Brilliant in its conception and brilliant in its execution, SpaceChem is a puzzle game like no other... if you possess a single geeky gene, this game will meld with your soul and possess you completely.

Truly the greatest puzzle game of all time. Not for the faint of heart. Shortly after the tutorial levels your intelligence will be challenged. If you're one of the elite few who have what it takes to make it to the last levels of the game then your sanity will be challenged.
I'm sure I've gotten hundreds of hours of quality puzzle time from this game (I was playing the Linux version before Steam was available on Linux) and I consider completing this game the greatest gaming feat I will ever accomplish. Mostly because no one makes games this challenging.
"The second incorrect assumption we made was thinking that puzzle games need to be difficult and long to be good. Although challenge is essential to making puzzle games "work", the difficulty that emerges from the mechanics of SpaceChem can be bewildering, even if it's what makes the puzzles feel so open-ended. Combining this intrinsic difficulty with an abundance of puzzles that must be beaten to "complete" the game gives SpaceChem an oppressive 40+ hour difficulty curve that only 2 percent of players reach the end of."

Very good logical puzzle game, but check out the similar, but free games "The Codex of Alchemical Engineering" or "Manufactoria" to see if you like this style of puzzle game. Also has a nice long demo you can check out.

I wake up in a wonderful underwater world. It’s magical, large and full wonderful things to discover. I have no clue how I got here or why I am the only one besides the normal sea creatures. I am Naija, a beautiful mermaid-like woman, trying to discover the past and find out what happen to everyone else.
Aquaria is a 2D underwater adventure where you need to recover your past and find out what happen to everyone else. All other intelligent life seems to have been wiped out and you can’t remember anything. What discoveries and treasures will you find on your large adventure?
You will discover songs that will give you special powers to help you on your journey. You can get one that will shoot like a fire blast, another which will let you swim against strong currents, or one that will let you light up deep dark caverns. You can earn these by fighting bosses or finding them in hidden caves. You will also need to learn recipes that will help heal you and give your powers a boost. These are all found when dropped from defeated enemies or plants you can pop by certain music tones.
It’s a beautiful world of varieties of sea creatures that range from friendly to violent. Everything looks really colorful and vibrant. The world under the sea is very large and when you think you’ve discovered everything you discovered another huge area. You’ll have plenty of backtracking to find all the hidden secrets in the old-school Metroid style. Get a new power and go back to a previous area to access new areas.
There wasn’t really any problems with the game in my opinion. I do wish the final fight was a little better but it wasn’t really an issue. I also wish I was able to zoom in on the map a little more as sometimes it was hard to see where I needed to go. Those are minor issues though and never pulled me out of the experience.
Aquaria is a low priced indie game that is superb and wonderful to play. You have a good story with a twist, beautiful world to explore, fantastic music, and many hours of enjoyment. I sank 24hrs into the game and enjoyed every minute of it. There’s also some mods you can download to add more to the game if you’d like.

Aquaria reminds me in feel quite a bit of Super Metroid, though with an even larger world to explore and much more dynamic and fluid (no pun intended) controlling.  The music and graphics of this 2D, sprite-based game are lush and beautiful and really draw upon the heart and soul that made some of the Golden Era of Gaming from the SNES-Playstation 2 time period truly golden.  The only real negative I can cite on this game is that it seems almost certain there won't be a sequel, and in an age where those seem a constant to games that *don't* need them, this one truly would have been spectacular to continue.  Nonetheless, I can't recommend this one enough, especially for the low price they're asking.  Pick it up, take it for a swim--you won't regret it.  (Do make sure to use WASD for movement rather than the mouse, though, unless you're a real ace with that!)

Aquaria, the other indie game by bit blot, is a 2D Action Adventure game that has the feel of a Zelda game.  What I mean by having the feel of a Zelda game is that in this game there is a large open area that allows the player to go anywhere that you can go providing you have the proper unlocks or tools. In this case it is her [Naija’s] Song forms. These allow her to do different things needed to get to certain parts. One of the downsides to this is that this game doesn’t really give a clear direction of where to go. You start at a certain point and you are told to just go. In a way I appreciate the game for not hand holding me like so many AAA titles of recent but on the other I got bored at times trying to swim around and find where I needed to go next.

The main character in this game is called Naija but in the beginning that is all she knew about herself, her name. You travel on through the world of Aquaria trying to find what happened to everyone else. In the process you slowly learn that the “Creator” created different races and for whatever reason became jealous of them and destroyed all of them but those races Gods. Each time you find the different Gods you find out a little more about your past and who this “Creator” really is. Eventually Naija comes across Li, who I can only assume is a human, that when she pulls of his helmet she has to kiss him in order to keep him alive and learn about him. Naija keeps mentioning that she is finally not alone but several instances of him being kidnapped by the Creator gets her angry and fights towards an inevitable final confrontation with him, the Creator.

The gameplay isn’t too much different from that of say Darksiders or Zelda: Majora’s Mask where each form of Naija’s gives her unique abilities and allows her to progress through the game.  But unlike in those games in order to change forms she has 8 notes that when she sings a certain set of them it changes her into one of those forms. I would say this is a pretty unique gameplay mechanic if it wasn’t for the fact that you can just hit 1-8 on the keyboard to change forms as you learn it. Though this does make it easier it also takes away from a unique mechanic that could have really added to the game. However there are certain times where you need to either use songs you know or songs that appear in the game to progress including games of Simon Says.  Her different forms include Song form (her standard singing form), Energy form(She can fire energy to combat enemies),Beast form (allows her to swim through strong currents and eat creatures),Nature form(Opens big blue and red bulbs on the map),Sun form(allowing her to see in the dark places of Aquaria),Fish form (small form that allows her to slip past enemies and travel fast), Spirit form(pretty useless, allows her to pass steam vents) and the most powerful form Dual form. Dual form combines Li and Naija into one. Li’s version of it fires very powerful charged up shots that when he kills 3 enemies with it allows Naija’s form to scream and kill just about everything on the map. On top of her different forms another nice mechanic is the crafting/cooking system. In the game there are 52 cooking recipes that have all sorts of different effects that include healing, stat enhancement and even boost attacks/skills. In order to get the materials to cook however you must either kill the creatures (some of which will fight you some won’t) or harvest them out of song plants. Song plants are unique “chests” that in order to open them you need to sing the note corresponding to the color of the plant.

I’m going to mention to talk more about the art than the actual graphics. I absolutely loved the art style of this game, everything all the way down to the plants and small creatures were well drawn and looked amazing. Each area was unique and looked nothing like the others. I will say though just like in every Zelda game, Aquaria did have its own “Water Temple.” That really annoying mechanical temple that had several puzzles you want to forget about. On top of that the sound was really well done too.  Each area in the game had its own music playing and even most of the bosses had unique music for the different stages of the fight. I will say that the music really added to the last couple of levels and made that part feel really awesome as I was fighting through hundreds of enemies to get to the final boss.
My final thoughts about the game is that this indie game isn’t one you should miss. I really enjoyed the game even if some parts were tedious and difficult to find where I was going. The graphics/art and sound was top notch and it even had an ending song with vocals that was really well done as well (felt kind of like Enya’s song at the end of Fellowship of the Ring).  The difficulty of the game wasn’t too hard and wasn’t too simple. Your amount of health you had was very similar to that of a megaman game that if you were hit perhaps only 5-10 times you were dead if you didn’t use any health items. I had a lot of fun fighting the unique bosses and figuring out how to beat them.

Mechanics 6/10: The controls are easy enough to comprehend......and perhaps its too simple
There are two parts of this game which are; The mech battles and the third person shooter combats.
You can upgrade your wanzers by customize four parts which are: head, right and left arms, and the legs.
You also can costumize the colors of your wanzer extensively. This includes; The color, camo pattern, decal and the glossiness of your wanzers.
Your wanzers also can be equipped with melee weapons and shields for close-quarter encounter, standard firearms (rifles, shotgun etc...), extra guns/missile batteries mounted on both of the wanzer's shoulders and a backpack as a passive aids in battle. Each of those weapons and parts can equipped with skills cards (of some sort) to enhance your arsenal's ability like explosive ammunition and so on (though they are pretty limited. As an FPS veteran and someone with almost 1,000 hours in Red Orchestra 2, I feel I can now properly review the game.
This game is hands down the best realistic multiplayer immersive WW2 Shooter available on Steam. It takes strategy, raw aim, and countless hours to master the nuances of the game's diverse maps and mechanics; but it's definitely worth the time you'll put in to it, if you can stick with it and brave the steep learning curve of course. This game is not easy. It will not hold your hand. You WILL die, and you will die CONSTANTLY. Not for the first 10 hours, or even the first 20 hours, but likely until you reach around 50 hours of gametime you will be dying frequently. But do not despair. Try to learn something from every death. Where did you die from? Did you see the enemy? Was there a safer way to get to the location you were trying to get to? If you'd like to improve your skills in the game quickly you need to pay attention to the high-level players around you on the map and try to follow them and learn the maps from them. There are many places that are "kill-zones" on the map, where you will likely die near instantly from machine gun fire or a snipers well aimed shot, so try your best to listen to experienced players over voice comms and follow your team commander's orders. For example, if the commander or your squad leader calls for the team to bum-rush through artillery or machine gun fire into the capture point in order to hold it for 10 more seconds (and possibly causing a map victory) you better risk your measly life to accomplish the specified order.
All-in-all, this game is one of my favorite PC shooter games and I hope to pour countless more hours into it and guide and help new players to learn the game. If you are new to the game do not hesitate to add me on Steam and I will gladly help you or answer any questions you may have.
If I had any criticism at all for Red Orchestra 2 it would be directed specifically to Tripwire's development team. I wish they would continue to improve and update the game. There are many small bugs and quality of life fixes that they could address to make this game a true masterpiece, a description it deserves.
-Johan

You can almost feel the G's as you hug the ground to gain speed or fly knife edge between two pilars to snag a power up.  The controls take a bit of getting used to, but they work really well.  Control over your plane feels nice and tight, even during the more hectic moments.  You'll definitely want to play this one with an x-box game pad.

This is based on the type of game and size of the team. Early access is almost guaranteed to have bugs, the whole point of going into Early Access is to fund the game, test the game, and also get input from the community on what they want added or changed in the game. The last comment I saw that really annoyed me was this "it's more than likely that the developers are just going to abandon this game". Where is the proof for this? I will admit that not all updates are monumental, but the devs have been so kind and listen to the community. Good things are worth waiting for. I have faith in this game and in the dev team. I'd originally bought Project Zomboid five years ago, when it was in early, early alpha. It is a descision I have not regretted.
PZ is at its core a survival simulator; your character has very real needs, from food and water to entertainment and advanced nutritional needs. The zombies are indeed quite present, and present a very real threat. So real, in fact, that it took some adjusting for me; I'm too used to the classic shooter feel in which scores of enemies are dispatched at a time. In PZ, you have to leave that behind; even a single zombie can be deadly if it gets the drop on you, and one bite means you're done for. Balancing the need to go scavange for supplies or a new book so you can learn how to make this device or that tool is a constant and very interesting task.
The versatility in this game has me astounded; you can build a base, chopping down trees for lumber with which to fortify it. You can install a generator, or build rain collector barrels for when the power and water go out. You can roam about, picking what you can from the city while hiding, silent in an upstairs bedroom, ready to abseil out the window if you hear a zed knocking on your door, never saying in the same place twice. You can team up with friends to try to make a community togetehr in the multiplayer, or you can go solo and experience the lonliness of a sole survivor. You can scavenge for canned goods to eat, taking the dangerous but simple path to getting the calories you need, or you can start a farm or forage or trap, much safer but also much more difficult to stave off long-term malnutrition.
The zombies do what few other non-horror games manage; they're scary. Not because each one individually is too frightening, but because a group of three or four can easily mob the unwary, because they're so many that killing them all simply isn't a viable solution, and because one bite or even a scratch for the unlucky may leave you alive, but doomed to a slow death as the zombification sets in. I find myself, every morning when my character wakes up, doing a patrol of the secure house and grounds, because it's happened when I didn't that a zombie lunged out of the bushes and bit me before I could put it down. When traveling, I constantly check over my shoulder. I walk or even sneak, because the noise will bring more of them. I curse whenever I hear a helicopter or gunshot in the distance because I know it means more zombies will be coming my way. I run from more fights than I have in any other game. I avoid yet more entanglements with small groups because, while I PROBABLY could take them, I also might not; it simply isn't worth the risk for my monthlong survivor.
The skill and trait system likewise offers both tremendous freedom of choice and the rewards and risks to go with it; you can play an asthmatic carpenter, who may not be able to run fast but will have a leg up in building a base. You can make your character athletic, but at the cost of making them hard-of-hearing or feeble. And once you've made your character, there are enough skills in the game that you can develop whatever role you like; experience is gained not merely by killing enemies, but rather by doing what the skill is about (similar to the Elder Scrolls series.) If you find yourself using an axe instead of a bat, your blade skill will increase regardless of your plans. If you run everywhere, you'll find that your sprinting skill is increasing. It allows for a very dynamic and yet deep approach to character customization.
Really, the only thing about this game I DIDN'T like was that it removed the "story" mode from the earlier builds. However, it appears there are plans to bring it back, which I personally am thrilled about; I've played AAA RPGs who don't give me the feels this game did in its first ten minutes.
In summation, this has the distinction of being one of the best zombie games, or even just one of the best games in general, I've had the privilage to play. 10/10 would impulse buy again.

I recently reviewed this game for my game review blog, Five Penny Review. If you enjoy this review, please visit my page:
What sets this game apart?
Aquaria is a robust, independently developed adventure game.  I was originally planning to review it as part of Indy April, but in order to diversify the titles covered, I elected to include a different production created by Derek Yu, Spelunky.  This game features a huge area to explore, a variety of available powers that must be used to reach new areas, and an item system with over 50 recipes.  Given the underwater setting, the normal platforming elements of this sort of adventure game are transported into the weightless environment, instead utilizing the mouse and keyboard together to swim and interact efficiently with the environment.  Most of all, the environment itself is captivating and complex, with an exciting array of sea life en encounter.
What is the difficulty factor?
The basic controls of the game are very simple and well explained.  Movement can be achieved with the mouse or keyboard, and most actions are taken using the mouse.  I find that precision movement is easier with the keyboard, while dashing or jumping about is easier achieved with the mouse.  Once new forms are unlocked, they give you new powers, most of which follow the same basic formula where the controls are concerned.  Overall, while movement can be a bit strange, especially the few times you venture out of the water, it has an extremely fluid feel once you get used to it.
From a challenge perspective, Aquaria is rather hit and miss.  Many times, being caught off guard against a regular enemy or running into a few damaging obstacles can be just as deadly as fighting a boss, if a bit less urgent.  This can be especially frustrating given the spacing between save points.  However, farming a good amount of healing items before you go exploring and paying close attention to your current health can actually make the game rather easy by comparison.  As far as a goal goes, Aquaria is very open ended and encourages exploration.  This can be frustrating at times, given the size of the world and the number of dead ends you will likely encounter that cannot be addressed until you unlock a new power.  Personally, I got as much satisfaction out of the exploration as I did from moving forward in the game, and there are often rewards for leaving the beaten path.
Does it use media effectively?
Aquaria is a beautiful game.  The sea life is recognizable, ranging from colorful fish to terrifying eels, and each area seems to have slightly different creatures appropriate to the area.  The backgrounds are colorful, vibrant, and living, often featuring crystals you can move behind or grass that moves as you swim through it.  The environmental effects such as sunlight and darkness, and the constant water effects that are hardly noticeable until you leave the water and return to it, all add a great deal of depth to the already rich graphics.  The designs for all of Naija’s forms and costumes are creative, reflective of the creatures they mimic and the powers they bestow while still maintaining her own appearance.  The cut scenes are simple but elegant.  The music perfectly reflects the various areas of the game while being subtle enough that it never feels invasive or repetitive.
Best moment in the game?
Aquaria is most of all a game that celebrates the environments it creates and encourages players to explore those environments.  For me, the pinnacle of this exploration was the first time I reached the surface of the water, exploring either The Veil or the Frozen Veil areas.  While the surface of these areas had very little to offer in the way of hidden treasures (although the few treasures I found are definitely good), there is something deeply satisfying about jumping over rocks along the surface like a dolphin, swimming up waterfalls, and shooting monkeys out of trees while flopping along the surface.
I do not mean to undermine the more serious parts of this game in naming my casual playtime as the best moment.  The bosses are interesting and often require you to utilize your powers in creative ways.  There are other great environments like the Kelp Forest and the darkness of The Abyss to explore.  The cut scenes and story are gorgeous and well told.  For me, the fact that I could have so much fun doing nothing productive in this game shows just how great it is.
Who needs to play this game?
If you have a computer and the time to spend exploring Aquaria, this game is worth checking out.  The strange controls and lack of direction require you  to have a bit of dedication getting started, which may cause some more casual players to lose interest, but once you get started you will likely find yourself addicted to the adventure.  Aquaria is available on Steam and iOS.

Cuphead is Fantastic.  There's no beating around the bush.  Even when whiny game journalists cried about it, the developers didn't back down from the game they wanted to make.  Something where an actual challenge is presented, and the only way to get past it, was to get better at the game.  This giant middle finger to the SJWs who think they are owed things they didn't earn is fantastic, and gives me hope for more developers who won't cave into the SJW narritave.
Now that that's out of the way, lets talk about the actual game.  The name of the game is trial and error.  I know some people aren't a fan of this style of game, but I think it works very well here.  You will die, and change your aproach next time.  "One more try" is a phrase you will say a lot, and repeat it until you realize that it's 5:30am and you work at 6.  It's a game that forces you to adapt and try different strategies.  The game is both increadibly challenging, and also increadibly fair.  There were very few times when I had a death that was because of poor game disign, rather than my own shortcomings.  This makes it a game where the real enemy isn't the boss in front of you, but yourself.
The other thing, of course, is the art disign and music.  If you've seen anyone else talk about it, you know what I'm getting at.  The game sounds and looks like a 30s cartoon.  The one thing that often gets overshadowed by the artstyle is the music.  While the visuals are amazing, the music is the real star of the show for me.  Even when I was stuck on that MOTHER♥♥♥♥ING DRAGON for an hour and a ♥♥♥♥ING half, I couldn't help but tap my foot to his theme music.
This game is awesome.  I will be revisiting it at some point in the future, and it is well worth the $20 entry fee.  Unless your name is Dean.

As an FPS veteran and someone with almost 1,000 hours in Red Orchestra 2, I feel I can now properly review the game.
This game is hands down the best realistic multiplayer immersive WW2 Shooter available on Steam. It takes strategy, raw aim, and countless hours to master the nuances of the game's diverse maps and mechanics; but it's definitely worth the time you'll put in to it, if you can stick with it and brave the steep learning curve of course. This game is not easy. It will not hold your hand. You WILL die, and you will die CONSTANTLY. Not for the first 10 hours, or even the first 20 hours, but likely until you reach around 50 hours of gametime you will be dying frequently. But do not despair. Try to learn something from every death. Where did you die from? Did you see the enemy? Was there a safer way to get to the location you were trying to get to? If you'd like to improve your skills in the game quickly you need to pay attention to the high-level players around you on the map and try to follow them and learn the maps from them. There are many places that are "kill-zones" on the map, where you will likely die near instantly from machine gun fire or a snipers well aimed shot, so try your best to listen to experienced players over voice comms and follow your team commander's orders. For example, if the commander or your squad leader calls for the team to bum-rush through artillery or machine gun fire into the capture point in order to hold it for 10 more seconds (and possibly causing a map victory) you better risk your measly life to accomplish the specified order.
All-in-all, this game is one of my favorite PC shooter games and I hope to pour countless more hours into it and guide and help new players to learn the game. If you are new to the game do not hesitate to add me on Steam and I will gladly help you or answer any questions you may have.
If I had any criticism at all for Red Orchestra 2 it would be directed specifically to Tripwire's development team. I wish they would continue to improve and update the game. There are many small bugs and quality of life fixes that they could address to make this game a true masterpiece, a description it deserves.
-Johan

For casual players this is a great game to pick up and play whenever it goes on sale. The content currently found in Tetris Ultimate is nowhere near the value of $15-$19. Tetris by default has a ton of replayability though, and the core concepts of Tetris go uninterrupted for the casual fan. There's several game modes as outlined, and each one barely scratches the surface of where these styles of play originated from. However, even with the shallowness of these modes, they're all bundled together in a package deliverable to the casual player.
Big negative points given for no native button mapping nor controller remapping support. Casual players, the targeted audience of this game, are the ones who require this feature the most. It is 2015 right?
Negative points are given for a lack of colour and style choices. It can be difficult to make out the ghost pieces, and not everyone tolerates the default colour scheme or skins. Not to mention there's no colour-blind mode for those impaired.
If Ubisoft or TTC provide 'DLC' (should be free content patch) then this game will certainly be a requirement in any casual fans library on Steam.

Absolutely no rush work. Pretty decent debugging. Complexity increments not too fast so u can catch up i guess.

Stonehearth has the positives of Dwarf Fortress (DF): a simcity style game that focuses on individual citizens, their lives, attributes, and abilities without the difficult learning curve that makes DF so in-accessible for people. It has beautiful graphics, and has the option for a peaceful setup (for those not interested in fighting).
It is by no means complete - but the team has been steadily working on the core functionality - and the improvement shows with each new alpha version.
Update:
Alpha 17 is quite playable - once you decide to focus on what works rather than what does not  -Lots of content. High quality UI. They have chosen well when they copied Dwarf Fortress (attributes, farming, combat, 3D) and chosen well even, or particularly, when they diverged from it (RPG-type-classes, experience, levels).
The game creates interesting decisions -
Embark - Race, difficulty level, choice of location
Start - Which classes to focus on, etc
Worth buying not just to support but also to play.

I bought this to a group of friends a couple of years ago to play together. We played it a couple of times (a few hours) and had fun trying to beat "the story missions". I forgot about it for a long time before coming back on a couple of occasions to beat the rest of the levels by myself. I consider it one of the hardest platformers I've played.
is perfectly described by its name. It's a precision platformer where a tiny mistake means death and you may die hundreds of times before beating a level. The traps are everywhere and deaths paint the levels red (unless you turn off the gore). Adding some chaos, you can play it co-operatively or competitively with your friends.
Played multiplayer, like it's probably meant,
is good fun for a while. The bipedal cat furry humanoids run through the obstacle course that is the trapland and try to reach the door to the next area without dying. Jumping on a fellow furry kills them in a bloody pop, similar to the obscure multiplayer deathmatch
.
There's also a deathmatch and race modes with their own levels. To perfect the game, a par time has to be reached in the race levels that may benefit from or even require playing co-operatively.
Level design is nice, levels are fairly complex or sometimes there are two alternate routes to the end. The story mode also has several routes through it, some requiring co-op to beat.
It's too bad controls cannot be changed, and only one local player may play on keyboard with arrows. Up to four players may play with controllers though (I've tested and played it with Xbox controllers).
Name fits the game very well: Levels are filled with traps. Sharp traps, squishing traps, and surprise traps. Bottomless holes, guns, aiming cannons and bouncing fireballs. There are the classic spikes and sawblades, both moving and retracting ones and they come in several sizes. Occasional teleporter makes it initially impossible to tell how the level should be played out.
Fundamentally, the traps are of four types: stationary, moving, periodic and reacting ones. The moving ones
have a distinct pattern of some kind (however see below). Periodic ones
go off at set intervals (again, see below).
Reacting ones are mostly fine: there's a gun, it's going to shoot when you go in front of it, and there are falling blocks that go when you step under them and get squished. These are all fine if initially surprising.
However,
hosts two kinds of traps that I absolutely abhorred:
The hidden blocks are literally inside the wall, impossible to see before they first strike. The jumping lava balls bounce from the lava at quasi-periodic intervals at various different heights, impossible to anticipate.
Both of the above traps can be kind of fun when playing with friends. When playing solo, they become extremely frustrating. The blocks because they artificially prolong the levels before you know to even try to avoid them, fire balls because they cause totally random deaths. You can pull a perfect speed run (required in the race modes for gold status), taken away from you at the very end through sheer chance by a fire ball that jumps at the same time as you, it's rage-inducing.
I spent 19 hours with
before beating every level. That includes about 5 hours of co-op play with friends. Hardest levels/challenges were likely those that required co-op play because of the inherent requirement of coordination.
I am left with mixed feelings of the game. With friends it was quite fun, and many levels were pretty fun even in solo play. But some of the lame traps made solo play incredibly frustrating and that utterly ruined some levels for me.
So if you can live with that and/or you and your friends are up for Nintendo-hard platforming,
might be an alright investment. And if you really dig it, there's a level editor and so an infinite amount of custom content, if the extremely challenging original levels are not enough. Still, because of the above qualms, I'd wait for a sale.

I am not a very big fan of shooters, my first being Dirge of Cerberus (for the story) and my second being Borderlands. I will say that this game really drew me in. On easy difficulty, I was able to comfortably be challenged by the game but not feel like it was too easy or too hard. The looting aspect of the game might turn some people off, but I thoroughly enjoyed the many mechanics, the story (which got more dark as the game went on) and the way they unfolded the story. The player was encouraged to explore and find the various recorders to figure out what really happened down in rapture. If one is smart, the signs for the infamous twist are there, but (also having the fortune of not having the game spoiled) when the grand reveal happened, I was pleasantly surprised and enjoyed the game that much more.
What I liked:
- Different endings based on moral choices in the game
- The opportunity to stun/kill for players (like myself) not as whip accurate at shooters
- Hacking minigame was fun, and was a worthwhile challenge in many cases
- The storytelling as a mix of live recordings, left behind tapes, and sifting through the ruins
- The concept of the underwater city of Rapture was fascinating, given the time period they placed the game in
- The twist in the game messes with your head as a gamer, and was well worth the slow reveal and wait
- Ability to revisit earlier levels to search for things I might have missed
- Plasmids are awesome, that is all
What I didn't like:
- I would have liked to move faster
- Achievements are only for the remastered version, which is buggy as hell
- Battles got a bit repetitive after a while. Once you ujnderstood the flow, it was easy to predict the outcome
- The final fight was a lot easier than I'd anticipated.
- I want to be able to save my game after the final battle. The completionist part of my soul hates that the file is just eternally unfinished.
- I wish there was some downside to using more plasmids. Lorically, allowing your character to become plasmid OP seemed out of place in a city where the natives who did the same go crazy.
Anyway, Highly recommend this game to folks looking for fun game mechanics and a fun story.

Dungeonmans is an accessible and fun rogue-like with well thought out meta-progression elements that give future characters a better chance to survive. You can also choose to have a single life and character should you desire a more traditional experience.
You can expect to run into plenty of jokes and puns which keep the game lighthearted and relaxed when it comes to the presentation. You should take the time to read the enemy and item descriptions. There are some knee-slappers waiting to be found.
You can also expect turn-based combat with grid-style 8-direction movement. You can use the arrow keys, the numpad, or the mouse to move out of the way of certain death. It helps that the GUI is generally clean and clear. You're not going to be making many mistakes because you couldn't tell what was happening on the screen despite all the spells, buffs, and debuffs happening.
Where the game really shines is how it handles progression with leveling up. If you ever dreamed of making an archer that uses a wizard's energy shield while also being able to dual-wield two swords and drop banners that provide buffs, this game will let you do that. The ability to pick and choose skills from different classes make customization both interesting and wacky. You'll eventually have all the key skills for your preferred playstyle once you learn not to die and have the chance to branch out to try different things.
The academy part of the game kept me coming back for me. The meta-progression is dependent on you bringing back relics to the headmaster. That can result in new functions for the academy such as automatically identified items, crafting recipes, powerful item storage, random item drops that can be redeemed by a successor, and more. The super important one are the "Proofs of Stremf" which help both your current and future characters purchase stat increases at the trainer. You'll always come back stronger unless you royally mess up a run.
The only problems I have with the game are certain strong enemies that can "one-shot" you. Most of the time, they'll have a tell with the red zones indicating an incoming attack. Those situations are live and learn, but some of those red incoming attacks you can survive without an issue and you won't really know which one is the truly lethal one. I kind of wish those extremely high damage attacks had a purple zone or something different. Maybe I'm missing something. Dodge everything.
Anyway, the bigger problem in my experience are parry chains. Normally, parries are great and let you attack the enemy during their turn. Later in the game, certain enemy types will come at you with their own high parry chance, which lets them parry your parry. However, you can then parry their parry. And they'll be able to parry that one and so on. It leads to an uncontrollable exchange of blows that can go on until the death of you or them. It also cost me my last character's life which soured me quite a bit since the monster hit me back for a surprising 400 and 1600 damage. I never understood what happened exactly there.... Anyway, the back and forth parry brawling happens far too frequently. I used to think of parry as a positive stat, but then also considered trying to make it deliberately low just to be able to control damage intake.
Still, Dungeonmans is my current #1 rogue-like, dethroning Dungeons of Dredmor (I stick with the more friendly ones). It's worth a try and offers hours upon hours of entertainment. You'll probably lose some characters horribly.

I remember playing Navy Field 1 years ago, and was quite excited to see what the sequel brought to the table.  Unfortunately, I can tell you that I am quite disappointed after spending a fair amount of time on NF2.
Navy Field 2 is a WW2 naval battle simulator where players take command of a ship (or submarine) of varying classes: destroyers, light cruisers, heavy cruisers, battleships, aircraft carriers, and submarines.  Progress towards higher tier ships is accomplished by completing ship research towards the next ship, which in turn can be done with "ship exp" earned in battles.  Ships themselves as well as some items to boost ship performance can be bought with credits earned in battle.
With that quick summary it sounds like NF2 could be quite fun, and it could be--except whatever fun I derived from the first week or two of blasting other ships slowly dwindled.  There are several fundamental problems with NF2 and the company that supposedly supports it.  I will list what comes to mind:
-There is only one battle mode.  NF2 is a multiplayer-only game where players are placed on a team of up to 16 players and pitted against a team of up to 16 players with ship tiers roughly matched.  Then it's basically a death match for up to 15 minutes.  That's it.  The only variations are the maps, so playing NF2 will become repetitive.
-A beginner doesn't have a whole lot of documentation to help overcome the learning curve.  In fact, there's very poor documentation for a NF veteran!  Game mechanics are not fully explained in-game or on the website, and often I had to figure out a number of things on my own.
-NF2 is free to play, which also means cash shop items.  That's right, there is a pay to win aspect of NF2.  Personally I haven't had much of an issue against pay to win, but the setup is very poor.  I will only address pay to win aspects that affect gameplay.  The system is that players have "sailors" who gain experience in battles.  There are various specializations for sailors (ex. a gunner can be specc'd for faster reload speed), but all of them have this variable called "morale."  Morale has a hard cap of 200% and an initial maximum value of 120%.  Morale affects sailor performance, and increases when battles are won and decreases slightly when battles are lost.  Now for the nasty part.  Maximum morale can be raised by buying an item in the cash shop.  There exists a version of this that can be bought for a tidy sum of in-game credits, but this version actually has a risk of failing.  As you can guess, a risk-free version exists for cash.  Besides the obscene amount of money you'd need to max out morale for just one sailor, there is very close to no official documentation on anything related to morale.
-Updates are frequent (usually weekly), which is good, but are generally awful.  Many weeks have featured a "patch" where a ship gets some adjustment.  Okay.  Problem.  There is no context provided for many changes, and many undocumented (utterly unannounced) changes take place.  As of the writing of this review, a recent patch 2 weeks ago introduced a large number of new ships, but undocumented changes nerfed a number of existing ships that the community would agree are completely uncalled for.  No GM on the forums has commented on these changes.
-There's no incentive to keep playing.  Seriously.  The only possible goal in this game is to get a higher tier ship, but after tier 5 (tiers go up to 11) the requirements for the next ship increase steeply.  Players can join fleets, which are kind of like guilds, except there's pretty much no point.  There are no fleet battles or other incentives to join a fleet other than to have a tiny pixel of a picture next to your name in battles.
I was hoping things would get better, especially with the latest big patch introducing more ships, but it's clear that NF2 lacks developers who know how to support and develop a game.  I definitely would've stayed away from NF2 months ago if I knew what it was like and how it wouldn't change.

Incredible, atmospheric experience and a work of art.
From the design standpoint Aquaria is a Metroidvania 2D game with big underwater world to explore. Those ideas aren't that special on paper, but the strange mix of climactic locations, fitting music and hand-drawn graphics makes this title not only joy to look and hear, but also leave so big impact on the player that after you finish the game you will know that is one of the best indie games out there yet to be recognized by most of gaming community.
The story is simple, but it is told extremely well by the voice of the main protagonist as you play the game. It starts out interesting, but it ends up strongly heart-touching. The plot is slowly revealed through the game and the next surprise around the corner will be bigger than the former. Aquaria is one of those indie games that had a ton of potential. The graphics for the most part are super detailed and varied, the soundtrack gets you into the right mood efficiently, and there are a lot of powers, enemies, and bosses to keep the gameplay interesting. I don’t even know where to start with the problems. The biggest one is probably that you don’t know what you’re supposed to be doing in this game in a very minor and large ways. I spent an hour just swimming around because I had no idea where I needed to go or what I needed to do. Then some bosses have a very specific way you have to beat them and the game never tells you even how some of the steps necessary are possible. You just have to keep guessing and dying and hopefully not give up. Some of the puzzles are like this, too. You know what the answer is going to be like, but you just have to keep guessing every possible combination of possible answers to finally get it right. That’s not fun or engaging. One of the more minor complaints is that the writing is pretty awful. I couldn’t help but to roll my eyes over and over to some of the narrative because it just sounded so childish and maybe what an immature writer would consider poetic. Also the animations look cheap but that’s the key thing to remember here is that to make them better would’ve probably extended the production time of the game by years. Indies are cheap due to a lack of a huge budget so I’m willing to give that one a pass. They did the best they could. Over all, if you think you might enjoy the concept of the game and some interesting ideas in a metroidvanoia type of setting, I’d give this game a try.

I'm going to start my review of TLD a little bit differently. I am going to start with a short bit about the developers of this game, Hinterlands. As a person that was around, back when the patching process first started and can tell you the exact company and game that made patching to fix, a mainstream practice for Devs, to this day( FYI, it was Epic Games and the title was Unreal), I can say that Hinterlands is not one of those Companies. Anyways, just to say, I have seen MANY, MANY BAD devs, in my days. I can say with complete honesty and trust my statement, when I say, Hinterlands will be one of the best Devs that this industry has ever seen. My hours here don't reflect true play time, as I was playing this on XBox1, before PC. Hinterlands has been on top of the development of this game since day 1, with steady patching for bugs and issues, adding content, staying current with the community. They are truly dream devs. You can tell, right away, that TLD is a project of love and passion for them, not a cash grabe, or claim to notariety. They truly love and believe in what they are doing with this game and it shows. Hinterlands didn't just put their hearts and souls intto this game, they left a little piece of each there.
Now, on to the game.
TLD is set in the Canadian north. The Devs have done an absolutely amazing job in creating this "dream" world. I cannot even call it a simple environment, sandbox, world, setting, etc. No, this is a dreamscape of etherial magic and beauty that can be so stunning, yet so cruel and brutal, all at the same time. You will almost feel the cold embrace as you explore this wild and enchanting dreamscape. You will almost feel the hunger, as you hear your stomach grumble in pain, from being empty. You will almost feel the energy draining from you as your character slows and weakens, in game, from pure exhaustion. Your throat will nearly dry up, as your character thirsts for a life saving drink, you will feel the fear and anxiety, as you spot wolves, or a bear, off in the distance and you will most certainly feel the urgency, to survive, when you are on the verge of starving, freezing, dehydrating or being eaten alive. The Devs have really done an amazing job in creating a very immersive reality. The game can be frustrating at times, as it should be, There is nothing simple about trying to survive in a frozen, windswept, wild environment. Life is brutal and mother nature is apathetic(she doesn't care if you live or die). You will make mistakes and die, BUT if this game is for you, like me, you will be driven to go on and on, to push farther and farther, to see how far you can make it, how long you can survive and even try to get beyond surviving, to thriving.
For a good while, there was just the sandbox mode, which involves simply trying to stay alive, for as long as you can. That aspect, in itself, is quite entertaining and carries GREAT replay value, as there are multiple areas to explore, map out, hunt and gather, with enthralling scenery and diversilty in locals. Then they added challenges, which adds a great addition  to the sandbox mode. As the name would suggest, you are provided with a certain end goal, to achieve. There are multiple challenges for you to try your hand at, each in a different local, of the game. Finally, with the addition of story mode, they have made this game the absolute premiere survival game, IMO. I have obviosly not had time to complete the story mode yet, but from what I have seen so far, it is a masterpiece of a game and certainly a steel for $35, IMO. Honestly, to me, this game absolutely does NOT feel like an indie title. Hell no, this feels like a top grade AAA, full release title, from an experienced and well respected Developer. The sky is the limit for Hinterlands.
In ending, I feel like I stoled this game for $8, when it was on sale, but I would gladly pay the full price of a AAA title for this game. I don't usually rate games with stars or numbers, but for me, this game is a 10/10, 5star, AAA game, in every aspect. I absolutely LOVE IT. This game has actually somewhat saved my gaming for me. I have played sooo many games, for sooo many years, that I have a very hard time finding games that will hold my interrest for very long. TLD doesn't just hold my interrest, it grabs it by the throat, squeezes the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it and refuses to let go. Would I recommend this game? Without hesitation and I already have, to numerous people, who also bought and love the game.

Epic could NEVER patch the MP aspect of Unreal to work for many players, so they decided to create a stand alone MP version and sell it. That is how you got Unreal Tournament. The first, EVER, abandoned MP, that came with release, that was repackaged and resold.
One thing I will say, that I forgot to add. The story mode is not an open sandbox, it is actually quite linear and not really what I expected, but I still like it. A very polished and very difficult dungeon crawler/roguelike/tower defense. The game flow is similar to Faster Than Light, but the mechanics are very different. So you basically do an action that advances the game, a random event is triggered (combat, loot, new hero, merchant, etc.), you have to react to it, manage your base and heroes according to the changes in the last round and then go for another round.
The visuals are pretty nice and this is coming from someone who loathes gimmicky pixel art execution. Somehow the "modern" colors, lighting and 3D modeling of the dungeon blends really well with the 8-bit FX and character models.
I would also add that DotE is a good example of Early Access done right - a solid concept, design and roadmap that materialized in a very stable and cohesive game.
My only complaint is that none of the game's aspects is very complex, even if they seem to take a while to understand when put together. Character management is simplistic, combat is very basic, base management pretty much the same. The challenge actually comes from having to plan your moves well and using the least resources possible for the task, because one needs to stockpile for the toughest levels. Going too conservative on your resource usage results in an early loss, while not stockpiling enough results in a loss on the later levels.

I can't say anything else, except to buy this game.

This is probably one of the best Roguelikes i've played in the last year or two.  It manages somehow to pull off sythesizing squad based tactical combat with tower defense in a really innovative and fun way.  It's difficult, but when you fail you almost always have something you can point to that caused your run to fail that you can improve on next time. There's also a lot of variety of unlockable characters and synergies between them that are fun to explore.
I only have two (mild) criticisms of the game:  Once I finished it, I sort of lost motivation to keep playing.  The fun of the game is mostly its challenge, and when that is done, there isn't a lot of content to compel you to explore further. I didn't unlock every character, but enough that I didn't feel the burning desire to find the rest.  There also could be a little more depth and variety in the monsters.  There were only a few I felt I had to develop specific strategies to deal with, but honestly it felt ok; perhaps more complexity would have detracted from the core gameplay.

The sniper rifle was one of the least satisfying guns I've used in any game, and whenever I had to use it that mission just dragged on and on.  In general most of the weapons outside of melee weapons and shotguns leave a bit to be desired.  All of the others are just pretty dull feeling and boring to use.
In general most of the combat and gameplay is extremely repetitive. They also force you out of the mech from time to time to do a standard third person shooter segment, which is easily the worst part of the game to me. Okay finally arrived better late then never. I have played only about an hour and dabbled in most of the game types (Except the ones that crashed) and here's what I think.
Lets start positive because there are some good things. It looks great. I like the aesthetics it is probably one of the better looking versions of Tetris there is. People who prefer the really really minimalist designs in some of the unofficial variants like Lockjaw or Nullpolimo might not like it but I do, especially when you compare it to last gen which i really did not like. There are also a good number of game modes so every kind of player will find something they are after, whether its Marathon, Sprint or Battle. Okay thats all I got for god things so lets move on.
My criticisms are divided in 2 minds, one as an aspiring game designer and one as a Tetris fanatic.
I really dislike the approach to TU's Menu design. It looks good, and animates well. But its not intuitive and clutters the screen with a lot of information most of which is hard to direct around at first. Especially since there is no real tutorial. Or I should say there is one but its placed in a spot that no first time player is gonna find. And when you do get to it you are faced with an encyclopedia of text. If you were trying to follow the instructions you would have to constantly flop back to that menu.
I could understand if the dev team wanted to not have the players go through menu after menu but I would of rather something simpler. A starting menu that says "Online, Solo, Settings, Profile" which then opens up into something else. instead of an overwhelming amount of text as soon as you hit start.
On the subject of clicking things. I'm not sure why they decided to make somethings clickable and somethings not. Everything in the footer requires key presses and somethings require clicks. You have to be a little more consistent than that. Its like trying to play an FPS in an options menu. Also who thought it was a good idea to make the two keys to press "O" for confirm and "Backspace" for exit. Those keys are in the middle of nowhere and doesn't relate to any of the keys during play.
And now we come to some issues with the gameplay.
Something happens the faster you want to play and it comes from your expectation compared to what happens. 2 things that are really critical is line clear speed and when you are allowed to rotate the incoming piece. The longer that delay is between what you want to do next and when the game allows you to do it Is very important especially the faster you want to play. Very important for sprint players.
I am not that quick of a player, relatively speaking compared to the really really hardcore players, but even I am getting irritated with the delay. When you know what to place next, and when you know you hit the button to rotate, but the game lets you down by not keeping up with you. Its very frustrating aspect.
The decision to allow sensitivity was good. Maybe not to the degree I'd like, something finer than a 1-10 scale would of been nice, but a lot of variants don't have it so fine. The decision to Lock the Controls and the Piece orientation on the other hand is baffling to me. I had no idea they did this because I thought it was a given before it came out. I play with the numpad because it means I can rotate both ways with just my right hand. Thats how I play thats whats comftable for me. I also don't like using the space bar for drop, I prefer a smaller key and one next to my hold like "z" because i prefer using my index finger instead of my thumb.
these specific issues for everyone to play a certain way makes me think Tetris Ultimate had a very clear goal in mind and I'm not one that likes it.
If you are a casual player who doesn't play tetris often, maybe occasionally a long time ago. The game is fine. There are bugs here and there (3 of the game modes crashed on startup for me in the first 20mins) but its manageable, and if you are able to navigate the god awful tetris party up system, its okay.
The problem is I don't think its worth it to get it on PC. because if you are playing causally, 4 controllers will work, 4 keyboards won't.
More pressing is I don't think its worth your $15USD. You can get the same things from other outlets that let you satisfy that craving and then move on... and get back to Fallout 4 or something. If you hadn't already bought the game on your XBone or PS4, theres no reason to get this version.
If you are like me and you are a Hardcore player. This game is missing far to many options and crashes to many times to be taken seriously for your time. If you are a marathon player you would rather play TGM, if you are a multiplayer player you would rather play Top or Cultris. If you are a sprint player you would rather play Nullpol or Lockjaw. Most of them cater what you are after, better. and most of them are Free to play as well.
The only reason you would play Tetris Ultimate is if you hadn't tried any others.

As a lover of tetris as a child, I was more than excited to see it appear on PC at long last.
Although the game clearly still has some tweaks that needs to be sorted out, the overall appearance and action of the game is good. I am having no issues with lag whatsoever and the modes of the game really do bring a new element.
However sadly there are a couple issues, such as the game crashing frequenty when certain modes are switched on which is disappointing and I hope this is solved soon.
Also I am not a huge fan of the controller, controls as the hard drop button does not feel natural, would much prefer it to be on the X button or something similar as you can easily accidently shift your tetronimo to the left or right whilst trying to use the hard drop.
However overall, although I have just started playing I am throroughly enjoying and will get many hours out of it!

Where to start...
The game is free-to-play, which also means there's a pay2win aspect somewhere in the game. However, unlike most others, you don't pay to get ships, you need to earn them. The only thing you're paying for (or at least want to pay for), would be the premium 50% boost that helps in the grind through ship tiers later, the officers for an extra boost, and/or extra ship slots to keep more ships (honestly, you don't need more than 5 if you plan on sticking with one or two classes). Otherwise, everything is obtainable through just playing normally.
Now, the matchmaking. Yes, it needs some tweaking. You're not always going to be placed against people of your tier level, but I believe there's a good reason behind this, being that you get to experience fighting against different types of ship classes. And remember that the matchmaking puts you against a fleet (not clan fleet, just a fleet) equal to yours, meaning if they have Tier 9, you have buddies who are Tier 9 as well (or Tier 9 equivalent). The downside? You get wrecked if you're not careful.
Best advice for new players is to capture islands, sub detect and provide AA, while trying to support your team from behind and survive. Everyone starts out as a Destroyer so you don't get to do much unless you're really good with your torpedoes and shelling first hand (I've sunk Battleships, just saiyan), it's pretty easy. Heck, you might even manage to land a kill steal and get that huge amount of XP.
Eventually you'll reach Tier 3 in a few battles if you try to power through all the upgrades and not invest in any of your ship equipment. My friend did it in less than 30 minutes. You CAN face against stronger enemies even at low levels, but that relies on teamwork, not charging into everything.
The community. I haven't really talked to many, so I can't really say, but I've had battles won with teamwork where we were outnumbered, some cooperative, some not. It happens.
The grind. I'm a fairly new player myself although I've played since February (before dropping it for a while cause gemes), so I have yet to reach that part of the game. I'm still at Tier 5, using Destroyers, and I can tell you the amount of XP and credits you accumulate increase based on the ship tier you're using, so you might get like 300 or 400 at say, Tier 2, before getting 2000 to 3000 at Tier 5. Then again if you think the game's fun and all, it might not be so bad to invest time to grind, but if you're not that kind of person, better decide now whether you want to drop it.
Graphics? Ship docks look good. Actual game? Not so much. What, were you expecting some WoW or WT tier graphics?
My opinion? The game isn't nearly as close to frustrating me. I just like naval games and try to have fun. :v
Should you play it? Well I mean, just because there's a lot of mixed reviews doesn't mean you shouldn't try it out and see for yourself.
(NOT SPONSORED BY NAVYFIELD 2)
EDIT: So after countless battles, I am now at Tier 7, with ships of different classes also at Tier 7. To be honest, the game isn't really that frustrating once you get used to it, since you win and lose (although you lose more and that's kind of a good thing since XP gain is much faster with losing compared to winning).
The grind, however, becomes increasingly harder. And it's more around the amount of XP required for each upgrade before you get to the next ship than the XP gain itself. For me though, it's not a problem, since I enjoy playing the game either way. It gets a bit repetitive here and there, but eventually I managed. With 4 ships at Tier 7 equivalent (under 2 weeks of grinding; 1-3 hours a day), what's to not get bored of?
Psst, the maps.

I'm going to start my review of TLD a little bit differently. I am going to start with a short bit about the developers of this game, Hinterlands. As a person that was around, back when the patching process first started and can tell you the exact company and game that made patching to fix, a mainstream practice for Devs, to this day( FYI, it was Epic Games and the title was Unreal), I can say that Hinterlands is not one of those Companies. Anyways, just to say, I have seen MANY, MANY BAD devs, in my days. I can say with complete honesty and trust my statement, when I say, Hinterlands will be one of the best Devs that this industry has ever seen. My hours here don't reflect true play time, as I was playing this on XBox1, before PC. Hinterlands has been on top of the development of this game since day 1, with steady patching for bugs and issues, adding content, staying current with the community. They are truly dream devs. You can tell, right away, that TLD is a project of love and passion for them, not a cash grabe, or claim to notariety. They truly love and believe in what they are doing with this game and it shows. Hinterlands didn't just put their hearts and souls intto this game, they left a little piece of each there.
Now, on to the game.
TLD is set in the Canadian north. The Devs have done an absolutely amazing job in creating this "dream" world. I cannot even call it a simple environment, sandbox, world, setting, etc. No, this is a dreamscape of etherial magic and beauty that can be so stunning, yet so cruel and brutal, all at the same time. You will almost feel the cold embrace as you explore this wild and enchanting dreamscape. You will almost feel the hunger, as you hear your stomach grumble in pain, from being empty. You will almost feel the energy draining from you as your character slows and weakens, in game, from pure exhaustion. Your throat will nearly dry up, as your character thirsts for a life saving drink, you will feel the fear and anxiety, as you spot wolves, or a bear, off in the distance and you will most certainly feel the urgency, to survive, when you are on the verge of starving, freezing, dehydrating or being eaten alive. The Devs have really done an amazing job in creating a very immersive reality. The game can be frustrating at times, as it should be, There is nothing simple about trying to survive in a frozen, windswept, wild environment. Life is brutal and mother nature is apathetic(she doesn't care if you live or die). You will make mistakes and die, BUT if this game is for you, like me, you will be driven to go on and on, to push farther and farther, to see how far you can make it, how long you can survive and even try to get beyond surviving, to thriving.
For a good while, there was just the sandbox mode, which involves simply trying to stay alive, for as long as you can. That aspect, in itself, is quite entertaining and carries GREAT replay value, as there are multiple areas to explore, map out, hunt and gather, with enthralling scenery and diversilty in locals. Then they added challenges, which adds a great addition  to the sandbox mode. As the name would suggest, you are provided with a certain end goal, to achieve. There are multiple challenges for you to try your hand at, each in a different local, of the game. Finally, with the addition of story mode, they have made this game the absolute premiere survival game, IMO. I have obviosly not had time to complete the story mode yet, but from what I have seen so far, it is a masterpiece of a game and certainly a steel for $35, IMO. Honestly, to me, this game absolutely does NOT feel like an indie title. Hell no, this feels like a top grade AAA, full release title, from an experienced and well respected Developer. The sky is the limit for Hinterlands.
In ending, I feel like I stoled this game for $8, when it was on sale, but I would gladly pay the full price of a AAA title for this game. I don't usually rate games with stars or numbers, but for me, this game is a 10/10, 5star, AAA game, in every aspect. I absolutely LOVE IT. This game has actually somewhat saved my gaming for me. I have played sooo many games, for sooo many years, that I have a very hard time finding games that will hold my interrest for very long. TLD doesn't just hold my interrest, it grabs it by the throat, squeezes the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it and refuses to let go. Would I recommend this game? Without hesitation and I already have, to numerous people, who also bought and love the game.

This is an unusual game. Imagine Rogue Legacy, but as a ToME-style Roguelike instead of Metroidvania, and you pretty much got it. Personally it just didn't last for me. It is not a fault of the game, but of the genre it created. The hallmark of a roguelike to me is being able to consistently win if you have skill. This game will brutally kill you for no reason, and you are supposed to shrug, spend your stuff to make the next character a little stronger, then go again. Builds are also rather shallow and I found myself struggling to try anything new or interesting beyond the obvious.
Ultimately what killed it for me is that it was just too easy for 99 percent of it, then I'd run into some bullcrap boss like a Warlord that still oneshot what I thought was a very powerful character. I got sick of spending a couple hours to probably die on a random boss that took 1,000 turns to die and only got difficult due to complacence or RNG. I was hoping there would be a way to skip to a certain level and just play challenging content. There's a brief zone between a very dangerous  new group of monsters and potentially being weak that I enjoyed, but that went away pretty quickly with the global buffs you gain from doing runs.
Would I recommend it? 30ish hours for 15 bucks is a good deal for me, so yes, because Steam doesn't have a 'neutral' option. Did I enjoy every hour of that to the extent I did games such as ToME or Cogmind? No. Ask yourself if you liked the simplicity of Dungeons of Dredmor. If so, this is like a much more expansive version of that, with similar humor as well. If not, then head towards Dungeon Crawl: Stone Soup, Cogmind, return to the wilds of Tales of Maj'Eyal, or what have you.

Like many of you, I've had Early Access woes and let-downs, but I gave this game a try.  After playing it and getting involved in the community, I can honestly say that I believe in these developers.  They actively engage with the players (via their website forums especially) and seem to really listen to suggestions and bug reports - and that is the mark of a good Early Access.
My recommendation:
If you are willing to have patience and help with the bugs and new features, buy this game.  It's worth it for the game, and it will be even more worth it if you get involved in the community too.

After first trailers I thought it was great idea, but was afraid that it would be not polished enough and decide to wait free weekend. And it fully proved that statement. Details:

- Too fast and too chaotic, hard to monitor health and hard to aim

- For monster health bar is on top, which is completely out of sight, when you always concentrate on center screen. That leaves you too often in heat of battle with very very low health :) but you notice it too late and there is no time to maneuvre in safe place

If you would have chance to get it for free or with discounts for about 5$, you could try it. If there still will be players, you could have 3-4 hours of some kind of interesting experience. But in general it is too boring too fast, even with those cool ideas and structure.
Enjoy your 75% loading and 25% playing.

Free weekend? Absolutely!
Evolve......Evolve never changes....
No, I sure don't have a lot of time with this game, but it was about all I needed to get my fill. I went into the free weekend hoping maybe some updates and patches might have made this game decent as it was always a game I HAD WISHED done well. Sadly, it comes down to it's core mechanics that make this game...not great.
The team composition is static; you cannot do any unique compositons of maybe 2 trappers (which I could understand that being a little OP) or multiple medics, or whatever. It sounds OP with how the current game is built and is why that would never work. They should have built this game with the idea of having unique compositions - but balancing is tough :< boo-hoo.
Each character you can select is also stuck with whatever weapons they have; no unique loadouts here. So you may like one characters design, but hate their equipment. Well too bad. that's what tou get. Once again, this to me feels like the devs were too lazy to actually spend time to balance custom load outs, forcing static equipment since that's mountains easier to balance.
The game itself mostly winds up in a tepid game of hide-and-seek. In the hour I have on my steam record, I was able to only play 4 games. Let me just recount that whole hour for you to understand why this game is fundementally flawed:
Game 1: I played medic. Dropped in. Immediately saw the tracks. in under 1 minute, we found the stage 1 monster and at 2 minutes we won the game.
Game 2: I played the medic. Dropped in. Immediately saw the tracks. in under 1 minute, we found the stage 1 monster and at 2 minutes we won the game.
Game 3: I played the medic. Dropped in. Couldn't find the monster, couldn't find the monster, couldn't find the monster. Some kid raged at us since we were 10 minutes into this and the monster was near stage 3 - saying we sucked. oh the good ol Webholez :> Finally after 15 minutes of doing nothing but running around in circles, we found the monster at stage 3 and got curb stomped by him.
Game 4: We dropped in. We were all pretty new. The first minute was the awkward moments of none of us knowing who to follow or where to go. Finally the monster scared some birds, and I decided I would make my way toward it. Within a few minutes we caught up to him, but the bugger slipped through our trap, and I slipped into the mouth of some deadly wildlife. Combat became a game of saving me, then waiting to try and track down the monster again. I could see him in the distance and was able to tag him with my tranq. It wasn't long before we caught up, but he had reached stage 2. Once we faught him, it was a close encounter. He was smart; taking me down first, eliminating their healer. Then the trapped, and next our assault. Our support was nearly dead - running for his life. Just as he died, the 3 of us managed to drop back in, right on top of where the monster was. This final encounter was quick, but intense. We all nearly died, but managed to slay the beast.
In total, I spent about roughly 40 minutes actually playing the game. So what did I do during the other 20? waiting. Lots and lots of waiting between matches. I appreicate the new matchmaking system, but it seemed to struggle connecting me to parties. Often it would tease me or the other members who were in the lobby by finding a player, letting us select the role we want, then the new player would D/C and we'd wait some more.
This brings me to my final critique since I know not only Steam review readers only want "HAHALAWL" reviews and don't have the attention span to read this whole thing, but also Steam has a character limit.
Why does the game finding players, then have us select our role, then load the next screen, then have us select our character, then load the game? I feel like this could have been streamlined to save on the amount of downtime between matches. Why not have us select our character when we select our role? I'm not a dev, so I guess I will never understand this reason.
Either way, I'm glad I got to give this game that ol' college try, but it saddens me to play this game. I loved the idea of tracking the monster in an asymmetric multiplayer game...but it kind of just boils down to a rather tepid alien-planet, countryside strole. Even if this game was permenently free, I would find it hard to enjoy, because, at it's very core, this game is flawed. Had the devs given more choice to how the team or even the player would like to play, I feel like this experience could be slightly more interesting, but tracking is a boring slog, and the player who plays the monster makes or breaks your experience, and he has no one to fall back on to pick up his slack. *sigh* I wish - I wish, this game was better, but as it is: I cannot recommend it.

Let me first say that I am a huge Front Mission series fan, and played the 3rd, 4th, 5th and now this one, hence the negative recommendation.
This installment, unlike its series predecessors, is a third person shooter instead of the series’ trademark turn based RPG gameplay. But that is not the main reason why this Front Mission is mediocre.
The gameplay is easy to catch-up and to play, I really enjoyed how the game played; nothing wrong here.
The wanzers we see are all from the series (except one or two), so you can somehow relate that you are playing a Front Mission game, even though their designs are ugly (I speak of the Grille Sechs for example).
The story could be good if it was longer and with well written dialogue. Character progression is weak and seems a lot happens of the screen. One second you meet Adela and she hates you, then on the next mission she is jealous of Dylan’s old friend and apparently now loves Dylan? Also Dylan gets involved into the UCS military no questions asked I mean … it makes no damn sense. Characters die for no reason, are enemies in one mission and on the next are you best friends …. In the end, the story is really bad written, full of clichés, and does not make up to the series.
Also the characters have no personality that makes us love them or hate them. They look like random guys with names and no propose.
