While I may not have been aware of PZ from the start, for all intents and purposes, PZ is a complete game. In fact, I'd think it's the most complete and realistic zombie survival game out there.
Like many others, I was originally concerned that this had been in early access for many years, with no signs of final release. There were also no NPCs for single player mode. However, when I start playing it, most of these fears were unfounded. The game is still in early access because the developers are still finetuning it, improving it, which is great in my book, because as it is stands, it's already an excellent game.
As for the absence of NPCs, well, if you want a truly realistic interaction with others in this world, I'd suggest playing multi player on the Redboid server. It's like you are immersed in the world of TWD, with other survivors like yourself. Some will be hostile and some will be helpful, and some will rob you blind when you are not looking. :) Serious fun.
Also, if you find the base game too plain for your liking, check out the mod scene. PZ has a lot of good mods. Do check out the Hydrocraft and ORGM mods once you are used to the base game as they add a whole lot of depth, providing a plethora of items and weapons that you can craft and use. Check out the map mods too, that will help expand the world of PZ with new and interesting locations.
Overall, this is likely the best bang-for-buck game I have ever invested in.
And oh.. I have spent 1,060 hours playing it and counting.

Loki is an isometric action RPG, where in control of one hero based on famous mythologies you have to find out what happened to your local gods and fight some bosses after you get the big picture and who is behind all the madness happening around.
The gameplay is absolutely dull in this action RPG. You receive one (or for some characters two) quest and just run through areas killing hordes of monster with mostly either modified basic attack or a simple spam spell. The whole story is told by one main quest at the start - the local God from the mythology you picked gone mad and you have to find out why. You dont have to be a Sherlock to understand that the game's name is the evil behind it all. Having tried all the mythologies I can easily tell - its the same for all characters.
The combat in Loki is absolutely dull - If you play a melee character you simply spam potions to stay in the fight (they have a really small cooldown) while as a ranged you can just skill full damage and one-shot most of the enemies in the game even before they reach you. There have been no challenges at all in the the time I played it before I got bored besides some bugs like getting permanently stunned, or not being able to attack due to a stun bug (you can still move, but do no actions until you quit and re-enter the game). The skill trees are really boring aswell, you basically pick your main spell and stick to it the whole game or until you get an upgraded version of the same spell. Playing a ranged character it was absolutely easy to kite since enemies base movespeed is slower. Overall absolutely boring combat for an action RPG.
The graphic is a shame for 2007 release and feels more like Diablo time, so 1996. The effects are cheap, areas have no detail at all (egyptians run around in the desert that is simply a huge yellow square), towns look like they were last minute implementation. The interface is not fitting the game at all, since you have tons of slots for skills but you will mostly use 1-2. The bag window is a mess, the skill trees are not structure at it took me a while to figure out how to change skill tree focus, it overall does not feel polished at all.
There is no progress in this game besides running through the area killing everything and reaching the next area. Since there are no mini-games or anything else to do in this game besides smashing your mouse for hours, not a high rating to give here.
The only immersion I had was on the main screen where you have to select your mythology / character. It was underline with fitting music while you decide if you want to be an Aztec Shaman, Norse Warrior, Greek Fighter or Egyptian Mage. Sadly, after picking the hero you wont feel much immersion anymore and since there is nothing noticable about the music or the sounds, it gets a terrible rating aswell.
Loki feels unpolished and sometimes even broken, looks old, sounds bad and does not have any feature to make you stick with the game. It is one of the very few games that I have not finished (if you read my reviews, I finish 99% of my games) simply because it felt like wasting my time. Killing hordes of monster in Loki is simply boring and unrewarding, there is neither challenge nor a story to back up your progress. Since there are tons of action RPGs that do quite everything much better, I would suggest you dont waste your time or money on Loki.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

Hack 'n slash RPG in what players as mythological heroes fight against evil. Each character like Egyptian sorcerer, Aztec shaman, Greek fighter, and Norse warrior has their own three Gods to call on for power, but it will cost 25% of the experience points you earn battling enemies. Nevermind the slower leveling, though, because the only way to advance your skill trees is to do all your deeds in the name of some god or another.
Norse warrior can specialize in two-handed weapons, dual wielding, and lances depending on how you allot the points between Thor, Tyr, and Odin. The Egyptian has fire, darkness, and lightning spells, while the Aztec can summon animals, transform herself, and fight from the spirit world. The Greek is more hunter than fighter learning swords as a supplement to her bow and trap use.
To accelerate your skill trees, you can make offerings to the gods at the same altars where you switch alignments between the three.
Loki motivates players to complete all the difficulty levels like Diablo II did. Better loot and level uber characters. The "timeline" a character plays through their own world first, then the other three characters, and then moves up in difficulty to do it all again. You can reset enemies and dungeons to gain extra experience, but the important part is that by continuing, you keep your level and inventory each step of the way.

This is unfortunately it when it comes to positive things about this game. Some of the negative ones are really what set me off this game:
- The movement is clunky, the terrain(doesnt matter how small it is) is an obstacle to gap-closer abilities.
- It is very hard to get aggro of large group of enemies. They wait until you kill 5-7 of them and then attack you. This one is very apparent in the Greek world.
- The Worlds are very similar, you either fight through a Square map with similar topography in every world, dungeons with identical pathing or  islands connected with bridges through mountain cliffs. The only difference between world are the colours of the levels.
- The skill trees are very straightforward and are not rewarding to mixed leveling of abilities (some might like this, well I do not)
- The items are not diverse enough. Unique items are just stronger statwise than their normal counterparts.
- Crafting is suboptimal.
- This game crashes frequently while teleporting and transition of maps.
If you are a die-hard fan of the Arpg genre and want to kill some time go for it, else dont waste your time.

I don't know how much time I've wasted on the Baldurs Gate games, been playing them on and off since release. Baldurs Gate is the entry drug for Dungeons & Dragons. Some reading is still recommended as advanced features such as dual- and multiclassing (and how they are related, their pros and cons) is still poorly explained which is actually kind of dangerous as the game is over when the main character dies, and how easy you die depend on hitpoints and other values which are increased as you level... you see where this is going. The original Baldur's Gate is one of my favourite games, second only to its successor and is a game any rpg fan must play. Due to its art style for a game that came out in 1998 it still holds up well today. Graphically this game still looks beautiful due to 2d painting-esque backdrops and thirdperson isometric viewpoint.
The gameplay also has an incredible amount of depth to it and the combat is very tactical and varied depending on the class you play and the party setup you choose. The game is also from an era when games were unforgiving and actually provided the player with a challenge. The combat is similar to Dragon Age: Origins where it can be free-flowing and action oriented but it is highly recommended that players take it slowly and utilise pausing to setup properly between rounds during combat.
The game being built upon the ruleset of Advanced Dungeons and Dragons has a lot of depth to classes and the classes will all playout and feel very different which offers a lot of replayability ontop of just choosing and adhering to different alignments.
Also due to the game being built upon AD&D and being set in a D&D realm the game has an incredible amount of history and backstory in there that the world feels real and is incredibly dark and gritty which ties in great with the dark tones of the main story.
Without spoiling too much of the story it starts with very humble beginning and quickly thrusts the player into a world descending into turmoil with bandits and bad guys wanting to kill you at every turn you must uncover the sinister plot that is unfolding and discover your own dark heritage in the process.
I would wholeheartedly recommend this game although I will warn that there is a lot of reading involved and that the combat is designed to played slowly (unlike diablo and games of its ilk) and very tactically but for those that love a game with a great story this game is undoubtedly one you should play.

This game is abyssmal. The only reason why I finished was because I put money in it and I didn't want it to be wasted. With that said let's get to the trial. Where to begin; it's boring, I just wanted to quit halfway through the game, but you know, money spent, and with that said lets get down to the boring aspects. My biggest gripe is the weapon system, a single gun alone is underpowered, I went into battle weilding two, in addition Front Mission Evolved puts an emphasis on shooting body parts, such destroyed body parts leave the enemy at a disadvantage, which really doesn't matter because you blow them apart seconds later for the effect to be relevant.
The gameplay is very linear, the game won't let you play certain missions unless you have a sniper rifle, kind of legs or something or other. The controls are also pretty clunky, mouse movement is fine but the controls on your keyboard are a different story.
Speaking of which, you get a relatively small variety of weapons, rifles, SMG's, swords, sniper rifles, shotguns, and shields (why the ♥♥♥♥ are these here?), but you also get should mounted weaponry, which are pretty nice, mainly missile launchers, rockets, miniguns. These help out a lot, because as I cannot stress enough, your guns are pretty weak. Not to mention the sniper rifle is useless in boss fights and around the end of the game. The guns also have an overheat system, as do the shoulder weaponry, pretty annoying, like the SKATE's recharge. However you can also utilize just a sword and shield if you want a swordsman style gameplay but I'll touch upon that later.
Then comes along the movement system, walking is mind numbingly slow, as such the only way to get around is to use the SKATE System, and the disadvantages mean life or death in some cases, burning out the entire charge for SKATE forces you wait 8 seconds for a recharge (or less depending on customization), a lot of stuff can go down in the time, especially near the end of the game, and that's time nobody has either! You also get the EDGE system, time slows down, you become invulnerable and deal out godly amounts of damage, the EDGE system is recharged through fighting.
The enemies are all cookie cutter-type enemies, they pose no challenge, little threat, their just...there pretty much, yet they remain durable enough for me to need two guns, at times a new type will be introduced but really it's just the same thing with a different gun or body type. This all makes the combat and gameplay repetitive, as the only things getting changed up don't make an impact, and there are no enemies that try something dramatic or pull a twist., it's 5 types, they're all fodder. There's also bosses, and around the end you fight 4 you met earlier and you fight them alone, pretty darn difficult, only interesting moment really.
The story, CLICHES GALORE and it's dull and typical like a lot of things Hollywood pumps out. Unknown bad guy decides to be a terrorist and destroys space elevators to make a statement about the world, and the young perky engineer guy (protagonist) must rise and stop him. No plot twists, it's just...bland. Which brings me to the characters! Oh boy are you in for a treat! One dimensional! The characters don't change, they don't adopt new viewpoints, get different outlooks on life, you know the symptoms, voice acting is fine, but the catchphrases are a pain. Hope you like cutscenes, you'll get endless amounts to progress the story.
With that said lets get down to the maps, LINEAR ON-RAILS SHOOTER HO! Summarized it, you're forced down a path with the same enemies (stated earlier) all to get to something. With occassional breaks into large areas to move around and fight enemies, bosses, only to be shoved down the same forward path again. But it's got collectables laden along the way, a ♥♥♥♥ton, have fun finding 20 sensor nodes in nooks, crannies, you name it. However there are three emblems per level, these unlock decals and emblems for your mech, basically the only collectables that matter.
Now from time to time, you won't be fighting in a mech you'll sometimes be on foot in third person, and the weapons selection is small, rifle, rocket launcher, shotgun, grenades, and the enemies this time around are just as cookie cutter! The on-foot segments are a change of pace, but they don't break the monotony, as it all delves back into the same formula as when driving a mech. Same goes for gunship landing segments, however, I did find those a bit fun, mainly because I got guns that were actually powerful, but it all boils down to 'circle area, and land.'
Are we done? Nope! Remember when I mentioned that bit about swordsman style, well were getting into customization! Now to the games credit, customization is pretty nice (of course, they posted it all over the videos and pics). You get to compare weapons, body types (this is the armor), backpacks, legs and arms, and really you can customize to some pretty big lengths. There are three types of legs, bi-pedal, multi-leg, and hover, their all just about the same though as what really matters is the skate system, but multi-leg does let you carry more heavier weaponry while hover gives you more manuvering. You can change up your weapons to become like, a dual sword weilding person, a heavy sniper, or just do what I did and fit as much OP stuff on as possible.
Backpacks give you all kinds of benefits, more energy for SKATE, anti-missile systems, more power for carrying heavier weaponry, faster recharge, movement and such, and the game won't force you to use a certain kind of backpack for missions. And while were on customization, you can choose decals, colors, you know the jist.
But the biggest incriminating factor about this game is the fact it has multiplayer, BUT NO ONE PLAYS IT, it's dead. makes the DLC pretty useless, along with the customization and decals mentioned earlier. Also to addon is that the end of the game, the final part, is very unforgiving.
All this combines to make little to no-replayability.
The designs and looks of the mechs are pretty nice though, that's the only redeeming factor.
TL;DR: Front Mission Evolved is boring, linear, on-rails, and it's a massive time sink for such boredom, multiplayer is non-existant, the story is dry and flat, and it's all stuffed behind pretty graphics. Don't buy it. It's not worth anything.

Maybe it's just the Front Mission fan speaking, but I can't shake this impression that Evolved finds it at best extremely uncomfortable operating within the existing IP and at worst, it seems to have nothing but contempt for it. Obvious genre bender might seem as a surprise, but it's not the first time the franchise had a spin-off title, it's the fact that the execution of TPS gameplay seems clunky is what really brings the game down from a mechanical standpoint. Especially the completely tacked on infantry levels which were obviously an afterthought and come close second to the annoyance that are rocket-sponge bosses who will test your patience towards the end. Overall pacing of the game is also very lacking and at times it seems as if there are entire chapters missing which would've facilitated smoother flow instead of the current rushed narrative.
Speaking of which, the story is probably the greatest offender in the entire game and takes a very liberal, but ultimately misunderstood take on the existing setting. No tropes or cliches are left unchecked as the story forgoes franchise's signature politics-heavy approach in favor of merely dropping acronyms whenever it can and expecting you to give a damn as you follow a very bland main character doing his revenge thing which never evolves into anything beyond that very simple concept. Characters at large aren't treated any better and just fill the utterly predictable archetype role, especially the villains who are so by-the-numbers I first thought it was perhaps some kind of irony at work. You will forget what you went through the moment you finish the game and be glad you'll never again have to deal with all the manufactured EDGE drama.

After playing more than 100 hours in this game i dont recommend it here are reasons why:
1. 0 Rewards for being usefull for your team - you dont get more credits or exp for great battles and that leads to super slow progression through tiers. So one can ask how do you earn credits well there is some bonuses to "normal" earnings when your ship have reasearched  every single node avaible.
2. Upgrades and consumables - there is no such thing as upgrades for few ships at once. Developers aparently thought that every cannon and gun avaible for any ship were designed as completly new construction so despite spending a lot of effort to max out your battleship and after that moving to next tier you cant use previously reseached technologies. (ive double checked that guns with same calliber, barrel lenght and markings cant be transfered to other ships within nation). Consumables are some kind of joke even premium ones - i could understand 1 battle only and then re-buy i could understand higher prices for pernament but buying armor of airplanes for 7 days is just riddiculus. Even if you spend gold (premium currency) for consumables you gonna get it for 7 days .
3. Tutorials and in-game information - while movement tutorial is covered rest of tutorials like: how to use planes, how to use sonar etc. are in form of non interactive screen shot (yes 1 screen shot) with MISSING (sic!) information text. Also there is no such thing as shooting range or training mode to find out for yourself when to drop bombs or lunch torpedoes.
4. Economy - ive said about battle rewards and let say you can handle it and you are thinking well maybe i should check out other nations i have some credits accumulated i wont need to go through every tier. Nope you wil have to there is no such thing as common  "bank account" for all your captains you cant transfer funds between them.
5. Controls - just nightmare. Best example is playing carrier: you cant leave your planes unattended they will crash into gound (isnalnds), also you cant just order them to execute attack on given position you will have to manualy drop bombs/torpedoes, you dont even have decent minimap to know where you are needed most or if you are in danger (in game minimap just shows red and blue ship-dots only)
6. Balance - Personaly i dont care with what tiers im matched and like in every tier based game you will be matched with higher/lower tiers thats perfectly fine becaues there is always room for outplay but you can be matched with subs without any means of fighting them (only detect them) with ships that was meant to fight them or ships without any AA guns (except "AI" controled) fighting air planes. Also you can be matched up to 7 tiers difference but for me its just different game play and i dont really mind it as long i have ANY ability to defend myself.
Things like gameplay, graphics, stability etc. are fine. Ques are fast, gameplay is good, graphics have their charm despite bing outdated, didnt encounter many bugs. Conclusion is that game will die as soon as world of warships will be released its unfriendly to new not stubborn players and i do not recommend playing it

Artifex Mundi sp. z o.o. is one of the best Puzzle/Hidden Objects developer I've found so far BUT this game is the worse one I've played !
The story is good and graphics are fine if we don't talk about the main cute scene issue !
The puzzles and hidden objects scenes are fairly shared. The game features an inventory where you can store items to combine with the environment to go deeper in the story.
The game have two difficulties and have a guest feature : all the family can play the game and resume it where they left.

There is also a map which is useful to not get lost despite you can't fast travel with it but can show some hints if you play in the easy mode. Also you can use the Hint/Skip hourglass whenever you want and wait until its refill to use it again. But be warned that you may not skip or use a hint in any puzzle or hidden objects scene if you wish to have some achievements.
There is some choice of puzzles and there are two kind of Hidden objects scenes. The first Hidden objects scene features the name of the objects to find some are found easily (normal one) and some others need you to interact with the environment or to combine two items to found them. The second Hidden objects scene let you find the shape of the items to find.
(#):
From the beginning to the end I've a very bad issue: all the cut scenes were full of pixels and I've seen one or more discussion on steam despite I didn't read them all. I tried to switch to the lowest resolution, I think its changed something even if the cut scenes are still bad.
(*) :
The game has some achievements that can be missed, mostly challenging achievements, including finishing the game on hard mode or using no hints in the puzzles or hidden objects scenes. There is currently a good guide for that (Chapter 0 - Achievement / Arquivamentos):
The challenging achievements require you to finish a puzzle or an hidden objects scene or a domino game under a minute. And two achievements require you to find 3 objects in 3 seconds or find all objects with a few misclicks in the hidden object scenes.
(@):
As I said in the key features, you need two playthrough to finish the game. One to finish the game with all the puzzles and hidden objects scenes perfected and another one playing the mahjong game instead of the hidden objects scenes. The good thing is you can skip all the cut scenes and puzzles in your second playthrough if you succeeded your first one. The mahjong game consists in taking all of the mahjong tiles, to do so you need to make couples. BUT there is one main trap to not fall in... you need to play a new game in the same user ! If you don't you'll not have the last achievement that require you to have all of the previous achievement in one user session !

EDIT:
To give you guys an idea of what the gameplay is like...
There's no storyline to this game, your only goal is to survive for as long as possible. You'll start off in a random tiny 1-storey house in one of the major cities and will spend the majority of first few hours going from house to house collecting food, water, tools/weapons and other supplies and eventually securing a building to serve as a safehouse.
You'll encounter zombies everywhere, especially in big open areas such as parking lots and on major highways. Occasionally, you'll get spooked by a zombie in a building as you go from room to room looting it in dark, often cramped rooms.
After a while (depending on your difficulty settings), water and electricity will shut off forcing you to build rain collection barrels for water and boiling it to sterilise before drinking. Restoring electricity is pretty useless as petrol for the generator is scarce and the noise attracts zombies.
Every so often, random meta-events will occur such as screams and distant gunshots which will draw zombies in the direction it came from, often making them pass by or overwhelm your safehouse.
Once you've looted all nearby buildings and built up a decent safehouse, you'll either migrate to a different area for supplies or begin farming (which takes a long time to yield crops).
That's about it... as I mentioned above, the game is fun for a little while but then once you're set up and fully self-sufficient... the game gets incredibly boring and unrewarding.

My favourite game series - the setting & lore of this science fiction masterpiece is so fascinating, one that I return to regularly. Rapture feels like such a real and fully developed place, full of amazing characters - Ryan, Tennenbaum, Atlas, Cohen, Suchong and many more than you uncover through the wonderful dialogue over the radio and the audio logs that flesh out the backstory brilliantly. The story twists and turns in wonderful ways and has many iconic moments.
The art design is peerless - beautiful, horrifying, darkly humourous, all of which portrays the insanity and egotism of Rapture. It immerses you into the world with it's wonderful use of light, colour and sound in a way that keeps it fresh even ten years on. The atmosphere is really incredible and often terrifying - there are jumpscares but they don't feel cheap because there is plenty of psychological horror and creepy mind♥♥♥♥ery that keeps you on your toes. The Big Daddies & Little Sisters are iconic for very good reason - their dynamic is wonderful, especially when you have played the entire series and gotten the whole picture. This is a game about parenthood as much as it is one about Objectivism after all.
The gameplay is very rich and entertaining - streamlining ideas from it's spiritual prequel System Shock into a kinetic action game. Weapons have a good kick to them, with multiple ammo types for use in different situation. The plasmids are great fun to use and are integral to the plot & lore. I really enjoy the research camera too, it's just wonderfully funny to be casually taking snaps while Splicers are trying to rip you to pieces.
Level design is excellent, full of environmental storytelling & room to explore within hubs. Every area has it's own feel to it and gives you a more rounded feel for the city of Rapture. The second half of the game feels a little less inspired and is more linear which may disappoint some but I still felt there was lots of interest to see.
Flaws - I'm not a big fan on the Pipe Mania minigame for hacking. Bioshock 2 improved hacking hugely with a remote hack dart weapon & a quicker interface.
The save/harvest choice for Little Sisters isn't much of a choice - there's not much room for grey morality as you ultimately get rewarded more for saving them, making it ethically and pragmatically the right and only choice to make.
The boss battle at the end is pretty mediocre aswell. It isn't bad, but it feels too typical for a game that otherwise has so many atypical and original ideas.
Still, these flaws don't in any way make Bioshock less than a masterpiece. It's a great game, it's a great story and it's great art.

As someone who doesn't typically enjoy shooters, and someone who has no nostalgia for the title, I can safely say this game is legitimately worthy of it's praise as a classic.
The Good:
- Beautiful environments and a wonderful overall aesthetic. The immersive undersea late 1950-60s city that you find yourself exploring is not only a very unique location for a game, but it's also just masterfully crafted. They really blew me away with just how interesting they were able to make every area. It was the kind of location I seriously would love to see in real life, a sort of dream environment as it were.
- Equally interesting storylines, all told through various cassette tape diaries you find while playing. You rarely see any direct character interactions to tell the games story, but the voiced diary entries really tell well crafted stories, allowing the player to "imagine" what happened between these characters for themselves (often times with evidence of what went on being found later in your playthrough.) The overall theme hits on Ayn Randian ideology and it does a good job of getting the players to think a bit without it feeling too much like the devs were pushing some agenda on you. It's just a great game with unique storytelling, while the compelling undertones are exactly that; undertones.
- The game does a good job of rewarding you for exploring it's environments with very gamey hidden stashes of Ammo, currency, food and powerups. This might seem to be a smaller deal, but I found it to be a core part of what had me interested in the game. They put a lot of "secret" areas and locations in the awesome zones you find yourself in, and you're almost always rewarded for finding them. Sometimes the reward is cheap and insignificant... but that's fine, at least the game puts in effort to show that things may not always be as they initially seem, and it really makes the zones feel dynamic and meaningful. You rarely enter a new area thinking, "well this is obviously an empty room" and as a result, you can look forward to uncovering whatever secrets might be hiding there.
- The powerups themselves are pretty well fleshed out as well. I don't want to go too specific here, but there is a lot of customization options available to you when it comes to deciding how you want to play. These powerups also do a good job of making your progress feel meaningful in the game. It's fairly well paced as well, although I do have to say I felt like just using a select few the entire playthrough, but that could boil down to personal preference.
- The game does linearity right. Open world syndrome is something I've come to dread from recent games, and honestly, this game realizes that simple objective based gameplay can be perfect, boundaries and walls can be a good thing in the same way that rules in sports don't ruin the fun as a result of how "restricting" they might be on the players. That said, even though you have very clear objectives throughout the play, the zones are large enough, and linked together in such a way that you could deviate if you were so inclined. This is my opinion of how games like this should be structured.
- Spooky enemies with spooky sounds really do a good job of making you feel threatened at all times, even though the enemies were rarely actual threats on normal difficulty. It might be a bit gimmicky and jump scare-ish, but the voice lines of the enemy splicers are really crazy and fun to listen to, and they did this cheesy thing where they make an enemy sound like it's right behind you in loud volume, which just gave me the chills frequently. The enemies weren't behind me mind you, so it really was a misleading gimmick, and this could be argued as a Con for the game just lying to the player, but for me, it made the experience feel more like exploring a haunted environment, and that was enjoyable.
The Meh:
- The gunplay itself just isn't my cup of tea. I didn't feel like the gameplay was particularly fast paced (like counterstrike or something for example) and as a result it just felt like bullet sponge encounters all day. To be fair, the powerups and your wide arsenal of weapons (which you're able to carry every weapon on you at all times) led to a sort of rock paper scissors mini game of using the right tool for the enemy at hand, lightning for electronics, armor piercing for big daddys, fire attacks on oil patches etc, but yeah, I personally found the combat to not be as compelling as the rest of the game (as I said, I'm not big on FPS gameplay.)
The Bad:
- The hacking minigame. I couldn't stand this aspect of the game after about the fifth thing I hacked, and believe me, it doesn't go away any time soon. Your lategame somewhat compensates for how tedious it becomes by offering you several powerups to make the process easier, but they also ramp up the difficulty of the hacks as the game goes on as well... I literally quit the game halfway in because of this stuff, and only recently jumped back in to finish it.
So yeah, overall the game was fantastic. Even one of my only complaints (the gunplay one) could be entirely disregarded if you happen to like FPS gameplay more than me. This was one of the more surprising games I have played to say the least, because I fully expected to hate it, and ultimately, I just really enjoyed my time with it somehow.
9/10 if I had to score it (for those that enjoy FPS games), fk the hacking minigame basically.
My personal enjoyment was more like a 7/10, but that's just because I'm not into FPS games, but I can clearly tell it's amazing for people that do enjoy that stuff.

Aquaria is a very beautiful game that follows the style of Metroid or Castlevania Symphony of the Night in which you have a generally 2D open world in which to explore and discover. Best of all, it is even moddable.
Controls are absolutely fluid (pun intended), and the music/soundtrack is especially fantastic. Its really a treat for the senses, every pulsating beat, every emotional feel is conveyed extremely well.
The story is well presented and is quite a long adventure spanning at around 13 hours (More if you take the time to fully explore the environments and do all the achievements) Some scenes are also very well crafted. (Eg: Really felt very special first time at Veil especially at that special sequence)
Downsides tho, the game sometimes feels directionless, especially during early game. Unlike Castlevania or Metroid where players are given gentle nudges via story cutscenes, In Aquaria, you are basically left on your own to discover the world with very little hints. Some puzzles are also very obscure. This game makes uses of save points to save your game, and some locations are just downright stingy with save points.
One gripe i have is the ending. While the normal ending ends at a satisfactory note, there is another secret ending which ends with a cliffhanger and hints at a sequel. Sad to say, the team that made this game has disbanded and we will not see a sequel anytime soon.
Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10

This is my second or third review of the game, however it's my first review since the game has come out of early access with the Wintermute update.
This game...has a special place in my heart. I could go on and on about it, but there's no true way to describe it, as each time I play a new sandbox it's a new adventure through the frozen tundra. The past two years, I saw this game grow into one of my favorites of all time with each update. Hinterland is one of the few dev companies that listened to the players while having an early access game out. They heard us loud and clear, and now the story mode is finally here. Within the first 20 minutes of story gameplay, I was astonished. I was sitting there thinking "this was worth waiting two years."
Hinterland has given us a gem of a game in an overcrowded genre. I'm not a fan of the survival genre typically, but this one is different. There is just something about this game that makes me want to get through another night in the quiet apocalypse. The story so far has me on the tips of my toes, and I have only encountered the first wolf thus far. It's far more intriguing than sandbox mode, yet has the same pleasures.
It's not the most graphically stunning game in the world, but it's beautiful in its own rite. The art style is perfect for the environment, and despite the cartoony-like style, it makes it all the more real.
I was delighted to see newer texture packs for in game items, like sewing kits or beef jerky. The gameplay got a bit of an upgrade as well! The two layer system is amazing. It's nice to not have to go back and forth into a menu for everything. Hinterland gave us a radial wheel, similar to GTA Vs weapon wheel, but for use of everything. Since the faithful cartographer update, I've been enjoying the game to its fullest extent.
Now with story mode, I'm in for a rough and emotional ride, only to probably freeze to death 60 days in.
I give this game a full 10/10 for being an instant classic, and for having a special place in my heart.
I also give Hinterland 10/10 for being an outstanding dev company, listening to the players throughout the years, and actually fulfilling their promise to deliver a one of a kind experience that is The Long Dark.

Stonehearth is a great game. It's a merge of Dwarf Fortress and Minecraft; The former for it's 'base-building' and management aspects, the latter for it's voxel graphics.

Good replay value

Looks great

Large amount of craftable items and professions

Building Designer

Villagers level up and unlock skills

Frequently updated

Rather buggy, villagers tend to get confused very often and so on

Combat is slow and iffy at times

Game will often break if you don't save often to avoid doing things that break it

Some 'texture' issues

Few pre-built structures

Lack of game customisation (monster spawn rates, villagers, etc)
In Stonehearth, your goal (if any) is rather simple: to build a thriving medieval village/city, and take care of the various needs of your villagers (known has hearthlings) along the way.
You don't have direct control over your villagers like an RTS; you give them orders to perform and they'll find a way to do it (most of the time) themselves.
As you progress in-game, and your villagers level up, you'll slowly unlock more proffessions for them to practice, and thus more furniture, decoration, tools and weapons for them to use.
You will not, however, unlock new buildings, as the game only has 5 (I believe) pre-built ones. The rest is up to you to build, using the game's Building Designer feature, which works more or less the same as 'The Sims' Build Mode, with a tab bit less freedom.
Hearthlings tend to have issues when building; I have had to help them off of roofs, demolish a building because they couldn't build scaffolding or because they just go on strike and won't build anything at all.
Decoration-wise, there are tons to choose from, ranging from beds, to flower pots or braziers. Each crafting profession has some form of decoration. My villages have gotten prettier and prettier over time as I've discovered new crafts.
The game's replay value is rather high, as attempting to create a functional village in different environments can be a challenge at times (on top of a mountain, for example ^^).
The game is also rather buggy in it's current state; several times I have had to start a new game because I placed a path over another and the villagers refused to build anything else, or because I was planning a custom building and none of my orders would work anymore.
Many blocks/items sometimes overlay eachother as well, causing flickering textures which can get rather irritating at times.
I've also had issues where my one fighter hearthling has gotten themselves stuck in an infinite loop of 'Attack Golbing Chieftan > Run away from Goblin Chieftan'. Seeing as there is no direct control over the villagers, I can't do anything to get them to stop, and just have to wait for something to hopefully kill them.
All in all, Stonehearth is a great game to own if you're into the genre and I highly recommend it.The frequent updates make it a great game to come back to from time to time.

So. Very. Japanese.
It's bad enough it's a game about giant mechs (not that I have anything against games with giant mechs) but Front Mission Evolved seems to be making a point to hit every single anime cliche that it can. Young man inexplicably talented at war suddenly drafted into the front lines of the conflict. Revenge for the death of a family member. The brunette love interest and the geeky girl with glasses. "Meaningful" sacrifices of a friend and unexpected reversals of fortune. Giant bosses unsurprisingly hampered by giant orange weak-points. It's unsophisticated, sophomoric pabulum that makes the Modern Warfare franchise look deep in comparison. Aging graphics, uninspired sound design and dull level design don't help. The combat is colorful but the levels are too constricted and linear. The third-person camera too often wedges into a corner leaving me with a useless view of my mech's (sorry, my /wanzer/'s) back. And the boss fights go on forever.
FME's only saving grace is that, ultimately, it does involve giant robots, and it's hard to hate any games involving 100-ton walking death machines. But that's barely enough to keep one playing; it certainly doesn't warrant a recommendation. It's trite, unimaginative and poorly designed. But, sadly, that seems par for the course for Japanese video games.

You don't like point-and-click adventures? You don't like puzzles?
Neither do i, and yet... it took all of about 2 minutes for this game to reel me in. It's a casual point-and-click adventure where the protagonist is on a quest to rescue her daughter from a risen-from-the-dead (or was he ever truly dead?) pirate (which may sound horribly campy, but it actually fits the story very well). It offers a "hint" button to help the... ah... less puzzle-oriented of us out when we're stuck, and offers an alternate mechanism for finding hidden items in some contexts (namely, a Mahjong mini-game, where matching tiles substitutes for finding items). As others as mentioned, the quality of the cinematic cutscenes is rather poor (specifically, each pixel is about 15mm across, but the motion _is_ fluid), but the cinematics are nonetheless used to great effect, providing cohesive transitions between non-cinematic scenes, which ties them to each other in a way i've not personally seen in games of this type (admittedly, my experience with them is limited, as it's not really my genre - perhaps that's a common thing to see in other games of this type). The non-cinematic parts are of course graphically impressive and the controls are trivial (well, the singular control - the mouse). The voice-overs are a definite "meh" but they aren't bad. (Some of the pronounciation irks me, but there's no accounting for taste (tomato, tomahto, and all that).)
At 8 Euros for parts 1-3 (on sale), i kinda feel like i've cheated the publisher, as opposed to feeling cheated myself.
So... back to playing... where were we... right, we've just left the museum and... aaaarrrrggghhh! A pirate! Click it! CLIIIICK IT!!!
PS: plays flawlessly on my Mint Linux.
PPS: After having finished it, some closing thoughts:
- None of the puzzles felt "arbitrary" to me, in contrast to some puzzle games i've played (i'm looking at you, Lego series!).
- A couple of the words for hidden items were a bit confusing (or completely new to me), but the "sonar" feature made that a non-issue.
- It felt a bit short - roughly 6 hours (without using the Hint feature), including the  Extra Adventure which gets unlocked after the main story. Nonetheless, the pacing felt good - it never went long without something to do and i was never left scratching my head for more than a few minutes at a time. Likewise, backtracking was not problematic because navigation is swift.
- Unlocking all achievements requires 2 play-throughs (once using the Mahjong search feature and once without it), and i'm very unlikely to play any game of this type twice.
- i feel that 8+ Euros is a tick too high for today's market for this type of game, but not overly so. i won't impulse-buy an 8 Euro game, but will certainly bookmark it so that Steam notifies me if it's on sale.
- i will likely impulse-buy future titles by this publisher if they're priced at 4 Euros or less.

Ummm... sure. Why not. Might as well give this game a thumbs up.
I'm an old-school 80's and 90's gamer. Back then, games were made and sold "as is" once they hit the shelves. There were no patches, no promised features and no DLC. You bought a game, went home, played it and that was the end.
That's pretty much where I'm at with Project Zomboid. I didn't buy it for planned or promised features. I bought it on a whim because it looked fun. And it was fun. Mission accomplished.
So this game is very much a "what you see is what you get" purchase. Don't buy it because they promise anything or it has potential to be anything other than what it currently is.
Is it fun, though? Yes. Definitely a worthy, fun experience for the money spent. Lots of detail has gone into the survival aspects; food, water, sleep, physical and even psychological health. Zombies also behave naturally (if that's even possible...?) Items in the game seem balanced and practical, no "uber shotguns of d00m" or anything. And you can adjust many settings for each game, making each play through unique.
This game becames short though, once you have it down. It plateaus at a point where you have plenty of food, water and defense. There's not much left to do after that, except ride it out and see how far you can get comapred with the other players.
Reminds me of Cortex Command.

As Fallout was to Wasteland, so too was Baldur's Gate to the text based fantasy adventures and RPGs that came before it. An isometric classic, Baldur's Gate paved the way for now-legendary D&D PC Forgotten Realms RPG titles like Baldur's Gate II, Icewind Dale, Planescape: Torment, and Neverwinter Nights.
With the Enhanced Edition, Baldur's Gate has now been repackaged to include the expansion, Talers of the Sword Cost, and been reoptimzed with modern resolutions and compatability fixes.
Potential customers should know that with Baldur's Gate they are getting an epic classic RPG adventure and the ability to import their playthrough into Baldur's Gate II, also released with an Enhanced Edition.
The price you pay for this adventure is an RPG that, like many of its time, does not hold hands. You will be expected to make a charachter and maintain that charachter and a party of adventures through the archaic (even at its time) AD&D 2nd Edition ruleset. Conversation paths and encounters can open up or lock you out of future quests without warning. A single unprepared encounter with a greater basilisk, a web trapped giant spider enclave, or a wizard ambush can decimate even over-leveled parties in seconds.
While many classic RPG fans would call Baldur's Gate a "must play", I fully acknowledge that the depth, openness, and difficulty of the series can be a major turnoff to modern gamers. To those who take the plunge, feel free to hit me up with advice for charachter creation and remember that the Q key is for quicksaves. Use it often.

Gonna keep this quick, if you are a person who liked the original Dungeon Keeper, get this game. It is nothing like a clone of Dungeon Keeper, instead it just clearly has influenced Dungeon of the Endless. As a veteran player of Dungeon Keeper you will go through this game constantly being reminded of your favourite classic. The thing that most reminds me of DK is that feeling of opening up a door and never knowing what is at the other side waiting for you. Every time you click on a door (in the same way you would knock down a door or tunnel out into the unknown in DK) you get a sense of excitement waiting to see if it is treasure, enemies or both on the other side.
An utterly addictive and fun exploration game, which due to the random level design will keep you coming back again and again. Several different game modes change it up even more.
Though I aimed this review at Dungeon Keeper players, I imagine anyone who likes exploration, adventure, surprise and killing monsters this game is for you. The game can be frustratingly difficult at times and attempting to move foreward before you have laid enough traps can be fatal within seconds. This game may make you 'rage quit' but believe me in 5 minutes you will be back on the game.

One of my most favorite games.  Very unique and love the concept.  Simple, pretty, with great functional design and love the music.
Dungeon of the Endless is a mix between tower defense and hero wars type of a game.  Each door you unlock essentially ends your turn.  Rooms you have not powered, whether intentionally or unable, have a chance of spawning waves of monsters.  At this point, hope your defenses are good enough to beat back the hordes and your heroes are leveled up enough and equiped well enough to help.
Part turn-based, part stradegy, I find this game to have a very refreshing asthetic.  Mixed with a reasonable price, why have you not purchased this already? ^-^
Oh, you want to hear more?  Well, how about that this is a rogue-like.  No two games play the same, no two maps are the same.  Each time you play, it will be different.  Also, this game features a ton of unlockables, from ships which change your game type, to different chracters, of whom have different abilities, strengths and weaknesses.
Multiplayer has always seemed to be pretty stable as well.  This also presents more challenges if you play with friends, as your resources are pooled.  How well will you be able to work together.  Can you make it to the final levels?  Maybe you just do not want to stop.  Try Endless mode for a really challenging experience!

This game came out at around the same time as Titan Quest, yet Titan Quest looks 100x better graphically. Heck, Diablo 2 looks better. This game has unpolished looking graphics, a horrible UI, a rather badly made loot system, a frustrating skill system, and lousy combat.
The character balancing was pretty godawful too. You choose one of four characters (Greek Archer, Nordic Barbarian, Egyptian Wizard, Aztec Shaman), each of which have three skill trees that you can access by worshipping one of three different dieties for that particular class. You may only put points into a tree if you are currently worshipping that particular god. It is a rather needlessly complicated skill system.
The difficulty of this game is also a tad skewed. Picking anyone other than the Egyptian and you're gonna have a hard time with this game, the difficulty curve spikes pretty high, even on Normal difficulty. Picking the Egyptian however gives you access to various AOE spells in each of his diety trees, any of which you can use to nuke monsters from around corners and generally out of their lines of sight to kill them without aggroing them. Some bosses being the exception with this tactic, but still rather easy to kill with his spells regardless. The melee characters all have hard times avoiding great amounts of damage and the  Aztec Shamans pet spells seem lackluster by comparison to the Egyptians nuking.
The voice acting is subpar, even for this games time. The monsters themselves can vary soundwise from normal levels to occasionally ear splitting combat screams depending on the monster type involved. You have to slog through the story on each difficulty to actually get the final ending, and go through each other classes area on each difficulty fighting their bosses along with your own. Combat is repetitive, frustrating (if you're not the Egyptian), and boring (if you are). The boss fights are pretty painful to get through as well. Particularly the final boss in the Aztec area. I hated that fight.
All in all I'm probably giving this one a bad review because I had played Titan Quest right before it. Titan Quests only problem after release was a slight memory leak. This game had many more issues and overall can't compare to it. Or Diablo 2. Or Diablo 1 for that matter. Even the first two Sacred games have a certain charm that this one just....lacks. Skip it.

The year is 1960, and you're flying over the Atlantic Ocean. One mysterious plane crash later, you're floating in the water, apparently the lone survivor, surrounded by the flaming wreckage of the aircraft. But there's a lighthouse on a tiny island just at the edge of your view. You swim closer and discover a small submersible called a bathysphere waiting to take you underwater. You're sent into the secret underwater city of Rapture. Masterminded by a businessman named Andrew Ryan, this city is driven by its own idea of total freedom, with capitalism completely unhindered by governmental meddling and science unhinged from the pesky morals of organized religion. Before you step out of your bathysphere and into the city, it becomes obvious that everything has gone horribly wrong down here. The city is trashed, and genetic freaks called splicers roam around, attacking anything that gets in front of them. At the heart of the matter is a powerful, corrupting substance called ADAM, which makes all this genetic tinkering possible and allows you to get your first plasmid power, the ability to shoot lightning out of your fingertips.
Customization is a key. You have a limited but increasable number of spaces in various customization categories, and you can totally reconfigure all of your different plasmids and tonics at will at specific locations in game. Plasmids are the active, weaponlike genetic enhancement. Incinerate lets you burn things and melt ice. Telekinesis lets you use your left hand as if it were wand with Leviosa from Harry Trotter. Security bullseye is a little ball you can toss at enemies, causing any nearby security cameras, turrets, or sentry bots to point in his direction. Enrage can cause enemies to fight one another. Insect swarm causes your arm to shoot bees at your enemies, which unfortunately is far less cool-looking than it sounds. You can also place decoys, plant swirling wind traps for enemies, and so on. While it's fun to mess around with a lot of the indirect attacks, facing your enemies head on with the more direct plasmids feels a bit more effective. Tonics are skills that are slotted just like plasmids, but they have passive effects, like sportboost, which increases your movement and melee attack speed, or natural camouflage, which makes you turn invisible if you stand still for a few seconds.
Most of those plasmids and tonics will have to be purchased using the raw ADAM that you collect from harvesting vessels called little sisters. They're little girls with a big needle that they use to collect the sought after stuff from dead bodies, and they're protected by the baddest enemies in the entire game, hulking armored monsters called big daddies. This is where the game makes you decide to be selfless or selfish. If you harvest the girls, they die, but you get 160 ADAM from them. If you free them and return them to normal, you get only 80 ADAM. Either route has benefits and consequences, and there are story considerations as well.
Your melee weapon is a wrench, and you quickly collect a revolwer and machine gun like Tommy Gun, flamethrower and shotgun, grenade launcher and crossbow. All have three diffrent ammunition like burning one or antipersonal.
You'll find more important human characters at certain points in the story, and though these are set up like boss fights, these guys are just more powerful and resilient versions of existing splicers. You'll also have to deal with security robots, turrets, and cameras, though these can all be hacked via a neat little hacking minigame to bring them over to your side, allowing for more indirect combat options. Then there's the big daddy, which comes in two configurations. The bouncer has a huge drill arm that is used to, you know, drill into people. The rosie likes to launch explosives in your general direction. Both of them are fairly nasty, because they move quickly and dish out a lot of damage while not taking very much from most of your attacks.
You won't miss a ton of locations by sticking to exactly where the arrow points you, but the story fills out a lot more when you find and listen to as many audio diaries as possible. Hearing various characters talk about the problems leading up to Rapture's current disheveled state really fills in the blanks nicely and should be considered mandatory if you intend to play the game. Hearing the voices of these wide eyed idealists as their world falls apart makes the whole game feel more human. Playing through without listening to any of these optional audio clips would make the game quiet and fairly confusing, as you'd be proceeding with no sense of backstory about Andrew Ryan, fish magnate Frank Fontaine, and the bit characters who comment on their increasingly hostile struggle.
It certainly helps that the environments you find throughout the game look amazing and practically beg to be explored. For something as potentially dingy as an underwater city, you sure do get a lot of different looks as you move along, from the boiler rooms and workshops of the city's core to the forest that helps keep the entire thing oxygenated. You'll get a lot of great views of the sea through windows. In addition to a terrific artistic design that ties the visuals together, the game has a very strong technical side, provided you have a machine that's built enough to handle it. At least when it was done, now you can get revisited edition with better graphic but still same good game.

There are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of collectables, which is how you both gain new skills (hint: these are very handy) and cash (which is also handy, even though the cash system in this game is kind of a trainwreck?).

Some in on-rails shooter sections, some that you have to find in boss fights or arenas before your targets die and you're forced onward? Or enemies who will stunlock you while AI companions break randomly? Don't forget how slow you move in overly-large levels, or the wait-for-a-recharge special attack mode you'll basically require in most fights to speed them up.
The biggest sin of all, though, is that the game is BORING. HIDEOUSLY DULL. I could totally get into this as a mindless action game but it has cutscenes that go on FOREVERRRRRRR and takes itself deathly serious and none of it's worth a♥♥♥♥♥♥while the same 5 enemy types fight you all game and nothing ever breaks the monotony up. is a hack & slash RPG. The Norse God of Mischief is on the loose across the world, so local heroes must each travel across their lands and help their own Gods safeguard the world.
: This game has plenty of dungeon crawling. With each of the four characters, you have an entire campaign set in a different part of the world, interacting with different Gods and different enemies and creatures. There is a large variety of weapons and armors, and different levels of rarity very similar to the Diablo series. Graphics are ok if you're zoomed out, and you heal quickly enough when idle that you can jump right back into action after a few seconds of rest.
: The game is basic, story is bland and so is the voice-acting. Crafting is pretty good, or at least it would be if it was of any use: Why would you disassemble your Two-Handed Hammer's magical handle if you'll throw it away as soon as you start getting the Spiked Hammer a few levels later? Why would you recycle for material your old weapons and armor if you can't even sell the material, which will be outdated as soon as better material becomes standard a few levels later? The game lags terribly whenever you're walking along an invisible wall (whether a ledge or an actual wall). Game gets quite repetitive after a while. You'll find equipment for classes other than your own (example: finding an Aztec Shaman armor while playing the Norse Campaign), which doesn't make sense seeing you can't transfer inventory between the different characters, and the characters will never set foot in the other campaign settings. The advertisement in Steam would have you believe this plays in 3rd person mode, but you actually play in isometric view (image #11 is the only accurate representation of the game).
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you

This is one of the worst 3D platformers I've ever played. Throughout the entire game, you are navigating between tiny platforms hovering over a void, so there's a consistent difficulty in gauging distance. It only gets worse as the game progresses, when you come across glowing platforms and black platforms which you can't see your shadow on. Even the hub world is obnoxious with narrow platforms that coil upwards. The game also has ridiculous speed challenges with crushing walls or spurting lava(?) that I'm convinced have some kind of rubber banding, because the timing is just that tight. A constant problem in the game is that you need to adjust the camera, but you don't have the time to, and so you end up making blind jumps instead. I can't even imagine playing this game without a controller.
What's worse is that the game is often unintuitive, with no tutorials or visual cues. Like the critical mechanic where you have to walk off a ledge before jumping to get barely enough distance for a few gaps late in the game. In one level, the ceiling is a death field, even though it has no spikes or anything. There's also a minigame at the goal of every level where you have to jump through three rings in a time limit, but it would consistently fail the minigame instantly when I jumped through the first ring. I have no clue why. I only ever completed the minigame once in all of my attempts. I won't bother going into the platforms that act randomly different from visually identical ones.
The rewards the game offers up are almost pointless. After you defeat the first boss, you earn the ability to double jump, but every subsequent level demands vastly longer jumps, so it's a distinction without a difference. After the second boss, you earn a health upgrade... and immediately afterward encounter instant-death enemies and traps. You earn the ability to fly, but it can only be used during the final boss fight and in the hub world.
The game is riddled with bugs. You can die when selecting a costume in the hub world. A few times when I started the game up, it wouldn't allow me to choose the "Start" option, despite it visually reacting to button presses. If you collect more than one life at once, you will only get one of them, and the rest are erased. You can earn an infinite amount of lives from gumball machines and get your coins back if you kill yourself before a checkpoint. Some enemies just froze in place. I consistently got pushed through walls by crushers and had to restart the entire level because I was stuck. The final boss battle is a complete joke, a unending stream of bugs that ate upwards of 40 lives, forcing me to grind lives on past levels. It would even spawn you in already falling to your death.
The only positive things I can say are that the music is okay (it's Kevin MacLeod), and it's interesting that levels have a randomized assortment of obstacles for each playthrough, if you for some reason even wanted to replay them. On the whole though, I'd skip this game.

is a breathtaking cartoon style graphics 3-D platforming, an adventure game that stands out among other platformer competitors on the PC market.
First off, we can tell just from the title that the main character's name is Joe and from the screenshots, on Steam, we can also see that the word lolly is short for lollipop which is Joe's friend’s favorite kind of candy because it makes him feel better.
does everything right in its presentation, we have the early levels (world 1) that have donuts, pizza, french fries, burgers, tea cups, cookies and even telephones that you have to jump on top of to prevent yourself from dying. What Lolly Joe is not, is a platformer that wants to be another generic side-scroller. The ones in which use spikes, pitfalls, saws and other obstacles that gamers have to progress and jump over until they make it to the end of the level. No, imagine if you combine five platformer games, in particular,

,
and
.
Now you mix all the main elements into a pot and out pops an indie platformer known as
that is highly worth the money, platformer value for every single gamer. We have many sections in
that require exact precision, if you are off the slightest, two things will happen. You either will fall to your death, losing one of your lives or you will lose one of your hearts and only fall partially.

The main goal of
is to go through a surrealistic world full of this boy's dreams. The boy happens to be a friend of ours. Since we play a dog, Joe as the main character, we should be asking, is a dog really man's best friend? Yes, despite the dog not being able to communicate with the boy in the boy's dreams, we can see the heartache, sorrow as well as the joy and happiness that the boy experiences. This relationship centers around the boy and his mother. In fact, at the start, we even have the dog that is present in the house with the family. Everything in this game is fictitious and represents no symbolism to anything within real life except a storyline with real-life based situations that happen every day; the main theme is bullying through the first world.
In high school, I was skinny, slender, thin and I have never had much muscle to me, so upper-classmen my Freshman year in high school would lift me in desks and would joke that when I become a senior, that I would come back being buff and fit. I also used to have my Freshman year of high school; people try to take food from me when I needed all of it to eat. You know, the ones that do not care if they take your fries or even more than they can help themselves to.
The music and sound are ok. Normally on the boss stages, the music changes to fit the boss. However, throughout the majority of the game, the music switches from calm to sorrowful, the kind of music you would normally see in tear-jerkers and drama based movies. This is good since it blends in so well with the story. The music uses lower piano notes in order to create a sorrowful crescendo and an unforgettable emotional experience. In other words, the virtual stimulation of the images used in the second to none, incomparable immersive environments.
Many platformer games usually have higher scales of music in order to increase the action, mostly found in the side-scrolling sub-genre of platformers. Puzzle-platformers use a combination of electronic, house and calm house, techno music rather. Let me just say; I am very impressed with how well the music blends in 1:1:1 with the presentation, mechanics, environment and virtual stimulation contributed toward the unique objects and props used to make this game one-of-a-kind.
Levels differ based on props, objects used, depth, height and the difficulty of jumps. The main goal is to make it to the very end of the level while exiting out of a portal. However, in order to get here many levels in the game require the player to reach incredible heights. There are so many places in the game so far where I have not felt confident in my platforming abilities to make. This game is not a game to be rushed, but a game that is meant to take some time planning out.
Controls are tight for the most part. There are some areas where it seems like the controls feel loose. Yet, only it is because different objects have different textures that have to be taken on account of the distance, velocity, and angle in which it needs to be approached. For example, in the first world, the cookies crumble, it is hard at first to get a good grip and angle to hit the cookies and even donuts accurately. It must be timed perfectly, or else you are going to die. The cookie is one of the most innovative ideas, to have a cookie that separates into four different parts. Every time you jump back down, the cookie resets.
It is really awesome when you think about it, the donuts revolve as well and have a large hole in its gap, many of the earlier food objects such as the pizza, have a large incline that is solved through having the right momentum. Later in the second world, we have added streetlights, telephone pole wires, double-jumps off of window ledges and rooftops in which we have to jump from rooftops from balloon to balloon to get to other areas.

This is a very decent collection of hidden object puzzles that is encased in a shell of inadequate point and click adventure game conventions, and edutainment minigames.
First- The meat of the game, which are the hidden object puzzles, is quite scrumptious. It's as good as the best 2-d drawings, but with the addition of some animation tricks which only the video-game medium could provide.
However
Second- The rest of the game is lacking. The story is poorly written and poorly performed (from a voice acting and animation perspective), and the remaining gmaeplay is usually tedious.
A) The "narrative" experience this game has to offer is not captivating because of the lack of quality voice acting, the extremely low number of animation frames, and just inadequate writing and scripting. The only postive is that the setting is firmly in the "Age Of Sail" fantasy pirate genre.
B) The "point and click" adventure game aspects are usually illogical (as is typical for that genre). The puzzles are not solved by rational thinking, but rather by thinking within the perspective of the game developers.
C) The other minigames within the game are educationally entertaining at best, boring at worst. You have tile matching puzzles, tile swap puzzles, simple instruction following, and shape identification.
D) The game also offers Mahjong solitaire as an alternative to the hidden object game sections. The art assets for this are certainly less artistically drawn.
This is still a very good game if you want to play about 20 hidden object puzzle pages.

CONS:
-Sometimes hearthlings don't tend to certain tasks and will sit idle (can be bypassed in a few different ways)
-Designing multi-level buildings requires finesse and sometimes doesn't want to work the way you hoped
-Combat needs a little tweaking. If enemies run away, even if you hit them, they take no damage.
-Currently there are various errors and cpu-usage spikes.
-

Loki is an isometric perspective action role playing game.  There are different classes to play each entrenched in one of four mythologies; Norse, Greek, Egyptian or Aztec.
Character controls and the interface are functional, but lack polish and feel.
Individual enemies are extremely well drawn and animated.
The terrain feels blocky and awkward, almost as if it was an afterthought.
There is no smooth transition between zones, and the zones are all square tiles with portals linking neighbouring zones.  Moving between one square tile zone and the next brings up a loading screen.
The game balance in early game is among the worst I have ever experienced.  Your character will keep dying and respawning at the zone entrance.
Loki has a nice design concept which has been extremely poorly implemented.  This is a lack-lustre attempt to create a "me too" game to cash in on the Diablo / Diablo 2 franchise success.  The quests, storyline and mythology are the strong points, but these are let down by poor gameplay mechanics and lack of balance.
As an alternative consider playing any of the ARPG games in the Blizzard franchise (Diablo, Diablo 2, Diablo 3) or consider Titan Quest and it's add-on Immortal throne.  Sacred and Sacred 2 are also alternatives worth consideration.  Other alternatives include Spellforce, Spellforce 2, Dungeon Siege, Dungeon Siege 2.
Loki is not a bad game, but it lacks much of the finesse, polish and playability of the top games in this genre current at the time of its release.  In other words Loki is not to be considered a good game, but rather a mediocre attempt to imitate games that are good.  That said, Loki is not the worst game in this genre, but certainly could be contrived as making a half-hearted attempt at achieving that accolade.
Worth picking up when it is on sale at good discount, but Loki is not a game you will be tempted to re-play too often or remember with fond nostalgia.

After playing this nonsense for a few hours I checked the Steam page and did a doubletake. I swear it looks like a completely different game than the one I'm playing. I guess anything could be made more exciting if you zoom the camera in on action shots. When you actually play Loki you'll notice that you spend almost the entirety of it a mile away from the action, watching your hero slay countless foes in repetitive drab backdrops in the hopes of getting a hold of that phat loot.
If I had a grain of sand for every hour that I've spent with games like Diablo 2, I could create my own Sahara in the backyard. Naturally I'm easy prey for games like Loki. Eventually my better sense prevails and I realize that I'm playing with hot garbage.
The biggest problem with Loki is that you're staring at a giant middle finger while playing. It's in the background and it almost feels like if you alt-tabbed at just the right moment you'd see it. That middle finger doesn't appear until you start leveling up. Getting a level up is usually a good thing in Action RPGs. You become stronger, you gain new abilities, and you can proceed to take on new challenges. In Loki however the monsters level up with you, and they tend to do so at a better rate. The gear you find doesn't in any way compensate for this rapidly growing disparity.
I have no idea what happens 5, 10, or even 20 hours into Loki. Does that middle finger grow in size? Does it disappear for awhile and then come back with a vengeance? Or is it like a heart beat? Pulsating and thumping every second as a reminder that you're spending time with something that hates you almost as much as it hates fun? I don't know and I really don't care to find out.

If you want a more realistic approach to the zombie apocalypse get this game. Not only is killing zombies important but everything else is accounted for. Hunger, thirst, sleep, happiness, etc. There is so much stuff that you have to take into account if you want to survive. Just to put it into perspective, I will write about one of my first experiences in playing this game.
Me and my friend were setting up base in northern Maldraugh. We picked a spot not far from a warehouse and settled down. After having to clear about 15 zombies we figured it was a safe location. Fast forward a few days and me and my friend were going to the large warehouse specifically to find an axe in order to barricade our safehouse. There were too many zombies outside so we ran into the warehouse and began looting. Luckily, I was the one who found the axe. Zombies began to break into the warehouse through windows and doors. We ran upstairs and... the door was locked. Thankfully, I still had my axe, so I began to knock the door down as my friend held off the zombies at the top of the staircase. He went down fighting, and was surrounded and eaten by zombies just as I got through the door. I got through the door and it felt like a slap in the face as realized I was trapped on top of a roof with no way out. I tried to fight off some zombies but there were too many. As a last resort I jumped off the roof and broke both my legs. I tried to slowly crawl away but they caught up to me, and I died, only minutes after my friend.
This is only one of the many great experiences I have had in the game. The one and only complaint I can find about this game- is how slowly updates come out. I feel like I have been watching this games development forever and although it has come so far, it is still missing some important promised features. At the very top of this is survivors. And being someone who very much prefers multiplayer over singleplayer, this has not affected me much, yet it has still been promised forever.
In general though, this game is very much worth the money. If you are into realism and a challenge, get this game. If you expect badass zombie killing action at all times, this game is not for you because sometimes you have to run, or you die.

This game is probably the most realistic game I have played, however, it is also very unrealistic and irritating at times.
What Iike about this game is:
-It is realistic in how perfoming actions such as farming, first aid, and many more are completed.
-It is essential to avoid taking injury as those can become infected if not tended for, and especially do not take damage from them zambiez as you risk dying from zombification. It is very tedious to tend for those injuries as well, especially when you are running from hordes 24/7.
-The difficulty. With everyone complaining about making games overall easier and therefor making all games impossible to lose, this game is a breath of fresh air. I actually die on this game, which in every other game is impossible, even on the hardest difficulty! But for those who can barely play a game, don't worry! You can change the settings of this game to make it incredibly easy!
-You need to multitask and plan ahead. If you don't, well you know what happens. Plan your escape routes, your scavenging runs, and many more.
-Spawn zones of items makes some sense. If you go into a civilian household, chances are of finding a gun are very low. In a police arsenal, now that is a different story.

-How this game is mod oriented. They don't push out too much content and if one is to get a better gaming experience, looking to the communities' mods is their best bet. I do not like this as mixing mods sometimes does not work, corruption of save, etc. Just too much a hassle to deal with.
-They have no vehicles. You can get those in mods but still, not a fan of that.
-The occupation skills you can pick make very little sense as apparently a masters degree in medicine (physician) is not the highest level of first aid you can get.

I like this game. They are still releasing content, I however, wish they would incorporate mods like the vehicles into their game. My experiences in the game are hilarious and fun. Such as right now as I am currently hiding in my house with barricaded windows. I collected a good amount of supplies and was on a wood run and then suddenly, pineapples. But no really, a helicopter flew right on over like a fly in your face while at a part in a game that requires 100% attention. It attracts thousands of zambiez and I run to my base hoping for them to walk on by... they didn't. Thats where I am at. Thinking of of whether to accept my death or to deny it by leaving the game off.
