Cuphead is fantastic, but not perfect. Despite what you may hear, it's not comparable to Dark Souls in any way, or almost any difficult game for that matter. Almost as Cuphead is it's own, unique, game. Seriously though, this game works on nearly every front. The 30s art style and music are absolutely fantastic, and hits the nail on the head, but that was already obvious, so I'll talk gameplay. Almost every time I die, it feels as if it was my own fault. The only times it felt unfair were either very coincidental pairs of attacks, or RNG would ♥♥♥♥ me in tne wrong spot. No two bosses felt the same, and I can't think of a single one I disliked. However, while I might have no shortage of praise, I still have a list of cons, and I'll sum it up in a list.
PROS
-Fantastic art and music, it pays homage to countless animations from the 30s and 40s. It's fantastic and works so well because we've never seen it much in gaming, but countless times in old animation. Therefor, it feels so new, yet so familiar. I simply can't go on enough about it, so I'll continue
-Difficulty. No beating around it, this game is hard. So ♥♥♥♥ing hard. The type of hard that ♥♥♥♥s you in the♥♥♥♥♥and rips open your stomach. However, it is fair, at least 95% of the time, but I'll talk about that. Every attack has a tell, and every attack can manuevered through perfectly with practice. The only times it's unfair is when two non complementary attacks go together thanks to RNG. Again, I'll talk about that. The difficulty will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ but it's almost always fair, and the feeling of beating every level or boss is something indescribable.
-Story. This isn't the Citizen Cane of gaming stories, and that's what makes it so great. The story is simply that Cuphead and Mughead go to the Devil's Casino, and start betting. They are doing fantastic when the Devil himself walks into the frame. He explains that they can roll one more time. If they win, all the loot in the casino is theirs. However, if they fail, the Devil will take their souls. Cuphead, blinded by riches, goes for one more role. They end up losing because, well, it's the Devil, and the boys beg for their lives. The Devil makes a compromise, if the boys collect the souls of every other runaway debtor to the Devil before midnight the next day, he will spare them. The story is so simplistic, annd yet still interesting and fun, as it is a new concept. It isn't an overdone damsel in distress or saving the world, it's a story about two characters facing real consequences for their actions. This game certaintly should not have a deep plot or story, because it would not go well with how the rest of the game is made, and therefor detract from the experience. Overall, the simplistic perfectly complements everything else.
-Grading & Progress system. The way the game grades you based on HP, parrys, and skill encourages the player to try and push themselves to do better. Similarly, there are no health bars when fighting bosses. However, whenever you die, it shows you how far you made it to the end, while a message from the boss itself lingers atop the screen, usually mocking you in one way or another. The progress bar will always give you that feeling of either how much there is left to do, and that you want to see all the other phases, or that feeling of "I was so close, but I got it this time". It's genius, and keeps the player playing.
-Run'n Gun levels. For the most part, these levels aren't anything special on there own. In fact, very few stand out as being creative to me. However, simply, they provide much needed relief and variety from the normal boss rush gameplay.
I could continue going on and on with the endless praise I could give this game, such as all the different weapons, supers, charms, and even how each boss is so intricate, creative, hard, fair, and fun. However, I'm gettinmg tired of writing, so let's move on.
CONS
-RNG. The system itself isn't bad for most bosses or levels, but there are a few moments where I call rightful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Best example, genie fight. The very first phase can go down in three ways, all dependant on RNG. It can be either painfully easy, moderate, or borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. See, the very first phase, the genie has one attack. Well, three attacks, but he only choses one for each attack. One of which are these swords that are painfully easy to dodge, making the fight a pushover. The second possibility are these homing sphinx cats, which are somewhat hard to dodge, but still moderate. However, if he chooses the only other possibility, consider your fight over. He opens his chest, and a complete bullet hell of random items take any space on the screen by storm. However, unlike any other bullethell section in this game, there is absolutely no decernable pattern of the items, and at times they will appear out of the blue even after the phase is over. Had each possibility been similar difficulty, this wouldn't be a problem. However, since each different possibilty is so different in terms of difficulty, I've found myself restarting the fight if I got the wrong outcome. This is the only fight where it's this big of a problem, but I have a smaller example. In the Beppie the clown fight, the third phase can be a problem thanks to the coaster. Whenever the donkey shoots out the yellow magnets, depending on when the coaster comes, it can be impossible not to take a hit. Before the magnets reach the top of the screen, there is a short period of time where if you jump at all, you will take damage. If the coaster is coming during this time, you have no choice but to get hit. This is my biggest problem with this game, especially since one of it's biggest selling points is being tough but fair.
-Length. The game is worth it through it's duration, but the only thing making this game somewhat long is it's difficulty. If you beat every boss and level perfectly, this game could be completed in about 40 minutes. Again, it is more than worth it, but I can find it bogging down the expierence.
I have many more cons, but they are all so minor, such as some OP charms, and a strange flow of difficulty through some sections of the game. However, the two listed cons are the only ones I felt were worth listing.
However, no flaw can detract from how much I love this game. Even with it's difficulty, Cuphead is addictingly fun, and accesible to so many audiences, unlike games such as Souls (I know, comparing it to Souls yet again), for each level is so short that starting from the beginning is hardly a problem, and the enjoyment adds to it. Of course, the art and music more than anything make it stand out from any other game like it, and that's why I think it's so popular. But Cuphead deserves every bit of praise and popularity it gets. Overall, the game is fantastic, and despite its flaws, I would recommend this game for 30 dollars, and I think everyone needs to at least try it out. I hate number scores, so I won't be giving it one.

=[Heads Up]=
[This review is about a game in early access. The game might not be finished yet but it is already worth the money and the time.]
[This review is about my own point of view. If you should disagree or find it not helpfull, feel free to do the most obivous. Or write a comment down below.]
=[Review]=
First of all, I am just happy to say that this game actually got onto steam. Being on Greenlight for a while just after the succesfull kickstarter campaign, I was hoping for it to come on here. Which brings me to my first and probably most important point.
- Is the game good and enjoyable at its current state?
To answer that question I must tell you this: I got this game before it hit steam. It was the first ever time that I backed a game on kickstarter and I didnt regret it one bit. Granted, this was quite some time ago but back then it was already worth the money I had spent for it. And now, with all the updates and improvements it is even better. Overall the game works well and flows well. You can have a really peaceful experience to gather experience or jump into a world filled with monsters. Either way, your settlers have to survive and build up their settlement/village/city.
The cute style of the game is honestly something that I just had to have. The overall style alone, the animations that are well done. The ideas within the animations and how they interact with other animations as the little Hearthlings interact with each other. All ties in well and makes up for a rather enjoyable experience.
- "But this game is quite old now. 2 years after all. And its still in early access?"
While I usually agree with this point, the team itself wasnt very big at the start. They slowly but surely were able to hire more people and actually kept everyone up to date via their youtube channel with the updates and ideas for future builds. Not only that. The devs are working together with the community as close as they can. They use their forums frequently and look for comments on youtube. Any bit of criticism and feedback is welcomed with open arms. I once reported a bug which made the game unplayable for many others as well. Overall the bug was about a gamestutter which made the game stutter so much when trying to do anything, that you couldnt play it at all. I reported it on the same day and not even 20 minutes after that, we got a patch with a fix.
So what can you expect so far into the game?
Well in my old review it was still simple. Mining, Crafting, Fighting and Farming. While those keyelements are still part of the game, you have the ability to do so much more now. From an entire party of fighters that patrol the area and keep your village safe to a simple smith, being able to make gold only for you to sell it for a bit of gold so you can buy other things. There is a lot more to see in the game and therefor I will not spoil it for you. Its much more fun for you, if you see it yourself.
What about building stuff?
Building before was a hassle and only improved till now. Before, building was a problem to be dealt with. While you could easily build your own houses and use templates, it wasnt the best system and easily bugged out to a point of your savefile corrupting.
This has changed. Changed to a point where you can build entire cities in the blink of an eye without it destroying your savefile in the slightest. And its fast.
Oh and did I mention that the game already has full on modsupport already? It may seem like a red flag to you, but the devs arent just resting on it, to take the idea and implement it themself. They keep on going strong on their own ideas and let the community have fun while its going forward.
Overall, I love this game and I couldnt love it more. I love it so much that I even rewrote this review of mine. And I hope that I encouraged some of you to get this game as well. Or at least to look out for its future.

It was my first experience with Artifex Mundi's games and I was so hooked that I'm buying any game from them once on Steam.
Nightmares from the Deep puts you in the shoes of Sarah Black, a museum curator in the Caraïbean Islands, and interested in the pirates stories. After receiving the corpse of the famous Henry Remington, don't ask how but you awakened him. Taking your daughter as hostage, you sneak into his ghost ship and find yourself in a race against the clock to save your child.
The story is beautiful as you're also diving into the pirate's past and love story. Besides, Remington is cursed because of a pact with Davy Jones, only you can undo it. And Davy Jones is important for the trilogy anyway.
The gameplay mixes point-&-click, puzzles and hidden objects scenes. It's well balanced: all the puzzles aren't too hard but are not too easy (though one or two of them could be seen as harder to understand). I didn't find anything wrong or buggy.
The graphics are correct but beautiful too as between the boat and the island, you have also that surnatural aura surronding you. As for the soundtrack, nothing bad can be said.
Also, you have a bonus chapter, showing how you rescued another poor soul on your way home.
A well-constructed plot, a nice ambiance, a balance for the difficulty, you have everything in this hidden object game. Never hesitate for this one!

While this game is not outstanding in the point and click genre, it's certainly not bad either. To sum it up, this is way I liked or disliked about the game.
Pros:
- Great art style, fits the gloomy setting of the game
- Well made soundtrack, setting an adequate mood.
- While the synch is not exactly perfect, the voice acting is good.
Cons:
- Hidden Object scenes are entirely random. You search for 20 objects, one of which you are actually looking for, the rest dissapears forever.
- Item Usage often doesn't make sense. At one point you need a stone to smash a window even though you have an iron wrench in your inventory.
- The quality of cutscenes is horrible. This may just be an issue I had, so I don't know if it's the same for everyone.
- Most items that you use are immediatly discarded forever even though you would need them later. Instead you have to search for a similar item all over again.
To put it in a nutshell, I miss the logic aproach that most point and click games should use. If you need a certain item for a situation, you should usually be able to figure out which one on your own. Also, If I have to find a total of 3 scalpels to use in 3 different situations, I'm beginning to question if my character instantly annihalites every item that has served it's purpose once as a personal one-use policy. However, the game can still hold it's own with it's art style and soundtrack, which is easily good enough to create the atmosphere required for the game.

...and here we have another Artifex Mundi caliber HOG. I've been meaning to play this game for ages now. Finally being able to find the time, I'm rushing here to give you my full review.
is one of Artifex Mundi's earlier games, thus it is quite possible to encounter amateur mistakes or some clumsy animations now and then. Yet, the charm attached to the developer’s name doesn't fail to entertain us anyway.
Here we have Sarah Black, the curator of the Caribbean Museum and the mother of one cheery teenage girl, preparing the exhibition of a life time. The mummified corpse of Henry Remington, most notorious pirate of the Caribbean Sea back in 1800s is finally discovered and retrieved from his resting place: "Davy Jones' Locker" a.k.a the bottom of the sea. The corpse is delivered to the museum for the exhibition, and Sarah prepares him to be displayed. Just as we were thinking that he seems kinda handsome for a corpse that's been lying at the bottom of the sea for some centuries, he comes back to life, kidnaps our daughter, summons his ghost ship and sets sail to Skull Island... Oh, where did I see that before?
Okay, okay, I'll say it. I have no idea about the rest of the series yet, but this first game is basically a retelling of
without Captain Jack Sparrow to lighten up the mood. But as the first instalment of the
series - and possibly the most clumsily done -
still finds means to keep you interested, with a detailed story of its own, weaved out of countless nautical folktales. Hey, I'm glad that we have a name for the protagonist at least, contrary to "Madame Detective" of
.
Artwork is most brilliant with its eerie depictions, nautical themes and an expected amount of undead roaming around. At this point, no one expects Artifex Mundi to present bad artwork, even with its older titles. What I do wonder though, is that how they've managed to make cinematics in lower quality than actual game artwork. Cinematics are blurry and less presentable compared to actual in-game artworks. Same goes for the voice acting: voice acting itself is beyond par, but the lip synch is non-existent: people do move their mouths rhythmically, that's all. I think this is forgivable considering that this is an older title though.
Here comes the gameplay: we have quite enjoyable and clear HOG scenes, some FROG scenes, a good amount of enjoyable puzzles and alternative Mahjong games if you are bored of object hunting. It takes at least 2 playthroughs to complete all achievements - one for HOGs, one for Mahjong games. The map is not interactive, but you get used to the environment quickly, and there is little backtracking aside going back to the ship to place a Dubloon on a chest and listen to an undead dwarf tell a story now and then. What's that about? You gotta play the game to learn!
is probably not Artifex Mundi's best game, but it is a promising title and the start of a possibly enjoyable journey on a series. If you'd manage to grab it on sale, you'd enjoy it thoroughly when you'd be in the mood for a pleasant little HOG.

I must say, I haven't completed a lot of HOG games. Three, if I recall. So, due to that fact, I can't really rely on past experience in order to review a game of this genre. But still, I can identify one that is of higher quality, and that title is Nightmares of the Deep: The Cursed Heart. I've also come to know that Artifex Mundi's games (most of them) are actually pretty good, overall. And that's exactly what I can say for the first entry in Nightmares of the Deep (NotD). It is a pretty good HOG.
Originality reigns in this title. And I love it. You'll find numerous puzzles, and all of them are different in such a way that it amuses me. Just like in all HOG's, you complete these puzzles in order to receive an item, unlock an object, etc etc. Completing this certain task will lead you to another, and another, and another, until you reach a critical point in the game and achieve some objective you were trying to accomplish. Same with HOG scenes. There is, however, a twist in this part of NotD. You can skip the entire section that consists in finding, or assembling hidden objects, and replace it with a mahjong game. I've found this feature entertaining and distinguishes this HOG from others out there.
Graphics wise, the scenarios are pleasant to look at. A negative aspect might be considered as the cutscenes, which are of lower resolution. Same with character animations, and the horrible lip sync, that are clunky and not really believable, which is obviously not the point of an HOG, to look realistic, but I'm sure they could have done a better job in this department.
Looking at the story, it's actually a strong point in NotD. I won't spoil it, of course, but I can say it's pretty interesting. I also enjoyed the fact that some storytelling is told through ghosts scattered around the different scenes. And I must indeed admit, pirates plus HOG equals and awesome combination. The soundtrack is catchy and it looks like we're searching for Jack Sparrow or something related. Achievements add replayability and a "bonus chapter" that could have been totally implemented into the main game is always compelling, I guess.

Let's be clear: The core gameplay here is very fun, there is a wide variety of skill trees and character types, the humor is spot on, and the academy building between-characters metagame is well implemented and feels rewarding. Enemy types are varied, and many have abilities that move themselves or you across the battlefield to keep things fresh. And honestly it works well as a roguelike.
I really, really want to recommend this game.
But I can't in good conscience, because it feels half-finished, like an early access game. And the developers show no signs they want to fix anything.
First off, there's bugs all over the place. Both big and small, including some that wreck people's save files. There's also lots of stuff (especially in the late game) that is missing its description because they never got around to it.
Game balance is also wonky. The defensive stats do practically nothing for your defense early on but makes you virtually invincible at high levels, except against a few specific enemies with specific spells. Some skills do virtually nothing but act as as stepping stones to more important skills, or are hideously weak compared to skills that are available earlier. You can tell at a glance that some character perks are stronger than others. The graveyard dungeons have way too high a loot-to-risk ratio. Many bosses are pushovers, except the final boss who has an instant-kill attack (yes, in a roguelike). And the holy/dark elements are given tons of weight in the random item abilities but are virtually absent except in the final dungeon (where everyone's dark).
So overall, this game is very fun but has massive flaws. I just can't give it a positive review when it's this obviously unfinished.

I've been following this game ever since its Kickstarter campaign. It had a bit of a rocky start, but as time went by we backers received a nice series of very interesting updates, fixing bugs and adding new features.
Right now the game is still in Early Access, mind that. It still lacks many stuff and bugs are prone to lurk around. Having said that, this what you can play here is a beautiful experience with tons of potential. Think of it as a kind of Dwarf Fortress, but with nice (cute, even) Voxel graphics and a much, much, much kinder difficulty curve. You will begin each new game with a group of settlers, and from there on you must help them survive. Gather raw materials. Craft items. Grow plants. Build your town. Survive.
One VERY interesting feature of the game is the building system, which allows you to design your own buildings, letting your settlers do the whole construction stuff. Of course, be aware that larger building will take longer to build (as well as require more materials).
Perhaps the current price is a bit steep, but if you like this kind of game (Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria) then StoneHearth might be just what you were looking for.

Brief: It would be good if it weren't so bad. Be ready for bad people, bad interfaces, and countless bad deaths (at the hands of both teammates and enemies).
They say the community is nice and helpful, but apparently "nice" means they shoot you for no reason and "helpful" means they yell "noob" at you and everyone else. The grind is... really wonky. One can get several new ships within a few battles  and apparently nothing really affects one's rewards from battle. So, even if you just get blown up with no idea what you're doing (which I did when I was starting out) you'll still have a full set of ships within minutes... if you can figure out how to get them, as the interface is strange and gives few to no hints about how to use it. Is that an icon or a button? Better check it all! The grind shows up after those few, but is more of what I'd expect from an early game experience for about one tier, then goes immediately into "Just imagine what that tier 5/tier 6 ship will be like when you get it next week!" I imagine the T10 users have been playing since before the game was released and just acquired them. Oh, and the "report a player" button on their site did nothing until I tried another browser, at which point I got an "Under Construction" popup. Their "Contact GM" area was apparently locked off because of some email verification thing. I couldn't be bothered... I figure any game attempting to be half-decent will not only have player reporting available but have it easily accessed in-game.
Oh, and people don't seem to care to play as any sort of team. Typically several ships will be found faffing about, maybe fully capping some base or just napping in a corner while everyone else dies. Apparently people will actually grind by capping something and then suiciding. I even saw a carrier torpedo bomb itself to do this.

One of my favourite games, Aquaria is just beautiful in every sense. The protagonist is easy to engage with, the maps are all beautifully crafted and the lack of specific directions on where to go simply makes Naija's isolation even more poignant rather than becoming mechanically frustrating.

In Aquaria, you play as a Mermaid who has amnesia/discovers her past/explores deep and mysterious waters. The first thing you need to know about Aquaria is that it was made by two guys whose lifelong dream was to make a great game. The second thing you need to know is that it is an absolutely beautiful, wonderful, intelligent, amazing game that is a legitimate contender for my pick as the best game of all time, even though it has a lot of things that I usually hate in video games [no multiplayer, little direction given to players, slow access to game content]. What Aquaria gives you more than any other game to date is the chance to discover
about the world. It demands that you be clever and observant about the world around you, but unlike many similar games, it's carefully crafted to give you the tools and chances to be clever in great ways. You're given a beautiful world, and everything about it is intelligent and engaging. That's what makes this game great. Buy it.

I had walked for a long time when I stumbled onto the cabin. It was far away still, but it made me renew my efforts. The snow was coming down heavy, like icy, suffocating feathers, and the cold wind cut me, almost physically. I was shaking by the time I arrived at the cabin, and by then, I barely knew what I was doing. I broke the window of the cabin door with my bare hand, cutting myself badly, as I couldn't think for long enough to get the door open any other way. I stumbled in and shut the door, cutting most of the deadly wind outside. Dusk was fast approaching, and it was hard to see the interior. The first floor was bare of supplies. Someone had been here already. I could see empty tin cans lay strewn on the rough wooden floor, and my initial hope took a tumble. I checked the fireplace, but there was nothing but ashes. Walking upstairs on shaky feet, I saw someone sit by a fireplace, next to a bed. I froze, but managed to call out a greeting a voice broken with the cold. I got no answer. It was a dead man sitting there, with an empty can of tuna. I sat down next to him and closed my eyes as the shakes started again. It would soon be dark.

TL;DR
A great Village building game with mechanics similar to Minecraft, Banished and Dwarf Fortress. Well worth the money asked. Developers are HEAVILY involved in development and community relations, along with consistant and crisp graphics.The community of Stonehearth show how amazing this game is, and how much potential the developers have.
---------
Where do I start on this brilliant game? I've been watching this EA game since Alpha 2, and have finally decided to buy it. There are hundreds of pros and minimal cons. It is well worth the money asked for (you could wait until the summer sales heil gabeN) Or you can spend it right now!
Pros:
- The Developers
The developers are heavily community focused, implenting features people think would suit the game, as well as fixing game breaking bugs that are encountered. They do frequent updates (Around one every few weeks) and keep the community informed with "Desktop Tuesdays" where they show off new features being implented
- Beutiful Graphics
I don't often judge a game by it's graphics. But this is an amazing exception. The graphics are smooth, clear, and crisp, it often reminds me of Minecraft (minus the 16 bit textures) due to its simplicity. The graphics are consistent, and don't randomly change with updates.
- The Community
The community is very well knit, and are welcoming of new players. You can often find them helping new players settle in to the world of Stonehearth, and help solve problems with bug fixes.
Cons
- Crashes
Like most EA games, there are lots of crashes, there are a few crashes here and there, but if you remembered to save, you're in luck, they've recently added an autosave feature, which is absolutely brilliant, to make up for these crashes. They can be often caused by new features (the 64 bit update)
- Steep learning curve
Like Banished, it's going to take A LOT of tries to hit the ground running, but after learning why and where you went wrong, it gets a lot easier (my current "village" is on 40 hearthlings) and eventually you will end up with a small town.
- AI
The AI in this game can be, at times, tedious, often when you mark a place to be deforested, they cut it down, but refuse to transport it to a stockpile (knowing me this will be the problem on my end), but eventually they get around to it.
CONCLUSION
I believe that this game has a HUGE potential, and that the developers are prime examples of what should be the norm in the game industry (I'm looking at you EA) The community is one of the huge aspects of this game, there is some mod support, but sadly most are either broken or outdated. This game is well worth the £19 asked, with many features still to come.

An innovative take on the rogue-like, Dungeonmans had me hooked for the first few hours that I played it.  The class and leveling system, though simple, was enjoyable.  The randomly generated world was a great feature for replayability and the legacy system capped it off with an academy that gets upgraded by your heroes exploits and offers perks to future heroes after your each one dies.  Unfortunately, the game seemed to quickly lose its luster when I realized that the difficulty seems quite easy for a legacy rogue-like.
The game begins with your character graduating from your academy.  You will select their stat package from several randomly generated ones and then choose your class.  From this point on, you'll adventure through a procedurally generated world that is done decently well, though it could use a bit more variety throughout.  Acquiring special items will improve your academy and the benefits that it offers to your future graduates are exciting to unlock as is finding stolen goods that you can return to a town of your choice to boost their prosperity.  This will in turn make that town have a more effective stock of items that are sold at cheaper prices.
In theory, this all adds up to a great game.  That changes quickly, however, once you realize that the game is fairly easy, especially when you consider that as a legacy rogue-like, a large part of its charm is death and moving on to your next hero.  With this foundation a bit shaky, the game's excitement waned rather quickly as the variety for a single hero seemed to be lacking.  I've now played multiple hours on the same character and, whenever a true threat revealed itself, I was either able to escape or outsmart it rather easily without ever being at risk of death.
If Dungeonmans were in Early Access, I would give it a positive review as it lacks enough content to keep me playing on a single player and also the difficulty to facilitate me moving through the generations of my academy.  However, it does have a very strong foundation if the developer were to continue adding content and it has peaked my interest enough that I will be coming back to try the game again in the future and will change my review accordingly if it improves.  However, I currently do not recommend this game if only due to the fact that Dungeons of Dredmor is a superior game in the RPG rogue-like category and Rogue Legacy is a strong platformer/RPG rogue-like with an impressive legacy system.

However, while I might have no shortage of praise, I still have a list of cons, and I'll sum it up in a list.
PROS
-Fantastic art and music, it pays homage to countless animations from the 30s and 40s. It's fantastic and works so well because we've never seen it much in gaming, but countless times in old animation. Therefor, it feels so new, yet so familiar. I simply can't go on enough about it, so I'll continue
-Difficulty. No beating around it, this game is hard. So ♥♥♥♥ing hard. The type of hard that ♥♥♥♥s you in the♥♥♥♥♥and rips open your stomach. However, it is fair, at least 95% of the time, but I'll talk about that. Every attack has a tell, and every attack can manuevered through perfectly with practice. The only times it's unfair is when two non complementary attacks go together thanks to RNG. Again, I'll talk about that. The difficulty will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ but it's almost always fair, and the feeling of beating every level or boss is something indescribable.
-Story. This isn't the Citizen Cane of gaming stories, and that's what makes it so great. The story is simply that Cuphead and Mughead go to the Devil's Casino, and start betting. They are doing fantastic when the Devil himself walks into the frame. He explains that they can roll one more time. If they win, all the loot in the casino is theirs. However, if they fail, the Devil will take their souls. Cuphead, blinded by riches, goes for one more role. They end up losing because, well, it's the Devil, and the boys beg for their lives. The Devil makes a compromise, if the boys collect the souls of every other runaway debtor to the Devil before midnight the next day, he will spare them. The story is so simplistic, annd yet still interesting and fun, as it is a new concept. It isn't an overdone damsel in distress or saving the world, it's a story about two characters facing real consequences for their actions. This game certaintly should not have a deep plot or story, because it would not go well with how the rest of the game is made, and therefor detract from the experience. Overall, the simplistic perfectly complements everything else.
-Grading & Progress system. The way the game grades you based on HP, parrys, and skill encourages the player to try and push themselves to do better. Similarly, there are no health bars when fighting bosses. However, whenever you die, it shows you how far you made it to the end, while a message from the boss itself lingers atop the screen, usually mocking you in one way or another. The progress bar will always give you that feeling of either how much there is left to do, and that you want to see all the other phases, or that feeling of "I was so close, but I got it this time". It's genius, and keeps the player playing.
-Run'n Gun levels. For the most part, these levels aren't anything special on there own. In fact, very few stand out as being creative to me. However, simply, they provide much needed relief and variety from the normal boss rush gameplay.
I could continue going on and on with the endless praise I could give this game, such as all the different weapons, supers, charms, and even how each boss is so intricate, creative, hard, fair, and fun. However, I'm gettinmg tired of writing, so let's move on.
CONS
-RNG. The system itself isn't bad for most bosses or levels, but there are a few moments where I call rightful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Best example, genie fight. The very first phase can go down in three ways, all dependant on RNG. It can be either painfully easy, moderate, or borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. See, the very first phase, the genie has one attack. Well, three attacks, but he only choses one for each attack. One of which are these swords that are painfully easy to dodge, making the fight a pushover. The second possibility are these homing sphinx cats, which are somewhat hard to dodge, but still moderate. However, if he chooses the only other possibility, consider your fight over. He opens his chest, and a complete bullet hell of random items take any space on the screen by storm. However, unlike any other bullethell section in this game, there is absolutely no decernable pattern of the items, and at times they will appear out of the blue even after the phase is over. Had each possibility been similar difficulty, this wouldn't be a problem. However, since each different possibilty is so different in terms of difficulty, I've found myself restarting the fight if I got the wrong outcome. This is the only fight where it's this big of a problem, but I have a smaller example. In the Beppie the clown fight, the third phase can be a problem thanks to the coaster. Whenever the donkey shoots out the yellow magnets, depending on when the coaster comes, it can be impossible not to take a hit. Before the magnets reach the top of the screen, there is a short period of time where if you jump at all, you will take damage. If the coaster is coming during this time, you have no choice but to get hit. This is my biggest problem with this game, especially since one of it's biggest selling points is being tough but fair.
-Length. The game is worth it through it's duration, but the only thing making this game somewhat long is it's difficulty. If you beat every boss and level perfectly, this game could be completed in about 40 minutes. Again, it is more than worth it, but I can find it bogging down the expierence.
I have many more cons, but they are all so minor, such as some OP charms, and a strange flow of difficulty through some sections of the game. However, the two listed cons are the only ones I felt were worth listing.
However, no flaw can detract from how much I love this game. Even with it's difficulty, Cuphead is addictingly fun, and accesible to so many audiences, unlike games such as Souls (I know, comparing it to Souls yet again), for each level is so short that starting from the beginning is hardly a problem, and the enjoyment adds to it. Of course, the art and music more than anything make it stand out from any other game like it, and that's why I think it's so popular. But Cuphead deserves every bit of praise and popularity it gets. Overall, the game is fantastic, and despite its flaws, I would recommend this game for 30 dollars, and I think everyone needs to at least try it out. I hate number scores, so I won't be giving it one.

Sometimes this difficulty is artificial though, as the game tends to have issues recognising mouse clicks, but this is still just an inconvenience next to the real problem: backtracking. Even with easy mode and a quick travel map, the required amount of backtracking is so ridiculous that it takes easily half of the otherwise substantial playtime.
Unlike in the first game, we only have one demoness to tackle: a succubus. Predictably, she kidnaps our protagonist’s rather dorky boyfriend, so the entire plot is about her trying to get the guy back, but to fill the game with some actual story, we also need to help four pairs of deceased lovers. It is all incredibly cheesy with somewhat amateurish voice acting, but the package is still delightfully charming as a whole.

I did a hidden object scene and when I got the object, I was able to click the scene and somehow go into it again, only with different items (it reuses the same art for some HOGs which is fine).  I got the second object, The game then said I could remove a stone, which was supposed to initiate the second version of the HOS.  I did so, the HOS glimmer reappeared, only when I clicked on it, it launched into a glitched version of a HOS where it loaded up the HOG scene, but no item list came up.  When I click on the map, to hopefully teleport away, it shows I'm nowhere on it, and I can't click any of the locations to get me out of it.  So, I am essentially stuck in the HOS, the hint button doesn't work, the map doesn't work, and I can't exit out of it.
I've played some great Hidden Object Games on Steam, and some bad ones.  Never have I run into one where it was coded so badly, I couldn't actually finish it.

Like going to the finest restaurant in town and finding your water is served in styrofoam cups, the flaws in this game do make you roll your eyes, but always over something that doesn't really matter. The core naval combat game seriously rocks. Zaggat rated 5 stars.
Battles are 15 minutes long, if you survive that long or decide to stick around and watch the end after you are sunk. Ship on ship combat is nearly perfect, though the boats move a bit too fast for my taste, but you do get used to that. Graphics are nice except for anything written. They use some font that doesn't work well on my PC. Legible when tweaked, but not great.
The pay-to-win elements are truly kept in check, unlike most games. To me, this speaks volumes about the devs. They actually understand that a well-balanced game will bring in more money. Every P2W element gives a slight advantage, but this game is so heavily skill-based that those slight advantages can be easily overcome by superior skill.
There are 2 main gaming areas: the Battlefield and the Shipyard. The Shipyard is where you get new ships, put equipment on your ship, train your officers, etc. The major flaws in this game have nothing to do with battle. Battle is great. I mean it. Great. The flaws are with peripheral things like: It is hard to register to get the game started, there is no steam overlay (at least for some users currently), when I started the game, I couldn't read anything. Their FAQ page said to make your GUI bigger in Game Options if you can't read the font. The real solution was to turn down my screen resolution one level. Everywhere you look in the Shipyard will be phrases that were obviously translated into English by a computer translator, and then never proofread by a person who actually speaks English. Much of the instructions are tragically non-sensical. Fortunately the wiki is getting bigger everyday, and the forums and guides are good. And players in chat are helpful (which is another nice change of pace). So the Shipyard can be a bit difficult to figure out, but nothing there is real-time. You can always stop and ask for help when confused in the Shipyard. But that's it for flaws. Minor flaws that make you roll your eyes, but nothing that affects the core gaming experience, which is happily rock solid.
Lots of newbies think this game is too hard, but it's usually because they don't understand that their small fast low-level ships can get to the enemies' big ships quicker than their own big ships can get there. Then they try to fight the big enemies without the back-up of their own big ships who won't arrive for another minute. This is a thinking-person's game. This game relies on understanding your role in a complex team, which few people seem to get. Then they complain that matches are made that put them up against top tier ships. Well guess what? You have the option to run away! Just at the start of battle, look to see the names of the players in high tier ships and avoid them, noob! It is a fun challenge if you don't play it like a boxing match where if you see an enemy you attack without thinking! There are things for low level players to do besides fight, like capture npc bases to give your team an airfield or something. Sheesh!

Dungeonmans is a neat game where you play as an adventurer, explore the realm, likely die horribly, and then - you start a new adventurer in the same world!
No, wait, don't go, this is still a rogue-like! You'll find that the dungeons you explored initially will all be procedurally randomized again!
Whoo, okay, so! -
Dungeonmans is essentially a Rogue-like with a persistent world. You essentially make a seed for a randomly seeded world map, and then spawn your character into it from the Dungeonmans Academy (more on this later). From there you venture out into the world clobbering enemies and likely eventually getting clobbered yourself! When you die, your remains will remain in the level of the world where you died (unless you get to a high enough level, in which case something else happens); and you will have to make a new character to spawn into the world with.
Spawning into the world again, you will find that the world map is the same, though there will be some negative effects from your last characters death. Bandits will have set upon the roads and towns, and towns you invested in on prior run(s), dungeons you visited will be randomized to feature new layouts to re-explore, and the remains of your prior adventurer will be around to collect loot and experience from.
And that pretty much sums up what this game is all about above. But there is more - and unfortunately, not all that good....
Essentially, if your character gets to a specific level, you can retire your character. Retiring your character you might go and opening an inn, go back to teach further recruits of the dungeonmans academy some learned tricks from your retired character, or just go about wandering.
The key problem here though is that is leads to a situation where you'll be doing unfun things like 'farming' characters to level 10 to retire so that you can essentially make better and better dungeonman characters to do things with.
Now, as a note, this game does now have an Ironmans mode as of this review, but playing on a single run will have a very generic rogue-like experience that gets away from what the gameplay of dungeomans is really all about - a persistent world.
This is one of the odd rogue-likes that I both 'recommend' but give a wary warning about. It is a really interesting example of a rogue-like because it has that persistent world concept, and it is worth experiencing because it is really neat.
However, because of the farming factor present, this is also a game I would suggest avoiding if you want a game you could really sink your teeth into and enjoy

When I took a screenshot of Stonehearth, and shared it with my friend, the first thing he asked was "Is that a Minecraft clone?"
Seriously, no. If you think a complex city building and management game is a clone of Minecraft, you need to really get a reality check, bud.
Anyway, moving on to the actual review. First, you should know that I've been playing Stonehearth since the pre-alpha days, and that this review is for Alpha 10.5. I'm also basing this only on the content that is currently available, and not promised stuff due out later in development. Though, I'm personally looking forward to PvP combat, which is going to be a feature later on.
SOUND
Sound design is average, and everything you'd expect to be there, is there. You've got grunts, a catchy (if not a tad repetitive) soundtrack, and all the other standard musical cues you'd expect from a video game.
-7/10
GAMEPLAY
You've got the foundations of a pretty awesome city building game, though there's a clear lack of content as of this writing. The core city building aspect is most definitely there, and you're able to build custom structures, mine for resources, and even fight invading monsters. I've yet to actually figure out what happens if you lose all of your guys to a city invasion, and the enemies don't seem to do much other than invade, and rush you with numbers. But at the very least, it's the start of something major. You're also able to create squads to better fend off enemy invasion, and the city building animations are fascinating. I found myself building random structures just to see how my little minions (yes, that's what I call them) would construct it.
-9/10
FEATURES
Unfortunately, the game is currently lacking in the feature department. While the actual gameplay is polished beyond what you'd expect for an Early Access game, it isn't without its faults. For starters, there is very little in the way of configuration. There's no graphic slider, or volume control. This is really just a core experience right now, and you know what? I'm oddly okay with that. This is just an alpha after all. Things will improve.
-8/10
CONCLUSION
All in all, Stonehearth offers a very solid city building experience. Considering as how this is only just in alpha, Stonehearth feels like a finished product. It has polish, it has style. It's just an all around fun experience. Sure, there's a fair number of bugs, though none of them are game breaking, at least in my testing. This is an alpha, so a bug or two is expected. But the fact that Stonehearth plays and feels like a finished product? Well, that's just darn amazing.
So yes, I recommend Stonehearth.
Final rating?
8.5/10.
(note: this review was for alpha version 10.5)

Sadly a game that has too many issues (and isn't polished enough) to be recommended.
The presentation isn't that bad, but you can see that the game is a bit older. The cutscenes are rendered okay-ish and the 3D models do look pretty dated. The main issue here is that the subtitles are horribly de-synced. Voice actors are okay and the music for the most part is very good.
There's a good amount of interesting minigames and while the hidden object scenes look nice, the hit boxes are awfully off. Since this is a big part of the game it really gets annoying. While this is bad the worst part is that some item based puzzles suffer from the same problem and especially one puzzle is nearly not completable as you have to click quite far from the item to pick it up.
I really enjoyed the story and atmosphere of the main game (the bonus chapter is the usual nonsensical excuse to throw some more minigames and hidden object puzzles into the game), but the technical issues really don't warrant the asking price. In a bundle or for a serious discount you might be able to overlook the problems and enjoy the game.

First of all this game is pretty old as it's been out since 2013, so I'm not going to compare it to any new hidden object game. It could be even better than any new ones which tend to be quite repetitive, this game does have a variety of puzzles, going from the easy ones to the extremely hard puzzles which took me almost 45 minutes to solve it.
The story caught my attention from the first moment. Two lovers were having a romantic dinner where he was planning to propose to his girlfriend but an unfortunate event stopped the proposal. A rather beautiful succubus showed up and ruined everything.
But of course no woman would ever let another woman steal her boyfriend, our protagonist will try to find her man no matter what. The theme of the game is all about true love. You will travel through the time and find tragic stories about two lovers. I liked the first two stories, but the last three were OK.
pros:
+Interesting story with a good twist.
+Beautiful graphics, the art of some of the scenes are great and detailed even though the game is old. but Alawar Entertainment are known for their amazing visuals.
+Fitting music.
+Fast traveling map.
+Good voice acting, not all of the characters though, but they did a good job so far.
+Very useful journal.
+Challenging puzzles and hidden objects scenes, they are not very easy and well hidden.
+Good game length.
+Easy achievements. (You get five of them once you finish the bonus chapter if you didn't use hint or skip puzzles/hidden objects scenes)
+Steam achievements.
Cons:
-Some of the hidden objects scenes were hard to click even though you know this is the item, it takes a while for the object to respond and be clicked, I think the area of the object is narrow or something.
-No replay value.
The bonus chapter is quite long, the whole game took me almost 7 hours to finish it without using any hints, plus one of the puzzle took me a while to solve it. It is as what someone else called it 'puzzle from hell'
I recommend this game to hidden objects lovers, the story alone is good to try it out, but if you know you'll get frustrated from the hidden objects and puzzles, I suggest you try another game.

Another superb entry in the series, and highly recommended for fans of casual point-and-click adventures and hidden-object games.
The game is heavy on adventure puzzles--lots of content--and they are pretty much always fair and satisfying. The hidden-object scenes are excellent, and the few puzzle mini-games are soothing little distractions, though they are usually too easy.
The story is, again, nothing to write home about, but it goes through several locales and feels diverse. The cut scenes are fantastic.
The weak point is the bonus story: unfortunately, though it has gorgeous graphics and adds important dimensions to the story, its puzzles are often obtuse. Also, the voice acting in English is truly awful: just pretend it's not there and you will enjoy the game more. :)
It's also worth mentioning that the game engine is a bit wonky. It seems I needed to click a bit above objects in hidden-object scenes for the click to register. Also, some users have reported bugs, though I'm happy to say that everything ran smoothly for me.

One of the best 2D platformer games I have ever played. Cuphead is a visually beautiful game, the sound and graphic design were expertly drawn to perfectly mimic the art design of 1930s and it is absolutely beautiful. A popular point of critiscm I have seen for this games is it's difficulty, although I do agree that this game could get quite difficult I dont see this as a valid reason to dislike the game, personally I thought that the difficulty only made you more anxious to beat the level and when you defeat the boss (unlike a lot of other 2D platformers) it gives you this great feeling of relief and satisfaction.Even at times when this game is seemingly impossible it still brings a smile to your face to watch the stunning animation. One aspect that I loved about this game was the fact that it wasn't meant to be beaten on your first try and makes the player strategise how to beat the boss, in many cases it is just the weapon which restricts you from defeating the boss. Many games seem to lack one thing which cuphead is thankfully excluded from; replayability, due to the vast variety of weoponry you can choose from, it is fun to try and use different weapons to try your way to defeat a boss over and over again. In retrospect i think Cuphead is one of 2017s best games and very well may just be one of gamings best 2D platformers.

The game has a system where you have to pay for engine wear, tyre wear, and fuel. They all go down when you drive the car at all. No, not  when you crash; when you DRIVE. You have to pay for these individually. My minimal pay for drifting is even more subtracted now. The heck am I supposed to buy anything at all?
Maybe this is normal in other games? I only fancy games where I am not limited in something like this. Honestly, the first person who thought penalizing your players for playing your game the way it's supposed to was a good idea should have their loved ones beaten. (Because they are probably equally as douchey.) If the developers wanted realism, work on the physics first.
-
The game countersteers the car for you when drifting in a game ABOUT drifting. There is no option to turn this off. There is also no FFB, at all. So yay.
I'm a wheel user. If I wanted the game to take control of my steering and assuming I'm a GTR fanboy who doesn't actually know how to drift, Christ, I can go to NFS 2015 for that.
If you have a good computer and are looking for a game with nice drifting physics and lots of upgrades and tuning, get Forza you madman. At least on that game the developers doesn't hate you and give the chance to earn money.
If you're looking for realism get Assetto Corsa. (But you're reading this so you're probably aren't.)
Positives? I can't really think of any that isn't already done better by another game. Drifting is okay? Graphics look very nice? Again, if you want pretty pictures get Forza.

Should YOU Buy The Long Dark? I have made a short video to help you decide that:
PROS:
- Most unique survival game I have ever played
- Extremely immersive and realistic - makes you truly feel "cold" and alone
- Outstandingly beautiful maps that manage to have very different looking areas
- No tutorial - immediately jump into playing the game
- Interesting cartography system - there is no in-game map, rather you draw your own maps by surveying the area with used charcoal from your fires
- Loads of achievements, difficulty levels, and challenges for the completionists
- 5 chapters of story mode(2 at release said to have 6-10 hours of gameplay) with superb voice acting
CONS:
- $35 may be a bit steep for a lot of people but I think it's well worth it if this is your cup of tea
- Lack of multitasking in the game - feels tedious when you have to sit and stare at a pot of water boiling instead of doing something else productive
- Loot spawn is somewhat random potentially causing you to die quickly if you're not lucky enough to find tools
- Animals have a patrol box making them feel a little unnatural at times
- No jumping! :(
Overall, The Long Dark is an excellent fresh take on the survival genre that you could easily find yourself sinking hundreds of hours into. If you’re the kind of person that enjoys nature and survival, I definitely recommend heading over to Steam or your console to start playing this game immediately!

+ Decent graphics and sound.
Cons:
- Unique mechanics make it difficult to get back into the game after a long break.
- Not too difficult to waste time going in circles, despite the useful map. If you fall through a hole to the level below, you need to replay that whole level (granted this won't happen to most players, I'm especially talented!)
- No option to save multiple checkpoints. Only the latest one is saved.
- So so story.
- NPCs have very limited AI
- A couple of boss fights (including the final one) are very annoying. If you find them as tedious and endless as I did, just check the community guide about how to enable god mode cheat. I found it essential to complete the game.
- Requires an Origin/EA account. Even worse, if you made the mistake (like me) of starting to play the game logged in to Origin, you need to log in again in every subsequent session to get access to your saved game. If you don't care about leaderboards (I don't), just start playing while logged out.
Bottom line: Worth playing for the unique mechanics and cute protagonist, but not without its share of frustrating elements.

First game in a present three game series.
Story: Museum Director Sarah Black is putting together an exhibition surrounding pirates and one pirate captain in particular, Captain Henry Remington.  Unwittingly Sarah triggers 'ancient' magic and revives the cursed Captain.  Captain Remington upon his revival steals Sarah's daughter, Cory.  Of course, Sarah follows and stows away on Captain Remington's summoned "ghost" ship as it sets sail for Captain Remington's island.  As Captain Remington's story unfolds the player discovers his personal history, his cursed 'life' and why he stole Sarah's daughter.  Sarah with the help of a surprising ally convinces Captain Remington that what he wants to do will only cause more tradegy.
Gameplay is basically set up to occur in three distinct arenas, the museum, Remington's ship, and Remington's island.  The tragic tale of Captain Remington is revealed through the various characters (mostly his undead crew, who were cursed when he was, assuming the player talks to them).  Rather reminscent of the 'Pirates of Caribbean' first movie and the tale of 'The Flying Dutchman'.   Captain Remington's entire tale is told by the Guardian of Remington's chest, which contains the collateral of Remington's Davy Jone's bargain, whenever coins are found and given to the Guardian.  Very keeping with the Davy Jones motif and legends.
The puzzles are classic, nothing hard or head scratching.  The game even includes a 'treasure hunt'.  (When I saw the 'treasure' map, it reminded me of 'Treasure Island'.)  There are enough hidden object scenes to keep this a Hidden Object game.  The puzzles and hidden objects scenes are intergrated well enough into the storyline that they do not stand out, which in my opinion is a very good thing.  However, since the gameplay arenas are limited to three areas there is a lot of back and forth movement within the area until everything is completed.  Some may find this annoying but the amount of things needed to be done and accomplished within the area keeps the gameplay moving.

Anyone who has already played an Hidden Object Game by Artifex Mundi, knows that this developer delivers beautifully designed games, which form the best the genre currently has to offer. The first game in the
series does not disappoint and proves to be another fine release from Artifex Mundi. However, the game does show its "age" a little bit: it was actually already released early in 2012, and this shows – it's not as meticuously polished as Artifex Mundi's more recent releases.
Don't take me wrong: I enjoyed playing this game, but I didn't felt "drawn in" as much as by other games from Artifex Mundi. This was mainly due to the voice-acting of the different characters, which proved something of a disappointment. This is a pity, since the story itself is more than interesting and offers  a nice twist on the well-known "Pirates of the Caribbean" theme, although the ending could hardly be more cliché.
Somehow the different elements of the game – point-and-click, hidden object scenes, puzzles and cutscenes – didn't add up for me to something really engrossing. Most of the separate elements are perfectly fine, with the hidden object scenes standing out as beautifully drawn as ever. The puzzles range from very easy to moderately difficult, and add some variety to the gameplay. I was especially pleased to find the option to choose for a game of Mohjang instead of the different hidden object scenes., with the Mohjang games gradually increasing in "difficulty". The music in this kind of games often strikes me as bland, but that's just a matter of personal taste I guess.
As is well-known among collectors of achievements, games by Artifex Mundi offer excellent possibilities to achieve perfect games without too much difficulty. As usual, two playthroughs are needed for this, but both need to be on the same profile in order to let all the achievements unlock. Something to keep in mind, as I made the mistake of starting the second one on a new profile, and playing through it for a third time would be stretching it way too far ;-).
Solid Artifex Mundi product. And dead pirates, yar!

This game has been in my library for about 2 years now, and i have to say, this is best FPS game i have ever played
and here is why.
Pros.
The Audio is amazing, esspecialy the native curses (german/soviet) they say to each other.
Your soldiers scream in agony when shot, even crying and stuff. I really like the ambience when you are behind a teammate and he gets shot and you wittness him getting shot and screaming at the top of his lungs before choking.
Alot of weapons to choose from, attachments are historically accurate.
To unlock an attachment, you need to rank up your weapon to level 25, even though it seems easy for the first 4 levels because you need 3-4 kills for a level, after a while, like level 30-50 it needs anywhere from 10-30 kills for a level.
Never knowing where you are shot from, unless you see the gun flash a milisecond before the gun hits you.
It's so satisfying killing your enemy from a flank being last alive in the flank, them not knowing you are there, the headshot sound is amazing.
The attention  to detail inside of the tanks is amazing. You play the tanks from inside, you can see everything, and when that enemy shell penetrates you, you better be ready to either die or be very lucky, because just 1 shell can damage you tremendously/insta-kill you if you are unlucky.
This game requires teamwork in order to win, between soldiers, the TL(Commander), the Squad Leaders,
ordinary soldiers resupplying machine-gunners for ammo so they can continue to pin down the enemy without having to run back for ammo.
Overall realistic things in the game, you know how in COD and other FPS games with bolt action rifles you shoot 1 bullet and reload, the soldier puts 5 bullets in instead of 1? Well in this game, if you shoot 3 bullets from you Bolt action, the soldier will put in 4 bullets not the whole 5-round clip. You must change your barrel for your LMG after 100-150 shots.
Alot of maps to choose from, currently there are 25-35 diffrent official maps, not counting the numerous workshop maps.
The commander system is way better than in battlefield or any other gme.
Squad leaders have to mark artillery so commander can choose where to rain down hell.
Commanders abilities:
Force respawn- Respawns entire team, people respawn in waves in this game to simulate reinforcements
Recon plane - Marks all enemies on the minimap for all the players
3 Artillery strikes
Mortar for  small radius nonstop artillery
Large artillery for a medium area
Rockets for a wide area to kill nyone that isnt in a bunker or any sort of cover
Reinforcements system is good  with the tickets
Cons
This game is not very friendly for new players, because you need to learn alot of things in this game, until i got good, i got to rank 60 out of 99, and from rank 10 to 60 is about 1-1,5 months if you play it every day like i did.
Some bugs.
Despite the realistic factor of this game, people run up stairs with their AT rifles and satchel charges and ammo and probably an SMG they found about 60 kg or 100 lbs like usain bolt.
Some tips.
Always use smoke screens
If you are on a low end pc like me, nd you can get about 40 fps on minimum graphics. I recommend you to use medium grphics, disable shadows and antistr- what ever the ♥♥♥♥ that word is filtering for better performance. Most important one is Lightning quality, if you put it on medium, the map will be way brighter so its easier for you to spot your enemies.
Play this game every day, so you dont get rusty. If you play the game about once every 3-4 days you will need about 8 months to a year to get good.
Overall this is the best FPS game i have ever played.

Clicker Guild is a fairly standard clicker game, but with a slight twist. Like games like Hero Clicker, you ostensibly control a group of heroes; the heroes all attack on their own, while you can upgrade yourself to improve your clicks.
Unlike many such games, the heroes you hire are actually displayed on-screen; they stand around the enemy and, rather than dealing a constant DPS, swing their weapons and deal damage when their swings connect. Adding to the complexity, they have a chance to critically hit, and unlike most such games, the enemies drop equippable items; each hero has three slots, and the item is automatically assigned to one of them when you pick them up. This adds a small element of strategy to the game – the items sometimes have slightly variable abilities, and while it is obvious that some are better than others, and they get better over time, deciding whether to prioritize, say, criticals or straight-up damage is at least one more choice than most such games have.
However, the game is still at its heart the same thing as every other clicker game; you click on enemies to deal damage, your heroes idly deal damage even when you aren’t clicking, and you have a handful of special abilities with cooldowns to temporarily boost your output of clicks or passive damage output. You can buy new heroes, or you can upgrade existing ones, and each one has a new (usually passive) ability that unlocks at levels 25, 50, 75, 100, and 150. Because of the scaling, it is mostly not really worth upgrading heroes above level 150, as the new heroes are better/more efficient and the upgrades are linear rather than quadratic, meaning that adding +1 level to your first guy is always about the same – thus, going from level 1 to 2 is a huge jump, but going from 150 to 151 is not even noticeable.
Unfortunately, like many such games, there comes a point at which you hit a brick wall and must “ascend”, restarting the game from scratch. And herein lies the rub – the game really gives you poor rewards for ascension. Like all clicker games, you gain some static boost, but in this game, the boost is very small indeed – you gain “stars”, which can be spent on permanently raising some global attributes, but the boosts are very small and the star cost is large compared to how much you get for ascending. This means that even after five ascensions, getting past the start of the fifth area (which is actually 40 levels in, as each area is split up into 10 zones, though the differences are purely aesthetic) remained basically impossible unless you waited an hour for a cooldown timer to expire. The game becomes extraordinarily grindy at that point, and it never got better, unlike other clicker games, where at least you can make additional progress after ascending.
That being said, this at least felt like a bit more than blindly clicking, though only a very marginal amount more. It still remains the same old core, bog-standard gameplay, with only very minor adjustments, and there also seemed to be a bug preventing some characters from having items spawn for them at all.
All in all, this is not something I’d suggest for general audiences to get, but if you’re a clicker fiend, this is at least a bit different while still being mostly the same.

Should YOU Buy The Long Dark? I have made a short video to help you decide that:
PROS:
- Most unique survival game I have ever played
- Extremely immersive and realistic - makes you truly feel "cold" and alone
- Outstandingly beautiful maps that manage to have very different looking areas
- No tutorial - immediately jump into playing the game
- Interesting cartography system - there is no in-game map, rather you draw your own maps by surveying the area with used charcoal from your fires
- Loads of achievements, difficulty levels, and challenges for the completionists
- 5 chapters of story mode(2 at release said to have 6-10 hours of gameplay) with superb voice acting
CONS:
- $35 may be a bit steep for a lot of people but I think it's well worth it if this is your cup of tea
- Lack of multitasking in the game - feels tedious when you have to sit and stare at a pot of water boiling instead of doing something else productive
- Loot spawn is somewhat random potentially causing you to die quickly if you're not lucky enough to find tools
- Animals have a patrol box making them feel a little unnatural at times
- No jumping! :(
Overall, The Long Dark is an excellent fresh take on the survival genre that you could easily find yourself sinking hundreds of hours into. If you’re the kind of person that enjoys nature and survival, I definitely recommend heading over to Steam or your console to start playing this game immediately!

Beautiful game and highly recommended. Here are my thoughts having completed it on its easiest setting and about 15 hours of playtime.
Dungeon of the Endless puts me in mind of FTL.  I've tried several times to explain the basic premise and deleted each effort. This is not a complex game, but like FTL there are so many elements - that can get as complex as you like - you really have to immerse yourself in the game to understand and enjoy them.
At its most basic you have to defend a crystal and transport it to the exit of a mysterious underground labyrinth. Along the way you'll encounter increasingly challenging monsters that seem determined to do nothing but murder your crystal. You'll build defences, upgrade your heroes and defences, you'll find mysterious shopkeepers, make mad dashes for the exit holding the crystal and watch your heroes get horribly murdered.
Dungeon of the Endless distills so many bloated game ideas, and so many 80's movie moments into a beautiful pixel-art rogue-lite. Its absolutely compelling and as you unlock new heroes and new ships the game gets increasingly difficult.
+ Beautiful art style
+ Clever and well-contained mechanics and gameplay elements
+ Diverse cast of characters you can lead to grisly deaths
+ Tense and atmospheric
+ Incredible art-style
+ Challenging even on the easiest setting
Dungeon of the Endless doesn't quite hit the heights of FTL, but if you enjoyed that game and are looking for a similar challenge, and a similarly beautiful soundtrack (which I recommend buying) this is a must-have.

Dungeon of the Endless is all about the joys of random loot and exploration of an interesting universe.
The music, atmosphere, and pixel art is all spot on (just don't look at the awful pixel portraits). The game also boasts a very pretty, albeit underused art style through an album of drawn out depictions of enemies, ships, and characters.
The characters themselves deserve a special mention, because each one has their own distinct charm and play. This is even further explored in that characters interact with one another in interesting ways, and even provide actual game altering effects to incentivize team experimentation and boosts the game's replayability.
As for the meat of game, you start by choosing a pod (game modifier) to crash land in and the characters to bring along in it. Gameplay then revolves around opening doors. No really, opening doors is integral to the experience and the way the game functions, serving as a sort of "turn" for generating resources, refreshing ability cooldowns, and sometimes spawning monsters. Most importantly though, it's why the game is so fun and absolutely absorbing. You see behind each door could be anything, maybe it's a really cool item, maybe it's a new hero, maybe it's even the shape and size of the room you discover that makes you shout with excitement, but whatever it is, it's what it COULD be that keeps you trekking through each floor, and ultimately what keeps you interested for so long.

As should go without saying with any Early Access game, only purchase if you are interested in seeing the game grow, and want the chance to add your voice to the development. The concept is fantastic, and there's a lot of potential in the game, but...
There's far too many issues with its current state. Building custom buildings is near-impossible, the controls are often non-responsive, there's a nasty memory leak (this game should not require +6 gigs of RAM), and that's only the biggest problems. Workers that don't work, ladders and furniture that can't be deconstructed, etc. There's many small things that combine to make the game very hard to enjoy.
Putting aside the bugs and building problems, the game is well designed. The progression of your minions is simple but effective, the resource harvesting likewise. My only quibble is that it takes a very long time to do anything with only a 2x speed option. I'd like the ability to go up to 8x at least.
Given the strength of the underlying design, I look forward to playing the game more once it's had some bug-fixing done. However, I can only review it based on what it is now, so I cannot recommend this as is.

I'm not the sort to prejudice games over things like their being hidden object puzzlers; and the Artifex Mundi games are by far the best examples of the genre. Nonetheless A.M. has followed the method of if it isn't broke don't fix it, meaning they reuse their puzzles with cosmetic variations from one game to another. This has the unfortunate result that if you've played one of their games you've played them all.
That's O.K. if you think of the games as more visual novels with bonus puzzle content. Granted the writing isn't amazing; but it isn't bad either. I know I've yet to play an A.M. game I could make myself stop playing before the end. That's, on average, over 3 hours in one sitting. And, most of their games include a bonus chapter that extends gameplay another hour.
They do manage to do this without unnecessarily padding game length that overstays its welcome. I know that doesn't sound like much in an industry with triple AAA titles that boast hundred of hours of gameplay. But, for cheap casual games this is an achievement.
My recommendation, because of the "if you've played one you've played them all" problem, is pare your selections down to their better games. That would be Enigmatis 2 (but not the mediocre Enigmatis: the Ghosts of Maple Creek) as a top pick, Grim Legends 1 & 2 if you liked that, and the Nightmares from the Deep trilogy if you just can't get enough of these games.

I finished it some tme back, so I can't remember specifics other than spending over half an hour on one scene, with my husband looking over my shoulder, trying to find what they called an "onion," only to discover through sheer random clicking that they really meant "(a string of) garlic." There were at least half a dozen instances like this throughout the game, into the bonus chapter, and it's severely annoying as well as a huge strike against a HOG.
If you like HOGs, I'd recommend picking this up, but only if you get it on a good sale.

Unique & entertaining platformer, in the vein of Super Meat Boy & Pinkman.
First thing - it reminds me games, like "Pinkman" or Messhofs "The Puinshment" just from his minimalistic looks.
It plays very similar to the both much much harder Pinkman or Team Meat's Super Meat Boy. The idea and mechanics are just the same. I think SMB has the only difference the run button - to both others.
I thought, its a very hard platformer, because of those other games mentioned earlier. but, surprisingly this one is by far the easiest of all. I was surprised, how easy it was - so its an easy 100% game.
Mechanics works well, and also the music fits the game just well. There arent that much levels especially compared to games-  like SMB or Pinkman, plus with its very easy difficult level, you wont spend that much time on this - as the others.
While, you play in both other games for countless of hours - due to their difficulty, this one doesnt even take an hour for an average platform gamer. This is like a walk in the park.
The controls just work fine - although, i only played it with the (xbox 360) controller. One thing, about the achievements:
I was very SURPRISED, that i did not unlock any auto chievos - like "First jump" or Press R button" - this bug is, when you play with a controller, they arent recognized, by your joypad inputs - so, in the end, i had to use keyboard, to unlock them. (i did in fact not press R on the keyboard, until the end of game). When you just use joypad, it just wont work.
So those would be my only 2 complaints about this game:
-joypad bug for auto achievements, like "pause the game" or"make your first jump"  - for a hunter a bit annoying.
-very short and maybe a bit too easy.
All in all, for its price and for its craftmanship (its a very solid platformer with very superb controls)
i would recommend this tiny gem to any fan of the genre. It the other games are too hard for you (like for me), then you will be surprised with this. Give it a try.

I would recommend this game. The developers are active and keep the community in the loop on what they're doing, even if there isn't much to loop us in on. Development is a bit slow, but they've made great strides for each update they've put out. Plus it supports workshop so you can add/change the game even more by adding in some fun mods. It's fun solo, add some friends and you'll have a blast.
Just keep in mind the game isn't very forgiving. You mess up, you will die if you're playing surivival. There is a bit of a learning curve in that regard, so I would recommend using sandbox first so you can ease into how the game works before jumping into survival.
Here are a few pros and cons to consider before buying the game.
Pro:
The developers are clearly active.
Development can be viewed as slow, but is still going and we're kept updated on how it is going.
The game is fully playable with few bugs.
MP is available to play.
There is a depth to the game that makes you think about long term choices when the season starts to change.
Workshop is available to add additional content to the game.
Challenging game play - have to work to stay alive as time goes by.
Con:
Game has been in EA state for over three years.
In solo game, the "world" is a bit empty with no interactive NPCs that are not zombies trying to eat your head.
Over all, as i stated above, I firmly believe the game is worth investing in. It has tons of replayability and gives a really good open world experience, where your choices you made early in the game turn around to haunt you later as the game evolves with seasons, and aging.
What are you waiting for??? Hurry up and buy it!!!
