Alpha 10 review
This game is a town building strategy game in some medieval time, semi-fantasy. You start with only a few people and have to collect all the resources from the environment. There are different professions to promote the people, like blacksmith, farmer etc..
More people will join your town over time, as well as enemies who you might encounter. It is a sandbox agme with no win objective, just surviving untill you are satisfied or defeated.
As an alpha game this game is not complete yet and has a lot of bugs. The things mostly done are the building system (for building the houses) and a couple professions, water and mining. Although these still have some additional features planned. Like internal walss and rivers to name a few.
Furthermore there are merchants visiting from time to time and a basic goblin campaign who might raid you from time to time. Also a mostly finished terrain generation.
As a kickstarter backer I played from the very first alpha. Don't be fooled by my ingame hours, most of them are from mod testing. Only about 10-15 hours are real gameplay divided over several alpha's.
To me the biggest draws are:
- the building system
- the charming art style
- the relax gameplay
- the modding opportunities
You can play buildings pretty fast, with whole walls and roofs in a few seconds or even from templates. Or you can design something block by block, click 'complete' and the litte hearthlings go build it block by block including scaffolding to reach higher places.
The game has a really relax atmosphere, both through the excellent music as well as the gameplay where you don't move your hearthlings directly, but indirect by creating orders.
The advantage of a 3D game is that you can see the whole underground complex you made in a single instance, which I find a nice feature. Although I am missing the opportunity to see both underground and above ground at the same time.
I like where the game is heading. But I hope/wish the gameplay will be more interesting in the planning and decision making part.
For example: Now it is like draw a farmplot and select plant type. That's all. I wish there was something like seeds to obtain somewhere which you can plant. Or animal breeding instead of infinite sheeps spawning in the surroundings.
And feeding sheeps so you have to devote some crops to animals for example.
All the resources are too infinite and too abundant imo (through merchants mainly and infinite sheep and seeds). It does not matter if you loose sheep (if you even can), you just get new ones easily. So more resource sinks and planning/decision making parts makes the gameplay less shallow.
Modding
Having no prior modding experience and no single line of code knowledge or ever made animations or art before, I dove into the modding of stonehearth. Modding being one of the main core features of stonehearth got me interested in modding. I saw Tom (one of the devs) making some models in qubicle and it looked really easy. Downloaded the dome of qubicle and made some modles myself, which was indeed very easy. Even implementing them in the game was not too difficult with just copying and changing some text files. Even animation is not that hard. So I have high hopes for a great modding community for this game
Summary:
+ relax gameplay / lovely artstyle
+ awesomel building mechanics
+ great game in the making
+ excellent modding opportunities
- still lacking in gameplay/bugs (early access)
- shallow gameplay (wish for more interesting planning and decision making parts)

Stonehearth is a very cute, easy-going city builder/sandbox with some combat, though that is a little broken at the moment, as some of the enemies don't even fight your hearthlings properly, and larger battles tend to hurt performance a bit.
You gather resources (mining, lumberjacking, gathering, hunting, farming etc.)  build your city however you want, you can use prefab buildings or create your very own designs.
Stonehearth has a job & crafting system, where you can give each hearthling a role, such as the carpenter or blacksmith, footman or worker. Each hearthling will gain experiance in their given field, which unlocks skills or perks that improve their job performance, unlocking more recipes and such.
The dev's are very active, they stream 2-3 times a week and almost always post updates on their website each tuesday, and update their game on a regular basis.
While it IS an alpha, there is already a lot of content, and more is always being added. Defs worth checking out the roadmap on their website, and talking to the community, which is super-friendly.
Multiplayer is part of stonehearths future - I know many will be wondering this! I believe it will be coop and pvp, so you can build your city with your friends, or build seperate and raid their stockpiles >:D

I don't really understand why this is reviewed so well. It's really not a well-designed rogue-lite.
So, what is dungeonmans? It's a rogue(lite) game in which you pick a character, customize some of it's stats and perks, select a class (optional) and off you go to slay random monsters around the randomly generated world. Or die horribly.
What is different from most roguelike games is,  that unlike most roguelikes where after you die you roll a completely fresh character, is that you can eventually upgrade your starting characters with various perks by bringing back various items to the starting zone: base stats, better starting gear, you can even unlock entire skill trees from the get-go.
However, this is where the core issue lies. The game balance is designed with this in mind. You will need to essentially farm stats for your future character to succeed. Otherwise you will literally get one shoted by higher tier monsters. And there is no way of working around it. The hordes of enemies and the lack of complex spells and abilities waters down the gameplay to "grind stats, die, start another characters, repeat" until you EVENTUALLY get strong enough to walk over everyone' faces.
The "randomly generated" dungeons are very repetitive with no interesting objects to interact with. The loot is tiered, meaning as soon as you get an item from a higher tier the other ones become obsolete. The skill "trees" are a sad joke.
Overall, not a good game, not even as a "babbys first roguelike".

I am now Dungeonmans, thanks to Dungeonmans Academy, and you can be too.
Serious Review:
Dungeonmans is tons of fun. It's the kind of game that looks at the concept of an inventory limit and scoffs. There are always more zones to clear, more loot to find, more artifacts to find. In addition, the NPC towns you encounter live and die by your success or failure. The death of a Hero causes all the towns to lose a stat called Prosperity (exactly what it says on the tin), but you can bolster a town's Prosperity by donating a "Purloined Inventory" or 3. You get those from being a Dungeonmans and killing named/champion enemies.
They also drop artifacts, which I mentioned earlier. You can turn those in back at the Academy, but here's the catch: your current run will not benefit from this in any way. It takes the Academy some time to figure out exactly what you've given them, and how to use it, but future Dungeonmans will thank you by killing lots of things presumably in your name.
And that's just what I've unlocked so far.

Found an Academy and create your first hero.  Strike out to make a name for yourself and your Academy.  Early on, while you aren't clear on how to survive well, there will be bumps in the road and your heroes will fall -- but "you" are not the heroes; "you" are a collection of heroes, the legacy of the entire Academy, and you will lead its graduates to make it great.  Knowledge your heroes live to bring back, the Academy keeps; your graduates steadily start better and better equipped through the efforts of those who came before, perhaps even taught additional skills by adventurers past who teach at the Academy.  Choose masteries from about a dozen possible disciplines (and counting), and build the Academy inexorably until none can stand against its heroes.
If you've never played a "roguelike", or you've never heard the term, there's a learning curve you'll find a little steep at first, but stick with it -- once you get the hang of it, the rhythm of this kind of game, it's addictive.  For those who've played a roguelike before, this is a new twist -- permadeath is totally a thing, but not ALL of you dies.
This game's graphics will not rival a console AAA title (though its music might).  Gameplay is turn-based and easy to pass up based on prejudice of presentation, but you will have missed out on a gem.  Not only is it fun to play, Dungeonmans represents a new step in the development of a very, very old legacy -- older than the Internet, older than Windows and even DOS, to when a computer had one -millionth- the memory yours does now.  Dungeonmans takes a fine, sacred tradition, adds generously in personality and presentation, and offers some of the best few bucks you'll ever spend on Steam.

The puzzles are not particularly inspired either, however, some of the hidden object scenes are fairly challenging, and there were word usages and terms I was unfamiliar with (e.g. cockade) that upped the challenge bar. It is a very well-polished game, and I thoroughly enjoyed it, but I cannot help get the feeling that it somehow underachieves. Recommended: [ 7 / 10 ]

I want to like this game I really do, and I would prefer if Steam allowed me to make a neutral review. Lets start with the positive aspects of this game:
-The visuals are stunning, truly this game looks amazing. the old cartoon austhetic with the filters makes this game insanely unique and I love it.
-The music is also superb. Almost ever tune is just so vibrant, you can always find yourself moving in time with this great music.
Now here are problems I have with this game:
-The controls are very annoying to work around. Aiming and moving are the same thing, so using a controller with the analog stick, you often move it slightly up while running, forcing your aim upward so you aren't hitting a boss/enemy.
-The difficulty, while nice and refreshing to have a difficult platformer, feels more artificial due to the annoying controls. This game could be made difficult, but seems the developers went for an artificial difficulty with how the game plays, just making some points of the game annoying.
-The sound levels. The the music and sound effects are amazing, but the levels seem to be off, some sound effects are just ear peircing while some are far to quiet to hear. I'm sure many of you now of how load the end of level sound effects when it adds up your total score is. Lowering that also means you lower other sound effects, to the point where you wont be able to hear anything else in the game.
Overall, I really want to like this game, austhetically this game is one of the best games to release this year, but sadly the controls and the way the game as been made difficult just ruin what could very easily be one of the best games this year. Darn Steam also need to allow me to give a neutral review as that is what I mainly feel about this game.

After spending quite some time playing, I feel I can say that Evolve is one of my favourite games right now.
What's so great about EVOVLE?  You get to play as a big huge monster and smash tiny little flying people with rocks!  You can play as this weird tentacle monster and electrocute people!  Or you can become a nasty sneaky monster and sneak attack people!
But it doesn't end there!  You can also play as the other side.  Thus the game is both a third person monster game and a first person shooter.  Playing as a hunter adds an interesting fresh perspective, with twelve unique hunters you can choose to play.  Each with his or her own special abilities.  So there is bound to be at least one you might like.
Evolve is asymmetrical, which creates some really interesting tactical scenarios, however, it is still remarkably well balanced and either team usually has a reasonably decent shot at victory.
There is also a really neat solo mode feature where one can customize match settings.  It's a very useful place to practice before you get into some real games as well as get up your character mastery.
DO I RECOMMEND EVOVLE?
YES.  Please buy this game.  It is a beautiful work of art.

Space Colony is a casual overhead city-builder with both sandbox and campaign modes. Once one of the best games for the Macintosh, Space Colony is constantly referred to as "The Sims" in space. You play as god, moving around a dozenish people to improve their relationships with one another, limited in pace by an economy of space mining and farming.  The best part is the voice acting, as the quirks of each character bring out light comedy to keep you entertained for hours. These quirks will have you build different entertainment venues for each character, to maximize the benefits of each worker's work.  Or maybe you won't, because some characters are pretty useless.  This combination of micromanagement and macromanagement is far from tedious.
The Steam adaptation of it has some flaws.  Modern day computers have bigger and HD screens so, the field of view is widened and the buttons are smaller.  This doesn't interfere with gameplay.  There's some problems with audio balance for some sound effects. Alt+tab (switching windows) crashes Space Colony.  I still think this is forgivable, and I'd be willing to give the game 5/5 stars.

The game, as is, isn't all too bad. The only thing bothering me is that, at some point or another, it wasn't clear to me what to do/where to go next. Either I'm really out of touch, or it's completely random as to where you get the next step to proceed (a certain monk comes to mind).
Had those moments not been random, this would've been a decent mixup of a game.
At the start I felt kind of tossed in. Maybe there was some intro I skipped. Possibly. Probably.
That being said, the puzzles were decent enough (and the variety was really good). The story weaving it all together was well enough to keep me going. But the game as a whole just had this arbitrary feel to it when it came to progression and length. At some point it felt like guessing what to do next was the only option (either that, or use the hint button). Sometimes there just wasn't any build-up to what came next. Talking to the aforementioned monk felt quite random at times, but was the only step left to progress.
All in all, the game is enjoyable enough to warrant a buy. Even at full price it gives me more than the usual four hours of entertainment. That being said, this is one of the few games in its genre where I actually needed a hint or two as to where to go next.
And that last part is what makes me *not* recommend it. I feel like I shouldn't be needing the help of the hint button. The random progression factor killed the flow of the game enough for it to not be worth it full price. On sale, though, it will give you more worth for your money than most games in the genre.

I want to preferace this review by stating I am not an avid fan of either visual novels or romance stories, and was trying something new when playing through this.
I can't say that I'm disappointed I did however, as the story was engaging.  The main strength it has comes from the relationship and the fact that the chemistry between the player character and Ceri is genuinly believable.  It does a good job of putting you in the characters headspace as the loner highschool student and gets you to sympathize with this lonely introverted girl who's hiding emotional stress.  You get truly invested in getting close with her and helpping her through her troubled situation and seeing her through to a happy end.
I can't give anything more than a light recommendation however, because while the relationship is a big strength, it is the novel's only strength.  Which isn't to say that everything else is bad, rather that everything else is there to serve its given purpous and nothing more.  The family isn't given much characterization beyond a few basic traits and don't play a very large role in the story other than to give arbitrary advice and at one point a contrived plot device.  (The father runs a publishing firm that just so happens to run with your girlfriend's favorite author)  I don't think the mother had any reason to be in the story at all, and as for characters outside the player's family they're all pretty much forgetable, only there to point the player from point A to B without much characterization given.
The plot itself is also becomes predicitable by the end.  We start off with some mystery airing around Ceri and the issues that trouble her, but around the last third of the story things unwind in a way in which even I as a new comer to the gener could accurately predict what was going to happen.  This was not helpped at all by the fact that there are several late game dialouges that outright tell you what is going to happen, thereby sapping what little stakes were left in the story out completely.  There was real opportunity to drop something unexpected into the mix, a detail or plot development that would've changed things and increased the stakes a bit, but unfortunatly it was an opportunity that sorely missed.
Since this is free however I still recommend the novel for its compeling romance and main characters, just don't go in expecting anything spectacular.

It adds the extra dimension of trying to set up a solid legacy with a new hero while still playing as your old character. Will Fredrick the Rangermans surpass the great level 12 Wizardman, Fizban? Or will he die at level two because you weren't watching your stamina and couldn't jump away?
Beginning a fresh game can be tough when you have no legacy. Its part of the game to overcome this, stick with it! That being said, the game is quite simple to pick up and play, and skills are not convoluted with text.
The main thing that will get you killed is your ambition to go one more floor of a dungeon rather than turn around and go home. It won't be until you open that next door that you'll realize you are in over your head.

I have been a supporter of this game since the kickstarter campaign. Regarding the game itself, its what I always wanted in a voxel style game; the freedom to create a city/kingdom from the ground up with my own unique band of citizens.
Building is fun; you can follow a few set blueprints or make your own from scratch. As the game develops you will eventually be able to make massive castles, but for the current version as of june 2015 multi-story buildings are the new thing.
Combat and resource gathering are about what you would expect, but agian this game is in its early stages and will become deeper as builds go on. Some of the stretch goals filled include elemental enemies and several magic using classes of hearthling. It is still in its early stages, but with the team behind it I am confident the potential will be realised.
Another commendation to the dev team behind this game is that from the outset they have encouraged modding. In the future I would not be surprised if the modding community embraced this game like they do bethesda games.
In closing, its a great game with a great team behind it and its only going to get better as it develops. Grab it now and become part of the community and help the devs out, because you will be hearing about this game in the future, and you will want it then anyway. Happy hearthing.

Dunegon of the Endless is a hybrid roguelike-tower defense game that centers around exploration of each level of a large ship followed by escorting the game's source of power (dust) to the next level. You use dust (found as you explore the level) to power rooms that you can place modules to generate the game's other 3 resources (industry/science/food) which are used to build modules, research technology, or level up and heal heroes among other things.
Along the way you can recruit additional heroes up to a total of four and purchase items from merchants to power them up. The difficulty curve starts out fairly low for the first 5-6 levels and then ramps up significantly as monsters get stronger and the amount of dust you get per level decreases (dust is the only resource that does not carry over to the next level).
Unfortunately, due to the roguelike nature of the game, RNG can totally shaft you on later levels and you may find yourself just making a run for it in order to clear the level, which can put you at a disadvantage later on. A few of the modules also seem to have no real use past the first few levels as they get outclassed fairly quickly or are just counter-intuitive to use. Additionally, some of the requirements to clear the later ships border on the insane and I don't see myself trying to unlock any of them in the forseeable future.
Regardless, I would recommend this game to anyone bored of a typical roguelike as there are a lot of things to experiment with due to the hybrid game mode and there is support for up to 4 people in multiplayer so it could be fun to play with friends.

A solid roguelike RPG dungeon crawler with tower defense mechanics.
Not that there are too many to compare to.
Dungeon of the Endless sticks a ragtag party of criminals and/or their escorts in a falling ship, and your goal is to take the powersource from the bottom floor to the top.  Managing resources, tower defenses for the powersource, and managing your party's stats and equipment make for some amazing surface level gameplay.
Those alone make for deep decision making and management; throw in unique events, floors, the ability to recruit more characters (max party 4), discover new technologies, and whatever else have you, while taking into account nothing will be the same two games in a row, and you got yourself a stew cooking.
Despite all these unique mechanics, the game never feels like it bogs itself down in complexity, and it doesn't feel too complicated to be able to learn.  Coupled with a gorgeous pixellated artstyle and a simple yet beautiful UI, it's a blast to experience time and time again.
Without even having touched multiplayer yet (and I plan to), I recommend the game for anyone who likes... well, the list is up there if you need it.
+Artstyle
+The blend of genres meshes extremely well together, fitting both thematically and mechanically
+Multiplayer, and as far as I've read works rather well. Was not just tacked on for the sake of
+Fun references, but never feels out of place
+Heavy replayability
-Arguably barebones tutorial, which leads to a steep learning curve

This was not nearly as polished as other Artifex Mundi games, but it was still enjoyable.
The plot is reminiscent of Pirates of the Caribbean, just slightly more convoluted and tragic.
The resolution of the artwork was somewhat blurry compared to what I am used to from this studio, which made cutscenes harder to watch, and many of the hidden object puzzles a challenge.  I found myself having to use the sonar feature fairly often because I couldn't distinguish one object from another, although it was never so bad that I had to use a hint.  I honestly preferred playing the mahjong.  The background locations were pretty, though.
The point-and-click puzzles were mostly logical, although there was a lot of backtracking for what felt like very little payoff.  Also, I really hope you like collecting ingredients for recipes.
The voice acting and music were decent, and there was even a bit of humor with the pirates on the ship.
I was slightly disappointed with the bonus mission.  While the puzzles were pretty good, the spelling, grammar, and word choices were terrible: "tukan" instead of "toucan," "perl" instead of "pearl," "wires" instead of "yarn with knitting needles"... it just got worse and worse.  I can overlook small mistakes, especially in bonus content, but some of the errors made finishing the hidden object games nearly impossible without resorting to sonar or hints.
Overall, it is a decent little game.  It has its shortcomings, but it was relaxing enough and interesting enough to occupy an afternoon.  It took about 8 hours to beat it twice through on expert mode (once for each set of achievements) including the additional mission, so I feel like I got my sale-price money's worth.
I would give it a 6/10.

Of the six games included in EA's very own "Indie Bundle", two titles had never crossed my ears: Gatling Guns and WARP. When I accepted from the latter its offer of a five hour journey, my expectations were low. I didn't expect anything earth shattering, but I also didn't expect WARP to be as fun as it is.
Played in aerial perspective, WARP's narrative follows the exploits of an alien named "Zero" who finds himself captured by scientists and held hostage by mercenaries. Using his assortment of powers (primarily teleportation), Zero must escape the lab that confines him.
WARP breathes fresh air into the stealth genre with its deceptively childish visuals. Make no mistake, this is not for kids. F-bombs are dropped quite often and deaths are particularly gruesome. The gameplay demands of you to not only think, but also act hastily.
At the price of $9.99, WARP won't give you the most bang for your buck. But should you find it at a discount of 50% or more, it's worth a look.

I praised the heck out of this game back on it's steam release, I was a daily member of it's forums, and I was in the twitch stream with the devs and hundreds of people during the steam launch. I stuck around before it was on Steam and the devs seemingly disappeared, playing the hell out of 1.5d. This game was amazing to me.
But here we are 4+ years of development and the game is well, the same. I know technically a lot of changes have happened, and a lot of improvements have been made, but fundamentally it really hasn't changed much at all.
But this review is more set for people unsure of the games Early Access tag, and honestly I really suggest steering clear until they knock some of those planned features off the list because they are taking immense amount of time to seemingly accomplish little, and they aren't the type to wait a long time and have some huge friggin patch come out either. So instead we have to wait day after day, months after months and years at this point for them to release NPCs or a campaign, the big stuff always being asked. You aren't allowed to complain either or they just ban you from the forums, take a gander itself, you'll get banned just because you are getting frustrated. I have never laughed so hard watching the moderators appear so personally offended by every negative thing to the point they are constantly defending the game in every post with long responses about how we are the ones wrong, you don't see this in AAA games, or even most indie games.
Anyway it's not as if the game can't be fun, but the map is still very very much unfinished with furniture and room layouts that make 0 sense, you will find bedrooms and living rooms being merged into being the same room, bathrooms blocking doors, some houses have rooms missing, they just ruin immersion completely and look terrible. I could never get how people would live in it or all have the same decorator and furniture, or that some windows in a house have curtains but others don't.
NPCs have no ETA STILL (June 2017). We still don't have the friggin new animations that I remember being mentioned well over a year ago, and some weapons still don't even have actual sprites in the game. I mean♥♥♥♥♥♥they are still talking about vehicles and animations and I am sitting here wondering what year it is, are they seriously not out?? Seriously check the mondoid posts from 2015 and you will see this stuff being "worked on" I can't tell what the hell these people are doing when they work on this full time with all the funds they amassed. WE ARE HALF WAY THROUGH 2017!
The general gameplay itself all works nicely for what it is, it really can be a fun experience, but it seems like most deaths will not be from you doing something stupid, but because i get bored and start playing riskier just to make things exciting. It just loses momentum once you get a basic grasp of the gameplay. I really don't know how anyone that couldn't pick up everything in a couple hours.
If we had NPCs and they lived up to half the promises then the gameplay would improve massively, things would feel tense as you'd approach a lot of situations differently, like will they attack or join you? Do they have a quest? The other AI would make zombies move about the map, and you'd have a lot of interesting encounters and a more ironically lively world.
But here is the thing, the game prides itself on keeping things to the George Romero lore established from his movies, but fails to bring the other elements that made his movies good, and that's the characters and environments. The zombies alone aren't entertaining, nothing is fun about dumb slow shamblers that make no effort to find you or change anything up. 7 Days to Die did this perfectly by having horde nights and zombies running at night, keeping you always working against the clock and prepping for the next horde.
Gameplay mechanics it follows the same issue a lot of these games have, it's repetitive and once you fall into a routine the game just loses everything. The character progression feels very stupidly thought out, requiring the more fun aspects like construction and wiring requiring your character have a profession in these areas. Or else you have to grind a lot to get anywhere.
So following up on the gameplay, you will basically only ever just loot the same old houses over and over again, since nothing will change and I highly doubt many people have the patience to wait until the water and electricity in town go out. Not like growing food and putting up rain barrels is the least bit difficult anyway so what's the point?
Otherwise nothing else will happen, you will hit the normal routine of hording materials at a location and you won't be compelled to do much else because nothing else is required. Throw a sheet over the windows and you're safe forever. I wish it actually tried to be a bit more arcadey and sandboxy and make it easier to build up large forts and take over sections of towns or overhaul a building. But gathering and moving loot is insanely time consuming and annoying with how heavy wood is to carry. And if you are only a level 1 carpenter you get these ♥♥♥♥♥♥ walls to build with until you grind a long long time to level it up to 3 where they aren't garbage anymore.
It's actually pretty comical how easy the game is when I am purposely playing wreckles to make this more fun. Zombies are easy to navigate around, food isn't really that scarce or difficult to grow, and I can take on a horde of 20+ zombies with a friggin hammer if I wanted to walk backwards and lunge forward to smack them. It all feels stale.
The UI and performance front seem shoddy, my RX 480 struggles to reach 60FPS at 1080p without experiencing drops or stuttering. The game actually suggests 720p and 30FPS funnily. The UI is one that requires a lot of clicking, and is just bad. Sometimes I need to click a few pixels over to select things properly, sometimes the window is stuck to my cursor, it looks dumb.
They mentioned wanting to overhaul it (3rd time) but we all know how long it takes for stuff like that to be finished..
There are more things wrong with the game, but these are the massive issues that need to be addressed within this year, Yall start releasing your♥♥♥♥♥♥ I don't care if the NPCs come out in a basic way and progressively get improved over time but just change something, rock the foundation of the game a bit, I really want to love this game like I did in the early days but at this point it's abundantly clear a lot of the popularity is about what everyone is waiting for the game to be and not what the game is currently.
(My hours are across 4+ years and 90% of it was at it's release on steam)

It's one of those hidden object games, which means I spent 10 minutes furiously clicking various parts of the screen whilst waiting for something to either happen or my mouse to break. It is beyond me how people can stand this sort of "gameplay", but I find it highly unenjoyable and absolutely dreadful.
You're  Melissa K, on a mission to do something...somewhere.. Suddenly a monk got lost and you have to look for him by doing the aforementioned furious clicking. The game offers a large variety of unfun things to do like
- clicking items and being told that your character should probably try that later
- clicking items, opening up a new screen in which you can't do anything since you're apparently missing something
- opening up other screens in which you have to find a multitude of items in odd shapes, which are conveniently hidden amongst a bazillion other items and getting spooked by some sort of red ghostly entity when you misclick too many times, just to annoy the hell out of you some more
- sending a lizard into holes and other small orifices to receive an item which, I grant the game that, often makes sense to use in a certain place
- clicking through a screen you already gave the click over once, again, because stuff does appear or becomes clickable at some point without you really knowing why or how
and so on and so forth..
I do agree that my 10 minute gameplay is probably not meeting the standards of IGN quality reviewing, but you should already know if you like this kind of game or not. If you do, then there's a high chance you'll enjoy this game as well, since the production values seem alright and there's a lot of puzzling and clicking to be done.
But if you, like me, are not a fan of this genre, then there's nothing here for you. Stick to something like the LucasArts adventures or The Book of Unwritten Tales or similar blends of "proper" adventure games for a more fulfilling experience.
This was my biased review, thanks for letting me enlighten you :p

This is a letter I just wrote to PC Gamer, they probably wont reply, but it reflects how I feel about dungeonmans:
Dear Tyler@pcgamer,
You guys ran an article a while back, giving  a tip on an "in development" game called Dungeonmans. I had already been a kickstarter backer when you ran the article, but really didnt have too high of hopes for the game. I was on a kickstarter binge for a while there, and dungeonmans was kind of my long shot.
In the time since you ran that article, dungeonmans has released, along with a few of my other kickstarter backed games (at least EA builds).
These games include:
Massive Chalice
Road Redemption
Wasteland 2
Shovel Knight
Dreamfall Chapters
Elite Dangerous
Godus (bleh)
Star Citizen
I have spent far more hours in Dungeonmans, than any of those other games. Not saying I dont like the others, they are all (for the most part) great, but Dungeonmans is up there with Spelunky for me in the roguelike genre. It is currently my 9th most played game on Steam with a library of around 300 games. Obliviously most of those dont get much play time at all, but I do game every day (95% Counter Strike), and Dungeonmans keeps drawing me back, especially when I'm in game downtime (waiting for a team).
My whole point in all of this is that it would be really cool for you guys to run a review on this game sometime. I think its fully released now, its been quite polished for some time.
It kind of makes me sad that this game didnt make a top chart once, I keep looking for it to gain some love, but I just havent seen much press on it. Get one of your rogulike lovers on it, I would be surprised if they didnt like it. Seriously, the game is like crack.
I bought it for my friend who is also my main CS teammate, we talk dungeonmans builds all the time. I honestly havent even beat it yet, I'm not sure I've even gotten close.
Anyway, I probably sound like I work for dungeonmans at this point (I dont, as far as I know its made by a single person, maybe two), I honestly just feel like gamers need to play this one. Its truly a hidden gem.
Thanks for your time

The game offers a few gameplay modes, which are actually the same game, but with some added gameplay conditions. For example, the goal of every game is to get through 12 floors, but in some modes you are not allowed to heal in certain ways, or your heroes are more powerful but you can't build defensive towers, or one mode in which the game is unwinable, and the goal is to get as deep as you can without dying.
The game also offers a multiplayer mode, in which you and your friends control just one character (unless there's less than 4 of you, then one of you can enlist an additional character you might find in the dungeon), which really adds to the longevity of the game. Recommended!

Okay, I've played the game for some time now and I feel comfortable enough to point out the good and the bad.
Frankly, the game -could- have been great, but I dunno whether Kalypso works hard so devs can't deliver a quality product or if the devs they find always skip Quality Assurance. It really feels like they made the game solely for the campaign, anything else was an afterthought.
- Nice graphics and style.
- Big Heroes of Might and Magic feel, upgrading cities, interacting with some stuff on the map and so forth.
- You upgrade your heroes much like you'd do in a typical RPG game, distributing attribute points and skills.
- Units needing to gain experience before they evolve is an interesting concept.
- You can revive nearly every unit, which makes it easier to deal with losses. Just make sure to retreat if things start to go down, if all units die, your party is wiped.
Bad (
)
- No hotkeys, save for spacebar to skip unit turn/finish turn. This alone is my
gripe with the game. Want to open any menu? Find the button and click it. Want to set your units on defensive stance? Click the button. Use an item in battle? Click the button to open the inventory, click the item and then the unit.
- No autoresolve. Every battle has to happen in the battle screen and "Quick Battle", the closest to autoresolve, makes your units dumb as rocks.
- No camera speed options. The first second of camera movement is ALWAYS too damn slow.
- No key binding option. Move camera with WASD, rotate with arrow keys. Don't like it? Too bad, sucker!
- If the map you're on doesn't have a Trainer building, the only way to get exp for your heroes/troops is fighting, which can be a problem when you only have lvl 1s and the lowest enemy around is 4 level 12 troops.
- Only the capital matters. Some maps have extra cities, but not having them wouldn't be much of a difference.
- It's hard to tell where you can or can't go in a map. In one map in particular, Islands (Hot Seat), a lot of interactive stuff in the map cannot be interacted with because your hero simply has no path to it. Oh, and that map also has a node that it's impossible to take by moving a hero there, you have to summon a unit, like a golem, to fight the creeps there.
- Most heroes move way too slow on the overworld map.
- Map selection outside the campaign is simply terrible. But then again, you probably won't want to play the skirmish.
- Can't select a difficulty for the CPU while playing in hot seat.
- No sense of empire building or even of territory expansion. Capturing nodes really doesn't feel like much.
- The game really feels like you're dealing with a small party of unique persons rather than a small army of units.
- Campaign lacks a difficulty curve, instead relying on a wall of sorts for each level. Once you get past the wall (by getting sufficient troops at the max level), the rest of the level is a smooth sailing.

Hidden object, point and click.  If you like those, you will like this.  If not, then no, you won't like this.  But what makes it a good hidden object point and click?  I'm not an expert, but I think I can say it was on the enjoyable side of such games.  The graphics are pretty but the animation is dated.  The story is followable (unlike certain "mystery" games) but simple and forced.  The puzzles... there are puzzles!  But their mostly chores and don't stand out as memorable or beneficial to the gameplay.  Ehh, it's a fine hidden object, point and click game.  If you're expecting something good, you'll likely be disapointed.  If you're expecting something horrible, you might be impressed.  It's fine.

For the type of game that it is, Nightmares from the Deep has more quality than i expected. Entertaining story, decent animation, and interesting environments. The game mixes point-and-click adventure with hidden object as well as a few mini-games sprinkled in. The puzzles are clever but not overly challenging. I never needed to use the "Hint" button.
Adding to the list of positive things are steam achievements, trading cards, a nice music score and zombie pirates.
If I have any negative marks against the game, it is a little on the short side. There is a bonus adventure that allows you to continue where the main game ended, but it too is short. I also wish the protagonist's daughter had a name. I don't feel as invested when I think of "HOLD ON! I'LL SAVE YOU.....WHATEVER YOUR NAME IS!". Maybe I'm supposed to be a crappy parent who can't remember my kids name.
Overall, it's enjoyable and if you feel the price is too high, wait for a Steam sale.

Here's another franchise I decided to blindly check out for the first time not too long ago, just like Resident Evil : BioShock.
I'm very glad I did.
BioShock is the first of the BioShock series created by Irrational Games. You play as Jack, a man who is on a plane when it crashes into the Atlantic Ocean. There, Jack swims to shore by an old lighthouse, and enters. From there, he discovers the underwater city of Rapture, created by business magnate Andrew Ryan, voiced by Armin Shimerman, who voices Dr. Nefarious in the Ratchet & Clank series, and best known for playing the Ferengi bar owner Quark in Star Trek : Deep Space Nine. Jack descends into the failed utopia, coming across many horrifying things like Splicers, which are the deranged citizens of the once prosperous Rapture, and Big Daddies, huge, hulking brutes in large diver suits which protect odd little girls refered to as "Little Sisters", while being guided by Atlas, an Irishman.
Now, let's just get to why I loved this game.
First off, the writing and acting. Wow. It's very believable, and sounds authentic. Those are some of the best words to describe it. My main praise for the acting goes to Armin Shimerman as Andrew Ryan. Not only did Shimerman do fantastic in the role, he also succeeded in making Ryan a very compelling character, and one of the most interesting villains I've ever seen in a game before. While I think The Walking Dead : Season 1 contains the best acting I've ever seen in a video game, this is probably the second best I've ever heard.
While it could be compared to other games like Half-Life for its weapon choices, BioShock does things differently. First off, the plasmids. They're quite useful and make for some interesting combat. Second, the different ammo types. While Half-Life only has usually one type of ammo per weapon, BioShock has usually 3 for each weapon that isn't a plasmid, some better than others. Third, hacking. A security camera monitoring you and about to send drones on you to shoot you to death? Hack it. Want to get a discount on ammo? Hack a vending machine. Hacking is one of your best friends in this game, and boy, it's useful. There's more in the game than that, like ADAM and EVE, and the significance both of those substances have, but I won't spoil it all here.
Now, I know this sounds crazy, but going to Rapture would be really cool, in my opinion. This is honestly one of the coolest and best settings I've ever seen in a video game. The atmosphere gives off a sense of uncertainty, and a really unsetling vibe. Almost like you're stepping into a shallow grave, which, in a way, you are. There was one part in the game that actually frightened me so bad, I screamed and hurt my throat quite badly. I didn't even know I could scream that loud.
There is a nitpick I have with the city, however. The city should have collapsed architecturally before the way it actually did, because there's giant sea-dwellers down there like whales and stuff. It just doesn't really make sense to me. But eh, it can be excused.
While I did summarize the story at the beginning, the story is much, much more rich than that. There's several different audio logs from different people, mainly the elite members of Rapture's society, describing the life they have in Rapture, and they also describe events like the civil war in Rapture, which was between Ryan, and the Bronx conman and criminal mastermind Frank Fontaine. All of these audio logs shed light on a once proud and beautiful creation, one which, by many people, would be considered impossible. That creation was Rapture, and its greatness has died out by the time Jack arrives, extinguished like a weak flame burning on a little match.
Overall, BioShock is fantastic. I consider video games to be a true form of art and expression, and this game nails that. It's quite simply art. It's original, creative, and very, very good. I believe there is no such thing as a perfect game. I may give a game a 10/10, like I did with Grand Theft Auto : San Andreas, but it's a flawed masterpiece. This is no different. But this game is also deserving of the legendary status it has achieved, and I loved it.
Final score : 10/10.

But there can only really be one true Space Colony; and it is back.
Note:
The HD edition adds widescreen support, higer resolutions, improved stability on newer systems and new mini campaigns.
The Steam edition adds all of the above, plus a further new mini campaign and Steam Workshop support.
My advice: If you've got the HD edition, you don't really need to splurge cash on the Steam edition unless you have plenty of spare money lying around. If you've got the original Space Colony or are buying for the first time, you will want the Steam edition. The Steam edition is also the most likely to get further updates as it is considered to be the definitive version by the devs.
Keep coming back to this game, unlike many others.

I'll start by saying that while I really love the game and the survival aspect I absolutely despise the game-y wolves. I greatly enjoy playing on Interloper difficulty because it feels like a true cold-weather survival game. Unfortunately most of my play-throughs end with getting killed by a wolf in an often very ridiculous fashion. To use my latest example, 9 days in and I am doing very well unforunately my hunger is running low so I am forced to scavenge an area I know that is frequented by wolves. But I'm hungry and desperate. Hunger is my only current issue as I am flush for resources and gear. As I approach two wolves begin to charge at me, fortunately there is a vehicle nearby and I hop in the vehicle and use my bedroll to sleep for a few hours. It's night time now and the wolves seem to be gone, I get out of the car and run about 200m to the building I intended to loot, there are no wolves in sight. Finally I am in the building I find enough food to allow me to have a good nights sleep, though I will need to search for more food in the morning. Fast forward the entire night and morning and it is noon. I ready my gear step out the instanced door, intending to take a quick look around and retreat inside if needed, but there is a wolf so close to me that I can only see the top of his head, and without time to do anything the wolf is immediately on top of me and at 50% health on Interloper difficulty I am dead.
I've seen this issue reported 3 years ago and it still seems to be a thing even though they said it's not intended. With the game nearing full release next month the fact that this still occurs leads me to think that it's just a part of the game. While the wolves can lead to fun and intense gameplay, more often than not they server as unfair spoilers without a weapon and a free source of resources when you do have a weapon. They are the zombies that are shoehorned in your survival game, they are the cliche jump-scare in your horror game, they are the antagonist that upstages mother nature herself in a game where she is supposed to be the star.
I hope someday they'll add custom difficulty or just fix many of the cheesy wolf interactions like the one I described.

WARP is an action puzzle game with a very unique twist, your character is able to warp through objects or into them, allowing for all sorts of possible ways to access different areas or complete challenges.  Initially the game felt a little too derivative of Wall-e in style, until you are introduced to the ability to warp inside of people and explode them from the inside out.  From that point on I was intrigued and enjoying the aesthetic of cutesy style mixed with over the top gore.  Both the Steam Overlay and widescreen modes are supported, as is the gamepad.  The only unlikable aspect of the game is the third party EA DRM, but it's significantly less intrusive than the Ubisoft launcher or Windows LIVE.  I would recommend this title to most gamers who enjoy twitch action and puzzle solving, but be prepared for some very difficult challenges and a high twitch factor similar to Super Meat Boy.

While still very much in the fledgling stages of the development, Stonehearth is still an amazing game that offers a voxel-themed sandbox/city-building experience that gives you plenty of direction with what to "do" next without being constricting about it.
About the biggest concern I have about this game is the lack of micromanaging. If you're a fan of games like Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria, or even Towns (or what you had hoped Towns would become), Stonehearth may leave you wanting for a bit more control over your individials and their priorities, or just the allotment of work between citizens.
I hope to see Stonehearth grow bigger and stronger, particularly with things like Seasons, expanded climates and map varieties, and some additional aesthetic content, but that's no reason to not pick up a copy and try it out for yourself. Stonehearth has got a solid foundation, a history of active and attentive devs, and a bright future ahead.

Stonehearth seems (even after about a year) very much still in the concept stage.  There's not much game here yet, but you can tell the devs are seriously devoted to making Stonehearth the best they can make it.  Even in this early stage you can tell it's the most charming, enjoyable 'concept' of a game out there (check my hours, and that's just through Steam).
The devs work closely with the community every step of the way and are immediately responsive to most all bug reports and suggestions.
The only caveat I can think of, is that it has been a long, long time getting to even where it is now, and it still has a long long way to go.  I do think it will get there and I have the utmost faith in the devs, but don't expect it in a mere few months.
Your money invested here is not to have a fleshed out playable game today or tomorrow, but to help ensure the devs can make Stonehearth all it can be.  You won't have a game you can play day in and day out... just yet.. but it will happen and it will be wonderful.
Edit:  I've changed my recommendation to NO for the time being.  There's just too little game here for the high price they're charging.  That high price was fine for kickstarter where you were investing, but now they're selling it on Steam and there just isn't much of a game here for that kind of money.  I also have concerns about how long development is taking.  Don't forget, this game has been in development for two years before it hit Steam early access. Over two years now and frankly, not much has happened for such a long dev cycle.  I honestly think the devs have gotten in over their heads and don't quite know how to dig themselves out of this hole.
I'll happily change to Recommended when I see this game kick into high gear, but for now, it's 'wait and see'.
Update:  I have to say after ANOTHER YEAR, the devs continue to dig themselve into a hole over their overly complicated approach to hearthling building process - to the detriment of the rest of the game.  The devs seem not to know they are fighting a loosing battle with the manual building process they've tried to implement.  A process so inherently complicated NASA couldn't figure it out.  But still they persist.
I'm afraid the game will go nowhere now.  All the 'positive' reviews are based on just a few hours play time and ignore the deep-seated issue of a building process in the game that doesn't work.
We could have had the nice rolling hills we were promised early on instead of the 'cliff' design we have now because it was easier.  If all the dev time was applied to landscape rather than this sink hole they've gotten themselves into with building, we'd have a glorious game by now.  And a finsished one.

I had a huge addiction for these hidden object style casual adventure games a few years ago until I totally burned out on them.
This game was my first, tentative, step back into the genre. And a good one at that. It's not the deepest game you'll ever play (no pun intended), but it entertained me enough to play it through to its satisfying conclusion.
Gameplay consists of traversing (pretty much) static screens of a museum, a pirate ship and a mysterious island, gathering items and solving decently fun puzzles. Items are generally gained by playing a mini-game, which is either the traditional hidden object one
a game of Mahjong. The critical detail here is that you can choose which one to play whenever you want!
I went through the game only solving the Mahjong puzzles and had a great time.
The game is a great introduction to the genre and a solid example of how to do a casual adventure game right.
Steer clear of it if you're looking for a particularly serious or challenging experience though.

I'll start by saying that while I really love the game and the survival aspect I absolutely despise the game-y wolves. I greatly enjoy playing on Interloper difficulty because it feels like a true cold-weather survival game. Unfortunately most of my play-throughs end with getting killed by a wolf in an often very ridiculous fashion. To use my latest example, 9 days in and I am doing very well unforunately my hunger is running low so I am forced to scavenge an area I know that is frequented by wolves. But I'm hungry and desperate. Hunger is my only current issue as I am flush for resources and gear. As I approach two wolves begin to charge at me, fortunately there is a vehicle nearby and I hop in the vehicle and use my bedroll to sleep for a few hours. It's night time now and the wolves seem to be gone, I get out of the car and run about 200m to the building I intended to loot, there are no wolves in sight. Finally I am in the building I find enough food to allow me to have a good nights sleep, though I will need to search for more food in the morning. Fast forward the entire night and morning and it is noon. I ready my gear step out the instanced door, intending to take a quick look around and retreat inside if needed, but there is a wolf so close to me that I can only see the top of his head, and without time to do anything the wolf is immediately on top of me and at 50% health on Interloper difficulty I am dead.
I've seen this issue reported 3 years ago and it still seems to be a thing even though they said it's not intended. With the game nearing full release next month the fact that this still occurs leads me to think that it's just a part of the game. While the wolves can lead to fun and intense gameplay, more often than not they server as unfair spoilers without a weapon and a free source of resources when you do have a weapon. They are the zombies that are shoehorned in your survival game, they are the cliche jump-scare in your horror game, they are the antagonist that upstages mother nature herself in a game where she is supposed to be the star.
I hope someday they'll add custom difficulty or just fix many of the cheesy wolf interactions like the one I described.

Bioshock is a fantastic and dark dystopia, with excellent narration and surprising plot twists, but it is not without flaws. While the setting, characters, and story are breathtaking, gameplay is way too easy and the protagonist is way too overpowered for the enemies to be able to even put up a decent fight. There are maybe half a dozen weapons, each with different ammo types that drastically affect weapon parameters and performance, and about a dozen plasmids. The game seems to throw an overwhelming amount of ammo at the player and I've left tons of it behind simply because I could not use it up fast enough! Similarly, I found only two of the plasmids really useful: Shock and Ignite, and mostly used those two exclusively throughout the entire game. Many of the plasmids are outright useless, mainly because of how easy the game is.
Graphically, the game still looks great, except for the Field of View, which is remarkably low for some reason, with no easy way to change it in-game. It's possible to raise it somewhat by editing configuration files and assigning keyboard shortcuts that increase or decrease the FOV, but I found it to be wonky at best and it would frequently reset back to defaults. It is not a game breaker by any means, but definitely something that should have been handled better, because in all other respects, Bioshock is a superb spiritual successor to System Shock. Now... would you kindly go play it?

I was a backer for the kickstarter for this because I enjoyed the demo versions available then and I like the way it has progressed to now.
This game has a bit lacking presentation quality compared some other paid rogue-likes (still above most popular free ones) using tiles so no animations, fixed tiles not changed by equipment, the help option opens up essentially a readme in another window. I was impressed when banners showed their new effects in tooltips when leveled up, but disappointed to find upgrading light armour didn't do the same.
The game keeps things interesting using lots of active abilities on the player but also monsters. However sometimes the list of actives to try to set up, as well as potions to quaff, can sometimes seem overwhelming, one character had 4 abilities to buff themselves up but focusing on that leaves no time to move or attack- and so I found myself focusing on the other 2 abilities that give enhanced mobility and attacks in one. Some longer, cheaper buffs are optimally constantly active but can be a pain to keep up- especially the light shield power offered by light armour skill as using it before it expires causes it to explode rather than refresh and that explosion puts a cooldown before you can make shields again.
In the kickstarter version my deaths were domiated by a few types of monsters putting out massive damage who thankfully seem to have been toned down- though the triger seems to want to take their place- and since then I've ran into some very nasty bone barons who create powerful summons as well as being strong on their own. Also unleashing ancient kings by opening secrets can sometimes lead to a quick death- unlike other secrets or exile chest which give you a prompt whether to fight them or not.
While the game has no strict classes you still have starter options, and even going for choice with the dungeonmans (as I tend to do) you still stick within skill trees so I'll mention as few things. I enjoyed and was pretty successful on the bannermans, though I'm not convinced using banners for buffs makes all that much of a difference compared to just buffing. Southern gentlemans have a fun theme and interesting gimmick of real time that is very flavourful for a berserkerish character but I don't think being encouraged to play quick and sloppy is that good a gimmick, and their skills seem random in a way you seem to need to react to, certainly not good for a character that encourages button mashing. Playing some other characters i found myself relying on archery powers even on characters that started melee focused and wonder if the ability to kite melee enemies and not be kited by ranged ones makes ranged characters too good compared to melee. I did still manage to have a lot of success on a sword and board, so it isn't needed. I seem to remember necromansers used to be very mage related but now aren't, which is nice for options but does leave necromancers (and southern gentlemen) without and clear idea or real synergies with any weapons set up, especially as the game doesn't really say what stats their skills benefit from.
One major feature, but unfortunately one I'm not a massive fan off, is the idea of a persistant academy you build up. It lets you make characters brokenly skilled, statted and equipped in the early game, but still doesn't really let you skip the early levels. There is also a lot of randomness, or sticking to what successful previous characters have done, that can make the usefulness vary massively between different characters. As strong as characters can be early later on is still a challenge, which is obviously somewhat good, but also means very successful early characters can easily find themselves underpowered. Really not a thing I am sure about, but hasn't been deal breaking and there are neat elements like avenging dungeonmans and aquiring some of their equipment, or gathering information on enemies.

Very short TL;DR at the bottom.
I had a long detailed positive review of this game after a good five or ten hours playing. I had to edit this review, however. It was even better than I imagined.
The game starts out as a fun roguelike and it is immediately endearing. The static character sprites become of little concern with all the wonderful animated effects and amazing soundtrack. It seems initially like a well-done roguelike with some cool mechanics involved. I won't get into those mechanics because it would be too hard to explain them without ranting about how cool they are.
Shortly after grasping the game and being on your way in a fun roguelike, you become somewhat awed by how well the game plays and how neat the Academy building, nemesis system, soul-retrieving mechanics work. Then, once that shock starts to wear off, you'll notice the many dungeon themes, each with a whole set of mobs to go with the theme, and you'll start finding new themes. It's like a whole world of oldschool Dungeons and Dragons that's just thrown down for you to explore. Towns to bolster the prosperity of, bandit blockades to raid, Scrobold warrens, crypts, mage towers, it's all here.
Now, there's a few key points that I noticed.
No worrying about food or inventory limit. That's right, no worries on that. This irked me slightly at the outset, but I rationalized that inventory limits cause you to have to do a lot of backtracking and it gets boring tedious, not fun tedious. And there's a TON of loot to nab! So, removing the inventory limit was a smart move for this game. Well,  with no inventory limit, then hunger becomes pointless as it won't be long before you can just shove a ton of rations in your pack and forget about hunger for a while. It might sound odd to oldschool roguelike players, but the ramoval of the hunger and inventory limit are actually very good for this game and it really works.
The loot system, while there's just a ton of stuff you're picking up, makes it very easy to manage the stuff you're actually interested in looking at as well as super easy to offload the stuff you don't want, through the clever use of tabs and sell/smelt selections when talking to shopkeeps/smiths.
The game also has a lot of really cool psuedo-hidden "secrets". Every town is worth exploring. At lower levels, it's easy to ignore towns and, indeed, ignore many of your consumables (not to say lower levels are easy, trust me), but as you start fighting higher level enemies, you start paying a lot more attention to what you're using and how you're using it and you start wishing you'd bought all those scrolls of combat blinking and pin to win, but you didn't need them back then. You'd better grab them up with the next character!
The combat itself defeats traditional roguelike standards in every way. The skills are all unique and build awesome characters and force you to truly pay attention to what spaces you're moving to. A fightermans doesn't just bump up against a mob until it dies - you have a number of special moves and you'd better make good use of them! What's more, you can customize your characters move sets and pick new skills from any class as you level. The classes are more like archetypes, really, just to give you a start, but you can choose a custom class as well.
There's a resource building mechanic so that future characters will be more successful, but you can opt to build up those resources and still not use them in the spirit of traditional roguelikes, but they're there if you want to give yourself an edge - and in such a way that you pick which edges you want and ignore the others.
There's a legacy system as well, but I won't try to explain it, just know that it's very very cool!
Procedural world, running legacies, themed dungeons - a - many, very tactical combat, tons of items and loot to find, towns to explore, libromancers to irritate, lots of enemies, champions, and named bosses, this game pretty much has it all!
TL;DR I honestly cannot give this game enough praise. It's hands-down the best roguelike I've ever played. If you like tile-based, grid-based roguelikes, DO NOT pass this game over!

If you like ToME or are familiar with its gameplay, Dungeonmans is similar but different in some areas.  I might end up liking it over ToME because of it's humor, charm and accessibility.  Both are excellent, so if you've played one of the two and like it, the other is a given.
I've spent about 12 hours with it (I play some steam-less so the hours played won't be accurate) and I've gotten quite far, yet I'm still surprised quite often.  I've barely explored the world map, but that's mostly due to my completely self-inflicted deaths.  I'm getting the hang of it now and the fact that you can combine any class skills together in combos makes for excellent versatility, replay and fun.  Right now, I'm playing a heavy-armor wearing ranger / necro hybrid.  It's awesome.
While ToME may be rich in story / lore, Dungeonmans makes up for it in charm.  The visuals, sound and music are excellent.  I especially love the over-the-top level up screen and boss defeat animations.  This game also has some persistence; that is, if you provide your starting academy with certain items you get when completing dungeons, you'll get to assign more stat points to your future "dungeonmans".  You also find rare skill books, and if you'd rather not use them, donate them to your library and eventually you'll be able to start the game knowing more and more scroll effects.  Provide your armorer with loot that's been molten down and you can start your future dudes with stronger armor, weapons, etc.
You have your overworld map, which is randomized and contains towns you can visit to buy/sell loot, dungeons, bandit barricades and other stuff.  Random battles rarely occur when you're on this overworld map, and you can skip most but not all.  I personally like them; they're different than your usual dungeon crawling and can have variety of enemies including champions.
What's also cool is if you die in a certain dungeon, you can go to that same area / floor with your next guy and collect some XP and possibly a weapon.  It's not game breaking but it surely helps.
Mouse and keyboard control work very well, but it would be nice to be able to remap the controls without delving into a text file.  Thankfully, the text file is easy to understand so remapping the entire keyboard can be done in minutes.  The file, along with Dungeonmans's savegames are located in \users\*username*\AppData\Roaming\Dungeonmans.  I think the file is keybindings.txt but if it's not, it'll be fairly obvious.
In conclusion, I'm addicted to this game.  I can already tell it'll become one of my mainstay roguelikes that I can enjoy for years.  To the developer - you should port your game to the PS4 system.  It is sorely lacking in fun roguelikes, and while PC is an excellent platform, your game would be the perfect mix of difficulty, charm and fun for the console community.

The Red Orchestra series is truly one of my all-time favorite FPS-series.

While there are unlocks, they only give you a mild advantage, which you do not need to succeed, something that modern FPS games don't do anymore.
Most importantly: there are no god damn micro transactions.
This is a pretty cheap game to begin with, and the publisher does not try to slow down your progression and force booster down your throat, which I feel is something worth mentioning.
This series made me aware of Tripwire interactive, one of the few publishers I truly like (though the KF1 DLCs were a bit over the top) and whose games I continue to look forward to and keep buying.

Melissa K. and the Heart of Gold Collector's Edition is just another point and click games with a lot of mini games on it. The game itself classifies the mini games into 2 parts: Puzzles and Hidden Object. The puzzles are basically a different and unique mini game while the hidden object is... just like other hidden object games where you have to find specified items. There are some collectibles in this game, although you can't see the progress unless you are in adventure mode (story mode). Other than that, it's basically the same as other games with the same type (read: Artifex Mundi games).
To be honest, i got some trouble in understanding the story. The story doesn't flow quite well, and the messed-up subtitle timing makes it worse. I like how they are talking in a normal speed in cutscenes, but other than in cutscenes, people are talking too slow for me. I know that it's kinda normal for a game like this to have people talking very slow, but i think it's not needed.
Switching to the plot, although the big picture of the story is given out, the story lacks detail, especially on how they are not even telling why they have to move to another place. The tasks given on the game doesn't really flow well (especially when you have to talk to someone out of nowhere and some items which are appearing out of nowhere) and i have to admit that i will have a lot of trouble if i'm not playing this game with a walkthrough in hand.
Because this is a collector's edition, there is a guide on this game. I just want to say that the guide section doesn't really well-made, and i rather use the steam guide rather than the in game guide. The guide is only listing pictures and youtube video, and it loads slowly when i open it for the first time.
The graphics in this game is decent. I hope you are not expecting graphics in AAA titles in this game, because it's far from that. However, i am impressed with the details for the face part and how the mouth are syncing with the voice. The environment details are made greatly, and i was really touched with how the artists were trying to make the environment as close as the real one (you can see it on the bonus track).
Well, i can't really say much about sound in a game like this, because they give off the same vibe. The music is kind of relaxing and slow, which makes a perfect sound, especially when you are doing the mini games. The voice overs are done beautifully, especially the "crazy monk", because imo, that's the one who were giving the most effort in doing the voice overs. However, i have to admit that the ghosts voice are hard to be heard.
There are a lot of mini games in this game, with some being easy and some being hard (this includes both the puzzle and hidden object games). Some puzzles have difficulty level which gives another difficult level to solve, while some hidden object games have a different type of hidden object: a hidden object game with a text as the list-to-find-items besides images. To be honest, i enjoy the mini games a lot, especially the puzzles. Although the hidden object is just the same as you'll expect, there are tons of variations in the puzzles.
This game can satisfy you in weekends with its long playtime and you can enjoy it to the fullest with tons of mini games on it.
Pros:
- Tons of mini games
- Collectibles
Cons:
- Story doesn't flow well

I've only been playing for about a month and I never played NF1, I just added this to steam with the new patch last week. I don't have a deep knowledge of every aspect of NF2, this is more from a new players perspective.
Basically, its a fun game that is flawed. The tutorial is short and nearly useless, but after going through that 2-3 times and playing a dozen or so battles and you get the idea. Once you get the hang of leading targets and using the focus fire you start to settle in pretty fast with the different ship types/playstyles.
There is a wide variety of ships in branching trees that work logically for the most part. There are a few ships which seem out of sort with dreadnought-era tiered against others from 20-30 years later but these issues end up moot through balancing. Each ship has upgrades for modules which are limited but do add to your ships capability.
Each nation you play will have a crew. As you play your crew levels up. This leveling up leads to an annoying amount of micromanaging after battle as you increase crew skills. As the commander levels up you can also add more officers to yield even better crew stats overall. You can pay for gold officers which yield slightly better bonuses than credit officers. There is also an aid you can buy (both silver and gold ones) which can help you gain XP/credits faster.
Then there is the economy. The first 3-4 tiers are pretty easy to unlock. After my first two hours or so I had a BB and CA.  Then it starts to slow down and feel a bit grindy by tier 5-6. Ships start costing a lot more but you don't earn much more XP/creds. Rewards for each game sometimes seem totally random. I have gotten near identical rewards for a game where I died early without landing more than a few shots and another with a few kills where I doubled my HP in damage done.
Overall, I like NF2. I can't take it too seriously with the P2W elements (consumables, crew/officers, consumable slots etc), but in my opinion its flaws are outweighed by the fun arcade shoot em up style of game play.

TL:DR Do you have a realistic expectation of alpha/early access games? Are you willing to wait for more features and enjoy the current game in the mean time? Do you like the genre of this game?

I have been playing this game pre-EA release, and honestly believe it is one of the most satisfying kickstarters I have ever backed and is already quite fun to play. It has a brilliant balance of city building, crafting and RPG elements, and rewards the player with a real feeling of progression. Each citizen has their own stats and skills which you can improve and you are able to get very creative with your architecture already with a little effort.
PRO
- Developer communication, every week there are numerous posts on their websites dev blog covering their progress and frequent developer streams where you may have direct imput in the creation of the game.
- The game is being designed to be ULTRA modder friendly, I myself, someone with NO prior experience making mods have already made a few myself without causing bugs in the game in an alpha state. (Expect workshop support)
- Frequent updates, the game is beginning to progress rather quickly and is adding features and busting bugs EVERY patch.
- A wonderful art style, it maintains a simple charm while still looking brilliant and handling rather well even on less powerful machines.
- Balanced progression, the game in this current state is slow enough to last but fast enough to hold your attention.
- A fast forward button, I personally find this extremely important for things such as building or mining, or passing time while not active.
CON
- This is an alpha, there are occasional bugs, especially following new versions, but far fewer than there have been previously. For an alpha I have seen a relatively low amount and they always seem to get fixed before I can encounter them more times but there will be some bugs and if you go in to an early access game not expecting bugs you will be dissapointed.
- Villager progression through classes is currently incomplete, quite a few are implemented so far but it does reduce the games variety.
- can be hard at times as death of a skilled citizen can set you back for a while.
