This is a highly enjoyable, in development, town building game. I have spent many hours building towns, learning the game, and enjoying the new game aspects they are adding from patch to patch as well as the bug fixes.
With all of the good things however, there are a few bad.
- The map generation takes quite a while per map roll (time consuming when looking for specific setups)
- Save files are not compatible with updates, meaning you will need to restart each time there's an update
These two things are not game breaking major, and they are wanting to implement the backward compatibility with save files, to prevent the need to constantly restart with updates, so it should no longer be a problem when they implement it.
This game offers unique textures and means to build your town as well as prevents the need to have them always be building whatever is placed, which helps prevent accidents. This lets you build roads, houses, and other structures the way you want it. Do you want a flat area? Doable, do you want a roof-less house? Doable. Multi-structured mansion? Doable. Throw your guys in a hole and never able to get out? This can also be done, and those who are fans of the Tycoon games, such as Rollercoaster Tycoon, you will be familiar with the ability to trap your visitors where they cannot leave, or killing them with rides. Make this your own experience with the city and enjoy yourself as you do so.
I will modify and go into more detail with this review as time goes on and as the game develops.
Update 11/27/2015:
This game has received quite a few updates since the original review. They have added the ability to create multi-tiered structures in the game, however this feature is a bit wonky and not 100% working in my opinion, as the settlers will often fail to build the bottom half of the house before the upper half or not build the building at all. They have also improved the errors that may happen in the game - if something were to bug out, it is no longer in a nasty developer box, but rather something a bit more user friendly to understand and depending on what fails, offers instructions on fixing the issue.
There are some present AI issues in the game that can make it a bit frustrating to have a large amount of tasks, I've been able to circumvent this issue in the developer versions of Alpha 13 - which is said to fix the AI issues in regards to building, etc, but may not be 100% done yet - by removing the request and redoing it or suspending/pausing the task then resuming it. Assuming there isnt still a ton of things already requested for them to do, they often figure out that it still needs to be completed. The game is still very much in a playable state and I still highly enjoy it and my original review still stands at this point in time. They are making progres toward finishing the game and adding features. Please note that at the time of this update, that saves are still not backward/forward compatible. And my original con of the map generation taking a lot of time still stands as well, but it feels a bit faster than it once was.
A few other major things they've added are a new style of settler and a new map biome type - the desert and raya's children. I've been able to play around with them in the developer build and its a very interesting change of pace to the normal gameplay that I had grown to love. This in combination with new professions and crafting systems in place permit for a more diverse and intricate creation system, making it feel like the crafters actually rely on each other to make the final product rather than it being a one man army. They have also vastly improved the game experience with making it run faster on my machine, and offering various options to help with slower/older machines as well as bug fixes. I haven't had massive bugs in regards to the UI or other pop-ups outside of one where I was clicking on buttons rapidly.
So let me mark off my cons at this point in time in regards to Alpha 12/Dev Alpha 13:
- Some AI issues in regards to tasks where they fail to complete (see above for my solution and some info)
- Map generation still takes too much time
- Save files are still not backward/forward compatible
This said, let me list some pros of this game thus far
- Multi-tiered structures
- Intricate crafting system
- Ability to trap your settlers
- Aggressive (normal surviving) & Peaceful mode (for building)
- Various travelling merchants
There's a lot more as well that I would list off but this review would end up to be too long.

Although Stonehearth isn't a revolutionary game, it is still very enjoyable. Even though I’ve only owned the game since Alpha 9, I have spent enough time in the game to get a good feel for the gameplay, features, and overall value of the game. At this point in development I can recommend the game for those looking for a fun game, but aren’t afraid to test out builds, and find bugs.
In the games current state your goal is to not kill all your hearthlings. When starting the game you are given virtually nothing to survive other than a tool to make a carpenter and a trapper. From there your job is to craft tools, give hearthlings jobs, and start to grow a tiny civilization. If you are playing on the Peaceful game mode then you really don’t have anything to worry about beyond keeping your hearthlings well fed. The other game mode at this time is Normal, and includes some nice goblins for you to fight with. The goblins don’t make the game overly difficult at this time and really just add another degree of play. Personally I enjoy playing Normal since it can be somewhat boring playing on peaceful mode.
As of Alpha 10 the goblins haven’t been in the game very long. They do a nice job of adding more gameplay options though. With the inclusion of goblins you will need to take defense into consideration while building. They will not attack you immediately upon starting a game, but they do increase in difficulty as you grow stronger.
One of the strongest points this game has is the robust building mechanic. You can build whatever structures you can imagine, as long as it’s within the boundaries of tiny blocks. The build mode is very simple to use and really help you personalize it to your taste. When you get a structure created you can even save it to use at any time after that. It’s a really nice feature since you don’t have to worry about designing each building every time you need it. The game also allows you to edit the building before placing it, giving you a chance to personalize each one without the need to recreate it from scratch. The only issue I have found when designing the buildings you can’t add in items like desks, beds, chairs, or other things of that nature without having them created and sitting in your stockpile. Luckily you just need 1 on hand to add them into the building blueprint.
At this time the hearthlings don’t really have traits, but they do have stats. The stats are things like speed, courage, diligence, etc. and can affect how well a hearthling does his/her given job. As development continues I am sure we will see more stats, traits, and other features added to the individual hearthlings.
That is really just a rundown of the main features the game has at this time. If you are interested in learning more about the game feel free to join us over at the
forums. We always have some discussion going about the game, and keep up with all the little bugs in need of squashing. You can also find my pros/cons breakdown below.

- Music
- Art style
- Crafting system
- Builing/Blueprint system is awesome
- Fun factor
-Replayability
-Great development team
- Occasional building issues
- LUA issues(LUA hits 100% causing game to lag and freeze)
- Ocassional errors while playing
- Lighting/Shadow issues
The only con that I’ve found to really be a hindrance is the LUA problem the game runs into. You can see the game resources in real time while playing via a small bar on the bottom right of the game client. Once the LUA usage hits 100% the game will lag completely out. This is a known issue and will hopefully be addressed soon.

I've put a lot of my time into this game since it's launch. I've played in the Alpha, Beta, and launch versions, so I've seen this game slowly warp into the game it is today. I've played on both the casual and pro level, but this review will only talk about the casual level.
First I'll start off with what it'll be like just picking this game up. This game will kick your♥♥♥♥♥if you aren't ready to spend a couple of hours figuring out the basics you'll likely not have fun with this game. You can't just pick up this game and start playing it like any other FPS or action game. the first thing you'll need to learn is how to track the monster, I recommend playing the T1 trapper Maggie in order to quickly learn how to properly track. Once you've figured out how to track the monster I guarantee this'll be one of the most exciting games you've ever played. If you want help on tracking youtube videos and guides can be found on Reddit/TRS forums.
Once you've gotten past the basic level you can have a lot of fun with the game even in pubs. Playing skirmish is a good way to play if you want to play hunter, but don't have a team set up. I also recommend playing Skirmish before you jump straight into the Hunt only playlist, as this playlist is highly competitive. At a casual level the gameplay is solid, quick, responsive, and addicting. Each of the classes of hunter point to a specific type of playstyle. Medic is your go to class if you want to be the difference between annihilation and killing the monster. Support is for the player that wants to buff the team, and debuff the monster. Trapper is for the player that wants to constantly outplay the monster. Assault is for the guy who just wants to shoot everything. If you don't want to play with pubs then you can pick the monster. The four monsters also pull at different playstyles you can pick stealth, bruiser, strategy, or tank. The hunters have similar gameplay differences, but they generally will fill the same role.
On the issue of DLC I feel this game has done a fair job of telling the consumer of what they're getting, and I feel the price of the DLC is justified. You'll pay 15 bucks for ~5 maps on some games while for 10 more bucks Evolve will give you 4 new hunters, and monsters that offer entire new mechanics to the game. All of the maps, and future game modes will always be free meaning that the community will never be segmented.
Overall this is one of my favorite games of the whole year, and I bet most of you guys here would enjoy the game if you gave it a chance.

One of my Biggest Regrets on Steam
Evolve is an FPS PVP sort of crossover where two teams fight to the death
On one side you play as the Hunters whos jobs are to kill the monster. The hunters are separated into 4 classes
Assault- Deals heavy damage to the monster and the offense of the group
Medic-   heals the group
Support- Supports the other classes
Trapper- Slows down the monster and keeps it away from the group. Also uses a pet to track the monster
My Opinion for these classes is that I don't care for any of them because most of the time you will be trying to catch up with the monster and that can get extremely boring. You can kill other small monsters so the monster can't eat them but that is pointless because there are small monsters everywhere around the map. When you do catch up to the monster then there is some actual action but if you don't kill it prepare for more boredom of running around trying to find the monster and if it reaches level 3 good luck even trying to kill it. Yes i know there are more hunters you can unlock by playing more of the game but i never had the paitence to do it I hated playing as the hunters.
On the other hand you can play as the monster where you must feed on small animals and grow big to defeat the hunters or an alternative is reaching level 3 and cutting the power. So far there are 4 monsters in the game
Goliath- Can do melee and ranged attacks to damage hunters and can jump a high distance
Kraken-Can generate electricity to deal ranged damage to the hunters and can fly
Wraith- Can pick off the hunters 1 by 1 and has the ability to dash
Behemoth- Can deal major Melee damage to hunters but has the inability to jump as it must climb
In my opinion the Wraith is my favourite monster to play, I enjoy playing as Goliath however i don't like the kraken and I have not played as the behemoth yet. When playing evolve I always find myself playing as the monster because he is FUN!!! When you start the game you are given 3 skill points to apply to 4 skills for your monster and as you evolve you gain 3 more skill points. The Max evolution level is 3 so you only get 9 skill points if you do get to level 3. The way to evolve is to attack and eat smaller monsters which can also restore your shield as you lose health permanently. This  is much more fun than running around trying to look for the monster. You can also kill rare albino animals which if eaten gives you a bonus ability but you can only have one at a time. Now I love playing as the monster but there because of the monster the game is also completely unbalanced compared to the hunters because  1. The monster has the ability to smell which is like a radar for the monster. Not only can it smell other small monsters but it can also smell the hunters so you know when they are getting close to you and you start to run causing the hunters to possibly not run into the monster once until it reaches level 3 where the hunters will most likely lose. 2. Some of the monster skills are downright BROKEN!!! including the wraith's supernova which if maxed out can destroy 1 hunter in mere seconds there is also the kraken's banshee mine where you are most likely to get hit by it when fighting the kraken. Those are the reasons why i sometimes find the monster to be broken. And there is one last flaw with the monster class where in order to unlock the other monsters you must play the same monster over and over again until you max out exp with skills you probably never use which brings me to the biggest problem I have with evolve. It is very repetitive and has little to no replay value what so ever. When you first play this game it starts out fun but after a couple of hours later you start to get really bored of it. The way they have you unlock new things is Bulls**t as you have to play the game over and over again just to level up the skill you never used in the first place. But overall I still like playing as the monster even with these flaws
There is also different game modes in the game but i Only played hunt because I did not care about the other game modes because I couldn't bring myself to try it out.
Extra settings include giving the hunters or monster a handicap which can favour the opposite team like man eating plants which can damage the hunters, clear skies and more birds to track the monster eaiser.  I didn't care for these settings because it just makes the game even more unbalanced.
Grapically speaking it is dark, edgy and grim which is what i expect for a game like this but you have to have a great computer to run this game smoothly. On my laptop it the frame rate started chugging not to the point where i couldn't play the game but It bothered me a little.
The Verdict: Evolve is one of those games where it would be great on paper but it is done horribly wrong. The Hunters are a Chore to play, The way you unlock new things is bulls**t. I didn't care for the other game modes other than hunt
extra settings just make the game more unbalanced than it already is and overall it is just A clusterf**k of a game. The only thing I like about this game is playing as the monster because he is much more fun to play than the Hunters.
I recommend waiting for a price drop at around $20-$25 as $40 is not worth it. I bought this game when it first came out and I payed $70 dollars just for this game! I wanted to like this game but in the end All i got was A feeling of dissapointment and A feeling that i Just got robbed of $70.
My Final Rating for this game is a 4/10

A great game with turn based, isometric map movement set in a medieval fantastic, dark gothic world. I like the improvements over Disciples II such as having a bigger party, having skills for your heroes, attributes, levels and even a paperdoll to equip items. The art direction or style remains the same as in Disciples II; It's gothic medieval fantastic and epic. The map, the units and the battles are all in 3d. In the single player campaign (only thing I've played), there are about 24 maps (I might be wrong) divided in Legions (Chaos), Humans and Elves. So about 8 maps for each race and each map can take more than an hour to finish. You can hire multiple heroes and transfer units between your heroes (as well as items) at will once both heroes are next to each other. There are permanent stat and skills boosters available to purchase. You can hire mercenaries, capture towns, build your capital, reinforce your "nodes". The battles are now played on a bigger board than in Disciples II. Each of your unit can move around the map and some spots you can move to have random bonuses specific to a unit's class (ranged, melee, magic).
Bad sides: I don't know why they removed the "wait" action. Sometimes, my hero would be surrounded at my first turn (by a rock in front of him and 2 units on each side plus a full rank behind). Since my hero has the highest initiative, he acts first and thus cannot just "wait" but ends up defending, which messes up everything regarding the deployment. The battles can be a bit long and repetitive, even with randomized terrain but I should check the options to skip animations at least.
Overall a must-try for Disciples fans and well worth trying for newcomers in search of deep turn based strategy and tactics with stunning artistic presentation.

I'll start by saying that while I really love the game and the survival aspect I absolutely despise the game-y wolves. I greatly enjoy playing on Interloper difficulty because it feels like a true cold-weather survival game. Unfortunately most of my play-throughs end with getting killed by a wolf in an often very ridiculous fashion. To use my latest example, 9 days in and I am doing very well unforunately my hunger is running low so I am forced to scavenge an area I know that is frequented by wolves. But I'm hungry and desperate. Hunger is my only current issue as I am flush for resources and gear. As I approach two wolves begin to charge at me, fortunately there is a vehicle nearby and I hop in the vehicle and use my bedroll to sleep for a few hours. It's night time now and the wolves seem to be gone, I get out of the car and run about 200m to the building I intended to loot, there are no wolves in sight. Finally I am in the building I find enough food to allow me to have a good nights sleep, though I will need to search for more food in the morning. Fast forward the entire night and morning and it is noon. I ready my gear step out the instanced door, intending to take a quick look around and retreat inside if needed, but there is a wolf so close to me that I can only see the top of his head, and without time to do anything the wolf is immediately on top of me and at 50% health on Interloper difficulty I am dead.
I've seen this issue reported 3 years ago and it still seems to be a thing even though they said it's not intended. With the game nearing full release next month the fact that this still occurs leads me to think that it's just a part of the game. While the wolves can lead to fun and intense gameplay, more often than not they server as unfair spoilers without a weapon and a free source of resources when you do have a weapon. They are the zombies that are shoehorned in your survival game, they are the cliche jump-scare in your horror game, they are the antagonist that upstages mother nature herself in a game where she is supposed to be the star.
I hope someday they'll add custom difficulty or just fix many of the cheesy wolf interactions like the one I described.

There are many (!) good reviews about Bioshock so there's no point in going on. And while I recommend it and think it totally deserves this positivity, I WOULD write a few (just a few) points which did bother me a little, and may be critical to other players:
*Game is quite linear. It didn't bother me greatly, but I know some wouldn't like it at all. There are plenty of corners for you to explore and look around for resources and cool stuff you collect throughout the game, so it really bothered me only at the very end when I felt I didn't have much to find anymore. So, not 100% linear, but mostly linear.
*Story is unfolded mostly with tape recordings. Actual happenings are really mostly at the very beginning and towards the end of the game. That one actually REALLY bothered me, I found it harder to concentrate and understand the story this way. It could also make things boring & repetitive at times. But all in all, the whole story of Bioshock is pretty much worth it.
*Game is completely playable on modern machines despite being old, but nonetheless it's not innocent some bugs and glitches, personally I've encountered a tendency of the voice acting so suddenly disappear at some of the non-tape-recordings moments, which are the most crucial ones, leaving me only with the subtitles which I couldn't even finish reading at times. I couldn't find a solution to this problem and that really ruined a moment or two throughout the game. From trying to figure it out I found that there are plenty of others encountering the same issue and some others as well. Ah well. Just some technical bugs, but really, they're not that common.

Space Colony was originally released in 2003 and then upgraded to HD in 2012. Steam Edition is now let loose in 2015 that adds all of the modern conveniences, including a brand new single-player campaign, achievements and both workshop and cloud support. Core of the game is focused on real-time strategy but it brings so much more. Great blend of  Sims, Time Management, City-Building, Strategy and Tower Defense gameplay along with a distinct 90s space vibe.
Initially getting given options of playing through the campaign (including cut-scenes and stats that carryover between missions), galaxy mode (choose your own planets and pathway), sandbox mode (choose your own planets and given access to more equipment without upgrading) or loading user-created mods. Included are a bunch of community favorites but there is a huge selection to choose from. With the addition of a reasonably intuitive level editor and steam workshop support it would be very easy to spend many hours just playing custom games.
Thankfully even though upgraded, Space Colony has kept all of it's original charm. The tacky yet amusing banter between odd-couple characters, the combination of 70s disco and elevator music and the space creatures straight out of your favorite B horror movies. For fans of the genres I mentioned above this is a game
, more so if you never had a chance to play the originals because (imo) you are in for an absolute treat. Just make sure you have the spare time as it can be quite addictive.
Few small downsides, Inability to zoom your view (older engine) but the wonderfully detailed pixel art makes up for this and sometimes the UI can be a little clunky though more a matter of playing the game longer. Highly recommended game and one worth shortlisting. Cheers folks. :)

This game has some serious balancing and design issues.
First, the game isn't really idle - main mechanic is about looting items that drop from monsters, and for that you have to be actively playing the game (items disappear after several seconds).
Second, the reason why looting the items is the main mechanic is because item quality keeps increasing as your average item strength grows. No matter which zone you are in or what heroes you have. So you could practically stay in one zone and keep looting better and better gear. And power from gear quickly overshadows base strength from heroes.
Third, because of the looting mechanic, and how gear becomes the main source of power - gold becomes useless. At first it may not seem that way because you keep unlocking new heroes which at first are stronger than gear. But as you reach final heroes you find out that gear is the only way forward and there is no point buying further levels for heroes.
Fourth, you quickly learn that the only factor affecting the speed of your progress is the speed at which you loot items. Which means that it's actually preferable to NOT move into further zones and just keep farming gear on monster which die in 1 second. Oh, you can't go back to earlier zones, so getting forward actually means slowing your progress (monster die slower -> you loot less items -> item strength grows slower)
Fifth, gear stats are messed up. Bonuses that increase critical damage or chance are useless. Bonuses that increase gold drops are useless because gold is useless. Bonuses that increase damage by percentage are useless, because they increase it by percentage of base strength, before items are applied. The only meaningful bonus is the flat damage increase.
Sixth, ascension bonuses are useless once you understand that 5% damage increase can be attained by simply looting items for 2 more minutes. Boss timer bonus is useless because you simply don't want / need to go ahead, because that will only slow your progress.

Simply put, this is one of the best WWII MP games ever, especially if you like more tactical and hardcore gameplay. The fact that this includes Rising Storm means that you get both the Eastern and Pacific fronts. This is awesome as both are very rare in the realm of WWII online shooters. Playing as Germany, Russia, Japan, and the United States is an awesome and varied collection of countries/weapons.
The multiplayer battles are an incredible mode. They obviously reward teams for capturing enough objectives to win the match, but also reward teams for inflicting heavy casualties on the enemy team. Doing so takes down their combat power for the next match. Having this progression in the campaigns means each individual match means more than just one long match.
This is a great MP shooter for those who appreciate attention to historical details. Tripwire clearly did research to capture the feeling of the war as closely as you can in a game. There is still a small but dedicated community for these games, which speaks to their quality as they've been out for years. They are the types of games where new players will be punished in the early hours while learning the ropes. However, having the patience to stick with it pays off in many ways and gives way to insanely fun gameplay in long hard fought matches that have an impact on the next battles to come.

An excellent, top shelf WW2 shooter. Even after many years, this game is still grand.
I've only played the multiplayer, but that experience is more than enough to convince me of this game's superb quality.
Red Orchestra 2 has a variety of engaging and inspiring stages set in WW2. Before each battle, you can choose whether to fight for the Russian or German side and the American or Japanese side, depending on the map. Each faction has a unique variety of weapons with distinct traits as well as a number of classes to choose from. However, the amount of players per class is limited-- and with good reasons, of course. Balance, mainly.
Choosing your role and playing your part in this grand spectacle feels immensely satisfying. As a flick shooter, this game is definitely on the slower side, but that doesn't tarnish the excitement value. In this game, you are constantly living in the moment and fighting to survive to complete objective after objective. Often times, you'll find yourself being the deciding factor in vastly improving your team's chances of success. Despite the huge battlefields and 30 v 30 lobbies, this game finds a way to make every player count.
The weapons are satisfying to shoot. Everything works well in this game. Even the graphics age well for their time and still looks good today. They obviously weren't messing around with this game. Unfortunately, the player base is dwindling, with about 700 players playing at a time. This means you won't always be able to choose what map you want to play.
Regardless, this is a game of quality. Play it if you can.

Where to begin? From the start, The Long Dark has been a very ambitious project by a small, experienced team dedicated to realism in conveying the beauty of the northern Canadian wilderness and the danger inherent behind it. The development process has seen incredible changes to almost all aspects of the game, and the polished amount of content seen in the current build - nearing on release - is remarkable, especially looking back on the humble launch in 2014. It's a 'post-apocalyptic' game, but in the complete opposite sense of the urban dystopia. Nature has reclaimed the desolate reaches of the world, and in this open Sandbox, the player struggles to survive amid picturesque scenery.
Naturally, much of the appeal of this game is in the atmospheric, stylised visuals. The artstyle is effective in creating an aesthetically pleasing, almost painted look to the world. One that draws you in and captures the imagination. It's gripping in how subtly everything comes together - the soundwork, music, designs and ultimately the lonely nature of gameplay (so far as Sandbox is concerned), create moments that are intensely visceral and often deafeningly quiet, to peaceful and serene. Calm moments of awe at the scope of your surroundings and your insignificance in comparison to it.
This brings me to the actual gameplay itself, which is intuitive, lending well to the setting and scenery. The stat system you rely on to survive is such that instead of being a micromanaging burden, it forces the player to be purposeful in what they do and constantly aware. Be it staying alert to the potential presence of animals, to scanning the horizons for clues of where to go next/ find food/shelter/supplies, or being conscious of changes in weather. It similarly adds all the more urgency in thinking through and planning your actions that you only have one save and one chance. Once your character dies, it's over. All your progress is lost and you have to start again.
But where this might've had the effect of discouraging starting anew, there's an excitement in once again setting out into the unknown with a randomised spawn location and learning from previous mistakes.
One thing to note, is the accessability in how the game can actually be played too. The variety of 'difficulty' settings change, among other things, the behaviour of predatory animals - from being another source of scenery in Pilgrim mode, to an ever-present and ominous, lurking threat in Interloper, with settings inbetween too (unrealistic behaviour for bears and wolves, but explained as being related to the post apocalyptic disaster). This, along with the versatility of having challenge modes and a fully fledged, authored, story mode, give the game a lot of replay value.
I look forward to see where the development will go in the future and how the story will progress, as the roadmap is ever changing. The involved nature of The Long Dark community and the team really create a feeling that this isn't a static project, but a living, breathing, collaborative work.
Truly a breath of fresh air.

I used to hate Bioshock. Even before earing about System Shock 2, it didn't really "hit me" as much as it did everyone else.
Bioshock is System Shock 2 without freedom of approach. Most people hadn't played System Shock 2 in 2005/6, so that shallowness kinda went unnoticed. It was hinting at great gameplay depth but it didn't require any. Nowadays, after seeing games like Deus Ex HR, Prey, Dishonored, Metal Gear Solid 5 and Zelda: Best of the Worst, etc. I can hardly believe even a part-time gamer wouldn't find Bioshock a bit wasteful in its design.
It's an FPS pretending to be an immersive sim... But, ultimately, it's a pretty damn good FPS.
The production value is incredible, the environments are non-linear and fun to explore, it sounds perfect, the story and its concepts wins in having lots of really interesting, extremely clever pieces (even though the whole "puzzle" isn't as great as SS2), it's memorable and iconic and proactive and whatever.
It's a special game that casts a huge shadow of quality over most other games. But it has shadows of it's own that not enough people know about. As far as quality goes, I'd say it's on par with the early Resident Evil games.

It has tons of replay value as there are many ways you can decide on how to kill enemies.  From straight up shooting them until they're dead with the various types of guns and ammunition you find to using different powers you aquire throughout the game which can levitate enemies, shock enemies, set enemies on fire you'll always have a different experience everytime you play.
Combine that with tons of side optional questing you can do, an array of secret rooms, chests you'll never get bored and you'll easily amass over one hundred hours into the game across multiple playthroughs.

Similarly, ammo is plentiful, you'll literally never run out of it even if you kill every single thing that moves.

Detailed:
I played Disciples 2 through the whole of 2014, and loved it. Disciples 3 is a modernised, but overall worse game than its prequel.
+ The core gameplay elements are the same as the previous game, aside of learning the 3D controls and upgraded battle mechanics, it's fairly easy to get back into the game if you played D2.
+ The graphics have been updated for the current decade, everything is "shinier", the capitals look awesome.
+ Very atmospheric and catchy background music.
+ The new interactive objects slightly enrich the experience.
+ The battles are more interesting with the added tactical movement map, though with manually controlling the movement of each unit they also take longer.
+ You carry over most items in the leader's inventory between campaign acts. Also the shop in the capital is quite handy for selling all the junk from the previous act to boost the starting budget.
~ Removing the rod-bearer unit is an interesting choice. Being able to conquer territory with the main team certainly makes the game flow smoother. On the other hand the vulnerable but essential rod-bearers added an extra tactical layer to D2.
~ The times of the day alternating each turn is interesting, though I wish there was an option to just leave it on daylight. The others add atmosphere, but make the various items and enemies on the map harder to see. This leads to...
~ Tons of achievements, but quite a few are unlockable without editing files or even with that. (
)
- The movement map is prioritising looks to the detriment of usability. Often interactive objects are only noticeable if you highlight them with the Alt key. Similarly the enemy units are mostly unnoticeable on the main map, and not even get highlighted by Alt.
- Inconsistent stat names, eg. a potion says it gives extra Dexterity, but when used it actually increases Agility instead of Dexterity and vice versa.
- The inventory feels a lot more cluttered than in D2 with the huge icons and no way to sort the items.
- Only 2 hotkeys (for passing turn and highlighting map objects), even though many functions would sorely need it.
- Buggy and not-user-friendly UI.
- You can only carry over your beginning Leader between campaign acts, and most plot triggers only unlock with him. This basically forces you to play the whole campaign with a melee leader :(
- You can only cast 1-2 spells
per turn, instead of being able to cast 1-2
of spell per turn as in D2.
- Each time the players casts a spell, they have to wait for the whole 10-11 sec animation to finish before the game becomes responsive again. This makes the spells giving extra movement mostly useless, as passing a turn takes a fragment of the time compared to the spell's animation.
- The Dwarf and Undead nations are missing. (Though at least they added the Undeads in the Resurrection edition, but we never get to play the Dwarves again.)
- When you type a space in Steam overlay mode, the game passes a turn.
- Way more so than the maps in D2, there's no feeling of open spaces, the maps feel very linear and railroad-like, robbing the sense of exploration.
- The tactical maps are randomly generated, and their layout can significantly affect the battle.
- The game doesn't show any more what percentage of land is controlled by the various factions, instead it shows the resource incomes in two different places. Also it's hard to tell apart the Empire territory from the Neutral lands, it was a lot better in D2.
- Clichéd story and mostly badly written dialogues.
- The narrator's voice acting is quite bad, he's trying, but his voice has no power or majesty to it, instead sounds like a slightly bored office worker. Also the elven unit voiceovers are horrible, instead of the previous game's "elven language", they speak English with a cheap "metallic" effect to distort their voice. Ew.
- Some pointlessly sexualised female outfits.
- Some of the sound effects are quite funny and unfitting.
I wanted to love this game, but I have strongly mixed feelings about it. It still provides some fun, but that's probably due to me loving the basic gameplay concept and its prequel. For someone else, who is not that much in love with these, it's probably a more frustrating than enjoyable experience.

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #48 - Disciples III: Renaissance
I'll start with a disclaimer that I've never played any of the other Disciples games, so I didn't have any particular expectations coming into this game.   But, having played some turn based fantasy strategy games before, I kind of had an idea what to expect.
I can't say my immediate first impression was that great, as the game opens up with a narrated cutscene that sounded like they just asked someone in the office to record rather than spending the money on an actual voice actor.
The game offered a choice of game modes when I started a new game.  For my review, I stuck to the Campaign game mode, and started with the tutorial, which acts as an introductory mission to the overall campaign.
Gameplay seems pretty similar to the other turn based games I've played, with my party moving around on an overland map gathering resources.  When running into encounters, the game will then switch to a tactical hex based map where turn based combat takes place.  It didn't seem like there were a lot of options in the actual fight.  Each of the party members has a basic "attack" which varies based on the type of character it is.  For instance my main character did a melee attack.  But other character types can shoot arrows, cast an offensive spell, or heal other party members.  Characters can also go into a defensive stance rather than attacking.
Another hallmark of these types of games are the towns that you can upgrade to add other building types, which in turn unlock other types of characters that can be recruited into your party.
There is some customization you can do with your main character.  As you progress and get experience, you will end up getting skill points which you can spend to buy skills.  You also get attribute points which you can use to up your main attributes.  Treasure can be found on the overland map and certain items will be equippable by your main character, which generally serve to upgrade stats.
I got through the tutorial and played about 30 minutes into the first mission.  It never seemed difficult to me at all, but I was playing on easy, so that is a reasonable expectation.  I'm just not sure if it's supposed to ramp up in difficulty in later missions.
The UI is servicable but felt a little clunky at times.  I didn't like the fact that I couldn't hit Escape to bring up the options menu.  Instead you have to click the gear icon at the top right.  In fact pretty much all of the menus in the game are accessed by clicking a particular icon, but it wasn't always obvious from looking what icon did what.  It took some getting used to.
I did like how right clicking on anything of interest would give you a popup with details on whatever you clicked on.  At a minimum the popup will tell you what the item is and what it does.  I also liked how if the item was 'recharging' (such as a well that you can drink from every 4 turns), it would tell you how many turns left until it could be used again.
Overall I found the game to be a bit simplistic for a strategy game, but reasonably easy to pick up.  I do think there are much better turn based strategy games out there that I would recommend instead of this.  Still, I had fun in the time I played so I can give this a lukewarm recommendation.
Make sure you get the Reincarnation rather than Renaissance because it is this game massively updated.  I don't think they should be selling this version anymore.

I can absolutely recommend this game to those who enjoy old-school time/building/resource management games. The original may be from 2003, but it plays like games from the 90's with similar charm and quirkiness: Theme Hospital immediately comes to mind, for example.
In a similar vein to Theme Hospital, a lot of the basics become a bit monotonous (once you've built one corridor, you've built them all), but there are enough new building types and scenario objectives to keep it interesting. There's a whole host of things to do too, ranging from harvesting crops to mining, keeping bugs at bay and cleaning up a dirty station, treating injured colonists, having them sit down at a restaurant...you get the idea, it's a long list.
What really makes the game, for me, are the characters.
They each have quirky phrases and character interactions, and can go from totally satisfied in a relationship to stir-crazy and requiring detention to calm them down pretty rapidly without the correct needs satisfied - the most obvious one being human interaction. They die if not looked after, have audible banter when they bump into each other, moan when things aren't going well...it's fun to work out how to achieve the objectives of a new mission, but far more so to try out the new characters as they appear in your base.

Nethack and Rogue Legacy had a baby. That baby is named Dungeonmans.
From Nethack, it inherited...well, pretty much everything from Nethack.
From Rogue Legacy, it inherited the recently-coined "roguelite" system, whereby your character right now works on building your legacy, leaving behind bonuses for later characters, created when your current character almost-inevitably dies. If you like the idea of Dwarf Fortress, but could not get past the interface, this is the game for you. It's like a god game where you boss around a group of Minecraft players. You don't control your hearthlings individually, you simply direct them on what to do and they go and do it. The most control you have is in putting down a banner to tell a group of footmen to fight in a particular area (useful for invasions). Of course, you also tell them exactly where to mine, what trees to chop down, and what to build, you just don't control your workers to do this directly. Do well, and more hearthlings will join your mighty settlement. Do poorly, and your hearthlings will die by the crude sword of a goblin or die of starvation. It's a fully 3D voxel game in a randomly generated world where you mine, harvest, build, and conquer. The crafting system is still a work in progress, but there is a lot of stuff you can build, lots of upgrades for your workers and soldiers, and you can pretty much do whatever you like in the sandbox setting. Just look out for campaign events sent your way by the Game Master system (right now there's one campaign in three parts, but many, many more campaigns are coming). In addition to the campaigns are visits by travelers and traveling merchants you can deal with. These will give you some opportunities for trade that may benefit your settlement. Oh, and did I mention the game is extremely moddable? Oh yes, this is an indie game company that recognizes the value of their community, and wants to put the same tools in your hands that they use themselves to create content.
Right now Stonehearth is in alpha, Alpha 10.5 as I type this. Please don't buy this game yet in Early Access if you can't handle some bugs, even game-breaking bugs. Don't get too attached to your settlements, either; your save game won't be compatible with the next alpha, and new alphas come fairly quickly. Radiant Entertainment is a fantastic company and they've been great about keeping players informed about what's going on, and fixing bugs pretty fast, but some of you may find the game unplayable at various times. If you're willing to help them test and submit useful bug reports, great. If you're coming here expecting a fully playable game hold off and wait for Stonehearth to get into beta, at least. You'll have a lot more fun then.
According to their roadmap, about 90% of their custom core engine and technology is built. They're still about 70% on world generation, 60% on building tools, 50% on classes, 30% on the Game Master, and 20% on monsters and denizens. Multiplayer is coming too, but that's a long ways off. It's also worth noting that Mac and Linux versions are coming too, once they've got the core game finished.
That said, Stonehearth has come a very long way in a short period of time.
There are now 8 classes in the game in addition to the regular worker type class you get as the base. These include the Carpenter, Farmer, Weaver, Footman, Trapper, Shepherd, Mason, and Blacksmith. These provide the raw materials, and food your settlement needs, as well as the various tiers of crafted goods that allow you to advance up the tech tree of the game. Workers wearing a fancy set of clothes move quicker. Footmen with upgraded weaponry and armor are a lot better equipped to handle invasions of zombies, goblins, and wolves. And, of course, unless you want your hearthlings to live in a hole in the ground and sleep on the cold hard dirt, you'll want your carpenter building doors and windows for your houses, and your weaver can build nice curtains and make the cloth for your upgraded furniture like comfy beds. The mason will build stone walls and gates to keep invaders out or your shepherd's sheep in. Your crafters will of course build the tools necessary to upgrade your workers to advanced classes, as well. You can't have farmers without a carpenter to build wooden hoes. The interactions of these systems, combined with the need to manage your limited workforce, make the game complex and strategic. A lot of farmers means lots of food to attract new settlers to join your community, but not as many workers digging out tunnels to mine for valuable ores and increase the wealth your community has, wealth being another requirement for attracting new settlers.
In terms of the rest of the game, the building and harvesting tools have come along very well since the earliest alphas. At this point you can actually play the game, and get pretty far, doing pretty much what you want. Want to build a gigantic fort with a moat? Yep, that's possible. Want to build a deep lair in a mountain, with the entrance looking like some kind of huge voxel head with flaming eyes at night? Yep, that's doable! Just carve away into that mountain. There is, as I mentioned, only one Game Master campaign at the moment, so each play-through will feel a bit repetitive, but they are still building the systems behind such things. Once these systems are in place, they will add a lot more Game Master content (and modders will be able to add their own campaigns as well).
What I like best about this game is that you can really just play it however you like. The settlement I keep building each new alpha is very different from the settlements I see other people building. Technically the game is a sort of RPG/RTS/Roguelike, but at its core it's a sandbox game. It's a very fun sandbox to play in. While I would recommend this game to everyone, I wouldn't recommend you play this
if you'll be bothered by pop-up error logs or if your game suddenly stops working and that settlement you spent hours building suddenly can't be played with anymore. These problems do happen. They've gotten a lot rarer since Alpha 1, but this is still an Early Access game in alpha, and you should only buy this now if you have a tolerance for bugs.

If you are even remotely interested in this game or supporting it along it's journey, I recommend you check out their website.

Alright, so I played this game before story mode was released. I loved it as a 'tester' for something I had high expectations for. I played survival mode to exhaustion. It was an interesting game, however the novelty wore off after a few weeks. I played the different difficulties, saw a lot of the map. After a while, I realized a few flaws with the game, but who cares, it was still in development. I noticed how ridiculously quickly itmes wore out (even solid crowbars). Noticed that falling from a foot high could lead to serious injury. Not being able to jump was frustrating. I noticed how quickly the day would go by relative to my walking speed. I figured all of this would be dealt with when the game was actually released........ NOPE!
I tried story mode. It failed to grip me. I was trying to find a way to exit tutorial mode and soon realized that is just how the gameplay is. I loved the alpha version because it threw you in raw and you had to figure everything out. There was a sense of accomplishment when I learnt how to make water, or how to create a map! This game holds you by both hands and spoon feeds you. The story wasn't even compelling enough to keep me going, even if I was able to.... which leads me to my next point.
The save game options are so limited that they are game-breaking. There are only checkpoints. That's fine, a lot of games save by checkpoint. What's not fine is the non-existence of choosing a previous checkpoint to load from. I have not been able to progress in this game without having to restart the entire game and play through the mind numbing 'noob zone' following the plane crash. My character was about to freeze and starve to death in the night as I crossed a checkpoint while mistakenly going the wrong way on the map. My character lasts for less than a minute as the same wolf chases me down as I try to find cover in a cold car. I haven't played the game in a while because starting from the beginning and going through the first few days of this game is something I can really do without.
This game initally caught my attention because of its aspects of realism. I thought this game was going to follow the reality of what would actually happen in a similar scenario (within the constraints of a video game). When story mode came along and all of the major flaws of this game were not corrected, I realized the developpers may not have been as clever as I had anticipated. It is as if they were guided into a really good direction that would have led to creating a groundbreaking survival game, but instead, about half way through they just gave up and tried to find creativity where there was none to be had.
I do not recommend this game unless you want to pay almost $40 for a flawed survival simulator that will likely leave you bored within a week. I would highly recommend just going into the woods and camping for a weekend and maybe do a little RPing with styrofoam crowbars and paper clothe for a similar experience.

In
, you play as a half-Japanese, half-English student attending an "international school" in Japan. There you meet fellow student Ceridwan "Ceri" Erwood, a very shy girl and an avid reader. You become curious about her and start spending more time around her as a friendship begins to develop.
This game is a visual novel, a type of video game entirely story-driven. Most of the game is reading the story, though there are a few decision points along the way that ultimately decide the course of the story. There are three different endings to achieve.
Overall, I felt this game was weak in several regards. Starting with the art, there is only one character sprite in the game, that of Ceri. Despite the presence of a few other important characters, such as the protagonist's parents and Ceri's father, no one else makes an actual physical appearance. Ceri also gets a voice actor in this game, in English, which is a bit different for a visual novel. However, I felt the acting often came off as very wooden and stilted.
The main problem of this visual novel is the writing. What we have here is a very shallow romance plot. Even though I clocked-in around two-and-a-half hours in this game, it felt like almost nothing happened. There was hardly any conflict or interesting or memorable points in the story. It just felt like some dialogue scenes with barely a plot to speak of. The pacing of the story is also poor. The entire story takes place over less than two weeks which makes the events seem ridiculously rushed. There was never much of a chance to develop the characters very much and I never cared about any of them. I must also especially fault the Ceri character. She is as cliché as they come being written as a standard cute, but shy, girl (complete with large breasts) that has trouble making friends for vague reasons and it is up to you, the player, to act as her white knight. It all just struck me as a terribly unoriginal story that was never interesting.
I find myself not recommending this visual novel. The writing and characterization is shallow, boring, and unoriginal. It is free so if you are really curious and like visual novels you do not have much to lose, but others can pass.

Like I said, the difficulty is hardly anything to shake a stick at, but the game is pretty good at providing feedback loop to the player to always make it feel like you're making progress.  The story is somewhat of a joke, but I can safely say that the 12-year-old me would have probably loved this game to death.  The guy over twice his age... you know what? I liked it for what it was.
One caveat, however, is if you're going to 100% the game (which I did, so that's saying something, right?) you might not enjoy a second trip around as you'll need to play the game twice to get every cheevo.  Normally I don't do this, but it was too easy to pass up.  So why is playing it twice so bad?
The game offers an alternative most of its hidden object puzzles (there are secondary HOGs to play that make absolutely no effort to hide anything; they are thematic bits to vary up the found-something-in-the-pile method of providing the player items) in the form of "Mahjong".  First off, I hate that anyone calls the matching game of mahjong tiles "Mahjong".  It's Shanghai, and Shanghai sucks!  If the game had real mahjong, I'd probably enjoy it a lot more (and no way that's going to happen).  However, if HOGs aren't your thing, but you would prefer to match tiles to pass puzzles, you're welcome to do that.  And you can't possibly fail, either as getting to a stalemate simply reshuffles the stack... which will affect your achievement hunt.
So, in conclusion:
- Great time waster with some interesting if not terribly difficult puzzles
- "Mahjong" tile matching will shrivel your sack and must be suffered if you want to 100% the game
- Recommended, but you might want to hunt for it in a bundle. It is not worth the price of admission, even with the extra scenario packed in for "collectors"
- Alternatively, get it elsewhere (cheevos are also in-game and just as useful off of Steam as they are on it) for much less.

~Overview~
STORY: 3/5
DIFFICULTY: 1/5
GAMEPLAY: 3/5
GRAPHIC: 2/5
REPLAYABILITY: 2/5
~My Personal Progress~
Story: 300% [beat the game three times, in regular and expert mode]
Time played: 10h05m total [3h55m 1st run (regular) + 3h15m 2nd run (expert, mahjong achievement) + 2h55m 3rd run (expert, hidden object achievement)]
Achievements: 100% [15/15 ACMs]
~Review~
"Nightmares From The Deep: The Cursed Heart" is a simple hidden-object-/puzzle-game set in a mystic "cursed Pirate"-Adventure.
The story is simple and straight forward: you're a museum's curator and proud mother. You receive the dead body of  Captain Remington, who was - back then in his days - a feared and cruel pirate. In fact, you are the one who brings him back to life and Remington flees with your daughter to Skull Island. Obviously, it is your task to rescue your duaghter and break the curse that keeps the old Captain alive. One should not expect a deep and emotionally moving story behind such a game and so didn't I, to be honest. That's simply because such games are ment to be played casually: easy to learn, even easier to master! In comparison to other games of this genre this game made a quite good attempt and at least tries to build up tension and most of the time keeps you a little curious, indeed. Of course, this isn't comparable to extraordinary RPGs, for example, but within its own genre this game knows how to sell its plot well (therefore my STORY-rating is pushed from a 2 to a 3).
The difficulty was mainly rated with the highest difficulty-level in mind. There are two modes you can choose from: "regular mode" that shows on your maps all places where actions are available and gives you a shorter charge time for hints, and "expert mode" that doesn't give you hints at all and lets your hint-bar fill up more slowly. If you play this game for the first time, expert mode can be really hard, indeed, because you have to spent more attention on clickable items and have to backtrack a lot to find spawning hidden-object-scenes, but there is one big downside: the game offers a complete "strategy guide" ... I would rather call it a "click-through", to be honest. It's an entire list of all objectives, you have to fulfill, including all clickable items with a beautiful photo gallery. This is ... *clearing throat* ... ment to be nice, really, but this game is simple enough and offering a complete walk-through is destroying the last bit of a challenge completely ^^" Without this "feature" my rating would probably have been a 3 of 5 due to the expert mode, but in this case I decided to reduce it to a 1 out of 5 because even the
(as stated in the game description) weren't clever enough in my opinion but rather easy-peasy.
The gameplay is solid and the voice acting is ok. This game is actually just a simplified Point&Click-Adventure (because the game chooses the appropiate interaction-method with objects automatically, e.g. "talking" while hovering about persons, magnifying things that can be inspected, and collected objects from your inventory aren't combinable, at all) with hidden-object-/mahjong-elements and - let's be honest - it's hard to screw something up that's as simple as clicking ; ) Autosaving works perfectly fine and I didn't bump into bugs or crashes of any kind. However, there doesn't seem to be a way of starting a new game as long as your current campaign isn't finished, despite of creating a whole new player-profile; not the end of the world, but mildly annoying. Due to some restrictions I had to play this game three times to earn all achievements. Mini-games can be played in two different modes: One is the common hidden-object scene and the other one let's you solve the object finding by playing mahjong. To earn the achievements "Self-guided Tour" and "Mahjong Master And Commander" you have to solve all 28 mini-games in a playthrough either only as hidden-object-puzzles or only mahjong-challenges, and during my first run I tried out both mechanics and wasn't able to complete these puzzles a second time in the other mode. I'm not sure if this was intended. If it was, then I've got to criticize that this design-decision artificially lengthens the game time for those who want to get a Perfect Game.
The graphics are generally good and offer a decent resolution, the only thing that disappointed me, was that the game description claims to have
that it clearly doesn't have! The cinematics didn't scale with the resolution and because I play with a FullHD-monitor, probably as most players these days, I had to watch horribly pixelated cutscenes. Either the devs didn't test the quality on a common monitor or they simply lied ... no matter what applies, it's awefully negative, in my opinion.
I decided to decrease the rating for the game's replayability, although I personally played it three times. The reason simply is, that on one hand I only would have needed two playthroughs - maximum -, if I had paid a little bit more attention. And on the other hand I want to evaluate games as objectively as I can, which means, that I have to be aware of people that don't care for achievements like  I do. These people would probably not consider to replay this game, because it doesn't offer new challenges, alternative endings or anything else that makes this game worth playing again.
~Conclusion~
"Nightmares From The Deep" is a decent game. Those of you who like hidden-object-games will probably have some nice hours to spend with this. I personally don't think that it offers any original ideas or breakthroughs in this genre and didn't create tension or fun above the ordinary, but on the other hand I don't see any severe reason to prevent you from buying this game, if that is the kinda game you like and enjoy, because despite the misinformation about the "AAA-cinematics" it offers a solid quality and I consider it as one of the better hidden-object-games on the market.

I'm bad at reviews. Now, my everyday advice for purchasing games is, glance at the reviews (read the long hate reviews), glance at the discussions (see if problems are solved quickly), and with Early Access games, check the update history and news.... ok, so if you did that, you're probably no better off than you were. There's a lot of love and hate for this game out there.
The love is well founded. This game has amazing potential, and "as is" is fairly decent and playable, if mostly as a multiplayer experience (the single player game is lacking, but, is worth a playthrough or two).
The hate may be well founded too. Some people have been waiting years for this game, and out of their love for it, became frustrated with waiting. Should you buy this game? Eventually, the answer will be a hardcore YES. But if you're mostly a single player, well, the regular game gets boring after a while, but there's an awesome survival scenario where you earn cash and upgrade your gear as you go (I hope they add more like this).
All in all, I think the game is worth supporting, that one day it could become THE game that other games like this are compared to. I'm happy with my investment, and I'm patient... as long as the developers are making some effort, then the game is moving forward, and I'm happy.

Dungeon of the Endless (DotE) is one of those rare hybrid games that manages to successfully mash together different genres into something enjoyable. In this case, Amplitude has developed a game that combines Tower Defense and light RPG elements into a rogue-like structure.
While somewhat light on graphics, DotE makes up for it in rather addictive gameplay. The basic premise of the game is that the interstellar prison ship you're on has just been shot out of the sky while on route to a penal colony. The survivors scramble into the escape pods, and after a huge explosion, you find yourself trapped underground on a mysterious planet full of things that want to kill you. You must escape through successive levels to reach the surface. Pretty standard fare.
Each level is randomly generated, and consists of rooms and doors. Each room can contain power nodes, resource/item drops, buff/debuffs, or special structures. It can also contain additional NPCs for you to recruit (Your maximum party size is 4) or a merchant. And of course, monsters.
The game uses doors to advance the game world - research, resource production, and monster spawn timers only move forward when you open a door. Your goal is to open eough doors to find the elevator to the next level. Once you do, you pickup your power crystal from your starting room, and use one of your heros to move it and your party to the elevator room, all while dodging the final, continuous spawns for that level.
It gives you a few choices on how you can do this, however. You can invest in researching new towers and making a protected path to the elevator. Or you can invest in your heros and level them up. I usually pick a middle path between them. The game uses three resources to let you do this, food, industry, and science, which are produced by building different structures throughout the rooms you open. Again, standard fare.
As you progress, you can unlock new heros and escape pods for future playthroughs. Which is important, because while there is a pause feature, there is no save/load, only a exit/resume. Therefore, you can leave/return whenever you want, but it will only delay the inevitable fact that you'll die a lot. Which is not bad. DotE effectively works its roguelike angle to make this process enjoyable.
The game has become polished enough that there are not many obvious downsides. As a story person, I'm obligated to not that, typical for a roguelike, there is little exposition or character development (Although this has been improved recently through some elevator banter amongst party members, but nothing serious). This is normally fine, except Amplitude has based it in an existing world structure (The "Endless" franchise), so if you own any of their other games, don't be let down if you can't find out how this connects to the broader universe, although they have hinted that it will. Possibly. Amplitude has promised to introduce new heros (Currently there is a healthy selection) as well as a faction system and some plotlines. But again, ROGUE-LIKE.
Another downside is the lack of a more detailed Bestiary, which is both good and bad. The upside is that it leaves something for you to figure out on your own. The downside is that it makes power gaming annoying, as the distribution of enemy stats will not be clear to you. Some of it is done through character design, however, for example, variations of a certain set of bug creatures will vex you when you expect them to chase your heros, but it instead beelines for the crystal, because that happens to be the PINK ONES, not the brown ones. Whether this is actually a downside is a function of how much your enjoy rogue-like games.
Overall, I'd give DotE something like an 8.5/10. Its a solid investment of your time and money, and if you enjoy tower defense games, rogue-likes, or hero based games, this game will have something for you.

TL;DR
This game should be early access. The core seems quite finished, but it is far from polished.
I have allmost 10k hours on Clicker Heroes and 7k hours on Time Clickers, so I know my way around clicker games by now.
There are just too many aspects that are not clear, unbalanced or even broken.
For now I do not recommend it until the major bugs are fixed, but I would really like to recommend it in the future.
Pros:
- The art is nice
- Relic (equipment) system for heroes (though unbalanced)
- Real idle clicker game (idle in the sense that you are not required to fight the monsters yourself)
- Treasure chests can contain more than just gold
- Ascending system
- Clicking actually helps also in the later stages of the game
- Options to help reduce CPU usage
- Plenty of heroes
- Plenty achievements
- Low CPU usage even though there are a lot of animations
- Use Shift to buy 10x or Ctrl for 50x upgrades for a hero.
Cons:
- Some ascension upgrades cost more than they display (e.g. it shows the price is 5 stars, but it is actually 6)
- Some achievements are bugged (e.g. you reach 1 billion cash and you get the achievement for 100 million)
- You cannot know how many stars you get on ascension (I consider this a bug, since it is a major flaw and breaks the gameplay for a clicker game)
- Gold gained while Idle is not worth it at all, I got more gold by leaving the game open for 1 hour than closed for 10 hours.
- Display of gold amounts is not consistent. "You received 1.23423423423423e17 while you were offline", yea great, is that 1 quintillion or 0.1 quintillion, or perhaps 10 quintillion?
- No zone or level navigation, so no optimal cash farming
- Appearently Shift and Ctrl help you buy more upgrades at the same time, but this is nowhere explained or visible.
- Some heroes's faces aren't visible because of UI elements overlapping
- Icons aren't intuïtive, for example, the chest icon does not navigate to the equipment section, but the ascension section.
- Equipment for higher level heroes are damage bound, you cannot get equipment for high level heroes when your damage is too low, you need to farm relics until you can.
- Most females are scantly clothed (con in my opinion)
- Relics drop like mad and disappears quite quickly, which practically removes the idle part of the game (yes, I know it is not tagged as such)
- No mannualy saving
- Legendary relics are flawed, they may help you for 5 levels, but after that the common relics are catching up, yet you get a pop-up asking whether you are sure the common item with 100x more dps should replace the relic with three +0% bonusses (not kidding, this is a real example and happens all the time).
- Found relics seem to target the relic spots where an epic or legendary relic is equipt instead of just randomly selecting a slot.

I think the best way to open this review is with an empirical statement: Dungeonmans is brilliant!
Now, I suppose to make this review a little more useful I should offer you some of the facts that prove my opening statement is unquestionably accurate. So, I'll do that:
First off, Dungeonmans is very true to the Rogue-like ideal. It has everything you would expect: Permadeath, turn-based gameplay, loads of unique creatures inhabiting a procedurally generated world, loads of nasty surprises that will make you think “Man... I shouldn't have gone through that portal”, and, of course, tons of unidentified and potentially deadly loot.
The classic formula is there: Go kill the bad guys, take their loot, get more powerful, go kill more powerful bad guys, take their loot. On top of that there are a number of ways to pass your progress on to your next character (and you need that because you're going to die a lot). Much of your forward progress comes in the form of upgrading the Dungeonmans Academy. You can find a number of artifacts to improve the academy making things easier for new recruits. In addition you can get relics which only “unlock” once the character that discovered them has died. So new characters can enjoy a number of benefits from those that have passed on before.
Of course, your current Dungeonman can also find artifacts that help them. Proofs of Stremf can be used to increase stats immediately, saved to give to future recruits, or both. Equipment can be enhanced using the smithy at the academy or by using magic scrolls you'll find in dungeons or shops. You can make some truly epic level gear. (And that's a good thing, because you're going to need it.)
The artwork is a beautiful example of old school 2D and it perfectly fits the theme of the game. On top of that Dungeonmans is loaded with humor that has quite literally made me laugh out loud time and time again.
All things considered the game is hours and hours of fun. I would love to tell you what the end game is like, but I haven't gotten anywhere near it yet. However, I am very confident that the game continues in the same vein. If I ever manage to hack my way to the Dread Purpleonians I'm sure there will be an interesting (and humorous) grand conflict.
So, the long and short of it is this: Dungeonmans is certainly worth the price of admission!

Long anticipated release answered by great disappointment. You would have thought the game would have come some ways from its 2013 beta release.
-Note: play time shows nil, but I've been on it before steam release.-
The game revolves around a tedious upward grind on different ship trees, some required to unlock another class (ex. Play as destroyer, unlock heavy cruiser, then unlock carriers). To unlock the next ships, you have to research a string of "upgrades" until next ship is available for research in the end. Quotations around "research" because they seem to have been chosen at random for each ship or are just meaningless (like gun or boiler upgrades that cost you thousands of exp but improves absolutely nothing). Each tier of each class consists of only one ship and even though the first ships come fast, gameplay eventually gets stale and boring. Wasn't a fan of Warthunder but at least they had more variety with several vehicles per tier.
Towards the endgame, exp walls take on an exponential climb. If you're a free user, its very unlikely that you'll ever get to touch the endgame ships. And before any SDE fanboy chimes in with "Stop whining, NF1's grind was even worse, this is nothing", then you're missing the point. Anyone can make a game model focusing entirely on a neverending grindfest (with cash/premium shortcuts of course!). It takes very little effort and imagination but it still seems good at raking in the cash from the whales.
Ingame:
Depending on ship, controls can be a bit clumsy and matches are always unbalanced to the point of being rigged. Don't be surprised to have your 1895 heavy cruiser facing Battleship Yamato or your submarine 1v2 against a pair of Destroyers on a tiny map. You don't see much teamwork either and ships rarely tend to play on their ship's main roles. And why would they seeing as how the game rewards all the same regardless of what you're doing. Despite the different classes, they all virtually play the same: cap a base, go deal as much damage as you can,  die/kill yourself, then quit back to lobby. Repeat. The faster you get at this, the faster you can progress. Without premium, however, it feels more like you're in a hamster wheel.
Surprised this isn't listed as an early release or beta as there's still some bugs. Some aspects like endgame rewards don't even make sense at times. Players that carried team often get rewarded less than the exp farmers who torpedo rush suicide or guys hanging out back taking random potshots. I guess its a work in progress and they'll iron it all out eventually. Right after they release that new set of ship skins in cash shop.
It wasn't all bad though. The music is okay I guess. It doesn't get as annoying as NF1's. The ship descriptions were interesting.
I haven't tried World of warships yet but from the videos I've seen it looks like a lot more action going on over there. The only people I'd see recommending this with a straight face are diehard armchair admirals who care nothing about gameplay quality or SDE fanboys and suck ups. To everyone else, I'd look elsewhere.

It takes an approach very similar to dwarf fortress, inthe sense that you learn through losing constantly and returning to the game with aquired knowlege from your previous character. This is definitly a game with a very realistic, and extremely unforgiving. The Long Dark will be sure to test the ability of any player who is willing to approach it and to invest their time into learning how to play it. Its a survival experience like any other and is worth any survival game fan's time.

Alright, so I played this game before story mode was released. I loved it as a 'tester' for something I had high expectations for. I played survival mode to exhaustion. It was an interesting game, however the novelty wore off after a few weeks. I played the different difficulties, saw a lot of the map. After a while, I realized a few flaws with the game, but who cares, it was still in development. I noticed how ridiculously quickly itmes wore out (even solid crowbars). Noticed that falling from a foot high could lead to serious injury. Not being able to jump was frustrating. I noticed how quickly the day would go by relative to my walking speed. I figured all of this would be dealt with when the game was actually released........ NOPE!
I tried story mode. It failed to grip me. I was trying to find a way to exit tutorial mode and soon realized that is just how the gameplay is. I loved the alpha version because it threw you in raw and you had to figure everything out. There was a sense of accomplishment when I learnt how to make water, or how to create a map! This game holds you by both hands and spoon feeds you. The story wasn't even compelling enough to keep me going, even if I was able to.... which leads me to my next point.
The save game options are so limited that they are game-breaking. There are only checkpoints. That's fine, a lot of games save by checkpoint. What's not fine is the non-existence of choosing a previous checkpoint to load from. I have not been able to progress in this game without having to restart the entire game and play through the mind numbing 'noob zone' following the plane crash. My character was about to freeze and starve to death in the night as I crossed a checkpoint while mistakenly going the wrong way on the map. My character lasts for less than a minute as the same wolf chases me down as I try to find cover in a cold car. I haven't played the game in a while because starting from the beginning and going through the first few days of this game is something I can really do without.
This game initally caught my attention because of its aspects of realism. I thought this game was going to follow the reality of what would actually happen in a similar scenario (within the constraints of a video game). When story mode came along and all of the major flaws of this game were not corrected, I realized the developpers may not have been as clever as I had anticipated. It is as if they were guided into a really good direction that would have led to creating a groundbreaking survival game, but instead, about half way through they just gave up and tried to find creativity where there was none to be had.
I do not recommend this game unless you want to pay almost $40 for a flawed survival simulator that will likely leave you bored within a week. I would highly recommend just going into the woods and camping for a weekend and maybe do a little RPing with styrofoam crowbars and paper clothe for a similar experience.
