As a casual gamer, I don't spend much time every week playing computer games. Whatever free time I do have, I like to use wisely. I've been playing this game for nearly a year now and have nothing but praise for Team Radiant. Stonehearth is being developed with the player in mind. They have taken into consideration our suggestions and concerns, providing regular updates to address issues and keep us in the loop.
So what is Stonehearth?
I like to think of it as a voxelized version of the Caesar/Zeus games from the late 90s. It's primarily a city builder with scenarios/campaigns. The focus is on building a small town, improving your buildings, specializing your villagers, and fighting off occasional waves of raiders. There are a lot of new features currently in the works, and greater plans on the horizon.
Yes, the game is still being worked on, so if you expect a 'final' product, you may be slightly disappointed at this point. Thankfully, the major bugs and game mechanics have been ironed out and improved over the past year, so I would definitely recommend it to anybody who doesn't mind the odd bug or two. Updates are always a pleasant surprise, creating new limits to push in building the ultimate village. One major 'plus' for Stonehearth is the developer's decision to make it mod-friendly. This includes custom resources, items, classes, campaigns, and scenarios to add to the pot and make every new game more unique.
Current features:
- Resource-to-voxel building -- your resources are directly used to create the buildings you design.
- Crafting jobs and leveling system -- more crafting is unlocked as your workers level up in their chosen job.
- Combat campaigns -- Random goblin and undead attacks.
- Mining
- Basic water (ponds/lakes)
Upcoming features:
- Other playable factions and races (dwarves!)
- Advanced water features
- Improved combat and variety of scenarios
- Enhanced building and added build styles
- Magic classes
- Explorable ruins
- Seasons / biomes
- Alternate planes
It's great fun in its current state, and it will only get better. If you aren't too keen on getting it now, definitely have another look in a few months!
On a final note, I'd suggest this to any less active gamers out there as it doesn't need hours of input to get anywhere. Your empire can be pieced together over many short sittings (though if you've got a weekend to kill, you can definitely keep busy for hours on end designing and building your dream castle!)

Re-review of Evolve Stage 2 Beta:
Jumping back into the game since free play weekend a lot has changed (review on freeplay weekend posted 03Sep2015 posted below).
They implemented a progression system where every game you play you are awarded “silver keys”. With this in-game currency system this allows you to acquire ALL characters/monsters/skins/perks just through gameplay. So far in the beta there is no indication of cash shop or other payment methods.
I suspect they will implement a “pay to skip” in the future to generate some kind of revenue. Servers and games development will not run on hopes and dream alone.
Gameplay:
There is a tutorial you can use to learn the basic gameplay of the current characters and monsters available to you. You can earn some silvers keys this way while you get your footing into the game. Gameplay as a monster requires a good amount of skill level to win. I have yet to win as monster but there is no penalty for loosing either.
As the game went to Free to play the player base has grown dramatically, so it’s not difficult to find a game.
The bases of the gameplay are to unlock perks to fit your type of gameplay.
Steam Controller:
Work great with x-input and mouse controls. If your using the combination set your promt setting in game, from auto to controler or you will experance HUD promt flickering.
Rumble works fine so far..
The Developer CS profile uses joystick simulated mouse input which is a joke for reaction time gameplay.
Other thoughts:
Seems that people who gave in and invested into multiple season pass’ are disgruntled, and they have the right to be.  Those who have purchased the game will be granted “founders packs”. It does look like they will be given the “pay to skip” feature in advanced as founder packs.yet people who paid dont feel compensate enough for the founders pack. Sad to see people who paid for the game give it bad reviews. The game is alive and people are playing agian. In general, its healthier to have a game that has a growing playing base than a dying game in your steam library.

Third playthrough.
Day 1:
I wake up and there are zombies outside. I grab my son’s baseball bat and a rucksack and I begin raiding all my neighbours houses. I sneak around with all the care of a teenager nervously reaching third base in the backseat of a car with the father still in the front seat. Occasionally I just lash out at shadows. I gather enough supplies to last me a week. I return to the house and sleep with two eyes open, still cradling my baseball bat.
Day 2:
I wake up screaming, batting at the shadows. Nothing there. After a nutritious breakfast of fruit, I begin mapping my surrounding area, locating my future safe house. I fill all my bags with everything I want and head over there. On the way there I accidentally kill a zombie, run and hide in a bathroom for eight hours, eat a packet of chips and cry uncontrollably in bowel loosening terror. Realizing it is now dark and I can hear weird noises outside, I sleep on the bathroom floor.
Day 3:
I wake up, climb out the window and make it to the safe house. I fill it with everything I think will be useful. I start worrying about water and spend the next week stockpiling water bottles. I fill every saucepan and bucket with water. I start reading books about water collectors. I sacrifice a dead rodent I find under the cupboard to Lono. I also convince myself that farming is easy.
Day 11:
I have a small farm and around my house there is a pleasing collection of scattered zombie corpses. I feel that I need to start building barricades though, so I embark on a journey to a warehouse where I hope to find tools and building supplies.
Day 12:
Huzzah! I have tools and building supplies. Time to start chopping wood.
Day 16:
I have now conquered the forest and carried 200 metric tons of lumber into my yard. With this I shall build an impenetrable fortress to last until the end of time.
Day 17:
I have used up all my lumber and there is a 60 meter gap in my perimeter fence. Too tired to build, tomorrow I head back to the woods. Side note, why aren't my carrots growing?
Day 18:
Chop chop chop.
Day 19:
Build build build.
Day 20:
More lumber is required.
Day 25:
I add butter to potato soup. I am a culinary genious.
Day 35:
My fortress is complete! I gaze proudly at its rickety walls and celebrate with some whiskey I had planned to save for disinfectant.
Day 36:
So bored. I nail some nails to my baseball bats and go out practicing my swing.
Day 65:
Whilst looking for cement, I cut my hand jumping through a smashed window. I bandage it with some ripped sheets and start looking for a pharmacy.
Day 65 (Update):
Why is there no disinfectant in this pharmacy?
Day 65 (Update):
Too tired to keep looking. I will sleep and look tomorrow.
Day 66:
My hand is infected. Of course it is. Why wouldn't it be. It will take me a day to head back, I think I have some disinfectant in the bathroom. I should be able to make it. Everything hurts though and Batty (yeah I named my bat, sue me.) is getting harder and harder to swing. Taking it easy as hell I creep through abandoned buildings past shambling zeds. One of them looks at me funny so I stove his head in. Crap, shouldn't have done that. There is pain shooting up my arm now. The bleeding appears to have started again. Oh balls, the zombie is getting back up again, and I hear movements from down the alley. I start to run, taking the back routes I have mapped out and turn onto the main road home...
Where 19 millions congregated zombies stand groaning.
I defecate in my trousers.
Behind there are 3 zombies purposefully shambling towards me. One of them looks like my ex.
Making an executive decision I bring out the Molotov Cocktail I prepared earlier.
Lighting it with trembling hands, I launch it into the crowd, screaming "Deus Ex Machina this you undead Foddermuckers!" and barrel past the distracted horde, lashing out with Batty whenever a rotting hand gets too close.
Dripping with sweat, gore and reeking of charred zombie flesh, I make it safely home, slam the door shut behind me and find some disinfectant for my hand. That night, I sleep the sleep of the righteous.

Wandering through my garden I accidentally brush past the fireplace, setting my trouser leg on fire. Panicking I run around screaming, set fire to my beautiful new watchtower and am engulfed in the ensuing inferno.

If you've ever wondered if you could survive alone in a zombie apocalypse then this is the game for you.
Good things -
Workshop for modding (get the cars mod, just get it, you'll save yourself hours walking around the massive map)
Large variety of zombie models
You can build a literal fort to keep zombies out
You can farm, fish, forage, trap, or simply loot food
A variety of survival items, guns, melee, tools
Customizable character skillsets with XP and leveling
Massive open world with meta events and zombie hordes
TV and radio reports covering the Knox Event Infection
Multiplayer
Lumberjackin'
Bad things -
- No NPCs,  you're just alone, and that gets boring if you don't want to do multiplayer for whatever reason
- Which means no quest based interactions or any such challenges
- Which means no real 'story' or 'story mode' of any kind (apart from a loose affiliation with broadcasts)
- Which means you don't really feel fully integrated into the world you're just surviving in it from a narcissistic perspective
- The developers, while well meaning, are super slow to bring out mostly mundane updates. For example it took Steam Workshop just to get us cars about 4 years into it. I'll probably be dead by the time they bring out NPCs. It's done under the excuse of 'we have to make sure it's perfect', but what they don't realize is that even if they released crappy NPCs, as long as they were there in the game files, we'd perfect them in about 1/16th of the time it would take them to release an update for the feature.
Should you buy the game? Yes. It's fantastic for what it is, a groundbreaking achievement in the zombie survival genre. Should you also learn to hack and rewrite the game's programming so that we can see NPCs in the game before we all die of old age? Yes for the love of God do it.
Review done.

After playing previous games in the series, and finishing all the Heroes games but still wanting a fix of this sort of game, I ended up getting this on a bundle sale.
Started disappointing due to the clunky dialog and lacklustre gameplay, but I continued on if only to keep me visually stimulated whilst listening to audiobooks (the background musics alright, but not for over 50 hours of play).
Midway the bugs started kicking in, including (but not limited to) units stacking inside each other, inventory screens and city screens remaining visible on the overworld, level ups not registering... but usually restarting the game would fix these and I figured I'd got halfway through so may as well finish.
Then I reached the elf campaign.  I pride myself on not resorting to easy modes as a general rule, but this game makes it nigh-on impossible to get past the first couple of enemies on any higher difficulty.  After that point I was disappointed to find I couldn't raise the difficulty, meaning the rest of the game I was auto-battling every fight including bosses with little to no casualties.  The only input I had as a player was clicking from fight to fight, following a relatively linear path until completing the map.  But still, near the end of the game... I may as well see how the (bland and generic) story plays out.
Final map.  I'm tired of this game now and just want it to be finished.  I level up my party to their highest ranks but then I ignore all treasure in favour of getting to the end.  I reach the final gate, get a cutscene preparing for the final boss, and...?  That's it.  A script error causes a new objective to come up to destroy the city you just destroyed.  Some say they fixed it by downloading a revised script, but no luck for me.  161 hours of gameplay (half of which was actual playing as I'm afk a lot), only to reach a brick wall at the very end.
Nevertheless I'll be playing the expansion, as I paid for it as part of the bundle, but seriously- don't bother starting the same journey as me.

Space Colony is the Steam release version a 2003 game with the same title. The game was developed and self-published by FireFly Studios whose most notable work includes the popular Stronghold franchise. The game draws heavy inspiration from the well-known 'The Sims' games, the 'Tycoon' series of games, and FireFly's own Stronghold titles which is reflected by the existence of a combat mechanic.
The game features a lengthy single-player campaign where the player takes on the role of Venus Jones and her diverse team of space colonists working for Blackwater Industries, a company hell-bent to increase profit and productivity at the expense of its own employees.  Travel to different worlds and follow one of the two branching storylines by either going through the military or civilian campaigns. Like a Real Time Strategy (RTS) game, it also features a 'skirmish' mode along side the campaign. Likewise, the game also has a sandbox mode like a regular Sim/Management game.
+ Classical HD remake of the isometric view of old games with some enhancement on detail
+ Colorful and goofy characters with different personalities and traits
+ Story mode is fun and offers a variety of challenges (limited resources, colonists, etc.)
+ Interesting new idea to mix different game elements such as: simulation (relationships, needs etc.), real time strategy (combat, base defenses and resource gathering), and management (resource management, work efficiency and trade)...but (See CON #1 and #2)
+ Fully voice acted with decent voice acting and dialogue
+ Branching story mode to showcase the civilian and military aspects of the game
+ Upbeat techno soundtracks that fits the game very well
+ Map Editor to make your own scenario or maps
+ Steam Workshop support
+ Contains all other bonus packages for the game
- The RTS elements are basic: It lacks essential features that should be mandatory for proper implementation of an RTS aspect of a game such as but not limited to: Unit groups (ctrl+1 etc.), Attack move, patrol, or just a hotkey to Stop units would be nice.
- The 'Sim' aspect of the game is also lacking in its complexity when it comes to colonist relationships.
- The isometric graphics does not allow you to rotate the screen or objects.
- Lacking in option menu: Hotkeys cannot be rebound
- Speed setting is lacking with only pause, normal, or fast as the only options.
- Base construction follows the 'Sim style of creation' where items are available at anytime (unless you are in story mode). This is under CONS because they could have gone with the RTS style of base construction which would follow a technology tree system which unlocks specific options based on existing technology or structures. This, in my opinion, would have added to the game's complexity.
The concept of mixing together the various aspects of Simulation, Real Time Strategy, and Management games is a great idea but only if the proper mechanics from each of those genres are implemented properly. Among other things for example, Space Colony severely lacks basic RTS controls such as unit grouping and waypoints which lead to some frustrating and clunky unit control. Another issue is with the Simulation aspect where the shallow relationship mechanics made for some boring relationship micromanagement and the lack of screen-rotation led to some mis-clicking accidents.  If these issues are ironed out, the experience would have been much better.
Overall I still enjoyed my experience with Space Colony and I can

Aquaria is a 2D action/adventure "platformer" (for lack of a better word), that blends stunning visuals and fluent controls with an incredibly emotional storyline about one girls journey of self discovery, newfound freedom; and her self motivated journey to find the existential answers to her questions about life: about who she is, what she is, and why she exists.
Aquaria dazzles with it's vibrant and artistic underwater setting, beautifully realized locations such as post-civilization ruins, coral reefs, trenches, and open stretches of water - complete with all the signs of life one would normally see, albeit life full of fantasy elements. Aquaria's atmosphere exudes despair, hope, and the sense that not all is as it once was, or should be...
In the end, Aquaria is a glittering gem of a product, a perfect example of what two very talented and passionate developers can do with their hard earned time away from reality, and is a result well worth every penny of it's current asking price. I highly recommend Aquaria for it's excellence, and all the praise I can muster for it's creative duo at Bit Blot!

Dungeonmans is an absolute blast to play for those that a fan of the Rogue-Light genre. It's chalk full of absurd puns, awkward enemy and item names, and you are always just one dungeon away from perma-death.
There is a great deal of continuity between characters in a mechanical way. That is equipment and stat boosts can be retrieved from graves of your former characters to boost your current(or future) characters. You can stock pile relics(randomly looted through out the game) and use them to acquire better equipment(a relic can only be used on future characters, and are tiered--each one giving a better quality item when expended) with new characters. Then there is the "proof of stremf" system wherein when you kill champions or bosses of your level or higher you receive an item(proof of stremf) which can be turned in at the head master for 2 bonus stat points on your current character--and 1 bonus point on all subsequent characters.
Other wonderful bonuses can be attained for future characters by maxing out your library(by handing in books at the head master). This allows you to retrieve 4 randomized books with each newly created character, and also allows each new character to inherently know what each scroll does(after talking to the librarian).
The ever-growing graveyard of your past characters while mostly benign, can be entertaining to take a stroll through. :)

Dungeon of the Endless (DotE) is one of those rare hybrid games that manages to successfully mash together different genres into something enjoyable. In this case, Amplitude has developed a game that combines Tower Defense and light RPG elements into a rogue-like structure.
While somewhat light on graphics, DotE makes up for it in rather addictive gameplay. The basic premise of the game is that the interstellar prison ship you're on has just been shot out of the sky while on route to a penal colony. The survivors scramble into the escape pods, and after a huge explosion, you find yourself trapped underground on a mysterious planet full of things that want to kill you. You must escape through successive levels to reach the surface. Pretty standard fare.
Each level is randomly generated, and consists of rooms and doors. Each room can contain power nodes, resource/item drops, buff/debuffs, or special structures. It can also contain additional NPCs for you to recruit (Your maximum party size is 4) or a merchant. And of course, monsters.
The game uses doors to advance the game world - research, resource production, and monster spawn timers only move forward when you open a door. Your goal is to open eough doors to find the elevator to the next level. Once you do, you pickup your power crystal from your starting room, and use one of your heros to move it and your party to the elevator room, all while dodging the final, continuous spawns for that level.
It gives you a few choices on how you can do this, however. You can invest in researching new towers and making a protected path to the elevator. Or you can invest in your heros and level them up. I usually pick a middle path between them. The game uses three resources to let you do this, food, industry, and science, which are produced by building different structures throughout the rooms you open. Again, standard fare.
As you progress, you can unlock new heros and escape pods for future playthroughs. Which is important, because while there is a pause feature, there is no save/load, only a exit/resume. Therefore, you can leave/return whenever you want, but it will only delay the inevitable fact that you'll die a lot. Which is not bad. DotE effectively works its roguelike angle to make this process enjoyable.
The game has become polished enough that there are not many obvious downsides. As a story person, I'm obligated to not that, typical for a roguelike, there is little exposition or character development (Although this has been improved recently through some elevator banter amongst party members, but nothing serious). This is normally fine, except Amplitude has based it in an existing world structure (The "Endless" franchise), so if you own any of their other games, don't be let down if you can't find out how this connects to the broader universe, although they have hinted that it will. Possibly. Amplitude has promised to introduce new heros (Currently there is a healthy selection) as well as a faction system and some plotlines. But again, ROGUE-LIKE.
Another downside is the lack of a more detailed Bestiary, which is both good and bad. The upside is that it leaves something for you to figure out on your own. The downside is that it makes power gaming annoying, as the distribution of enemy stats will not be clear to you. Some of it is done through character design, however, for example, variations of a certain set of bug creatures will vex you when you expect them to chase your heros, but it instead beelines for the crystal, because that happens to be the PINK ONES, not the brown ones. Whether this is actually a downside is a function of how much your enjoy rogue-like games.
Overall, I'd give DotE something like an 8.5/10. Its a solid investment of your time and money, and if you enjoy tower defense games, rogue-likes, or hero based games, this game will have something for you.

Re-review of Evolve Stage 2 Beta:
Jumping back into the game since free play weekend a lot has changed (review on freeplay weekend posted 03Sep2015 posted below).
They implemented a progression system where every game you play you are awarded “silver keys”. With this in-game currency system this allows you to acquire ALL characters/monsters/skins/perks just through gameplay. So far in the beta there is no indication of cash shop or other payment methods.
I suspect they will implement a “pay to skip” in the future to generate some kind of revenue. Servers and games development will not run on hopes and dream alone.
Gameplay:
There is a tutorial you can use to learn the basic gameplay of the current characters and monsters available to you. You can earn some silvers keys this way while you get your footing into the game. Gameplay as a monster requires a good amount of skill level to win. I have yet to win as monster but there is no penalty for loosing either.
As the game went to Free to play the player base has grown dramatically, so it’s not difficult to find a game.
The bases of the gameplay are to unlock perks to fit your type of gameplay.
Steam Controller:
Work great with x-input and mouse controls. If your using the combination set your promt setting in game, from auto to controler or you will experance HUD promt flickering.
Rumble works fine so far..
The Developer CS profile uses joystick simulated mouse input which is a joke for reaction time gameplay.
Other thoughts:
Seems that people who gave in and invested into multiple season pass’ are disgruntled, and they have the right to be.  Those who have purchased the game will be granted “founders packs”. It does look like they will be given the “pay to skip” feature in advanced as founder packs.yet people who paid dont feel compensate enough for the founders pack. Sad to see people who paid for the game give it bad reviews. The game is alive and people are playing agian. In general, its healthier to have a game that has a growing playing base than a dying game in your steam library.

Okay, so how do I start this off...
Since video games and reading romantic (and Adventure) novels are some of the things I enjoy, this was an interesting "Playthrough" for me. While this is only a visual novel you are given some choice throughout your gameplay, not too much but enough to affect the entire ending of the game. To give info on how easy the choices are, I, without knowing the outcome of my choices, recieved the best ending based on logic of relationships. So as long if you have basic psychology skills and pure common sense you should be fine getting through these decisions.
Getting into depth with the story, here's a quick review. I was pretty neutral about the start of the story, as it seemed to start off like a typical "Girl drops something, guy helps, Girl becomes flushed in appearance" sort of way. a bit after the start of the story (roughly 15 minutes in) choices become really logical as stated before and your character's decisions and dialogue stay rational. The story stays like this for sometime, with numerous yet slight differentials in story mechanics. However, the novel really starts to become riveting at the climax.
* I'm going to spoil some of the story here so DON'T put your cursor near the review while reading this *
I honestly thought the overall story was adorable, while it could use a bit of patching up in some places. For some reason Ceri's own life and decisions reminded me of my own life somehow, most likely because I had to move twice (from around the Southfield area to Kalamazoo and then back in the span of 2 years) and I would fake my own illness to stop going to school to prevent me from seeing this one group of people than would always tantalize me throughout elementary and the start of middle school. I would also fake illness to prevent going places where there were a lot of people. This was basically the borderline of social anxiety that I had thoughout my early life,
.
In the end, your reading a great visual novel and getting (basic) social advice by readin this, so you should probably get this visual novel before it becomes a pay2read.

2)  They haven't been able to find the issue.  (they created the port, not a third party, which means they are the ones that coded)

And through all of this, they continue to gleefully sell their game with no warning on their page that some of their achievements are broken.  Buyer beware, and oh thanks for your money.
I don't play games solely for their ahievements, but when they are there, I enjoy the extra challenge and replayability that they give.  I; however, also went to college not for the grades but to learn. With so many games on steam, I would love to see valve start holding devs accountable for selling broken products and ban them from selling here again. I love this game. It's very charming. It has a similar feel to building management games like Gnomoria, Timber & Stone, Rimworld and even Dwarf Fortress, but on a very "Lite" level as of course DF is the Grandaddy of them all in micromanagement and colony building as far as intense detail. It also has a Dungeon Keeper kind of feel since you can dig both upwards and downwards into mountains and the ground if you choose. The freestyle building is a bit like Minecraft with blocks and templates of walls and whatnot, but on a miniature scale.
The artwork and graphic style is adorable too of course and so far it's running great on my mid-range PC (my system is about 4 years old, certainly not top of the line).
The combat is pretty simple at this point. Monsters or invaders (goblins, undead, golems etc) will attack your town regularly - so you will want to build up some defensive walls and whatnot but it's nowhere near the complication of a Tower Defense game (like Craft the World for example). You can fairly easily manage your footmen (soldiers) into groups to patrol and attack invaders and you can craft better weapons and armor for them and it all works nicely. That aspect is fairly easy at this phase of the game.
I really enjoy it overall and the Developers are super responsive and discuss feedback on their forums a lot. They really listen to the players and that says a lot for the future success of the game

Original Review:
I've had this game for a few months before it was released on Steam and it's a great looking game with a lot of potential and a very active development team.
This is a CASUAL game. Very fun and easy.
If you're looking for a game that combines sandbox building with town/city management and some light RPG tower defense type elements, then Stonehearth is worth a look. Those who loved Gnomoria, Hearth and Stone, Game of Dwarves, etc will love this game and it's absolutely adorable graphics - kids are drawn to the anime look - My 5 year old son loves playing this game with me.
Do not expect a heavily detailed management system yet - it's still quite early in development and you're not going to get really complicated building abilities or city management simulator stuff at the level of some other finished games but this one does have a lot of promise for additional challenge and detail as it moves along in development.
Do not expect a heavy crafting system like Minecraft type games - it just doesn't have that. It does have invading monsters (goblins, zombies, skeletons) with survival elements necessary to help your "Hearthlings" stay alive and build a village/city. The job assignment system is nice as well and easy to understand who is doing what in your village as it grows.
You can do blueprinted (prefab) buildings or try your hand at free-form building - which isn't as complete and somewhat buggy at this stage in the game.
Summary: For an Early Access game, this one's surprisingly solid and offers a good deal of interesting gameplay that should appeal to builders, city managers and sandbox game lovers alike. I predict it's going to have a healthy modding community as well so variety will always be available.

Disciples III is a game that I ultimately expected more from. The Disciples series was something of a cult hit and Disciples II:Dark Prophecy was one of my favorite turn based games. The series has always been noted for its beautiful gothic art style that reminds you of Arthur Rackham's illustrations.
That said the artwork in Disciples III is what one would expect from the franchise. The maps, units, buildings are all detailed well enough. However the gorgeous art design can't hide some of the game's shortcomings when it comes to gameplay.
The story is ok but the narrator lacks the dark tone that the narrator in Disciples II had. And it ultimately feels like D3 drones on for far too long before you even get into the mission. There is also a distinct lack of the short animated cutscenes that punctuated each mission in Disciples II.
One change that I do appreciate is that when you equip your hero with items those items are displayed on said hero. Its a small cosmetic change but it is appreciated.
The new gameplay mechanics have you moving your units on a hex grid which is alright but ultimately does little to add any sort of meaningful depth to the series. Part of what made Disciples and Disciples II so appealing was that while simple; there was a surprising amount of depth in what unit types faced off, which units were in the front, which were in the back.
Also curious is the omission of the Mountain clans and undead hordes as playable factions.
Disciples III was terribly buggy upon its initital release and some may still be found now though I found it to be fairly stable from my playtime. In the end I would recommend the game if you are a fan of the series; but would suggest waiting for a steam sale as the price of admission is too high for what you may be expecting from the franchise. I can't help but feel part of that may stem from the change in developers from Strategy First to Akella.

if you're going to make a blatant clone of an existing game format (Heroes of Might And Magic) then you might as well pull out all the stops and make a better game.  And that's what they've done here.  A grown-up clone, without the My Little Pony and Tinkerbell stuff.  They've focused on the good bits -- movong your player piece across the board, entering into staged battles with enemies you encounter -- and dumped the junk -- all those dancing elves and glittery stuff.  The learning curve is steep at first as you have to work out the magic system -- different systems for on the board and in staged battles -- but once you know what you're doing it flows really nicely.  Can get a little repetitive, but then what game doesn't?  Lovely graphics, ambient music, altogether an absorbing game.  Don't get too attached to Lambert, as you lose him at the end of the "human" interest story, no matter how you play it.  Bit nasty of the authors to do that really....
The "achievements" aren't much, you win them during the normal course of the game, the only ones you need to look out for are the ones where you deliberately have to under-achieve, like using no magic, or finishing a level with no gold (spend it on teams in your capital or on upgrades from the veteran), or not building parts of your city that won't be used...only a perfectionist would want to do any of that.

The Long Dark is a unique and intriguing game that I would definitely reccomend for any fellow lovers of survival and the foresty wilderness in general. One of the first thing's that got me interested in this game is the artstyle, I'm not sure whether or not it has a name. I first saw this kind of artstyle in TF2, and then most recently in Firewatch (which kind of helped me live out my fantasy of TLD:Summer edition). It's got a charming sort of mid 20th century cartoonish feel, but more gritty and based in an unforgiving world. There's something about it that makes it feel nostalgic even though its new. Though I love the graphics and the tone set by the brightness levels at times in this game, the lack of animations is a bit disappointing. Being able to sit down in this game would be great as theres many a time you're waiting out a blizzard or a subzero morning near a fire and wish you could sit down on a chair or the ground and journal/read your skill books instead of just make believe crouching.
The gameplay itself provides a fairly steep learning curve. If you're used to more topical survival games like Minecraft maybe, this will be a dive into the deep end. I definitely wouldn't reccomend playing your first game on anything above the lowest difficulty unless you have the patience of a saint and dont mind losing your game progress each time you find out how easy it is to die in certain areas/scenarios. Once you get used the game's mechanics and have a good idea of where the shelters and supplies are in the game, you can up the difficulty and get a satisfying amount of challenge without feeling too overwhelmed. A co-op mode would be amazing, but it's a shame none is planned.
The realism of this game is also what made it stand out for me. It's a little bit silly that wildlife makes a bee line to kill you every single time you're in their vision cone (which is thankfully a little more fogiving than it could be realistically) but it makes up for it in regards to other realistic things you'd have trouble with surviving in the wildness. Food quality, water potability, infections, frostbite, and even mobility restrictions based on the denseness of your clothing are all very unique and well thought out mechanics. You truly need to make a plan each day for how you're going to do something and just jumping outside without thinking about the consequences will bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥just like it would in real life.
As far as functionality goes I've been spared in the bugs department. I haven't had any crash to desktop moments where I was nearly at my destination or anything. Random parts of the map can be a surprising FPS killer and with graphics like these that a bit more simplistic you'd think there wouldn't be such issues, but I suppose coding with Unity does pose unexpected problems with varying hardware. Recently though I did pay dearly for my relatively bug free experience in that when the most recent update came I lost my journals and badge progress when the dev team stressed that it would only be save games that were deleted. They still haven't gotten back to me on at least what went wrong in that regard. It was discouraging and I know I won't be dedicating the amount of time again that I did with my main save to write all those roleplayed journals, much less the extraordinary amount of playtime you'd have to accrue getting any of the badges in this game, but still it's a nice goal for people who have a true die hard love for the game.
Overall this game gets 9/10 for me because I really do love the art style,setting,survival mechanics, and general gameplay intricacies. Perhaps once it gets it's full release I'll have even more love for it to push it to 10.

My overall review is over but there are some small critiques I'll make about the game. The loss of the journals and badge progress isn't what made me think a little less of the game lately. That was mainly to do with the raising of the price months before their LOOONG awaited story mode (which they've been wanting to get into the game since late 2014) hit on August 1. I feel that that would have been the time to finally come out of early access for this game and start charging full price.
Also, the most recent update changed certain stylistic decisions that I dont 100% love. They really brightened up the indoor areas of the game that used to have a real moody and offputting tone due to their muted colors and darkly lit (even in daytime) interiors. Now there's a lot of odd reds and greens along with much higher brightness interiors that don't really fit in with the unforgiving nature of the game. The UI has taken a step forward and two back also. While I do like the new status indicators as they fit in with the game's "cartoony wilderness" feel, I really do miss seeing the more intricate information on the sidebars like calorie info. I realize that it's unrealistic to know precisely what amount of calories you sit at, but it was something that's been the game for years and something that I would hope they'd carry on, but it is early access so anything is up for change. The other drawback of the newer UI is the wind indicator. In the past versions of the game an icon of a shield appeared in the lower right hand corner of the screen which was very small and low in opacity to indicate that you were protected from the wind (protecting yourself from the windchill factor is extremely important) and it was simple enough. Now the icon is about twice it's original size, it's opacity is 100%, and it's right in upper middle portion of the screen which is detracts from immersion greatly for me. I don't know what was wrong with the previous one, if they wanted to update the graphic to have a more "cartoony wilderness" feel they should have just put the new shield graphic where the old one was with the same size and opacity.
There's some other odd decisions that made the game a little bit harder to play for people with certain real life problems. For instance their decision to make you click and hold to interact with things where it all used to be done with a single click of the mouse. This isn't great for me because I sprained my index finger badly years ago and it can bother me when holding left click too much. Thankfully they did add an option to disable this to keep it a one click interaction but why change that at all?
The other small thing is that the last time I played this game post update to get a feel for some of the new visuals I literally got snow blind from this game. My left eye was hurting me for days and I had to sunglasses to use the computer because my eyes were so sensitive to the light which they are already. I take care to lower the brightness of my screens because of my sensitive eyes and even after that the snow gave me fits from looking at it too long during the day time. However now the snow at day time in this game seem's brighter and whiter than it ever was and it even with my brightness and contrast all the way down on my monitor it instantly hurts to look at the snow in the daytime. I wonder if there's anything that can be done about that (perhaps some ingame sunglasses so my character doesn't actually suffer the same very real life pain of snow blindness?) because I really like to play this game from time to time, but the threat of eye strain isn't worth it.
In all seriousness though these problems I have with the game are minute in the grand scheme of the game and really go to show that there is no huge problems with the game that would warrant not giving it the gameplay it definitely deserves. With that said I don't how much more sandbox I'll be playing after having done so much of it already, but I do look forward greatly to the storymode coming in a few weeks.

1. TLD is a decent game in allowing a player to try to survive in a post-apocalyptic world in northern Canada (below the treeline). Think survivng in the Rockies. Lots of trees, snow and wildlife.
2. It allows a person to freely roam a vast world of multiple regions (exploration gameplay).
3. Players are allowed to harvest and do limited crafting (RPG gameplay).
4. Game can be easy to hardcore by chosing your play mode (FPS gameplay).
5. Strategy game that requires keeping an eye on your vitals, and preparing in advance of when and where you will travel to ensure you will survive getting there and back.
1.
That told me this was another wanton game of bang-bang kill them all or be killed game (something I was trying to escape from playing WoW).
2.
The clock starts ticking not only on your vitals even the items you carry decay -- like canned food, decays like it's in 100F jungle weather and by a nuclear reactor -- despite the weather is constantly freezing (which preserves food and items for even centuries!). Just a couple days of sleep and your canned food decays by whole percentages. Very unreasonable decay rates in a game that has achieves for 200+ game days of play!
3.
Problem is the tiny white dot so loved by shooters for interacting
Try picking up items when the dot can't even be seen on the screen to pick up items to center yourself to pick up items! Hope it isn't an arrow or you'll be cussing up a storm just trying to find that tiny dot to interact with objects against a snowy background ...
Sandbox mode also doesn't feel like a true sandbox with mechanisms to push a player along on a different type of script. Take for example, the new Cabin Fever mechanic. Designed to push people out of base camps and to trek in the cold. This on top of now blizzards tear and ruin clothing a mechanic that is with the Pilgram mode too (when did a blizzard rip clothing anyway??? Not even hurricanes rip clothing to 0% [totally ruined]. Fabric is quite strong or our hair would shatter in the wind even!).
One hand the game isn't at all about reality (like the whole CME that created this world that kills off every other human in the world but 2 people who survived a plane crash and wildlife), but it adds elements of gameplay that totally doesn't jive with surviving the near tundra conditions.
1.
Die you're dead forever. 200 game day toon ... puff ... gone. Game autosaves at critical events so you can't go back to a previous save. Will lose everything if you die. See The Bad #2 and the Cabin Fever mechanic and why turtling became a fact-of-life for long-term survival (so true in real life survival too).
2.
Lose it forever. Bullets are rare drops (no reloading in the game -- heck even the game
allowed reloading!!! -- and once gone you're reduced to using arrows. But they also limit the amount of arrows you can craft, as you only can make arrows out of birch saplings (a rare item that doesn't respawn -- think rare crafting hassles in MMORPGS).
Add the glancing arrow mechanic; arrows so thin that can't be seen at 10 yards away are so easy to get lost -- with your arrowhead that took ages to craft and feathers that was recently nerfed to dropping once around carcasses -- means little replay value for a survival game (it's mechanics tuned for weekend gaming, not passing 4+hrs a night in as the resources will be used up quickly).
3.
.
Worse, the clothes you wear counts against the capacity of your backpack -- yes, not clothes stored in the bag, what you're wearing, so the bag will never be 0 capacity unless you strip off every bit of clothing in the frozen North!
4.
. Each log can weigh 2.2lbs and remember that backpack limit? No firewood = permadeath hypothermia. But somehow with a Blizzard that can totally ruin your clothing, and temps below freezing, you need 20+lbs of it to keep alive -- when that backpack has the clothing you wear penalty and you got to carry your water and food, too.
5.
. Beautiful on an artistic basis, but practically painful and useless for anyone with a hand injury. Until players can toggle the UI on/off, the game is absolutely painful for people with disabilities playing (having to constantly hit the control key to preview your stats or die -- both with overuse of a damaged hand; to even seeing the world with mechanics that's for "challenge" only. That's NOT good game design. Good game design is thinking of what populations that would even play sandbox games in the first place ... at their pace and not having gamers scream of being "slow" or some "n00b" because you can't see well anymore in the larger social games out there.
If the devs would release a customizaiton menu for toggling the UI; respawning options; and choices for aim reticles this game can be 4 out 5 in quality. But "as is" the game suffers from "we make the game our way" syndrome, which introduces other problems as players aren't just one demographic and love more options, not less.

To those thinking about this game post- FREE WEEKEND around September 5th, 2015 and forward, this is for you.
TL; DR: DON'T GET EVOLVE (for reasons listed below from an active community member to one that has had his heart crushed with how this game came to be)
Four areas covered in review:
1. Context and Game Development
2. Product/DLC Release Cycle
3. Gameplay and Mechanics
4. The Community and Match Making
5. Summary
6. My Playhours justified!
Context and Game Development:
For those that continued reading, I'll start off with some context since the game's launch, in case many newcomers do not know or care to do the research. The game was released earlier this year, post a very productive alpha and beta. However, shortly thereafter, you may have heard of the DLC uproars and consistent bugs/glitches/fails that plagued the retail version for a very long time prior to any patches. Due to development focusing on the production cycle, the fixes were set in parallel to what developer provided the console version. Therefore, realize this that some bugs still exist (talking about the stupid cursor bug that happens once in awhile, and a few others) due to a delayed patch cycle. Even with patches, many things seem to be a "1 step forward, 3 step backwards" type of deal. That is, due to the rapid push-out of DLC, the game has continued to experience new problems most patches, or just pure errors that again take time to fix.
Product/DLC release cycle:
I'll be short and sweet with this. The DLC release for the game, many find exploitive and attrocious. As for my opinion, I am fine with the DLC, but as of late, it has become a disappointment. In the beginning, the DLC was standalone; most of the DLC was cosmetic as skins for weapons, character or class specific and what not. The skins themselves were weapons only, meaning the overall design of the characters would not be altered in any form besides weapons or color schemes, but this has changed with the release of the Meteor Goliath.
Upon release of new characters, monsters were sold individually and so were hunters (this individual sale was where the problem resided). After a community uproar, the sale policy was changed and those tier 4 characters were provided via Season Pass 1. Same to the tier 5 characters with the introduction of the Season Pass 2, yet it did take time to change to this bulk buy concept. To TRS' (Turtle Rock Studios) defense, this was their first AAA title and IP, so it was still a learning experience, but the overall monetization efforts between them as well as the publisher My2k was a big failure.
Gameplay and Mechanics:
Yet, the most upsetting part was despite the awesome content, the combination of new content and a fledging company resulted in terrible balance issues between hunters and monsters, even character specific. These problems still persist and despite the outcry, these problems will continue. The issue resides in the process of balancing where character trials are done by Pros and ESL Teams (keyword being TEAMS), meaning minor balance adjustments pros suggest catastrophically impact the overall public player base due the unreliability of solo matchmaking and metagame mechanics of tracking/hunting/team-composition.
To put it in lamens terms, the pro teams that provide feedback for character debuffs/nerfs or buffs run in teams far more efficient than anything you will encounter in public matchmaking. Therefore, if someone picks something out of the recommended team composition or perks, the entire team suffers as random teams cannot perform to the level of pros or regular teams which consist of friends willing to communicate. Some ways this misrepresentation has ruined gameplay/mechanics stems into monster health/survivability and just simple things like how ineffective the hunter jetpack has become as of late. This misrepresentation results in the whole community debates of "Monsters too OP, or Hunters too OP." This disproportionate representation inevitably leads to similar issues of player base segmentation due to skill gaps as described in the following category.
Community and Matchmaking:
Finally, the last category many will be most interested in as this is still an area of concern and all else aside, my main reason to recommend not buying the game. The community has risen and fallen multiple times since the game's release (which has been about half a year almost at the time of review). At the moment, the community has fallen under the 300 Steam mark, meaning you cannot view players online in game anymore since the number is so low. This inevitably leads to horrible teamplay as skill levels differ so much. Even more so, the new Matchmaking 2.0 makes the traditional Hunt mode to be a catastrophic failure as the skill segmentation is done poorly due to the inbalance between players. You may have experienced some form or another of said reasons in the free-to-play weekend, but these problems will persist post-weekend as the player base again levels out.
More so, the overall community is inaccurately respresented in many forms. The subreddit for evolve may have more members posting than those playing at a time, along with the game developers continuing to favor the input of pros to continue this infant dream of competitive gameplay. I say infant due to the overarching problem of a small player base negatively impacting any efforts to improve competitive matchmaking.
If unknown, Matchmaking 2.0 is an effort by TRS to promote competitive ranked play. Prior to MM 2.0, players could play the traditional Hunt mode without any penalty of leaving prior to match completion without penalties in the form of reduced Character rank or timeouts. MM 2.0 has shifted the traditional form into only ranked play, meaning the original Hunt mode was removed for this competive copy and there is no way to enjoy the original Hunt form outside of running a Evacuation gameplay (Evac being the 5 day campaign, either PVP or PVE, being 4v1 or 4vCP) or custom match with friends.
Summary:
To sum up my overall decision, with the reasons above and with foreshadowing as the game development is plateauing out due to the final push for DLC coming out soon in the form of the remaining Tier 5 characters, it is a good idea to avoid the game, at least until it is within the $20 - $30 mark. However, by that time, I assume the game's player base would have fallen even further, so its best to avoid purchasing the game.
Thanks for reading!
Edit Sept. 5, 2015:
My Playhours Justified:
Had this as a comment to address my play hours, but people skipped it, so here's my justification for play hours.
To those mentioning my play hours, realize my review is based off of the time since the beginning to now, post all that development. To be frank, as many others have mentioned it in other reviews, the game was extremely promising in the beginning being visually and mechanically fresh, so let's say ~250 of those hours were within the first 3 months of game release. By that time, many DLC and patches came out coupled with balancing issues where my play time dropped drastically as the appeal to the game fell.
Since then, the only real reason I do play, or continue to do so is due to my own friends playing it far more intensively than I am. I became a part of a team, and was the dedicated medic for most matches, so I can't necessarily leave friends hanging, as playing without a dedicated team is tough. However, recent changes are making that seem like a viable solution rather than continuing as my recent "hours played in the last 2 weeks show." I only say this as many can understand, playing a game to only experience frustration or ending on a sour mood post play is not appealing in any way.

Just one more door...
These few words describe the entirety of the game. The question of what lies behind that closed door. Whether it is the exit or a merchant or just a empty room. This single constant thought is what drives me to try and open every single door in this game. The chance of finding maybe the little bit of dust to power another room. The hope of finding the exit and going for a wild run to it. The fear of seeing three door in the next room instead of one.
So what makes this game special? It’s this feeling of dread and wonder that you will experience in every single game. Dungeon of the Endless is by no standard a content heavy game or even has a little of items and enemies. It’s how it works with this small amount of content that generates this feeling. Each level is randomly generate when you load it and you’ll often see the same rooms. Problem is the layout is always different and the exit might just be in the next room or at the end of a long hallway. So what you need to do is slowly room by room explore your own maze and hope that with opening the next door no monster spawn, because you won’t be able to light up all rooms. Especially later on when Dust, their energy currency, becomes a rare commodity.
Outside of the very well used game mechanics it also has a lot of hidden story about each character/heroes you can unlock. By pairing up two certain or more heroes with another everytime you beat a level you get a bit of story about them. And let me tell you some of these pairings aren’t good. You can beat a level with it but it will be hard.
So all in all I would recommend Dungeon of the Endless.
Yes, the pixel graphics are very fitting with the game and the soundtrack. The gameplay is solid and even after failing on the tenth floor of the first level after 2 hours you want to try again and again and again. Because you’ll always be telling yourself:
P.S. for the more hardcore of gamer: The game starts in Too Easy. You will fail on the Too Easy mode. Just throwing that out there.

Space Hulk: Ascension & Sanctum 2 had a mutant pixel baby and it's pretty OK I guess. One of those games you have to go read the wiki first because lazydevs couldn't be bothered to portray much info in-game. You can play it multiplayer - but it wasn't really designed with multiplayer in mind...
-resources aren't pooled, so you will be doing that manually to build / research things asap and survive.
-There are many enemies and random factors that temporarily render heroes pointless: Each Hurna Shaman in a room reduces (stacking) hero damage by 50% to 66%, randomly discovered Stele's randomly reduce hero armor to zero and cut hero damage in half.
-Operating resource-generating modules are required for survival, but in multiplayer that leaves one ore more players stuck in the same room doing nothing all floor long. It's fine in single-player or two-player co-op where you control multiple characters and can leave one to Operate, but it's a real problem in 4-player co-op.
The game is very much about towers... and there are those hero guys/girls/creatures too I guess...
It also bears mentioning that the controls are really strange. You can't move voluntarily or target something specifically within a room, you can only right-click to move into a room and then your character just kinda does whatever the heck they want there beyond you telling them to:
-move into a different room
-activating their 0 to 2 active abilities (depends on how much you've leveled up)
-eating food to heal
-resetting ability cooldowns... with 'science'
Actual control over your hero is extremely limited compared to most games you've probably played.
Despite all that, it's a good price point (also you can pick it up on sale) and can be fun with friends as long as you are eyes-wide-open aware that you will probably fail and don't sweat it. I'd strongly advise you buy the Pixel edition first, then upgrade to Crystal if you really like what you see - it adds some new heroes and game modes but doesn't drastically change the experience.

A prison ship crash lands on (or rather in) a hostile alien world, where creatures of the planet who prefer dark areas will kill you and destroy the energy crystal that powers your escape. If you are an indie supporter who likes to see a game evolve and support a project early on, then yes, it's a great buy. Also if you are content with what amounts to a sandbox that is still very much a trial run of the features in the design doc but are OK with may features still outstanding, then certainly dive in while the water is relatively clean. If you are looking for a game that is near feature complete with only minor bugs, then perhaps it's worth waiting. If I had to guess, Stonehearth is at least a year away from being ready for final release; so if you don't have the patience to wait until the features you want are in the game, then you may want to wait. Perhaps the Early Access money from Steam will afford a larger team and speed up the development...
In the end, be sure and check out the games website and watch some YouTube videos to help with your decision.

Stonehearth is a leisurely paced city-building game in which you guide your "Hearthlings," a tribe of hobbit-like people (dwarves and a rabbit-y race have been announced, but are not currently in the game), from an empty campsite to... well, that's up to you. The graphics are charmingly blocky voxels with a varied and vibrant color palette. The music is made up of similarly charming string-heavy orchestrations that set the mood for work, sleep, or combat. You can judge for yourself from the sample video whether this style works for you, but it works together marvelously, forming a cohesive vision.
In peaceful game mode you are free to make whatever kind of town/city you want. You can assign crafting/gathering classes to your hearthlings, like farmer, trapper, shepherd, carpenter, weaver, cook, and mason (many more classes are in progress, including animal trainer, engineer, geomancer, and magma smith). You can design custom buildings or select pre-made designs from a list. You can mine, lay roads, trade with traveling merchants, and more. If you meet daily food, comfort, and wealth goals, additional hearthlings join your community.
In normal mode you can do all that, but will occasionally be attacked by zombies, goblins, orcs, kobolds, ogres, and more. Here you'll want at least a few footmen, the basic military class, which can later be upgraded to archers and knights. (a magic class is coming later), and a blacksmith to create weapons and armor. Once in a while, a goblin camp will appear and threaten you with an ultimatum: give us resources or we'll attack. You can keep the peace and face further extortion, or send in your fighters to eliminate them. Combat occurs in real-time, albeit slowly, and there is basically no player input required aside from pointing your fighters in the right direction.
Right now, that's just about all there is to do in the game. However, these developers are very active and transparent. There is a weekly update on their website
, a development roadmap, user forums, Twitch streaming of in-progress features, and more. In fact, the game is progressing so much that my only annoyance with it is losing my save every few weeks when a new Alpha version comes out. The new features make that a lot less painful, though.

Melissa K. and the Heart of Gold is a 3D puzzle game, full of hidden object mini-games, and other assorted games and puzzles. As much of an adventure game as it is a 3D puzzle game, Melissa K. and the Heart of Gold takes you around the world, to various locations, some of which you will have to return to, in order to complete later puzzles and advance in the story. You can also replay puzzles to beat your old scores.
The visual appeal of this game is very well done. It looks very intricate and you can tell the developers put effort into making it have a high visual appeal, but the 3D aspect of it is very simplistic. The FMV clips throughout the game make you feel like you are playing through a movie at times. For a low budget, indie title, I thought it was exceptionally well done.
This game is trash.

If you like fragmented object scenes and want a bunch of difficult puzzles on top, buy this game. If you want an adventure game or you are a completionist, forget that this store page exists.
Melissa K. and the Heart of Gold is a collection of good fragmented object scenes (with some classic hidden object scenes here and there) and a large number of varied puzzles. All of these have additional challenges beyond the story mode to keep the game a little fresher, and play time surprisingly high for a smartphone title.
But it’s definitely not an adventure game. For starters, it has less than half dozen locations overall. They are all beautiful, and the pseudo-3D makes it unique among this genre, but said 3D is also the foremost tool to hide everything in the stupidest spots, turning the game into a tedious pixel hunt.
And there is the story… or more like the lack of it. It is supposed to be about the resurrection of an ancient Buddhist demon, but actually understanding it is impossible. The plot and the dialogues have zero cohesion or dramaturgy: events happen and people (dis)appear randomly, and all conversation is made up of awkwardly, boringly acted lines that have no logical dialogue structure whatsoever.
Therefore, this game is only good to play a bunch of puzzles. But Steam has better and cheaper alternatives for that.

With the astonishing amount of negative reviews for this game I feel like I need to clarify some things for anybody considering purchasing the game. At the moment the game could be considered finished, in my opinion it is the most immersive, deep zombie survival games out there. However the developers mistakingly made promises years ago that are yet to be delivered and it has cost them dearly, if not for this mistake the game could have been considered finished with overwhelmingly positive reviews.
They are a small, independent development team who are actively developing the game and including new features, do not get the impression that they have just given up. If anything their biggest flaw is that they are too ambitious. For $15, even in it's current build, definitely worth it. Just try not to hype yourself up for any major features 'coming soon'.

Project Zomboid. Should you buy it?
The short answer is yes. Project Zomboid is in my opinion the most realistic zombie survival game out there. The gameplay is fun and the atmosphere is exellent. Wandering the empty streets of Muldraugh and Westpoint makes you feel like you really are in the acopalypse. Again i have to emphasize the atmosphere. The feeling of hoplesness and inevitability really make the game that much better.
Project Zomboid can be played alone, but the co-op and multiplayer aspects increase the play time of the game almost indefinitely. While Project Zomboid is still in early access and may never be fully finished it is still worth your money even at this stage.

Come on. Seriously. How could the idea to use mindless clicking as a game mechanic actually become a trend worth capitalizing on?
Moving away from the idea behind it, and heading into the game itself, there's a good bit to talk about.
First of all, the graphics themselves aren't good for a game with so many intricate visual details, or at least, details that are unbecoming of a game that expects little of you other than just clicking.
Second of all, it's drab as hell. Clicker Heros is bright, colorful, and has a whimsical atmosphere. This game has a dull and damp atmosphere. Which leads me into my next point.
Thirdly, this game seems to take itself seriously. Click Heros purposefully takes the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of itself in quite a few text lines. It's monsters look silly, it's world is silly, the heros are silly. Here you have a failed attempt at making something as benign as a clicker game, as serious as an RPG. There isn't any stimulation. Good, deep games can be dark, because the game play makes stimulation. A clicker game needs to add it! Which again, brings me into my next point.
Lastly, the additional layer of complexity with the item system does not make this game less of a clicker game. Increasing necessary involvement in the kind of game in which the player wants to be idle, or at the very least mindlessly waste time, is such a silly idea.
Sadly, this is a well made game, that was definitely made to take the market over with a superior product. The problem is, there is really nothing clever about it other than some interesting game play elements, which aren't so much desired in a clicker game. Good on the developers for making it, but you should perhaps focus your talents on a different kind of game.

Clicker Guild is a free to play incremental clicker game sort of the same as Sakura Clicker and Clicker Heroes.  It worked on Win 10, looked good, sounded ok, played ok.  The negative reviews said the game didn't have a Save function, but when i tried the game, it saved when you Closed the game and even saved lootchests to be opened next time you are playing actively and save gold offline.  The music is boring and the sound effects is simple.  It has unique detailed animated hirelings that line up surrounding the single animated enemy in the center, but the enemy are average looking.
The difference in this game is the gear system.  RNG gear drop from enemy killed and you have to put your cursor on it to compare it with what you have, then you left click to wear it, and right click to sell it.  Dropped gear will disappear after 10ish seconds.  There is different levels of gear from common to legendary.  Gear you are wearing degrades after passing by a boss and each level drops slightly better gear.   You will be more busy checking and picking gear than to be clicking on the enemy.  The devs is actively fixing the game from the feedback.  If you are not paying attention you might put gear on that has lower dps than what you have in that slot, epic and legendary will ask you to confirm, or you might sell gear that you could have used.   Each hireling and your hero has 3 slots for gear.
Give this game a try, maybe you might like it.

I was surprised at how engaging this storyline is, especially for a scripted, and hidden-object puzzler, which don't often hold my interest for long; I played through the basic story in ~under 7 hours or so.
tl/dr:
Fun puzzler, will take 5+hours for an adult on first playthrough (with some use of hint button/strategy guide - which is provided in the options menu in-game); worth the price.
1.) Hint button timer can be set to fast or slow, and the difficulty of the game describes these options *clearly* at game start.
2.) Cinematics can be skipped - but there is an achivement for watching them all without skipping.  Some are annoying, and all take a bit too long imo, but they're tasteful, if low budget.
3.) Puzzle instructions are clear, but puzzles themselves can be challenging.  There are extra puzzles at the end, and three different difficulties for several of them.
4.) Music can be turned off, but if you like Enigma-type music it should suit some of your taste.
5.) Safe for kids, but not patronizingly idealistic/simplistic.
1.) For those interested in achievements/completionists, you will inevetibly need to play through at least twice if you don't carefully read the achievements.  Most can be unlocked in normal game play, but some are related to puzzles or events that are just tedious, and the skip button becomes so very easy to use, thus preventing the accumulation of a completion in some challenges.
2.) For those interested in stunning graphics, you will be nonplussed by the decade-old character textures and limited facial expressions, though animations are fairly fluid and overall animation quality isn't unbearable.  One character looks close to Nathan Fillian's appearance from his Firefly days.
3.) Some puzzles are dependent on spotting almost miniscule variations in item texture.  While the puzzle isn't hard once you figure out what to do, finding that first tiny button is sometimes annoying if you don't know that's what you're looking for.
~In terms of a puzzle game, this one get 7.5/10 from me, which means it's not a failing grade.
~In terms of creativity and clarity of puzzles, there were some good ones, and some were very well thought out; most will complete (and some even show the perfect solution) when you're 'close enough' that it's not absurdly tedious (the string puzzle will explain this remark): 8/10.
~In terms of a story game, this one gets 8/10 from me because there were things I didn't see coming, and yet those things weren't outrageously unbelievable, though some of the plotline was difficult to follow without using hints.
~In terms of technical difficulties, I ecountered
10/10 on this front.
Very nice work, SDP Games!
This review is based only on the base game, not the CE content.
- Having finished the CE content, let me add an 8-8.5/10 for that.  You learn more about the Nathan Fillian character (he has the right personality for this, and dialogue is simple, but engaging and amusing - well done, here!) and his motivations, and gain a new player ability that makes looking at things a new way an absolute.
CE content adds about 2 hours to the game (with some use of the hint button).
Good game overall in its genre.  As a rule I play wargames and puzzlers, with some side-scrollers and 3rd person shooters, and this game got my attention on content alone.  8-8.5/10 overall.

While I reccomend the game I feel it deserves a caveot. That is the gameplay is clunky. The game is a masterclass in its graphics, storytelling, sound design, atmosphere, characters, and everything not relating to the gameplay.
The gameplay is not bad, but in trying to add deapth and finess feels unpolished. most notably the various ammunition types feel like they get in the way more than adding a nuance to the game. There are already a slew of weapons and plasmids which act like spells giving so much freedom in how is played. Hacking is fun at first but then the difficulty ramps up on it and it needs to be done like every 2 minutes and just becomes a hassle later on.  I don't mind the scarcity mentality that the game pushes and in fact think that is good... That said I think the game would benefit from being a bit more streamlined. Fewer ammunition types, better descriptions/menus, pc controls can use some rebinding, and better pacing on the hacking.
The storytelling of the game is some of the best in all gaming though and more then compensates for any of these gameplay complaints if you go into the game knowing the gamplay is not perfect. The voice acting is great, the story is delivered as you walk around and almost never takes control away from you like half-life. Just everything is done so well and is so intentional.
If you are willing to learn to forgive some clunky gameplay and learn its systems, the games story and everything else about it will more than make up for its shortcomings.
This game got me into gaming, its art and a masterpiece. I highly recommend you get this game if your looking for good story with a good horror/action feel.

Game Menu Option: Two section – Volume and Miscellaneous settings. The volume section has the following: Dialogue, Music and Sound. The miscellaneous section has the following: Subtitles, Screen Resolution, Quality, Full-Screen, Custom Cursor and Camera Sensitivity.
Game Difficulty Modes: Three game difficulty modes – Novice, Adventurer and Expert.
Cinematic/Dialogue: All cinematic scenes can be skipped if you do not want to watch them. They can be watch over again under the cutscene section the extras. There is an option for skipping the entire dialogue scene without having sit through it.
Voiceovers: Nothing much can be said about the voice overs asides from that they are well done.
Game Music/Sounds: Nothing much can be said about the music/sounds asides from that they fit well with the game.
Game Graphics: Nothing much can be said about the graphics asides from that they are nicely drawn with a painted feel to them.
Inventory Panel: There is a lock option for the inventory panel. Easy access for the items that are collected in the game.
Notebook: Six sections – Achievements, Secret Letters, Chapters, Buddha Statues, Notes and Objectives.
Map: The map interactive with useful indicators; map icons/markers. The legend on the map explains the function for each of the map icons. The ability to fast travel to another location and back.
Hidden Object Gameplay: Shadow items, Find “X” amount, Fragment items with some and/or no interaction required. Most of the hidden object scenes can be replayed in the hidden object section in the extras.
Puzzle Gameplay: Most of the puzzles are fairly easy to solve. Some puzzles has extra puzzles in them to solve. There is a skip button if the puzzle(s) becomes too tasking to solve. Most of the puzzles can be replayed in the puzzle section in the extras.
Game Ending: There is an ending for the main portion of the game. The bonus chapter somewhat overlaps the main portion of the game. But is different game character's perspective.
Game Achievements: In game and Steam. There are total of 32 different achievements to earn throughout the game. Each of the achievements has certain requirements before they’re obtained.
Game Collectables: 21 Buddha Statues and 14 Secret Letters.
Game Concept Art: 12 concept art from the game.
Game Soundtrack: 17 soundtracks from the game.
Game Strategy Guide: The strategy guide can be access through the game’s menu only.
Game Length: The main portion of the game has nine chapter. The bonus portion of the game has three chapters. In total there are 12 chapters in total.
Game Trading Card/Badge: This a special feature only available in the Steam’s version of the game. The game drops three different trading cards only once and the rest of the cards: Community Market, Booster Packs and Trading. The game badge can be crafted after having all the card in the inventory then it can be upgraded four more times.

OK initially it was somewhat difficult to grasp the general playability of this game upon initial loadup. But the simple truth of the matter is that this game is a gem thats been dumped on repetetive disapproval of microwave gamers. By microwave I mean the influx of gamers who need immediate satisfaction in the form of rankless lobbies yet beg for a balanced atmosphere.
The game was intended to allow human players to communicate and work cohesively as a unit to hunt. Nothing new right but the greatest aspect of this is that you are hunting another human player who thinks, fears, and eventually develops an ego the way that you do as the match progresses. With this being said of course there would be certain imbalances as certain players develop skill with specific hunters, monsters, etc., and at times it is difficult for noobs to recieve a warm welcome when paired with experienced vets. But this, I feel, was intentional and even parallel to irl war fronts. The grunts would go into war not knowing what to expect, often paired with soldiers who had already seen their share of battle, and over time would steel themselves to usher in the next group of grunts.
Only two things keep pushing this game towards it's destruction leaving it just an uninstalled game in all our libraries. One is obviously in the creators hands in the form of constant rent, i.e dlc. The second is solely based upon the gamers, quit thumbing down a game purely because it doesnt fit into your gaming style, communicate in game and find a group that you can traverse the badlands of shear with. Evolve is one of the most underrated and improperly utilized games on steam currently.

This game is a turn based fantasy strategy game. Comparable to Age of Wonders or a fantasy version of a Civilization game.
What the game does really well is how it makes creatures beloning to none a good threat and force to be reckoned with. Varying from lonesome creatures to world threatning bosses that can devour whole armies. Don't worry though, with magical spells and heroes you made powerful by exploring the world and it's dangers your army still has a shot ;)
A feature that really deserves praise is the customablity. You can create your own leader and units. From scratch you can decide what weapon and armor they wear and what abilities they will have. Don't worry if this is not your cup of tea though, you can also train a list of standard troops ranging from simple scouts to real champions.
The only thing that could  be handled better is the time it takes to build and train buildings and units. For me the start of the game feels really slow because of it. You can barely face any real creature threats and since you don't want to waste more time by having to replace units it's a very carefull playstyle at the beginning, existing more out of skipping turns and waiting than anything else. Once you get out of that phase and your empire starts expanding this isn't that much of a problem anymore though.
