I was among those people who waited release of this game with excitement! However, as many other fans of Disciples II, I was disappointed.
I completed the story with the Empire (Humans) and started to play with the Legions (Demons), hoping that I will find something that will get me going, however I didn't. Although the story is quite interesting and I wanted to find out what will happen next, the battles are so repetitive, that I just caught myself thinking: why do I even play this game?
I guess it's faster to just watch the intro in Disciples 3: Resurrection - it gives a pretty good summary of what happened in Disciples 3: Renaissance.
I feel too much influence from Heroes of Might and Magic V in this game, which, in my opinion, is not a good example of turn-based strategy. I think the developers should have sticked to their own principles as seen in Disciples II.
This game is not all bad, there are also some good things and improvements, so to be fair I'll list both pros and cons.
Pros:
- Great graphics, although sometimes there are so many details, that it is hard to distinguish objects.
- Zoom in/zoom out - missed that one in Disciples II.
- The player has very specific choices about how one can develop his character. I particularly liked that you can develop your leadership up to 7 (and even 8 with specific items). Also transform, revive and other additional leader skills come quite handy.
- It's much easier to conquer enemy capitals. In Disciples II you had to use whole arsenal of potions, artefacts and spells to atleast have a chance against defenders of the capital (and not always it was enough).
- Node guardians is a good idea. They are strong and most of the time they are able to defend themselves, so you don't need to worry about loosing your resources and burdensome rod-planting character management as in Disciples II.
- Achievements. Atleast for me they provide a bit of extra motivation.
- Thief is a fully-functional leader with initial leadership of 3. In Disciples II, Thief had no leadership.
- You can carry all you items to the next act. In Disciples II, you could only take five items with you.
Cons:
- Battle system is the worst aspect of this game. The battles are long and repetitive. After few level ups, when it's not possible to lose anymore, I think everyone finds himself pressing the Quick resolve button. Also I found the obstacles annoying. They needlessly limit the movement of units. Also I'd rather prefer the static battles without tactical map movement as in Disciples II. Thus the initiative actually had some meaning.
- No shortcuts, except for Space (End turn)
- Camera rotation and zoom level in battles also are far from perfect. It's not possible to rotate the battlefield 360 degrees and zoom level is not sufficient - all units look small. The lower corners are almost out of reach. If an enemy is hiding in the right lower corner, you have to turn camera to that corner on every attack to actually perform it. And that is annoying.
- Sometimes it's hard to find the way, because there are trees or building covering the field of view.
- Not only spells are limited to once per turn (twice for Archmage), but this limitation apply to whole of the spellbook. In Disciples II, this limitation applied only to a particular spell. So, spells are not actually that important for victory and it's not worth to research them all. Most of the time I used only healing and damage spells.
- I never had a need to use a thief. I don't actually know what is his special trait. So Guild as a building is useless. Atleast for me.
- Due to spell limitations and lack of Thief actions, it does not make that much of a difference which gameplay style you choose (Warlord, Archmage or Guildmaster).
- Also the interface is not very intuitive. It took me about 45 minutes to understand how this game works.
My overall rating is 5/10.
I think I will return to this game just to enjoy the story and graphics, when I will have nothing better to play. And perhaps my opinion will change. But for now, I can't recommend this game to anyone.
p.s. Disciples 3: Reincarnation is out, which is sort of a remake of Renaissance and Resurrection. Perhaps it is better. So if you are considering to try Disciples 3 afterall, perhaps you should buy Reincarnaction.

I was a HUGE fan of the original franchise. Turn based, somewhat interesting combat, and all kinds of fun mechanics to learn and optimize. Disciples III seems to have precisely one thing in common with the previous games: the name. I guess the turn based combat is also shared, but is vastly different. Indeed, this entire game feels more like someone saw the gorgeous art of the first two, and thought, "Hey, we own this franchise. Let's make more gorgeous art, and redo everything else! They'll come crawling for it!" The only real positive I can say beyond how pretty it is is that I didn't pay full price. The engine is .... stupid. The world economies are 'smoothed out' to the point of being stupid. Now, suddenly, you can only control parts of the world with strategically placed control points: there are no 'holy person's to drop a control rod to annoy the opposition. The inventory system is atrocious (Really?? I have to scroll to the right one column at a time, after I select the right interface screen, just to consume the potion I just got??) as is the advancement system. I'm all for advancement trees, but this is just ludicrous. And the story is .... shallow, to say the least. Oh, and thank you soooooooooooooooooo much Game Designers and Developers for not allowing me to turn off the spell animations. Sure they're pretty once or twice, and I admire them for that. But EVERY TIME???? Come on!
EDIT: Oh, and I entirely forgot! I've watched the CPU's heroes literally walk through encounters to take over resources. Walking through encounters applied to my own avatar, so they could just go about their thievery and bypass me completely. And let's also not forget that not only can the computer target you with offensive spells when there is Absolutely No Way It Could Know Where to Target the Spell, but their low level attack spell does damage AND removes my ability to cast a spell that turn as well. You know, because it's "fun" and "challenging".
Trust me. Save your money and get Disciples 1 or 2. They're much better games.

Disciples 3 Renaissance tries to improve over D2 in several ways, and it succeed to a certain extent

+ Inquisition, Angels and Demons, Dwarfs, Elves !

+ the environment changes according to the owner (humans, elves or demons) as soon as you conquer or lose territory
It also has the same defects of its predecessor
- an army of level one units can be defeated by a couple of level 2 units, stats double from level 1 to level 2, you have no chance
- as a consequence combat is frustrating at the beginning of a game
- once your units have gained two levels through the corresponding buildings, your army is virtually unstoppable
- "Normal" difficulty is punishing
- units have only one line to say, which gets on your nerves rapidly
- the game has a chilly pace, animations slow down the game immensely and become rapidly repetitive
- bugs are plentiful
TL; DR
graphics and environment 10/10
units 10/10
story 7/10 (nobody expects the Spanish Inquisition)
combat 7/10 (from frustratingly difficult to quite satisfaying)
music 6/10 (meh)

It should be emphasised that the game IS still in its alpha stages - that means there's only a limited amount of content in it at the moment. That aside, it's definitely very enjoyable, and the building editor and the like allows for very complex structures to be built already, and a single game can happily last for a few hours before you've reduced the goblins & undead to little more than nuisances.

This game is one of those casual hidden object games, which one can find plenty of around. The game nods continuously towards "Pirates of the Caribbean" and similar "Cursed pirate stories", which could be a plus or a minus depending on your personal preferences. It does boast rather nice background art and multiple "exotic" objects to manipulate from "all around the world". There is also a variety of ages where objects come from - modern, XVII-XVIII century and end of XIX century (if you care to go for a "bonus" adventure available under "Extras"). Some of the foreground objects look a bit cheap, though, and cutscene video quality is really way too low. While being very accessible overall (as a casual game should be) "Nightmares" does not explain everything (like "Skip by playing Mahjong" option or how to start hidden object minigames) very well in the beginning. However, there are no giant mechanical flaws in it, and the ones existing do not detract too much from the experience. Although the voice acting and overall sound assets are so-so, they do help to complete the "pirate mystery" atmoshpere. The storyline is super-simple and although it tries to add a couple of twists, overall there is nothing grasping about it. There is a little humor to be had and there are even a couple of jokes that might make you smile, but overall the game tends to overplay "serious mystery" part a little bit too much for my taste. A couple of cheap jumpscares are also available.  Having completed all of the available adventures I can say that the game does provide some casual fun for those, who appreciate the appropriate setting and do not mind to solve some simple puzzles (with ample hints available). Overall it is a good title to buy in a bundle and casually enjoy when you don't want to strain yourself or spend much time with a game. Perhaps, it could also be worth a try for HOG fans when on >75% discounts.

Cuphead is a boss gauntlet with some light overworld exploration, a handful of platforming run-and-gun stages, and a gorgeous art style inspired by cartoons from the 1930s. It will challenge you, and even put you through the meat grinder at times, but every death takes you one step closer to learning and eventually conquering the game's many multi-staged battles.
Perhaps even more importantly, every death is a new opportunity to enjoy the beautiful animations and backgrounds on display; it's easy to miss the details when you're frantically dodging the immediate threats to your existence. True to the cartoons that inspired it, a sense of quirky liveliness pervades everything—even the things that aren't actively trying to murder you.
Cuphead has developed a reputation for being difficult, and it earns that reputation, but fans of video games and cartoons (taking a wild guess and assuming there are a few of us around here) shouldn't overlook this game, regardless of skill level.

I was actually surprised by how much I enjoyed this game and I think it's a great example of how much can be done with so little, everything from the gameplay to the graphics are extremely minimal, with the vast majority of the game effectively being still images that pan from side to side.
The best thing about the game is by far how it provides just enough story info to create intrigue, making me quite eager the play the rest of the series to see how it is expanded (Which, considering the amount of theories I've seen about the game, I'm fairly certain it will be).
Some things to consider though before purchasing the game.
Firstly it is not like any other horror game in terms of gameplay, and in fact if you (like myself) consider jump scares to be the lowest form of 'horror' then you'll likely not rate it highly as a horror game at all, which is true for myself. Where I do think the game holds up is as a game of strategy; Of course you have the obvious strategic element (Managing your power usage), but you'll soon find that to survive the five nights, there is more you'll need to learn.
Overall I definately recommend the game considering the price, especially considering this game has been on sale during every steam sale this year and I in fact managed to purchase it for just £1, and for that price I certainly am not disappointed.

Upon purchasing this game, I wasn't expecting much from it. Opening up the game, the front screen was already too much for my computer to handle. But after playing a game on easy mode and losing on floor one, I knew this game was worth my money. If you are looking for something hard and also fun to play with your friends, this is the game for you. The only game-breaking mechanic that I found was that you could not pause in multiplayer. This is one of the reasons the game is so hard. When the dungeon gets bigger and bigger and you and your friend are trying to do 10 things at once, when one of your heroes are dying, it is hard to miss it. Having played with my friend we lost quite a few heroes while learning how to play the game. This is definitely a game worth your time and money.

Dugeon of the Endless is hodgepodge of game mechanics that through the power of amazing game design come together to form something greater then it's parts. You choose your dropship [read game style/ mode] and as many Hero's as can fit inside it and begin your quest into the Dungeon. I should point out that this game has a phenomenally balance enconomy but many new players will see it as stingy. You have Food/ Industy/ Dust/ and Science or F.I.D.S. as the game call it for short. Using your F.I.D.S. wisely is a large part of the learning curve of this game a I'll admitt I had a fair share of fustration with this but I hope you have patience like I did because once you grasp this you really get to see the depts of this design. Now the game runs in turns that happen everytime you open a door. These can trigger a enemy wave, though not always. These enemies can only spawn in rooms that arent powered or occupied by your hero's. All of this adds up to giving you a lot of control over a slighty random system. This opening of doors to end/begin a turn is great to me. It makes you both excited to see what's in the next room but nervious at the same time. Like having your birthday on Holloween. [Shout out to all those whom know how that feels!] Now like all rogoue-likes there will be very dry runs where you just aren't getting enough Dust needed to power rooms, but that my fellow gamers is part of the challenge [Though be sure to check to see it's not one of your hero's passives that is choking you out of your Dust].
The multiplayer for the game is just sublime. You each get your own hero and the FIDS are split between you all. You're free to trade anything even hero control at almost anytime [sans inbetween levels]. This is great. It allows players to still contribue by placing defenses/ econ modules when they have lost or don't have control of a hero. Heck you could even decide to have one player in the group to do just that so they are never "distracted" by their own hero. Seriously this game's multiplayer is nearly on par with it's single player with the caveat that you have good friends or that you get lucky and don't get a rusher or tower spammer wasting your precious turns/ FIDS.
TL; DR Proof that a Frankenstein's Monster of game mechanics can if built carefully and with though be far greater than the sum of it's parts. BUY THIS GAME!

I bought this game on a whim since I enjoy roguelikes, and I was not disappointed. The game takes a little getting used to even with a passing familiarity with the genre.
There are certain aspects of the game that are not very intuitive right now. If you clear the dungeon closest to your starting Dungeonmans Academy, you'll already out-class all the other surrounding dungeons, with no option to go inside them. You do get an option to receive a handful of loot from them, but it's typically not that great. Once you find a dungeon you can enter, the difficulty is typically much higher than you can handle with just the first cave's loot and experience.
This quirk resulted in several futile attempts at the game until I figured out that you can enter a dungeon and leave, which marks that dungeon and lets you re-enter it later even if your level "surpasses" it. Since this issue has a workaround, it's not game-breaking or anything, but I do think the level restrictions could be loosened or allow a third option to enter a weaker dungeon anyway, rather than just "auto-clear" and "leave it alone".
There are some dialog options in your Dungeonmans Academy that seem to do nothing, particularly with the museum curator. I've not run into very many other bugs.
In all other areas, Dungeonmans surpassed my expectations. The graphics are simple but look great with some nice detail, and are suited to the old-school style of gameplay. There is a variety of classes to play as to change things up if you get bored playing the game one way. The music is pretty good, and gives a nice atmosphere to the various dungeons. There are multiple dungeon "types", such as swamp, catacombs/graveyard, ruins (typical dungeon), and tower. Each dungeon type provides a different experience, and I found it a nice changeup while playing.
There are also some nice touches such as secret doors, magic pools that will randomly help/harm you, and portals that may take you to rooms filled with either monsters, secret shops, or several strong "champion" level monsters. I've put about 15 hours into the game as of writing this review, and I plan to play it for many more.

Yes, developers of SDP Games, you actualy have acomplished to leave me very confused with this game. Why? Because I just don't know if I should give this game a praise for the sometimes marvelous graphics and Sound. Or if I should put you to the stockade of shame for bad voice acting, cutscenes that seem to sap even high powered machines and a very bad adventure script full of stereotypes and... literally superfluid sideploting.
This is more a solve a riddle game than a hidden object game. As said, the graphics are quite good and if the story of the game would be alone with the sound and the graphics be an emersive dream that you wish to go on forever...
Sadly, there are too many issues. The voice acting is at times a real pain in the neck, the cutscenes sometimes seem to stutter (even on a High-End Machine with new graphics adapter) and the story itself is lacking depth, logic and real suspense. The protagonist is too much of a Mary Sue character to be comfortable.
Some of the riddles are ... too easy to give them any credence here, it would have been nice to brew up some new riddles which weren't recycled for the 9th Million time since 7th Guest (And at that time some of the riddles in that game were already as old as Methusala... Shaving impossible... maybe that is not a beard, but some kind of fungal growth). Other riddles were well done and even though the basic concept was used elsewhere the solution was given a new image (the floating lotus riddle for example).
The hidden object scenes were used to give the game more a feeling like an adventure, and in my opinion that too ruined some fun in this game maybe a mixed solution (as in some construction HOG and more normal HOGs to liven the atmosphere) might have been a bit more into this genre.

I'm conflicted as to whether I could recommend this game or not.
-On one hand it had beautiful, intricate illustrations, a solid duration and a lot of puzzles which I found refreshing. It's been a while since I played a hidden object game that didn't feel too short. It also had some charming Indiana Jones references that made me smile and I really liked the protagonist. Bonus points for having different difficulty settings, that's always a nice and considerate touch. The best part is that this isn't a clear-cut hidden object game. It has many mini-games but also many adventure elements that kept my interest and made the experience even more enjoyable. Oh, and it has a bunch of extra hidden-object and other mini-games after you finish the game! Yay!
-On the other hand the 3d animation is almost funny in it's crudeness, which becomes even worse when compared to the aforementioned jaw-droppingly beautiful illustrations. The plot may be interesting but the writing is bad. Some scenes are so poorly written that they become disconnected from one another, to the point I thought I'd skipped some in-between ones that explained how we got from point A to point B (no, unfortunately that was not the case and yes, I double-checked). The voice acting was hilariously slow and boring.
But most importantly the puzzles were not challenging even on the expert difficulty.
I still had a good time it's true, but there's one thing that really annoyed me, and tipped the scale into me not being able to recommend this. There are 2 specific puzzles in the game, one being the final one, that are near impossible to complete on a pc. It was clear the game was meant for touch-screens and those 2 would have been a breeze if I had one. But I don't and neither should I since I bought this on Steam and not for my tablet. This is something that should have been addressed and fixed before it was released on Steam.
I spent the better part of an hour trying to frantically click through the tiles of the final door puzzle. That was obviously not intended by the developers, seeing how easy that task was on tablets. It wasn't fun and neither felt rewarding when I finally made it.
There are other minor problems like some pixel-hunting and adventuring that just don't make sense -you have to look through the weirdest places to find an item that will give you a solution to a riddle no sane person would ever imagine, but they are not even close to being as irritating as the final door puzzle.
So yeah, I can't recommend it although that doesn't mean it's bad. Overall I had a good time, even if I lost some sanity points somewhere at the end. It's rough around the edges and that simply did not rock my boat.
Try it at your own risk.

As others have said, this is better classified as a puzzle game than a hidden object game. Sure there are some hidden object scenes, but most of the time you are trying to collect objects to complete certain tasks that then result in solving a puzzle or riddle.
Compared to other games in the genre, the artistry in this game is much higher quality that others (you can actually play the game at 1920x1080 and not some upscaled lower resolution). The objects do not appeared muddied or distorted like other games. The view is not constrained to static scenes. It is actually a 3D view with a locked viewing window (different scenes allow different amounts of movement and viewing). There are probably about 25 different scene locations plus about 15 "hidden object"-esque scenes. There were also some additional puzzles.
The voice acting is average. Nothing to write home about, but I've definitely encountered games with worse. Sometimes it can get a little frustrating to sit through conversations where the speaking pace just seems very ... drawn ... out... It usually ended up back tracking to a previous location where a new item had appeared or something was now clickable. I was able to complete all of the puzzles and hidden object scenes without hints, but figuring out the next destination proved tricky at times.

A good
adventure game, mixing point-and-click puzzles, many cool mini-games, and a few hidden-object scenes. It's an Indiana-Jones-type adventure -- with
obvious homages -- but with a female protagonist, who is refreshingly not sexualized -- though she's also kept uninteresting in any other way. (And what's with the name Melissa K? Yawn.)
It's an easy play that won't tax your mind too much, but will still offer many diversely satisfying moments. You can sit back and enjoy the plot, engage yourself in medium-hard puzzles, or just marvel at the graphics.
The graphics engine indeed represents a breakthrough for this genre: 3D effects mixed with the usual lush 2D scenes, with excellent character animation direction. It is a treat!
The background story is based on Thai Buddhism, a topic that as far as I know has never been covered in a video game before this one. The research both in terms of story conception and graphics design are surprisingly good, within the limitations of the genre.

BioShock is truly a work of art, something I rarely say about any form of media. This game was way more enjoyable and better than about 90% of games that have come out after it. It truly is a timeless gem. The PC version is great, with no memorable performance issues. The game looks amazing even though it came out over a year ago, and the gameplay still holds up. While the final encounter and ending are very lackluster everything else about the game is great. This is a must have game for anyone that owns a system capable of running it. If you're debating whether to get this or Infinite, you should buy this instead. The story you experience (the story that affects you as you play) is absolutely amazing and unforgettable. The story you don't experience (why Rapture is the way it is, why people have become ♥♥♥♥ed up, what the ♥♥♥♥ Big Daddies are doing with Little Sisters, etc) is unexplained, or at least very unclear to me. It still isn't anything that impacts immersion. As of me writing this review the game has taken me about 15-6 hours to complete (I know what my record time says, but some of that was wasted time), and each second was great. The game has a great atmosphere that really sets the mood. Even in daylight when the sun is glaring into my room I'm still fully immersed in the dark world of Rapture.
If there is one tip I'd give to anyone playing BioShock, it's to rescue the Little Sisters. It WILL benefit you in the long run. Also, do NOT bother downloading the remastered version, it is littered with bugs. The original 2007 BioShock looks beautiful anyway.

Bought this early in the dev cycle and loved what was already there but every update has made the game a little bit worse.
Hinterland seems to favour form over function with it's user interface, brutally culling clear and concise text in favour of icons or pictures. Sometimes you get the impression that they just replace things to make translation easier/faster/cheaper.
Foraging for wood was removed in favour of picking up twigs, which don't appear to respawn. You spend most of the game surrounded by trees but Hinterland says they aren't a wood source so no fire for you. See that fallen-down tree? You could probably chop a branch off that for some wood, right? Of course not, you madman.
Your clothes degrade in quality because of... wind, I think? That coat offers good protection from the elements but is also destroyed by the elements. I dunno, it feels dumb.
I once sprained my ankle three times in a day by just walking around. No hills, no falling, just walking. Three times. Luckily you can munch painkillers like [insert inappropriate celebrity reference here] with no adverse effects.
Waiting for leather to cure? Got enough food & water to last the time it'll take? Want to just skip ahead by resting indoors? Screw you, we've added cabin fever so you can't spend more than 48 hours inside.
Hinterland likes to say that the game isn't meant to be realistic but whenever they make a change that slows the pacing of the game to a crawl, they do it under the excuse of realism.
They wiped people's saves because "the save architecture changed too much". This is a weak excuse. They could have loaded the saves under the old architecture, then saved into the new architecture. I suppose they just looked at the time it would take to program something like this and decided it was just easier to screw over the people who supported the development.
There's an episodic story mode because of course there is. This may be a plus for some people, I just have no interest in it and I don't think it fits well with the tone of the game. I'd rather the time spent on it was spent elsewhere.
My gripes all seem a bit trivial now that I've read it back. It's just that every mechanic has become a bit more inconvenient over time. It's not challenging, everything just takes a little bit longer. Survival feels like busywork. Now if that ain't a good metaphor for life, I don't know what is.

This game is incredibly creative, atmospheric, and addictive. Kudos to the developers for creating something so unique and evocative! TL;DR: Game is unfairly difficult, perma-death is unbalanced and animals are telephatically guided to you. Survival aspect is ok, progress is excruciatingly slow. Feels very much 'In development'-y despite launch date being near.
Coming from two sessions of about 8 or 9 hours each and a few trial runs, I got a pretty good feel for the game. You'll start off clueless, making a lot of mistakes, while the game mercilessly throws weather conditions, hunger, thirst and "energy" (or stamina, gets replenished by sleeping) at you. Your first hours in this game will be spent trying to figure out how to sustain yourself and have some sort of progress, while battling the unforgiving difficulty of it all. This will be the most fun you'll have with the game.
Then, out of nowhere, you'll find yourself in a place where you might have setup a "HQ", where you keep all your surplus of food and random beverages, as well as other resources that need to be "curated" to be used. Here, you'll have mastered the basics and will be making short work of food, water and handling your stamina. It feels good, but this is where things go down-hill.
In order to "progress" (I'm using the word lightly) in this game, you'll have to eventually hunt animals other than bunnies to craft your "end-game" clothing, such as deer, wolves and bears. The A.I. of the hostile enemies is VERY poorly implemented as it is at the moment, here's a common scenario:
- You'll be walking in your somewhat-end game gear and out of nowhere, you hear a growl or a bark.
- Having spent some time with the game, you're aware a wolf is nearby and is aware of your presence.
There are two possible outcomes here, the wolf is now eternally glued to you unless you have enough stamina to run for a while OR he'll attack you without a second thought or notion of self-preservation. The game gives you a single sure-fire way of dealing with it, flares.
When turned on, the flares will prevent wildlife from attacking you for a certain amount of time. Except, if the wolf is anywhere near you, your character's slooooooow movements taking forever to turn the thing on will either not succeed in turning the flare on at all OR the wolf will attack you despite you having the flare on. Fighting them off when they're on top of you feels clunky and sometimes idiotic when the game gives you multiple options on "how" you fight the wolf off depending on what equipment you have that don't seem to make any difference in the end. You won't die of hunger or thrist in this game, the aggressive animals and their laser guided attacks will. In a world where a stylised realism seems to be the goal and perma-death isn't an optional feature, it just feels wrong.
This is just one of the many "Hey, this feels broken" parts of this game. Perma-death in a game where the enemy A.I. is -very- poorly implemented isn't a feature, it's just an annoying bug. Resources like animal leathers take unbeliveably long amounts of time in order to curate, which in turn slows your game down into an awkward "okay, I guess I'll go get food now until I wait 7 days for this wolf pelt to curate". 7 days in this game is A LOT of time.
To reiterate, if you buy the game you'll have fun in the first 2 to 5 hours while you figure out how things work. Then the game will turn into an awkward waiting game sprinkled with survival fluff. I could go on and on about what's lacking in this game but, to keep this short, that's all I'll say about it.

I enjoy the Sandbox , however I cannot recommend this game in its current state. The Story mode should not have been released in its current buggy state, and its severe linear gameplay is disappointing, and the fetch quests are boring.
They need to focus on the Sandbox and make the game more realistic, with more crafting and more realistic wildlife.
The game needs more options to allow more styles of gameplay. This is the biggest problem of the game. The devs have a vision of how this game is to be played, and force this on the customers. They have forced the unrealistic, over-aggressive, omnipresent, unlimited respawning wolves onto the game to create artificial difficulty. In doing so, they break the game, as the games changes from and open world exploration game into a boring hibernation game, where you try and survive with the limited resources that you have, since it is too deadly to explore over the next hill due to the over-aggressive, omnipresent wolves.
The game is bi-polar. Its an exploration game that discourages exploration. Its a crafting game that discourages using your tools with artificial over-aggressive wear breakdown rates. Its a base building game that forces you to sleep outside. Its a survival game that creates artificial difficulty by not allowing you all the normal options to survive.
The gathering of resources is artificially limited because most of the visible items shown are unusable.
Everything shown in the environment should be usable. The tufts of grass peeking above the snow should be harvestable for tinder, the rugs on the floor of the cabin should be able to be crafted into a coat or blanket, The blankets on the bed should be usable, everything inside the cabin should be burnable. Why am I walking around in the bitter cold without a coat, when I just passed by two beds that have blankets on them? Why pass by a spare bedroll, instead of cutting holes in it to wear it as a coat? Not having any wood (in a forest), and freezing while inside the Camp Office, with a prybar or axe? The front counter is burning baby! There are boards leaning against the wall outside the Camp Office, yet I've got to go look for little sticks? I can chop a whole in the ice yet cannot get any water from there, and we are forced to melt snow? What?
One option to tune the difficulty would be to extend the time before animals respawn. This would allow a player to 'clear' an area of dangerous wolves and then explore. It would also force the player to move on to other areas once they have depleted the initial wildlife population. No wildlife, no food, time to move on. The current situation of unlimited respawn of all wildlife is incredibly immersion breaking. But these options are not available, and it seems that Hinterland doesn't approve of this gameplay option.
If wildlife respawned very slowly, the game would be much more playable, realistic and immersive. The current density of wolves and bears is far too unrealistic. They should be rare, and match the density of prey available. If you move into an area and harvest all of the available rabbits and deer, then you are then going to have to face hungry, aggressive wolves and bear. If there is no prey available for the predators, then they should move to adjacent areas. Eventually, you will end up as the only prey available, and all the predators from all of the areas will seek you out.
The Sandbox has the potential to be THE best survival simulation ever, but only if they make the game more realistic.

I've been playing Disciples II for a long time before I found some good offer on the following chapter: I've played Renaissance, Reincarnation and Resurrection.
Although Reincarnation was the one I enjoyed the most (but also the first I played), I have to admit I found Renaissance to be quite easier. And that appears quite strange and opposite compared to all the reviews I read on Steam.
The big flaws of the game, in my opinion, are three:
1. the fact you can't decide whether to attack or retire from a battle when you come across an enemy;
2. you can't use shortcuts (at least, I'm not able to use them on Renaissance while I used them all the time on Reincarnation);
3. battles can be a bit confusing if you don't pay attention when deciding every move: for example, if you click on an hex too far from your player he will go there on the next turn, but you can't set him on defensive status.
Moreover, I didn't like the fact that range attacks can hit everywhere on the map, even on most distan hexes. I way prefer Reincarnation battle mode on this sight.
Also, it's never clear which charachter got a level up, there's no sign to notify your hero can learn new abilities and so on.
All in all, I'd surely suggest Disciples III - Renaissance to anyone fond of the Disciples trilogy, but if you want a more challenging, refined and precise game experience then you should definitely go for Reincarnation.

Every piece of the interface, every sound effect, every background sets the mood wonderfully. The music and art create a fluid experience that engage a sense of wonder not often unlocked in games. Gameplay is simple and arcade-ish, but with enough meat to back up the audio-visual experience. The world is rather large and loads of fun to explore, though it takes a while for the game to really take off mechanically. Once you have enough songs at your dispossal to really explore you encounter interesting puzzles, exciting arcard combat, and  a marvelous world under the sea.
And if you're anything like me, you'll be too busy taking in the sights to really mind the slow start.

Pros:
- Nice relaxing cute graphics, that makes it a visual joy to play the game.
- Seems like the developer has some good ideas about the direction he wants to take the game.

Cons:
- Every update breaks saves, so you can't really play around and build a lot of fun things in this early version because when you return a week later your saves will be invalidated.

All in all, I like the idea about the game and it feels like there is a great game slowly being chiseled out, but it is not worth using money on yet. I am convinced it will be in time, but wait a while.

Ok, I have become shamelessly addicted to these hidden object games. Having played three, I now consider myself an expert on them. Definitely. Anyway, this is a good one. Just don't judge it on the quality of its story and voice acting, both of which are subpar at best. It seems to be a genre convention actually, so I can go with the flow. No, these games depend more on the quality of their artwork, the level of interactivity in scenes, the quality of the puzzles (if any), and how well things sparkle and zing when you click on them. No really, when you find that hairbrush hidden carefully in the background of a scene, you want some fireworks when you click on it. It's satisfying, I admit it. I get the impression, reading around, that this developer is considered a good one when it comes to HOGs. I wouldn't know, but on the strength of this it's well-deserved. The game's quite long; it took me a little over 6 hours to complete the game (including the two bonus chapters as this is the CE) which is about twice as long as some HOG games. Like most of these games, the difficulty level was towards the easier end of the spectrum, but frankly that works just fine inbetween bouts of Spelunky and Jets 'n' Guns. It's relaxing, and strangely compelling. Interestingly, each hidden object scene also offers a mahjong game. You can either do one or the other, and the more of the HOG you complete, the easier the mahjong game becomes (and vice versa). It's a good way of trying a different approach if you're stuck trying to find a particular object. That didn't happen very often with me, but I appreciated the option. There's no time limit on completing each scene, but if you do them quickly you can gather a few Steam achievements. The achievements were a little bugged though, not all of them registered, if that kind of thing is important to you. Puzzles? Yes, plenty of those, most of them very easy, but they're a nice change of pace. The game surrounding the hidden object scenes plays out like a point and click adventure, with an inventory and objects that must be found and used in the appropriate places, so there's plenty of variety to keep you going. There's even a map!
So overall then, the best HOG-like I've ever played (out of the three I've played over the last month). GOTY in the HOG category so far, in fact! But seriously, if you like this kind of thing you can't really go wrong. The artwork is excellent, the music and presentation are great, the storyline and acting are like fingernails on a blackboard, you'll love it.

This is the first hidden object adventure game I have ever played, but I am a veteran of the old 90's style point and click adventures.
For the most part you wander around, seemingly at random, until you find a "swirly" spot to click on.  This will start a hidden object scene search, upon completion you will be awarded an item, although some items are found without hidden object searches as well (general environment finds).
Some of these items are used in puzzles, some of them are keys, and the rest are your traditional use on environment items that adventure fans are familiar with.  None of the puzzles are challenging, and all are logical.  The only exception to this rule is the "Urns" puzzle - the final one in the game.  Thankfully you can hit a button and skip any puzzle if you want, but this version of the game also has a strategy guide which you can access from the menu (probably not during a game though, but I never tested this).
This version of the game does come with some digital "extras", most notably 8 beautiful (up to 1080p) wallpapers which are taken from the memorable scenes in the game.  In fact you can see three of these in the screenshots on the Steam Store page.  Naturally you get to play back any video you have already seen, and there is also some concept art (but not much, six images to be precise).
Oh, there's also a mahjong game if you want to play that instead of finding hidden objects, but I never tried that feature.
For the price I feel like the game is too short, versus something like Monkey Island II - another zombie themed pirate adventure, and probably the best adventure game of all time.  However, it's worth playing if you like pirates and the sounds of thunder and lightning and want to have the beautiful wallpaper art on your desktop (I do).

Dungeonmans is a great fantasy RPG (or rogue-like if you prefer) featuring a single character that you can mold freely along different skill trees to suit your play style. While fairly tongue-in-cheek, the game is constantly challenging you to adapt to new monsters and situations. I rarely felt that monsters got cheap shots in on me - careless mistakes were always my own fault.
Also the game features an evolving Academy, similar to that of Rogue Legacy, where each successive character that dies leaves something in the wake for the successors to benefit from, whether it is knowledge, equipment or skills. This helps cut down the whole starting from scratch and slogging through early areas repeatedly, as you become slightly more powerful each time. This keeps the game surprisingly fast moving for an RPG - I didn't ever feel that I was grinding a dungeon out in order to progress. The developer has also continued to make updates and refinements to the game in the three years since release, greatly extending the life of the game
It's somewhat similar to Tales of Maj'Eyal and just as enjoyable.

I absolutely love this game. I've only played 20hrs and I'm already addicted lol
At first it was hard for me to get into, I loved The Forest so I thought I'd try The Long Dark thinking "Oh.. I know what to do" FALSE!! haha. I struggled so much trying to play it with no idea how some of the mechanics worked. I literally had to "Google" "How do you get water in The Long Dark" until I looked it up I had relied soley on sodas figuring "If it works in New Vegas, it'll work here."
It is truly a test of skill and patience because alot of stuff is repeatitive, just like how it would be in real life. Surviving day to day involves going out exploring, finding loot, hunting food, surviving the elements, avoiding bears and wolves and trying to make it back to your home for the night (you can journey durring the night but I would advise against it).
Honestly the game is difficult to me and I haven't played it past the second diffuclty setting yet because I want to master everything. It is so rewarding to put everything you learn into action. Fighting off animals in other games is a cake walk compared to this game. "Oh you have 2 bullets left and there are three of us wolves? Good luck buddy may the gaming Gods watch over you." Finding bullets is like seeing your child take their first steps, finding a box of ammunition is like winning the lottery on the same day your child starts walking, finding a box of ammunition but you still haven't found a rifle is a sad sad day indeed.
I love how it's designed around "realistic" survival principles. You are encouraged to travel out and find more loot but you have to excercise restraint. If you're low on supplies but have no means to defend yourself or hunt you might be better off redoubling your efforts and really look in every nook and cranny to see if you missed anything (trust me this game hides stuff in the most annoying places lol, under beds, behind a sofa etc), of course if you have no way to survive sometimes your best option is just to run to a different part of your area or even leave your aread to a completely new location. Of course just like in a real survival situation you may find out that area has nothing at all and you'll cry as the wolves circle in and your guy dies of hypothermia running from them. :(
If you like survival games this is a wonderful game to buy. It's still in Alpha but it's well made and is starting to feel like it's almost complete. They say the release date is going to be in August and at the stage it's currently in I think they will definitely make that deadline, unless they add a bunch new stuff (which would be bleeping awesome!).
I highly recommend it.

I put a pretty significant amount of time into this game, but only because I'm a completionist, and once I start playing a game I generally try to finish it.  It's essentially a point & click and hidden object game, with a cliche plot and a pretty terrible script and voice acting.  The puzzles are often well made, and there's a option (and achievements) for playing every puzzle separately and beating all of the "best scores."  Despite putting in the time and doing this, I somehow and missing a bunch of achievements for them.  Perhaps part of the game/achievements are broken.  I know some of them art on Mac at least, because there are 5 more achievements I have credit for in-game that Steam won't register.
As far as the game itself goes, gameplay is a bit infuriating.  At times the narrative of the game and the nature of the puzzles are non-sensical... and you'll most likely need a guide even if you're a very seasoned adventure gamer, not because the game is difficult, just because the game doesn't always make sense within its own design.  Also, in an attempt to obtain the a final item for an achievement, I started replays of both the regular game and the Collector's Edition additional chapter.  Both of these replays are now "frozen" because of broken, insurpassable hidden object scenes that don't have the objects in them I'm supposed to be finding (this isn't a case of me not knowing what the objects are-- I've beaten these puzzles on speed runs for "best" scores and know all of the objects intimately-- they're simply missing from the puzzles).  As both of the games are now broken, I'm giving up on getting the last few achievements.
All of the achievements and broken elements aside, I'd probably rate the game a 5 or 6/10.  Because of them, we're down to about a 4/10.  Parts of the game look beautiful, but it's obviously designed for IPad.  There's one final puzzle at the end of the game that's impossible without a mouse, and seems best played on a touchscreen.  If you're trying to do it on a laptop touchpad (as I was for a time while traveling), it's impossible to complete.  Overall I found the game tedious and not very fun.

I'm not a huge fan of hidden object games, but I enjoyed this one very much.  For a game with such a low price, this has quite high production values. The voice acting is quite good, the hand-drawn art is beatifully done, and the 3D rendering was also mixed in very well for a seamless experience. Most of the point and click puzzles were challenging enough without being too overwhelmng.
That said, the final "reverse Tetris" puzzle was very annoying and felt out of place due to being more of an arcade game instead of a logic puzzle. I guess it's meant to be a bit of a joke because there's an achievement for failing this particular mini-game 10 times, but it still really didn't have a place when compared to the other puzzles.
My only other gripe is that a few of the individual solutions didn't make a lot of sense. There were a few times when the game (via the "hint" button) showed me the solution and I thought to myself, "Seriously? I would never have made that association."
Even with those bumps, the game was primarily a smooth ride. The story was enough to keep my interest and there were several nods to the various "Indiana Jones" movies and made me smile. If SDP games makes more games like this (minus the arcade-y bits) I'll be a repeat customer for their games.

The animation is fun and most all the characters have interesting designs. The gameplay is decent as far as clicker games go. It's a decent clicker game which is better than most I've played recently. It also has a fair amount of character and charisma thrown into the mix.
Now that I have that out of the way let's get to the negatives. It is full of bugs, most of which occur in the STR system which is filled with flawed math that does not add up and actually increase your overall DPS the amount it should. There are also bugs in the microtransaction store, but I haven't utilized the shop so I cannot say from personal experience.
In addition, progress becomes stagnant and slow after about halfway into zone 4 (which is early on) and takes hours upon hours to earn enough money to even afford one upgrade for someone you've already unlocked. When you ascend for Stars to upgrade global stats you barely get any and need to ascend at least 3 times to afford the first level of any upgrade. Given how long it takes to get to the point of ascension you could easily start from scratch on any other clicker and upgrade everything at least twice in roughly the same amount of time.
It's not a bad game. It's simply slow AF. That can be a good thing or a bad thing given who you ask.

I haven't played the other Disciplines games so I can't give you a comparison; however, if you judge Disciples III on its own or if you are new to the series, it is really a fun turn-based strategy/tactics game. Similar games that come to mind are King's Bounty or Heroes of Might and Magic VI. Personally I enjoyed this game more than those, and one of the features I really liked about Disciples III is that instead of just having 'stacks' of units like those other games, you create squads of units (you can hire multiple leaders) that will stay with you and level up, advance in ranks, and learn new skills. If you are familiar with the Ogre Battle series then this has some more similar aspects to that. There is a fair amount of depth to this game as you build up your castle, learn new spells, level up and choose your skill and class advancement paths, explore the world, and get involved in the story that spans 3 campaigns.
There are some minor bugs that I ran into quickly such as the right-click tooltip system not always working properly (only happened once or twice and restarting fixed it) and the Esc key not always bringing up the game menu (you can use the mouse to click the menu button instead), but these were not enough to hinder my enjoyment of the game.
Do not expect an improvement on Disciples II. This is diabolical in comparison.

Stonehearth is a game that has a lot of sources of inspiration, most noticeably Dwarf Fortress, but also old RPGs like Final-Fantasy-Tactics. Stonehearth wears its inspirations on its sleeve but has its own unique charm and play style.
Stonehearth is, as is described by its creators, "a game about exploration and survival in an epic fantasy setting where your job is to help a small group of settlers survive and carve out a place for themselves in a hostile land". In other words, your goal is to help a group of settlers (or "hearthlings" as they are called) to create a colony.
You are the mind beyond the operation, you do not control your hearthling directly, you lay out the general plan (mine, build, etc) and your hearthlings commit your plans by themselves. There are also a few RPG elements in the game, like a job three, levels, stats and percs.
Two things that i really like about the game are the art style and the emphasis on modding. The devs of the game have built their own game engine with emphasis on modding, which can only increase the lifespan of the game. The game has a really easy to use, and nice looking GUI. the animations are cute and i really like the character design. there is a lot of small things that makes the style of the game charming.
The last thing i would like to mention is the awesome community that as been created around the game. since the kickstarter days the game has come a long way, the devs are active in the forums and are actively engaging with the community, they even stream the game development 3 days a week on twitch!
All in all the game is very promising, and even though it is missing features it's very fun in is current state. it has a long way to go but I'm really hopeful for its future. if you like what you see give it a try!

I would like to talk about the development cycle of this game being that it is in early access. I backed the game for $30 USD in April 2013 on Kickstarter, while the project timelines of the original crowd funding were not met, the transparency and progress on the game by the developers at Radiant Entertainment have always been thoroughly communicated.
Despite original project timelines not being met, the team has continued to grow and be staffed were needed, which in my opinion demonstrates sound management on the part of team. This is not a pick up and run with your money type of project. Updates are provided consistently and feedback is incorporated via the games blog, forum, trello roadmap, and Tom and Tony's tri-weekly twitch development streams.
Radiant Entertainment was founded by evo2k (the fighting game tournament) and
, founders Tony and Tom Cannon, who had years of working at vmware before venturing on this project. Tony Cannon also wrote netcode middleware GGPO, which was a turning point for online play in the fighting game genre.  I backed the game because of their history, these two have remained accountable and have earned the FGCs trust having been a cornerstone of the community.
To conclude, the development of this game two years after its successful crowdfunding campaign continues to demonstrate a level of accountability and trust that is among the best of early access games.

The phrase "If you enjoy Roguelikes you will like this" is played out pretty bad, but it honestly fits here. Dmans is just a fun game about exploring dungeons, crushing monsters and looting all the loot. On top of that, you also get a good sense of humor and rad music and visuals. The Academy mechanic allows your next character to get a leg up if you so desire. Death comes swift in most RL games, and it's nice to have the choice to let your next character slingshot through the early game. But it's your choice if you want to take advantage of the boons, or start without taking them. Dmans plays fast and fluid, and a lot of dungeons can be played on the fly. Though, don't take that as this game being a brainless hack&slash for your cofee break. It's still a Roguelike where a wrong decision can doom you.
The game is stil fresh and needs to grow a little more as of now, but I seriously enjoyed every minute I've played so far.

I absolutely love this game. I've only played 20hrs and I'm already addicted lol
At first it was hard for me to get into, I loved The Forest so I thought I'd try The Long Dark thinking "Oh.. I know what to do" FALSE!! haha. I struggled so much trying to play it with no idea how some of the mechanics worked. I literally had to "Google" "How do you get water in The Long Dark" until I looked it up I had relied soley on sodas figuring "If it works in New Vegas, it'll work here."
It is truly a test of skill and patience because alot of stuff is repeatitive, just like how it would be in real life. Surviving day to day involves going out exploring, finding loot, hunting food, surviving the elements, avoiding bears and wolves and trying to make it back to your home for the night (you can journey durring the night but I would advise against it).
Honestly the game is difficult to me and I haven't played it past the second diffuclty setting yet because I want to master everything. It is so rewarding to put everything you learn into action. Fighting off animals in other games is a cake walk compared to this game. "Oh you have 2 bullets left and there are three of us wolves? Good luck buddy may the gaming Gods watch over you." Finding bullets is like seeing your child take their first steps, finding a box of ammunition is like winning the lottery on the same day your child starts walking, finding a box of ammunition but you still haven't found a rifle is a sad sad day indeed.
I love how it's designed around "realistic" survival principles. You are encouraged to travel out and find more loot but you have to excercise restraint. If you're low on supplies but have no means to defend yourself or hunt you might be better off redoubling your efforts and really look in every nook and cranny to see if you missed anything (trust me this game hides stuff in the most annoying places lol, under beds, behind a sofa etc), of course if you have no way to survive sometimes your best option is just to run to a different part of your area or even leave your aread to a completely new location. Of course just like in a real survival situation you may find out that area has nothing at all and you'll cry as the wolves circle in and your guy dies of hypothermia running from them. :(
If you like survival games this is a wonderful game to buy. It's still in Alpha but it's well made and is starting to feel like it's almost complete. They say the release date is going to be in August and at the stage it's currently in I think they will definitely make that deadline, unless they add a bunch new stuff (which would be bleeping awesome!).
I highly recommend it.

A mix of a point and click adventure and hidden object game, Melissa K and the Heart of Gold brings a refreshing approach to the genre. Alternates between hidden object sections and logical puzzles(where you need to find objects, combine them, use them somewhere specific, etc), and thus becomes more interesting than your average hidden object game.
It's not particularly hard and you stroll along just fine without getting frustrated, making it somewhat of a relaxing playthrough, which is helped even more by the charming artstyle.
Melissa K has a bit more care for the visuals and art than most game I played in the genre. The game is actually rendered in 3D yet it emulates 2D art quite well, making it rather impressive when you actually see that it's 3D and you can see it on a few different perspectives.
For a more casual playthrough, the game offers "Skip Puzzle" and "Hints" options, which can be rather handy when you can't find that darn last piece you need.
Definitely worth it for any Hidden Object game fan, brings a few twists to the genre and it's more diverse than most of the game of the genre because of the point and click/adventure section. Recommended.

With the tens of releases every month it’s hard to make your game stand out, especially if it’s a hidden object game and when there are already plenty of those available. Neither of those games bring new life to the genre but Melissa K And The Heart Of Gold makes a bold attempt anyway.
There isn’t much to tell because the game is meant for casual gamers and the gameplay is always kind of fun, but ultimately still too shallow. The story brings you to Thailand where you eventually have to solve a case about a missing Buddhist. Further into the game you’ll stumble upon new discoveries which require you to travel to new places and solve even more puzzles.
The game is shown to you from a first person perspective, which isn’t entirely fixed, but I’ll talk about that in a minute. Your objective is to then find the correct objects to click on and to occasionally solve a (relatively easy) logical puzzle. No, that’s right; it’s not all about hidden objects.
Clicking on certain objects will reveal puzzles or other objects. These objects can sometimes be used in combination with other ones, or you have might have to find a whole set of them. From time to time you have to click on an object and rotate it to unlock a certain item. So there’s actually a very decent amount of diversity to be found here.
Later on you’ll also acquire objects like a gecko and spyglass that you can have access to all the time. The gecko for example will help you grab items from tiny holes and the spyglass can be used to zoom in on far away objects, usually to find hidden/secret messages and codes.
If you don’t want to solve a puzzle or don’t know what to do next you can click on a Skip button (which becomes available after a few minutes) or you can press the Hint button. The Hint button doesn’t give any penalties and can be reused after about 30 seconds, free of charge. See it as some sort of ‘Win’ button. In my opinion, there should be consequences for using things like this, but on the other hand I can understand that the developers want anyone to be able to play and finish this.
A lot of the puzzles later on in the game are farfetched, however, and seem to be made to give the game a longer life. You can definitely tell that the developers stretched out the story. This ultimately hurts the game. Again, this is a game that would’ve been better if it was shorter. These games don’t have to be very long, as long as they’re enjoyable all the way through. I enjoyed it very much until 4 hours in, after that I couldn’t wait to just finish and quit it.
I do have to admit that this is still one of the better hidden objects/casual adventure games out there so even though it might seem that I’m bashing the game that’s not my intention. It’s just that with games like these it’s easier to talk about the negative parts since everyone usually already knows what to expect as far as the gameplay is concerned.
A cool feature that the developers introduced with this game is that the game looks 2D but in reality it is actually 3D. That perspective I was talking about in the last paragraph can also be moved to the left and right. It’s nothing fancy; don’t expect complete freedom here, but it looks great and it’s something that gives the game a little more depth. I wish more games would use this because it makes the game a lot more interesting visually. The art is beautiful and colorful and there’s plenty of detail to be found in them, but sometimes things are tucked away a bit too good.
The actors also did a good job with the voice acting. Some of it is still terrible, sure, but most of it is at least decent.
Melissa K And The Heart Of Gold is again one of those games that doesn’t reinvent the genre but hey, at least it tried. The developer has integrated some smart (gameplay) elements that should be available in more games like these. It’s nothing big or revolutionary but still good in any case.
For now this remains one of the better hidden object/casual adventure games. If you’re into those I can gladly recommend this. And if not, I suggest you wait for a sale before giving it a try.

Stonehearth is a sandbox strategy game, set in a (light) fantasy setting, with town building, crafting, and a military campaign.
Take Dwarf Fortress. Tone down some of the rogue-like elements. Replace the esoteric production chains and mood  simulations with more accessible and managable alternatives. Add a charming 3D voxel art style with tons of character. Introduce some truly innovative mechanics, including the way hearthlings simulate building. Voila.
Or, for readers that haven't had the privilege of learning how "losing is fun", we'll try a more popular game for comparison. Take Minecraft, pull it back to  a strategic level, give yourself hearthlings to manage, add in a bunch of depth with jobs and production chains, and smother it in buckets of charm. Welcome to Stonehearth.
I am recommending Stonehearth not only because it is already a successful sandbox strategy game in its own right, with truly innovative mechanics and an on-point blend of strategic depth and accessible fun, but because the small team at Radiant Entertainment have proven their exceptionalism. Since backing Stonehearth on Kickstarter I have enjoyed weekly updates, steady content addition that is continuously polished, and interactivity with multiple team members on their community forums. These guys care about making a great game, and it truly shows.
Stonehearth is a game that is worth your money and time right now, as of Update 10.x, and one that will only improve in value as those updates continue rolling in.

This is some seriously polished classic dungeon adventuring. For the most part it's traditional rogue-like fare, the few places where twists have been added work really well and only serve to improve the experience. There does not seem to be any of the more hardcore elements of some rogues (like hunger, involved sound/smell, etc) but the game still provides a rich, deep game play that is fairly quick and fun to jump into but involved enough to capture you for a LONG time as you experiment with different types of characters and strategies in an attempt to just not die.
The end result is a well balanced game that people new to this type of genre may find a little more "easy access" than some other offerings with various input options (that "just work" when you use them) to control your character and an easy to read/understand interface but enough complexity (and traditional rogue controls if you already know them!) and depth to keep those of us more experienced hooked for.. a long time. Just look at the play times listed for the other reviews. Great $/hr value!
Finally then: expect a world map you traverse to get between dungeons and towns, expect several varieties of dungeon (warrens, dungeons, crypts, temples, towers, etc) each with their own little twists, a "spend points where you want" skill tree, potions and scrolls to identify, loot galore and equipment (potentially cursed or magical or plain), champion monsters and dungeon bosses. The rest go discover yourself :)
ps: art is lush and music is awesome.

At first it was hard for me to get into, I loved The Forest so I thought I'd try The Long Dark thinking "Oh.. I know what to do" FALSE!! haha. I struggled so much trying to play it with no idea how some of the mechanics worked. I literally had to "Google" "How do you get water in The Long Dark" until I looked it up I had relied soley on sodas figuring "If it works in New Vegas, it'll work here."
It is truly a test of skill and patience because alot of stuff is repeatitive, just like how it would be in real life. Surviving day to day involves going out exploring, finding loot, hunting food, surviving the elements, avoiding bears and wolves and trying to make it back to your home for the night (you can journey durring the night but I would advise against it).
Honestly the game is difficult to me and I haven't played it past the second diffuclty setting yet because I want to master everything. It is so rewarding to put everything you learn into action. Fighting off animals in other games is a cake walk compared to this game. "Oh you have 2 bullets left and there are three of us wolves? Good luck buddy may the gaming Gods watch over you." Finding bullets is like seeing your child take their first steps, finding a box of ammunition is like winning the lottery on the same day your child starts walking, finding a box of ammunition but you still haven't found a rifle is a sad sad day indeed.
I love how it's designed around "realistic" survival principles. You are encouraged to travel out and find more loot but you have to excercise restraint. If you're low on supplies but have no means to defend yourself or hunt you might be better off redoubling your efforts and really look in every nook and cranny to see if you missed anything (trust me this game hides stuff in the most annoying places lol, under beds, behind a sofa etc), of course if you have no way to survive sometimes your best option is just to run to a different part of your area or even leave your aread to a completely new location. Of course just like in a real survival situation you may find out that area has nothing at all and you'll cry as the wolves circle in and your guy dies of hypothermia running from them. :(
If you like survival games this is a wonderful game to buy. It's still in Alpha but it's well made and is starting to feel like it's almost complete. They say the release date is going to be in August and at the stage it's currently in I think they will definitely make that deadline, unless they add a bunch new stuff (which would be bleeping awesome!).
I highly recommend it.

After 290 hours of game-play I feel like I can finally give a full review of the game.
Let's start with the good:
The game-play is fantastic. I have never had such a realistic zombie experience with an in-depth (But limited) world. The player really gets a sense of being alone, with zombies around every corner. You have to carefully ration food and manage your noise levels. Also, be aware of having a proper nutritious meal every now and then or you might still starve! This game can EASILY take 10 hours of your time if you let it. Not to mention the fun and engaging leveling system in which you can customize your character. I also REALLY enjoyed the food/cooking system. If you get this game for free, or for 10 dollars - hell yes.
Let's get to the point though.
After 290 hours of game-play, over ~4-5 years of development, the game has changed very little. Besides a graphical overhaul/engine overhaul the gameplay remains the same.
"Why is this a problem?" - you may ask.
Well I have to respectfully say that the gameplay becomes dull and repetitive once you reach the 'end game'. Once you learn the lack-luster combat mechanics (Which was promised an overhaul over 2 years ago?) zombies are no longer a challenge. That's right. The games BIGGEST BADDIE is no longer a challenge once you get a nice baseball bat. If you decide to turn up the zombie count...well...you are still faced with the eventual same problem except with the exception of a single helicopter bringing hundreds of zombies to your location, and the only REAL way to deal with them is by lighting the horde on fire or using those nice OP bombs. And forget being able to see the majority of this amazing map they created - there is no way to travel except by foot. Which becomes dull very fast if you want to go check out the mall on the other end of the world. And while exploring the world is initially exciting there is not much to find besides an empty world full of zeds. No other AI survivors. No vehicles. Just woods and a few buildings.  The world feels empty and lifeless, and besides nature slowly taking over the world it, the environment does not change with any interesting or challenging mechanics.
So that's my biggest complaint.
Now for the 2nd challenge this game has.
The multiplayer.
The multiplayer makes the game so much more enjoyable...except for the fact that it makes the above problems WORSE. And if you have too many zombies on the screen they begin to warp around and teleport (MAGICAL ZOMBIES!!). I have seen this on several dedicated servers.
Sigh...that's not all. Because my friends and I LOVE this game. We thought "HEY! The game has SPRINTING zombies!!! Those are good because they are DIFFICULT and make the game SCARY and a small group of zombies is VERY FUN to fight against!"
Well. Sprinting zombies work good in singleplayer. But DO NOT work in multiplayer as they warp around terribly and teleport every which way. This has been a bug for YEARS.
Which leads to the 3rd challenge this game has:
The development team. The development team moves slower than any other team I have seen. If you do not watch the news of the game you would believe the game was abandoned. Sure, they have frequent updates. But no true new game mechanics that actually create new challenges for the game.
Enemy AI have been promised for ~2 years and they are using valves "It's done when it's done" as an excuse.
When reporting the teleporting sprinting zombie bug for nearly 2 years the dev's eventual response was exactly this:
"The option will be removed from MP at later date." - EngimaGrey
No explanation as to why. Just simply saying "It would be too hard to do". Come on.
After nearly 2000 hours in development for ArmA mods and talking to many other developers I know that "It would be too hard" = "We don't want to tackle that challenge because we are lazy." (Or as others say "Too busy", because prioritization is NOT a thing with this team).
It simply comes down to the developers struggling to put the work into their game that it desperately needs. It is difficult to compare apples to oranges, but when looking at many other EA games their work pales. I can do without the additional food recipes, please give me AI to interact with. Please give me a difficult zombie curve. Please add more gameplay options for the late-game.
Please add a purpose or goal for this world. Why am I surviving? What obstacle is there to overcome once you have that nice baseball bat and enough food?
I will change this review as updates come along but I am significantly dissapointed with the direction of development.
To wrap it all up
This game offers a VERY FUN experience for the initial few run throughs and I recommend it for free to 10 dollars (Which is subjective, I know)
I would wait to purchase this game if you are waiting for more meaningful mechanics to come into play. Because you might be waiting another 2-3 years for the first introduction of anything really impactful to gameplay.
Frequent Responses:
1) It is difficult to include feature X! You can't expect them to include feature X because of that.
Coding and working on a game takes massive time, dedication, patience, and skill. Just because something is difficult does not exempt it from examination. Having a proper working government is difficult to do, however that difficulty does not exempt it from criticism. Still, it is the developers right to NOT do something and I can not fault them for taking the game a direction they want. However, this does nothing to lessen the dissapointment of NOT having sprinting zombies just because of a percieved difficulty. It was one, of several promising mechanics to keep the game fresh which was removed before it ever really worked.
2)You played it for 290 hours...How could you not give it a good review?
Hours played have no bearing of my final satisfaction of the game. After 290 hours of gameplay I feel very dissapointed in the state of this game and very doubtful of the future of this game.
Compare this to other games in my library: (Only 2 due to space issues)
7 Days to Die : 906 Hours - Still love this game to death. I don't play it as much but would still recommend it heavily.
Doom: 49 Hours - I do not play this anymore, but would still heavily recommend this to people. Not dissapointed with the purchase.
At the end of the day I can look back at MANY other games with over 50+ hours and not feel regret. Project Zomboid, for many reasons, has left me with no urge to return to the game as the development team continues to abuse the early access system and continue to pat themselves on the back for next-to-nothing updates.
