As many other reviews have noted, the base game really should be free to play. It certaintly isn't worth the launch price, or the current price.
I can't admit to having played more than a dozen multiplayer matches before uninstalling, but I think that's enough experience to comment on how the game plays and its core problems. At the top of my list on these and probably the most damning is that the actual concept simply doesn't play out well. It strikes me as an idea that was playtested by the developers in the office, rather than designed for online play - it's reasonably fun with 4 other people you know and have mics or are sat next to; with 4 random strangers (which, let's face it, is how most people will play it), it's simply not fun.
The problems of playing with random people are exacerbated by a tiered matchmaking system that puts pressure on people to play to win, and which is buckling under a lack of players. Expect to spend at least as much time in a lobby trying to start a game as you will playing it, and very probably more. That's 15 minutes of staring at a lobby for every 15 minutes of actual gameplay; and don't dare doing anything other than staring at the screen, since if anyone in your team goes afk and fails to select a class, you'll all get dumped back to square one. Expect also, due to the ranking system, to have an even harder time getting the first 10 matches under your belt, as you'll be listed as unranked, which other players will read as 'n00b'.
To go into the mechanics in a bit more detail, as any reader probably knows, 4 hunters have to chase down a 5th player as a monster, trying to take them down before they level up and stack the odds in their favour. In gameplay terms, this boils down to a lot of running in circles around awkward terrain using a jetpack with a fuel system that's understandably necessary but feels irritating. Hunters get 4 abilities which can be synergised between classes, but there's limited depth; it has a hint of that 'forced teamplay' feel you get from games like Brink, where each class has a role and god forbid they should think or play outside of the box. This is compounded by a progression system that lacks any real depth or desirable unlocks (beyond new characters, of which some can only be purchased as additional DLC).
The monster is perhaps more fun to play, as at level 3 you have to try pretty hard to lose, and odds are unless you're up against 4 buddies on teamspeak it will be relatively easy to get there. The process of getting there, though, is rather tedious - run away, in circles round the map, killing and feeding on livestock. This comes back to my central point - the core idea for this game just doesn't work too well. Many of the things that made Left4Dead (the game that gave these developers their name) great have been lost, and what's new isn't better. Pinging away at something with massive hp in an FPS has never worked well; it's a bit like Left4Dead if the only content were non-stop tank fights. Hide and seek can easily become a tedious exercise in circuit running, and that's also a trap Evolve falls into far too often. Yes, there are other game modes, but they're equally unremarkable. Finally, considering some people actually want to play games casually for fun rather than MLG-style, the lobby and matchmaking system are far too time-consuming when a simple AI drop-in / drop-out system would alleviate the waiting and let people play quickly.
Summary:
Pros
- Decent graphics and performance
- Potential for fun if you're playing on TS with 4 buddies
- Good tutorial videos for new players and simple mechanics make it easy to pick up and play
Cons
- Far too much time matchmaking
- Core gameplay concept and execution isn't great
- Not a fun game to play alone or with randoms
- Can't justify it's purchase price. Can't come remotely close to justifying it's DLC prices.
In short:
Wait for free to play or avoid; if you want a good 4 player co-op experience Left4Dead plays vastly better, if you want a team-based shooter with a simlar feel Team Fortress is the way to go. If you already own both and are looking for something new, expect to be underwhelmed.

Nice and difficult indie platform game with a twist and unique visual style. You play as Naught, an undead cat-like creature that travels through dark levels filled with traps and monsters. You don't move your character directly - instead of that you fluently turn his whole world around to make him slide in the direction you want. If you wish to survive, you have to be extremely cautious and fast about it.
There are new enemies, deadly traps and rules introduced every few levels to keep it interesting and challenging - you'll learn how to swim, how to make use of the tree spirit following you, how to use bubbles of air to enhance your maneuvers and so on.There are three boss fights with giant creatures as well. There's no way you'll feel bored.
Naught Reawakening is quite difficult. Of course if you simply rush through all 30+ levels it might appear easy and very short - it takes less than two hours to get to the end. But its beauty lies in collecting diamonds. To overcome all dangers lurking in the dark and collect every well-hidden diamond you will need patience, wits, good reflexes and at least four hours. Beating time trials is even more challenging and requires a lot of practice, but awards the player with lots of achievements.
Naught's visual style is very similar to Limbo - the world is dark and atmospheric, almost entirely covered in shadows. Cratures inhabiting it are kind of creepy too. There are no graphics options available, but that's understandable, since it's a 2D game. Rest assured, though, that it looks good in FullHD resolution and runs well even on older rigs. It sounds nice as well since music makes the game even more psychodelic and strange.
The only major flaw of Naught Reawakening is its price. PC version costs more than twice as much as Android and iOS editions for no apparent reason, which is simply unfair, since it's exactly the same game. It might not be worth 9,99€, but be sure to give it a try as soon as it's on sale.

Otherwise you have to do it all over again (fortunately the levels are not very long).
I recommend it to those looking for something "different" and "difficult"

Gioca con la forza di gravità e accompagna Naught nel suo viaggio attraverso un misterioso mondo sotterraneo, dove l'oscurità è un nemico instancabile che può assumere mille sembianze differenti. Naught, il Risveglio è un mix tra un'avventura e un platform game che metterà a dura prova le tue abilità, affidandoti il controllo completo di Naught e dell'ambiente che lo circonda.
Naught, il Risveglio possiede delle caratteristiche uniche nel suo genere, che rivoluzionano il concetto di platform game. Grazie all'uso dell'animazione procedurale, puoi calibrare i movimenti di naught adattandoli all'ambiente che lo circonda, ad esempio puoi farlo aggrappare a una parete, modificare la sua andatura in base alla gravità e alla superficie del suolo, e farlo interagire con vari oggetti in un modo dinamico e mai visto prima. I haven't played any of the previous Disciples titles. Maybe that's my advantage, because so far I like it.
What you certainly should not expect is a challenging strategy game of the good old days. This is a dumbed down version with a lot less freedom and strategic variety and you possibly will play the campaign only once and possibly never touch multiplayer at all because the game does not really allow enough strategic options for that and the gameplay by itself is not as compelling.
That said: what you should expect is up-to-date graphics (with a darker theme than the Heroes series), charming musical themes and a nice story with some twists. The story itself is not new I'm afraid: fallen angel trying to take over the world (again).  To do that the dark overlord needs a "Mc Guffin" that in turn everybody chases after. That's it.
Same old story of the devil taking over the world that has been told so many times now that it's hard to tell which game is a rip-off of which. However: it's nicely told and has some compelling bells and whistles and twists.
Three factions are available in three campaigns that build up on one another. Cutscenes (so far as I have seen any) are rare and are mostly zooming in and out of hand-drawn black and white still-images with (really good) voice-over.
Over all the game will keep you busy for a few days.
It's not brilliant, it's not perfect. But if you are looking for an entertaining, easy-going distraction with simple (not too complicated) gameplay, it is worth taking a look at. If you are a looking for any more than that, this game is not for you.

I've been playing this game on and off since last July (before the Steam release), and I love it. Here are some of the things I particularly like:
+ The graphics are extremely cute. It can be heartbreaking to have to kill the evil goblins who come to attack your village, as they look so adorable!
+ The building system - it is so easy to use and customise, and has many different parts to use (different wall types etc). As well as this, it's great how the "Hearthlings" build scaffolding and ladders (much more realistic than just hammering the ground until a building suddenly pops up, which is what happens in other games).
+ The goblins and zombies add a more challenging aspect to the game. You must keep your Hearthlings safe, and this is no mean feat when you reach the late-game and your village is assailed by the goblin army. Do note that you can play in a "peaceful" game mode where there are no enemies, if you prefer.
+ Modding - the developers have specifically made it easy to modify the game. In fact, there are already a few mods to choose from, with many more to come.
+ Lots of small things, such as the ability to craft a toy plushie, or to buy food/furniture/materials from travelling merchants, or to give your footmen special swords crafted by the blacksmith.
However, you must keep in mind that there
, as this is Early Access. I haven't experienced any game-breaking ones, but there are some which are slight nuisances. You can report them on the Stonehearth Discourse.
Also, if you are used to playing finished games, you may feel that Stonehearth has few features. There are certainly enough to make a fun and immersive game, but not enough to last say, a month of gameplay. I guess this is also to be expected of Early Access. But this hasn't been such a problem for me, as the game can be replayed many times and still be thoroughly enjoyable - I have played since July and am not bored yet!
Overall, I would certainly recommend this game. It may have the usual problems of Early Access (bugs and fewer features than you might hope for), but it is certainly great fun. And exceedingly cute.

I have been playing this game since the first Alpha release, in early 2014. I mostly played after feature patches to see what's new and to spend a relaxing evening with the game. In this review I want to give my oppinion about a few aspects of the game and it's development.
The vision:
I really like what the devs want to achieve with this game. The voxel style is really cute and in my opinion, it does not look like it's just copied from another voxel game. I look forward to playing a game which can follow in the footsteps of the old Settler games, combining a strategy game with having a village inhabited by scurrying inhabitants.
Communication:
The developers are really active with their community from what I saw. There are weekly updates on their website, regular livestreams (not at the best times for Europeans) and active discussions in the forums. I always felt like I knew what was happening with the game, even if there was not much progress, for example due to moving to a new office.
Current state:
Currently, this is not a game to spend a lot of time with for the average player. To see all the content, a few hours will be enough. But, after all, this game is in early access, so I think that is to be expected. You can already see the direction in which this game is heading, you will be able to have some fun for an evening or two, and you probably want to check from time to time what new patches added.
All in all, this game is heading to a promising direction, I never regretted backing it on Kickstarter, and I'm still confident that it will be a great game. There is enough content to spend a few hours playing it and updates are always coming.

Stonehearth is a cute little game in the vein of Dwarf Fortress (though with less madness and fewer death spirals) though the Hearthlings don’t seem to like living underground.  It’s very cute, and it’s looking at the ASCII code of DF saying “ooh, I want to be like that when I grow up!  Only better!
Unfortunately, that’s all it is right now.  It is full of potential, as well as glitches—I won’t outright call them bugs.
•	Hearthlings occasionally just drop what they’re carrying and it stays there indefinitely, unusable by anyone.
•	Hearthlings get confused about what furniture goes where and nothing gets placed ever again.
•	Hearthlings will occasionally decide that they’re just done working and never do anything (other than eat or sleep) again.
•	Hearthlings will teleport to inaccessible locations and you have to figure out where they are and how to get them back.
•	Goblin Raiding Parties will, sometimes, just run into an empty area of your village and . . . loiter.
None of these actually cause the game to crash and burn, but they are incredibly annoying, usually requiring you to start a new village.  Now, don’t get me wrong.  When the glitches don’t show up (which is happening more and more regularly), you get a cute little village and get to watch your little Hearthlings build a basic village.
But, all that said, this is still in Alpha, so, you should expect worse.  However, there isn’t much worse.  For an Alpha, it’s pretty stable and they’re working on it regularly.  I’ve only had it lock up on me twice and force me to kill it.  I’m sure there are people who have had worse issues.
As it stands, if you’re looking for a polished, DF-like game, then this isn’t for you.  If you’re looking for a cute little society building game that plans on drawing its own future, then take a harder look.  But, even if you don't get it now, if it interests you, keep your eyes on it and see about getting it in the future, when it's closer to completed.

Cuphead is a Run-and-Gun game developed by Studio MDHR as their debut project. Borrowingly heavily from the narrative tropes and art style of the western cartoons of the 30s (with the works of Max and Dave Fleischer being a major inspiration), the videogames is about the adventures of Cuphead and Mugman, two young brothers with a liking to gamble. After loosing a bet with the Devil himself, the two boys are tasked by the demons to collect the soul contracts of the Devil's other runawayd debtors by any means necessary, with their own souls on the line.
Cuphead's gameplay is clearly inspired by the Run-and-Gun games from the 80s/90s (think of Contra, among others). You can either play solo or with a second local player in co-op and you move from isle to isle to clear the various levels or bosses and unlock greater and greater challenges. Cuphead's signature gameplay mechanic is the parry: by jumping and pressing the jump button again as you are about to land on a pink object or enemy you can "parry" it, destroying it and filling up your super meter. As the game progresses, being able to parry at the right time and several times in a row becomes increasingly important.
Cuphead features two kinds of levels:
1) Boss-only levels, which are arguably Cuphead's main attraction. Each boss features a sequential battle where the more you damange your enemy the more attacks and gimmicks you'll have to face and learn to counter as the boss will change patterns and stages till it'll be defeated. This game's bosses have a lot of tricks up their sleeve and aren't even shy about summoning help or even full-fledged mini-bosses.
2) "Run n' gun" levels, where, as the name would imply, you must run from the beginning to the end of the stage while dodging or defeating the enemies barring your way, defeat the occasional mini-boss or think of ways to bypass your obstacles.
At the end of each level you'll recive a score based on several indicators, which also varies depending on the difficulty you are playing the game on: Simple (easy), Regular (normal), Expert (hard). Simple can be considered a trial mode of sort and will halt your progress in the game sooner or later. Expert changes the bosses' patterns and attacks significantly and provides a huge jump in difficulty for people in search of a better challenge.
Aside from the proper levels, Cuphead's world map features other objectives you can pursuit and means to make your life easier:
1) The Run n' Gun levels contain coins you can spend at a dedicated shop in the world map. The shop contains new bullet types you can equip to better prepare yourself against the boss you are currently facing and charms giving your character useful passive abilities.
2) Each isle features a mausoleum where you can compete in a parrying challenge to unlock one of the three super moves available to you.
3) The world map is also filled with NPCs you can interact with to have either useful hints or start side quests. While some of these side quests will award you coins, some will unlock more unusual rewards for you to enjoy.
There's no going around it: Cuphead is a very challenging and difficult game where memorization and reflexes are usually the key to overcome your current obstacle. It also doesn't help that the majority of the bosses have some randomness factor to them that may frustrate some people (as to say, every time you face them they'll summon different mini-bosses, dish out different attacks or attempt other combos, with some being far easier to deal with than the others). That said, one of the main charm of Cuphed is that even players unfamiliar with the genre can face and win everything the game will thrown at them with enough dedication and mastering. In that regard, Cuphead is both fair and extremely rewarding.
The art style is the second feature people will talk about regarding Cuphead and is as gorgeous and unique as you'd expect: every sprite was hand drawn, the backgrounds were all painted with watercolors and attacks behave and characters morph wildly before your very eyes (sometimes in extremely unsettling ways) as to emulate watching one of those old cartoons from the last century. In this regard, there's currently no game like Cuphead. The beautiful jazz soundtrack performed by a live orchestra only enhances an already great set mood.
In short, Cuphead is a very unique and gorgeous game, should you have the patience to learn its dangers and resident baddies, and I'd reccomend it to anyone anytime, even people (like myself, mind you) who really didn't grow up with the kind of games Cuphead pays homage to

Alright, so let me just say first off that this is the best rouguelike I've payed for to date.
First lets examine how it shapes up as a roguelike, its got all the elements that I would consider defining for the genre. Turn based combat in a square tile grid, full keyboard controls, randomly generated loot and monsters, secret passages and a progression system[levelling up] for your character. Diverse and varied classes, albeit in my opinion there is a distinct lack of classes, which I would count as a negative but hopefully classes can be added later or modded in. It also has the characteristic difficulty, if it is slightly easier than most rougelikes but, if you're not careful you can find yourself out of your element and dead quite quickly.
What it lacks in the hardcore area it makes up for in the actual playability, graphical fidelity and clarity. While there are some elements of the UI I'm not super impressed with generally speaking its miles ahead in terms of accessability so - if you've been looking to get into the rouguelike genre I think this would be a good place to start. The only problem is that you will probably miss out on a lot of the genre related jokes but there is plenty of humour to be found here which is tucked away in descriptions and text which you only read once.
In terms of graphics its not amazing, but compared to others of the genre I feel its miles ahead, which a strong aestethic and good clarity you'll never be squinting at the screen trying to see if thats a goblin[g] or an arch wizard[Z].
The combat, in my opinion is very advanced for a game of the genre. It takes the basics of rouguelike principles and throws a few wrenches in the works. Time honoured tactics of hiding in doorways to funnel enemies in one by one work great. That is until you encounter more advanced monsters - who can fling you around the room, dash through you to surround you and knock you back either throwing you into a room filled with bomb throwing maniacs who are as much a danger to themselves as you or getting behind you turning your careful funnel into a two versus one. Additionally some monsters will spawn barricades and ice blocks to trap you in with their friends which keeps the combat frantic and yet the player must be deliberate and pray that the carpenter bee doesn't summon ANOTHER barricade in the way of the door lest the swarm of blue lizard men things do horrible things with their claws and spears to the heroes hasty behind.
Each class has a distinct playstyle, the gentleman AKA barbarian builds up fury when hit and can unlease it in a tantrum, giving them a lot of buffs to damage as would be expected. The Bannerman fights with a spear and favours being fairly immobile with lifesteal and ranged purity magic - though he can get a move on when he needs to, opting for a more mobile polearm and bow style or entrenching with a heavy shield and poleaxe to cut down multiple foes at a time. You'll be spoiled for choice as each class can be played in a variety of ways. Even the necromancer doesn't really use magic as you would expect, instead generating a resource from corpses that forms the basis of all their spells. Summon the undead to do your bidding or blow up a corpse potentially chaining through an entire infested room causing utter destruction and chaos. There are meaningful choices and paths to take for each class and I think this is one of the games biggest strengths.
As for the permanent buffs that can be obtained from adventuring and making it back to the Academy alive? They are, for the most part, fairly underwhelming and are more of a kickstart to your adventure allowing you to optionally identify some of the potions and scrolls in the game although - if you like to kick it old school you can and instead discover things as you go. To be fair though, as you progress later in the game some of the artifacts can be quite awesome. Even the stat gains you earn permanently seem to have diminishing returns meaning its hard to get to the point where every character will be utter ownage and its more of a long term slight boost with each run.
All things considered, this is a refreshing and interesting title in the rouguelike genre. Rouguelike players are notoriously new-game-ophobic as they're comfortable in their habits. This title makes some great efforts to shake things up and I think it has done so tremendously. My only real negative for recommending it is the price point, I'm not sure the game feels justified at the 15$ mark[15Euro for us europeans] but I have got nearly 3 times the entertainment time of a movie ticket for around the same price so I can't complain too much. I probably would have avoided this title at the 20$ mark, but at 15$ it less questionable. If you're not sold on this review but are interested I'd recommend picking it up on sale for anything around or under the 10$ mark. At the time of writing at least, with 7 hours in.

As a big fan of roguelikes/dungeon crawl games, Dungeonmans is a solid addition to my collection.  For a bit of background, I have played quite a bit of the genre from the original Rogue and own Tales of Maj'Eyal, Dungeons of Dredmore, etc.  I bought this for full retail price, and at the time of this review have 14 hours completed over 4 characters.  So why was this worth my $14.99?
Streamlined Gameplay:  Dungeonmans provides a streamlined experience with lower barriers to entry than most other games in the genre.   With about 75 skills spread over 8 or so categories you can mix and match your build to your tastes.  While fewer than Dredmore and ToME, I was easily able to understand each category quickly while providing enough flexibility to create interesting decisions during my character progression.   Another great feature is the ability to autocomplete dungeons (with a nice jackpot of loot) that would be of trivial difficulty to your character.  This cuts down the grinding a great deal.
Permadeath and the University:  Yes this game features permanent character death, but unlike most games in the genre Dungeonmans has your core base of operations: the University.  The University contains lots of fun *persistent* features that allows your next run to be that much easier.  These include autoidentification, bonuses to your starting equipment, additional mob information, and free stat boosts.  This greatly cuts down on the intimidation factor since you know each successive run you'll be just that much stronger and wiser.
Sense of Humor:  This is hard to describe without experiencing it yourself, but this game has a cheeky sense of humor that I appreciate.  The main tips area in your University is literally a Wall of Text.
Accessible Developers:  If you couldn't tell by the discussion responses, the developers care about their product enough to invest their time to address issues, concerns, and even thank those that are enjoying their experience.  I have seen one even visiting Twitch streams providing advice and support.   I would take a dozen developers like this over a Triple A company that puts out a broken and unsupported product.
Value:  With so many games left unplayed, I started to valuate my future purchase differently.  How much per entertainment hour would I get?  Honestly I can't answer that question for you.  What I can say is that I am at nearly $1 per entertainment hour and the value is only getting better with every playthrough.

Dungeonmans is a rougelike with a delightfully snarky sense of humor. As a recent graduate of Dungeonmans Academy, you are sent forth to make the world safe for ordinary townsfolk. You'll face dozens of dungeon-dwelling enemies, from strange and exotic creatures, to knights and wizards, and eventually come face to face with the Dread Purpleonians.
After picking from among some truly abysmal starting stats, your hero-to-be can select from among several pre-built classes, or mix and match masteries to create a customized monster-bashing powerhouse. Each of these classes has a very different style of play, allowing for different tactics. Whether you favor a Wizardmans, Necromanser, Rangermans, or Southern Gentlemans, you'll need to keep an eye on important resource pools like Health, Stamina, Foom, Ire, and Deadpulses to unleash powerful attacks or invoke defensive manuvers.
The overworld is persistent -- although you can generate a new world map at any time --but each dungeon or tower is randomly generated, as are the beasts and treasures within. Defeat Champions to collect Proofs of Stremf, trophies that allow you to enhance your hero's stats and boost those of future graduates as well. If your hero can fight his or her way back to the Academy, you can deposit these Proofs of Stremf along with books, equipment, and other trinkets that can be used by other Dungeonmans in the event of your untimely (and highly likely) demise.
I've played this game since its early beta days, and it's gotten better and more polished with each update and expansion. I've sent more than 30 adventurers to their deaths so far, and never had a single one make it beyond level 10, but there are always fresh faces back at the academy eager to test their mettle, and I keep coming back for more.
Someday I'll crush those Dread Purplonians. I won't let you down next time, Headmaster!

Hue is a fun puzzle platformer with an interesting mechanic. The puzzles are unlikely to trouble experts, but for the rest of us they ramp up to pretty challenging as the game goes along. The mechanic makes the puzzles very enjoyable and unique, and the more difficult puzzles are very satisfying to solve. Also despite the game's focus on colour, there is an option to add symbols to assist those who are colour blind. The only problem I had with the game was that sometimes I found selecting a colour fiddly, which is not what you need in the middle of a big puzzle. But other than that the game is definitely worth checking out.

I thoroughly enjoyed it. Not sure it's worth £12 but I got it during the winter sale, and I'm more than satisfied with what I paid for.
The puzzles aren't particularly difficult until late game, and even those don't require any Herculean effort, so if you're looking for a
puzzle game you won't find it in Hue - but if you like good puzzle platformers and/or interesting mechanics it's absolutely worth picking up in a sale.

Initially I was put off this game by the lurid colours in the screenshots, but once you see the game in motion it makes far more sense. What lies beneath is actually a really nicely handcrafted puzzle game about single room puzzles based on blocks, switches, and a bit of platforming, all based on one key mechanic. When you change the background colour, all objects matching that colour disappear. This enables you to walk through blocks, hide lasers, hide falling rocks and use all of those things to solve a puzzle and open a door. The ‘story’ is a bit pretentious, but the gameplay is great.

Hue is a two-dimensional puzzle-platform game where the protagonist (Hue) has a task of collecting color segments of a special ring to find out what happened to his mother.

Depends how quickly a person is able to solve the puzzles and how much time they will spend exploring for beakers. On average, I would say that people should spend from 5 to 10 hours playing the game.
This game is really enjoyable, alongside sharing a similar theme of a black and grey background with

main gameplay is the addition of a mysterious ring called the Annular Spectrum that allows Hue to change the color of the world around him.
The very simplistic art style of the game is what makes the hours played fun. One complaint I would have about the graphics would be the colors on the color wheel. They are very close together, and at times I had a difficult time distinguishing between the colors, espically when I needed to think fast. With all the shades having a
look to them it was hard to determine whether an obstacal was yellow, yellowish-green or yellowish-orange. Same goes with the purple and pink shades down at the bottom which were just as confusing.

As you have an option of returning to completed levels to search for hidden beakers, going through the featureless areas is tedious with no narration to cause a distraction.
Hue's movset is very simplistic as he is mostly able to jump, move from left to right and move objects such as boxes. With the left mouse click controlling the color wheel it is fast and easily accessible, but at times may become confusing.

After months of this game's 'development' it's clear now that this entire concept is a complete miss as far as 'competitive' games go. The biggest issue with this game is that it's so called balance extremely favors hunters.
Here are some issues:
"Balance" is based on pub(completely random) matchmaking, resulting in hunters being far overpowered compared to monsters when hunters play as an actual team and communicate.
Hunters keep getting annoying as♥♥♥♥♥♥abilities that completely ruin the fun for monsters and add endless frustration, such as Slim's Spore Cloud which makes the monster effectively blind. The funny thing is, a lighter version of this was originally planned for a monster, but wasn't implemented as it was thought to be 'not fun to play against'. But hell, lets buff it and give it to hunters, who cares about monster players, right?
Certain combinations of hunters are plain overpowered. Normally, in other games, if you saw that teams nearly exclusively pick a certain combination that completely outshines all others, steps would be taken to lessen the effectiveness of that combo. In Evolve, the devs say hell no and leave it as it is since launch, resulting in 90% of games having 2 specific hunters paired up which completely ruins the fun for monster players.
Some hunters are plain better than others. Such as an assault class character that requires no aiming skill and has the highest DPS output in game. This used to be balanced by the fact that said character's ability had a negative effect for the hunters as well, but TRS devs say hell no. Lets remove the negative effect for the hunters and buff that character, resulting in that specific character also being selected in 9 out of 10 fights.
Hunters, who are already overpowered, are constanly cradled like babies thanks to the that fact that there's theoretically 4 of them for 1 monster player, so of course it's more important to keep them happy. This resulted in the latest moronic decision to completely remove any skill requirement from the skill that often determines the outcome of the match, and while previously it was possible to dodge the said ability for a couple seconds after it was used, it is now impossible to do so. This was done to 'reduce the stress of a certain class'. Get it? You had to TIME the use of this huge range potential game ender ability to hit, so that was removed. But that's cool, that specific class wont be stressed so much anymore. Who cares we tripled the stress for the monsters, right?
The game had audio cues which gave both sides crucial information. Monsters could hear the potential game ending ability I mentioned and know they have to run, while in return monster's 'smell' ability could be heard by the hunters. Guess what? The audio cues from hunter side were removed, while the ones on the monster side were naturally kept making it so that sound helps only hunters.
Introduction of game breaking bugs on the monster side is the last on the list of priorities to fix, such as the auto aim bug that basically takes away your ability to decide which hunter to attack has been in game since launch, or another latest screw up which now made movement auto lock onto hunters. But hey, we're told it'll be fixed in the future update. Just a few more months I guess. Of course, if a bug is introduced on the hunter side, it'll be patched as soon as possible.
If you want to play as a monster, save yourself the time and money.
If you want to play as a hunter, buy the game right away. Any wish you have will be swiftly granted if you whine loud enough.

After 290 hours of game-play I feel like I can finally give a full review of the game.
Let's start with the good:
The game-play is fantastic. I have never had such a realistic zombie experience with an in-depth (But limited) world. The player really gets a sense of being alone, with zombies around every corner. You have to carefully ration food and manage your noise levels. Also, be aware of having a proper nutritious meal every now and then or you might still starve! This game can EASILY take 10 hours of your time if you let it. Not to mention the fun and engaging leveling system in which you can customize your character. I also REALLY enjoyed the food/cooking system. If you get this game for free, or for 10 dollars - hell yes.
Let's get to the point though.
After 290 hours of game-play, over ~4-5 years of development, the game has changed very little. Besides a graphical overhaul/engine overhaul the gameplay remains the same.
"Why is this a problem?" - you may ask.
Well I have to respectfully say that the gameplay becomes dull and repetitive once you reach the 'end game'. Once you learn the lack-luster combat mechanics (Which was promised an overhaul over 2 years ago?) zombies are no longer a challenge. That's right. The games BIGGEST BADDIE is no longer a challenge once you get a nice baseball bat. If you decide to turn up the zombie count...well...you are still faced with the eventual same problem except with the exception of a single helicopter bringing hundreds of zombies to your location, and the only REAL way to deal with them is by lighting the horde on fire or using those nice OP bombs. And forget being able to see the majority of this amazing map they created - there is no way to travel except by foot. Which becomes dull very fast if you want to go check out the mall on the other end of the world. And while exploring the world is initially exciting there is not much to find besides an empty world full of zeds. No other AI survivors. No vehicles. Just woods and a few buildings.  The world feels empty and lifeless, and besides nature slowly taking over the world it, the environment does not change with any interesting or challenging mechanics.
So that's my biggest complaint.
Now for the 2nd challenge this game has.
The multiplayer.
The multiplayer makes the game so much more enjoyable...except for the fact that it makes the above problems WORSE. And if you have too many zombies on the screen they begin to warp around and teleport (MAGICAL ZOMBIES!!). I have seen this on several dedicated servers.
Sigh...that's not all. Because my friends and I LOVE this game. We thought "HEY! The game has SPRINTING zombies!!! Those are good because they are DIFFICULT and make the game SCARY and a small group of zombies is VERY FUN to fight against!"
Well. Sprinting zombies work good in singleplayer. But DO NOT work in multiplayer as they warp around terribly and teleport every which way. This has been a bug for YEARS.
Which leads to the 3rd challenge this game has:
The development team. The development team moves slower than any other team I have seen. If you do not watch the news of the game you would believe the game was abandoned. Sure, they have frequent updates. But no true new game mechanics that actually create new challenges for the game.
Enemy AI have been promised for ~2 years and they are using valves "It's done when it's done" as an excuse.
When reporting the teleporting sprinting zombie bug for nearly 2 years the dev's eventual response was exactly this:
"The option will be removed from MP at later date." - EngimaGrey
No explanation as to why. Just simply saying "It would be too hard to do". Come on.
After nearly 2000 hours in development for ArmA mods and talking to many other developers I know that "It would be too hard" = "We don't want to tackle that challenge because we are lazy." (Or as others say "Too busy", because prioritization is NOT a thing with this team).
It simply comes down to the developers struggling to put the work into their game that it desperately needs. It is difficult to compare apples to oranges, but when looking at many other EA games their work pales. I can do without the additional food recipes, please give me AI to interact with. Please give me a difficult zombie curve. Please add more gameplay options for the late-game.
Please add a purpose or goal for this world. Why am I surviving? What obstacle is there to overcome once you have that nice baseball bat and enough food?
I will change this review as updates come along but I am significantly dissapointed with the direction of development.
To wrap it all up
This game offers a VERY FUN experience for the initial few run throughs and I recommend it for free to 10 dollars (Which is subjective, I know)
I would wait to purchase this game if you are waiting for more meaningful mechanics to come into play. Because you might be waiting another 2-3 years for the first introduction of anything really impactful to gameplay.
Frequent Responses:
1) It is difficult to include feature X! You can't expect them to include feature X because of that.
Coding and working on a game takes massive time, dedication, patience, and skill. Just because something is difficult does not exempt it from examination. Having a proper working government is difficult to do, however that difficulty does not exempt it from criticism. If the naysayers writing negative reviews are to believed, the developers of this game are stringing us along with weekly website posts that promise big changes to this game, but significant game updates have been limited for a long time. "For years," apparently.
Well, I don't really care about that. I bought this game years ago in early access because it looked interesting. It has provided me with a couple dozen hours of suspenseful fun. I'll come back to it occasionally to see how much it changes, if at all. I don't need to become upset over how complete one early-access game is. As I understand, the modding community is taking care of some changes itself.
Anyway, about the game: it's an isometric zombie apocalypse sim. You start alone (hopefully) in your house. You are the only uninfected human being in a town of thousands. You can only see the things in the direction your character is facing. If you're wearing too much clothing, you'll get hot. If you eat rotten food, you'll get sick. If you stay inside for too long, you'll get bored. If you get too bored, you'll get depressed. Eventually, the water and power for the town will get shut off, so you'll need to find a reliable and safe source of water. Also, the non-perishable food in the neighborhood which you start in only lasts so long. You'll eventually need to venture out into the huge game world to find more food. If you make too much noise, or if you're seen, nearby zombies will come for you. Potentially dozens of them. And unlike you, they don't need to sleep. If you are bitten once by them, you'll die a slow and miserable death from infection. The game, then, is a mixture of balancing your biological needs with the necessity of managing the size of the horde you have to fight at any given time. Eventually you'll learn enough about crafting and farming to be able to be safe and self-sufficient. Perhaps the negative reviews are by people who want more of an endgame. At any rate, you'll have to play for quite a while before you get to that point.
On an unrelated note, when I was very new to this game, something interesting happened to me a couple of times: I would enter a building looking for things to eat or use as weapons. I turned my character around and a zombie entered his field of vision, inches away from him, and I screamed out loud when this was accompanied by a musical sting. If a game has never made you do that before, perhaps you should try this one out.

Cuphead is quite an interesting game. From the artstyle, to the boss design, to the soundtrack, to the infamous tutorial jump, it has a lot going for it. But is it as good as people say it is? Well, here's what I have to say.
First off, is it as hard as people say it is? Ehh, not really. The reason why I don't think so is because I've played a lot of platformers before, like Hollow Knight, Cave Story, Ori and the Blind Forest, Super Meat Boy, and quite a few other things. All of those are awesome games, by the way. But since I've had experience with both 2D and 3D platformers in the past, I guess that's why I didn't find a lot of it too hard. That doesn't mean there wasn't any hard parts, however. Believe me, there is.
Next, is the game actually good? Yes. Yes it is. It's really good. It's fun, and quite nostalgic for me, considering my early childhood (probably from when I was about 4-8) was filled with Disney cartoons, and that I just love the animation style.
The boss design is amazing. Cuphead is home to some of the most creative and memorable bossfights I have ever gazed upon. Some bosses have some clever jokes, and everytime you die, you get a nice rhyme from all of them, mocking you. Many of these are quite funny, and they give you the urge to play more so you can finally beat them if they're giving you a rough time. There's also a lot of game references scattered around the game, as well as some great easter eggs, but I won't spoil them here.
Anyways, now to the core gameplay. Basic platforming with enemies attacking you, and you have weapons, or powers, to defend yourself. When you collect coins, which you can get in the run & gun levels, as well as some secret areas, you use them to buy new weapons or abilities to help you in the future. Some are quite good, and some are quite not so good. There is a small nitpick I have, however. I feel that the game wasn't entirely suited for running & gunning. Now, while most of those stages are fun and are creative, there's one or two of them that are just really a chore to complete.
Oh lord, the soundtrack. Now, I've heard a lot of jazz in my life, but this stuff? This is classy, grade-A stuff. I found that I loved and adored almost every single song in the game, especially the later ones. They fit the tone perfectly, and provide some entertainment on top of the already entertaining spectacle that is the game itself.
There isn't much else to say, so let's get to what I think about the game as a whole.
Cuphead is a great game. There isn't much to say other than that. The boss designs, the killer jazz soundtrack, the jokes, the references, the artstyle, all of it. It works very well, and I'm glad I got it when it came out.
Final score : 9.5/10.

Cuphead is a boss gauntlet with some light overworld exploration, a handful of platforming run-and-gun stages, and a gorgeous art style inspired by cartoons from the 1930s. It will challenge you, and even put you through the meat grinder at times, but every death takes you one step closer to learning and eventually conquering the game's many multi-staged battles.
Perhaps even more importantly, every death is a new opportunity to enjoy the beautiful animations and backgrounds on display; it's easy to miss the details when you're frantically dodging the immediate threats to your existence. True to the cartoons that inspired it, a sense of quirky liveliness pervades everything—even the things that aren't actively trying to murder you.
Cuphead has developed a reputation for being difficult, and it earns that reputation, but fans of video games and cartoons (taking a wild guess and assuming there are a few of us around here) shouldn't overlook this game, regardless of skill level.

First, I am not going to compare this game to what will (or might be) WoWS, or the WT version of naval battles, as those are different games with a different aproach. I will try to give an objective review of the game and not its competition.
Second, I won't review balance, or what I think are temporary issues. The developer is fairly reactive and each weekly patch brings a lot to the game in my opinion. There are still issues, but I judge a game by its fun and its potential.
Pros:
- Gameplay is fun. Very fun. It is fast paced, team-based, strategic, and skill and positioning are a huge part of the game. You'll never get bored during a game. Guaranteed. Too much to do and think about.
- Gameplay is varied. Playing a BB (Battleship), a DD (Destroyer), a CV (Aircraft Carrier) or a SS (Submarine) is very different, so that you can add variety to your gameplay from one game to the other or just find your playstyle. Each ship has its role (even 2 CLs can have very different roles depending on their loadout). You constantly switch between weapons (guns, torps, planes, mines, depth charges, AA, ...) and try to make the most out of it while navigating your ship. Significantly different maps. Game is surprisingly deep.
- Beginning progression is very fast so you can get any class of ship within hours, and then you have to invest your time to get the top tiers. They just boosted permanently XP and credit gain by 2 and 1.5 respectively, for everyone.
- Game makes it in a way that a tier I can take out a tier VII if played correctly/smartly. Very rewarding.
- NOT Pay 2 Win. Premium account gives you the usual XP and Credit boost for faster progression. Some real money items give increased (temporary) stats in game but to the order of 10% max; which is definitely overcome by skill and teamplay. It is more P2W than games with a pure cosmetic cash shop, but I strongly believe the advantages are not significant.
- Developer is its own publisher/editor, on this instance of the game, which means faster development cycle and patches.
- Easy game to get into (simple basic controls, basic goals, immediate action, ...) ...
Cons:
- ... but difficult to actually understand. Poor documentation and tutorials forces you to discover things by yourself, or ask the community, to understand better how to play. Community is decent and people will answer your questions. This problem sometimes leads to frustration, but it is rewarding to get to know the game better. Lots of "Eureka" moments.
- Linked to the above, but the game has its quirks, ie some unintuitive stuff from controls to interface. You get used to it after a few hours.
- "Korean grind" game. You will 100's of similar games (but never the same).
- Graphics and effects are outdated
- historically inaccurate

I've played this game a few months and have about 900 games under my belt.  If you're looking for a free-to-play naval game with arcade like gameplay then you should give this game a shot.  I only recommend it as such though, do not expect 100% realistic gameplay or you will be dissapointed.
Pros:
1)  Ship types are not only useful but neccessary for a team to win.  A team with 10 Battle Ships will lose to a mixed force that plays the map properly.
2)  Similar to World of Tanks there are smaller vessels that exist in high tiers.  Think of it as light tanks or medium tanks at high tiers except with ships.  They all have their role on the battlefield.
4)  Personal skill means a lot.  You cannot simply stomp someone just because you have a higher tier ship.  If you rush in without care then you will see lower tier ships mop the floor with you.
5)  Rock-Paper-Scissors balance.  As stated above you need a mixed force however you can get hard countered by certain ships.  Submarines are able to take out Battle Ships and Aircraft Carriers with ease if the Destroyers and Light Cruisers do not hunt them down.
Cons:
1)  As in World of Tanks or War Thunder there will be games you just cannot win due to having a team that does silly things.  Personal performance can only carry you so far and some games are just unwinnable.
2)  Aircraft have no fuel gauge so if you plan to roll up the CV line you better have good micromanagement skills.
3)  Some people say the game is insanely grindy.  In the past that has been true however the XP gains have been adjusted to reasonable levels.  This makes it possible for anyone to get into ships earlier than they probably need to be.  It only took 400 games to reach Tier 9 in the CV line but then again most people would say that's too much for an arcade like game.  XP has been doubled since then so hopefully that issue isn't around anymore for newer players.
4)  No physics for ships.  You can stack all the ships together and have them occupy the same space.  If anyone shoots they'll hit the others which leads to people never "crossing" eachother to avoid accidentally blowing up the ally who cut across them.  A very cheesy tactic is to move your ship into the same space as the enemy ship so that their team cannot help them without blowing up their ally.  Meanwhile you can just pound away at their ship from within their footprint in the water.  Some ships have no way to lower their guns and cannot hit targets that close... all they can do is hope the smaller ship inside them runs out of ammo as they die a slow painful death.
Is this game good?  I think so.  I'd pay $20.00 for this game if they asked since it's on par with the quality you would expect from a $20.00 game.  The matches do not last very long, 15 minutes tops, which means you can knock out a round or two before work or whenver you got a bit of free time and I like that.  Many tactics have evolved as people unlock different ships and soon organized Fleet Battles will come out and give the game a competative aspect.  Give it a shot if you love skill based Free-to-Play games that have no Pay-to-Win.

I have played both Navyfield 1 (started mid 2009) and Navyfield 2 since launch. I have 3 level 50+ captains in NF2 so ignore what steam says about me not playing for very long.
I'll try to be as in-depth but at the same time I'll give you the straight truth on what's going on with this game...
Box art description: Navy Field is a game about WW2 naval battles where you choose a nation, decide which ship line to go down, then play out sea warfare in glorius 2006-era graphics. Where the game lacks in graphics, it makes up for in strategic combat that can actually be quite thrilling if you're into this sort of game.
Now let me get this out of the way first: This will be the make or break the game for most of you out there.
There is a term for what this game puts you through and that term is "Grind". This game will require days of your life in order for you to play ANY ship beyond Tier VII. There are 11 tiers.
The good news is that the first 6 tiers are fairly easy to get to by playing normally without any sort of booster or Premium(More on this later). The better news is you can get to every single ship class by Tier IV so you can try all different playstyles before you uninstall this game because of the crazy grind to Tier X.
All in all, this game is only truly about
15% Pay to Win. There are no "Premium Ships" in NF2 (unlike NF1), and there are no Premium Weapons or Premium Planes or anything. Every ship/item in the game must be earned with XP from battles.
The P2W currency in this game is "Gold". With Gold you can buy  "Premium", which is like a subscription and does a few 'subscriber'-like things. The main reason anyone would buy premium would be for the Credit and XP boost that comes along with it, a whopping 50% boost. ... Not the most P2W I've ever seen by far but maybe that's why it's so cheap.
I've paid for Premium before, and battles where I'd average 800 xp I'd be getting about 1200 xp so there's a decent boost from it.
EDIT: After further review, it appears as though these slots are unlocked by default. Which means I would change the amount of P2W this game is down to about 15% from 20%.
But either way, that's the most pay to win aspect of this game. There are a few other things, such as items for your ship you can buy that will give you a 15% boost to your engine recharge speed or for 1000 gold (roughly $10) you can straight up buy 100,000 credits from the store. But the truth is without the EXP you gain from battles, you can't even unlock anything worth buying.
So the grind they've implemented actually cuts their P2W factor down by quite a lot. Whether this is a good thing or not is up to you.
ATTENTION:
If you've gotten to this point and are still on board, congratulations! You might not hate this game after all! I mean, I do. But I still play it. It's a love-hate relationship. Anyway, I'll actually outline some game details so you can know what to expect.
First, each nation has it's own advantages and disadvantages. For example, Japanese torpedos do WAY more damage than UK torpedos. But UK's armor on their ships can take IJN cannons all day.
The different ship lines are: DD (Destroyer), CL (Light Cruiser), CA (Heavy Cruiser), BB (Battleship), CV (Aircraft Carrier), and SS (Submarine). They're each good at different things, and to win you must play on your strengths as a team of different ships.
When you first choose your capatin, you'll enter into the harbor to inspect your ship and enlist crewmen. There are 4 types of crewmen: Weapons Officers, Support Officers, Engineering Officers and Aviation Officers. Each one has 3 different stats you can put points into as they level up along with your captain, who has his/her own 5 stats you can level up. All of these stats change the way your crew works. For example, if you have Weapons Officers that are high in Reload but low in Accuracy, then you'll pump out the shells but they'll spray everywhere at longer distances.
Finding a battle is easy enough: Click the "Battle" button. They have a "Platoon" system in place that will allow you and 2 friends to enter in the same battle. If you have a larger group however just have everyone hit "Battle" and you'll find each other :)
During battle, the goal is to be the best (insert ship class) you can be by racking up damage points and capturing objectives. If you are sunk during a battle, you can wait until the end of the battle to receive a larger EXP and Credit bonus towards your ship and crew.
I would recommend this game to anybody looking for something different and interesting to play. I mean,♥♥♥♥♥♥.. it's free. What's the worst that could happen? You actually like it?
HINTS:
Ask questions. People will answer.
Give your torps at least 1 second to arm.
VISION IS OP
If you're a DD and there's a sub around, use your damn sonar.
'Gradual' firing mode is good for learning how the shooting mechanics work.
AP ammo removes the armor so HE does full damage.
Think ahead: Put points into your commander as if you were playing the ship you want to play from Day 1. You'll be way better off. Ex: If you're building an aircraft carrier, give your commander aviation points instead of weapons.
Thanks for reading, and I apologize for any misspellings. If you need a friend to roll with, send me a request and I'll support you as best I can. I have one of each ship class and would be happy to help you in any way I could if you need it :)
Just send me a pm or comment and I'll do my best!

I have been playing this game since the first Alpha release, in early 2014. I mostly played after feature patches to see what's new and to spend a relaxing evening with the game. In this review I want to give my oppinion about a few aspects of the game and it's development.
The vision:
I really like what the devs want to achieve with this game. The voxel style is really cute and in my opinion, it does not look like it's just copied from another voxel game. I look forward to playing a game which can follow in the footsteps of the old Settler games, combining a strategy game with having a village inhabited by scurrying inhabitants.
Communication:
The developers are really active with their community from what I saw. There are weekly updates on their website, regular livestreams (not at the best times for Europeans) and active discussions in the forums. I always felt like I knew what was happening with the game, even if there was not much progress, for example due to moving to a new office.
Current state:
Currently, this is not a game to spend a lot of time with for the average player. To see all the content, a few hours will be enough. But, after all, this game is in early access, so I think that is to be expected. You can already see the direction in which this game is heading, you will be able to have some fun for an evening or two, and you probably want to check from time to time what new patches added.
All in all, this game is heading to a promising direction, I never regretted backing it on Kickstarter, and I'm still confident that it will be a great game. There is enough content to spend a few hours playing it and updates are always coming.

Stonehearth is a cute little game in the vein of Dwarf Fortress (though with less madness and fewer death spirals) though the Hearthlings don’t seem to like living underground.  It’s very cute, and it’s looking at the ASCII code of DF saying “ooh, I want to be like that when I grow up!  Only better!
Unfortunately, that’s all it is right now.  It is full of potential, as well as glitches—I won’t outright call them bugs.
•	Hearthlings occasionally just drop what they’re carrying and it stays there indefinitely, unusable by anyone.
•	Hearthlings get confused about what furniture goes where and nothing gets placed ever again.
•	Hearthlings will occasionally decide that they’re just done working and never do anything (other than eat or sleep) again.
•	Hearthlings will teleport to inaccessible locations and you have to figure out where they are and how to get them back.
•	Goblin Raiding Parties will, sometimes, just run into an empty area of your village and . . . loiter.
None of these actually cause the game to crash and burn, but they are incredibly annoying, usually requiring you to start a new village.  Now, don’t get me wrong.  When the glitches don’t show up (which is happening more and more regularly), you get a cute little village and get to watch your little Hearthlings build a basic village.
But, all that said, this is still in Alpha, so, you should expect worse.  However, there isn’t much worse.  For an Alpha, it’s pretty stable and they’re working on it regularly.  I’ve only had it lock up on me twice and force me to kill it.  I’m sure there are people who have had worse issues.
As it stands, if you’re looking for a polished, DF-like game, then this isn’t for you.  If you’re looking for a cute little society building game that plans on drawing its own future, then take a harder look.  But, even if you don't get it now, if it interests you, keep your eyes on it and see about getting it in the future, when it's closer to completed.

Hue had so much potential to be a great game, but it feels like the developers couldn't decide whether they wanted a platformer or a puzzler. Instead of doing one genre well, they did both poorly.
The game features a lot of slow walking around, especially during story segments where you walk through a boring environment while the story is narrated to you. The story is fine, but having to walk through a long hallway to kill time is annoying.
The platforming segments are just frustrating - they present no challenge to either your brain or your reflexes, and instead feel like pointless filler. The same exact type of platforming section is repeated multiple times within the game, sometimes even back to back. It almost feels patronizing considering this is supposedly a puzzle game.
The puzzles are okay, most are of average quality and the difficulty curve is fine. They never get challenging though - right before you might ramp up the difficulty, a new color or game mechanic is introduced and the difficulty curve starts over. Instead of iterating designs with the elements they had, they just added more elements.
What really annoys me is the lack of a proper checkpoint or rewind system - if you make one mistake in a room and die, you have to start completely over from the beginning of the room. Many of the game mechanics are deadly, such as spikes, lasers, thwomps, bottomless pits, etc. and you will die a lot from simple mistakes. The worst part is that I frequently knew exactly what I needed to do, but a simple mistake in execution meant I had to die and start completely over from scratch. I feel like a different choice of game mechanics could have made for a much more fun experience with a lot less death and restarts. At the very least, being able to rewind a few seconds or create quicksaves would be a much appreciated band-aid. The game recommends a controller but I really don't see how that would help.
Another major annoyance is that when you are selecting a color, your character keeps moving in the same direction even if you let go of all movement keys. Time is slowed down but it's still very annoying that you have no control over your character while selecting a color - the slow motion is very useful in execution-based situations and is completely ruined by the lack of control. Many of my deaths are attributed to this, and the game requires this kind of quick maneuvering frequently.
There are collectibles in the game, but their placements intentionally hostile to the player. You will frequently see an obvious collectible in a level that you don't have the right color to access until later in the game, meaning you have to backtrack or replay levels to access it. This is beyond lazy - none of the collectibles require any challenge or puzzle to access, so requiring the player to replay levels to reach the spot once they have the right color is just insulting. The fast travel system in the game only lets you travel to the start of huge sections of the game, there is no way to travel to a specific level without replaying all of the levels before it.
The color palette seems to have too many similar colors. These are not your typical shades of colors as you would expect from opening up MS Paint or Photoshop, these are hand-tuned colors to fit the theme and art style of the game. While it does make the game consistently look pleasant, it also makes it really hard to discern colors. I am not colorblind, and I frequently had trouble telling apart yellow from orange, pink from purple, and yellow from yellow-lime green because they were so close in shade, especially when various elements tweak the shade slightly. This meant I frequently selected the wrong color, half the time resulting in death.
As for the story, it's okay. Just okay. It explores some interesting ideas but never follows through with them, instead stopping short to move on to a different topic.
On the bright side, the art design is beautiful, and I'm a big fan of it. The music is also pretty good.
Overall, I'd rate the game at 5/10, which is average and not a bad score, but I can't recommend it for the asking price. Get it when it's on sale for 50% off or more.

This game is great, the setting and characters are amazing, the story is great, the gameplay is good, although it can get a bit frustrating at times.
Ammo is scarce, and the enemies are bulletsponges. The plasmids save it for me. If you run out of ammo (which you will) you can always freeze, burn, electrocute or melee enemies. If you do die, you just get teleported to the start of the level and the enemies you've killed/ damaged will stay that way. This means that if you encounter a lot of enemies of just one really tough enemy, you can chip away at them without having to worry about losing progress. This means it's basically impossible to get stuck on any part of the game. I'll leave it up to you to decide whether that's a good thing or not.
The Big Daddies are another cool addition. What I really like about them is that you don't necessarily have to fight them. If you're low on HP or ammo you can just ignore them, and they won't kill you.
The story and setting are really what make this game for me. The setting is unlike anything I've seen before. It really drew me in and made me want to keep playing to see what the next area looked like. The characters and story are pretty unique as well, as long as you've never played System Shock 2. It's basically that but way better and with objectivist philosophy and moral dilemmas. It really stuck with me and I think it's the main reason why you should buy this game.
In conclusion, buy it. You owe it to yourself to see and experience this game.
8/10

Underneath the silly, this is actually a pretty fun & well put together Roguelike (a REAL roguelike - not those games with permadeath and level generators that call themselves "roguelikes"), with enough unique features to keep it interesting. Its more than just running dungeons, you have your "Dungeonmans Academy" you need to bring things too to make it better, an overworld to explore, ect. Theres lots to do, many character class & traits choices. I havent played too much yet, but this looks like a Roguelike I'll have fun with.
The silly, however, is overpowering. Sometimes its amusing, but IMHO it beats you over the head a little too much. It may be funny if you're a teenage guy, I'm a 30-something chick, so I can't judge there. Still, theres lots of clever Roguelike humor for long-term rogue players.
It is out of E. A. but still seems a bit incomplete (the "help" button in options does nothing that I could see), there are gender options such as "beast" and "who cares" but the only images are of stereotypical fantasy males and females. Come on, if youre going to be silly, give us some funny icons to work with those genders!
The graphics are pixel tiles. They are colorful and cartoony and fit well with the style of the game. My one (minor) complaint is getting new weapons and armor does nothing to your tile. Like if you have the barbarian shirtless guy with the sword, he remains the shirtless guy with the sword even if youre wearing platemail and carrying an axe. Its kind of nitpicky, but Roguelikes have progressed from the days of "@", or even the tile systems of *Angband. I love games like Tales of Maj'Eyal, or Rogue's Tale where your tile changes depending on what you have equipped. It would be an asset here.
Overall though, this game is defintely worth taking a look at for Rogue fans. It has a lot of content and is something a little different.

Dungeonmans is a thoroughly enjoyable rogue like with several innovations that add depth to the genre. The Dungeonmans starter area known as The Academy is the main hub of these innovations. The Academy allows you to make subtle tweaks to your experience. For instance bringing artifacts back to the academy lets future Dungeonmans use stronger weapons and armor then would normally be available to a new graduate. There are several non-player characters at The Academy who can increase new graduate advantages with the riches that your last Dungeonmans gave their life for.
This game also has a fully realized class system using an intuitive point allocation system.  You also have the freedom to build your own Dungeonmans instead of using a prebuilt starting class. You are allowed to mix and match between magic, melee, and ranged skills over your career. This game has soundtracks, sound effects, and sprite based art that helps to create captivating rogue like environments. The world of Dungeonmans is populated with towns and dungeons galore.
Dungeons have ominous soundtracks and gritty sprites, while the towns are depicted with cheerful music and colorful sprites. Towns provide another place to enhance your experience. Towns can be upgraded like The Academy to give you better shop items from the local merchants. The dungeons vary in size, design and difficulty. Besides being filled with monsters, dungeons can have traps, secret treasures, and ultimately end with a showdown with its powerful master.
The advantages of the Academy are completely voluntary. If you’re looking for a harsher challenge simply don't enhance The Academy and your new Dungeonmans will have no advantages when they start out. Even with the advantages that the Academy provides, you'll still find that the best equipped and experienced players will find challenges in Dungeonmans readily available. This game has provided me with many hours of entertainment. If you’re looking for a rogue like with something new to offer, but the difficulty the genre is known for then look no further. Dungeonmans is the game for you.

A long time ago when I was only young I played a Roguelike- This Roguelike was pretty much perfect in my eyes. It had a great mix between being challenging and being accessible. The name of this Roguelike was Castle of the Winds and it has long held a place in my heart as being the best of show out there for this genre. Now I think after many years Castle of the Winds has finally been toppled in my eyes.
Dungeonmans is the best Roguelike I have played in a long time- it has an easy to learn and use gameplay which is unforgivable the further out you go. The game captures everything that I loved about Castle of the Winds- the crisp but simple art, the spellbooks for learning new spells, the absurdity of monsters you find in the deep... Then it puts everything into overdrive. With Dungeonmans one of the most innovative features is the Academy which grows based on deeds, you don't simply pour money into this academy to make it better, you fill it with the blood and sweat of a ton of dead dungeonmans. As someone who always likes persistant strength options in Roguelikes, this is good, but what makes it better is the fact that all of the unlocked perks are optional to pick up. If the game is too easy for you, just don't pick up the perk at the start. No harm done. You will still do awesomely if you are skilled enough for the task.
The music of Dungeonmans is also pretty phenominal due to being the work of the great Zircon, a remix artist who makes the game come alive. The art is pretty standard, but the simplistic nature of it actually works well with what is trying to be achived. As you go deeper into the many dungeons you will find an increasingly powerful variety of loot capable of making you feel like a king- and if you die while carrying one of your favourite swords it is even possible to find the sword in a later playthrough in a more powerful form.
There is so much to unlock in this game too- you can find hidden skills, dungeons, artifacts of power and more based on how you play and what you do. I won't spoil them, but basically the game rewards you all the way in the best possible way. Overall- this game scratches many itches for me. The itch for a good Roguelike, the itch for constructing my own "x", the itch to find a game I can happily play for countless hours-
Full disclosure though- At the end of this I feel that I should say I was a kickstarter backer. While I don't belive my experience has been coloured by that fact, it is possible that some of my praise is the work of a Rosetinted Glasses look of someone who didn't want to have wasted their money. So please do take my review with that in mind,
EDIT: Also one slight warning- The game is best played with the numpad for movement so if you have a laptop which does not have one... keep that in mind. There is mouse control but it makes the game seem a lot more "slippery". Though, it should also be said numpad controls is just another reason why this game is rocking it CoTW style.

This is a traditional roguelike with a tileset, and a persistent base called the Dungeonmans Academy that can be upgraded, and all features unlocked/improved can and will be used by future characters. In the beginning, you make a world, then you make your character. The character starts out in the Academy in your world, and you go forth from there. The Overworld is generated when you make your world, and stays the same, though the dungeons continue to be randomly generated. When you die, you make a new character, and go back to the same world with the Academy you've been working on. You can have 3 seperate worlds at once.
There are plenty of skills and passives you can unlock when you level, supporting many styles of play: Dual Wielding, Sword and Board, Magic, Two-Handers, Necromancy, Bows, Spears, Light/Medium/Heavy Armor(or Light "Armor"/Medium Armor/Real Armor as the game calls them). And I know I missed a few.
There are also unidentified and randomized names for scrolls and potions too. The large variety of potions and scrolls reminds me of Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup.
There's also a lot of goo humor in the game, from the dialogue, item/skill/spell descriptions, and events.
I definitely recommend this game to any fan of roguelikes.

Dungeonmans is a
. I'm over 100 hours in and it still provides new and interesting moments every time I play.
It's a rogue-like and that means challenging permadeath gameplay; however, the game also has the "Dungeonmans Academy" which provides limited permanence and can make the game more forgiving over time for less skilled players. The combat is highly tactical (all turn-based) and different combinations of enemies continue to provide unique challenges even after you're familiar with how to defeat each enemy individually. The main level cap is 15, which sounds low, but each level represents a significant bump in power and challenge.
Character advancement is simple, yet rewarding. Powers can be chosen freely without class restrictions, so you can have a wizard clad in full plate wielding a giant axe if you want. Some powers can only activate with certain gear equipped and a small handful of the most powerful abilities have to be "unlocked", but those restrictions all feel quite reasonable.
One aspect of this game that's hard to describe is the humor and the overall feel. As you well might gather from the title "Dungeonmans", the game doesn't take itself too seriously. Oddball monster varieties, subtle self-reflective mocking of RPG/adventure game tropes, and humorous flavor text are woven into nearly every piece of the game. It helps balance the seriousness of the gameplay, frequently giving you a reason to smile while playing. It's also nice that the humor is unimposing and unpresumptuous--it doesn't try too hard to make you laugh. It reminds me a lot of the feel of a tabletop D&D session with old friends--occasionally serious, sometimes laugh-out-loud funny, always enjoyable.
The game is highly replayable for a number of reasons. 1) You usually know exactly why you die when you die (needed to drink a healing potion 3 rounds ago, shouldn't have entered that large room at half health, etc). 2) Since the academy makes subsequent attempts incrementally easier, there is always the challenge to complete the game in fewer characters. 3) The randomly generated dungeons occasionally have hidden rooms with very challenging encounters (sometimes optional, sometimes not). On later playthroughs, you can keep it interesting by opting in to these big challenges. 4) There are enough rare/unique items that I still see new loot nearly every playthrough. 5) The developer has teased several types of end-game content which will likely be available once the game is out of early access.
The last thing I will say is that the developer has done an incredible job with the "early access" phase of this game. He is highly responsive to individual players, he openly shares progress, and regularly incorporates community feedback into the game development. He streams development on Twitch and releases updates regularly. That's exactly why a lot of gamers prefer indies over AAA publishers, so we need to make sure to show our appreciation for the ones who go out of their way to focus on community.
