Stonehearth is a sandbox-rpg town builder with a lot of heart. I’ve been playing the game since Alpha 3 and it’s the only early development game i’ve had zero regrets about purchasing.
Community And Developers:
The Stonehearth Discourse is full of awesome and helpful people. It’s a very good grouping of gamers really trying to help each other out. Friendliest discourse on the net.
The developers at Stonehearth truly are one of a kind. They continue to be very open about what is happening with the game and participate in discussion on the discourse. They REALLY do listen to feedback, i've seen it happen multiple times where the community will spotlight a great idea and it makes it into the game.
But the main thing is… they stream THREE times a week on Twitch, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. Two design live streams and one coding stream. Tony and Tom answer questions accept feedback with the best of them.
On top of this, they do a development blog once a week, sometimes twice.
Alphas get pumped out one every 6-8 weeks on average. In between that, they update the unstable branch that allows you to play test the upcoming features, and those come pretty quickly after main Alpha releases.
Gameplay:
The game plays great You set up the tasks and then can kick back and watch as your Hearthlings go to work. Farmers need to direction as they constantly plant, harvest, and replant food. The trapper will automatically head to the trapping zones you set up, survey the lands, and place out traps to catch small game. And one of my favorites... footman will patrol along your roads and stockpiles, wary for danger.
With the Dungeon Master Ai system, it spawns events and campaigns (I won't spoil what) that come to mess with your village. In some cases, you are given multiple options on how to handle it.
Overall:
I think the Devs said it best
"It’s important to understand that Stonehearth isn’t finished yet. Not by a long shot. But Stonehearth, as it stands now, is a game with fun, robust gameplay and plenty to do and explore."

Numerous times I FOOLISHLY passed over this title, for whatever reason it never grabbed me. I am so glad that I gave it a chance, because in many ways it is the game that I have been seeking out for years. I'll point out the strongpoints for me, because if I had known these things about the game I would have purchased it much sooner.
-Create YOUR OWN FACTION, along with your own hero to lead it!
-Excellent faction customization: edit uniform/armor colors, traits (boons), weaknesses, and even your own backstory!
-Excellent hero customization: Edit appearances, choose from many races, alter equipment, mounts, and their backstory!
-The awesome customization doesn't end there. Once you start your game, you will be able to customize your own units!
-Rename cities and units to anything that you'd like, custom tailor everything to your faction.
Why is it so important to have custom factions and all this, you ask? Why not just play with the epic unique original factions? Do that too if you wish! All of the lore in this game seems epic, but I will explain to you my appeal with this extensive customization. I am a fiction writer, in particular, I enjoy writing fantasy novels. Being able to bring the factions from my stories to life is something that I have craved, as I have found that games have helped inspire creativity when I have writer's block or low motivation. This game is inspiring, to say the least. I created 7 custom factions from my story, and I set up a game on a large map using only my custom factions! For some reason, I was only able to have 6 out of the 7 custom factions selectable when I started the game (though, in all fairness I believe I needed to exit the game and re-enter to let my newest faction "set in" with the system, idk). Overall, I am proud to say that I spent the first 7 hours of the game creating my 7 factions. Before you ask, no, it does NOT take 1 hour to make a faction. You could probably throw one together quickly. I just spent a lot of time exploring all my options and picking the best factions from my stories to include in the game. I set up an alliance between my faction and another, while setting up an alliance between our 2 strongest foes, with 2 other bandit/merc factions... this was all done in the options before I even started the game!
So customize to your heart's content, and let the creativity flow. I am excited to explore the lore, creatures and other factions from the game, as they all seem really unique and appealing. I am so pleased that I finally gave this gem a chance, I am going to look into the Sorcerer King one next, I think that is next in the series. Anyway, I don't understand why people aren't shouting to the heavens about the customization here! I am simply blown away, and on my first day playing this I have fallen in love, pumping 11 straight hours in already. Can't wait to enjoy this game more, and to explore this wonderful game! Don't make this same mistake that I did in passing this one by, I can't tell you how many games I bought in search of a game like this. A game where I had true freedom in my faction customization. While I do wish there were a few more options at times, I am nothing but pleased with my game experience so far! Overall, I'd give this game a 9.5/10. Yes, the graphics may be a little dated, and I'm sure other people have plenty of gripes with this or that. I am just in love with this game as it has given me something that I wished to have for so long. I know this will aid in getting my creative juices flowing as I set off on many adventure with my favorite factions and heroes from my stories!
TLDR: 9.5/10 This is a high quality turn-based strategy game (like the Civ games), with an in depth turn-based combat system (like Wasteland 2, Gladius, etc.). Strong features include: faction customization, character customization, great world/lore and much more!

I don't quite remember where this game came from, as I am a pretty avid subscriber to Humble Bundle. It probably came from one of those. That said, this review will short.
Hue is a game that explores the ability of incorporating colors into puzzles. Say you need to get through a blue wall. If you have the blue piece of the ring, you can get through it. This can apply to just about any object, making just about anything of color invisible. This gets more and more complex as you go, as there are lasers, balloons on crates, springs that change color when you step on them, even boulders of various colors rolling after you.
There were a few moments where I had to use the "Restart Level" button from the menu. This does detract from the experience, and it gave me this feeling that I had done something wrong, when I had merely been going through the process of trying to solve the puzzle. There aren't many levels that will do this to you, as I can only count about 2 or 3 that were particularly specific in how the game developer wanted it to be solved. Most times, you are never painted into a corner that says you can't undo what you've done. Because you are able to push and pull crates with the action button, it gives you a lot of forgiveness in pushing things too far to one side, or needing to drag a crate here or there.
The music is amazing. It seemed to capture those moments that were dangerous, without overplaying itself. It also blends well into the background, so that solving the puzzles doesn't become difficult with a distracting background music. The voice acting is also great. There is a feeling of real emotion in the words, and it helps to draw a connection to the characters, as well as give a new insight, through the writing, on how we perceive colors.
I won't give away too much more with this game. It didn't require me to go outside of the game to find solution for it. I recommend it to those that are keen on solving puzzles of a creative nature. Few puzzles deal with the idea of making an object passable, while not moving it in the slightest.

I think there are better idle / clicker games out there to spend your time on. For the most part this does not have anything that you haven't seen before.
This game could have been really good, but they missed some major points. In it's favor, I will say that the one thing it has going for it is decent graphics.
-Poor interface.
Having to scroll through a list is suboptimal. You can only see a handful of heros at a time. Combined with the fact that you have a bunch of different tabs, that is no good. I'm willing to put up with that kinda stuff in a game with more depth, but not from a clicker. The fact of the mater is, its not even like it needs to take up that much space. Your only option is to buy more levels. The only important information is their strength and the cost to buy more levels.
-Poor feedback
The graphics are this games one highlight. All of your "guild" members are fully animated. That's great. However, their idle animations have a lot of bouncyness which makes it look like their attack animation. It would have been easy to make the enemy flash when your guys attack or damange numbers appear over their head. Instead, it really doesn't feel like your guys do anything other than dance around.
-Missed opportunity
OK, this game could have been something really different. For example, the monsters could do damage back to your guild members (and every wave they all get back up). Then you could have heros that heal, heros that debuff, heros that buff. It could still have the same core clicker growth and feel, but with at least the illusion of depth. It would have been something we haven't seen before.

This game is great, the setting and characters are amazing, the story is great, the gameplay is good, although it can get a bit frustrating at times.
Ammo is scarce, and the enemies are bulletsponges. The plasmids save it for me. If you run out of ammo (which you will) you can always freeze, burn, electrocute or melee enemies. If you do die, you just get teleported to the start of the level and the enemies you've killed/ damaged will stay that way. This means that if you encounter a lot of enemies of just one really tough enemy, you can chip away at them without having to worry about losing progress. This means it's basically impossible to get stuck on any part of the game. I'll leave it up to you to decide whether that's a good thing or not.
The Big Daddies are another cool addition. What I really like about them is that you don't necessarily have to fight them. If you're low on HP or ammo you can just ignore them, and they won't kill you.
The story and setting are really what make this game for me. The setting is unlike anything I've seen before. It really drew me in and made me want to keep playing to see what the next area looked like. The characters and story are pretty unique as well, as long as you've never played System Shock 2. It's basically that but way better and with objectivist philosophy and moral dilemmas. It really stuck with me and I think it's the main reason why you should buy this game.
In conclusion, buy it. You owe it to yourself to see and experience this game.

The graphics are stunning, but you will not find photorealism here. The game has a very unique art style, with faded colors and beautiful art direction. It kind of adds to the feeling of melancholy and despair of being alone in the wilds.
Game mechanics are deep enough to keep you satisfied, and living just another day becomes a huge victory for you sometimes.
It does get a little repetitive after a while, but the devs have been adding content all the time, and are really good at communicating with the community.
Overall, this is a recommended game to buy. I know it's not finished, but the final product will surely be damn good.

This game is one of my favorites that I discovered this year. Its uniqueness of being a roguelike combined with a tower defense is what drew me to it. Initially I didn't know that was what this game was, becaues the trailer didn't show much of how the gameplay works.
The premise is that a ship crashes and you are in control of up to four people who escaped in an escape pod. The escape pod buried itself deep into this planet which you landed on and there are thirteen levels in this "dungeon" which you have to go up. Each level has a certain amount of rooms, and when you open the door to a room enemies may spawn. You also collect Food, Industry, and Science (FIS) each time you open a door. Rooms can have up to 1 slot for a major module like a FIS Creator (one type for each resource), but may also have none. Rooms can also have several minor module slots which can have laser turrets which are the starting minor module. Industry is what is used to build modules and different modules have different Industry costs. Throughout the game you can use science in certain rooms you find to research new modules. There are minor modules that heal your heroes, slow enemies, and much more. However, only powered rooms can have working modules. Rooms are powered by Dust, something that you can collect when you open new rooms and kill enemies. Unpowered rooms that you have opened may spawn enemies each turn, but not every turn.
There is a room on every floor that has an exit, and you have to bring the crystal from the first room of the floor to the exit via one of your heroes. This starts a turn and enemies come from every unpowered room. If you successfully get the crystal to the exit, you get onto an elevator and are done with the floor.
Heroes are used to attack enemies, increase output from modules, and carry the crystal at the end of the floor. Food can be used to instantly heal them whenever you want, or to level them up and make them more powerful. In some rooms you can find a chest with an item which you can give to one of your heroes, or you can find a merchant which will buy your items or let you buy theirs for FIS or Dust. There are three types of items: weapons, armor, and equipment. They can improve your heroes stats in speed, damage, or defense, or also give them bonuses for fighting with other heroes in a room or alone. There are 16 heroes (now 20 with the latest update) and each one is unique in the type of weapon they use, and the abilities they have. You have control the heroes in your game and can move them to different rooms as you please. They will attack enemies on their own and focus certain enemies over others. I didn't realize this from the trailer but found that it works well instead of having to manually attack enemies. Heroes also unlock active abilities as they level up which you can use for various effects.
I've played a ton of this game since I bought it a couple months ago and I love it. The multiplayer is fun, but there are rarely people hosting matches. If you want to play multiplayer then get this game with a few friends. The multiplayer works well and doesn't require any server hosting or anything. For single player the abilitiy to save the game and come back to it later is great, but there is only one save slot. I would highly recommend this game as it is quite cheap for how good it is, especially so on sale! Also it seems that the developers still work on this game, as shown by this latest update today which added new heroes and items. If you enjoy roguelikes, tower defenses, or strategy games, I would highly recommend this game!

TL:DR;
Possibly most complex zombie survival out there, despite it's granularity I cannot recommend it without few warnings.
First, it has been in Early Acces for like what? 3 years? Development come to nearly a stop. For the other reasons, read on.
Review:
Project Zomboid is complex zombie postapolacyptic survival game. Name 'dwarf fortress' can come to a mind for quite a few reasons.
Reason one - number of small things and items and map size.
Reason two - never ending development and bugs
Gameplay in this game is very uneven and under designed. You start as a survivor in one of the locations on a VERY large map. From there on, you have to cloth yourself, eat, drink, creaft weapons and kill zombies.
Sounds good? After all who woudn't like good old zombie killing and survival combo?
The problems however can break even the greatest enthusiasm.
So let's name them.
Starting new game - there is no real tutorial, except for very basic movement. Worse, sandbox settings are so uneven, that it beggets belief. On weak setting zombie takes 4 hits of crowbar. On normal, 12. How much it takes on strong?
Numbers of zombies on survival setting is so huge, you will constantly bump into groups of 10-20 zombies.
On basic perception settings they will spot you on sight. On basic speed setting they will keep following you everywhere.
There is no story line to follow. Except some gibberish new feed on TV. No notes to be found (there is even a mod that adds them!). No NPCs to save and care for. Absolutelly no point in doing anything no reason for you to keep going. No achievements. Not even a sense of achievement, if you manage to put up a decent base.
But lets back to ur zombies, mkay?
Oh and I see that Random Event just spawned a horde after us?
Now, maybe it's time to fight back?
There are no real weapons to craft. What you find is usually crap, best of weapons being axe, which is also critical to crafting. And items do wear out!
Guns - they miss most of the time, and draw more zombies. Swinging your axe at them will get you swarmed or will eat your stamina and get you swarmed.
There are little traps, bombs, etc.
Worse is that on hardcore setting you can't just shot your gun. You have to load, rack it, aim and shoot.
I believe that complexity is welcome, but there are reasons why in games you do certain things by yourself automaticaly.
So maybe let's build a base to put up a wall between us and zombies.
Suprise - you can't. Once you level up carpentry so that you actually can, you discover that cutting trees exhausts you after 3 trees. And they overburden you. And you have to carry them to the place where you build and drop them on the ground. Only to discover, ground level has capacity limit(whaat?) to a maximum 5 wood logs per tile.
And once you build the wall you suddenly discover zombies will simply swarm it and keep bashing it untill it breaks.
There are no stone walls to build, no steel reinforced barricades, only wooden crap that lasts few minutes against the zombies.
There is not real base building. No real sense of reward after tremendous work it takes to fortify anything.
Mkay, but perhaps we can craft something otherwise usefull?
No, despite having tons of crap. You can't attach a knife to the mop and make a spear.
You can't upgrade your pistol with a stock to make it more accurate, put a flashlight on it to see in the dark etc. Predefined mods are very few.
Top line craftable weapon is spiked baseball.
Something else maybe? Like what? Radio, that doesn't reach anywhere?
To add insult to injury, Inventory management is troubling, at least.
There are very few slots to put anything in, two hands, chest, legs, boots, backpack slot. Nothing else. No careful arming and protecting youself.
FFS damn wound system points to more slots than you can actually equip something to!
Ok, so the basic game is bland and pointless. Maybe mods will help?
Yes, there are certain mods that do improve the game. For example burning corpses in the fire mod. Or different book colours to help you tell them apart. Or perhaps more zombie loot - finally they carry something more than just clothes.
But some mods add things that are completelly pointless.
Biggest one, called Hydrocraft, allows you to establish an entire  industry.
But ask yourself this:
In zombie survival game, wouldn't you like to be able to craft solar panels to heat water and cook food rather than build a mine and cast tin ingots?
Perhaps you would like to make a solid spear instead of bronze halebard?
What about putting leather wraps around your legs and arms, rather than cast steel morning star?
You see. Adding few hundred recipes that are useless unless playing with people in multiplier, which isn't working quite good, doesn't help.
Knowing all the above you have to make a hard decision wheter to support a game from Early Access limbo with your money.
After 55h hours of my gameplay I feel like I have achieved completely nothing. Make sure you will not make the same mistake.
Edit:
Also, keep in mind. Devs were seen arguing with negative reviewers in steam comment section.

What is best in life?
I started playing this game around Early Access v1.2, with diminished expectations. It looked like a typical sprite-based permadeath fantasy roguelike-like, something I'm not the biggest fan of.
Appearances can be deceiving. Having logged many hours since, I find
rather unique. There are roguelike elements, yes, but also a plethora of accessible game design concepts from other genres, some of which have been unjustly abandoned for years, all stuffed into the trappings of a modern indie game.
Remember the simplistic visual charm of early turn-based PC RPGs, such as the SSI Gold Box D&D titles?
has that. How about the grand, synthesized orchestral scores of early Playstation JRPGs? That's here, too. Weaponry with dramatic prefixes and suffixes that denote their crazy powers? A wide variety of procedurally-generated dungeon styles? Humorous tongue-in-cheek dialogue and item descriptions? Skill trees? Potions galore?
is both a parody and an homage to the best aspects of role-playing games over the past two decades, and a sort of fast-paced frustration-free approach to the roguelike model. Yes, each Dungeonmans (or gender-equal Lady Dungeonmans) gets but one life to live, but they leave behind a wide selection of enhancements for the next adventurer in line, some more difficult to retrieve than others. Defeat is quickly forgotten, vengeance is sworn, and progress resumes on the path to crush your enemies.
While all the post-mortem handouts make the game less punishing than the average roguelike, mistakes made in combat still lead to a swift death. However, once a player learns the effect of each skill, and how they interact with statistics and potion-based enhancements, progress is limited only by how aggressively you wish to press your luck. Bigger risks bring bigger rewards, and it feels pretty great to outsmart a party of high-level monsters, see them driven before you, then return triumphantly back to the Dungeonmans Academy with many Proofs of Stremf.
The numerous skill trees lead to many different but equally successful play styles, which keeps things fresh. Speedy players can blast through dungeons as a rampaging “Southern Gentlemans”, while methodical players can become a plodding pillar of death with “Sword & Board”. Understanding the abilities in each tree is essential when taking a Dungeonmans and the Academy to the highest level, and the truly skilled will leave behind only a few grave markers on the path to ultimate success.
The visual presentation is a good fit with the gameplay, with colorful sprites and environments hearkening back to the pixel art of the 1990s. The avatar selection for the player is limited but memorable, with a range of exaggerated, comical designs to choose from. Distinct sound effects make in-game events easy to identify, and Zircon's soundtrack is fantastic, especially for fans of Hitoshi Sakimoto (Final Fantasy Tactics, Vagrant Story).
So what's missing in Early Access, as of the current v1.6c build? Odds and ends, really. Some graphics are absent, or need to be reworked to better fit the style. There are loopholes to farm stat bonuses that haven't been closed. End game content is sparse. The highest tiers of weapons and armor aren't available. However, unlike other alphas, the game is stable and highly playable. You can create characters, kill monsters, hear the lamentations of their gender-neutral life partners, buy stuff, sell stuff, read books, burn books, slam bad guys, slam potions, and I have yet to get tired of any of it.
On top of all that, the creator of the game is extremely accessible. Jim hosts bi-weekly live development streams, where soon-to-be-released content is tweaked before an audience. He checks social media and forums regularly, and I haven't seen a question or suggestion go unanswered. This is about as active and transparent as Early Access gets, and may very well be the best part about
.
If you're looking for a pure unforgiving RNG-heavy dungeon-crawling permadeath fix, look elsewhere. If you fancy genre mash-ups chock-full of swords, sorcery, sandals, monsters, monster blood, traps, digital die rolls, throwback charm, and use of the word "enstremfinize", then I highly recommend
.

You can take as long as you like on your turn, and you had better use that time wisely.  Dungeon of the Endless is made by the folks who created Endless Legend, Endless Space, etc.. so if you've played those it will help with the terminology of the game.  Okay let's get into some high points.
The graphics sport a nice retro look with some amazing lighting and particle effects to give the game a modern coat  in an older time.  Being from the Nintendo/Sega Genesis Era this really resonates well with me.  As for the leve and character design, not only does each character sport their own unique look, they also have their own whimsical personality to boot.  Not to mention the dozens of enemy designs, unique randomly generated level placement, and of course, the ships and artwork itself.  There's real talent in the art team here.
So what does this game entail exactly?  Well, you have a turn or round if you will that you may take as long as you want provided that you don't open any doors.  The gist of it is, a door is a "turn", so opening one will give access to new areas and potentially new dangers.  Your job is to find an exit on each floor, smartly utilzing these turns, your characters, and turret and hero placement to not only find the exit, but to move your ships core to the elevator (exit) as well.  Sound a bit chaotic?  It is, but the game will ween you into it nicely.  As the difficulty goes up, so does the dangers, and the cringeworthy choices.  You WILL make hard choices, and maybe not all your heroes make it?  Yes, permadeath is a main feature in this game and it is glorious.
The last thing I'll mention, is there's a bit of background story here but most of the story is the adventure itself.  Will you make out alive?
10/10 Hands Down     Replay Value:  Very High

Snarky, violent and in-between a Conan slash-em-up and a cartoony strategy, Dungeonmans has the potential to become one of the more remembered and loved roguelikes that have been gushing in the last few years.
You are a recent Dungeonman graduate, ready to face the dangers of the land and bring glory to your name and that of your Academy. To do so, you delve deep into the several dungeons, ruins, temples and other dens of danger waiting for you to make one wrong move.
In the vein of Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, the game is turn-based, with the "You move, I move" style in that sort of game, but that simplicity gives way to the dozens of skills your enemies wield to make your job a bit more difficult: cryomancers summon deadly icenados to stop you dead on your tracks, Giant Carpenter Bees block your way with ramparts, and let us not forget the Dreaded Jabber-Snap... It's up to you and your inventory to sort these motley miscreants out, whether by sword, spell or scroll.
Leading these dangerous mobs are the Champions, souped-up, buffed-up monsters well capable of turning your Dungeonmans into Dungeonmash if you're not careful. Should you succeed in delaying your inevitable demise by killing them off, you are rewarded with Proofs of Stremf and Relics, oh so useful for upgrading your stats and your Academy. You read that right, the Academy: with each successful item return to the Headmaster, you are granted boosts and passive buffs to your Library, Alchemist, Blacksmith and Museum, giving future graduates a  handy leverage against the dangers awaiting them.
Finally, there is the death system: when you die, and you will, your Dungeomans is dead and gone, with only a tombstone to remember him by. But fret not!: you did not die in vain. When exploring your previous place of death, future graduates may find the body and soul of the Dungeonmans, which grants you stat boosts and, were he powerful enough in his previous life, an artifact weapon, infused with the true Dungeonmans power.
As the game is, it might seem short in content at times (the developer admitted to the need for more unique weapons and mobs), but what is there is enough to leave us oogling at and begging for more. I heartily reccomend this game, if not for the sake of its quality, then for the value it brings to this generation of rogue-likes.

This game showed a lot of promise back when I bought it but after coming back to this product now that it has been in EA for 3 years I gotta let others know about the issues I have with this game.
There is no point.
I'm not even going to get into the whole lack of meaningful updates and promises that they've yet to fulfill in detail, I'm not all too savvy about it. The problem I have with this game back when I bought it which hasn't changed at all is that there is no long-term point to anything. You create a character with its pro's and con's from the use of a profession and negative/positive traits and then the game lets you out into the gameworld (which is massive). The game doesn't really inform you well about how things work so you'd do best to look up stuff on google but whatever, you find a neat weapon, a good bag to carry loot in and then set off to find a house to claim for yourself.
After you've found a nice little house that seems appropriate for defense and accessability(?) to the rest of the city so you can gather supplies you start the old crafting formula of building a base. Well, I found an axe by using a online map to find a hardware store and cut down trees and started crafting walls so I could keep my house as safe as possible, cutting off access to a lot of windows and putting sheets up on the doors which had glass windows on them so zombies couldn't see inside.
In the process I've been scavenging nearby buildings for supplies and I have a revolting amount of preservable food and access to a nearby pharmacy that has any healing items I could possibly need. My house is safe. I'm well stocked.
...
Now what?
That's the problem I've faced in other survival games before and Project Zomboid is no different. You've caught the carrot that has been dangling in front of you, pushing you forward and now there is no carrot, so you look around and see nothing of interest. Why keep going? Why not just go home(stop playing the game)?
The problem with PZ in its current state (and considering I haven't seen much changes in its gameplay formula for years I doubt this is going to change, regardless of how much the devs are promising things) is that there is no point to it. There is no end-game. In fact there is no early-end game, middle-late game, middle game or early middle game either.
If the point of PZ is to survive for a very long time then the problem is that there isn't anything to hold your attention for such a long time. I had everything I needed within one day (I played yesterday offline on another computer) and once I had secured my future... Then what? What do I do to pass the time? Explore? And find what exactly? More loot so I can horde even more excess? There aren't any diaries or anything around that gives depth to the games world. There are no NPC's or quests. There aren't much unique stuff to find either. It's just more of the same.
So what else is there to do? Craft more stuff? Sure, you could do that I suppose. But I've learned my lesson from other games and I know that I will just reach that point of "now what?" again  when I run out of stuff to craft. So why bother? I'm not crafting anything unless I need to. I don't find it enjoyable to gather resources and craft things when there is no reward that feels like a saving grace.
You could go around killing zombies. But the problem there is that they respawn. So if your goal is to cleanse the world of undead filth then that's not possible. Besides, it's not really that much fun in the first place. The game was hardly ever difficult and you don't want too much difficulty when out ♥♥♥♥ing around killing deadheads either. Why? Cause the game uses a one-save system and if you die then you stay dead.
So I can't recommend this game.
It showed promise back in the day but at this point it is laughable how little progress has been made on the game and how many excuses they are pulling as to why nothing of substance has been added. The game is a big sandbox of nothing. No matter what you do to try and pass the time it is inevitable that you will reach the point of "now what?" and would you rather feel like you've wasted a couple of hours or that you've wasted dozens of hours on a game with no conclusion?
Maybe the multiplayer is better since you can always♥♥♥♥♥♥around with a comrade, wouldn't know. Don't care to know. The solo experience of the game is severely lacking.
Save your money and wait, if they update the game so that it finally has a damn point to playing it then great! Buy it then. And if it never reaches beyond a "now what?" then hey, at least you won't have to feel like you've wasted money on a product that never amounted to anything.

Dungeonmans is an incredibly satisfying roguelike, in whose current incarnation bosses literally explode into piles of loot. A solid, enjoyable game. It's very similar to Civ 5 and the like, but it has a more complex battle system. It's not overwhelmingly deep, either, but I dare say it's better than what Civilization series usually has. Also, there's magic, which means using cool spells and fighting dragons, and that's always a plus in my book. It also grants a greater variety of enemies and unit options. Randomly generated maps with a plethora of quests and neutral units makes for an interesting gameplay experience with lots of replayability. You can also create your own hero, faction and even customize your units in game (although it feels like cheating vs. AI default units, so I don't really do that). There's multiple victory conditions, you get bonus heroes, collect items and spec your characters upon leveling up, so it's a nice mixture of a turn-based civ-like strategy and an RPG. It does feel a bit unpolished, and there may be some framerate issues (especially on larger maps or late in the game), but it is in general a fairly pleasant experience. 7.5/10

The AI is rough around the edges in single player, but this is a great introduction to wargames and to Ancient Chinese history.
Warring States' art style is unique from the few (if any) wargames like it, and games are usually buttery smooth to play, no matter how many units are being fielded.
The single player campaign is ripped from the history books, and follows the Chinese kingdom of Qin (which is also followed in the "Kingdom" anime) in their unification of China. Each battle, be it campaign, multiplayer, or single player skirmish, starts with each side purchasing regiments of melee troops, archers and cavalry with a limited pool of points.
If you're looking into wargames both here on Steam, or those made of plastic, cardboard, and wood, I say Warring States should be your entry point.

BRAVISSIMO! I had heard good things about Hue, but my GAWD, what a fantastic experience. This is indie game perfection. I cannot find one fault with it. I can name perfect games on one hand (Spelunky and…?), and this one grabs the title.  It is now right up there with The Swapper as one of my two most favourite platform puzzlers of all time.
The balance between head scratchers and skill-based puzzling is just right. The pacing is perfect, titrating out new colours and new mechanics at just the right speed. The voice acting is superb, the music is melancholic and beautiful. The end-game puzzles certainly had me stumped for long minutes – just the right amount of difficulty.
My favourite aspect was the sheer joy of colour swapping. Putting the colour wheel on the right stick, adding a nice whooshing sound as you engage, sprinkling lovely musical chimes as you spin through the colours and slowing down time as you do it, made the mechanic just feel so good. There’s nothing else like it in any other game.
I completed the game but did not go back for all of the collectibles. If I weren’t a father of two with a full-time job, I probably would…
If you like platform puzzlers in any way, make sure you don’t miss this. It’s probably the best one out there.

Not an original concept, but executed with very beautiful design and music...Sadly, I am mainly not recommending this one, because I don't feel the price fits the value for the game.
It is a cute little puzzle platformer where you have to change the color of the background in order to either make parts of the environment visible or invisible.  This concept uses more colors than I think I have seen the mechanism implemented before.
The puzzle design is not bad, but can feel a little repetitive and tedious, rather than a feeling of true accomplishment.  I don't feel like I really have to think, rather I have to do way too many mundane movements of self and blocks to move such a short distances.  I would much rather have level design that makes me think about the task at hand, rather than knowing what I have to do and just taking forever to execute!
I have said this before about other puzzles games..When you introduce new mechanisms, simply show how they work and then give the player interesting ways to apply them.  In this case, the same puzzles only more color only gets more tedious, rather than more challenging.
Not a bad game, but I don't think I can suggest it for the price...It is obvious that it has had a good reception, but it feels more like a $5 puzzler, rather than $15 title.
Too often, developers will create long and drawn out puzzles and levels, thinging they are adding value.  Novel ideas and levels adds value, long simple puzzles add frustration and boredom.  It has good length, but I don't feel like I am gaining anything by playing longer, only trudging through to completion.

"What are you going to play next?"
"Umm. Outlast I guess. It's been in my backlog since summer. Supposed to be scary or something."
And there I went. Oblivious to what I was getting into. Honestly, I had only watched 2 minutes of vids online and a Conan O Brian review. Then came the game; immediately creepy. And it quickly moved on to scary and terrifying. The world seemed a bit Portal 2-ish, but the actual gameplay...was amazing. Pacing, story, real HORROR, and tension like I had not really felt in a horror game. Not that I have played a ton of horror titles, but I would put it on par with early Silent Hill games.
I won't go into the details. Really, it would spoil it for you. Honestly, very basic. You are a reporter checking out the weird stuff happening at the aslyum. And then you walk in into an evil Wonderland complete with menacing large evil killers and a nutso with no pants.
Speaking of that, tweedle-nude and tweedle-nuder didn't get me once. I was kinda proud of that.
You can't fire a gun or use a weapon. The only defense is running, hiding, ducking, and having your heart up in your throat as Chris Walrider walks by you...aw! He found me! AwHHHHHH!! RUNNNN!!!
Of all the games I have played this year, this has to be one of the best made in totality. The length is just right. Cues and progression move at an exact rhythm that does not allow you to slow your scare down. The jumpscares are there, but are by no means the meat of the game. There are no useless time wasting missions. Everything has a reason and the most annoying mission in the game
is perhaps one of the most terrifying when you do not know what will happen next at all. Normal difficulty is not impossible and not once did I get stuck on geometry. A few things are not apparent - that much is true. Granted, if they were, the game would not be hard enough. It's just right. Really. It's absolutely just right. Kudos to the dev team.
At one point I told my buddy I was really wasn't super scared anymore by about the middle of the game. BUT. I could not play for more than an hour or so or my heart would not slow down enough for me to sleep well. Too much tension. Then he said "Isn't that what terrifying means?"
He was right. Even when the horrific graphics no longer phased me, it was the sheer tension of the game that kept me in it's grip. That is amazing, and impressed me more than many AAA titles I've played in the past.

I don't like the idea of Early Access much, and have had my share of disappointment with the games I tried. This one is not one of those. It is a good example of Early Access done right.
The Long Dark is, simply put, a real survival game. There are no zombies, no enemy players, no superhuman powers. This game is about surviving through a cold wild enviromnent, with mundane tasks like feeding and finding shelter becoming huge struggles for survival.
The graphics are stunning, but you will not find photorealism here. The game has a very unique art style, with faded colors and beautiful art direction. It kind of adds to the feeling of melancholy and despair of being alone in the wilds.
Game mechanics are deep enough to keep you satisfied, and living just another day becomes a huge victory for you sometimes.
It does get a little repetitive after a while, but the devs have been adding content all the time, and are really good at communicating with the community.
Overall, this is a recommended game to buy. I know it's not finished, but the final product will surely be damn good.

What a gorgeous little game! I picked it up during a sale a while back and finally got around to sitting down and playing through the whole thing today. As a self-confessed bird nerd who dreams of flight, and as someone who enjoys classical music this game intrigued me when I first saw it and prompted me to snap it up on the cheap.
I played using a controller and whilst I found it a little janky at times (the game would sometimes pick up both thumb sticks and not know which one to 'follow' resulting in some flock/rock collisions!) which could prove a little frustrating, otherwise I found things a smooth experience.
I'll be honest, I got to halfway through and my interest began to wane. I felt things were getting a little 'samey' and I was contemplating playing something else to get a break from it and coming back later until I saw a note that the game could be completed in around an hour, so made myself stick with it. I completed the my current stage and progressed to the penultimate 'level'...wow! Won't spoil it here, but it was the change of pace needed to get me right back into the game.
After which followed the final stage which actually made me gasp aloud a little because I found it so beautiful. I had a tiny bit of trouble right at the very end finding my final spot, but when I'd finished I felt satisfied :)
I'm not sure I'd call it a game so much as an experience of sorts, but it's refreshing to play something that's more about the journey rather than the end goal for a change and a pleasant way to while away an hour. I'm not sure if I'd go back and play it again - maybe sometime in the future - but for a couple of £ or $ whilst it's on sale, it's well worth it!

The game is available for android phones and tablets and it feels like it was designed for touch interfaces first and adapted with minimal effort to the PC.
It's also a very short game (a 45min at my first playthrough) and seems to not have much variation if you play through it a second time.
At full price it looks a little expensive taking all these limitations in account, so I'd recommend this game when in a bundle or at a discount (that was my case), and only for people who are looking for the art and/or the relaxation, because this is what it does very well.

After this new patch I find it very hard to recommend this game to anyone, I do love the artstyle and really appreciate the amount of effort the developers have put into this game, but after this patch it seems like the devs are just making the game harder, it's really hard to appreciate the animation and music when 90% of the game you see is the "YOU DIED" screen.
Maybe this is just a "Git Gud" situation (definitely not, but I know that's what people will say to me), but a lot of the time I didn't feel like I died because of a fault of my own, it was either a huge barrage of attacks that were impossible to avoid, or an attack that was not telegraphed at all.
For a game to be a fair challenge, it has to make it feel like it was your own fault for dying, and I just don't get that feeling with this game. Most of the bosses are too unpredictable and it entirely just comes down to a dice roll, as ironic as that sounds, considering the games story.
The only thing that made this game worth it for me were the run and gun sections. While they are crazy and unpredictable like most of the bosses were, they actually were the only sections that made me feel like it was my fault for dying, and I honestly would've preferred having more of those sections in the game, it was a fair balance of craziness and quick thinking. But there are hardly any of them in the game, and I feel like that's what stops me from actually enjoying myself in this game.
Again, I can really appreciate the animation and music, the amount of work and effort that the devs have put into the game really shows, it's just too hard for me to consider it a fair challenge.

A game that was previewed at E3 2014, Cuphead is a game that is meant to combine 2D side-scrolling shooters with 1930's cartoon style. It is an ambitious undertaking from Studio MHDR Entertainment. There is a very heavy focus on boss fights with a break in the form of side-scrolling levels that have coins to pick up and use to purchase more powerful abilities.
Graphics
A gorgeous, colorful, piece of art. It really was made using techniques from the 1930's cartoons. It uses hand-painted watercolor animations to capture the essence of that era's cartoons. The actions are fluid; more fluid than what you see in a lot of games that are produced by larger companies. There are a huge variety of different enemies; each look unique and act differently. Each of the bosses are also different in look and feel; keeping the numerous boss fights fun and engaging.
Controls/Complexity
Controls are smooth, which is a must for a game as difficult as this one. There are six different weapons, a handful of different power-ups and supers for your character, and everything is very distinctive from each other. That said, it's really easy to pick up; but each level is punishing to the max; challenging your skills as far as you think you can go; and then further. Every boss will destroy you until you learn what each attack looks like. That said, no boss has a set pattern to their attacks, as the boss fights are not set patterns like most games of this type. They are random attacks; so learning what each one looks like to start and how to dodge them is pivotal to beating them.
Expect to die often.
That said, the game does a good job of making you feel like the deaths are your fault, and not due to some arbitrary luck from the computer.
The game feels like it was meant for controller, as it was supposed to be an Xbox only release that was put out on Steam as well. Unfortunately for the PS4 owners, there has been no word on a PS4 release as of the time of this review.
Story
Story is pretty simple. You control Cuphead (Mughead in 2 player games) after he has a really good run of luck at a casino, and makes a bet with the devil. He loses that bet, and begs to keep his soul. The Devil tells him that they can keep their souls as long as they act as debt collectors and retrieve the contracts on souls that other people owe him.
You set out to collect those souls, and hoping to find a way to get out of your debt with him.
Grade-A
A solid A. Almost perfect in every regard. Even the music; which is very reminiscent of the 1930's jazz is beautiful. Studio MHDR has created what might be the best first release from a company that I have ever had the pleasure to play. Everything comes across damn near perfectly.

Before I start this review I just want to say the overreaction to the comparison to Dark Souls & difficulty towards Cuphead isn't fair at all in my opinion, the best way to describe this game is that it's a 1920-1930s cartoon version of Metal Slug, Contra & Mega Man.
The laughs were great though at all the fails this game has delivered from streamers & etc. with no self-awareness for their surroundings at all even if I don't understand how Cuphead can make someone break their keyboard or controller at all (it's really fun to play with a friend & is more of a chill game for me) when the game makes it clear that every death is the player's fault.
The only way I would understand anyone raging at this game is if your playing pacifist on a Run 'N' Gun level or Expert mode.
The tutorial debacle was honestly the cringiest thing I ever watched though & for anyone that hasn't seen it prepare to lose some brain cells.
Now to start with this review the only con I can give the game is the default keyboard controls (they're really bad) & my personal preferred control scheme for this game if I do play on keyboard is:
AWSD - Move Cuphead
Space - Jump
Up Arrow Key - Fire Gun
Left Arrow Key - Dash
Right Arrow Key - Lock
Down Arrow Key - EX Move
E - Change Weapon
The game plays well with a controller too so it doesn't matter what you pick.
If you delve into Expert mode I would recommend the Spread & Charge gun combination.
You might have to change the gun combo up a bit for hard to hit bosses like the Dragon for example which I would recommend the Lobber & Spread but overall I think the Spread & Charge Combo does the job of finishing boss battles as quickly as possible.
For the rest of the review all I can say is that this is the most original game I have ever played.
I'm extremely impressed that the 2 brothers that are responsible for every animation in this game used the actual old methods/techniques that Warner Bros, Fleischer Studios, Disney & etc. used to make Cuphead so unique & I would watch a Cuphead cartoon series if it was possible at all.
I don't have any words on how amazing the Jazz (Maybe Blues too) soundtrack for this game is & the behind the scenes for some of the tracks is extremely impressive.
No DLC at all which is how games used to be so A+ for none of that crap in Cuphead & an extremely fair price for 15+ hours of gameplay.
2 player local co-op for this game was the most fun I ever had in a long time since I barely play any multiplayer games anymore because in my opinion online multiplayer was a nice thing for a while but then it got boring when game studios got less creative & I wouldn't be shocked if Cuphead does get an online co-op feature in the future.
Every boss battle on this game was fun for me to play against (King Dice is my fav boss & the Phantom Express was my least fav on regular mode + I'm still playing through expert mode so I might update this review) & I hope to god the two brothers behind this game don't dumb the game down in anyway because this game to me can motivate anyone to improve their skills in platformers.
The story to the game is pretty straightforward about Cuphead & his brother Mugman owing the Devil money at the Casino so I won't talk much about it.
Overall if you haven't played this game yet I would strongly just buy it full price because it's one of the few games in my opinion that deserves it & Studio MDHR don't let greedy corporations like Microsoft or EA for example buy you out.
P.S. As irrelevant IGN is here's the 2 brothers fighting the bosses
2 vids I found showcasing what old cartoons inspired Cuphead's characters
For Xbox One owners (Not sure about PC) you can expect a physical copy of Cuphead in the future
For something really cool I found a vid of someone playing Cuphead on an old Black & White CRT TV
EDIT: After doing further research I just noticed that the 2 brothers might be Street Fighter enthusiasts if you compare Ryu & Ken with the frogs + Balrog (Bull), Sagat (Tiger) & Vega (Snake) with the slot machine symbols off the final phase of the Clip Joint Calamity level.
The Rat Pack (infamous jazz music group from the 1900s featuring Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin & other famous jazz singers) is a huge influence for the very 1st boss battle in Cuphead
King Dice (my fav boss in Cuphead) is heavily inspired by famous Jazz singer Cab Calloway who was featured in Fleischer cartoons like Betty Boop's Snow White for example (the singer for King Dice's theme song has a resemblance to Louis Armstrong)
One of the animators for Cuphead has revealed that the Baroness Von Bon Bon boss was heavily inspired by starlets from the 1900s
Archive:
Grim Matchstick's name is a reference to Grim Natwick of Betty Boop fame (responsible for drawing/animating her)
The Game Over Screen for the Cigar's face in the King Dice battle is heavily inspired by Lou Bega
One of the Studio MDHR animators explains the creation process of Cala Maria
There's a ton of videogame references in Cuphead but I'm not going to name them all because that would take forever.
EDIT 2: After playing for a while on Expert mode my least fav bosses have been Cala Maria, The Devil & Wally Warbles.
If you value your sanity I would advise doing both Wally Warble & Cala Maria (both of these bosses are pushovers in regular mode) 1st if you're going for the expert mode achievements because they both have terrible patterns to memorize & most of the time the RNG will screw you over.
Sally Stageplay, Captain Brineybeard (I struggled with him on regular mode but I had fun learning his pattern) & King Dice are my fav bosses to go through on Expert mode.
EDIT 3: Studio MDHR's future is looking very good & I'm happy that they're going to continue using the old 1920s-1930s animation style in their future games.
I don't care for any type of award shows but it's still good to see that the gaming industry still values creativity.
EDIT 4: I nominated this game for the “Even Better Than I Expected” Award for Steam's 2017 Autumn sale (probably a bit contradictory since I mentioned in EDIT 3 that I didn't care for award shows at all)

SUMMARY: A humorous, sprawling, fun, .complex, and deep roguelike game with a persistent world , plenty of player customization, and great replayability/continuing play.  Dungeonmans is a must-buy for fans of RPGs, Roguelikes, and fantasy.
I've played this game through from Early Access  (ver 1.5.1 to be precise) to Full Release (ver 1.02), so I can comment both on the game and it's evolution.  The short form is "it's great and a lot of fun and you should buy it," but to really appreciate Dungeonmans, you have to go into the details - because there's so much to it, and all the elements come together to make something truly special.
Dungeonmans is a mix of Roguelike, mild setting building, character improvement, and humor that's quite enjoyable and good-natured, while taking some real planning and tactics.
Start an academy, go forth as a Dungeonmans (the term is gender-neutral) of a given class.  Find loot, bring back artifacts, improve the academy, die horribly, come back as someone else, and venture on.  Much like Rogue Legacy and similar games as you adventure you find things that improve  things for future characters - in this case the academy, your starting character's equipment and knowledge.  Books improve the library, equipment improves the alchemy lab, knowledge improves the museum, leftover equipment lets the blacksmith make new things, and so on.  Sure your character may die, but their legacy lives on (and dies on as you burn through characters).  High-level characters that die can come back as teaching ghosts and characters can retire to teach or do other things.
Character building presents you with plenty of choices.  You can start with a premade class or customize from the start with a general Dungeonmans class.  Pick the skills you want to learn and build, and develop your own playstyle.  My personal favorite is a kind of arcane archer, but maybe you'll favor a heavily armored necromancer, a dual-wileding trickster who creates duplicates, or a warrior armed with magical banners.  There's plenty of fun strategies you can come up with depending on playstyle.
Improving the academy and towns, finding resources, and more enhances the chance of current and future Dungeonmans to live longer, venture further, and perhaps unlock the mystery of the game.  Strategic choices, management, and thoughts of the next student really weigh on your mind.  Take a special weapon knowing it may end up collecting dust with your corpse - or that it may let you survive.  Melt down enough gear to build upgrades or sell it for cash (and knowing a future Dungeonmans can buy it later)?   Options once chosen affect the game later.
There's enchanting of items as well - though unless you spend the resources to do it specifically with Upgrade Hammers (that can break overpowered items), it's random.  Still, with a few scrolls and luck (or blowing a lot of resources recovered from old weapons) you can craft some enjoyably insane stuff.  Want a sword that freezes people in place and sets them on fire?  A suit of armor that resists, well, everything?  Go ahead and make it - or use a Solvent scroll to start over.  You can even find blueprints to make special items if you have the resources.
Adventuring starts out as pretty straightforward adventure-battle-loot.  Over time it evolves as you face more and more powerful enemies, make decisions about using artifacts and crafting items, or figure which towns to upgrade.  The game never becomes too complicated, but it does ramp up in complexity over time.
Finally, there's a lot of depth to the game.  Right when you think the dungeons look alike, you discover something else.  A random boss gives you a chance at improvement. or death  A new monster surprises you.  An item you find is enjoyably bizarre and useful.  Modified towns have new inventory.  Character's that have passed may leave surprising legacies.  Dungeonmans is packed with things to discover.
Best of all, as of this writing, the developers are actively bugfixing and improving the game.  That's the kind of commitment to quality that not only makes it more fun and gives me more confidence, but speaks to the level of commitment to making a good game.  As of this writing I'm on my third playthrough, which should give you an idea of just how fun the game is and how much is in it.
An enjoyable game with a sense of humor that delivers adventure, challenge, and surprises - all with a sense of sheer, good-natured fun. Well worth the purchase.
Also worth playing through twice.  At least.

Having played the Alpha the game has progressed significantly since it started 5 years ago.
Since the game is still early access expect some of the weak points and criticisms to be fixed in later releases.
The pre-alpha was released in 2009 and was very rough but was an original concept for Roguelikes that poked fun of the gentre well before "Dungeons of Dreadmor" was released.
Graphics
- Although the graphics are 2d they have a charm to them and Monsters and Boss monsters can be easily distinguished.
- Each Character class has a Male and Female icon although it would be nice to see more Fightermans Icons and not just the Barbarian archtype.
Characters
- The class name are not Roguelike Standard names which gives the game some style and charm. more classes have been hinted at for later releases.
Plot
- Like other Roguelikes there is not a given Big Quest, it's more explore and discover.
Magic
- Scroll system has humorous names for spells and potions. As usual drinking and reading unidentified scrolls and potions can have negative effects.
- Identified magically enhanced items are blue and identified cursed items are red. All unidentified equippable magically enhanced items are blue so be careful.
This game has both dungeons and towns to explore. You start at the Dungeonmans Academy where you can get basic training and upgrade later as you complete dungeons. The advantage of upgrading the Academy is that new characters star with better equipment and more knowledge.
This is a hard game don't expect your first character to survive the first dungeon, half the fun is trying out different characters and playstyles.
I recommend this  for people who are tired of standard Roguelikjes and like homor in their games.
I've not given class , monster , item or skill names to avoid spoiling the fun.
Although the sound effects are fairly minimal the music is exceptional and very reminiscent of Tangerine Dream's 1980's period.
Expect me to update this review as the game is updated.

Dungeonmans is fun in short bursts. As a graphical rouge-like it has a wide over-world as well as many dungeons to explore.
What sets it apart from other rouge-likes is the persistence of the world. As your heros explore and return with knowledge, this can be passed on to the next hero, or not. It is up to you if you want to have scrolls and potions identifed before setting out.

I supported this game's kickstarter on the basis of a very strong pre-alpha demo, and since then, the game has continued to get better and better.  This is a roguelike, but with an academy that is persistent between characters, that you can upgrade in a variety of ways in order in order to make the game slightly easier for each subsequent character (these improvements are all optional, so if you want to treat this as a more traditional/dangerous roguelike, you can).
The game includes several classes that you can play, but this is misleading, since every character can potentially learn every skill.  The classes serve more as a good starting template for a particular play-style.  You can also select the 'Adventuremans' class and build your own from scratch, if you prefer.  Classes include Warriormans, Wizardmans, Rangermans, Necromans, Southern Gentlemans, and Bannermans (as well as the blank slate which is the Adventuremans).
Even though this is early access, it feels like a fully fleshed out game.  The devs are VERY responsive to problems and active in the Steam forums.  And there are more features coming in at a slow but steady pace (crafting, for example, isn't quite there yet, but it's on the horizon).
Even in its early access state, this is one of the best roguelike games currently available on Steam.

This game showed a lot of promise back when I bought it but after coming back to this product now that it has been in EA for 3 years I gotta let others know about the issues I have with this game.
There is no point.
I'm not even going to get into the whole lack of meaningful updates and promises that they've yet to fulfill in detail, I'm not all too savvy about it. The problem I have with this game back when I bought it which hasn't changed at all is that there is no long-term point to anything. You create a character with its pro's and con's from the use of a profession and negative/positive traits and then the game lets you out into the gameworld (which is massive). The game doesn't really inform you well about how things work so you'd do best to look up stuff on google but whatever, you find a neat weapon, a good bag to carry loot in and then set off to find a house to claim for yourself.
After you've found a nice little house that seems appropriate for defense and accessability(?) to the rest of the city so you can gather supplies you start the old crafting formula of building a base. Well, I found an axe by using a online map to find a hardware store and cut down trees and started crafting walls so I could keep my house as safe as possible, cutting off access to a lot of windows and putting sheets up on the doors which had glass windows on them so zombies couldn't see inside.
In the process I've been scavenging nearby buildings for supplies and I have a revolting amount of preservable food and access to a nearby pharmacy that has any healing items I could possibly need. My house is safe. I'm well stocked.
...
Now what?
That's the problem I've faced in other survival games before and Project Zomboid is no different. You've caught the carrot that has been dangling in front of you, pushing you forward and now there is no carrot, so you look around and see nothing of interest. Why keep going? Why not just go home(stop playing the game)?
The problem with PZ in its current state (and considering I haven't seen much changes in its gameplay formula for years I doubt this is going to change, regardless of how much the devs are promising things) is that there is no point to it. There is no end-game. In fact there is no early-end game, middle-late game, middle game or early middle game either.
If the point of PZ is to survive for a very long time then the problem is that there isn't anything to hold your attention for such a long time. I had everything I needed within one day (I played yesterday offline on another computer) and once I had secured my future... Then what? What do I do to pass the time? Explore? And find what exactly? More loot so I can horde even more excess? There aren't any diaries or anything around that gives depth to the games world. There are no NPC's or quests. There aren't much unique stuff to find either. It's just more of the same.
So what else is there to do? Craft more stuff? Sure, you could do that I suppose. But I've learned my lesson from other games and I know that I will just reach that point of "now what?" again  when I run out of stuff to craft. So why bother? I'm not crafting anything unless I need to. I don't find it enjoyable to gather resources and craft things when there is no reward that feels like a saving grace.
You could go around killing zombies. But the problem there is that they respawn. So if your goal is to cleanse the world of undead filth then that's not possible. Besides, it's not really that much fun in the first place. The game was hardly ever difficult and you don't want too much difficulty when out ♥♥♥♥ing around killing deadheads either. Why? Cause the game uses a one-save system and if you die then you stay dead.
So I can't recommend this game.
It showed promise back in the day but at this point it is laughable how little progress has been made on the game and how many excuses they are pulling as to why nothing of substance has been added. The game is a big sandbox of nothing. No matter what you do to try and pass the time it is inevitable that you will reach the point of "now what?" and would you rather feel like you've wasted a couple of hours or that you've wasted dozens of hours on a game with no conclusion?
Maybe the multiplayer is better since you can always♥♥♥♥♥♥around with a comrade, wouldn't know. Don't care to know. The solo experience of the game is severely lacking.
Save your money and wait, if they update the game so that it finally has a damn point to playing it then great! Buy it then. And if it never reaches beyond a "now what?" then hey, at least you won't have to feel like you've wasted money on a product that never amounted to anything.

Fallen Enchantress Legendary Heroes is one of the most criminally underlooked 4X strategy games out there. It doesn't help that Stardock itself doesn't understand the franchise and radically changed the game's structure with the inferior Sorcerer King games.
What sets FE:LH apart:
- A unique world setting. The gameworld is ruined at game start. All civilization has been destroyed by the Cataclysm and you are tasked with rebuilding. Most of the world is uninhabitable with only select places on the map being suited for colonization and wild enemies roam the map. You'll encounter quests and events from those surviving and those regarding the history of the world and its twisted creatures where even living gods were perverted.
- Many victory conditions including your usual 4X conditions such as conquering, but also an ascension to god-hood and a master quest to redeem the world itself.
- Each faction in the game can be used by different leaders and each faction plays differently allowing for quite a bit of replayability and roleplaying.
- Strong creation tools and modding allowing you to create or change the game significantly. The modding scene has dried up but many mods are still compatible.
Negatives:
- DLC is pretty lackluster with Stardock clearly trying to mine the fans of the game for more money. Among the more damning is The Dead DLC where the AI is completely inept at playing with the new faction's unique mechanics.
- Tactical combat isn't the strongest but functional. It's not anywhere near the complexity of something like Age of Wonders.
- Stardock in general. The game still has issues that they never fixed or modified and it's become clear over time that Stardock has abandoned what made this game good in order to repackage and appeal to new customers with the more limited "streamlined" Sorcerer King games.
While not a perfect game, Fallen Enchantress Legendary Heroes is a great 4X game taking place in a unique world. I highly recommend any serious TBS fans give the game a look.

Bioshock – one of the most critically acclaimed video games from the last decade. Well is it as good as they say? Maybe to you, but I found it to be much like Half-life 2 – overhyped and underwhelming. But make no mistake, they are both landmark games, unique with plenty of fresh ideas and an interesting and entertaining combat system to compliment a distinct world.
The story is eerily similar to Far cry in my opinion. It even shares some characteristic gameplay elements with that game. Bioshock is just tackling other themes and the story unfolds in a more sophisticated and mysterious manner. Unfortunately I didn’t find no character likeable which is pretty abysmal considering the scale of the game. The moral decision the game presents once in a while (harvesting) isn’t really impactful from a currency point of view, but also I failed to sympathize with the victim there. But if you decide to harvest 2 little sisters then the game automatically labels you a heartless, malicious madman who wishes to hurt innocent people, as evidenced by the ending. I wish there were more contrasting stuff between the good and bad. Because the game tries to be a horror game, you rarely see any good in Rapture or anything reminiscent of the pre civil war era. I do like the whole concept of the game though. It is very unique, there’s no denying that.
Audiologs – the way the story unfolds (pretty much). I have a serious issue with them. First of all, they are pretty hard to understand meaning they are pretty much all in a thick accent and using plenty of slang. This isn’t a problem to a native speaker, but I failed to understand a substantial part of the story because of it. I’ll be honest, I still don’t quite understand how Rapture ended up in the state it is now. I don’t know if splicers are even human any more, I don’t know wtf a splicer is. Secondly, the placement of some of these audiologs are dumb. For example, you go into a room, find an audiolog in the corner, you pick it up, press play, turn around and... jumpscare. Now you’re in the middle of a fight with an audiolog playing in the background, not paying attention to neither of them. All you can think then is – this is a really bad design choice. On some occasions, the background noise is so overwhelming that you can’t hear them at all (escape sequences and stuff).
The world is jam-packed with sounds. You can stand still and just be overwhelmed with all types of background noise. You’ll hear a vending machine go off, you’ll hear a splicer who is on another floor in a closed room shouting about tenderloin, you’ll hear the groaning of a big daddy, you’ll hear a security bot flying about and bumping into stuff, you’ll hear an advertisement coming through the loudspeaker, you’ll hear your character fiddling around with the current weapon. It’s pretty annoying. There is a lack of ambient music. When it is used, it is used to great effect, but most of the background music is just filler.
Now the map. It gave me literal headaches. The remastered version eliminated that but something about that engine, that lighting and those textures really hurt my brain. And I think visually the remastered version is so much better. The old game looks like a bouncy castle. Most of your environments look exactly the same from afar (disregarding the obvious landmarks). I found it very disorienting the first time and I was still getting lost the second time when I played it. Even if you understood your current objective, good luck finding your way around the map. It is also very linear, you can’t really play around with how to approach an enemy but fortunately the abundance of weaponry and plasmids make it a different experience every time. Surprisingly, there is plenty of room for exploration as you can find valuable hypos and ammo in discreet, hidden places throughout the game.
The gameplay was good. Setting out traps and sniping people with the crossbow is really fun. Even if I ended up using only 3 weapons and plasmids, I do appreciate the abundance of options. Same with the tonics. What I didn’t like was switching between plasmid and weapon. Too many times I would accidentally choose smth that I didn’t want and lost 2 or 3 full health bars because of it or died. Speaking of dying, I think it should have imposed a bigger penalty, because as long as you have money or ammo, you essentially lost nothing. Towards the end of the game, you’ll find so many things on the floor that there is no reason to save your ammo or eve or health or hack anything because in a 100m you’ll have enough money and ammo to do it all over again. And the final boss battle is broken. He gets caught on the railing and you just shoot him until he retreats. If you decide to do it properly though, then it is fairly easy as well. But the combat situations in medical pavilion were very random and I found that part of the game to be particularly underwhelming. And the hacking mini-game feels out of place and occurring way too often so most of the time I didn’t even bother to do it or used the auto hack device instead.
The game starts off slow and weird, but it evolves into something pretty entertaining in some form or another. I did not find it to be likeable, but it’s definitely a classic and I encourage everyone interested in video games to at least try it.

Dungeon of the Endless is a hard game to summarize. To call it "part roguelike, part tower defense" hardly does this game the justice it deserves. After crash-landing into the heart of an improbably deep labyrinth, your two surviving heroes must find the elevator up and deliver the shuttle's power core to it in order to advance to the next floor.
In classic roguelike fashion, you explore one room at a time, triggering events. The catch? There's only so much power to go around, and monsters will spawn from the rooms you've opened but can't keep powered. If they deal too much damage to your power core, then that's all she wrote.
And that's part of where the tower defense elements come in. In addition to moving your heroes around, you can build a variety of modules which create resources, damage monsters, provide various buffs to your heroes, and likewise debuffs to the monsters. The different types of monsters have different strengths and weaknesses, and many are more than willing to attack the modules you've built, with varying priorities.
The further you go, the more challenging the game becomes. Careful resource management and building decisions can give you an edge, but this game is well-balanced and will provide a challenge to the very end. The basic concept is good, the art is pleasant and the music excellent. The player's view is a little narrow, however, and the game quickly exhausts its repertoire of things going on, to the point where some of its additional plot features end up feeling a little contrived. Moreover, the overall story is short and fairly predictable.
Some people have found it relaxing and replayable. I disagree. I suppose if you easily get stressed, perhaps this will ease your lot, but if you're already laid back, this game will probably make no difference. More importantly, I think this game's replayability is very limited: there are only so many places to go and you can't really get far off the path it's encouraging you to follow, nor can you vary what you do much.
So do I recommend this game? No, not at full price, even though it's already fairly cheap. If it were discounted by 50%, however, maybe I would. And then I would say, "Play it once through - maybe twice - but don't expect too much."

This is my favorite new rogue-like game. This is a serious rogue-like. The gameplay is nearly identical to T.O.M.E. when it comes to combat. It is very hardcore. Many of your would-be heroes will die during their first quest.
Several things set it apart from TOME etc... The sense of humor, which is rather wry and very genre-self-aware. The addition of the Dungeonmans Academy, which is improved by the exploits of your individual chracters, and which in turn improves the lot of your new starting characters and the skill system which allows your character to train any set of class skills, regardless of whatever class you start off with.
You start by naming your academy, followed by a brief introduction by the headmaster of the academy. Then you name a hero and pick a starting stat set out of several options, followed by a class and two perks. Maybe your would-be hero's stats aren't up to par - you can dismiss him from the academy and pick another candidate.
Then you go out into the world map, like in TOME, looking for monsters (random encounters) and dungeons. During your questing you will find loot - equipment which you can use or melt down for scrap, which you can then use to upgrade your forge, books that teach you skills, or that you can bring back to the academy, rare artifacts that improve the academy, and proof of victory over powerful foes, which you can trade to the trainer for stat increases. Everything you bring back to the academy improves the academy and contributes to the future success of new recruits.
Since this is early access, they are still working on balancing issues, and sometimes bugs pop up (I've encountered them mostly while using skill books), but the game plays very well and is very fun.
