I bought this game back when it was on Desura for like $5. It was really fun, then. It's improved so, so much since. It's the only zombie survival game that comes to mind when I think 'has a chance of actually seeing a full release,' and that is due greatly in part of the very transparent development scheme that they have, with weekly updates on what they're doing with the game on
. But, I digress. Onto the actual review!
Firstly, the customization. At the moment, character customization is (visually) unimpressive. You can change your beard if you're a male and your hairstyle as either gender, along with the colors of your starting clothes (which you'll probably rip up into sheets to wrap that bite you got from a crawler in the bush, anyways.) The trait system, however, allows you to put together a diverse character who's got a completely different starting skillset from any other. You can start as a construction worker who is handy with tools, thus making you good at fortifying, but is hemophobic and hard of hearing, making you panic while performing first aid and decreasing the volume and distance you can hear noises from. All in all, I think it provides plenty of diversity to make every character that little bit different, so you don't feel like you're playing the same person with a different coat of paint (though the only occupation in the build as of this review, Build 34, that actually changes anything is the Electrician, who starts with the ability to run a generator. Every other occupation has to learn how to use one.)
Past character customization, you can also change just about everything about your zombies. Do you want them to be slow, feet-dragging shamblers that struggle to keep up with you, yet are superhumanly strong and extraordinarily tough to kill? Do you want 28 Days Later or Left 4 Dead style sprinters that are no more able to survive an axe then a human, and yet are fast enough to catch you unawares? Do you want to have The Walking Dead lore, where everyone is infected and no matter how you die, you come back to life unless your head is pulped? Or do you want classic Romero, where a bite is what's needed to infect and you''ll die within a few days after one unless you're extraordinarily lucky? Up to you.
Secondly, the early to mid game. At the moment, this is the most fleshed out part of the game. NPC's are planned to flesh out the late game, but they aren't implemented yet. (don't hold your breath, I have been since they removed the bare-bones NPC system 5 years ago.) Generally speaking, you start inside a house that is unfortified, with the water running and the electricity on. There are multiple weapons available, techincally, but there are only two you really want to look for. The baseball bat and the axe. Baseball bat because it can be made into the nail bat, which is pretty good at making zombie heads go squish, or just used plain if durability is an issue, and the axe, because it's good at killing zombies and chopping down trees. Of course, you could go the knife route, but that's best used for taking out single zombies and can only hit one. Knifes can instant kill, though. Past those, there are numerous small things you can try to bring to bear in fighting the undead, such as pens, forks, spoons, and sledgehammers, but all of these have their issues. Pens, forks and spoons breaking in one attack and swinging a sledgehammer being exhausting. In addition, this is probably the time where you'll be seeking out food. The game handles food... realistically. That is to say, you generally aren't going to want to stockpile what you find in the fridge, due to it likely being perishable. However, as long as you have the power running, you can store these in a refridgerator. It gives you good reason to go out and scavenge houses for whatever food you can, and bring up a stockpile, thus forcing you into danger and keeping you from holing up and waiting for it to all blow over.
Events can happen at any time. Currently, they're tied to an AI director, but in the future they'll be part of the NPC metagame. (Again, don't hold your breath.) If you hole up in one place and make a few very noticeable additions, like big old wooden walls, for instance, it's possible that a news helicopter observing the restricted zone will do a few flyovers to get some footage on how not everyone is dead. Of course, in a small town populated by exactly one living human being, there is very, very little louder then a helicopter, and zombies are attracted to noise. Other things can happen, mostly to add ambience, and some to create stimuli for the zombies and ensure they aren't simply immobile. Gunshots in the distance, a man or woman screaming, a dog barking. Some events are caused by player interaction. Breaking into a house can, for instance, trigger their alarm, which brings every zombie for miles.
Finally, lategame. At the moment, as I've said, lategame is fairly uninteresting. Farming and rain barrels provide a replenishable source of food and water, respectively, enabling you to, if properly set up, survive out in the middle of the woods for basically an indefinate amount of time. However, as I'm sure you could assume, this can get boring. Very, very, VERY boring. Zombies don't really wander too far out from the towns unless you set zombie distribution to uniform. You'll be out there, playing Stardew Valley: Zombie Edition for as long as you want before chugging a gallon of bleach or loading up a shotgun and running in to die in a blaze of glory.
All in all, I think that for a price of $15, Project Zomboid is worth what they're charging now. In addition, the game has incredible potential, but you should never purchase a game off of potential alone. Right now, for the price it's at, I'd say that it's worth the money, if you like zombie survival games.

This used to be my favorite 4x of all time, despite all the issues it has.
Pros:
-It is extremely customizable, down to the units, faction, sovereign (unkillable faction-leading hero) and, if you find and use the right mods, town layout and optional buildings and even gameplay systems if that's your thing.
-The early to mid game opponents put up a good challenge, especially early game.
-The spell and mana system is broken, but in a fun way.
-It's interesting to see what herores you have access to when the opportunity arises.
-Early to mid game expansion is as exciting as most 4x's, finding resources and potential good settling sites, and dangerous when you come across enemy dens you can't deal with yet, but will have to soon.
-The tech trees clearly, with the exception of magic, give you an idea of the types of buildings or equipment they'll unlock, making it easy to plan in advance for your next moves.
-Leveling up cities to choose between bonuses either to those cities or your faction as a whole is a fantastic idea that I'd say is underused, but fantasy 4x's in general just don't exist in great variety.
-If you have any knowledge about editing XML files, you can correct a great deal of issues you have with the game by modifying them that way.
-Buying items for your heroes that are available to make for your troops is a nice addition.
-Swarm, a combat bonus for attacking with friendly units next to the target in melee range, is an incentive to play a little more tactically, and sometimes worry a little more against high troop count units.
Cons
-The game is just ugly. They tried with particle effects but there's no hiding this is an early Unity game, and they chose the wrong engine to make it.
-Speaking of the engine, the game runs horribly. I play far better-looking games that run much better and load several times faster, and they have never corrected the performance issues. Do yourself a favor and play on low settings, removing all the non-essential gussiness for your tastes.
-The loot system's awful. There are plenty of worthless items, and I don't much enjoy taking out that camp of Strong enemies to find a ruined chain shirt there. Thanks RNG.
-Speaking of RNG, most things in the game are based around some amount of it. The variation of everything in combat you can do, or prevent, is dependent on RNG to an extent. The world generation, obviously, while dependent on RNG, isn't very good without mods, and even once you get that working to your taste sometimes you'll find yourself in a position where you'll be at war constantly for expansion. And then there's the loot system RNG. You won't be pleased early-game to fight off a strong monster den only to find a ruined shirt of some kind, or a piece of equipment you can already buy in your cities, or a crummy potion, or yet another -initiative maul for heroes.
-The loot variation would be nice if it wasn't fairly obvious by the time you become familiar with the game that there is one stat which is best above all - INITIATIVE. Any equipment or spells which boost initiative give you more turns and more chances to beat the enemy down in combat, usually before they have the chance to move. And after that comes whatever else you want to focus on; Mages will stay behind and cast spells, Assassins and Warriors will Maul the enemy up front (get the Maul skill on any melee heroes asap).
-Ranged heroes and units are awful by the time they could be useful. Since combat map generation is somewhat randomized, the distance between units can never be counted on. Even though ranged units can attack any enemy unit on the map, EVERY RANGED WEAPON HAS A HEAVY INITIATIVE PENALTY. This means that the enemy will always catch up to your ranged units within a few turns or, if not, that ranged unit's spot in the army could have been better used by a faster, more damaging, more armored melee unit. So basically the game boils down to stacks of melee units against eachother, where whoever has the better gear (and sometimes better positioning) will win.
-The late game. No matter what happens, either you or an enemy will be overpowered and unstoppable in late game, on respectable difficulties. This is a problem in nearly every 4x, but this one in particular has it BAD. Micro-management late-game is also an issue.
-Not to harp too much on the RNG, but sometimes the game will spawn very powerful, dangerous monsters in the game and if they attack one of your cities, you can usually count on losing that city. I'd be fine with this if there were some kind of obvious timer to give you time either before it spawns or starts rampaging, but there is no such thing.
-The AI is bad. Diplomacy, strategic map, combat too though it did get better over time.
-Cheating. The AI cheats HEAVILY, especially early game. I once watched another faction's city start building three seperate upgrades in a row, with the progress bar stating 13 turns left on the first, 14 on the second, and 20 on the third, but they were all built in three turns. This is a sign that the AI is rudimentary to the point of mental retardation on the faction-managing scale, and the only way to make this challenging to a player is by giving you nothing but robust mongoloid opponents.
-Speaking of cheating, the Betrayers trait Broken Loyalties spell, when under the AI's control, lets them by turn 100 use it every turn. This spell costs 1000 gold to cast. This means by turn 100 this faction is making 1000 gold per turn, when you as a player probably won't even be scratching 50, and effectively not just reducing the production of that one city they keep retaking to 0 but allowing them to destroy/sell my buildings when they take control of it. This is THE MOST BROKEN THING IN THE GAME. You'd be doing yourself a disservice not to mod this yourself to either remove it, or make its cost a little more appropriate to how powerful it is. (I modded it to make it cost the same as other city-destroying spells mana-wise, once I play against the faction again I'll see if it's still broken.)
-Stamina from this year's update is a mistake. I understand why it was implemented, but I don't understand why now, and why so shoddily. The skills it nerfs or makes are underused or never used. For instance, my first turn moves usually involved taking my mounted spearmen to the enemies' front line and using impale, a spear ability that lets you hit two units at once in a line, usually doing less damage than a regular attack but letting me whittle down more of the army at once instead of one unit at a time. Now those units need to generate stamina on the first turn... So instead I just charge ahead and stupidly swarm the enemy, both with units and the Swarm mechanic. Stamina makes me want to use abilities LESS, especially since they added perks in the hero skill tree that you have to devote to gaining it or using it, when I'd rather grab a better passive bonus instead.
I could go on here, but any more cons or pluses would be fairly minor to most players.
Despite all these issues this is still my 3rd favorite 4x of all time. If the last patch to the game had never been applied, and wrecked at least two things, Broken Loyalties (presumably fixable) and Stamina requirement (not fixable), it would probably bump up a slot on that list, maybe reclaim #1 for me.
There's a lot of complexity and choice in this game, and all the information you want, both of which are missing from a lot of other modern 4x games, and these are its biggest strengths. If you can overlook the many, many, many, many blemishes it has (or learn to fix them yourself or find some mods online that do) then you will find something very special here.

There is a lot to like about the game, but also quite a few areas where it falls short.  I am not sure if I really want to recommend it, but I don't want to give it thumbs-down either, so it's a reserved recommendation.
I bought Fallen Enchantress looking for an updated version of the classic Master of Magic.  In many respects, that is what this game is.  It has pretty much the same gameplay, with added complexity, detail, and flavor.  You have a wide variety of options to build the perfect city or the perfect unit.
Where the game falls short- way short- is in the opponents' AI on the strategic level.  The AI faction opponents are as dumb as a box of rocks.  Units seem to meander with no real purpose.  Sovereigns declare war on you without ability to wage it.  AI factions beat up on each other pretty well, but can't figure out how to come at you.  They do not seem to pursue any particular victory condition.  They expand well early, but inexplicably stop.  They do not seem to be able to take advantage of the higher end of the technology tree when building units.
Of course, no game of this type has an AI that is remotely as smart as a human player who understands the game.  But in the classic games like Master of Magic and Master of Orion and Civilization III, AI opponents were not outsmarting human players, but AI opponents did act with rationality and/or purpose.  The AI faction opponents in Fallen Enchantress seem to act with neither rationality or purpose.
The deficiency in the AI is magnified by all the complexity and options of the game elements.  The human player has a wide array of options and killer combinations that the AI factions simply cannot use.
This game perhaps has much more potential as a multiplayer game rather than single-player.  Unfortunately, it is single-player only.
I have nevertheless played the game quite a bit, looking for different ways to add challenge.  It is possible to make the early part of the game more challenging.  But there is always a breakpoint- after getting a  few level 3+ cities, a couple of higher-end spells, and advancing to the latter half of the technology trees- where my AI opponents just start stagnating while I take off.  (Honestly though, if the graphics of Master of Magic did not hurt my eyes, I'd probably be replaying Master of Magic instead.)

Warring States is basically turnbased tactical combat on a hex map, among forces of ancient China. Basically units can move, attack, special attack, or regenerate, depending on special points gathered, and the idea is for you to defeat all enemy units with just the units that you have (try not to lose too many). There are flanking bonuses as well as bonuses for having your flanks covered. There are terrain bonuses for attacking downhill. There are broken units (units that suffered too many casualties)
In a way, this is a little reminiscent of Civ5's combat, but with far fewer variety. The special ability points can also be spent on a special attack, which does extra damage.
The story are of significance only to people who know Chinese history, and we're talking about the Romance of Three Kingdoms and thereabouts. And they are not important.
The emphasis is on tactics, i.e. how to move optimally to force the enemy to engage on your terms, that you can surround it and flank it, pound it from afar with archers, and so on, while preventing the enemy to do the same to you.
The scenarios can be challenging, and the main emphasis is multiplayer, which can be brutal. the SP are more of a tutorial.
All in all, it's not a terribly good game, but it's fresh take on an area that's not widely explored out of China. Worth a try at least.

For now I would recommend to simply follow the game. In my opinion they have a good basis, but there's not enough content to keep you interested for more than 2 or 3 hours.
What we have at the moment is a pretty easy game with few tactical elements, you choose your units at the start of a mission, you move them on hexagons and try to get rid of the enemy, and this is pretty much it. The missions are independent one of the other and they all offer the same things to do, no RPG elements, no persistent units, and the placement is not really important vs the AI, or is, most of the time, pretty obvious, warriors first line, archers back line. You have to manage a 'tactical' gauge (do good actions) in order to use the special power of your units, but you'll probably only use the self heal most of the time. This reminds me a little the combats in AoW 3, but simplified and easier. The game is visually good and there's a nice background. The choices they'll take in the next weeks will be determinant for the future of the game.
At the moment, the game is boring after a few hours because it's too easy and not really engaging, even repetitive, but they really have something with the potential to become a good game. They also release regular updates. And for these reasons, the game deserves to be followed if you are into tactical games.

I am absolutely loving this game at the moment. As others have mentioned, it's very much a modern take on a classic roguelike game with all the key elements: permadeath, classes, turn based, etc. All of the things that are in traditional roguelikes are in here.
But what really seperates this game apart is the academy you build up over time. When you find relics and historical artificacts, you can turn them into the academy and it will get bigger and better and thus make your new adventurers better as well. Your first few people may die in the earlier dungeons, but as you get better and your character benefits more from the academy upgrades, you'll be able to make it farther and farther into the game.
The class system is very basic at the moment, but still feels fun to me. Fighters run up and smash things, rangers use bows and shoot them, wizards blow things up with magic. Solid for the moment, but I hope the dev does more later on to expand on them (it's early access, so it's understandable to be basic still). When Cuphead was originally shown at E3 I was blown away by its presentation. However, leading up to the release, I was concerned the game wouldn't live up to the expectations, either due to length or mediocre gameplay. I can now say with certainty and incredible joy that Cuphead not only delivers on what it sets out to accomplish, but also manages to place itself among the best games of the year and perhaps of all time.
The charming, cartoon story of Cuphead fits well and delivers the motivation you need. However, it's the art style where this game really shines. Cuphead's 30's cartoon style is pulled off flawlessly. The animation is as smooth as butter, the personality expressed in the enemies is phenomenal, and the color palette is perfect. This game blows every other release out of the water this year graphically, thanks to a gorgeous visual style that manages to perfectly replicate its inspiration and produce a timeless look. If there is but one complaint I could note, it's that I wish for slightly more visual feed back when shooting enemies. There is barely any and since there is no health meter the only way to know is by watching the phase change and looking at how far you made it when you die.
Cuphead not only succeeds graphically, it's also a musical tour de force. It boasts a stellar jazz-filled soundtrack that is catchy, fitting, and not at all grating which is impressive when you have to retry about 20 to 40 times per level. The sound effects are also snappy and satisfying, however, Cuphead's weapons could use a bit more punch to their sounds. They sound a little too weak.
As for gameplay, Cuphead somehow is basically perfect. Every level is methodically plotted out with clear visual cues for obstacles and traps and a good pacing to levels. I could go on for a long time about how each boss fight is brilliant but needless to say, they're all unique, fun, challenging, just long enough, and built with a perfect flow for retrying after dying. The weapons and charms are hit and miss. Some are fantastic and really helpful, some are basically useless. Most have at least one situation where they're beneficial but some like the lobber and whetstone are really not that good. All in all though, the gameplay is 10 cuts above the usual serving from indie and AAA devs. Finally, the brutal difficulty allows this game to take up around 12 or 13 hours which means it's not that short despite the levels not taking very long in one go.
Aside from a few little flaws I notice, this game is fantastic. One of the best indie games I've seen and one of the best games I've ever played. A meticulous passion project that proves the industry has been aching for something fresh. The price is fine in my eyes for the amount and quality of content you get. These devs gambled with their lives to make sure Cuphead succeeded and I highly recommend you buy this game to show you appreciate their effort and talent. I look forward to whatever Studio MDHR decides to tackle next because they have some serious skill in terms of artwork and game design.

Dungeon of the endless is a mix of quite a few genres, including rogue-like and tower defense. You start the game crashing into a planet after your ship was shot down by a nearby planets defenses. You will have the choice of 4 characters in the beginning, but you can unlock many other unique characters by finding them, buying them, and playing 3 floors with them or beating the game. Once you have picked your characters you will spawn in your crashed escape pod (which you can unlock more by doing certain things) and you will open the door into the dungeon, and likely into certain death. Whenever you open a door it has a chance to spawn monsters in that room, or in any other room that is unlit. You can light rooms by using the dust you get from killing monsters and opening rooms, hitting your middle-mouse button on the room you want, will light or unlight it depending on which it was before. Dust is probably one of the most important resources, among industry, science, food, and weapons and armor and tools that you equip on your characters. You will use your industry to build defenses, your science to improve the things that you can place and build with industry, and food will allow you to upgrade your characters, heal them, and pay for characters in the dungeon to join your quest to escape this hell hole of a dungeon. This game is also multi-player allowing you to get a group of your friends and conquer the dungeon as a group. Whether playing with friends or alone this game has many different escape pods (which change up settings in the game making it easier and harder), characters (up to around 20 I believe with the DLC's), and with the levels always different and the items being random, you can either get screwed or be the luckiest man on earth. But what makes this game good is that even if you get screwed in the beginning with good setup of your defenses and wise use of you characters and abilities, you can pull through and win.
I would recommend this game to anyone who likes a mix of luck, tower defense and the planning aspect of that, and the constant fear of the perma death from rogue-likes.

After many years, I think maybe this is finally the roguelike for me. Manages to both appeal to my strategic turn-based urges (with its door-opening advancement mechanic) *and* scratch that real-time fighting itch (as everything busts loose after opening the next door). Manages to have just enough resource-and-defense management to be fun as a tower-defense type game but also has just enough character-advancement-and-development to feel like something of an RPG. After about a dozen failed games (including a couple of almost-victories) I got out with a thorough enough victory to unlock almost all of the other pods simultaneously, and now it's just freewheeling terror-fun - sometimes playing slowly and cautiously, building out level by level with brutally effective strategic defenses, other times playing fast and furious by focusing on jamming up the heroes' power levels and just winging the fights as they come. And sometimes it works perfectly while other times... well, let's just say that when things go wrong, they go completely wrong very fast.
Also, I have never once used the pause key deliberately, only ever bumped it by accident. You should adopt the same policy.

One of the best "4x" games I have played. Takes the best of empire building and macro management from the 4x genre and melds it with levelling, talents, spells, skill trees etc that you would see in an RPG game like Dragon Age.
The battle system is hands down the best one that I have come across in a 4X game. Once you engage an enemy, you move your units around on a grid and use skills and spells - turn based like Heroes of Might and Magic.
There are so many spells and skills, and various roles your champions can take on.
Many spells can be used on the map itself, to enchant cities, change the landscape, summon armies, and my personal favourite - dropping a 1200 mana cost volcano in the middle of the enemy capital city.
The maps are beautiful and draw you into the world, there are so many different monsters (barbarians) to slaughter, camps and dungeons to loot, countless quests to undertake, all the while keeping your enemies in check and managing your kingdom/empire.
Units can be customised with the unit editor, they have included all the developer tools - so the the limit is your imagination. If you ever find yourself getting a bit bored (hasn't happened yet for me!) there are many mods to download and try!
It may have had a rough start, but it is very stable now and I have not encountered any major crashes / bugs as of yet.
Highly recommended!

Gathering Sky is a shorter casual game which substitutes the typical gaming tropes out to create an experience that is much more emotional and story driven.  Despite the lack of any dialogue or voice over, the aesthetics and music alone were able to convey the story and mood to me. About halfway through the game I found myself growing attached to the small flock I had gathered.
Coming in expecting a relatively bare bones game, I was pleasantly surprised to find a relatively large array of gameplay mechanics for such a small game.  The new mechanics, when introduced, never needed tutorials or explanation.  Their purposes were made obvious through the story and aesthetics.
I would recommend this game to any fans of Indie games in general, as well as any fans of casual or narrative-based games.

I have invested more hours into this game than any other in my library, and I am far from done. Like Civilization, X-COM, and other greats this one keeps pulling me back in. And it’s not even finished yet.
Replayability is a big thing for me, and PZ has it. Difficulty and settings are highly customizable to get as easy or hard an experience you could wish. The map is HUGE; I haven’t even begun to explore all of the civilized parts let alone the wilderness, and there is more planned. The solo game is fun and intense, and while the MP needs a little more polish, some of the most fun I’ve ever had with any game took place on an RP PZ server. The developers listen to concerns and attempt to address them, and the modding community seems very solid.
Much of the negative feedback I have read about this game center on the long time people have waited for specific updates, like NPCS and vehicles. I personally am not concerned about this. The developers have made it clear they will not rush; they want their baby to be done properly. NPCs were actually IN the game at one point, and they were implemented so lacklusterly that they were pulled until they could be done right. Good things come to those that wait.
Even so, if the developers abandoned PZ tomorrow, the game is well worth the 15$ even in its current state.

Cuphead is a Run-and-Gun game developed by Studio MDHR as their debut project. Borrowingly heavily from the narrative tropes and art style of the western cartoons of the 30s (with the works of Max and Dave Fleischer being a major inspiration), the videogames is about the adventures of Cuphead and Mugman, two young brothers with a liking to gamble. After loosing a bet with the Devil himself, the two boys are tasked by the demons to collect the soul contracts of the Devil's other runawayd debtors by any means necessary, with their own souls on the line.
Cuphead's gameplay is clearly inspired by the Run-and-Gun games from the 80s/90s (think of Contra, among others). You can either play solo or with a second local player in co-op and you move from isle to isle to clear the various levels or bosses and unlock greater and greater challenges. Cuphead's signature gameplay mechanic is the parry: by jumping and pressing the jump button again as you are about to land on a pink object or enemy you can "parry" it, destroying it and filling up your super meter. As the game progresses, being able to parry at the right time and several times in a row becomes increasingly important.
Cuphead features two kinds of levels:
1) Boss-only levels, which are arguably Cuphead's main attraction. Each boss features a sequential battle where the more you damange your enemy the more attacks and gimmicks you'll have to face and learn to counter as the boss will change patterns and stages till it'll be defeated. This game's bosses have a lot of tricks up their sleeve and aren't even shy about summoning help or even full-fledged mini-bosses.
2) "Run n' gun" levels, where, as the name would imply, you must run from the beginning to the end of the stage while dodging or defeating the enemies barring your way, defeat the occasional mini-boss or think of ways to bypass your obstacles.
At the end of each level you'll recive a score based on several indicators, which also varies depending on the difficulty you are playing the game on: Simple (easy), Regular (normal), Expert (hard). Simple can be considered a trial mode of sort and will halt your progress in the game sooner or later. Expert changes the bosses' patterns and attacks significantly and provides a huge jump in difficulty for people in search of a better challenge.
Aside from the proper levels, Cuphead's world map features other objectives you can pursuit and means to make your life easier:
1) The Run n' Gun levels contain coins you can spend at a dedicated shop in the world map. The shop contains new bullet types you can equip to better prepare yourself against the boss you are currently facing and charms giving your character useful passive abilities.
2) Each isle features a mausoleum where you can compete in a parrying challenge to unlock one of the three super moves available to you.
3) The world map is also filled with NPCs you can interact with to have either useful hints or start side quests. While some of these side quests will award you coins, some will unlock more unusual rewards for you to enjoy.
There's no going around it: Cuphead is a very challenging and difficult game where memorization and reflexes are usually the key to overcome your current obstacle. It also doesn't help that the majority of the bosses have some randomness factor to them that may frustrate some people (as to say, every time you face them they'll summon different mini-bosses, dish out different attacks or attempt other combos, with some being far easier to deal with than the others). That said, one of the main charm of Cuphed is that even players unfamiliar with the genre can face and win everything the game will thrown at them with enough dedication and mastering. In that regard, Cuphead is both fair and extremely rewarding.
The art style is the second feature people will talk about regarding Cuphead and is as gorgeous and unique as you'd expect: every sprite was hand drawn, the backgrounds were all painted with watercolors and attacks behave and characters morph wildly before your very eyes (sometimes in extremely unsettling ways) as to emulate watching one of those old cartoons from the last century. In this regard, there's currently no game like Cuphead. The beautiful jazz soundtrack performed by a live orchestra only enhances an already great set mood.
In short, Cuphead is a very unique and gorgeous game, should you have the patience to learn its dangers and resident baddies, and I'd reccomend it to anyone anytime, even people (like myself, mind you) who really didn't grow up with the kind of games Cuphead pays homage to

Mans! Womans! Are you Dungeonmans material?
Bash mans with mighty stremf, blast mans with mightier foom, use the power of science to discover new and powerful methods to crush mans.
Build your academy and pass down your mightiest weapons and armor to future students. Train your trainers to train your new mans to become mightier Dungeonmans before they step foot in a nasty smelly dungeon (or inverted dungeon, we call these towers).
Is Dungeonmans for you?
Do you enjoy bashing other mans and womans?
Do you enjoy a freeform skill system that allows you to
create the custom mans of your dreams?
Do you like the thought of exploring a persistent world and building your own Academy
the towns in the world?
Do you enjoy a dungeon crawling rpg with all the fat trimmed and nothing but lean purple muscle remaining?
Dungeonmans is not yet a fully polished game, there are skill, equipment, economy, monster, and dungeon imbalances. The final purpleonium (really) area isn't quite done yet. The Academy still has more renovating to do.
But that said, Dungeonmans is a fully playable game from start to finish, has charming sprite work,
music, extremely simple controls, great tactical combat, enemy and dungeon variety, some very sharp design concepts, and a
of potential.
For veterans of this genre you will probably knock out the final boss in a few days (and a few dead mans) and be left thirsting for more.
For players new to the idea of permadeath, Dungeonmans is a great introduction to the genre, as the Academy ensures that each new character you create will be just a little bit more powerful, and game mechanics are largely intuitive and easy to grasp (... which is not to say the game itself is easy, you can and will die quite fast if you don't pay attention!).
Dungeonmans is a fun game right now, and it is simply begging for expanded content and more refinement of its already enjoyable mechanics. Dive in now if you like (or think you might like!) this sort of game, otherwise, slap Dungeonmans on your Wishlist and keep an eye on it, it's only going to get better from here.

BioShock will have been out ten years ago tomorrow (August 21, 2007), so i figured it was long overdue to post a quick review of one of my favorite games of all time. With all the versions combined (the Xbox, original PC release, Remastered) i've easily spent over 500 hours playing and taking screenshots of the game, and to this day, it has never lost its special quality that hooked me from the very first time i booted up the demo.
Rapture is a city like no other. Built on the seafloor of the North Atlantic ocean, it was a place to escape the growing threat of nuclear war, as well as government and religious interference, while at the same time championing things like personal freedom, science and industry. Construction began in 1945 and it was officially opened up to its carefully chosen guests on Nov 5, 1946. With its grand Art Deco architecture, glowing neon signs and glass tunnels connecting the towering buildings, it was a spectacle that could take your breath away, time and time again.
BioShock as a whole hits so many right notes and i feel it’s one of gaming’s crowning achievements, especially when it comes to its visuals. Something that’s quickly apparent is that you’ve never played a game that looks quite like this. Its well researched art direction is flawless and coupled with creepy atmosphere and the huge glass windows looking out into the depths, it has a way of mesmerizing you from the second you start playing.
Since this sunken metropolis is crumbling around you, letting the ocean leak in at any structural weak point, Irrational devoted an entire team to just the water effects. And it’s something you can see and feel at every turn, with each flooded room and cascading waterfall reminding you that the ocean is relentlessly beating down on Rapture. The fire and particle effects were cutting edge at the time back in 2007 and still look fantastic to this day. Tons of little touches help to immerse you in this dystopian world, like the eerie patches of thick fog and the always entertaining advertisements plastered around the city. The contrasted lighting fits the game perfectly, bringing tension and uncertainty to every room you explore. Level design is also top notch, with unique and well laid out areas full of visual storytelling. The amazing detail in every level truly helps to drive the narrative just as much as any character. From the the beautifully overgrown Arcadia to the glamorous and extravagant Fort Frolic, Rapture is an unforgettable place to visit.
In addition to the wonderful setting, the rich gameplay, time period music, interesting characters and engaging story, all help to make BioShock a classic. If you haven’t played it yet, it’s definitely worth your time to try it out, especially with the remastered version coming out next month! And even if you have, it’s never a bad time to take one more bathysphere ride under the waves.

Marble Duel is a match 3 puzzle game developed by HeroCraft Krasnodar and published by HeroCraft. This game takes a very interesting spin, no pun intended, on the typical match 3 title. Instead of using gems as most of the other games do, one uses what are referred to as "spheres" or "marbles" to do battle with. At the start of each battle, the spheres roll out onto the battlefield in a string all linked together. The strings can vary on occasion as some may be completely motionless while others are in a constant state of flux. The goal is to match three or more marbles of the same color causing them to explode and build power for your character. Said power can be used to augment a particular ability depending on the color or colors of the spheres that you destroy such as health, defense, offense, etc.. The battle is over when you or your opponents health is reduced to zero. It's a simple enough premise and is actually quite entertaining in small doses. There is also a modest element of strategy involved in the gameplay especially if you want to be successful in your marble dueling.
Graphically, this game is quite impressive. The marble battlefields are brightly colored and smoothly animated. The art used in the game looks excellent and, in my opinion, has a Disney-esque style to it. The sound effects are crisp and the music fits the fairy tale like theme of the game but is not very memorable. However, the overall presentation of the title is professionally done and looks very solid.
For me, Marble Duel is game that you can pick up and play for a couple of rounds before moving on to something else. While it is a fun and different match 3 game, it's just not as great as the Puzzle Quest titles which I could play for hours on end in one sitting. If you're a fan of match 3/puzzle games then I would recommend that you give Marble Duel a shot but if you're a more casual gamer then I would merely suggest that you try it...or not. It might not be your cup of tea is all I'm saying....somewhat recommended.

This 4x (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate) fantasy strategy game does many things right, but also has some bugs/issues.
+ Highly customizable heroes and standart units. From their looks, to their weapons, armor and equipment. You can even change the background of their picture to your liking. This way even the most regular game units can look unique.
+ Nice and interesting selection of units, each with their own traits and skills. From weak wolves to the almighty dragons, every one is made with passion for detail.
+ Intelligent bulding queue. When you had your town producing currency for example and you decide to add an actual unit or building to the queue, the town will properly priorize the later and put it in front of the infinite currency production.
+ Instead of just having you fight enemies for rewards the game uses well-written sidequests. In some of them you even get to make a desicion - which affects the outcome.
- Unlike the sidequests, the main story mode barely has any story worth mentioning. One map, some general directions about where to go next every 20 hours or so and a few lines once you reach the goal. The end.
- Loading times are surprisingly long, compared to most other games. Usually if you load or reload a game after a bad decision, you are back in a couple of seconds. Here it takes up to one minute.
- Loading causes your units to continue on their planned way even if you hadn't hit the move button when you saved. Saving after you have selected to go to an enemy in the distance will have them run all the way to the enemy by themselves when you load, engaging him in a fight. Even if you found out that it was a poor decision. I mean, you can still cancel the fight. But you will have to walk back again, which leaves you exposed to the enemy.
-  The game uses "influence zones" that show the area you and your allies/enemies control. Most of the time, that is. Sometimes it won't show the zones at all.

I know that the later Age of Wonders games included repeatable "missions", but they didn't have much of a story.
Fallen Enchantress equals even some full-fledged roleplaying games in that aspect. Collect spider webs, find lost stuff, save villages, hand-feed out of control monsters to tame them... just to name some of them.

Ok, outline review and then I'll get to my main complaints.
-The tutorial was lacking. For example, it glossed over how yields work in this game and explained with concepts foreign to a first time player(what is essence?). Most of it was in video format which was a waste of time when I could've just read one or two lines to understand.
-Graphics are not my style at all. Black outline around everything. Cartoony (which i dont mind) yet ugly.
-Lots of unit customization which I've recently started enjoying from other games like Endless Legend and AoW3. Except I still usually prefer Civ style units that all fill a niche. If you like customization then you will love it in this game.
-I heard multiplayer crashes alot.
- Mostly combat based game. Diplomacy is lacking, rather than strategicly choosing city locations it's about getting lucky with finding good tile yields.
-Combat is mostly simplistic. Think of heroes of might and magic or a japanese SRPG. Does not account for facing. melee units try to gang up on units, ranged stays away. includes a turn order bar. I prefer AoW3 for this.
-The magic system is (again) comparable to the heroes series or age of wonders.  upkeeps, strategical map spells as well as combat spells.
-You can make OP imba builds. AFAIK, the AI can't.
-As usual the AI cheats at higher levels. Not complaining. How would you make a superhuman chess algorithm with a thousand more variables and with gameplay mechanics that were constantly adjusted through patches? As long as its passable.
- Quests are randomly placed but chosen from a small pregenerated pool. These are a neat fluff to accompany the constant combat but you start seeing the same ones again really quickly. The writing isn't too shabby.
The UI *SUCKS*. The load button is hidden behind 4 keystrokes. There are no screens showing data for all cities at once. want to see unrest? you have to open click them individually and hunt for the stat. Did you just level up or get a new hero? You're not allowed to minimize the selection screen to check what else you have. With auto end turn enabled, the game will execute commands  you queued on other armies even though you need to make an adjustment. Without auto end turn, the game lacks clear notifications. Oh, it has some but its certainly not clear. Where is the hotkeys list? Gotta look that up online. On that topic, this game actually has a convenient quick save button unlike a lot of other 4X games. In game manual lacks a search function but at least its alphabetically ordered.
I want to say that the game isn't too shabby... except it is. It's not for me but I know there are people out there who would enjoy this. Recommended for people who want a customizable, combat based, fantasy themed 4X. Just check out the other games I mentioned in my review first ;-)

Gathering Sky is incredibly relaxing, immersive and cute.
A Gameplay & Review video showcasing features I'm about to mention:
You start the game as a lonesome bird, and slowly add to you flock by passing by them.
Before you know it, you'll have a bunch of birds on screen, and will find that the game pulled you in as you followed drafts of wind at high speeds, accompanied by beautiful music.
Seriously, the music in this game is amazing. The best part is it's designed in a way to match what you are currently doing in the game, be it calmly floating through the sky, being pulled by a fast current, or being chased by a predator.
The game's levels add new music, environments and mechanics. Which keeps the game fresh
The art style is simple, but really nice looking. It goes with the relaxing theme of the game very well.
The fact that you control the entire game using only the mouse (Or analogue stick for controllers) also keeps to the simple nature of the game.
I really loved the game, and if you like the look of it, you probably will enjoy it.
Enjoy!

Buy this game if you want a short sit-down-and-play-to-completion experience full of flow, exploration and charm. Don't buy this game if you've already decided "what's the point?"
You are the unseen guide to a flock of birds on migration. Using your mouse, you set where you want them to fly to - you start with one bird, but you'll quickly find more birds, who keep joining your flock until it's so large that it becomes a challenge to maintain order.
And the point? Either take your time to enjoy exploring the level and finding lost birds, or push on to your destination at the far right of the sky, where entering a thick bank of clouds will guide you seamlessly into the next region.
Gameplay video:
Get over your fears that this is a insubstantial non-game and you'll find this to be  compulsive. It's got a great responsive classical score that uplifts when you're soaring along air currents, and makes you nervous when there's danger around.
And yes, there are dangers. Not "game over" situations, but things that threaten the unity of your flock, such as mountain peaks that split your flock in two, or eagles that chase your birds into a panic - providing the game's main heart-stopping moment.
The game is stripped to the bone to offer full immersion. There's one basic control - the mouse - and there's almost no HUD unless paused. Instead of telling you how to play, it allows you to work it out, using gentle prompts such as a wisp that you'll immediately realise should be followed. All this is why it works as well on mobile and tablet as on desktop. But you'll really want a large screen and some good heaphones to get the best out of Gathering Sky.

The Long Dark is an example to all early access survival games and what they should be. In fact, an example to all survival games. The Long Dark is a unique expirence that no other game currently can match, even while having the same core mechanics as all other games of the genre.
This is the silent apocolypse, not a Mad Max wasteland or a Fallout nuclear future with mutated animals running around. No, the only thing in this game you need to fear is Mother Nature herself. From the wolves that roam in packs, to the fearsome bears that lurk in their small caves, to the cold eternal winter of the wilderness, danger is everywhere. And upon first getting a weapon, most players first instinct is to go crazy with the .308 rifle and fire upon the first living creature they see, this isn't the wisest option as players soon will discover and shows how exactly you'll learn throughout the game: through trial and error.
Yes, there are no hints or even a tutorial, instead, you're dropped randomly somewhere in the region you chose and its up to you to figure out how to survive from there. And while there is a map, it does actually require exploring on your part, making it more effective to learn your way around the world yourself, a system that has proven to be sometimes even better than a map.
Within sandbox mode, a basic story forms, you've crashed your plane down in the middle of no-where-Canada during the snowy apocolypse, and you're job is just to survive for as long as you can before succumbing to the long dark that we all fear.
The game's artstyle is incredible to look at, I personally have some of the game's art as my wallpaper. The mix between a cartoony style and a more gritty style blend perfectly together to make a comfy and menacing enviroment at the same time. The same can be said about the game's soundtrack, its an erie yet calming mix of string instruments that fit the enviroment well, and most of these tracks will play outside so you can listen to beautiful music while looking around at the beautiful enviroment.
The Long Dark truely is a great game, if not the best game ever made, and I highly encourage those reading this to pick this game up.

I got this game because of the "great story", "unique atmosphere" and "intuitive" combat system that was praised by many reviewers, also because it could run on py potato PC. The idea of an underwater "Utopia" that is ruined by corruption and failed attemtps at making life better is a good start, however, I feel that the story doesn't focus on that, but focuses more on simply completing objectives (highlighting combat) instead of focusing on the atmosphere and story. Unfortunately, I had to force myself to finish the game, it was not done with an interest for the actual entertainment expected from a game, it was more of a quest to understand why people thought the game was fun. I found that the environment was quite dull, linear, and generally lacking in the drive that draws you to explore the map. The combat was synchronously linear (it allowed combination of "plasmids" and weapons to create a synergy, but I felt that some synergies were overpowered, which restricted you from trying new types). Voice acting however, was very very well done, emotions were effortlessly conveyed from the game to the player, and this enhanced the story to a certain extent. The story was not interesting except for the last missions (because of a plot twist, which was annoying because a good story has a build up to the climax, this game was very sequential, and then unexpectedly reaches the climax, then progresses to be boring again) and this is the main catalyst to my rating. Overall, I think that this game is not suited for a person who enjoys adrenaline-inducing combat, nor for a person who enjoys a good story, but maybe for a collector who wants to have a taste at 2007 gaming.

I backed this game on Kickstarter many months ago and it has been one of the few games that hasn't disappointed me at all.
I'll start by saying this is my favourite game out there, literally.
I must have clocked in hundreds of hours since I backed this on Kickstarter last year and i've loved every moment of it.
I've always been a fan of traditional roguelikes, even those that use a ASCII style interface and though recently i've seen more and more games being released as roguelikes none of them really seemed to feel like them to me. That was until Dungeonmans. Dungeonmans is a roguelike in the purest sense made by someone who clearly loves the genre.
In Dungeonmans You start by picking from 4 random rolled stats (Stremf, Skills, Science and Foom) and then your class from many different classes. Each class starts with different player abilities which you can choose to level up as you play on through the game.
A key feature to me that makes it stand out is the fact that when you level up and choose new abilities you can choose any from the skill tree, even if that was not the class you chose to play in. Feel like running around with a shield as a Rangermans? Well, you're free to do so. Just...don't.
The game, like all roguelikes, has permadeath but that's not the end of your adventure. As you travel through the world and various dungeons you'll kill bosses and collect artifacts and books. Both of these things can be used to level up your 'Academy' which is where you, and all new-spawns will start. Upgrading the academy and bringing back artifacts unlocks things like 'all level 1 potions identified for every new Dungeonman you play with, so even though you lose your progress and level on your Dungeonman when you die, you don't feel like you're starting over entirely.
I've played games like Dungeons of Dredmoor, Rogue Legacy and other modern Rogue-likes and they are great but there is something about Dungeonmans that keeps me wanting to come back and die just once more.
And you will come back to it, over and over, and most likely die, over and over, but dying never felt this good before.
I should also mention that whilst I play keyboard-only, for those who aren't too comfortable with that there is an option to use your mouse aswell :)
There isn't too much else I can say about the game, the simplicity and beauty of it is in playing it for yourself. Now that the game is out of Early Access it's content rich and even more fun than before.
So if you want a modern yet honest-to-the-name rogue-like with tons of loot, enemies, a soundtrack that really makes you feel epic and dungeon after dungeons after dungeon then this is the game for you.
Just remember, as the developer says himself.
Don't. Get. Surrounded.

Very cool game. I didn't expect as much depth to it as it had.
It was also freakin' hard! The first dungeon has 2 difficulties, "Too easy" and "Easy", which really rather felt like "Normal" and "Hard mode". I haven't managed to clear it on Easy yet (so, "Hard mode"), but the too easy variant was indeed pretty easy to beat. I never ended up bothering much with the other dungeons, I tried them but in the end the original dungeon was the most fun.
There's lot of variety in the game. You can go at it from a lot of different approaches (Tower-Defense style or rather Hero-Defense style for example) which isn't explained in the game but you figure it out on your own, or through YouTube videos.
Multiplayer mode adds in a lot of fun and really enhances the game. You have to decide together with someone else which way to go, what to build, which stuff to research and how to spend your resources as efficiently as possible. Also you cannot pause in multiplayer, which saved my life very often in single player mode. That makes it a lot more challenging, but since more players can watch over things it's well-balanced.
Multiplayer mode does have one big downside: it's messed up resource system. It would've been more fun if resources were either shared or something else. Now each player has their own resource pool of which the income is based on a formula that goes (normal resources gained/amount of players), rounded up. Usually I ended up passing all science resources to one player, that would do all research and then I'd do all production so they'd give all industry resources to me. Every round. Super annoying.
All in all, definitely a fun and challenging game. I'd recommend it to others, both single- and multiplayer. It's easy to pick up, hard to master, and throws a serious challenge at you. It's definitely worth the price, compared to what you get.

Marble Duel (originally named Evy's magic spheres) is in essence a simple marble popper.
But don't let appearances deceive you, cause it is anything but simple!
There is a bit of a backstory were a liitle orphant girl is left, as a baby, on the steps of an orphanage.
10 years later the little girl ventures into the attic and sees a shiny light behind the doors of a closet.
When she opens the closet it turns out to be a portal to some kind of fairy land.
She enters the fairy world and then encounters all kind of weird creatures which she has to defeat.
It starts out reasonably simple and straight forward, but just when you start to think: "Ohh this is easy, maybe a bit boring even...."
Then it starts to get hard, really really hard, even wicked hard and (seemingly) unfair even!
You start with 1 sphere, that doesn't have additional features and only some health points.
Beating a level gives you points you can use to boost your power-ups.
Initially you can pnly boost your health points, later on other power-ups get added/earned and in the end you have: life, attack, healing, defense, attack power up and reflection.
You also get additional spheres, which give a little boost to either your healing, your reflection, your defense or your attack.
So plenty choices!
But......
the AI is really powerfull and no matter how many power ups you have earned you seem to be always outskilled and overpowered. So you"ll face defeat after defeat after defeat after......well you get the drift!
I started to get frustrated, I started cursing at my screen, I was constantly on the verge of abondoning the game, because it is so unfair and so unbalanced!
To name a few unfair features:
-The AI always has the better view over the battle field and can reach corners you can't
-When there are separate rows for the AI and the human player, the AI always can reach your rows as well, and vice versa: nope!
-When you get to the point were you get 3 balls, instead of the original 2, then the AI always gets the perfect balls to make great line ups! Why? Because it "knows" what the 3rd ball is. You don't. So very very often you start to line up a perfect cascade only to find out that the 3rd ball is not the one you need! And then the AI uses your line up against you!
-And ohh wait, we also have exploding balls! They have a timer and have to be used in match before the timer runs out, otherwise: instant kill! No matter how many health points you still have! And those exploding balls? They only hurt you, not the AI!
Frustration upon frustration upon frustration.........
So why keep trying?
Because it is annoyingly addictive!
So at some points it must be doing things right!
How does it do things right?
Because it is just not a simple marble popper!
There is strategy involved.
Remember those points you get for power ups? They can be reassigned, over and over!
And you reaaly need to do that constantly!
Some levels are defense powers, some about attack powers, some about deflection.
High attack power certainly isn't the answer to everything!
So don't make the mistake of assigning your points and leaving them there, cause you will get beaten over and over!
Reassign them and decide upon strategy over and over!
But......
The reassigning is a reall pain!
You can't toggle them on and off: you wipe the sheet clean and have to reassign all points again!
That is A LOT of clicking! Very annoying!
Clicked a time too many? No taking it back: start over!
IMO this power up points assigning system needs to be redevised so that you can just take points down and add them to another skill. And preferably with a +/- button AND in batches of 5.
Cause in the end it is like 50 clicks to assign all points!
Can I recommend the game?
Yes, but not wholeheartedly, cause the frustration gets so high!
I can recommend it, because it is a real challenge, because it has a twist, because it involves strategy.
But there is also a number of reasons why I can't recommend this game, but those flaws I already described.
Ohh and then there is this after level 119:
Seriously!?
I tried so hard to beat this game and getting the upper hand, only to find out it isn't even finished!
To sum it up: highly recommended if you are a glutton for punishment!
Otherwise 3 out of 5 at best.

Marble Duel is a casual mobile style game created by the indie developer Hero Craft. Taking a refreshing approach to the puzzle genre, this game is similar to Zuma’s revenge. Although, while the latter is based on the concept of spheres being thrown to stop a moving line of spheres reaching the boss in each level, Marble Duel instead sets a game up with stationary spheres making for a slower paced game than alternatives, each colour sphere can deal damage, heals, shield or launch special attacks. The catch is, however, you and your opponent are given certain spheres to use in each game which you can switch using the right mouse click. For many of you out there, who are quick to be irritated- just a heads up: I found it quite frustrating when the game forced me to heal in a turn.
The game’s simplistic design allows for quick loading time which is ideal for mobile gaming while moving about. Thought has been made in designing the artwork for the game with typical fantasy characters. Dialogue between characters add another level of immersion as you play through levels, hence the RPG tag under the game. Despite this label, the game is misleading because little role playing elements were implemented. Instead the game has little to no storyline choice other than winning or losing a battle which can be replayed if lost. Upon completing each level, you are rewarded with gems which you may use to purchase buffs in a duel when spheres clash such as healing, health or damage. Gems are rewarded according to the turns you take in completing a level and can be replayed, obviously, the fewer turns you take- the more gems you receive! You are able to reset upgrades allowing you to prepare for another opponent where you may be better off focusing on healing upgrades for example.
Each sphere in the game applies something different for your character to do, green spheres heal, blue spheres shield an attack and red spheres attack. The concept is easily understood for a new user and the game does introduce more colour spheres and further abilities gained by upgrading later in the game for a greater challenge. To apply the above trait in a turn you need to clash two or more of the same colour spheres by launching a sphere. There are combos which you can get by breaking the same colour in the middle of three of the same colour on the outside, when a combo is made you are allowed to make an additional turn. Green and Blue spheres affect your own attributes and overheal is not in this game so bear that in mind when healing at max health! Red spheres are your fighting power and deal damage to an opponent in every game, therefore your upgrades are usually focused on attacking.
In each duel the opponent has different levels of upgrades as well as different spheres to choose from. Early introductory games were easy to complete, however the challenge of completing each level gets harder and harder until the point later in the game where completing a level is next to impossible. The difficulty is also determined by your own upgrade choices so by collecting gems from previous levels and the game makes it so that later in the game it is crucial to replay previous levels for gems. The game also has bonus rounds where you do not face an opponent and need to complete an objective such as stop a circle of spheres from hitting a beam of light. These bonus games were far from challenging and if anything became like a chore, these could be easily beaten by simply breaking spheres without mistakes by not colour matching them. The rotation of the circles made these bonus levels unnecessarily longer than needed, which is a shame as the game is brilliant in the main levels. While we are on the train of complaints the background music when starting up the game and dialogue deterred from the overall experience, this was not appealing to listen to but sounded familiar to other music I have listened to. Sound effects in this game however were superb and triggered dopamine in my brain that made me want to play more and more for the reward of hearing the sound again, ridiculous… I think not!
Marble Duel offers a highly addictive game similar to Zuma’s Revenge made by Pop Cap but is far more strategic and slower passed than this alternative. I love both games, however I prefer this turn-based variation of the sphere clashing style of gameplay. This game is a brilliant choice and to be honest I have been long awaiting another game bearing this the sphere clashing style of gameplay since I got bored of Zuma’s revenge for IOS. I recommend this game for anyone who wants a fun game to play on a laptop or tablet device in their spare time. This is an excellent choice to buy.

The Long Dark is an example to all early access survival games and what they should be. In fact, an example to all survival games. The Long Dark is a unique expirence that no other game currently can match, even while having the same core mechanics as all other games of the genre.
This is the silent apocolypse, not a Mad Max wasteland or a Fallout nuclear future with mutated animals running around. No, the only thing in this game you need to fear is Mother Nature herself. From the wolves that roam in packs, to the fearsome bears that lurk in their small caves, to the cold eternal winter of the wilderness, danger is everywhere. And upon first getting a weapon, most players first instinct is to go crazy with the .308 rifle and fire upon the first living creature they see, this isn't the wisest option as players soon will discover and shows how exactly you'll learn throughout the game: through trial and error.
Yes, there are no hints or even a tutorial, instead, you're dropped randomly somewhere in the region you chose and its up to you to figure out how to survive from there. And while there is a map, it does actually require exploring on your part, making it more effective to learn your way around the world yourself, a system that has proven to be sometimes even better than a map.
Within sandbox mode, a basic story forms, you've crashed your plane down in the middle of no-where-Canada during the snowy apocolypse, and you're job is just to survive for as long as you can before succumbing to the long dark that we all fear.
The game's artstyle is incredible to look at, I personally have some of the game's art as my wallpaper. The mix between a cartoony style and a more gritty style blend perfectly together to make a comfy and menacing enviroment at the same time. The same can be said about the game's soundtrack, its an erie yet calming mix of string instruments that fit the enviroment well, and most of these tracks will play outside so you can listen to beautiful music while looking around at the beautiful enviroment.
The Long Dark truely is a great game, if not the best game ever made, and I highly encourage those reading this to pick this game up.

Hue is a charming 2D puzzle-platformer themed, as the title suggests, around color. Specifically, your character, a boy oddly named Hue, has the ability to change the color of the background, which has the side effect of making any onscreen object that matches the background temporarily cease to exist; barriers disappear, deadly lasers vanish, and crates that were formerly being lifted up by colored balloons fall to the ground. You start out with only one color available to you, but as the game progresses, you’ll gain access to a full rainbow of eight.
This may not sound like wildly inventive territory for a puzzle-platformer, and to be honest, it’s not; while I’m not aware of another entry in the genre that uses this specific color-switching mechanic, much of what you do still boils down to pushing Block X onto Switch Y, or getting a key to unlock the exit to the room you’re in.
But while Hue doesn’t reinvent its genre, it does what it does with ample polish. The difficulty curve is wonderfully smooth, with new puzzle elements being gradually and carefully introduced to ease you in. Checkpoints are forgivingly spaced at the beginning of each puzzle, and time slows down while you switch colors, giving you plenty of time to avoid a laser or solidify a crucial platform in mid-air. And while the story is simple - Hue embarks on a quest to rescue his disappeared inventor mother - it’s well told, through excellent voice-over narration. My only real complaint is that two pairs of colors (pink/fuschia and orange/yellow) are a tad too similar to consistently tell apart in the midst of gameplay, resulting in a few unnecessary deaths.
For any fan of puzzle-platformers, Hue comes highly recommended.

with this one. The concept is pretty simple, you arrive at this fantasy land and you progress through various areas, each with their own monsters. If you're familiar with Luxor or Zuma then you'll feel right at home playing Marble Duel, if not then don't worry too much as the gameplay is very quick to learn.
There are two main features that separate Marble Duel from Luxor and other games inspired by it, firstly is that Marble Duel faces you off against AI opponents every round and your goal is to beat them rather than amass points. Secondly the game play is turn based so rather than a continual flow of spheres, you take turns against your opponents. This makes playing a little more relaxing as you are not rushing against anything. Instead of the clock causing difficulty you have an AI. The aim of each mission is simply to reduce the health of your enemy to zero.
You start with just one sphere: the red sphere. This will allow you to match three reds with each other to deal damage to your opponent and once his health hits 0, you win. Though you only have one colour starting sphere this will quickly change; as you advance through levels you'll unlock a variety of different coloured spheres. These include blue spheres for defence (blocks a percentage of damage), green for life (heals an amount of your health), purple for attack damage (gives your next attack extra damage) and yellow for attack deflection (sends a percentage of the damage you take back to your opponent). There are also white spheres which don't seem to do anything but block matches and black spheres which deal damage to whoever matches three of them together, though you cannot fire either of these spheres yourself.
When you complete a mission you are awarded with gems which can be spent to upgrade your various spheres and your health. Each stage can be completed in a set number of turns to earn yourself gold, silver or bronze stars which will reap you more gems and consequentially more upgrades. Once a stage is completed it can be revisited at any time to earn any bonus stars you missed and this can be very helpful if you're struggling with later levels because your stats aren't high enough. The stage will remain the same difficulty and chances are you'll have upgraded your stats by then making the stage easy to complete within the allotted turns. It's worth trying to get as many stars as possible as the stats of your opponents will increase over time and you'll need plenty of upgrades to fairly compete. You can view your opponents stats before entering each level allowing you to reset and redistribute your own if you see fit.

Marble Duel is mess of a game that should've stayed on mobile platforms, or at least, been properly rebalanced for PC gaming.
Before I launch into everything that's bad about this game (and there's LOTS to say about that!), let me give you some background on Marble Duel.
Originally, the game was called Evy: Magic Spheres and sold on mobile platforms, as well as Desura. When coming to Steam, the name was changed to Marble Duel. Personally, I think the old name sounds better, as the current title reminds me of Marble Madness, which is nothing like this game at all.
Marble Duel looks similar to games like Luxor or Zuma, but it plays very differently. You need to match three or more colors to do something (e.g. damage the enemy, raise shields on yourself, heal yourself, or increase your attack power), but unlike those two other games, Marble Duel is turn-based as opposed to real-time action.
The goal is simple: kill your opponent before they kill you. During the game, you'll be able to increase your skills, which directly translates to differently colored marbles. You can respec at any time, so if you put points into something you don't need much, it's easy to fix.
The graphics are entirely 2D and the artwork for the cutscenes are passable. The audio is okay, but I prefer it turned off so I can play my own music.
The story is utterly forgettable and more a nuisance than anything else. In this sort of puzzle game, I'm far less interested in the storyline (especially when it's written so poorly) than I am in actual gameplay.
Now the bad stuff... yeah, what I wrote up above is what I'd consider the "good" part of Marble Duel.
The developer KNOWINGLY placed false screenshots on the store. His response to this when someone on the boards called him out on it was this:
In other words, the developer doesn't really care that he use false imagery to sell his product.
Because Marble Duel was designed with mobile games in mind, the game was balanced for in-app purchases. Fortunately, the developer removed those before putting it on Steam, but in the process, failed to rebalance the game as well. That means the game's difficulty is such that it expects you to purchase gems or coins (or whatever stupid in-game currency was used in the mobile version) and without that feature, Marble Duel quickly becomes so difficult that it's impossible to play.
Here are three examples:
1. When playing the game, the line of marbles extends off the screen and wraps around elsewhere. The AI can apparently "see" what's off screen and can make moves based on that knowledge. The player, however, cannot see off screen and is therefore at a disadvantage.
2. Which marbles you get to shoot and match is randomized. That's supposed to be part of the strategy in learning to make moves with future moves in-mind. Unfortunately, the AI will ALWAYS receive whatever marbles it needs to make a move. If the AI needs a red marble or a green marble, it will get them, whereas the player will have to rely on pure chance.
3. I've played one stage over 60 times (and lost each time) where if I win, I get a new amulet with bonus health. The problem is the AI starts with huge advantages over me. The AI has 400 HP, and can make THREE turns each round. In contrast, the highest my health can be right now (with all available points redistributed to my health stat) is 80 HP, and each round I get TWO turns.
All in all, I'd strongly suggest staying away from Marble Duel. If I could get a refund, I would, but I've played more than two hours worth of the game.
