BioShock is easily the best game I have ever played. I have probably played over
. The gameplay, story, environment, weapons, characters, enemies, and graphics. They just all add up into one big pile of fun! Not to mention very time consuming. I had first seen this game about 7ish years ago. My dad showed it to me and i'm still very grateful for that. This game was a big part of my life, I watched my dad play it every time he did. So if you haven't played it yet, what are you doing with your life? Go get it!.... Your still here? Ok well, I can tell you need more convincing, let me do my best!

Though this game is a fps
It does it so well, I have no idea how they managed it! First off, the hacking system is one of a kind, until other games copied it. You can hack turrets, some that can fly, to help you fight off your
! Also you can hack camreas to send said flying turrets to kill them once your enemies step in it's vision! And of course vending machines are hackable, to reduce prices and give you free items to help you in combat. Then there are the tonics! They pretty much make you a walking killing machine, some of them will let you hack easier, be more sneaky. Do more damage and or take less damage.
They are only a few slots to hold them and you have to choose which one suits you. Do you get health when hurting enemies, or do you set everything on fire in an area when hit? The combinations are endless!
And then there is something that makes this game so unique, it's an edible liquid that makes you the scariest man or woman in the world! If you want to find out what it is your going to have to play the game yourself, but trust me. If it weren't for this feature the game would be x10 worse, but still a fantastic game! The combat it self is very intriguing. I could play for hours, and I did. And I will some more! Also, different ammo types! Regular bullets, armor-piercing ones. And another kind, find out yourself, again! I spend almost all my money on these in-game. They are life savers!
Even tho the weapons in this game is probably the low point of it, it's still amazingly fun! The wrench, revolver, tommy gun, shotgun and grenade launcher are just a few to come to mind. The others you'll have to see on your own! And though they might seem like the typical
weapons, they aren't! Not even close. Your first weapon is the wrench. Just like Gordon's crowbar. The wrench is your only melee. And it's pretty much your signature weapon. But it does a very good job. And personally, my favorite weapon in any game ever!
The revolver has a very... interesting opening. See for yourself, but other than that it's your trustful long-ranged weapon for a while. And just like all other weapons
it's upgradeable! More ammo capacity, or more damage? Which to choose? Of course they can only be upgraded at upgrade machines, which when used shuts down forever. And since there's only a dozen or so in the game, you can't upgrade everything. So again, which to choose? The tommy gun a machine fun, and a very effective one at that. And the shotgun... well the shotgun is just so good. Please use it, for your safety! And the grenade launcher helps take down the big guys. You know, the one of the covers!
The enemies can be easy, hard, and also very scary. Did I mention this is a scary game? Only at some parts. But they still do it better than most modern horror games! I'll start off with the weaklings, the splicers. They are the everyday crazy, mask-wearing, murdering, psychopaths. You know, like the one that's right behind you. Since they have low health and bad weapons, they team up most the time. And if your hurt enough, and they're group is big enough, they might manage to kill you! Especially in the early part of the game! But they are still wanderers, they can catch you off guard sometimes, but most the time you'll hear them from their singing.... they should definitely audition for America's got talent. The spider splicers on the other hand are the ones you need to look out for. They are more mobile, can take more damage, deal more damage. And sneak up on you. They're weapons are hooks. That they can slash or throw at you. If you are unlucky enough to have more then two fighting you, then you should probably pause the game and find some. You'll need it! The most interesting and terrifying part about them tho. Is that they can climb on ceilings. So keep your chin up! And your head. There are many more I haven't mentioned yet. And I won't, except for one.
They are the ones you hear first, the ones that have the most loot. The ones that protect something that is crucial in your survival, and the ones that are actually peaceful. But they are the ones you dread the most. to put it simply: save your game before fighting one. Please.
Probably one of my favorite parts of the game, the world that you survive in, is almost worth dying for! The city you fight in takes place in Rapture, an underwater city! Which has "partially" been destroyed. Sometimes when nothing is trying to murder me, i'll look out a window. And look upon the city, seeing distant flashes from broken billboards, and the occasional shark. Look up and you can see sun rays hitting sides of the buildings. Look down and you can see the darkness and depth of the ocean! But the interiors are equally,
, amazing! When first entering Rapture, you can tell there was a panic. With signs protesting "Ryan is not our friend" and suitcases everywhere. You can tell something horrible happened! The further you go in, water is leaking. And blood and corpses are everywhere! Flickering lights and debris can be found everywhere. And i'm pretty sure that corpse just moved. The tunnels connecting the buildings are just beautiful. Every time you finish an area, a new fresh one comes. My favorite has to be Fort Fr- hold on, not supposed to spoil it....
There I said it! Don't hover over that if you don't want to be spoiled. Probably too late tho, sorry. Also, one thing this game teached me is that you can't trust
So avoid those, unless you want to get scared!

This game...
This is the only survival game that has ever challenged me.
The only thing that I think would be nice to have is a coop multiplayer. A multiplayer with one or two friends tops to work with. That would be AMAZING. I know, part of the atmosphere is to be alone, but being with just one or two friends will feel almost the same. If they venture to get food or wood and they don't return in a while... hehe
First time:
I had to go get wood for the fire, but since I was just starting my gear wasn't pretty good. But I didn't know that at the time, and my mistake was to travel too far, and wait too long. While breaking bigger branches to small ones, I started to notice the trees were moving a little more than before, wind was building up. But I didn't think it was a big deal, just a little windy.
Oh boy was I wrong. I continued with my search, and the conditions worsened by the minute. When I decided it was time to go back, it was too late. The blizzard was at full throttle, and I was too tired, too far, too cold.
On my way back, the hypothermia started to settle in. My movements were slower, and I couldn't run much. I started to feel warm (yes, a known symptom of hyporthermia) I started to get dizzy. Next the sleepnes came... and the long dark.
I lasted for 30 minutes, and learned a huge lesson: nature does not forgive.
You want to survive? Play safe, as you would in real life. This is the game's best achievement: you end up being afraid of doing things like you would in real life. What if a storm comes in? Or a wolf... or a bear. Do I have enough food for the trip? What about water? Is your gear good enough to endure the weather?
If any of those answers is "no", then you better be prepared. Cause only the tough ones survive against the long dark!
Gameplay 9/10
Graphics 7/10
Atmosphere 10/10
TL;DR: if you like survival games, get this one. If you want rust but hardcore mode, get this one. If you want a real challenge, GET THIS GAME.

As someone who enjoyed playing Red Faction: Guerilla long ago, I don't think I quite recall or welcome the idea of aliens and the silly Ultor story reference from Saints Row being brought up in Red Faction: Armageddon. Red Faction: Armageddon pulls a full-on Crysis on its predecessor by shoving you into the damp caverns of the underground. Amongst destroying this centries-old artifact, you unleash a Pandora's hole, a monstrosity of different monsters.
If you're looking for classic Volition game design, its mechanics are pretty much the same, except it's switched over to linearly instead of having an open-ended world on the side. I guess if we're talking about convenience, you can run through the game without ever taking a break to consider how much debris you've broken down or repaired out of necessity. It's pretty much lined up in a conveyor belt; cutscene, explore, cutscene, escort mission, cutscene, scary exploration, cutscene, triumphant ex machina weapon, challenging cutscene, boss, cutscene.
I haven't played through the game in its entirety, but right now, I wouldn't judge it as a sequel to Guerilla even if the devs say that it's canon. I'm viewing it as an over-the-shoulder third-person shooter, and so far, I'm entertaining the thought that if instead of the title, "Red Faction", it's a knock-off of a Starcraft title where you're that heroic Terran soldier saving the idiots who decided to reside in Mar Sara, and so far, I've been enjoying it a bit more since.
It's an okay experience, probably worth picking up if someone convinces you at best.

There are many mysteries in this world. One of them is the lack of attention Full Bore has gotten, since it’s such a great Metroidvania puzzle game.
You play as a boar in a mine populated by talking boars. You’re in debt and you need to repay it by finding blue gems hidden all over the map. There’s also lore to find that will tell why the boars closed off an area of the mines, and who left all these computers and junk everywhere.
The puzzles are all block pushing puzzles. There are blocks that do different things and you are going to hate the ones that disintegrate after you climb on top of them. I cannot recommend this game highly enough. It's a simple, rogue-like, game that I think is best described as a Dungeon Defense. Your team of up to four heroes are trying to reach the surface of the planet Auriga, which you crashed through after an attack on your spaceship. In order to do that, you will have to navigate 12 (13? I haven't reached the end yet myself) floors of an ancient dungeon left behind by the enigmatic Endless from when they colonized the planet. In addition to collecting more resources needed to continue on your journey, each time you open a door in the dungeon one of several things will happen: monsters will attack from the open room, monsters will spawn in other unlit rooms throughout the dungeon, or a random event (mostly positive, such as finding an item or another hero) will occur. You can't light every room in the dungeon, but you can build defenses in the ones that you do. The monsters will try to attack your dust crystal (an item you NEED to progress through the game), so the game is about lighting paths through the dungeon to funnel the monsters down and wear them down with your defenses.
I know I might not have made it sound like it, but this is a surprisingly simple game that is also surprisingly complex and nuanced. Easy to learn, but difficult to master.
In later levels the game does start to throw some curveballs your way, such as monsters with erratic behavior and more imfamously those that go after your defenses and not your crystal itself.
As I mentioned before the game is rogue-like, so sometimes things do just come down to random chance, but there are plenty of unlockables to be had that don't require beating the game itself, so most always I feel that I gain something on each attempt. Multiplayer is almost none existant, and so the rogue-like elements manage to keep the game feeling fresh and new even after many hours of single player.
All things said though, this game is extremely difficult. Harder I think than FTL, I'd say. I know the only two difficulties available are called "Easy" and "Very Easy", but they're anything but; "Very Easy" is more like "Normal" and "Easy" more like "Hard". There are different escape pods that you unlock by beating the game and after reading about them I don't see how they can make the game anything but nightmarishly difficult.
Fluff wise, those of you familiar with Endless Space or Endless Legend will find a lot of lore related to the two other games in the franchise, and in fact this game serves as a bridge between the bigger, grander, 4X stratedgy titles that Amplitude is known for. It also takes itself far less seriously, and goes out of its way to make fun of itself in the flavor text. It's my opinion that all the heroes in the game are on a sliding scale of insanity, and the game takes every opportunity to remind you of that.
The art work itself, well, look at it. It manages to pull off pixel art as beautifully as Hyperlight Drifter.
If anything that I said above sounds appealing to you, than pick up Dungeon of the Endless right away. I can't recommend it enough.

A fantastic blend of real-time and turn-based strategy, roguelike difficulty and randomization, resource management, and beautiful pixel art, Dungeon of the Endless is by far one of the best games I have ever played - lumped together in my top 3 with Risk of Rain and Magicka.
It brings together the best aspects of several genres while being sarcastic, intelligent, funny, and downright unforgiving.  It takes itself seriously while still allowing room to make fun of both the player and itself, and the game is riddled with tongue-in-cheek references and jokes that will make you chuckle and grin.
The characters are unique, interesting, and have very well thought-out interactions, hinting at a deeper story than at first glance.  The variety of game modes keeps the action interesting - even though replaying the default game mode never gets boring - and the vast array of characters leaves many opportunities to discover new character stories, new favorite combinations, and new gameplay in general.  Each and every aspect of the game is designed in a way that makes it fun to play, and that same intelligent design guarantees a decision is not without consequences or some sort of risk-reward tradeoff.
And, with the improvements and alterations to multiplatyer mode, it's more than a blast to have fun with, yell at, and weep with your friends.
PROS
--Beautiful visuals: pixel art was a perfect choice to convey the game, and anything else would be an injustice
--Great character design: each one feels unique and special, and each one has his/her/its own unique niche in the gameplay
--Varied gameplay: even with the same characters, no two playthroughs will ever be the same
--Great story: even though it's not a plain-and-simple spelled-out story, it's told in such a way that lets the adventurous player discover the story that is artfully placed throughout
--Responsive and responsible Dev Team: there is a ton of interaction with the community, and it's underappreciated in general how important it is to be able to give feedback to the devs - they take everything in stride and when bugs are brought to the surface, the dev team squashes the problems
--Fantastic multiplayer experience: not having to futz with a third-party program to hook up the multiplayer, having quick and responsive connections, and allowing everything necessary for a smooth experience really pays off in the fun department
--Fun: plain and simple, it's enjoyable
--Unforgiving: if you mess up in this game, you have a one-in-ten chance of recovering from your blunder, and that's good - any mistake deserves to be a fatal one
CONS
--Difficult to learn: now, that's not to say it isn't easy to pick-up-and-play, it's to say that some people who aren't a fan of the genre or who aren't that good at strategy games will have a difficult time getting a grasp on this game; it's unforgiving and cruel
--Strange controls: granted, you can change literally every single thing in the game to a different hotkey, but that doesn't mean that the base controls are easy to get a hang of - they're simple, but simple isn't always good
--No controller support: granted, again, that you can find ways around that and that there are technical limitations, creative players have discovered ways to make it work - I think the devs should make it an option that is built-in
OVERALL RATING
9/10 - BUY THIS GAME

Cute art and story, as well. Overall a fun, memorable game that stands out in its genre.

When Cuphead was originally shown at E3 I was blown away by its presentation. However, leading up to the release, I was concerned the game wouldn't live up to the expectations, either due to length or mediocre gameplay. I can now say with certainty and incredible joy that Cuphead not only delivers on what it sets out to accomplish, but also manages to place itself among the best games of the year and perhaps of all time.
The charming, cartoon story of Cuphead fits well and delivers the motivation you need. However, it's the art style where this game really shines. Cuphead's 30's cartoon style is pulled off flawlessly. The animation is as smooth as butter, the personality expressed in the enemies is phenomenal, and the color palette is perfect. This game blows every other release out of the water this year graphically, thanks to a gorgeous visual style that manages to perfectly replicate its inspiration and produce a timeless look. If there is but one complaint I could note, it's that I wish for slightly more visual feed back when shooting enemies. There is barely any and since there is no health meter the only way to know is by watching the phase change and looking at how far you made it when you die.
Cuphead not only succeeds graphically, it's also a musical tour de force. It boasts a stellar jazz-filled soundtrack that is catchy, fitting, and not at all grating which is impressive when you have to retry about 20 to 40 times per level. The sound effects are also snappy and satisfying, however, Cuphead's weapons could use a bit more punch to their sounds. They sound a little too weak.
As for gameplay, Cuphead somehow is basically perfect. Every level is methodically plotted out with clear visual cues for obstacles and traps and a good pacing to levels. I could go on for a long time about how each boss fight is brilliant but needless to say, they're all unique, fun, challenging, just long enough, and built with a perfect flow for retrying after dying. The weapons and charms are hit and miss. Some are fantastic and really helpful, some are basically useless. Most have at least one situation where they're beneficial but some like the lobber and whetstone are really not that good. All in all though, the gameplay is 10 cuts above the usual serving from indie and AAA devs. Finally, the brutal difficulty allows this game to take up around 12 or 13 hours which means it's not that short despite the levels not taking very long in one go.
Aside from a few little flaws I notice, this game is fantastic. One of the best indie games I've seen and one of the best games I've ever played. A meticulous passion project that proves the industry has been aching for something fresh. The price is fine in my eyes for the amount and quality of content you get. These devs gambled with their lives to make sure Cuphead succeeded and I highly recommend you buy this game to show you appreciate their effort and talent. I look forward to whatever Studio MDHR decides to tackle next because they have some serious skill in terms of artwork and game design.

Rise to the top or crash and burn, will your city survive your incompetence? How high can you build? Watch your hard work crash down fast. I love this game! It's simple, clever, creative and lots of fun! You have to build a beautiful city as high as you can while balancing your creation on a platform, which is more difficult than you think. The building items have various shapes and sizes so you need a good stacking strategy.
The game has 10 missions in tutorial style that guides you to build the best city in the 2D world. There are 12 scenario's where you have to "rebuild" existing cities like New York and Paris, that once completed, will make you "lol" at your work of comical art when you stack certain landmarks in the most crazy ways. I managed to place the statue of liberty on top of the Brooklyn Bridge, while half an island sunk, hilarious :D.
There is free build option, where you let your city building creativity run wild. Do beware, once you feel save, you have a beautiful city and you think there is not a care in the BalanCity world, Godzilla will pay a visit to trample on your citizens and buildings and wreck your day. Better prepare your military.
I played for more than 14 hours now found a few little bugs, but mainly had an incredibly fun time. A minor annoyance is the music, it's been stuck in my head for 2 weeks now (O_O). So it could use another soundtrack.
In the end I'm in love with this little gem. It is one of those games that I keep installed and play every month or so, it makes me smile and sometimes shout "NOOoooooo" when my city crumbles and falls in the sea. Only to start rebuilding your city once again.
I do hope and wish the developers will add more scenarios and other fun updates.

I'd say this is a wholly worthwhile game. Its just not as exciting and fresh as RF: Guerilla. At a glance, I'd describe this game as sort of a weird synthesis between Guerilla, the original Red Faction, and Dead Space.
Its linear and mostly underground like the original which some might see as a step back, but I find I actually prefer *some* linearity in my games so I don't mind that part. My main issue with the gameplay is that the combat is mostly all that is here and its not all that amazing, just good decent shooting. Lack of emphasis on destruction compared to its older siblings is disappointing.
Armageddon is a bad sequel to Guerilla. But its still a decent linear third person shooter that can be a fun romp.
More specifically, Its weakness are its emphasis on cheesey and dumb plot and somewhat dull start with too many cutscenes, lack of effective use of destruction like Guerilla (except for maybe the Magnet Gun being fun). In fact, the game turns destruction somewhat into a chore, as the upgrade system is still dependant on finding scrap. So inbetween killing enemies you'll find yourself dully grinding random structures down for xp to some degree. Luckily, this doesn't take too much of your time and can at least be somewhat amusing break from combat. It's also got some somewhat dull vehicle combat parts.
Its also crash heavy by default at the time I played it. On the plus side, if you opt into the public beta it should run fine (check the communitty pages for details).
It's strengths however comes in the form of arguably better shooting combat than Guerilla with a better variety of enemies and combat scenarios. The aliens are in general a bit more fun to kill than hordes of guys with guns that we got in RF:G. I reccomend that when you play it you stick to using explosive weaponry, as they are the most fun to use in this game and ammo is plentiful. Also play on the hardest difficulty, its rarely particularly hard and if you struggle you can always turn the difficulty back down mid game. Its also got a decently interesting set of missions in the second half of the game in particular, the game changes things up just enough to keep things interesting.
Keep in mind, this doesn't come with all the DLC, its missing an additional set of 4 "prequel" missions that you can buy separately. It does however come with all the weapon DLC extras you'd have gotten from pre-ordering, and they're decently interesting weapons that aren't over powered, so the balance remains.
It also comes with some "horde mode" style game modes, I haven't tried them but apparrantly its co-op. I might have to try them and update this review sometime.
If you are looking for more Guerilla, look elsewhere, if you enjoyed the original if you enjoy linear horror action shooters like Dead Space you'll probably enjoy Armageddon.

I think the thing that makes this game stand out so much from the rest of the survival games out there, is that it mixes feelings of awe and exploration with desperation and sometimes even fear. It puts you in a place where people do not belong. You often get a sense of handicap, at your need to survive in ways that seem so easy to the animals that live there and have the home field advantage. It makes you feel vulnerable, and can sometimes make you nervous to the point of apprehensiveness. And then you turn around and see a devine, silent beauty of it all, and it kind of captivates one for a moment, making one forget about anything else. Which makes the experience all the more immersive.
It is for these reasons (I think) that the game is so much more adamant in it's ability to make you WANT to survive, to make you WANT to push through even to the very last, hopeless, second of your inevitable death. When compared to other games of the same genre.

Every few months I try to return this game...
I've waited a while to write this to make sure the media hype train was long gone and my initial frustration was tempered. In a nutshell: Don't buy it.
Unfortunately the game is insanely repetitive with a rapidly dwindling, tiny player base. The game came out at a full $60 only to be a platform to sell more DLC. The single player game forces you to play the tracker class as the AI hunters simply follow where you go and will not do their job (IE: Tracking the monster). Playing the Monster in single player is frustrating as the AI immediately knows where you are and takes the fastest path to you, immediately redirected their course if you try and double back or take a different path, effectively forcing you to play hunters and even then, forcing you to play the tracker class. Fully 80% of the game will be you running the same loop through the same maps complaining about how tiresome the game is with nothing to do except treat it as a running simulator.
This forces most of the small player base online immediately with zero knowledge of the maps or group dynamics, making for frustratingly inept groups that result in an instant monster death because the player running the monster doesn't know the map and makes a poor turn, immediately running into the hunters, or the hunters not being able to form a group dynamic worth a damn and immediately dying to the monster, or providing no threat and the monster hitting lvl 3 way to soon and then wiping the party.
If there was a single player aspect worth playing, we might see more competitive players online, but as it is, players load into online, get discouraged because they don't know how to play, then stop playing, which is why there will be an average of 500 people in the entire world playing an any given time, most of them far enough away to give you a 200+ ping and terribad lag.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a very simple, jump scare, point and click horror game where your objective is to complete your work shift without being killed. You're a security guard and your job is to stay from midnight to six watching over a children's pizza place, however, its not interference from the outside that's trying to kill you but what's inside. The animal mascots are trying to kill you and your job is not to fight back but to keep them from getting to you until your shift is over(They're only evil at night, they're perfectly fine in the day). Essentially, what you have to do is use the camera to spot each mascot and close your doors if they appear in front of them. Successfully accomplishing this goal until 6 A.M. grants you a victory fanfare and you continue on to the next night for a total of seven nights.
This game has incredible atmosphere with spooky noises, laughs, wheezing, and constant pitter-pattering of feet as the mascots move around. Now I use the word "move" very loosely as you only see actual animation unless you fail(get killed). As you poke around each camera the mascots are always still when you spot them. The reason for this is explained along with various other ambigious dialogue by the phone guy at the beginning of each level. The rules are pretty clear: check the cameras to spot and stop the mascots, check the cove periodically to prevent foxy from getting you, and try not to use the camera system, lights, and doors too much or you'll run out of power. If you run completely out of power everything shuts down which means instant death. Its a simple game with simple rules. Its a shame that the game doesn't seem to want to adhere to its own rules.
clickclickclickclickclickclickclickclickclickclickclickclickclickclickclickclick       RNG
I've already given my opinion on RNG in Equin:The Lantern so I won't repeat myself here but that's the least of your problems. You need reflexes of the gods as you continue to progress through the levels. The mascots move so fast and if you're a casual, like I am, you won't get far playing this game like your supposed to. This goes far beyond git gud. Unless you have that kind of time you are going to end up playing the game "wrong". Left light-close right door-check foxy-right light-repeat. This is what allowed me to beat the game. By playing the game as intended, I was to slow, kept getting killed and hit a dead end at night 4. The game has 11 different rooms for you to check and all of them are absolutely pointless except for one. Sometimes you will find yourself doing the EXACT SAME THING with each repeated playthrough with an entirely different set of chllenges each time. To be perfectly honest, I can't even take full credit and claim skill for beating the game when I truthfully feel that the only reason why I won was because of a set of circumstances that were in my favor. It makes the game feel...sloppy. Now if this was part of the extra days, 6 and 7, I suppose this would be different since its extra but to have this insanity as part of the main game is bothersome. From night 4 on I wasn't really playing but following a repeated pattern and praying for a good run set. Through repeated playthroughs the scares do eventually die down and when that happens your left with the goal of beating the game which means either git gud or git ready for a commitment of a pattern with alot of patience.
Despite the glaring flaws, I highly recommend this game as a group scare fest between friends. Its been a long time since any form of media has actually made me jump with my heart racing and that reason alone in enough for me to recommend.

Every now and again a little bit of magic happens. This game is one of those little bits of magic.
In a nutshell Dungeon of the Endless is a hybrid realtime/turn-based, procedural, squad survival strategy game, with RPG elements, resource management, research, building, maintenance, permadeath, humour, and a large roster of unlockable characters to play with. Quite a bit in that nutshell right?
Generally when game designers try to create hybrids it all goes horribly wrong and you end up with something that's mediocre at best. That is not the case with Dungeon of the Endless. After 20 hours of trying to rise above the deceptively simple challenge of fighting my way to the surface through 13 floors I have come to the conclusion that this game is flawless. I cannot fault it. Everything just works and feels right. It is simply a gem of game design.

Every year around Christmastime I try and atone for my sins by helping out the less fortunate. 2016 kind of was s*** and I can't be bothered to actually stare my fellow man in the eye. Instead of, therefore, saving some orphans just so that they'll get burnt in the apocalyptic wildfire 2017 is sure to bring, I'm reviewing a game I really like, yet somehow never got off the ground. This is charity work, and I can declare it on my taxes.
I think I got Full Bore in a bundle last year, and I played it more or less just to humor it. To my surprise, 25 hours later (I think around that timespan, this is a LONG game), I had 100%ed it. This happened for a few reasons.
This happens every time I get my hands on a well-designed puzzle game. I play it an unhealthy amount of time, to the point where I put off my real-life responsibilities as much as possible. It's probably indicative of some greater underlying mental health issue, likely having to do with that summer at camp I can't remember.
I can't for the life of me recall what that game was, but I remember being upset enough to slip into a rage-induced coma, probably one that explains why I didn't review Full Bore when I actually played it.
In preparation for someday being a father, despite reason #1's clear indication that perhaps I shouldn't, I am attempting to construct an encyclopaedia of ghastly jokes to embarrass my offspring with, and this game helped.
So, onto the game proper, and why I think I like it more than almost any other 2D puzzle game I can recall:
Simply put, it has the same sort of elegant design eventually found in The Witness. Every puzzle is solvable from the moment you start the game. However, they are all reliant on a complex ruleset that will not, initially, make much sense. You must learn and explore to determine how to progress, and the knowledge gained applies to earlier puzzles that may have seemed impossible at the time. The game will never tell you how to solve a puzzle - it's entirely on you - and each solution requires its own little ah-ha moment.
This results in a constant cycle of feeling stupid, and smart, in a way that I find more addictive than crack.
This game is impeccably designed in that regard. It's not exactly a looker per se, but the design is so fundamentally good, I can't help but recommend.
Right, now onto trying to find something else to scratch my moronic puzzle itch before I have to deal with celebrating the birth of some guy with a cute beard.

First, to save you time before reading an in-depth review, here's the pros and cons.
- Good graphics
- Fun destruction physics
- Compelling Story (For the most part)
- Fun Gameplay (For the most part)
- Honorable 'Red Faction' title
- Likeable Characters
- Wonderful environment
- Good character design
- Stable Frames
- FoV [Below 40!] (Brutal unless you get a fix here, which I highly suggest:
- Repetitive
- Story gaps
- Annoying enemy placement
- Enemy Encumbrance
- Lack of variety (in multiple areas)
- Short Story (About 6-8 Hours of just plowing through)
- Ocaisonal crashes before cutscenes
Now, on to the long review. (no spoilers)
RF: Armageddon takes place years after RF: Guerilla. Following the Mason bloodline, you play as Darius Mason, a Red Faction Soldier who develops a name for screwing up. Your time fighting pre-armageddon is very short, which is mildly upsetting, especially if you've played RF:G. The groundwork for the different regions was laid out in that game, and all you ever get to see is slivers of Dust (Post Armageddon), and the Terraformer before everything goes downhill. Even more of a slap in the face is the fact that you hear and see other places like Oasis mentioned, but never get to see anything of it. The marauders are back, and like they were in RF:G, they're inclined to reclaim their home. Events transpire in the Terraformer, and it forces the Red Faction and all colonists underground into old mining tunnels. After this event, Darius leaves RF, and does excavation work for whoevers willing to pay. This is how an outbreak is eventually released. with (somewhat familiar if you've played the original RF) aliens. You should get used to these aliens, because that's all you'll be fighting for most of the game minus a few boss battles and marauder gunfights. On that note, this game ditches the open world of RF:G for a classic level-bsaed shooter. In essence this isn't bad, and the game generally executes it well. Where the downfall comes, is in the late game battles. At first the swarms of enemies are cool, and using your environment to defend against, and attack them is really neat, especially with new game mechanics like reconstructing dilapitated buildings, and blasts of force to push them away. unfortunatley, about 40%-50% through the game, this get VERY repetitive, and the enemy waves only gets bigger. You find yourself wanting to explore and look at the enthralling environment around you, but can't because you're constantly fighting off enemies. The endless horde aside, the marauder missions are very well executed. Not too encumbering, still a good fight, and plenty of time to admire your surroundings. The vehicles missions are a shining point of this game, as controls are fluid and the devs found ways to design levels around each vehicle you use in the missions. On a story and level design aspect, there are two polarizing sides to each. Starting with the level design, in many scenarios it's unique from mission to mission, but much like the aliens, their architecture becomes encmburing. You get sick of seeing the same biomass infested scenes over and over and over again. The first few feel unique, and then by the mid to late game, it's just a bunch of biomass. Other than the alien levels and infestations, the other architecutre generally feels unique and enjoyable to be around. The environments their built upon are also well executed, and above surface Mars is breathtaking in all of it's ruin and grit. Perhaps my favourite levels are the ones with Ultor ruins. being a big fan of the original game, Ultor holds a place in my heart, but unfortunatley this game suffer the same fate as RF:G, in the Ultor is touched upon but never really explored to it's full potential. In regards to the story, it's a bit above generic. You'll care about the characters, and you'll feel urgency for the missions, but I never found myself in shambles at a majot death, or smirking when it was time to kick♥♥♥♥♥ I don't want to say too much about the campaign, as I do think it's fun, and worth playing for the story. As mentioned in the line about level design, Ultor comes up a few times in the story, and you even have to explore some of the old ruins, but in the end the mention of Ultor will tease old fans, and leave news ones with too many un-answered questions. We also never get a viable explanation for who the marauders are, and where they came from (my assumption is Ultor descendants, but that's been my theory since RF:G and it still ahsn't been answered). All in all, the story is a wonderful continuation from thr game RF:G, and the way they executed it, you don't even need to have any past Red Faction experiance (but it does help, and make certain scenes & scenarios make more sence) In conclusion, I think RF: A is a welcome addition to the Red Factoin series, and a fun game in all. It suffers from minor gameplay inconviences (FoV, fixable, See Pros.Cons), and many little annoyances and missed opportunities, but in the end delivers a compelling story with unique gameplay and mostly excellent level design. I suggest buying this game on sale, but I do think the $22 price tag is justified.

This is the saddest review I've ever had to edit.
For those of you who don't know, Turtle Rock Studios didn't give up on this game. 2K decided that, after the less than preferable response to Evolve going FTP, that they were ending Turtle Rock's contract and cancelling all updates until further notice. It's been months now and still no word, so I've come to the conclusion that 2K has little interest in trying to revive this game. With that assumption, I sadly have ceased playing this game.
I've seen so many people blame Turtle Rock for the fate of Evolve. Please don't; they fought with all their might to keep this game alive, through the thick and thin. I was active in the game forums, and I made friends there; it was a community that shared, discussed, fought, laughed, and came up with some great ideas. It was also a community that was shared by the devs (and still is), who would interact with their players on a one-to-one basis. They shared thoughts with their players, listened to ideas, and modified their game from the ground up in order to make it a learning, growing experience with their playerbase. Turtle Rock created something magical with Evolve: it was a close-knit community that truly interacted and almost felt like a family.
I loved this game. Look at my hours played; I loved this game. When I heard that Turtle Rock was being released from the project, I wept. I literally cried. I met people on these servers that are now good personal friends. I had the time of my life panicking and running from the monster, BEING the monster, and sharing a heart-pounding huzzah whenever we successfully defeated a tough monster together. It was the perfect combination of cooperative and competitive play, and it captured the hearts and imaginations of sci-fi fantasy enthusiasts like myself. The effort and care that went into this game astounds me, especially considering the wall of opposition and criticism this game undeservedly received early on. I've never had a game impact my life in the same way Evolve has done.
Evolve was always a niche game, true, but it was something amazing and breathtaking for many of us. I believe in Turtle Rock Studios, and I eagerly await to see what they do next.
So, with happy memories and optimism to fuel me, I bid you all one final "Happy Hunting."
Until next time...

For an early access game this game has very few bugs and a vast world to explore. There are few games like this one, as most survival games like to throw zombies or PvP into the mix. This game is just about surviving.The survival system is also more in depth than most games.
Depending on the game setting food and calorie counting is something you need to pay attention to. On the easy setting you don't need to worry about much, but on the harder settings just collecting firewood becomes a question of exposure to cold and calories consumed.
I won't give away all the inflictions you can get, as that will spoil the fun, but I have not seen another 3D survival game structured like this one. I still think their could be some improvement to the injury/illness system, but this is still more than what I have seen in other games.
Even though there is no story mode at the moment in this game, the harder settings prove enough of a challenge just surviving to keep it engaging.
I am a big fan of this game, but I'll try to list some cons to give a more balanced review.
On the sandbox mode once you have good gear and you are setup for survival there is not much point in playing further. The challenge is surviving and once you have met all those needs then the only point to continue is to explore areas you have not been or for the achievements, which can get a bit boring. Personally I just start a new game.
I would like to see a greater variety in wild life, dealing wolves all the time can get old. I think you could add moose and mountain lion, maybe even badgers.
Overall a great game and I think it is worth the money you spend on it, as, if this is your type of game, then you get tons of replay value out of it. To me having a video game you can go back to over and over and still find it fun is a game worth getting.

This game is amazing, the fact that it came out like 10 years ago and still holds up it's fascinating.
The story is mysterious and involving, the main character is awesome, the world built from the story is fantastic, Rapture is a place that feels real even though is just fictional.
The gameplay is solid and very good, it plays out like a shooter but the integration of "Tonics" (basically powers) is genius, the limitation of how many "Tonics" you could have at a time is very good, because the fights are more challenging and also some enemies requier more than a few bullets just to kill them. Generally the controls are very responsive.
The visuals are amazing, they aren't the best, but take note that this game came 10 years ago, the scenery of the outside Rapture is gorgeous, the inside of Rapture is very creepy and mysterious given by the plot of the game.
The sound and music are excellent, the music captures the feel of being in a  underwater city, the themes around the places you are are excellent, when you engage in a fight it's a very good transition from the exploring to the fighting.
But there are some things that I don't like, when you are near the end the fights with enemies are repetitive and sometimes not even necessary to do, some of the bosses aren't as good, they don't expand the motives of their actions and it feels like forced, there are some difficulty spikes depending in which mode are you playing and that's all of my complaints... I think.
Overall, it is a great game, I highly recommend it, even if you already know the story or the end, I recommend playing it because it is a blast to play through

I enjoyed this game because of its main mechanic, the color wheel. Basically you can change the color of the background to make objects of that same color blend into the background, which makes them temporarily disappear. The developer did a great job of filling the world with fun puzzles in a vivid world.
My only complaint really is that the structure ends up being very repetitive. There are eight colors, and each color's gauntlet is essentially structured the same. First you are forced to walk through a maze while a voice-over reads the story, but there's no way to skip this or reach the end of the maze before the voice finishes. Then you solve the puzzles, which can sometimes be a bit too easy and repetitive as well. And then you obtain the next color for the next area. I suppose it's simple and it works, but they could have probably done something slightly less predictable.
Overall it was a fun experience, with definitely a lot of effort put into it.

I had a great time with Full Bore.  I bought it expecting just another puzzle platformer, but it's much more than that.  It's a free-roaming open world exploration game, like Metroid without the enemies.  This means it's probably closer to Fez than any other game, but I enjoyed it more because it generally avoids  esoteric puzzles that require out of game knowledge.  The main mechanic of the game is digging in unstable soil, which will be familiar to anyone who played Steamworld Dig.  It works just as well here, but unlike Steamworld Dig you're expected to backtrack if you want to explore and the whole map isn't digging.
The music is great, the story is surprisingly complex, it has multiple endings but you can play after the two to three of them, and NPCs acknowledge your success.  All in all, I highly recommend for fans of 2D puzzle games.

Full Bore is the kind of game where everything feels like it was really well thought out. The central concept of the game is solving puzzles while you explore the game's world. Along the way you collect gems and read about the lore of the events that happened leading up to the present time within the game. Because of some excellent puzzle design and well paced introduction of new puzzle mechanics the game never felt boring to me. Full Bore also features a time travel mechanic that lets you undo the last number of things you've done as well as soft resetting the current puzzle you are working on. This alone helped make what would have been frustrating and tedious puzzle solving into fun and difficult puzzle solving. Only major gripes with the game are that you have to re-solve a number of puzzles when you go through a previously explored area for some, but not all areas. This is exacerbated by the lack of a clear map and very conservative fast travel locations, which make traveling to certain locations to clear out the map a bit of a pain. Overall I quite enjoyed Full Bore.

Full Bore is a story-driven puzzle-adventure game in which the player plays a boar.  The goal of the game is to complete the story and be the hero of boarkind, but exploration and treasure-hunting are other goals.  In order to progress through the game, the player must solve puzzles.  As one progresses farther into the game, the more complex and difficult the puzzles become.  The mysteries unfold as the player reads lore from many years ago, enters another dimension, and explores 5 different regions of the world.
The game is usually paced at whatever speed the player wants, allowing for think time to figure out the puzzle.  A few levels are high-speed action levels, in which making a mistake can be deadly.  Thankfully, a handy rewind feature can help solve the trickier puzzles, and the world map keeps track of which areas have been completed and which areas have not.
The world also contains a handful of non-player-characters that the player can chat with, gaining more information about the world of Full Bore.
The levels themselves tell stories--blast marks, skeletons and broken trusses tell the stories of what people did long ago.  The background music is very catchy and I love hearing it over and over.  The game designers did a good job of giving levels atmosphere, some levels I feel at home in, others creep me out. The game map can be explored freely and at the player's pace, and a warp system allows the player to teleport from one region to another very quickly.  In most cases, if you get stuck on one puzzle, there are plenty more to figure out.
Even after game completion, there is still stuff your boar can do--find hidden rooms, talk to NPCs, or try to solve the puzzles again!
I liked this game--a thinking game with a great story beneath it.   This game is good for people that like logic puzzles and working out their brain.  If you love good stories, this might also be the game for you.  Depending on how easily you solve puzzles, this game may take anywhere between a few hours to a few days or more to solve.
I would recommend this game for anyone who wants to stretch their mind, learn a good story, wander aimlessly underground, race through a mineshaft, or just have fun in general.
A game to play when you are BOREd

The action of Full Bore takes place in a post-apocalyptic world(?), where a new sentient race of boarkind (and a few more animals) is ruling. It's a puzzle platformer in which the player controls Hildi, a boar that is accused of stealing gems from a vault of a digging company owner. As a punishment, it's sent into the mines to retrieve all the stolen treasures.
The game is a puzzle platformer, which means the (almost) only gameplay is solving environmental puzzles with your own hands (hooves?). The player has the access to a map that allows to check, if there is still something left to explore in each location, which saves the time greatly and indicates the general direction of where should one proceed. To solve the puzzles, one usually needs to dig through or move some blocks. If mistakes were made, it's always possible to "rewind time" to specific moments, so that it's possible to take off where the last right step was made. On your way down (or up), more and more secrets are discovered that put the story into context. The game is an open-world one - there's no requirement to explore many of the maps, but they often hold some additional information about the past of the world or extra gems. Moving throughout the locations and maps takes some time, but a mechanism of fast travel makes it pretty convenient.
The puzzle solving is actually really absorbing and fun. First puzzles are rather straightforward, but the game gets progressively harder with new locations. There seems to be a big spike in difficulty at one point towards the end, where puzzles get really challenging and it wasn't unusual for me to spend up to half an hour solving one problem.
The controls are smooth and reactive, which is really important for a platformer. The only issue I had was with jumping down from blocks, where the boar is somewhat hesitant to do so, which costs some extra time, so much needed in many scenarios. Another thing that I found a bit disappointing is that, there seems to be no use for gems and most of the items. I mean, I wouldn't really like to see collecting those a requirement to finish the game, but an additional incentive would be ever so nice. Because of that, the last few maps, I just went straight to where I needed to go, without caring much about clearing the locations thoroughly.
I found the pixel graphics in the game very appealing. Surface is nice, cheerful and green, while digging deeper and exploring lower maps brings some darker and more volcanic colours into play. The main characters are made carefully and look really pretty (like the shaman), their animations and also animations in general are also nice and smooth. Overall, I found the graphical design really charming and detailed enough to be able to keep my attention, but not too crowded to obscure the view of the objectives.
As I've already mentioned, at some point I've noticed that going for gems and collectibles is not too rewarding, however, I kept on exploring. The reason for that is the story or more like - the history. The story itself is pretty straightforward and could be probably written down on one page of paper. Still, throughout the game, it's possible to find notes and terminal data that introduces the player to what actually happened before the current game world existed. Maybe, it's just me being a fun of post-apocalyptic settings, but after completing the game, I've spent some time reading the other players' theories on the in-game history, just out of curiosity.
The background music is quite catchy and I never felt the urge to mute it, as I sometimes do in many games. It changes from location to location, each one has its own tune. Changing maps also changes the music sometimes to a different variation on a theme. It definitely wasn't a kind of a music I'd listen on a daily basis or while commuting to work, but it was really fitting to the game and just sounded nice and right.
It took me almost 10h to beat the game, but if one wants to be really thorough and get all of the collectibles, I think there would be somewhat 20-30 hours of playing there. Shame that except for achievements there's little incentive to go for it all. Still, I believe this is a really decent amount of content and fun for a cheap little game. It kept me interested and it was always fun to try and solve the puzzles to get some more diamonds or reach more lore secrets and that's what's important to me.
Full Bore is a really solid indie game, all pieces just fall right into place. The puzzles are just challenging enough to keep one entertained and thinking, but not too hard, discovering the lore is actually quite interesting, the graphics are all nice and charming and the music just completes the image of a well-made game. I probably wouldn't pay the full price for it, but it's a great catch if it's bundled or on a discount. So, if it's discounted somewhere and you want to put your brain to some work, grab it - you won't regret it (probably).

This is the saddest review I've ever had to edit.
For those of you who don't know, Turtle Rock Studios didn't give up on this game. 2K decided that, after the less than preferable response to Evolve going FTP, that they were ending Turtle Rock's contract and cancelling all updates until further notice. It's been months now and still no word, so I've come to the conclusion that 2K has little interest in trying to revive this game. With that assumption, I sadly have ceased playing this game.
I've seen so many people blame Turtle Rock for the fate of Evolve. Please don't; they fought with all their might to keep this game alive, through the thick and thin. I was active in the game forums, and I made friends there; it was a community that shared, discussed, fought, laughed, and came up with some great ideas. It was also a community that was shared by the devs (and still is), who would interact with their players on a one-to-one basis. They shared thoughts with their players, listened to ideas, and modified their game from the ground up in order to make it a learning, growing experience with their playerbase. Turtle Rock created something magical with Evolve: it was a close-knit community that truly interacted and almost felt like a family.
I loved this game. Look at my hours played; I loved this game. When I heard that Turtle Rock was being released from the project, I wept. I literally cried. I met people on these servers that are now good personal friends. I had the time of my life panicking and running from the monster, BEING the monster, and sharing a heart-pounding huzzah whenever we successfully defeated a tough monster together. It was the perfect combination of cooperative and competitive play, and it captured the hearts and imaginations of sci-fi fantasy enthusiasts like myself. The effort and care that went into this game astounds me, especially considering the wall of opposition and criticism this game undeservedly received early on. I've never had a game impact my life in the same way Evolve has done.
Evolve was always a niche game, true, but it was something amazing and breathtaking for many of us. I believe in Turtle Rock Studios, and I eagerly await to see what they do next.
So, with happy memories and optimism to fuel me, I bid you all one final "Happy Hunting."
Until next time...

Roguelikes are a dime a dozen these days, but this one should turn your head for 4 reasons:
1) It's like nothing you've played.  Is it a Roguelike? Tower defense? An RPG? A 4X game?  All of the above.
2) It has polish to spare.  The pixel art is beautiful and bursting with character, the soundtrack establishes a strong sense of place, and every bit of the UI feels well-considered.
3) It's fair.  Unlike many other roguelikes, when you die, there's a very high chance it was your fault.  The mechanics are slowly doled out, some of them rather subtle, and your mastery of them typically dictates how far you advance.
4) It's packed with content. There are characters to unlock and any number of alternative modes to try on top of two difficulty levels, the harder of which I've just toppled at 30 hours.
Amplitude is quickly becoming one of my favorite devs, and here they've created something frighteningly compelling with all the compulsive one-more-turn-itis of a civ game.  Handily one of the best games of the year.

Dungeon of the Endless is a beautiful mash up of different genres that is really hard to identify.
It is a rogue lite, tower defense, survival, resource management game with a bit of rpg thrown in, let me elaborate more.
You begin the game after you choose your starting party of two people, these characters are the survivors of an attack at your ship near a mysterious planet. You choose a pod your heroes escaped in, which dramatically changes the rules of the dungeon, and off you go in your emergency landing, deep inside this strange complex. From there on, your only chance to escape the planet, is to carry your crystal from the damaged pod up to the surface. You have to use elevators to do this, they effectively mark the start and the end of each level. The game consists in exploring every floor searching for the exit, but also for resources, merchants, weapons, other survivors or who knows what your next objective might be. In the meantime, your dust reserve is used to power up the complex while you explore, because dark areas spawn monsters, and monsters have a nasty habit of wanting to break your crystal... so what do you do? You build minor modules to protect the path you carve in the complex, you build major modules to help you attain resources every door you open, you research new or upgraded versions of the modules you can build and onward to adventure. As for your heroes, every character has his set of skills, level up progression, statistics and possible equipment slots, which promotes customization and adaptability. The game has two levels of difficulties, one is doable, the other one is pretty tough.
Of course the game has tons of replay value, everything being randomized except items, modules and heroes, every room and branching is randomized so there is no chance you will have the same game twice, even the merchants sell not only different stuff, but even accept a random resource for trade. The multiplayer is great but I suggest grabbing a friend since this a highly strategical game, more than an action one, but I've met my fair share of reasonable people online.
If that wasn't enough, we are talking about the Endless lore, the same you find on Endless Space and Endless Legend, which is really cool if you're fan of the work Amplitude is doing, even the resources represent the FIDS system from the game (Food, Industry, Dust, Science).
Overall I had a blast with this little title, I wasn't even expecting much but it became one of my favorite indie rogue like titles really fast. Not everyone appreciates it though (like one of my friends) though I still can't understand him, this game has everything one could ever hope for, it's original and cheap too!

Being perfectly honest I have no idea how I ended up getting this game. Not sure if it was a gift, part of a pack of games I got for free on a random page or whatever, but it’s an actually quite interesting game. However as usual, I will start with the negative parts of it:
You know, this game let’s you create your own race, heroes and♥♥♥♥♥♥WHICH IS QUITE COOL, however something I totally HATE is not being able to edit that race. The first time you make your own, you'll have NO IDEA WHAT YOU’RE DOING, so being able to test it out and change what doesn’t work out should be a pretty normal thing to have. But no, the option isn’t there, which is disappointing.
Something that I also don’t quite like is how passive the AI always seems to be. If you don’t play in really high difficulty matches, it always seems that it’s me the one being an #sshole and invading others, as they never seem to make a move. And when they finally do, it’s some sort of suicidal attack that’s as pointless as a submarine on Mars.
Lastly, the game has a feature of not letting heroes die, but instead damaging them permanently. It’s a system I like, however if a hero gets killed by the last damn enemy, doesn’t matter how many heads he bashed into the ground, not only he doesn’t get ANY EXPERIENCE but he also gets injured for life. That’s bullsh#t. At least give him less XP, but not NO XP AT ALL!
However, ignoring the negative stuff, what do we have left? A weird mix between Civilizations and Final Fantasy Tactics… Of all things. Yeah, it’s a weird f#cking mix but it actually works quite well.
As I’ve said before, you create your own race and play against custom or default other races in open maps, what sets this game apart from other Civ clones however, is the RPG style it has. There are items, quests and monsters out there, and your heroes level up and get quite powerful as they grow.
The game also has a unit creator tool, quite basic but it gives you the choice of setting your own troops by default, as expensive and game-breaking as you see fit. It’s quite fun… But since enemies won’t use it, their troops usually never catch on to you.
Maps usually also have some story and mayor quests going on, something that I totally like. And since most players on the map will want to clear those out, it adds to the competitive nature of these kind of games.
Is it a good game? Yeah, it is. However it seems to be kinda obscure and not well known. I would recommend it for any Civilizations fan who wants to try something new, although as usual, on a good sale.
TL;DR Edition: Civilizations mixed with RPG and turn-based elements. A good mix, with a few problems that are easy to overlook. Good for fans of strategy games, and a solid purchase on a sale.

I read the reviews on this game and honestly, I don't know if can go by them or not anymore.  I ordered the ultimate package so I would have the add-ons, paid the full $40, and for that amount I will be replacing every other game I own.  Here is why...
I love Civ series games, Heroes of M&M, Age of Wonders, Endless legends, GalCiv etc, those types of games, but they always had me looking for ways to make: decisions, resources, battles, buildings, etc to mean more and to be more meaningful, more important in the game while not sacrificing anything too much.  For me, Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes Ultimate pack is the game that finally did that in a satisfying way.
The Civ aspect in FE:LH is that you will need to establish cities to expand and keep up with the game.  Now there is not unlimited city placement freedom, as in you cannot build just anywhere, but just pick a bigger map and there will be plenty of places.  Picking a location is much less complex since you base it on just one tile and then primarily its resources instead of mostly tiles.  From there, your city is a lot more about what you build in it and the path you take with your city.  There are many paths your city can take.  In fact, just to start it will become either a Fortress, a Conclave, or a Town, and what you want and in which order depends on your style and position your kingdom is in, because each of those choices branch into choices of their own set of choices.  So it isn't Civ, but it does what Civ does in a less technical, more obvious and transparent, yet sets up meaningful choices and decisions for developement, not resting on just placement and specialization.
One thing to note is there are no airplanes are boats, that part of Civ is gone from FE:LH.  There is no underground like in AoW either, so there is only one dimension, but in this one dimension is actual multi dimensional exploration; the land is broke into areas that feel like their own and require more of your army to be able to explore.  Even when you reveal the whole map, the world just unfolds into a giant search for a bigger army, better loot, with the constant hope of finding something else awesome with the epic you just got until the map is cleared...basically, it is an epic waiting to unfold as you explore the world each time.
Another big thing that is different in FE:LH is battle.  You can do battle like in Civ in this game and just let the computer throw dice for you... or you can actually control the field and make combos and plans that make losing numbers an invincible force.  It isn't always that way, sometimes you are just s.o.o.l. but that is how it goes.  This difference makes the whole feel of battle change, it feels meaningful and important.  Not only does it decide the fate of your army, but each battle can cost more or less depending on how much you pour in to it.  The battles are simple and fast, but require good use of characters to change the tide of victory.
The fantasy thing isn't my real calling, but the fantasy nature is one that is both fitting and natural, to the point where the fantasy world seems believable.  The art is considered less than good by many, but when I play it I see detail and character, clean and easy to look at, I wouldn't change a thing about it.
The real draw for me though, besides the customization and how you can make your Civilization as many ways as you can think of, is that figuring them out in a game so full of characters that also have their own paths, that just exploring the map is fun each and every game, because it is so different and it is how you build your character.  Character building is now as important as empire building and for me, that is worth trading in underground, sea, air, and space tiles.
If you want a spin on world building that includes character building and kingdom design and you don't mind having to get creative to get the full experience, say goodbye to Sid and your family and try out FE:LH Ultimate Edition.
This game is buggy as hell; extremely unpolished and unbalanced 4x experience. Definately look elsewhere if you're looking to scratch that 4x fantasy itch.

Fans of the Red Faction series should be weary when making the decision to purchase this game. Although this is a canonical installment that follows the events of Red Faction: Guerilla, it's quite a departure from the games before it and thus a total disappointment.
The story in this game is extremely lackluster and forgettable, which is too bad. Without giving too much away and ruining the fun, they essentially discarded the core of what made the RF games so great. So, instead of playing through a turbulent revolution on the barren red planet, the main character must ward off the threat of "Aliens", which may or may not be some strange Ultor experiment gone astray and hid deep underground. Again, the plot is extremely loose and riddled with holes, none of the characters are particularly unique but it serves as a passable backdrop for the action. Looking back at this game, there were a lot of missed opportunities to make it a really special experience, despite the choice to go with the whole "Alien" threat.
I enjoyed this game for its simplicity..a return to the roots of the franchise. It grabs elements of the first two to make for a vaugely nostalgic linear romp through tunnels, caverns and the windy plains of Mars. Some forced vehicle segments and a ton of weapons to play with. There's also a small skill tree you can customize to help buff character stats. It's a pretty easy game on Normal mode, but this may come in handy for hardcore difficulty settings.
Objectives become rinse and repeat after a while. You'll find yourself basically clearing spawn rooms of insectoid foes, and repairing junk in order to proceed through a level.
If you played Guerilla, you might recall the Nano-Forge. Instead of being installed in a rifle, it's now built in to the main character's gauntlet. Being able to recreate demolished sections of stages to build bridges or create cover for yourself turns out to be an amusing gimmick, and it gets pretty engaging when chaos erupts during firefights. So much more could have been done with this idea that I find it a tad lamentful. Just like the story. Oh well.
Clocking in at around 12-15 hours for the single player campaign, this is a pretty short game that will leave little to no impact on you upon completion. There's a New Game + feature which is a nice touch, but I'd be forcing myself really hard to want to play this a second time, and so soon. Forget the Infestation mode, it's worthless at this juncture in time. It's redundant but might be have some fleeting value if you have a group of buddies or miraculously find one or two strangers online wanting to play it..but the chances of that are slim to none.  To no surprise,  Ruin mode was the more neglected of the two extra features paired with the single player campaign. There are 8 timed stages to play through in which the player must cause as much chaos and destruction as possible. This deserved way more attention than the copious Infestation levels, that featured 30 waves a piece!! (!???)
Alas, from what I gather, the incentive for playing these two modes are pretty worthless.  A few guns to enhance single player that won't add much variation to the mix. Skip them, or dabble with Ruin mode for a bit. That's what I did.
Lastly, I will touch upon the Path To War DLC. What a stinker. I bought this on sale for like, 1.99. I don't really regret it, nor do I feel cheated due to its short length. What this DLC really felt like was carved bits and pieces from the main game that Volition/THQ felt the need to remove in order to charge desperate suckers like myself a few extra bucks in order to milk the most cash out of the game.
In all honesty, these were some of the better experiences I had with the game though. Mostly Human VS Human fighting, which the single player campaign really needed more of. However, the levels just feel like content that never made it past the cutting room. They are poorly threaded together with little to no story inbetween, and suffer from lazy level design. There's one particular tank stage that could have been amazing. Instead, you find yourself carefully moving up and around a linear winding path blowing up stuff here and there. Major let down.
Listen, I love the Red Faction series. I grew up with the first one, I kind of hated 2 and adored Guerilla. I won't compare Armageddon to any of these..it's just not a fair assessment. If you're like me and want to take a trip down nostalgia lane, play it..It's okay. It kind of jumped the shark with the whole insect "Alien" baloney and settled for being completely generic. For a Sci-Fi Third Person Shooter, it had its moments. It's a decent distraction. As a Red Faction game, quite watered down and skippable. There are tons of other games similar to this with way better stories, set pieces and game design. Maybe play those instead, or get this when its under 5 bucks.

You will build a base, cover the windows with curtains, learn skills to help you survive, and become complacent that you have comfortably beat the game... You will be wrong, and you will die... horribly.
You will strike the forums, complain and whine at how unfair the events that just transpired. You will read, and learn, and come back to the game better than you were before.
You will ravage your neighborhood for supplies.
You will build up a base to survive in, and enforce it with barricades, walls, take out the stairs, strike out and loot half the town. Surrounded by guns, axes, melee weapons, and an arsonal of equipment, you will overcome the challenges before you. And just when you think you've beaten the game... The game will throw a curveball at you... and you will die alone, hungry, huddled in the dark...
You will hit the forums again, aggrivated and frustrated that your character surivived weeks this time, just to die such a meaningless death. You will do yet more research, learn so much more, and come back into the game a zombie killing champion...
You clear your own place.
Build your own base.
Build your survival resources to last you long past the fall of the civilization you once clung to.
You will watch the coming challenges, and this time... you will still die... because this game is about how you died...

A dull, shallow game about changing colors and moving boxes. And moving boxes. And moving even more boxes.
Normally, I don't write reviews for games I don't especially like since they aren't worth the time to dole out a simple 6 or 7 and be done with it. They're mediocre, but never offensively bad. Hue is the straw that breaks the camel's back and is everything wrong with indie platformers in this day and age. It's all frills and dressing, but no substance. It's all about flash and pomp, but as shallow as a puddle when it comes to gameplay.
You play as the eponymous Hue, a kid who's looking for their missing mother and along the way, discovers the power to render the world in specific colors to get by obstacles and clear rooms. On paper, it sounds like nothing special but with a lot of room for potential. However, I don't think I've ever played a game that so undermined its own concept to the point where the puzzles are both tedious and mind numbingly easy. Boiled down, puzzles are based around the concept of making certain props vanish or appear based on the color you select. Instead of having creative enemies, platforming, color combinations, or anything remotely in-depth that would require strategy, the developers present the player with two types of puzzles. Reflex puzzles, which can be fun but are still relatively easy, where you switch colors to avoid obstacles and jump from platform to platform. These are okay.
Box puzzles, which make up the vast majority of puzzles in this game, are not okay. These puzzles require you to push or move boxes in specific colors or ways, sometimes swapping the colors four to five times just to reach one end of a platform to another to block a specific laser from zapping you, in order to reach a key, and then repeat that in reverse order, spending a good minute or two getting through it while thinking over the puzzle takes no more than 10 seconds to figure out. I don't understand why the developers would limit themselves to puzzles that remain the worst aspect of other puzzle games such as Professor Layton, but without any ounce of charm, endearment, be it through visuals or music.
From a graphical standpoint, the game relies too much on minimalism to hide the lack of thought and effort that went into the game. Details are limited to prefabricated tiles, backgrounds, and occasionally items in the world, and partway through, I found myself somehow wanting to play Fez instead. Fez, for all its faults, had gorgeous artwork and environments that still hold up today. Hue, on the other hand, is like looking at a sheet of charcoal with bright primary and secondary colors interspersed through outlines and empty space. Normally, I'm not too hard on artstyle choice or graphics, but when the gameplay is irritating and dull, it makes me wish I was playing a Professor Layton game instead. At least those games had a wonderful variety of puzzles, charming characters, and a cozy aesthetic with wonderful soundtracks.
In other words, if you like games that try to dress themselves up as being particularly deep or introspective without having an ounce of anything fruitfal, or if you have a particular fondness for puzzle games that are more like chores than actual puzzles,  then maybe this is the game for you. Otherwise, I cannot recommend Hue to anybody in particular. It does too little of anything to leave an impression and too much tedium to make it worth revisiting. Avoid it and save your money.

Highly recommend this game. I enjoyed the puzzles, and the unfolding story. Reminds me of Toki Tori 2+ (though more similar graphics to the original toki tori), another game I have sunk many hours into.
Initial gameplay can be a bit confusing - while the controls are easy and the puzzles are easy enough initially, growing in difficulty as you progress - the open worldness of the map tends to make you feel rather lost. If you can ignore the fact your digging randomly deeper into the unknown without a clue as to where you are heading, you eventually gain your bearings and the navigation isn't too bad after that. There is a teleport feature to help you get back to previous explored regions as well, which comes in handy when you are going back to solve those puzzles you couldn't figure out first time.
The simple story of gathering gems and rescuing the miners can be done very fast avoiding most maps areas and puzzles but you can go back to regions and complete afterwards, with new conversations and a more complete ending (roll the credits a second time when you are done).
Only complaint are the two 'boss' type levels. There is one race which takes quite a bit of skill to win (though you don't need to win for storyline), and the 'dark sun' level which is frustratingly difficult and requires a bit of rewinding to get it done. Also didn't feel the game was complete until I had managed this though, as it gave the full ending. Felt out of place with the rest of the puzzles you could stop and think about, rather than dashing around unable to stay still for more than 2 seconds!
So anyone buying needs to be aware there is a high-speed element to the game, but mostly just logical puzzle solving that's heaps of fun! Almost didn't finish the boss levels, but with some determination I managed and was def worth it :)
