I don't particularly enjoy giving this game a bad review, because it's evident so much effort went into it. But...
"Full Bore" is an open-world 2D puzzle-platformer where you assume the role of a boar that has to, well, bore around. There's no intro, you're just thrown into an adventure where you gradually discover the story
. The game doesn't hold your hand. Beside the most basic of commands, you're given no explanations or hints, but are instead left to figure it all out for yourself. The visuals and audio are likewise very nice.
However... the game was simply...
. The core gameplay consists of digging through the Earth, solving a series of block puzzles in order to progress and collect gems. Each puzzle is solvable as soon as you chance upon it, and there are no hidden abilities, or power-ups, or unlockables of any kind. Your only ability is a time-rewind function, which is really just an implementation of an undo button. You can't run out of the rewind power, like with the sands of time in "Prince of Persia", for example. Not even enemies exist here, not in the usual form, at least. In "Full Bore" you just kind of go, and dig.
So, why explore the world and solve puzzles as all? To collect gems and unravel the story. The story, while certainly promising, isn't THAT good. The gems themselves don't seem to give you anything tangible other than the satisfaction of having collected them. The visuals get a bit confusing here. Because of the 2D sometimes it's hard to distinguish what's the foreground and what's the background. With some timed puzzles and/or mini-games, it'll be a source of frustration.
Personally, I'm not much of a fan. If you're different in that regard, then "Full Bore" should be a no-brainer.

After this new patch I find it very hard to recommend this game to anyone, I do love the artstyle and really appreciate the amount of effort the developers have put into this game, but after this patch it seems like the devs are just making the game harder, it's really hard to appreciate the animation and music when 90% of the game you see is the "YOU DIED" screen.

A game that was previewed at E3 2014, Cuphead is a game that is meant to combine 2D side-scrolling shooters with 1930's cartoon style. It is an ambitious undertaking from Studio MHDR Entertainment. There is a very heavy focus on boss fights with a break in the form of side-scrolling levels that have coins to pick up and use to purchase more powerful abilities.
Graphics
A gorgeous, colorful, piece of art. It really was made using techniques from the 1930's cartoons. It uses hand-painted watercolor animations to capture the essence of that era's cartoons. The actions are fluid; more fluid than what you see in a lot of games that are produced by larger companies. There are a huge variety of different enemies; each look unique and act differently. Each of the bosses are also different in look and feel; keeping the numerous boss fights fun and engaging.
Controls/Complexity
Controls are smooth, which is a must for a game as difficult as this one. There are six different weapons, a handful of different power-ups and supers for your character, and everything is very distinctive from each other. That said, it's really easy to pick up; but each level is punishing to the max; challenging your skills as far as you think you can go; and then further. Every boss will destroy you until you learn what each attack looks like. That said, no boss has a set pattern to their attacks, as the boss fights are not set patterns like most games of this type. They are random attacks; so learning what each one looks like to start and how to dodge them is pivotal to beating them.
Expect to die often.
That said, the game does a good job of making you feel like the deaths are your fault, and not due to some arbitrary luck from the computer.
The game feels like it was meant for controller, as it was supposed to be an Xbox only release that was put out on Steam as well. Unfortunately for the PS4 owners, there has been no word on a PS4 release as of the time of this review.
Story
Story is pretty simple. You control Cuphead (Mughead in 2 player games) after he has a really good run of luck at a casino, and makes a bet with the devil. He loses that bet, and begs to keep his soul. The Devil tells him that they can keep their souls as long as they act as debt collectors and retrieve the contracts on souls that other people owe him.
You set out to collect those souls, and hoping to find a way to get out of your debt with him.
Grade-A
A solid A. Almost perfect in every regard. Even the music; which is very reminiscent of the 1930's jazz is beautiful. Studio MHDR has created what might be the best first release from a company that I have ever had the pleasure to play. Everything comes across damn near perfectly.

Before I start this review I just want to say the overreaction to the comparison to Dark Souls & difficulty towards Cuphead isn't fair at all in my opinion, the best way to describe this game is that it's a 1920-1930s cartoon version of Metal Slug, Contra & Mega Man.
The laughs were great though at all the fails this game has delivered from streamers & etc. with no self-awareness for their surroundings at all even if I don't understand how Cuphead can make someone break their keyboard or controller at all (it's really fun to play with a friend & is more of a chill game for me) when the game makes it clear that every death is the player's fault.
The only way I would understand anyone raging at this game is if your playing pacifist on a Run 'N' Gun level or Expert mode.
The tutorial debacle was honestly the cringiest thing I ever watched though & for anyone that hasn't seen it prepare to lose some brain cells.
Now to start with this review the only con I can give the game is the default keyboard controls (they're really bad) & my personal preferred control scheme for this game if I do play on keyboard is:
AWSD - Move Cuphead
Space - Jump
Up Arrow Key - Fire Gun
Left Arrow Key - Dash
Right Arrow Key - Lock
Down Arrow Key - EX Move
E - Change Weapon
The game plays well with a controller too so it doesn't matter what you pick.
If you delve into Expert mode I would recommend the Spread & Charge gun combination.
You might have to change the gun combo up a bit for hard to hit bosses like the Dragon for example which I would recommend the Lobber & Spread but overall I think the Spread & Charge Combo does the job of finishing boss battles as quickly as possible.
For the rest of the review all I can say is that this is the most original game I have ever played.
I'm extremely impressed that the 2 brothers that are responsible for every animation in this game used the actual old methods/techniques that Warner Bros, Fleischer Studios, Disney & etc. used to make Cuphead so unique & I would watch a Cuphead cartoon series if it was possible at all.
I don't have any words on how amazing the Jazz (Maybe Blues too) soundtrack for this game is & the behind the scenes for some of the tracks is extremely impressive.
No DLC at all which is how games used to be so A+ for none of that crap in Cuphead & an extremely fair price for 15+ hours of gameplay.
2 player local co-op for this game was the most fun I ever had in a long time since I barely play any multiplayer games anymore because in my opinion online multiplayer was a nice thing for a while but then it got boring when game studios got less creative & I wouldn't be shocked if Cuphead does get an online co-op feature in the future.
Every boss battle on this game was fun for me to play against (King Dice is my fav boss & the Phantom Express was my least fav on regular mode + I'm still playing through expert mode so I might update this review) & I hope to god the two brothers behind this game don't dumb the game down in anyway because this game to me can motivate anyone to improve their skills in platformers.
The story to the game is pretty straightforward about Cuphead & his brother Mugman owing the Devil money at the Casino so I won't talk much about it.
Overall if you haven't played this game yet I would strongly just buy it full price because it's one of the few games in my opinion that deserves it & Studio MDHR don't let greedy corporations like Microsoft or EA for example buy you out.

EDIT: After doing further research I just noticed that the 2 brothers might be Street Fighter enthusiasts if you compare Ryu & Ken with the frogs + Balrog (Bull), Sagat (Tiger) & Vega (Snake) with the slot machine symbols off the final phase of the Clip Joint Calamity level.
The Rat Pack (infamous jazz music group from the 1900s featuring Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin & other famous jazz singers) is a huge influence for the very 1st boss battle in Cuphead
King Dice (my fav boss in Cuphead) is heavily inspired by famous Jazz singer Cab Calloway who was featured in Fleischer cartoons like Betty Boop's Snow White for example (the singer for King Dice's theme song has a resemblance to Louis Armstrong)
One of the animators for Cuphead has revealed that the Baroness Von Bon Bon boss was heavily inspired by starlets from the 1900s
Archive:

The Game Over Screen for the Cigar's face in the King Dice battle is heavily inspired by Lou Bega

Sally Stageplay, Captain Brineybeard (I struggled with him on regular mode but I had fun learning his pattern) & King Dice are my fav bosses to go through on Expert mode.

Outlast + Whistleblower DLC: Fun times in the mad house. (Warning of ending spoilers for Outlast)
Outlast is considered to be one of the scariest games of all time. I was well aware of the game’s reputation. When Humble Bundle emailed me about a giveaway for this game with the Whistleblower DLC I had to take it. God, what a game....
Outlast opens up with Miles Upshur, an investigative journalist arriving at the sinister Mount Massive Asylum after receiving an anonymous email about inhuman treatments at the Asylum. Miles, always wanting a good story sneaks inside to see for himself and everything goes downhill from there for him. Now he must try to make it out of the Asylum and avoid the violent patients while discovering what happened at the Asylum and record as much evidence to destroy the Murkoff Corporation who drove the patients to murder in the first place.
Gameplay is simple at first glance, you are armed with a camcorder which has night vision and is used to record sightings for Miles to build his report. While you have night vision on the battery life drains so you have to balance using the night vision and finding batteries which are scattered throughout the Asylum. You can peak around doors and you can run, you can also hide in the lockers and under tables to help escape should anyone spot you. That is it. There is no combat in this game and it does not need it. It helps add to the nightmarish situation Miles is in. He is just a reporter lost in a place where almost everything wants to kill him. Miles and the player have to use their wits if they want to survive and it is done so well in Outlast.
The atmosphere and the sound design are the strongest points of this game. Just playing this game puts me on edge, the simple act of pausing the game makes the smallest unnerving sound that puts the player on edge, there is very little music with the exception of key moments to insure the full effect is set in. But asides from that all there is Miles terrified mummers, irregular breathing patterns and whatever sounds the docile or hostile patients make while hunting you or busy warped up in their own little world. It is so effective. One standout moment for me is when I was trying to escape one special encounter, hiding in locker hoping and praying that he would not find me. I was such an emotional wreck. That was one of many moments that bring Outlast close to my two favourite horror games, System Shock 2 and Bloodborne. I do not say this lightly. The game’s atmosphere is that brilliant.
So with all of that said Outlast should slide neatly into my Hall of Fame correct?
Wrong.
If it was not for the final moments of the game it would have been in the Hall of Fame quite happily but it sadly does not stick the landing due to one stupid element that is out of place and unnecessary.
Please be warned I am about to spoil a bit of the ending so if you do not want to read this part then please skip over the next paragraph now.
Outlast is one of the best horror games out there, that is a fact. I am really disappointed that the final stage of the game had to take such a silly turn.
Whistleblower is a short (about 2 to 3 hours give or take) piece of DLC that serves as a prequel and parallel story to the main Outlast story. You are Waylon Park this time, a software engineer who was working at Mount Massive and is the one who tipped off Miles Upshur to the treatment of patients. He is discovered and is placed in the Asylum to shut him up. After all hell breaks loose he tries to escape and tell the world. Gameplay is not different at all from the main game and a few familiar enemies appear and some new ones which I will not spoil here.
I would say that Whistleblower is better story wise because even though the silly element is still there it is not quite as prominent in the DLC as it was in the main story. I do consider it a plus.
Outlast + Whistleblower is a terrifying nightmare though hell. It is one of the best horror games out there but sadly it just barely misses being one of the best games due to that one stupid story element.

I'm not going to tell you about the gameplay or the graphics or the performance of Project Zomboid. That would be pointless for a game that has gone through so many different iterations of all of those - an ongoing process - that it could be completely wrong by the time you read this.
Instead, I'll tell you about what really matters for an Early Access game: The developers. I've been following Project Zomboid almost since it's inception, and I've never interacted with a more transparent, good-natured and hard-working bunch of people. If things go wrong, they'll tell you. If things are delayed, they'll tell you why. Community suggestions are heard and are often incorporated into the base game - they've even taken some popular mods and integrated them fully.
I won't lie, PZ has been in development for a long time, but the consistent communication and honesty of the developers makes the waiting that much easier. There are a slew of zombie survival games on the market these days, some of which do some things better than PZ. But they don't have one thing that the Indie Stone has: the Indie Stone team.
I could only recommend one survival game available right now, it will always be Project Zomboid.

Project Zomboid is one of the best zombie games of all time although it is still in development.
Some people might rant about the long time this game has been on Early Access and that some promised features are still yet to come. But they seem not to see the advantage in this longer development period. The devs really care about this game and every detail is made with love.
I spent more than 1.000 hours in PZ and with every little update there is something new to explore. Bugs are rare and I never encountered any game breaking bug in a stable Build. There are frequent updates and if a bug is reported it usually gets fixed within days. But one of the best things in PZ is that the devs are in close contact with their community and a lots of suggestions made by the players have found their way into PZ. Moreover, there are plenty of options to customize your game and PZ can be easily modded and has a great modding community.
I fully recommend this game if you are looking for a Romero-like zombie experience and if you are not too impatient in terms of ETAs.
New features like cars are close to make the zomboid experience even more perfect than it used to be.

Still, there was a demo on Steam, so it couldn't hurt to try that.
Downloaded the demo version, and it worked amazingly, I mean … this was like magic — in 11 minutes, IPT had reduced 81.09% wasted space on a very dense cluster of UV islands down to 19.17% wasted space (retested this a few times, but it consistently achieved this reduction). Unbelievable results and £49.99 was nothing to pay for the full, Indy version, especially considering such UV packing would have taken hours/days by hand, and I'm not sure I could have matched the software's UV density.
Purchased the Indy version, waited a few minutes for the 180 MB install to complete, and fired up the same FBX model with exactly the same settings (made a note of them from the demo beforehand), and clicked the 'Start Packing' button. Within a few seconds the software analysed the mesh, decided there was 100.1% wasted space, and then proceeded to have a go at solving this mathematical impossibility.
Twenty'ish minutes later, it had made not a single iota of progress. There was still 100.1% wasted space, that progress bar kept creeping to the right only for it to reset a few pixels' of movement later, and at this point all those negative Steam / forum reviews — that I had dismissed earlier as the rantings of noobs or people with weak PC setups — suddenly sounded a lot more like the truth.
I tweaked the UI, retested, with the same ridiculous results. I restarted the software, tweaked, retested and was greeted by the same idiotic results. I went through the imported mesh (again) in Blender to make sure I wasn't at fault, re-exported the FBX anyway, retested, and nope full-priced IPT still thought that not only was the UV space in the FBX empty but that I had also, somehow, taken emptiness to a whole new level of impossibility.
So, yes, people — I gave the £49.99 version of IPT 25 minutes of my time, and that is all it deserves, especially considering that the DEMO version CONSISTENTLY solved the imported mesh moreorless PERFECTLY (80.83%) in 11 minutes EVERY SINGLE TIME. And, for anyone thinking I should have tweaked this or that or something else — in the demo, you load in your model, click the 'Start Packing' button, and it just works; you
tweak the hell out of everything, but you can, if you so desire, just click a button, and the demo software works. It just friggin' works. But, no, not the version that costs money; that'd be just too friggin' easy, wouldn't it, [PB]Snoelk?
Who's / what's [PB]Snoelk? This is the developer who introduced IPT to the world on the PolyCount forums (
). So, from one coder to another: Snoelk, fix your code, mate. It's knackered. Worst case scenario, just revert the release code to the demo code and give us all something that works. Or, enable the save button in the demo and return the event code (assuming you removed it). Job done. Everyone's a winner. Until then, it's refunds all-round, though I'll happily re-purchase this software after you've taken a few minutes to fix it.
Until it's fixed (please, fix the software!), just download the demo version, use it to create a super UV layout, and then copy this by hand. Yes, it will be a major pain (especially if you've got lots of tiny islands), but IPT has created the best arrangement of the islands for you; all you've got to do is copy / rotate / scale.
And, thankfully, this story has a happy ending: it took Steam a mere 1 hour, 23 minutes to agree to a refund after my refund request (thank you, Steam).

This game is very well thought through, and has a very high replayability seeing as the many different scenarioes combined with the 4 different classes of hunters, each containing three base characters and more in the form of DLC, and different monsters keep you very well entertained. I loved the premice set for the different hunterclasses, and how each character within a class offers a different way to approach the role. This setup also makes for fantastic co-op plays, as a skilled monster-player can be exstremely difficult to take down if he/she knows how to tear apart your team, avoid your traps and set up traps her/himself or even mislead you in the hunt. The monsters in this game are also very well balanced between endurance and mobility and damage. So when one monster might be very large and tough (As the Behemoth), it is also slower and earthbound, as opposed to the Kraken, for example, that flies and damages players from a large distance, but also can't take as much of a beating as the Behemoth.
The game can easily be played as singleplayer, seeing as the AI's function very well. The only problem here might be getting the trapper-bots to actually track the monster for you. This is a minor thing though, since the first trapper available has a tracking dog that you can "activate" even when not playing as the tracker yourself.
So all in all, I really enjoy this game, and i can only recommend others who like co-op shooting games to try this one out aswell!

Just one more.
Just one more.
Just one more.
Eventually, just one more can kill ya. Because at some point, you don't have enough resources to keep the darkness at bay. And as most adventurers will tell you, the darkness is where the wild things are.
Dungeon of the Endless pits you and up to 3 of your friends against a randomly-tiled subterranean bunker, where you'll have to explore, strategize, and ultimately gamble your way back to the surface. So you open a door. Then another. And that's where the game gets interesting. Because while you plan where your nodes are being placed, and where you're placing your heroes, you're trying not to overextend yourself, and betting that you can face whatever holes there are in your defenses. For the enemies, meanwhile, time stops, and all is quiet. But as soon as you open that door, you have to face the consequences. The back and forth between having as much time as you want, and then having to cope with all your plans going awry, is what gives the game its roguelike edge. And the decision players have to make at some point when they play, is "Is that one more door worth it?"
But before you reach that point, you have to learn what the game doesn't tell you. Also like many roguelike games, Dungeon of the Endless gives you just a taste of the game's fundamentals, before leaving you to figure out other things on your own. That in itself is part of the appeal-- finding things out for yourself as you play, and using that knowledge to play your next session better.
(Psst! Here. The first one's free: heroes placed in an unpowered room count as "lighting" it.)
For me, a lot of the appeal of Dungeon of the Endless is in its pixel art, and by extension, all of the colorful heroes that can be unlocked. That tiny bit of persistence makes it easier to swallow when it all comes tumbling down on you. Hi, i'm Don, and i'm junky...a rogue-like junky. See, a game that challenges you to try again and again, hoping for that run that merges luck and skill into the best outcome, it's fun, and great, and will make you lose track of time because you will be more concern in making risk decisions rather than going to bed, or talk to your dog, or eat. With that said, does Dungeon of the Endless achieve this? The answer is yes... and no.
Let's just say that the presentation and the set are fine, they inmerge the player into the odd world that surrounds the heroes. The plot reveals itself in tiny bits, mostly through concept art that you unlock achieving objectives, wich is a rather nice and interesting way to tell a story. But, what matters here is the gameplay and here is when things start to get clunky.
At first, the experience will engross you. You will rapidly star to make strategies on how to manage your resources, where to build modules that help you to repel enemy hordes, which hero is better for exploration or combat, which rooms are convinient to power up, how to use items and abilities, etc., and that will make you have a blast through the first 6, 7 floors. But when you reach floor number 8, a factor that's always present in a rogue-like game, but in a tolerable quantity, will dominate your♥♥♥♥♥ That factor is LUCK.
Of all my playhtoughs on the hard mode (which the game list it as "easy", something i find awkward), luck was the definitive factor in my failure. You may say, "You suck, ♥♥♥♥♥.", but when you open several doors without finding ANY resources, when you don't get ANY item that favor any of your heroes, when suddenly a EMP discharge breaks every module on a room next to the cristal, when the swarms of enemies are just too large because you weren't lucky enough to find energy to power up rooms, when the research crystal throws at you tecnology that's useless, when the heroes that you find sucks balls because they don't go with your team, when the bloody exit it's in the last of 30 doors you open, you will blame LUCK, and you will be frustated, i guarantee it. Add the fact that the runs of this games are long, like 3 or 4 hours, so how do you think you will feel when you spend 3 hours only to reach a floor cursed by mother♥♥♥♥in' Fortuna, that throws away all your effort? And you wanna know something? I wanted to finish the game, so i turned down the game to normal, and guess how many tries did it take me to finish it? ONE.
In the end, the biggest flaw of DotE, is it's balance. The hard mode (or in other word, the FUN mode), depends greatly on luck when your reach the few last floors, and the normal mode it's just to easy to even think about an strategy. I will not say that it's a bad game, but try to get it on sale, or if you want to try a rogue-like game, go with angband or risk of rain or rogue legacy.

I really, really want to like RFA, but I just can't. Light spoiler ahead.
It mostly addresses problems that RFG had, like providing an open world-ish environment, but then making it nearly impossible to find all the collectibles scattered around that world. (Finding all the audio recorders is still a matter of ignoring the plot and wandering all over the area you've just completed in hopes that you'll spot a recorder. You won't ever be able to go back, so you have to hope you find them on this run.)
This time, though, you'll actually NEED the Nano Forge's reconstruction ability--it's not clear why it even existed in RFG. Nanite reconstruction is fun to play with, but, in RFA, you'll actually need and want to use it. This was a rather glaring omission in its predecessor. Also, the range of the reconstructor has been extended, and it's not nearly as fiddly as in RFG. (In RFG, it was too easy to point the reconstructor straight at something that you wanted to rebuild, and watch nothing at all happen when you pulled the trigger.)
The story is a bit more wobbly than RFG's relatively simple good-vs.-evil plot. It suggests, heavy-handedly, that the entire opening sequence was orchestrated by the Red Faction leadership in some way, but doesn't bother to provide a plausible reason why. Instead of dropping small hints and letting you form your own suspicions, you're fed other peoples' suspicions via the audio recorders... if you can find them. Since I haven't finished the game, I can't tell whether this is a heavy-handed setup for a twist that will see the RF leadership cleared of suspicion... or if it's ruining a major plot point by revealing it in well in advance.
Despite a few story issues, overall I was having fun. The controls seem a bit tighter than RFG, and you'll be playing with a mix of RFG weapons and new-for-RFA weapons. There's a nice new upgrades system, although upgrade tiers are still locked behind story progression, so the end result isn't very different from RFG in the end. You just won't be visiting Samara or an equivalent; there are upgrade and weapons locker stations scattered along your path--you may even have to rebuild them from scrap. Progression is notably more linear, and you can't wander off into a Martian desert to fight randomly generated Marauders and scrape together some more ore. I tend to view that as a good thing.
So, I was having a reasonable amount of fun, and I'd completed the prologue when--crash. To desktop.
Thus began a long run of playing with recommended tweaks and fixes, plus a few I made up myself. I discovered immediately that task-switching, while it doesn't crash the game, does make the Windows desktop unusable. Input latency shoots up into the range of seconds-per-keypress, so don't expect to be able to do things while the game's still running.
Unfortunately, nothing I did seemed to trigger a crash or reduce the number of crashes. Switching from the DX11 executable to the DX9 one was an obvious fix... except nothing was fixed. Fiddling with other game settings like fullscreen/windowed didn't help, and you wouldn't expect running RFA with elevated privileges to help, either, RFA being a firmly post-Vista game. A few hidden settings changes didn't make a difference, either.
The switch to DX9 did seem to reduce crashes a bit, to the point that I could at least get to the next checkpoint before a crash. As the maps got larger, crashes started to happen more often again, and finally I gave up when I could no longer reach the next checkpoint before a crash--somewhere around 37% story completion, I think.
Unfortunately, at least one problem here is a clear case of subpar console port: you can save at any time, but a save between checkpoints will kick you back to the most recently completed checkpoint when you load the game. I wasn't paying attention to whether scrap or ammo levels were being restored, but it doesn't make a lot of difference in the end: the important part was saving my progress in a map, which the PC-appearing save system doesn't actually do at all.
I love the series, I loved RFG despite its warts, and I'd love to be able to recommend RFA. Since I've been prevented from finishing it, or even getting near finishing it,
There've been no updates in a long time, and I don't expect to see any.

This game has honestly surprised me. The middling reviews and general lukewarm response this game got had me pretty wary, especially since I'm honestly not a massive fan of Guerrilla.
Armageddon is as straight as a side-scroller. Get past that, and you might find, like me, that it's better in virtually every way.
Tight controls that encourage constant movement over seeking cover. Great enemy design with lots of aliens of different shapes, sizes, and attack patterns that attack from all angles - above and below. Fully destructible environments that melt, explode, shatter, crumble, and disintegrate with every impact. Gloriously brutal weaponry including sticky grenade launchers, flamethrowers, beam cannons, singularity bombs, and a magnet gun that, combined with the highly destructible arenas throughout, make for the most entertaining weapon since the Portal gun. Fantastic pacing with tons of action moved along by a number of great vehicle sections, including mechanized attack suits, walking tanks, and even a 6DOF corridor shooter setpiece that pays loving and very un-subtle tribute to Volition's heritage with Descent - all in a hilariously destructive and very Red Faction manner.
The story's just a big, loud, dumb, and plot-hole riddled excuse to shoot up aliens, but it doesn't take itself seriously and totally works in a Sci-fi B-movie kind of way. It entertains with some impressively animated cutscenes - I haven't seen characters look and move this good since Uncharted 3 - and the voice acting is better than expected, with some genuinely charming dialogue and banter. It doesn't hurt the game is absolutely gorgeous and superbly optimized.
Bottom line - Armageddon is fun. It doesn't change the world, and it doesn't need to. It knows what it does, and it does it arguably better than most of it's over-ambitious and too-serious competition. It's a shooter where the mere act of shooting is an absolute joy. Sit down, relax, have a laugh, blow stuff up. One of the finest shooters I've ever played.

Block-pushing, dirt-digging, gem-collecting puzzles with no jump button.
I didn't do a lot of research before trying this game, so I was basically expecting a different flavor of Steamworld Dig.
Full Bore is, at its core, a series of increasingly complex block puzzles, but the puzzles are strung together to form a somewhat open world. It's kinda like Fez in that several of the puzzles are actually your travel route between areas, and other puzzles are optional for collection of treasure. On the plus side, it provides a nice cohesive framework instead of just giving you a typical puzzle game menu where you choose your next puzzle from a list. The downside is that backtracking can be a pain, although there is a warp system.
The actual puzzles generally involve a combination of digging and pushing. You can't jump. Different types of tiles behave differently: Some are suspended in place unless you dig through, some are unbreakable, some are fragile and will break just from the shock of you using the Stomp command from a close distance. Also, there's no jumping.
Did I mention you can't jump? For the uninitiated, this is extremely disorienting. You can hop up one tile height increment at a time (like stairs) by holding down a particular button (It's actually the same button that causes you to dig out the tile directly above you, which was very confusing to me when I came back to play months after doing just the tutorial).
There are no player "lives", but there are checkpoints in pretty much all of the active puzzle areas, and there is a somewhat Braid-esque rewind function. If you get stuck, you can rewind incrementally or all the way back to the checkpoint (or the door you came through, if you haven't touched a checkpoint since then). The downside to combining the open-world format and the checkpoint system is that if you get stuck on a puzzle [after touching a checkpoint] and you just can't figure it out, you pretty much have to quit to the main menu and reload your file in order to access a different route. With very few exceptions, you can follow any path you want. There are no incremental powerups that you need to unlock in order to access The Next Area. If you can find a puzzle or a secret, you have the means to solve it. I got stuck a lot in the early stages because I didn't understand the different tiles & their properties, but getting stuck in later stages led to a lot of "a-ha!" moments.
Some of the puzzles have time-sensitive elements, but the majority of them are pretty generous about giving you plenty of time to make your moves. The rewind function is a great asset, especially during the more complex multi-stage puzzles. Using time controls feels a little clumsy at times, I guess due to how it decides which points to remember. It's not that it smoothly rewinds playback (a la Braid), but it jumps back from point to point based on when it decides you made a significant-enough movement or action.
I'm going to talk about the racing segment now.
There is an extremely frustrating race against an NPC. You're required to do it, but you don't have to win to progress. You don't have to win it at all, as long as you don't care about getting 100%. In order to win, you essentially have to have flawless control of your boar through a really long obstacle course. Since the majority of the game is a series of low-stakes thoughtful non-time-sensitive puzzle solving, a high-speed high-precision segment is extremely frustrating, and the hit-or-miss nature of the rewind system means you might do more harm than good by trying to rewind partway.
There's a lot of atmosphere in this game, and I'll admit I was a little put off by the aesthetic in some areas, which is not to say that it isn't well-crafted! It's grungy, punky, and bluesy all at the same time. The sights and sounds definitely contribute to the mood and feeling in a major way. It's easy for me to imagine how different the game would feel if the exact same maps had been skinned and scored differently. The lore is interesting and ominous, and builds up very slowly. The other characters that you meet aren't especially deep, but I can easily forgive that since so much of the game involves being isolated.
I definitely recommend Full Bore to anybody who likes tough-but-possible puzzle games, or who wants to have more games starring boars.

BalanCity is, at its heart, a city building skin on a physics based puzzle game.  The premise its a simple one, build a city on a platform resembling a seesaw with the goal being to get it as high as possible while still functioning as a city and not falling over.  This is of course made more difficult by the addition of  disasters like meteors, attacking monsters, earthquakes, fires, and so on.  These aren't a necessity, however, as you can increase or decrease their frequency to zero if you want to remove that portion of the game.  It also includes various challenges that have you doing specific tasks like building under dire conditions or on oddly designed platforms, and also scenarios where you're tasked with recreating twisted versions of famous cities like New York and San Francisco on set maps.
All of this seems appealing on paper and that's why I initially picked it up.  The low price tag also contributed to that (it's even cheaper as of this writing on Steam than I paid a week ago on Chrono.gg).  However in practice it seems a little less engrossing than I had originally expected.  There's very little  of the standard city building gameplay that you find in classics like SimCity, where you're trying to maintain a profitable budget that also attracting new citizens, industry, and commerce.  Instead the only limitations between you and the goal of ever-taller balanced cities is having enough housing,office buildings, and power to run each.  There's some mechnaics involving grouping housing and offices together to be transformed in to more stable and effective building blocks, but I rarely see a way to keep them going past some of the initial placement.  The real meat of the game simply comes down to you trying to keep everything balanced – not so much on the seesaw - but in placing the many irregular  buildings you need for raising your height limit, providing power, or housing your police/fire/hospital/military services.  The latter of which exist to face off against disasters.
BalanCity does appeal to me in small doses, but with the gameplay revolving around balance beyond nearly everything, it almost feels more like it could just be any generic puzzle game involving the balancing of irregular pieces.  After watching the initial trailer I kind of thought that was the way it worked – you'd randomly be given building pieces and the goal was to keep them balanced and still have a functioning city.  I feel like that could even be a game mode that would lead to some crazy situations.
Even though it didn't meet my expectations, I do see the merit in the game and I don't feel that it's fair not to recommend it to people interested in what I've described.  Personally, I don't see myself playing it all that much more, or if so only just to see if I can beat my last high score in the free build mode.  So I'll go ahead and say this is a recommendation due to the obvious care in its design and the tiny sale price tag, but be aware it's not so much for fans of city builders and is probably more at home for people interested in physics puzzles.

Crouching mid-air

"F you"-moments
Hidden blocks smashing you out of nowhere. Not a lot of these and you learn them quickly, but they deserve a (dis)honorable mention as not having random deaths is game design 101.
Multiplayer
Not being able to access the entire game without playing with others is a choice I'm highly skeptical of considering the active player base will dwindle (and probably has already).

This is an incredibly addictive game with some real innovative twists on the roguelike genre by introducing some tower defense elements to the same formula.  You play with a team of up to 4 adventurers and work your way through 12 increasingly difficult levels by opening one random door at a time.  In each room you can build towers which provide resources or have offensive, supportive, or defensive attributes.  Most towers feel useful and provide varied effects which is interesting.  The characters also play differently overall, although many moves are shared which feels like a missed opportunity to create more varied character selections.  The games are relatively long for a roguelike, lasting up to about 2-3 hours.  Games can be saved in single player, but not in multiplayer which makes it an issue to play with a friend in one sitting unless you both have a large amount of free time.  Overall, this is a very fun roguelike with a lot of interesting twists on the formula but still gives the addictively varied random gameplay.

Let me start by stating this: to anyone who says this game is "easy", you're either as skilled as the guy who beat Cuphead with a DDR pad, or a dirty liar who's only fooling themselves. However, this is also not "HURR DURR CUP SOULS LOL HARDEST GAME ON TEH PLANET", in fact it's far from being unbareably difficult. Instead, it's a fantastic mix of classic arcade difficulty with modern precision platforming. It lies perfectly within the realm of skill-based difficulty, with only a few rare missteps into unfair luck-based difficulty. Almost every mistake falls onto the player, with nothing feeling completly unfair. As a proof of point, particularly skilled players can beat the game in about an hour.
Another thing to make note of is that Cuphead is an obvious passion project, with the concept first coming to fruition in 2010 and an overall seven year development cycle. Seven years. Seven years for a $20 indie game. Does this time and effort show?
Hell yes.
First and most famous thing about this title is the animation and art style, which takes heavy inspiration from the classic "rubber hose" cartoons of the 1920s and 1930s. They could've cheated by mimicking this animation on a computer like most studios would, but the developers instead patiently drew over 120,000 still frames to produce beautiful hand-drawn animation. They even could've simply drawn 12 frames a second and played each frame twice like many animation studios from the time period did, but instead they went for the full-fledged Disney technique at a costly and time-consuming 24 frames a second. Their dedication to the animation and art style shows, with smooth, vibrant, and creative visuals that will most certainly withstand the test of time.
And with the inspiration of rubber hose cartoons comes all the whacky things you can get away with in such a cartoon. A queen bee transforms into a bomber plane, a boat comes to life to shoot lasers at you, and even a clown turns into merry-go-round while green penguins lob baseballs at you. In short, every level is both a visual treat and a challenge as the player is constantly on edge for unexpected and nonsensical attacks. While this is a double-edge as nonsensical attacks can work against the overall fairness of a game, the bosses in Cuphead clearly telegraph their attacks in advance to give the player just the right amount of time to prepare to dodge or parry an attack.
The music is another area where Cuphead really shines, with a big-band orchestra playing the original soundtrack for this game. Every song matches the boss fight, and no two songs sound alike. Some tracks that particularly stand out to me are Railroad Wrath, Botanic Panic, Floral Fury, Junkyard Jive, Firey Frolic, and One Hell of a Time (my personal favorite). These tracks absolutely match the kind of boss the player is facing, and really add to the tension and excitment of the fight. To understand what I'm saying, simply play the game with the music muted and see how different the gameplay feels.
The only thing that sorta falters for me is the run and gun levels, they're not quite at the level of polish that the boss fights are. Some do stand out, like Mountain Ascent and Perilous Piers (with this level in specific being notoriously difficult), but for the most part they pale in comparison to the boss levels. It is worth noting that Cuphead was originally going to exclusively feature boss fights with no platforming stages to speak of, so these stages didn't receive as much attention as the boss levels. It's nice that they thought to design and include them, but I thought I should still mention that the platforming stages aren't as good as the boss stages. This doesn't really detract from the overall experience, and  in my eyes the platforming stages are just bonuses to the boss fights.
Overall, every piece of Cuphead is fantastic, the gameplay, the visuals, the sound. Combine these together and you get a stellar experience that leaves me excited to see what other games StudioMDHR will make in the future. It's challenging, it's beautiful, and most importantly, it's fun.

Hue makes me tickled pink, but that might be because I'm looking at it through rose-colored glasses. Other game developers must be green with envy because of what Fiddlesticks Games have accomplished. If you haven't guessed by now, Hue is a game about puns. No wait, that's not right. Hue is a 2D puzzle-platformer that involves the region of the electromagnetic spectrum between the wavelengths of 400 and 700 nanometers. It's a game about color, and it is excellent.
In Hue, you play as Hue, and change the hue. What a delightfully simple concept. Charmingly voiced by Anna Acton, who gingerly guides the player with some conveniently-placed letters, you will be treated to a loosely-defined story about love and perspective. You must find the author of these letters who has found themselves trapped outside the monochrome world. The young boy, Hue, must find eight colors: red, orange, yellow, lime, aqua, blue, purple, and pink. As Hue stumbles upon each, he gains the ability to change the background to that pigment at the press of a button. Changing the color of the background is surely a novelty. You can't make a platformer based on that alone, can you? Well, color me impressed, you can.
Whenever the background changes, all items in the world matching that color will effectively cease to exist. Boxes, ledges, balloons, lasers, and deadly boulders disappear from the world until the background is switched again. To get through a red wall, Hue can switch to red and now there is no wall. So, basically, Hue can give himself the red carpet treatment at any time. This color swapping is used well for both puzzles and platforming.
On the puzzle side, you might have to place an orange box behind a yellow one by making one invisible and dragging the other through it. You can use these boxes to trigger pressure switches that open doors by cycling through the palette. Later, Hue will need to deal with lasers that instantly kill and nozzles that spray paint to change the color of objects. There are even platforms that will cycle through to the next color each time Hue jumps on them. In all these cases Hue will need to consider his surrounds and swap to the correct color(s) to complete the puzzle.
While the puzzle side of things sounds basic, the implementation is nearly perfect. If it weren't for a few boxes getting caught on flat surfaces and dodgy ladders, there wouldn't be any issues with the mechanics. The gradual introduction of new devices matches the need to think in multiple colorized dimensions. Most of the puzzles take place in fairly small rooms, often with a key that needs to be acquired to open the exit. These contained areas ensure the puzzles are fairly manageable despite their purplexity. Most puzzles cannot be broken, so the game allows players to try bad solutions, before moving onto greener pastures.  While the game world is not strictly linear, the acquisition of colors and their corresponding areas tends to follow a direct route for a smoother experience.
The hectic platforming sequences are interspersed between these chains of puzzle rooms. Platforming challenges require much faster switching between colors, as you avoid deadly obstacles. Fortunately the swapping of colors slows time, providing a fraction more tolerance to make the required jumps. Nevertheless, some of these sections are tricky. Ledges will crumble and boulders will tumble. You need to quickly determine whether you want a specific color enabled or disabled. Pick the wrong color and you'll be black and blue all over.
These faster platforming sections can take a minute or two to complete and have a small margin for error. The tolerance for making some vertical jumps is fairly low; Hue might need to quickly swap colors after jumping up through an invisible platform. Horizontal jumps are sometimes made in advance of seeing what color needs to be disabled or enabled. In both cases, the main caveat is that the background cannot be changed when Hue is inside an object, so there is a little bit of dexterity involved. Platforming is also made a little harder because the swapping color wheel can obscure nearby ledges. While there will be a few deaths during platforming, the difficulty is quite fair when contrasted with the slower puzzle challenges.
These two main parts of the game provide a good balanced mix. None of the puzzle mechanics are overused, and the same is true with the slightly different faster challenges. Both elements get slightly trickier as the game progresses, following the general blueprint set by similar platformers. The game will take around four hours to complete, with more time needed to backtrack and collect some achievement-related objects. It’s a good length and there is plenty of variety.
Fiddlesticks Games have done the impossible—they've hit a purple patch after creating only one game. Hue is a 2D platformer that cleverly integrates the switching of background colors. Switching between each pigment will make objects invisible or visible, necessary to complete the good-sized puzzle rooms and leap onto ledges in the frenzied platforming sequences. Mechanically it is quite sound, with only a few red flags linked to boxes and ladders. After finishing Hue, there will be no grey area—this is a blue ribbon experience worth every cent of your greenback-equivalent.

It is hard not to recommend Hue. It is a charming, inventive little puzzle platformer and you surely have not played anything like this before. However, don't go in expecting the best puzzle game experience you have ever gotten - the game has its down moments.
Hue revolves around a clever color changing mechanic where you can control the background color of the stage. However, in my opnion the game falls short on discovering this mechanic to its fullest potential. The game tries to add more complexity by adding more colors to your wheel but ends up using only about 5 of the colors in the later levels. When most of the wheel colors have been opened, I had to turn on the colorblind mode to make things clearer.
Most of the game is moderately easy - you can proceed with flying colors. During the last hour of the game the difficulty ramps up. Some of the puzzles near the end are great, some just make you frustrated for other reasons than not figuring out the solution.
All in all, the game sort of fails to surprise player with its puzzle design. Nothing that Hue 2 cannot fix. Still a unique experience that is worth having.

I expected Full Bore to be a fun little puzzler, but I became engrossed in its mysterious world and by its devious puzzles.
You begin as boar walking through a tranquil field, only to be caught in a sudden explosion and thrown into the mines of the Full Bore Mining Co. You make your way up to an empty fault, which you're accused of raiding and then charged with finding gems to compensate for those that you "stole" You'll explore the mines, talk to other boars and find out more about this strange place.
The world and puzzle design are excellent. There's a vast network of caves to explore and plenty of secrets to find. It will take you many hours to find everything there is to find. The mechanics are simple: you can dig blocks, push blocks, climb blocks, and stomp on blocks, that's it. There are no upgrades to be found, so every puzzle can be solved immediately, but you'll need to understand how everything works to succeed. The challenges start out simple, but you'll tackle progessively trickier puzzles as you go along. There's a great rewind feature allowing you to undo any of your mistakes, which cuts the repetition to a minimum. You can always return to a difficult room later when you figure out how to solve it. The map does a great job of logging all the places you've traveled and all the collectibles and lore you've found or missed, so it's never hard to find your way around.
The story is mostly told through logs and books you find as you go, but there are also events and characters to talk to as well. The writing is charming and engaging. You'll discover that the history of the boars goes much further than you initially think.
The aesthetics are great as well. The pixel art, lighting and sound create a superb dark and sometimes forboding atmosphere. The rock soundtrack is a nice backdrop for puzzle-solving, never obtrusive to get in the way.
Overall, I was really pleasantly surprised with Full Bore. There's a lot to love here for puzzle game fans. If you're a fan of games like FEZ or Antichamber, I highly recommend checking this out.

I am a fan of strategic RPGs. So I might have had high expectations towards FE. There are several aspects worth mentioning.
1. Movement: most units have a movement range of two squares. None can pass mountains or oceans/lakes. There are no teleporter. But in later game you can learn a spell to transport your troops to any location you desire. This makes the game extremely lengthy and IMHO dull. Having learnd the spell of transportation it is giving too much of an advantage.
2. Tactical combat: your maximum number of attackers is nine units (i.e. a group of soldiers) or champions. When you attack a city, any defending unit or champion will be supported by a number of city units, depending on the buildings errected in this city. There are no obsticals like city walls to hinder the attackers. This makes every battle follow the same pattern: try to kill the archers as quick as possible and mob up the rest. Even if you bring more troops you cannot stack them. My city was once attacked by four groups one after the other in the same round and for every city unit that was killed a new city unit (level 1 though) stepped forward. After a while that is boring.
3. Diplomatic system: normally every fraction is going to negotiate with you. And normally you can persuade every fraction to do what you want regardless of their opinion towards you. It will just cost you more. You can trade knowledge and resources but no citys or resoureces pits. Your opponents switch their alliance at random. Or so it seems to me. What is the use of a long-time friend to turn on you whilest every other fraction already is at war with him? That has to be done better.
4. Game stability: crap. I dont have to go into this deeper. Just read some of the other comments.
5. Research: there are just very few research differences for the different races.
6. Injury system: whenever your monarch or one of his/her champions is beaten they will not die. They start over in the nearest city with all their equipment. All the receive as a punishment is a recreation period during which they cannot move and to a champion a random injury. That injury gives the champion a malady: for example less hit points or less strengh. Such injuries will stay with the champion until they are lifted by a potion which can be produced as a consequence of a city achivement. Even a level-up will not effect the injury. So when my champions were defeated several times, they literally became cripples. Moreover, there is a potion to lift all injuries of a person at once but you cannot produce it in your cities. So you have to buy the healing potion several times for 400 gp each.
Conclusion: FE: Legendary Heroes is way behind other products of the genre. Even the older Age of Wonders 2 (which I still do recommend as ground-breaking) is better and more stable.

I've been a long time customer. I also played this game several years ago, and recently came back, hoping I could make it past 20 turns or so without crashes. Unfortunately I was let down.
This game has amazing potential but seems fundamentally riddled with bugs.

The problem with Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes is *not* simply that it lacks Artificial Intelligence, but that lacks any intelligence at all. The amount of noise simply overwhelms the information and that is a design flaw that permeates the game. The designers simply do not understand that communication is about *meaning*, and you cannot meaningfully communicate if everything that you say is interrupted by something else, which in turn has been interrupted . Or that you drown out what is important by endlessly repeating statements about the irrelevant. Granted that these half-spoken communications eventually unwind off the stack to finally speak the rest of what they were supposed to have said, but the connection between pieces has been lost.
Stacked Modal dialogs that are half-statements of things interrupted is an idiotic paradigm beyond comprehension. Yet this is the paradigm that the designers of Fallen Enchantress have built into the control loop of the game.
But the basic principles of communication are not just abused in this manner.
Some guy will complain that you are intruding on his territory, but not tell you where. So that intrusion could be a transient event created by an automated scout or it could actually be a meaningful complaint about an army. But you don't know which because city boundaries are often not clear. All that you know is that something has happened someplace and maybe you should do something about it if you could.
Some alert will announce that there are enemies in your territory, and it has announced it for dozens of turns. But the alert is not relevant because the beasts are holed-up in their cave and still remain too strong to take on. That information then should be check-boxed and excluded from the alert, but instead it is repeated turn after turn, to the point that it is eventually ignored. Yet *all* intrusions use the same alert and so ignoring that one can leave other, more serious intrusions, ready to pounce from the bushes.
Tactical combat takes place in an arena that reflects the locale, and there are often building and trees in the area. This is a nice aesthetic touch and a sensible paradigm. But unfortunately, in Fallen Enchantress, those buildings and trees are fixed objects and do not become transparent when the space gains focus. That means that these objects can obscure armies and placements behind them, leaving you blind when you try to move into that space or attack enemies on it.
Possible movement squares of armies are highlighted as are those of the opposing armies. Unfortunately, the base color is light blue, and the movement squares of friends is light green. Closely examined, the difference is clear, yet errors in placement are often made because those colors are transparent pastels and not easily differentiated with a quick glance. Again, clear communication was not the objective and so it doesn't take place.
There are various other problems, and others have talked about them and the poor AI in the game, but the problem is deeper than any. The problem is that the developers do not understand what they are doing. They might be competent programmers but they do not understand design and the necessary flow of communication and execution that makes working within the world they've created a pleasure. This game works, but working within it is a pain because you have to fight with it to get what you want done.
Behind the mess is a game worth playing, but you'll need a fair bit of patience to reach it.

+ Needs of the city dictate your long term goals.  (Not simply a "plop" game).
+ Art style is minimalistic, colorful, and very attractive!
+ Music goes well with the game.
+ A fun, nay, HILARIOUS way to spend some minutes in between life's other tasks.
+ Disasters provide an extra difficulty level.  (Thank goodness they can be turned off, if desired!)
+ Tutorial is very good, providing a seamless way to get into the game.
+ There are several game modes to choose from, each of which have their own variations.
Negatives:
- At some points, it can seem "too hard", especially with the uniquely-shaped landmarks in some of the levels.  However, I must put that on my own shoulders -- I just need to play more and develop a better strategy!

Dungeon of the Endless, to put it simply, does everything right.
At its heart, Dungeon of the Endless is a relatively generic hero-based tower defense game. You defend your core node against spawning armies of increasing difficulty while building modules to defend and support your heroes. If this was all Dungeon of the Endless was, it would really just be another Kongregate tower defense game.
However, the mechanic that Amplitude chose to focus their core gameplay on is exploration, and what a glorious implementation it is.  I've always been a fan of games that use exploration as a resource mechanic. I enjoy puzzle games and this one simple mechanic can turn nearly any game into thought-provoking puzzler.
The premise of the game is simple. You're on a ship and you crash land. The only thing salvageable from your ship is a power source. You need to protect this power source and drag it through each of the levels until you reach the top and can be rescued.
Of course, it's not that simple.
Dungeon of the Endless uses a resource system comprised of industry (for building things), science (for learning how to build things), and food (for keeping your dudes alive and leveling up). You gain these resources by opening doors (exploration). There is also a concept of Dust as a resource, which you find in some rooms or from some monsters.
By allocating Dust, you can light up different rooms in the level. Lighting up rooms does a few things: powers your devices in the room and prevents monsters from spawning. However, you don't have enough Dust to light every room, so it becomes a puzzle of what rooms to light up and/or occupy to minimize the spawning enemies.
When you do find the level's exit and you plan to try to move your power source to it, the fun truly happens. From every dark room, enemies constantly spawn. The person carrying the crystal moves at half speed, so it's up to everyone else to defend that person until they reach the exit and your team can leave the level.
Speaking of your team, you start with two dudes. They all have different abilities and different stats. Over the course of the game, you can use food to level up your guys (up to a max of level 15) which helps their stats, gives them new abilities, etc.
All of these concepts work completely and are executed flawlessly. There is a sense of constant panic and dread when you're exploring, particularly when you're short on resources or dust. You want to spend resources to improve your team, but want to save some for emergencies.
If I have a complaint about the game is that it's a bit too easy. Once you understand the fundamentals of the game and have a good strategy, it pays to just keep repeating that strategy for the entire game. However, the developers very intelligently added a variety of ships that change the rules of the game. This is where the future challenge lies.
One of the best titles in recent memory. Well worth the low price.

Lets address the elephant in the room. It has the red faction name. but its really not like the other red faction games. Its like they have the havok destructible scenery system....and thats it. This is a standard third person shooter with aliens. You can destroy and rebuild the scenery...but there isnt actually that much you can destroy and rebuild in all fairness so its really not that impressive.
The story:
mars is ruined somehow, you are a "mason" part of the great line of masons who saved mars blah blah, some cultists destroy the terraformer, damn mars to hell, then you have to go do some mission (no one says why) and you release these hidden aliens.
First problem....its not open world and this is what made guerilla the phenomenal game that it was. It could get away with a crap story because guerilla was amazeballs fun. this is not. The carnage and chaos within guerilla is gone.
gameplay: it is a mediocre shooter, just an avergae run of the mill third person shooter with a few cool mechanics. Honestly nothing special. The magnet guns novelty wore off in about 2 mins.
Enemies: I made the mistake of putting it on normal mode. I could literally stand in the middle of a firefight, go make a cup of tea, come back and I think I would be ok. I got to the first boss, they are all like "you gotta rebuild your cover" I literally stood in front of him with a plasma cannon and drilled away. Yawn. put the difficulty up otherwise you will think you are in a star wars simulator and all the bad guys are stormtroopers (cause they really cant hit anything)
The aliens are absolutely rubbish. Was expecting creepy alien...instead I got some unscary bouncy little things running at me, missing me (of course) with their poison spit attack, and then running up to me to stab me in close quarters. When I realised this was the attack pattern, rather than trying to shoot the jumpy little s**ts, I just pulled out ye olde hammer, stood in one spot and let them come to me. yawn.
ultimately, combat is a complete yawn fest with predictable enemies and nothing interesting. HOpefully it picks up....
The sheer chaos that made guerilla fun is gone. The cool story that made 1 +2 fun is also non existent. This game is quite honestly....pretty awful. I mean, I bought it at a ridiculous discount so Im not complaining too much but they have taken everything from the red faction series that made it fun and added "red faction" onto the title to sell games. this is not red faction.
Many reviewers here have mentioned that if it wasn't named red faction it would have more recommends...I disagree. At best it is an average shooter with great mechanics that it fails to implement too well. This game could have been so much fun. That havok engine is made for exactly that...havoc, and that is not what you get with this game.

Development? Yeah, it's slow. It's also early access. By buying, you're acknowledging that it may never be finished. I did. I like to think that I got my $15 worth, and will get more than that with every update, regardless of the time it takes the team to get the updates out. I have the utmost respect for the devs, putting up with all the crap a lot of folks are putting them through in terms of how long updates take. By now, if I were TIS, I'd go the route of, say, Interstellar Marines and just leave everyone in the dark to shut most of them up so I could work. But, instead each week they put on their gloves and get ready for the **** that gets slung their way because they choose to keep us in the loop.
Now that I'm done with that, on to gameplay.
Even in its current state, in the off chance of zombacaylpse, I've learned a lot from PZ. Stockpile water in anything that can hold water. Turns out the people that keep the water running stop going to work after the world ends. Keep some books and toys handy (the toys may be part of the Hydrocraft mod, I'm not sure). Boredom is nobody's friend. Stockpile food, obviously. Non-perishables don't grow on trees, unfortunately, and besides, you're gonna cut all the trees down to make walls and other things. Perishables perish shortly after the power shuts off, too. Learn how to grow food. It's a marketable skill during the end of the world.
And when the animations update arrives, you're probably going to want several changes of clothes rather than wearing that one sweat shirt and that one t-shirt for the rest of your life. Blood stains and all.
I think it's worthy of the "something in my eye" award because you will get attached to your character and all the progress you make with him or her. You'll have killed lord knows how many deadoes, and then, when you least expect it, the sound of your flesh being torn open by a rotting hand or a decayed jaw. You suddenly aren't long for the world. You spent so long trying to ride out the storm, only to become a part of it. You think back to the first one you killed, then the first building you cleared. Staring in horror at that first house you saw boarded up, filled with rotters trying to break out and devour your flesh. Fast forward to the lights going out, or the water shutting off, and wondering
and finding a way. And for however long you kept finding a way, beating in heads, looting the homes of the deceased, fortifying your home (whatever or where-ever it may be). And now you flash forward to just a moment ago, as Rodney Rot-Face there just took a bite out of your arm. You are not long for the world now, and with this realization, and perhaps a tear in your eye, you can decide to hole up and wait to die, or you can take revenge on the world that did this to you.
Be lovely, I'm out, dropping the mic!

As a puzzle platformer, this does a lot of things well. It's a challenging, charming game at times and the initial hook is pretty decent. It's also for the most part fun. There's a story there but it's paper thin and the music is basic but nice enough. It's a good game for a quiet change of pace.
However, once the story is over, it's not worth playing again. The collect-em-all side quest which can't be completed until you finish the story really is a showcase for the games flaws. You repeat the same puzzles over again, areas where the collectables are do not offer any new challenge and are usually hidden in inaccessable holes in already completed puzzles. Without the story, the bits which had the exposition are now shown to be long featureless, puzzleless corridors, something you don't notice on the initial playthrough, but are very apparent and shows a bit of disappointing programming and you eventually realise how repetitive this game can be at times.
That's not to say it's not fun. It really is. But only once, because of this and the length of time to complete the game I would recommend not getting it at full price, wait for a bundle or a sale, but I would say £6/£7 is about the most you should pay.
tl;dr Fun puzzle game with flaws that are hardly noticible the first time you run-through, very much so when going for 100%. Too expensive though, buy on sale.

Hue is a 2D puzzle platformer where you can manipulate the world by altering the background color of the levels. You play as the small boy Hue looking for his lost mother.
The art in Hue is rather stylistic and vibrant. Some graphical elements are little amateurish, but overall the game looks quite beautiful and unique.
The sound effects and voice acting are decent enough. Music is quite nice too, even if slightly repetitive.
Pretty much all the puzzles and action sequences in Hue are built around the color switching mechanic. Any map elements that match the current color of the background simply disappear temporarily and you can freely pass through them.
This mechanic is then used in various puzzles and more action-oriented platforming sequences. While the color switching itself is quite an clever idea and the game keeps adding more potential colors to the mix, the actual puzzles remain fairly simple. I would have liked to see bit more depth and complexity with the puzzle design myself.
One minor annoyance is also the lack of checkpoints during the levels. Some of the larger levels take a while to go through and the game has quite a few hazards that can kill you.
Hue is a rather easy game, only the last few puzzles are slightly more complicated.
Controls are somewhat floaty and not terribly precise on a gamepad. At least the game doesn't really require precision jumping.

This gaming is AMAZING. It's like the honor-roll love child of Cave Story, Castlevania SOTN, and Adventures of Lolo, with maybe a streak of Portal. Simply fantastic.
I don't have enough good things to say about this game. If you are on the fence, just buy it. Even if you don't like it, the devs deserve your money. I guess I'll write a short summary about why I liked it so much. The game is an open world block puzzler. That may not sound like the greatest thing ever, but the world the devs have created oozes mystery and begs you to explore every nook and cranny to find both it's arcane secrets, and to find more puzzles to solve simply for the sake of solving more. The exploration has the same sense of wonder that SOTN or Dark Souls has, but without any real enemies to speak of. And without the stress of Dark Souls constant deaths. And when you finally do find all the pieces, the story is quite compelling, well thought out, and plotted at a masterful pace (despite the occasional typo or misspelling). The pixel art is sometimes amazing, and sometimes just ok, but they do some kind of 2D normal mapping or something to have this neat dynamic lighting. It looks great sometimes, but sometimes it looks like prerendered graphics from late 16bit early 32bit era stuff. The music is also amazing. Good tunes that are appropriate to the scene when they need to be, and entertaining when you are working out puzzles.
Things I didn't like...Not much. The occasional puzzle stumped me, but that's cause I'm too dumb. I ended up having to look up 2 of the puzzles on Youtube, which I'm fine with. Most of the time when I got stuck I would put the game down and come back later and something would pop out at me. The time rewind mechanic was helpful, but it often didn't go where you wnated it to go, and that was annoying. The race can suck it, the control just isn't built for it, and I frankly didn't find it fun. But those are totally forgiveable complaints in the grand scheme of how amazing this is.
Probably in my top 20 gmes of all-time.

I feel super bad that I got this game in a $1 bundle 'cause, damn, do the devs deserve way more than that for this game.
Full Bore is, at heart, a puzzle/exploration game. Not a platformer, you see, as there is no platforming, and you cannot even jump. But a puzzle game with the occassional action-demanding section.
And it's really, really good. Like, wow. The puzzle variety throughout the game is astounding, every puzzle felt unique and interesting. And the difficulty curve was smooth, too; as I got better at understanding the game's logic, the puzzles got more demanding themselves, so the entire way through, the game was certainly a challenge, but never an unfair one, and never too easy. The game world's design, as well, is really great; there are 5 main areas to the game, each pretty self-contained, but each is pretty expansive as well. The game is made up of puzzle rooms connected by doors, some rooms large with multiple puzzles, some rooms small with only a single puzzles, and plenty of rooms outright hidden by puzzles in other rooms. You can go through the entire game seeing less than 10% of what there is to see (if, well, you know exactly where to go, but yes) yet the game never feels too long because the puzzles remain enjoyable the whole way through.
The presentation is also great, the game is pixelated, yes, but it has a distinctly modern look to it, one that makes every main area look different, one that almost never has any visual confusion, and one that's just a joy to look at. The soundtrack is also very interesting too, I don't know exactly how to describe it but it fits almost too well. The story is pretty interesting though mostly conveyed through logs (that you don't *have* to read, either, and many of them are hidden... but let's be honest, why are you playing this game if you aren't going to attempt to find everything there is to see?)
I guess. There are a few puzzles that can be a bit tedious to solve, but they aren't common. The game's never too demanding action-wise, either, and the puzzles are tight and focused, maybe with the occasional red herring thrown in for good measure.
I don't really have much to say against this game... I enjoyed it from beginning to end, it's just a really enjoyable experience and you should buy it.
