So what is Full Bore? It's a puzzle game, which was described by some as a "metroidvania with boars", but that is entirely incorrect. It has an open world with rooms full of puzzles, but there are no ability unlocks at all. Your abilities are moving, digging and stomping, and that's it, from start to end. You roam around, collect gems, search for secret rooms and advance the main quest at your leisure. All of it involves puzzles of the digging and timing kind, though the timing aspect is not critical. It's much more about understanding how the elements interact and planning ahead than the execution itself.
So yeah, it's a semi-hardcore puzzle game about the cutest boar ever going on an adventure and you all should totally check it out. Really a hidden gem, I give it four out of four boars.

Basically, this game would have done better as a new and seperate IP. It trades the oppressive military for generic alien bugs, trades wide open scenery for claustrophobic, linear cave systems, and large destructable structures for little shacks and nameless machinery that sort of fall apart with no real effort. The destruction that made Guerilla fun is now a hindrance, as the spaces are so small and linear that debris will just get in your way. Vehicles have all but been removed, which is probably a good thing in these enclosed spaces, in favor of a couple different exo-suits. These are great fun to mow down bugs in, but again, it doesnt fit a red faction game. There is some weapon variety, but there is rarely a need to switch up your loadout since there is little to no strategy required for most fights. Adding to this problem is the "nano-forge" which is a very loosely "sci-fi" way of giving your character (and only your character) abilities that basically amount to The Force. Also worth mentioning is the generic A.I voice-in-your-head, named SAM, like every generic A.I should be named, that conveniently gives you all relevant mission objectives.
Visually, the game looks great, and runs smoothly even at max settings, including 4K (played using a GTX 1070). Lighting is very well done and provides a gloomy atmosphere with ominous glowing bug silhouettes dashing around and bright energy weapons flashiing across the screen. However, the majority of the time, the lighting is the only thing you'll get to appreciate, since the game is too dark to notice any other visual effects.
However, If you can get this game on sale, need something to play in Steam Big Picture mode, and/or want to mow down generic alien bugs in exo-suits, this is a fairly good title. Just ignore the fact that it is supposed to be a red faction game, and dont bother listening to the "story". Just go shoot stuff.

Before getting into this you should be aware of what RF: Amrageddon is not.
It is not an open world game. If you are looking for a continuation of RF: Guerilla than this is definitely not it. Armageddon is completely linear. Make sure you get this clear or else that's going ot be 2 hours of "I wonder when the map is going to open up" feelings.
It is not open at all in fact. Pretty much the entire game happens in caves. Just caves caves and more caves. The environments are well crafted but way too same-ish to appeal to the eyes.
It is not demolition paradise. Now whilst there are a few spectacular buildings to demolish, and the demolition physics are really sweet as usual with Red Faction, you can only fit that many types of building inside caves. No demolition derbys and challenges.
So once you take all these things that made Red Faction games away from Armageddon, what is left?
The answer is a pretty damn good shooter. The levels are (mostly) well balanced, enemy AI is effective, and most of all there are a ton of varied, whacky, or overpowered weapons to use. Flinging parts of buildings into giant insects with a magnet gun or detonating the (too few) buildings in the game with your remote charges is nothing short of awesome fun.  There are some short, but sweet, vehicle sections which add variety. The challenge level is just about right and outside a very annoying rail shooter bit near the start, I pretty enjoyed the whole thing from beginning to end without getting bored.
Unfortunately the game is not bug-free. I encountered a few random crashes, could not alt tab without crashing, and most annoyingly the difficulty changed itself from hard to normal at some point during my campaign without me noticing.
If you can overlook these shortcomings and know to expect something very different from the previous series, Armageddon is still worth playing to this date.

This game is amazing. i love the hidden depth of it with the character dialog that can only be found with certain combinations of characters turrning the deploy scenes. i love the colorful/lush/alive feel of each map. i love how each character actually feels unique, and that every one of them feels like they need improvement (i only say this because to me its makes them feel more realistic, even though annoying based on certain character kits). although i also hate it, i like how unbalanced the game can be at times, like how each match is different even with the same hunters, monster, and map. over-all, i give the game a solid 8.5/10 due to how much it captured me.
*However*
This game still needs a lot of improvement. I still experience horrible bugs (although not so often). I've had players fall through the map either durring the dropship sequence, or through some hole in the corner of the map that the monster forced them through. on multiple occasions, certain models will bug and revert to an idol "T model", whether a player or an npc (one example was a Parnel hunter. when we went through water, he didnt have a swiming animation, he stood in a static upright position with his arms straight and at a 45 degree angle). certain monsters are obviously extrememly powerful compaired to others (cough cough, wraith) and i would assume are going to be tweaked to be balanced the longer the game is out. some hunters, based on their kits, are easily inferior to other hunters of the same class. i find that Lazarus is quite useless as a medic, since he doesnt actively heal, but can have his only "medic ability" easily shut down by a monster that uses the dead hunter's body as bait or easily stands over it, and either cannot be revived, or lazarus himself dies. he doesnt compare well to any of the other current 3, as they can ALL revive AND actively heal downed friendlies from a safe distance under similar conditions.
the actual offense i take with this game, is not the game itself (i LOVE the game), but the marketing. i hate how the dlc has been conveniently labeled similar to other marketing strategies that offer ALL later released dlc in one bundle, but has been sectioned into different dlc releases. "Season Pass" has been universally marketed as such. adding "Hunting" to it is like making a loop hole to decieve the consumer. it's highly unappreciated by the community. another is that each individual dlc character, or even skins, are grossly overpriced. other games that offer pay-to-unlock chracters have a much wider variety of characters to unlock, and all of them can be unlocked by free means, but require more time to be spent playing the game (hint hint). there's be a huge drop off of players/consumers with this game (originally due to bugs/programming, now due to marketing schemes).
The game is great as it is now, but if the studio showed a bit more sincerity with the release of new content, the fans would slowly return. sure, take a small blow to the profit margin and release some legitimate free content, or implement a system that rewards the players for commiting their time and effort into the game, that allows them to aquire the new content through effort and continued play, thus holding a larger consumer base, and in the end, less need for shifty marketing and high prices. the lack of "care" for the consumer as a CONSUMER and not a dollar symbol really bleeds through.

This game is awesome. A perfect mix of teamwork, skill, and strategy. There are dozens of unique maps as well as dozens of 'effects' that can help or hinder you when you play in campaign mode as each victory or loss will have an affect on the next map. The matchmaker also keeps things fresh by switching up everyone roles if two people want the same role. This can also be over-ridden as you can swap roles with anyone else if you both want. There is also an auto-balance system in place when you play the campaign mode, which helps prevent the game from being one sided. Overall, the gameplay is fantastic and so are the graphics. The game really takes that co-op tactics style of left for dead, payday, or Socom and then amplifies it by making everyone truely needed. Then it adds a player as your opponent to top it off. (Or you can play vrs AI, and the AI is actually pretty good)
All the negative reviews are about the price and the day 1 DLC. But this in no way affects the enjoyment you can have in the game. The base game has 3 characters for each of the 5 classes(Assualt, Support, Medic, Trapper, and Monster). Seeing as no specific character is better than any other in the same class, this means everyone is viable when your team works together with each others strenghts. The season 1 DLC just adds 1 more character to each class, and they are no more powerful than the originals. Even if you never buy any DLC, you will not be left out as it doesn't prevent you from joining any game. In fact, if a game had already started with an AI playing a character from DLC, when you join you get to play that character that round. The DLC is very much all skins, even the additional characters. You don't have to spend any extra money to enjoy this game. That means the only negative of this game is the price. And honestly, its just the same price on PC as it is on console. So it's not even that bad. And if you wait for a steam sale then it's a hell of a good deal.

This is a game that tries to mix some unusual set of mechanics into one game. I used to play this during early access and I could see the potential back then but it was far from balanced; it had one particular winning strategy that rendered most of the mechanisms in the game pointless.
I'm happy to say that these days are long gone, the final version of Dungeon of the Endless is a very successful experimentation in game design that will keep you entertained exploring different strategies you never thought you'd use together in the same game.
There's a lot of luck involved though, keep that in mind if that's not your thing. But luck is a factor in many games considered good, specially in rogue-likes. In these games the fun is like a good game of cards, you develop skills as you play the game over and over again until you know the best strategies for the hand you were given. And there are many cards and possibilities in Dungeon of the Endless. I totally recommend it.

The best way to describe the state of this game is with this short story (that is well known in the software development world):
The monster and his shoes
Imagine you are an ugly monster and you are preparing for a party. You hava a very nice pair of shoes. You spend a lot of time cleaning and making your shoes look even more amazing, you go to the party and everyone runs away from you. - "The next party will be better" you say, and then you start to work on your shoes again... ignoring the fact that you are a big scaring ♥♥♥♥ing monster.
-- end of short story --
Analogy whit this game
The monster:
- super slow development pipeline
- NPCs (long promised)
- Vehicles (long promised)
- broken multiplayer (needs a ton of work, bug fixes, features to even start to make sense)
The shoes  (things that were already good enough or totally unnecessary):
- nutrition system (really?)
- metal crafting
- ultra detailed over complicated health system
- painting stuff (what the actual ♥♥♥♥)
- communication with in game devices (solving a problem that is already solved by external better voip apps)
- the list is really big ...
For that reason I think the team behind this project lacks knowledge on basic software development principles, like prioritize work that delivers real value not nice-to-have small stuff.
Stay away from this game until they start to deliver value with consistency.

Good game. It is extremely rare that I play early access titles, but this one is worth the $$, even to me. It is a good investment, and I reccomend it even in its early state. That being said, I have suggestions for the developers:
1. Fires.   Starting fires is a task that will be 10-20% of your in-game time. And it takes foreeevverrr. Starting a fire should be something that is sped up in-game to minimize the amount of time the player has to wait. I will begin starting a fire in the game and turn my attention to my phone for the 2 minutes it takes for the animation to complete. And it really sucks when I start a fire, wait 1 minute and 50 seconds, and then the fire dies. Hello Facebook. (I know accelerant makes this faster but it is an uncommon resource). Tasks that the player performs often should be fully-featured and feel intuitive.
2. Extinguishing fires.  It is equally frustrating to finally get a fire going and realize that it is not where I wanted it to be. For example, putting a fire on a frozen lake means I cant roll out a bedroll next to it and sleep. Moving the fire is virtually impossible (only achievable by  taking out torches and starting a new fire with the torches). If one could extinguish the fire and take out the wood, it would be easier to move. Plus, the utility of ending a fire early gives one the benefit of not wasting fire mats. Again, tasks that the player performs often should be fully-featured and feel intuitive.
3. Lockout tasks.   When I start a task like breaking down wood or harvesting venison, I should get some kind of warning before I die of frostbite, bleeding, etc. It is frustrating to die of hypothermia with 8 chair legs in my inventory because I started breaking down a crate that took too long and didn't get the opportunity to stop. I would reccomend that when the player falls below 15% health or so, a warning pops up saying, "Would you like to continue performing this task?" If the player selects yes, then they will continue until it is finished or they die. If the player selects no, then they stop and gain a yield proportional to the amount of time they've spent thus far. For example, if I've spent 40 / 45 minutes breaking down a crate while losing health due to hyperthermia and fall below 15% health, I should be able to stop and receive the 40 minute's worth of wood and then go build a fire to warm myself (I may die while building the fire, but that's a risk the player has to determine for themselves).

Full Bore is a indie 2D puzzle platformer developed by three man studio Whole Hog Games. The game was Kickstarted just over a year ago to the tune of $16,383.Full Bore has lovely 2d 16 bit pixelated graphics that not only add a retro feel, but add a degree of both humour and charm to the title. Environments look great with some really well designed levels, nice use of lighting. Levels are colourful and vibrant and the whole game is easy to look at. The soundtrack of the game is also wonderful created by Miguel Acuña and the Adjective Plural Noun. It boasts a great variety of tracks that range from happy go lucky to dark and atmospheric.
The games controls are simple and easy to use, movement is controlled with WASD. The space bar is used to make the boar stomp, which is used for crumbling loose blocks of ground and for moving certain blocks. Sadly there’s no jump feature which on one hand is necessary for the way the game is designed but I personally would have liked one. One thing I like is that you get all the abilities you need in the game at the start, as levels increase in difficulty its all about using your brain rather than just using in game abilities.
Full Bore has three main elements to it's gameplay, puzzles, platforming and exploration. Full Bore isn't just a level by level platformer, you have a world to explore. By entering different doors and entrances you can go to different locations. To manage where you are and find your way around you have the handy tool of having a world map so you can track you way back should you need to. As you explore you'll come across computer control panels, books and characters, all of which you can interact with which will progress the games story, offer information and some funny jokes.
Full Bore is a highly polished indie title that is packed full of character, humour and a bloody good challenge. It brings back memories of playing Fez for the first time and I would certainly argue that its up there with Fez in terms of indie titles in the puzzle platforming genre. All in all if your a fan of puzzle platformers or just charming indie titles in general I would certainly recommend picking Full Bore up, there’s plenty here to get your monies worth and you'll get a laugh or two out of it.

There are box-moving puzzles out there and then there is FullBore...
I hope I won't sound very biased saying that FullBore stands a bit aside from most of such games. Granted, it did not invent absolute novelty in the old genre. Instead, it used a different approach to it. There is a quote floating out there, "metroidvania with boars". I guess you can say so, because FB features a lot of exploration aspects and freedom of movement. And more than that, a lot of puzzles with less platforming. You aren't forced to solve them (many of them are optional), but the way these placed and designed - simply attracts you like a butterfly to the light. What could be hard in simple box moving and dirt digging..?
Don't even get me started on puzzles, these are simply fantastic. They make
sense that by the end of figuring out another one you will feel like a pure genius. They deliver insane amount of feel of accomplishment. Soon you will realize it is not about the gem or a secret you want to get or discover, it is about solving the damn puzzle that taunts you. And the most interesting part is that none of the puzzles require from you any special ability or an item - it is all knowledge and experience. The way blocks and boxes work or interact with each other and your understanding of this mechanism is the key to solve all the puzzles.
But hey, a fun gameplay is not the only thing FullBore can be proud of. Quite lovely and pretty 2D graphics with awesome lighting and "fake" 3D effect will catch your attention at once. They fit the game surprisingly well, just like an amazing soundtrack by "The Adjective Plural Noun". But this is something you'd better to experience yourself, rather then read about in in a sloppy review.
Long story short - FullBore was quite pleasant surprise of 2013 for me (The First Dig, part 1 of the game, was released earlier; Steam version features full game). It came out of nowhere and since then I fell in love with it. Really, how could you not love these adorable little boars?
You won't get bored with Full Bore.

This entry isn't exactly any different, save for a few more in-depth things that have been added. 6 more game modes have been added to the line up of variations with billiards. A Hustler tournament mode. A Pro career mode. Both of which are pitting you against the A.I. There is of course, online capability both through off-Steam and on-Steam means to play against players of many skill levels and online tournaments to partake in.
Most importantly...you can play against a cat! A fricken cat! His name is Boots and he's a cat! Dead Eye Dan has nothing on Boots!
All in all though, if you're a veteran of this series, you'd know what to expect from this well-made game. As well as this is a perfect entry for beginners to get used to and I will be biased by saying that Pool Nation and other steam pool games, don't have a thing on VP.

Pros:
Semi-decent bolt action play, traditional aiming style for a FPS.
Free humble bundle game.
Better hit reg then CSGO (not a huge complement or standard achieved)
Cons:
Artillery Strike quite OP and poorly implemented.
Friendly Fire on all Realism servers, poorly designed HUD
Friendly player tags are invisible until close range
Uniforms are similar for axis/allies in the Pacific Campaign, combined with poor HUD of realism mode and new players = TK fest.
1,500 players online, pretty small community; few 64 man servers to play in on ranked servers in the NA EAST region about it.
Out of Bounds areas are somewhat pro-defense, and invisible to new players so you will be caught outside of bounds many times during your first playthroughs on the different maps as your defending team looses as objective.
Take away for me:
Defending objectives is essentially moot if the airstrike has not been called in yet, as the airstrike will clear out a entire objective of enemies; rendering objective defense relatively inadequate in terms of defending. Not all objectives have buildings to hide in, so essentially a buildingless objective is a free objective for a team that has a competent commander, and the counter is non-existent. A recent game I witnessed a player achieve 94 kills utilizing artillery strikes only, typing half the time in chat about how he was getting so many kills. This seemed counter intuitive to a FPS, and relatively low skill level. I seen a constant trend of team and squad leaders receiving points on a scale not linear to other players on the team. The 94 kill guy was not even first place, Lol. It is a bit of a mess of a FPS, but for free I had to atleast add it to my inventory. I like WW2 theme FPS, but heroes and generals; a highly criticized F2P FPS has 5k players online atm, much more active and updated with WW2 theme environment.
There is a high skill curve in knowing map control in this game, not so much with aiming as its pretty rudimentary, and bullets deviate very little from where your aiming, which is a positive aspect in my opinion as I dont care for RNG in FPS, but that is just a personal opinion.
Movement can be a skillful aspect of this game, and important in positioning to get kills on advancing enemies; but the movement itself is kin to call of duty 1, very clunky and 2001; which ultimately some people like the older style feeling of FPS movement with a box feet like movement feel to the game, everything is very mechanical down to the prone function. Hit prone and it might take nearly a full second to prone, by then you have hit it a second time thinking it was cancelled by the terrain, only to be unproned and die 2 seconds later. That is the type of mechanical feel to the movement and functions of ADSing, Proning, or crouching. A minor few hundred millisecond delay of older engines feel is the best way to describe it from personal experience.

This game is amazing. i love the hidden depth of it with the character dialog that can only be found with certain combinations of characters turrning the deploy scenes. i love the colorful/lush/alive feel of each map. i love how each character actually feels unique, and that every one of them feels like they need improvement (i only say this because to me its makes them feel more realistic, even though annoying based on certain character kits). although i also hate it, i like how unbalanced the game can be at times, like how each match is different even with the same hunters, monster, and map. over-all, i give the game a solid 8.5/10 due to how much it captured me.
*However*
This game still needs a lot of improvement. I still experience horrible bugs (although not so often). I've had players fall through the map either durring the dropship sequence, or through some hole in the corner of the map that the monster forced them through. on multiple occasions, certain models will bug and revert to an idol "T model", whether a player or an npc (one example was a Parnel hunter. when we went through water, he didnt have a swiming animation, he stood in a static upright position with his arms straight and at a 45 degree angle). certain monsters are obviously extrememly powerful compaired to others (cough cough, wraith) and i would assume are going to be tweaked to be balanced the longer the game is out. some hunters, based on their kits, are easily inferior to other hunters of the same class. i find that Lazarus is quite useless as a medic, since he doesnt actively heal, but can have his only "medic ability" easily shut down by a monster that uses the dead hunter's body as bait or easily stands over it, and either cannot be revived, or lazarus himself dies. he doesnt compare well to any of the other current 3, as they can ALL revive AND actively heal downed friendlies from a safe distance under similar conditions.
the actual offense i take with this game, is not the game itself (i LOVE the game), but the marketing. i hate how the dlc has been conveniently labeled similar to other marketing strategies that offer ALL later released dlc in one bundle, but has been sectioned into different dlc releases. "Season Pass" has been universally marketed as such. adding "Hunting" to it is like making a loop hole to decieve the consumer. it's highly unappreciated by the community. another is that each individual dlc character, or even skins, are grossly overpriced. other games that offer pay-to-unlock chracters have a much wider variety of characters to unlock, and all of them can be unlocked by free means, but require more time to be spent playing the game (hint hint). there's be a huge drop off of players/consumers with this game (originally due to bugs/programming, now due to marketing schemes).
The game is great as it is now, but if the studio showed a bit more sincerity with the release of new content, the fans would slowly return. sure, take a small blow to the profit margin and release some legitimate free content, or implement a system that rewards the players for commiting their time and effort into the game, that allows them to aquire the new content through effort and continued play, thus holding a larger consumer base, and in the end, less need for shifty marketing and high prices. the lack of "care" for the consumer as a CONSUMER and not a dollar symbol really bleeds through.

This game is awesome. A perfect mix of teamwork, skill, and strategy. The matchmaker also keeps things fresh by switching up everyone roles if two people want the same role. This can also be over-ridden as you can swap roles with anyone else if you both want. There is also an auto-balance system in place when you play the campaign mode, which helps prevent the game from being one sided. Overall, the gameplay is fantastic and so are the graphics. The season 1 DLC just adds 1 more character to each class, and they are no more powerful than the originals. Even if you never buy any DLC, you will not be left out as it doesn't prevent you from joining any game. In fact, if a game had already started with an AI playing a character from DLC, when you join you get to play that character that round. The DLC is very much all skins, even the additional characters. You don't have to spend any extra money to enjoy this game. That means the only negative of this game is the price. I originally had recommended this game, but I feel that I am unable to anymore. As people have pointed out, the updates have come to almost a complete halt. The devs get very angry when anyone points out that their updates are rather uncommon, and protest that they're doing their best to get everything out, which I don't doubt, but the delayed updates are pretty tiresome.
As well, the game has become much more centred around multiplayer than anything else, with the latest patch being entirely based around multiplayer, save the two maps which are both multi and singleplayer.

Those on the fence, this review is for the vanilla version without mods as it currently exists on 11/13/2016.
Pros:
*Default maps are big.  Tread carefully.
*Complex (not overly complex) crafting system
*Price is right and usually on sale during big steam sales
*Not in development hell like a lot of early releases
*Updates are frequent but varied from minor bug fixes to new items/maps/etc
*Multiplayer implemented with ability to make own server on steam as well as private servers
*Hard or as easy as you make it.  Sandbox mode allows you to control how quickly you die.  Slowly or on day 1 =P
*Mod support, mods can enhance the game greatly for some without being necessary to have a good time
Neutral.
*Sometimes updates are minor bugs.  Neither good nor bad right?
*Perma-death.  Once you die, that's it.  You lose your character progress (not what they built).  Some like it others don't.
Cons.
*Community is active, but with more players PUG multiplayer would work better.  Even public servers are mostly empty.
*Have to walk/run.  Without mods you can't travel very fast or check out other maps without starting over due to it taking so long.
*Dev team is small.  It's not the dev's team it's small, but because it's Indie a lot of "things-to-come" have been in the works for over a year like cars and updated animations.
*Lack of end-game content.  Once you have the knack of surviving you're almost invincible and end-game becomes a bit boring without adding mods.
There you have it.  For those thinking TL:DR.  There's a lot to do.  The learning curve will be difficult without tweaking the options in sandbox.  Multiplayer or single player is fun, and mods are REALLY fun (In my humble opinion).  Definitely doesn't hurt that you get a lot for only $15.00.

Bloody Trapland is a hardcore platformer that encourages Cooperative play.
I only played this solo so I won't have that much to say on the multiplayer front.
The game itself is a simple platformer, the only real mechanics are jumping and crouching, however you can use your first jump as an air jump if you fall off a ledge. It is a very challenging game, and I was not able to complete the last level, however I was able to get there and play it for a while in about 5 hours. I feel like the playtime will mostly come from having to repeat the challenging levels over and over again. If you are not up to the challenge, this will probably just frustrate you.
The levels are designed well in that they will make you think very hard in how to approach the different parts of them, and you will get penalized heavily for making mistakes. The game is very cycle based, which is one of my main gripes about the game. If you aren't familiar with cycles, it basically is the concept of things being time based such as moving platforms. The game is full of traps, and a very large portion of them are on a time based system. Because the game is cooperative, the timers are always going, the level does not reset at any point. This can be extremely frustrating. It is normal for cycles to be in platform games, but here it adds to the challenge in an annoying way. Let's say you attempt to do a level right when you load in. You die because you were 2 seconds too fast getting to Trap A. Now you start the level 2 seconds later, however you die to trap B because you were 1 second too slow. This is a constant process of trial and error that becomes more obvious in later levels. There is still a large amount of normal platforming challenge, but I feel the emphasis on cycles as well as the tons of layered time based traps in later levels, adds to a game you will want to stop playing. I feel like this would be made impossible in coop play. Cooperative play would be very fun but I can't imagine you would enjoy it at the end of the game, where you have to make extremely careful decisions about cycles to move on.
There are also a few other multiplayer modes, but as I was playing this solo it wasn't really of interest to me. It still might be fun to try those out with some friends. There is also a level editor, which is always a really cool thing to have in games to keep things fresh and try out your ideas.
There is the main set of about 60 levels but there are also secret levels you can find which can be a neat way to get through worlds.
I don't think there is any story in the game. You're just a bunch of cats jumping around.
Cooperative Support
Very Challenging
Solid Platforming Mechanics
Large amount of levels including hidden worlds
Extra Multiplayer Game Modes
Level Editor
Unforgiving or downright impossible to casual players
Multiplayer might be more trouble then it's worth
Cycle Based Level Design
No Story
All in all I did enjoy the game, but I really hated having to "watch the clock" per say just to beat levels. It made me want to stop when I got to the last level just because there were about 20 different timers I had to keep an eye on. If you have some friends that want a very difficult platforming experience, or you yourself are a hardcore platformer lover, you should pick this up

Out of This World/Another World was a rare pinnacle of side-scrolling platformer design, the sort by which few tried to emulate because it was so outside of the ordinary.  This small French company is practically unknown outside of the greater Europe area and I am very sad by this.  They released a game called Flashback which was the "spiritual successor" to OotW/AW.  The game plot isn't related, but it uses practically the same kind of gameplay mechanic and rendered everything in the same visually unique roto-scoped flat-shaded polygon engine.  The game has the plot of the movie "They Live" merged with "Bladerunner" and it was amazing for its time.
Fast forward to here and now.  And this is a spirtual successor to Flashback.  It's a completely 3d remake of the original game.
And oh boy, does it stink.  The controls are awkward and unforgiving.  It tries to have mouse-aim gun play mixed with cardinal-direction-only D-pad control scheme of the original game.  My character can only walk left/right and change elevation at select points, but I can fire my gun in a 360 arc?  It just feels odd and isn't well thought out, particularly since some enemies can ambuse you from any angle now instead of in pre-defined locations as in the original.
The voice acting is bad, the sound effects are mediocre, and the visuals are nice at points but feel very flat.  All in all, this game plays and looks like a fan-made remake that somehow got access to a bit of a budget.

Pros:
Semi-decent bolt action play, traditional aiming style for a FPS.
Free humble bundle game.
Better hit reg then CSGO (not a huge complement or standard achieved)
Cons:
Artillery Strike quite OP and poorly implemented.
Friendly Fire on all Realism servers, poorly designed HUD
Friendly player tags are invisible until close range
Uniforms are similar for axis/allies in the Pacific Campaign, combined with poor HUD of realism mode and new players = TK fest.
1,500 players online, pretty small community; few 64 man servers to play in on ranked servers in the NA EAST region about it.
Out of Bounds areas are somewhat pro-defense, and invisible to new players so you will be caught outside of bounds many times during your first playthroughs on the different maps as your defending team looses as objective.
Take away for me:
Defending objectives is essentially moot if the airstrike has not been called in yet, as the airstrike will clear out a entire objective of enemies; rendering objective defense relatively inadequate in terms of defending. Not all objectives have buildings to hide in, so essentially a buildingless objective is a free objective for a team that has a competent commander, and the counter is non-existent. A recent game I witnessed a player achieve 94 kills utilizing artillery strikes only, typing half the time in chat about how he was getting so many kills. This seemed counter intuitive to a FPS, and relatively low skill level. I seen a constant trend of team and squad leaders receiving points on a scale not linear to other players on the team. The 94 kill guy was not even first place, Lol. It is a bit of a mess of a FPS, but for free I had to atleast add it to my inventory. I like WW2 theme FPS, but heroes and generals; a highly criticized F2P FPS has 5k players online atm, much more active and updated with WW2 theme environment.
There is a high skill curve in knowing map control in this game, not so much with aiming as its pretty rudimentary, and bullets deviate very little from where your aiming, which is a positive aspect in my opinion as I dont care for RNG in FPS, but that is just a personal opinion.
Movement can be a skillful aspect of this game, and important in positioning to get kills on advancing enemies; but the movement itself is kin to call of duty 1, very clunky and 2001; which ultimately some people like the older style feeling of FPS movement with a box feet like movement feel to the game, everything is very mechanical down to the prone function. Hit prone and it might take nearly a full second to prone, by then you have hit it a second time thinking it was cancelled by the terrain, only to be unproned and die 2 seconds later. That is the type of mechanical feel to the movement and functions of ADSing, Proning, or crouching. A minor few hundred millisecond delay of older engines feel is the best way to describe it from personal experience.

Hue is a brilliantly charming narrative that serves as a platformer with a twist: You have to change the color in order to advance through the puzzles. It certainly challenges you to act quickly -  time is never frozen, but it does slow. It's simple, but this means that there aren't too many features or attention grabs stealing from the essence of the story. It's meant to be thoughtful and clever, and it succeeds.

The art direction and gameplay concept are both certainly charm points for this game, however I feel like as a puzzle game it starts out very boring, and the aforementioned charm points wear off by the time the puzzles start to become challenging and engaging. Early puzzles, when you don't have many colors, are often hilariously trivial and play like the same switch-based platform puzzles you see in any platformer. Another thing that may be up to preference but that I really did not care for were the long corridors designed so that you aren't distracted from your mother's voiceover; to me that's just poor design and I'd rather control be taken from me for a cutscene or be shown a pretty setpiece. This segues into another point, the distinct lack of setpieces, particularly in points where the player has nothing to do but appreciate the art direction; not enough is done with the art in these moments as you're still mostly getting corridors with the same background as every other area in the game. All in all, it was a relatively short game with a decent premise and art direction, but I feel like the game still lasts too long for its own good.

LBA 2 is one of the first games I remember owning as a kid, and from the moment I started playing, the nostalgia instantly came flooding back, from the way the characters spoke, to the music, to some of the little puzzles hidden here and there. I adored it then and I adore it now!
Quite obviously the graphics and cutscenes haven't aged well, but for a game originally released in the late 90's this can be easily forgiven. One thing that brought it down for me is the quality of the voiceovers. Twinsen's VA in particular very clearly sounds like he's reading lines off a script. There was one very humorous cutscene where Twinsen discovers the moon base and his mouth drops open in shock. There's a half second of silence, followed by a tame "wooo..." Surprisingly there's a flubbed line that somehow made it into the final game. The French ferry man on Otringal noticably stumbles over his lines. This is all nit-picky though and I don't mean much by it. It certainly doesn't take much away from the game. But then again when it comes to dialogue, the standard wasn't the highest to begin with.
Aside from this, the world is vibrant, and I love the characters to this day as much as I did as a kid, wooden VA's aside.
I'd definitely recommend this game to my friends, although I feel that a lot of the nostalgia might be lost on them. For younger players that crave cutting edge graphics and instantly lose interest in anything less (GENERALISATION, HO!), this might not be the game for them, but I could definitely see myself mentioning it to someone my age or older who has a taste for these sorts of games.
Money well spent and I'm still enjoying it! Planning on buying LBA 1 next because oddly enough I've never played that one!

This game is amazing. i love the hidden depth of it with the character dialog that can only be found with certain combinations of characters turrning the deploy scenes. i love the colorful/lush/alive feel of each map. i love how each character actually feels unique, and that every one of them feels like they need improvement (i only say this because to me its makes them feel more realistic, even though annoying based on certain character kits). although i also hate it, i like how unbalanced the game can be at times, like how each match is different even with the same hunters, monster, and map. over-all, i give the game a solid 8.5/10 due to how much it captured me.
*However*
This game still needs a lot of improvement. I still experience horrible bugs (although not so often). I've had players fall through the map either durring the dropship sequence, or through some hole in the corner of the map that the monster forced them through. on multiple occasions, certain models will bug and revert to an idol "T model", whether a player or an npc (one example was a Parnel hunter. when we went through water, he didnt have a swiming animation, he stood in a static upright position with his arms straight and at a 45 degree angle). certain monsters are obviously extrememly powerful compaired to others (cough cough, wraith) and i would assume are going to be tweaked to be balanced the longer the game is out. some hunters, based on their kits, are easily inferior to other hunters of the same class. i find that Lazarus is quite useless as a medic, since he doesnt actively heal, but can have his only "medic ability" easily shut down by a monster that uses the dead hunter's body as bait or easily stands over it, and either cannot be revived, or lazarus himself dies. he doesnt compare well to any of the other current 3, as they can ALL revive AND actively heal downed friendlies from a safe distance under similar conditions.
the actual offense i take with this game, is not the game itself (i LOVE the game), but the marketing. i hate how the dlc has been conveniently labeled similar to other marketing strategies that offer ALL later released dlc in one bundle, but has been sectioned into different dlc releases. "Season Pass" has been universally marketed as such. adding "Hunting" to it is like making a loop hole to decieve the consumer. it's highly unappreciated by the community. another is that each individual dlc character, or even skins, are grossly overpriced. other games that offer pay-to-unlock chracters have a much wider variety of characters to unlock, and all of them can be unlocked by free means, but require more time to be spent playing the game (hint hint). there's be a huge drop off of players/consumers with this game (originally due to bugs/programming, now due to marketing schemes).
The game is great as it is now, but if the studio showed a bit more sincerity with the release of new content, the fans would slowly return. sure, take a small blow to the profit margin and release some legitimate free content, or implement a system that rewards the players for commiting their time and effort into the game, that allows them to aquire the new content through effort and continued play, thus holding a larger consumer base, and in the end, less need for shifty marketing and high prices. the lack of "care" for the consumer as a CONSUMER and not a dollar symbol really bleeds through.

This game is awesome. A perfect mix of teamwork, skill, and strategy. There are dozens of unique maps as well as dozens of 'effects' that can help or hinder you when you play in campaign mode as each victory or loss will have an affect on the next map. The matchmaker also keeps things fresh by switching up everyone roles if two people want the same role. This can also be over-ridden as you can swap roles with anyone else if you both want. There is also an auto-balance system in place when you play the campaign mode, which helps prevent the game from being one sided. Overall, the gameplay is fantastic and so are the graphics. The game really takes that co-op tactics style of left for dead, payday, or Socom and then amplifies it by making everyone truely needed. Then it adds a player as your opponent to top it off. (Or you can play vrs AI, and the AI is actually pretty good)
All the negative reviews are about the price and the day 1 DLC. But this in no way affects the enjoyment you can have in the game. The base game has 3 characters for each of the 5 classes(Assualt, Support, Medic, Trapper, and Monster). Seeing as no specific character is better than any other in the same class, this means everyone is viable when your team works together with each others strenghts. The season 1 DLC just adds 1 more character to each class, and they are no more powerful than the originals. Even if you never buy any DLC, you will not be left out as it doesn't prevent you from joining any game. In fact, if a game had already started with an AI playing a character from DLC, when you join you get to play that character that round. The DLC is very much all skins, even the additional characters. You don't have to spend any extra money to enjoy this game. That means the only negative of this game is the price. And honestly, its just the same price on PC as it is on console. So it's not even that bad. And if you wait for a steam sale then it's a hell of a good deal.

I wholeheartedly recommend this game, due to what it goes for with the story. I used to play this a lot back in the day and still find it good now a day.
BEFORE YOU READ ON: THIS REVIEW CONTAINS (MINOR) SPOILERS.
The story starts out quite small with the lighthouse keeper missing, but it will see you travel over 3 planets in total by the end. Every character I spoke to in the game is fully voice acted. Although I would like some options when talking to someone it is also funny when Twinsen asks someone out loud if they are part of the underground movement planning to overthrow the current goverment.
The game overal is light hearted, but does have some more serious undertones. For instance several alien races bickering with one another over a lot of things and instead of working together they expect a magical prophecy to solve everthing. The goverment has soldier/policemen everywhere to make sure nobody misbehaves.
Locations you visit are nice and varied. At the start you are on an island with a small town and a cave system in the slightly more hilly part of the island. On one of the alien planets however there is a town with a castle, a store, 2 ferries, a casino, customs, a spa and some more. And even then I said nothing about the military island, or the elevator that takes you under the mists, or even the moon.
Most of the puzzles are quite easy like using lightning to light all candles in a room. There are a few acceptions like getting a very important package out of the store house manually (though you can skip this one by paying money to an NPC).
However that is not to say that I don't have any nitpicks, with the biggest being that this rerelease doesn't make use of any enhancements that are available now a days. For instance the resolution is still that of when it was originally released and controls can feel awkward at times (you can rebind them, but there are still times where they don't feel quite right).

I loved the original. I have many fond memories of it. I loved the soundtrack of the original. This game isn't even worth the effort of shovelling it on my lawn and I'm fairly certain if I did it would kill it. This game isn't necissarily bad if you've never played "Flashback: The Quest for Identity" but if you're seeking the nostalgia of your childhood, this game will♥♥♥♥♥♥you off very quickly.
The only thing this game has in common with the original is that the levels are very slightly similar and the main character's name is Conrad. The end. The game felt very "dumbed down". There are popups on the hud EVERYWHERE that say, "Go here. You can climb this. Talk to him. There's only one path you can take but we're going to tell you to take it anyway!" Luckily, those can be turned off. I decided to play the game on medium and found out immediately that the difficulty settings were made for console♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ There's a health bar, light falling damage, enemies attempt to tickle you to death, and healing stations are closer together than Starbucks. They also tried to add an RPG aspect by allowing you to gain experience, level up, and spend points in different skills. In a few ways this is good but mostly makes me ask, "Why the hell would anyone add RPG aspects to a Prince of Persia like?"
The controls feel similar to the original but they added an extra jump button and an arc style aiming system. The controls were definitely made for dual thumbstick controllers and then (horribly) modified for pc. Aiming is done by moving the mouse up and down to adjust angle and then moving the mouse left and right to switch sides. This gets annoying when you're trying to adjust your angle and accidently move your mouse too far to one side, causing Conrad to turn around and take it in the butt. If you have a controller to use with the game then it might not be that bad but mouse and keyboard controls get frustrating.
Bug time! This game contains bugs. There were a few times while aiming that the mouse would become locked in one place and I had to right click furiously to get control back. There are also times when grabing onto a platform would cause Conrad to get stuck and stand in mid air next to the platform. I only encountered this a few times and it did not deter me from the game but then again it never happened during a part where it actually mattered.
Playing this game does bring back warm nostalgic memories in the sense that I want to go dig out my old SNES and play the original game. Overall I feel like someone who played through the original once when it released is attempting to remake the game on age old memories. The only consolation I have is that I purchased this game during a Steam sale and didnt pay full price.

This is not the best game i ever played, just decent. While it offers a large amount of content, there is still something missing.
Well, what is good:
Many different nations to play, and this is not orcs, dwarves and other elves we already seen in hundreds of other games. This is unique nations, mainly based on humans, with their own history.
You can create your own nation and choose its strengths and weaknesses, i especially love this aspect of game.
There is a constructor of units, you can create your own troops - arm soldiers with different weapons and armor, give them abilites and perks, this is quite complex system which offers a lot of tactics.
Lot of different technologies to research, separated in three groups: economy, warfare and magic. You need to build cities carefully and specialise them, city focused on training troops is very different from city focused on research.
Exploring of map is good too, there is different quests you may find as well as lot of treasures and monsters roaming around. Hiring heroes and developing them are important, in fact first part of the game, where you explore the map, hire heroes, locate resources and fight wildlife is the best part of the game. It is really good.
Resource management is simple and logical. There is resource spots on map and you need to build cities or outposts to control this spots. For example, if you have an iron mine, it will provide some iron each turn and you can spend this iron on units with iron equipment. And so on.
Well, it sounds like perfect game, but there is several moments that can not let me call Fallen Enchantress "perfect".
First of all, there is very weak AI. Almost non-existent. AI nations are very passive, they can not offer a challenge. AI can not use all possibilities that game offers. And if you decide to increase difficulty level, AI will just have extra resources and bonuses. This is simply not interesting.
You ask about balance? There is some issues with balance, it will take some time to explain this problems anyway... they exist, balance is not perfect at all.
Diplomacy is plain and simple. If your nation are weak then AI will declare war on you. If your nation is strong then AI will not declare war on you. That is all. Of course, there is pacts, alliances and trade treaties, but i do not think there is much benefit from this.
As for quests. In general, they all fit in simple formula "go somewhere, find something and maybe kill someone in process". But, to be honest, it is hard for me to invent something different so, well, quests are OK.
Boss fights become disappointment for me. From very start, game told me a scary story about "big, giant, enormously huge dragon that is extremely powerful". Well, alright, i methodically gathered all my best troops and cautiously approached to boss domain, ready to retreat in any moment. There i saw a dragon and, well, my archers shot him and my pikemen poked him. Dragon died. That was all. It was not the epic battle i expected for...
Pace of game is very slow. Really slow. You can find yourself not playing but just pressing one button - "end turn", waiting for something to happen. Yes, you can regulate the pace of game, but even on fast speed it seems slow for me.
I did not finished any games i started in Fallen Enchantress. Because when you have a powerful army and strong economy, there is nothing that can stop you. It is simply not interesting. I can conquer all map and resistance is futile... preparations for war is much more interesting than war itself. And it was a huge disappointment for me because complex system of troop creation is really good and combat system are well designed.
Last drop is multiplayer. I mean there is no multiplayer. You want to proof your friend that your strategy and tactics are superior? Not in this game, unfortunately.
Well. Can i recommend this game? Yes and no. If you love to slowly and carefully build your Glorious Empire in fantastic world - this game is just about it. But if you want challenge from AI or want to play with friends - this is not good choice, try to check Dominions or Age of Wonders.
For me game is good enough, i will play it from time to time.
I was hoping for something like a fantasy setting civilization, it was not what I was looking for. Everything looks washed out and the controls are really clunky.
Great fun, very addicting fantasy strategy game. Not the best graphics, indieish game, but fun gameplay.

Honestly, I don't know how to rate this game. So in this review I'm going to talk myself through formulating a rating, and maybe you'll see why I am so confused by how to rate this game.
- To start lets point this out. This game is HORRIBLY optimized. I averaged 40 FPS as low as 20 and I have a beast rig. But I averaged these fps on EVERY graphical setting. Max, medium, and low. Did the devs even aim for 60fps? I guess not.
+ These graphics are good enough for me, I enjoy them. But a lot of persons today may want something better. The game was released in 2012 though. We didn't have any Witcher 3 graphics back then, remember?
+/- The sounds were decent, but nothing to write home about.
+ The game has a story mode with two scenarios. One is essentially a "Squad-based" campaign where you mostly use "hero" units to accomplish quests. The second plays essentially like the main "skirmish"-esque game mode plays (Which is called "new game" and that's it), except with some added story that keeps it far more interesting than the regular skirmish mode.
- The repetition in the game is....ugh. Its the same quests over and over again. If you play "new game" first, you'll never enjoy the story mode because you've already done everything you can do in the story mode for 9 hours at least beforehand. If you do story mode first you'll never appreciate "new game"due to its lacking of the main story content that kept the scenarios interesting. The game's formula grows old after 5 hours.
+/- The turn based combat is something unique for this game in the 4X scene. It keeps the game very interesting, an even a little hard in the beginning. Eventually you learn the perfect strategy for each map because honestly, it doesn't have many. Then it just becomes a chore, and since auto-resolve tends to favor you anyway, you tend to skip the feature entirely. It's good...but becomes bad.
So I still am lost about what to give this game. Honestly, the game has a very mediocre feel in every aspect of it. From the studio that made so many good RTS games, you'd think they'd be able to get a turn based game down pretty easily. But honestly,
It was fun, eventually the repetition and lack of optimization got to me. (Eventually being 5 hours in. Its amazing that I made it to nearly 20 hours). It's a very AVERAGE game with some very poor design decisions. Mostly bug-free though.
So do I recommend it? Well.....no. It was more of a chore than it was fun to play. So even if it was fun for a little bit. Well...It's really just not worth your money, ok? Please save yourself the  headache that this game induces and just avoid it.

This is a game that I would really, REALLY like to enjoy. I've installed and uninstalled it repeatedly, trying to get into it. There are SO many good ideas in here, but it's just TERRIBLY executed.
Tile yields for cities seem to be completely random, with no bearing on the type of tile or any kind of visual cues to clue you in. You can't check what status effect icons mean in battle, which wouldn't be too bad except that each icon can mean multiple things, so good luck with that. Haven't been able to find a way to check a unit's range in a fight, either.
It's a shame, because I love the way the overworld drops into the fights, which gives a double layer of strategy, plus the use of outposts to grab resources without having to start a whole new city if there's one spot you want to grab is something a lot Turn Based games could learn from.
This is a perfect example that just having great ideas doesn't necessarily translate into a good finished product. Pretty much every issue this game has stems from an awful UI, which seems like it could have been solved with a little playtesting.
Hoping to see another crack at it, in the meantime, Civ V is that-a-way.

I recommend this game highly. Especially if you are into horror.
Keep in mind that the game is indeed graphic. Yet, the fear given to the player is normally not actual fear. The majority of the fear comes from sudden noises, sudden movements, music, and random flashing lights. Not only this, but the fear is also caused by chase scenes. The player will experience an adrenaline rush as they are being chased. The fear is increased by the items mentioned above.
With this stated, there are some parts that cause actual fear. The moments where you have to actually hide or are being lectured by a psychopathic ex-doctor that wants to sell you body parts to a market he can not even reach because he is stuck in the place due to a spirit. The fact that you are running from someone and then have to hide builds up the fear.
This is why I would state that when you buy the game, TAKE BREAKS. You are not a wimp if you do so. The game is graphic and terrifying. Having too many rushes of adrenaline will cause you to shake and not think correctly overall causing you to become angered. If you take a break to collect yourself, you will be able to calm down and think a lot more clearly. But, it is your choice, not mine.
Overall, the graphics are amazing, the story is rich and fun to try and figure out, some parts are a bit annoying (why the hell can't you just wait until morning to go into the place or bring a friend. Maybe a weapon. Maybe jump out the window into the bushes instead of going back into the hell hole where the two naked brothers are wanting to crush you. Just normal horror fustration.), the music is outstanding, the acting is perfect, and the animation and gameplay is just amazing.
I highly recommend this game to anyone.

It's hard to describe this incredible game to someone who hasn't played it.  It's a science fiction, fantasy, strategy, roguelike, dungeon crawler, tower defense, hoarde survival game with squad combat, RPG like progression and permadeath; It's a wild mashup of genres to say the least!  On paper it has an identity crisis, but the developers did an incredible job stitching everything together, and it feels amazing!
None of the mechanics feel gimmicky.  Decisions have weight, and create a strong sense of risk versus reward.  It has that addictive "one more turn" feeling, with each "turn" being one room explored.  Combat is played out in realtime, with heavy emphasis on tower defense mechanics. After you find the exit on each floor, you must escort your crystal through the dungeon to the exit, while hoardes of enemies chase you down.  Ship and character options offer a ton of replay value with drastically different play styles.  Graphics and music are beautiful.  In a sea of bland forgettable roguelikes, this is everything I've been looking for in the genre, not to mention the only tower defense game that has ever grabbed my attention.
PS. If I could find any fault, the tutorial doesn't explain all of the mechanics.  Only takes a few minutes to learn though.  Do yourself a favour and watch a quick video tutorial on youtube.  You'll find more enjoyment if you know the reasons for your frequent death ;)

Hue was introduced to me on Twitter when the developpers followed everybody who had an interest in gaming, and each of their profile transpired seriousness, commitment, passion and pride that Hue demonstrate.

You control a little guy wearing a tie, similar to the main character "Tim" in the award-winning indie game, Braid.
The gameplay may, at first, seem to be a simple platformer, but do not be fooled.  It is a deep exploration of a single creative mechanic; use lateral thinking and your "magic verb" to get past an array of mental challenges.  The easiest comparison I can make is to Jonathan Blow's famous first project, Braid.
The game is divided into different zones that present different twists on the main gameplay idea.  I believe the first game to use this structure is the well-known time-reversing platformer game, Braid.
The story is told in vagueries, mixing simple emotional hooks with philosophical discussion.  Themes include the subjectiveness of human experience, the sacrifices one makes to quest for knowledge, and the melancholy of remembering better times.  You may notice that these are quite similar themes to a certain other game.
There are optional hidden items to collect across the game world.  I did not, personally, find every one of them, but I wouldn't be surprised if doing so caused the ending of the game to change significantly, since that is one of the most talked-about features of what I believe to be the primary inspiration for this game (Braid, Number None Inc., 2008).
Final Score: 2.71828 Braids out of 5

It's not for everyone and is generally a slow paced experience with time spent following monster tracks in the mud than actually shooting the beasties but for those with a bit of patience this is a rich, rewarding game to master.
The teamwork required as the hunters does mean the game can be a bit dire when you're paired with numpties but when it comes together or you get some friends in, fun times are had. When you're pitted against a smart player in the role of the monster and clever team mates, it's a very tense and testing game that's quite different from anything else out there. I'm not much of a fan of multiplayer shooters but this is much more satisfying to master than twitch reactions.
Of course playing as the monster is a whole other game unto itself and requires a different mind set to master but only understanding of playing as both sides will give you a real edge. Not enough games let you play as big horrible nasties like this and it's a part of Evolve that almost feels under developed given how fresh it is, especially in a multiplayer game.
I think the tiers of unlocks is a bit needlesss though, something to pull in the CoD crowd but thanks to some great balance and smart design, it's usually very rewarding regardless of which class you play as. The one upside to the avalanche of characters is that each one is unique beyond the superficial, with their own weapons and play styles. Same goes for the monster. Learning new characters and whole classes becomes its own little mini-game.
So basically if you can get it on sale or cheap, absolutely worth your time provided you're willing to come to it with some patience and perhaps a few friends.

-Through an array of intelligent design choices, developer Turtle Rock Studios has created a smart, asymmetric, multiplayer monster-hunting game that plays unlike anything else. It’s tactically deep, bursting with character, and once you get past its mildly obtrusive progression system, it offers a level of nuance rarely found in multiplayer shooters.Turtle Rock extends that “easy to learn, hard to master” virtue across most of the experience and Evolve benefits immensely from it.
-The monster needs to move quickly and carefully, balancing the need to put distance between itself and the hunters with the need to find food to level up. It’s ahigh-stakes tightrope act that requires good map knowledge, and a strong grasp of the monster’s surprising number of non-combat abilities like climbing, sneaking, and sniffing around. For as effectively as they exude an intimidating physical presence, playing the monster successfully requires patience and skill. Overpowering the hunters is really just your reward for outsmarting them, which makes ripping them to shreds as a max-level monster feel just as satisfying as it looks and sounds.
-As the hunters, the continually interesting challenge is to find a cunning monster that doesn’t want to be found amidst the sprawling and beautifully realized planet of Shear. Fresh tracks and startled birds are among the more obvious clues, but following them like a bread crumb trail is rarely enough. You need to reason out where the monster is headed, and make effective use of your team’s amusing sci-fi gadgets. You might tag tempting wildlife with a tracking dart, so that when the monster eats it you can get a bead on its location, or pursue a monster with an unmanned drone to relay his position to your teammates. Since every second that passes without the monster in your crosshairs is another step closer to it becoming nigh-unstoppable, hunts are every bit as thrilling as they are nuanced. Though it’s hard to take it all in when you’re embroiled in an intense monster fight, Evolve looks and sounds remarkably good. The ground rumbles deeply with Goliath’s every step,  Kraken’s Lightning Strikes light up the screen, Wraith's extraordinary agility, and Behemoth the "tank of a monster" who can morph into a massive, sending Hunters tumbling in every which direction while startled wildlife scatter in fear.
-Each individual element is well executed, but combined as whole during a match’s most pitched moments, the complete picture really is a sight to behold.
The true beauty of Evolve, though, is in the subtle details that flesh out its world, its characters, and its mechanics.
Very high reccommended.

GAME SUMMARY
Yrminsul is a tower defense with a unique overworld/conquest mechanic. With the conquest mechanic you are challenged to 'aggressively defend' new worlds to gain power and unlock upgrades. It features 3D graphics for tower defense battles supported by 2D art for interstitial screens, including some comic-like story art.
THE GOOD
-Passable tower defense.
-Passable story.
-Unique overworld/conquest mechanic.
-Built towers on early stages remain in later revisits.
THE BAD
-Upgrade system is heavily gated on progression. Some levels containing powerful core upgrades are pretty much impossible in the early to mid game.
-Dialogue in the tower battle screen is very slow and must either be endured or skipped completely (no next line, as available in other screens).
-The 3D graphics are quite poor and not what I'd expect from a game in 2016, they do a disservice to the 2D art style which is otherwise acceptable.
VERDICT
Some interesting ideas but nothing revolutionary here. I'm going to give this a passing rating though I neither recommend nor do not recommend this game. This game will likely only entertain a very small subset of players but there is a fresh idea or two in a genre that is mostly chiseled in stone at this point. I got this in a bundle. I would recommend trying to do the same or picking it up on sale if possible just in case it doesn't tickle your fancy.

First off I'd like to say I'm not a big fan of tower defence games. That said this game blew my mind.
*GAMEPLAY (8/10):
Basic tower defence gameplay upgraded with skill tries, corrupt/defend and random events.         (can get repetitive)
*GRAPHICS (9/10):
Models and art style is what made me want to try this game. It's just so colorfull, and that's a lot to say for tower defence game which are usually plane looking.  (beautiful)
*SOUND (8/10):
Music and sound effects are appealing. They go along gameplay so well sometimes you don't even notice them. But if you turn sound off you'll see a big difference (tried).
*PHYSICS (9/10):
Physics are what makes this game so good. Difference in enemy healt, speed and effect and your towers and powers are what makes this game so good. Good placement and cordination are key to victory. But game uses enemy placements good too so it can get challenging very fast. (easy to understand, hard to master)
*STORY(10/10):
In my opinion story is best thing this game has to offer. It's given to you via a comic book that you unlock as you progress. Skiped a part you didn't want to? Don't worry you can replay it in menu again and again. It's kinda childish but really creative and different, also it has some psychological values.
*CONTENT/PRICE (9/10):
Map in huge and there are a lot of events that can happen at any given time. There are skill tries to upgrade and seeds to collect. You will face many different enemies including boss fights. I guess it has around 20-100 hours of gameplay.
***OVERALL SCORE: 9/10
Recomendation:
Overall this is a great game I recommend to everyone who likes tower defence. If you don't like them but still buy this game it will surprise you. And if nothing else if you're bored and are looking for something different look no further.

The thing that most intrigued me about Yrminsul was the area control mechanic. I have to say that I really liked this mechanic since it really makes you feel like you are becoming more powerful in the game. As you gain control over more areas you get more abilities and can build more towers. This works well with the story of you playing as the bad guy that is trying to take over the world. While the game starts off a little slow, it started to grow on me as I built up my empire and became more powerful.

The other problem I had with the game is that at times there are some areas that I wish were a little more polished. The first couple days I played the game, some of my saved games disappeared for some unknown reason. This problem seems to have corrected itself when I last played the game though. It is also way too hard to click on the small and fast enemies which is important for a lot of the special abilities in the game. Finally I don't think the game gives you enough time to collect the infamy dropped from enemies.
If you like tower defense games I think you will enjoy Yrminsul. It is not the best tower defense game I have ever played but I still had fun with the game.

Unlike traditional tower defense games, this one has a large world map filled with small skirmishes
each skirmish map is fought over and if you lose, you lose that part of the map until you conqeur it back again. I like the concept because your towers are persistant, so once your killing engine is in place you can then plant future turrets for future wars! This rewards forward thinking and also makes you think; "do I place a tower to deal with this problem here and now or do I plant a better turret for future battles?".
This is a regular tower defense game with a few puzzle defense stages thrown in as optional extras. A nice compromise and it shows a real love for tower defense games in general to include both types.
You can also gain the ability to upgrade towers (its complicated) but once you gain the ability, you can freely switch it around so I would re-enter a stage and upgrade tower type 1, leave, come back and upgrade tower type 2. A nice touch.
The game is overall okay, nothing offended me but a lot of things bothered me.
You get access to 4 skill trees however everything in all 4 trees unlock at exactly the same time and you are free to delve into all the trees at once. This makes it seem pointless, to seperate the trees and makes the gating system very apparent. What would have been better, would be if each tree had different unlocking tiers so I had more to look forward too as opposed to just grinding out till the next milestone.
You also never lose territory. I mean you can and will if you play the game the way its meant to be played but you can just alt-f4 out of a lost battle and poof, you are free to lose as much as you want. It kind of defeats the purpose in my opinion and you can also quit a losing battle and reload your save game from the regular in game menu anyway. I don't feel like I am struggling against the forces of good, because I am free to cheat my♥♥♥♥♥off anyway.
Okay, you got me, I hear what you are saying, its my own fault if I cheat right? Well remember those gated skill trees? You need to own so much territory to unlock more skills and the skills are, you guessed it, more and better towers. So losing territory is really a set back both in terms of the games narrative but also you as the player. You get
new to look forward too until you hit x territories so if you lose even 1, it may have a chain reaction as you lose all the connecting islands too and you are right back to winning them all back with nothing new or interesting going on in the meantime. To put it a simpler way, lets take Sonic the Hedgehog. Lets say you die in scrapbrain zone and that sends you back to greenhill zone act 2. Its needlessly annoying, oh and we take away any chaos emeralds you found beyond greenhill zone as well.
Other niggles with the game come from balance. A lot of the early towers are really quite pants and you are stuck with them for longer than you would probably like. While you wait for the more exciting towers you try using the not so good towers in different ways but nothing changes the fact that they just suck. Enemies move fast, even the slowest of the slow monsters still move fast so when you have a tower that attacks every 10 seconds and a large, high HP monster whom only gets hit by that tower twice, well you lean towards faster attacking towers, naturally.
The game does limit where you can place towers so it is closer to a puzzle defense game but most of the early towers feel so rubbish that I just used the two towers you start the game with in addition to the starting spell up till about tier 3. Not even the slowdown tower was worthwhile because it only slowed 1 target at a time and even worse, the slowdown wears off!
upgrading the tower increases the enemy slowdown, naturally, but it also increases the refire rate so upgrading the tower makes it
not better!
The same can be said for most of the later towers as well because anything that hits slower than 5 seconds will only hit a mob once and I have limited space for these towers anyway so it's not efficient to use anything slow.
There is a spell that makes a tower shoot faster...But it has a cooldown on it because of course it does. Make it a passive and a lot of the towers would become viable.
Overall I'd like to sit down with the dev team and tweak the towers, make autosave either happen during the game or as soon as a fight starts with a 'you lost' flag on it until you win and the flag changes and rejiggle the skill tree and then i'll be happy.
Everything else with the game is fine and I have no complaints and the presentation is pretty top notch on this one.
If you love tower defense games, I actually find it harder to recommend this game since it will drive you up the wall, however if you are new to tower defense games then this one is okay.
I also found it a nice touch that you can kill the wildlife for money. Oh thats right, we play as the bad guy in this game and whilst it does the cliche thing of 'we are bad so we do bad things, of course' I liked the fact that they allow us to freely kill wildlife with no prompt or encouragement and that it can be beneficial to do so as well. A good example of meta-storytelling.
