I really haven't get into this game and this review has nothing to do with the game itself, but I just want to warn what kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ company Take Two is:

Disclaimer: I no longer play this original version of the game and highly recommend the remastered one since they finally got it working properly. With that being said, I can't rate this one down since it is still extremely good fun and is in my opinion one of the 5 greatest first person shooters of all time.
The level design and environment that this game brings with its underwater city and dark steampunk themed hallways and corridors are one of a kind. The BioShock experience is as unique as it gets. This game is one of those select few that belongs up there with the likes of Half-Life and Doom.
The characters and the voice acting is tremendously well done. The gameplay and combat is fast paced and exciting. There are so many different ways of defeating your enemies that you can never get bored with it.
The audio though is atrocious and this game is well known for the bugs detailed below.
The audio for many won't even work at all. In my case I originally tried to play this game on a Windows 7 machine with my audio going from HDMI over to a surround sound receiver. It was impossible for me to get this game's audio working at all. Years later I had a Windows 10 machine and used headphones plugged into the motherboard's Realtek audio which allowed the game to work properly without modification. For people with speakers though you will likely need to plug something into either your microphone jack or the headphone jack on the front or something. It is a strange bug but you should hopefully get past it.
The next most famous bug is more just poor coding. The physics and I believe animations are capped at 30fps so they look funny compared to the rest of the game which is running smoothly. There is a physics patch out there you can download which replaces a few files and works fine. All of these problems are gone with the remastered version so it is better to just get that one instead.
This game is a true classic and one of the most entertaining experiences I can ever recommend in a video game. The game is also incredibly long. If you take your time and fully explore every level you will easily put more than 20 hours into this game from beginning to end.
I can NOT recommend this game enough. Please do yourself a favor and try it out.

This is a game that will test your skills in a zombie apocalypse. The content in the game currently is nearly enough to call it a full game, however, the developer ambitions wanting the NPC fully working the game is a large challenge and continues to be a hurdle as they are constantly adding and improving this survival simulation. The atmosphere that is present right now makes you feel like your playing the walking dead (season one) but without the dialogue.
The two maps available (Muldraugh & West Point) are reasonably large and can take some time to memorize where you are. This game is at best harsh and you will have to learn how to become self-sufficient in all aspects crafting, cooking, first-aid, foraging, sneeking etc. But that is all part of the fun. The music in the game is completely amazing and go well with the theme and atmosphere that the game tries to give to the player. The tension in this game is real, especially when theirs is a large horde of zombies right in front of your house that you can see, as you are peering your nicely nailed barricaded windows. Then it becomes a dramatic scenario where to decide a course of action to take even tho your options may be limited.
You will have to give some time to learn the environment whether it may be winter or summer, sad or happy, alive or dead. You must learn what the best choice of action to take in those critical early days of the apocalypse. Cuphead set out to be a tribute to the 1930s cartoons and it succeeds. The game itself, even when leaving the gameplay out of the equation, is a work of art. The seemless, smooth animations, paired with the art-style and authentic music create an atmosphere worth experiencing. Oh, and it's a tough game.
The basic premise is simple: You lost a bet against the Devil, and now you must collect the contracts of his other ''debtors'', in order to save your own... Cup. This basically means you are mostly walking around the map, engaging bosses in fun, interactive, hectic and very diverse battles. Not all bosses are of the same quality, but on the whole you're in for plenty of memorable fights, each with its own distinct character. In between the game offers some traditional Run 'n Gun levels, which are challenging and fun in their own right. There's a shop where you can buy upgrades, which are just diverse enough to give you some sense of tactical decisions as far as what weaponry you take with you for a particular boss (though one shot type is grossly overpowered). You are, for the most part, left at the mercy of your own skills, however. The art-style lends itself for a rather over-the-top-style and it fits this game like a glove. There is always something going on in this vivid game.
In the end most of the game boils down to a bunch of trial and error session, where you learn patterns and tells to get further and further in order to defeat every boss and clear every level. The high production value and diversity of bosses/levels keep it fresh, however. And there's a co-op mode, so you can laugh at each other's pathetic skills.
So should you get this game? I'd say yes, definitely. However, to help you decide, here are the pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Amazing art style and animations
+ Amazing soundtrack
+ Gameplay is smooth. Personally I'd suggest using a controller, however.
+ Variety in bosses and stages
+ Co-op mode is great.
+ Modes to unlock, grades to earn. There's plenty to keep the perfectionist busy.
+ Winning is very satisfying
Cons:
- Some bosses can get a bit too hectic, resulting in some luck involvement. Not all boses are of the same quality, mechanic-wise (visually they're all stunning).
Mixed:
+- The difficulty can be off-putting if you are not into bullet-hell and punishing gameplay, which means you may not get to see all of the designs the creators put so much effort into. If you like a challenge, however, this is your kind of game.
Convinced? Get it. There is no game quite like it.

I have played the Long Dark for sometime now and watched its development.  Up until the last patch there were a lot of issues that I felt made the game very difficult to play and actually survive.  Post the most recent patch and the game is so much more intuitive, fun, while remaining very challenging.  Part of the issues with the survival genre is that once you get to a certain point, the challenge goes away and you are coasting because you have the best gear, an endless supply of food/water, and no reason to leave a certain "home base".  The long dark fixes that simply by creating a true survival game that is based on "how long can you survive"?  You cannot stay in one location as there is no endless supply of food, fire making material (which impacts abillity to melt snow for water), gear etc.  This forces you to move and brave the elements while exploring and finding new areas.  Eventually you will fade into the long dark, the question is how long before you do...

Hue is a game simplistic in style and deep in gameplay. One of the most difficult puzzle-platformers I've ever played. Difficult, but not punishing, the game never throws crazy surprises just to screw with the player, but simply has a steep learning curve.
That was good. The story behind Hue is threadbare, but sufficient. You (the titular Hue) are trying to find your missing mother. She was a scientist who invented color and somewhat made herself invisible. The entire story is told through a dream sequence in the beginning and scattered letters. It actually has a fair amount of thought-provoking questions regarding the nature of color, language, and communications, coupled with Hue's mother talking about how she and this scientist partner of hers plowed way back when.
All in all, worth it. You can finish it in an afternoon, but the challenge is rewarding, and the game cheerful soundtrack and quick thinking puzzles are actually quite revitalizing.

I absolutely love this game.  Four human players VS one monster player. There is so much depth and strategy to this game once you put the time in to learning all its nuances and intricacies.  It's very much a team oriented game though, so you might not get as much enjoyment out of it as others that play with friends do.  I play solo the majority of the time though and I still love it.  No two matches are ever the same, and the game runs well.  There have been some hiccups along he way, but TRS has been very good about patching and balancing the game since its release.
Be aware, this game is not for the casual crowd.  If you want to enjoy this game, you have to put the time in to learning all there is to learn and getting good at it.  If you don't, you'll find yourself getting destroyed over and over, and that's no fun for anyone.  This game takes skill to play, so you have to keep at it.
Lastly, don't pay attention to all the people who boarded the hate train for this game because of their DLC pricing.  Yes, there was a ton of DLC on day 1 for the release of this game.  But ALL of that DLC was purely cosmetic stuff.  Nothing that adds or takes away from the game experience.  And as far as the pricing for DLC hunters/monsters, the opinoin on that is going to vary from person to person.  Because of how much I enjoy this game and how much game time I get out of it, it's totally worth what I've paid in to this game so far.  For others, it might not be worth it.
All in all, a solid game.  Anyone who enjoys team based games like Left 4 Dead will love this.

This is not Red Faction Guerilla. It's a linear shooter.
'Salright though. It plays like an improved but heavily restricted RFG.
The story follows Darius Mason, Alec's grandson, and occurs after Red Faction Origins, a movie nobody on the internet knows about because it was only shown on something called a "telly-vision". You work for the Red Faction, now a professional military, and you have to save Mars from a maniac who wants to destroy the atmosphere.
and everyone hides underground, until
an apocalypse of killer aliens. C'est la vie.
The game proceeds with Red Faction's signature destructive, fast-paced, slightly OTT mannerisms. You kill aliens and blow things up. There's a lovely variety of weapons, by the way - Rocket launchers, wall-piercing plasma cannons, vaporisation flamethrowers, a magnet gun that weaponises terrain (The best weapon), a nanite grenade thingy, laser guns, assault rifles, a unicorn...
The Force... yes, the Force. You also have a thing strapped to your arm that lets you do things with nanites. You can repair any structure (This is incredibly therapeutic and I advise you do it at every opportunity), blow things away from you, trap enemies in zero gravity, make yourself a shield, or go insane and shoot everything really bloody fast. These are all on a cooldown basis, but they're lovely to use, and this combined with the weapons makes the game passable.
The enemies are annoying. They're all alien things that can jump like Spiderman and cling to the walls and ceilings a lot, so combat can be really confusing if you lose track. The gunplay itself is pretty tight, with a variety of weapons I mentioned earlier, each with their own niche. Also, their heads explode if you kill them with a headshot, so that's nice.
Campaign's good. It's maybe two thirds on-foot stuff with the occasional level in a vehicle or on a turret to spice things up. I do not like this spice. I want more magnet gun. But they're not too bad.
Aside from the main campaign, there is ruins mode, which is an open playground of destroyables and access to all destructive weapons with infinite ammo, either on a time trial or free play, which is really what we all wanted from this game. There's only five maps however, and while they're nice, they have explosives lying everywhere that you can't remove and which can rather spoil the feeling of slowly tearing buildings apart.
There's also wave survival, which I usually go on singleplayer and kill things with chunks of wall with the magnet gun to intense music. I advise you to do this as well as soon as possible.
This game has crashes! And they tend to happen at random when reaching checkpoints and
which is very irritating. There is a patch for MOST of them, which is literally just debug mode, which can be accessed in the betas menu. No password. Slightly intrusive debug readouts in the corner. Whatever, it does the job.
All in all, RFA is a deeply alright game. I'd say it's worth £15 if you're desperate for new ways to tear buildings apart. RFG may be a superior game format, but all games get stale, and this one breathes just enough life, if through gritted teeth, to keep Red Faction fun.

The environment and narrative were a bit bland (aside from the audio which was really great), but honestly they aren't the main selling point of the game anyway. If you're just looking for a fun corridor shooter that rewards you for blowing up everything around you, I recommend this game.

I highly enjoy Bioshock. Before you get this, do know that the gunplay isn't great, but the game doesn't ever give you too much ammo, so it's not a big deal. You'll end up doing a lot of combat with the plasmids, which are kind of like spells. Plasmids are generally simple, nothing to advanced, but you can carry 8 at a time and get some good combos, and some are used for more things. For example, the lightning plasmid deals light damage to enemies, but it also stuns them. These stund enemies take increased damage from you wrench afterwards. It can also electrify water for high damage, and fix some doors. You'll figure these out as you go, and it's fun to try different combinations.
Bishock is also a bit on the easy side. You really wont have much trouble up untill the final 2 or 3 levels, where enemies deal high damage and have high health, but they're never really bullet sponges. Big daddies are the toughest enemies, but they're aren't too bad. They're mini bosses you'll encounter that are neutral to you, unless you threaten them or their little sisters. Little sisters are guided by these beasts so they may collect adam off of dead bodies. Adam is used to buy Plasmids and other buffs. Big daddies are a challenge your first few times, but they're also easy to cheese, and have various weaknesses to ammo. Each gun has 3 types of ammo, a more generic ammo, and 2 special kinds. They can be crafted or found.
What Bioshock excels at though, is the story and atmosphere. You'll find tape recordings around the game, and they'll teach you about the backstory of the game. A lot of back story is told through imagery, and whats laid around in the world. The main story of Bioshock is Ok up until the last 2 or 3 chapters, were you learn some things and the story ends up becoming quite engaging. The atmosphere of this game is also superb, with the intercoms coming on to give pre recorded messages, and the splicers speaking to eachother, and a lot of the ambient noise. While Bioshock isn't scary, it may creep you out with some of the stuff that happens.
In the end, I like this game, so go buy it.

I can not be impartial.
Because this game was a huge part of my childhood. I remember sitting in my room, flipping through magazines and discovering an advertisement for Little Big Adventure 2. THEY'RE MAKING ANOTHER ONE!"
I can still feel the slap on my face from my father for cursing ...
Amazingly well done for the time the game was released. So much little details and the outdoor areas were in real 3D. Well, kind of. Static 3D images which rotated accordingly to your movement. The sound design was nice; but nothing world changing. At this time, I only had the German version of the game so the synchronization was a little odd. Like it used to be for nearly all German synchronizations back then. But it was okay, I was a child and I was happy with it.

Wandering around the beautiful crafted environments, talking to the cute rabbits, running from the police, sabotaging a space station, relaxing at the pool site or drive around the desert; you name it. The ammount of activities were insane and ... and ... and ...
If one could marry a game ... it would be this gem.
This brings me back so many memories, great game for it's age. 10/10

This game runs in DOSBOX, if you want to increase the resolution:
-go to the game's folder(generally %ProgramFiles%\Steam\steamapps\common\Little Big Adventure 2)
-find the DOSBOX configuration file(LBA2.conf)
-change either the windowresolution or fullscreen resolution to your desired resolution(I had the best results with windowresolution=1024x768)
-if you wish to always start the game in windowed mode. Change the fullscreen configuration to false aswell(fullscreen=false)
Here's a small copy of the configurations I had the best results with:
fullscreen=false
fulldouble=false
fullresolution=original
windowresolution=1024x768
output=overlay

Virtual Pool 4 - It really makes your game better
After playing the hole franchise I really need to say that, in my opinion, this is the best game ever made. It simulates in a perfect manner the real cue games and offers a true and immersive experience for any gamer out there.
Story time...once upon a time I was very excited about playing snooker for real. But having some limited financial possibilities and a snooker table being a must for top performance, I started to play Virtual Pool, hoping that it will improve my average game. Soon I was going to be the first junior champion of my country, by only playing a computer game. Sounds silly but it's absolutely true. Years later when I became the owner of a real snooker table and after winning the senior national championship, I still play Virtual Pool for fun. Transposing from the snooker table to the computer game comes natural.
The angles are all the same. The effects and cue action are a little more pronounced in the game, as we are dealing with 1s and 0s here, and not real physics. Also, impossible shots can be achieved in the game, while in real life the table's architectural design will reject some of the object balls. Very, very few flaws, that naturally come from the limited possibilities of today's gaming engines and design tools. Except for the technique - not needing to keep a stable position with firm hand bridge and feet in the right angles, head straight with chin touching the cue; no feather movement back and forth, no movement of the eyes between the cue ball, object ball and pocket - this game simulates the real deal frighteningly accurate. It's sick and I can assure you that what they say is absolutely true: It really makes your real game better!
I would like to thank Celeris developers (I always do when I have the chance) for bringing to the public this masterpiece. And of course, many thanks to Steam for making this game available. I waited a long time for it and I would of bought it eventually from the original website, but Steam is better.
Enjoy your 147 potting zone! :D

This game came off as a huge disappointment and I found myself struggling to even keep giving it a shot.
Now, I don't mean to be rude to the people behind it, I'm sure a lot of fair, valuable work went into this game. But to be honest, this really feels more of a "practice project" than anything that should legitimately be on Steam for 7 bucks.
The game feels kinda sluggish and slow, and I don't find myself as comfortable with it as with most tower defense games control-wise. The graphics are a weird mix between a Flash game (mostly in the menus and interface) and something like Rayman 2 (The original PC Release), devoid of dynamism and far less appealing visually. The gameplay itself is nothing that creative or appealing. The 2D graphics are neat, however !
I found that it was a bit of a shame that, with such a focus on the "story" part of the game (there's a big emphasis on the movie clips and such), there wasn't much more effort put into the actual story, character design and storytelling parts of the game, which, wether it be through the dialogue or plot, are...rather shallow. The kind you usually quickly give up on and find yourself skipping through to get to the action.
Another thing that was a big turn down was how...uninished the game felt. It crashed the three first times I tried to open it and I never managed to get the resolution and screen width to match despite my best efforts, and it doesn't run...so well anyway despite my computer handling more requiring games perfectly fine. The aforementioned "Flash game" menus and how it took me multiple attempts to simply rebound my keys validated the impression that I shouldn't have paid money to access this.
If this is the first (or one of) game you guys made, then...great job, it's actually good for a first try. But in my opinion, something so...low-quality (to be charitable) shouldn't be showcased on Steam for 7 bucks when you can find much, much better and more enjoyable, dynamic and functional Tower Defense games for free online on whatever flash site. What felt the most disappointing to me was that the artwork for the game looked really amazing and fun, and what I ended-up with was outdated, sluggish, and, honestly, ugly and uncreative 3D for a tasteless gameplay.
You guys have all the ingredients to make great games (kudos again to the 2D artist, since their awesome art is actually what decided me to buy the game) but this just felt like there wasn't enough effort and creativity put into it. In addition, the gorgeous artwork being anecdotical in the ACTUAL gameplay (and having "Ew 3D" instead) kinda felt like a scam, though I'll give you the benefit of the doubt on this not being intentional.
I hope you'll find this criticism to be constructive, apologies if it happens to sound angry or salty ! I do hope to see the aforementioned possible improvements in your future games if there happens to be !

Hue is a delightful puzzle-platformer with a interesting machanic that makes for a charming, unique puzzle game that I would recomend to anyone interested.
The machanic pretty simple. You have a color wheel, and you can use it to change the color of the background. Any objects in the foreground that match the color of the background will dissapear. Not just invisible, but completly cease to exist (if you've ever played Runbow, this probably sounds familiar). They can easliy be brought back into existence by changing the background color again. You'll have to use this to solve your way through lots of tricky scenarios and avoid deadly traps. The game gets more advanced by adding not only more items to interact with, but more colors to use on your color wheel.
This game looks fantastic, and since the game is based on colors - and therefore visuals - it's really important that it does! The art style is great, most of it being silhouttes (they can't exactly use colors, after all).
This game's pacing is incredibly good for a puzzle game. The game can kind of be divided into three different kinds of levels:
Mostly, there a puzzle rooms. These are rooms that present you with a challenge to solve at your own pace, using the tools you have.
Often, you'll get a break from puzzles and have to get through what I call an action room. These rooms don't require solving - instead, you'll need to use your color wheel to dodge obstactles and navigate platforms (think of Runbow, except you control the color of the background). There are a lot more puzzle rooms than action rooms, but the bursts of energy sprinkled about the game can help give you brain a break without losing your engadgement completely.
Lastly, there are narrative rooms. This game does have a story, and it tells that story by having you walk down an effortless hallway while narration happens. Not the most interesting way to tell a story, but the story is pretty simple, and actually pretty touching at times. A majority of the narration is letters that you're "reading" (listening to), so it feels a lot like flipping through diary pages more than a heavy plot. A lot of the entries explain backstory, but some of them are just sweet, and a surprising amount of them are pretty deep. Nothing that will radically change your life, but interesting food for thought nonetheless.
Overall, this game has a fun new puzzle machanic, gorgeous visuals, great sense of pacing and a story that is enjoyable enough that it doesn't feel like it gets in the way. Easily one of my favorite puzzle-platformers of all time, and I highly recomend you gvie it a try if it strikes you as something you'd like!

The problem is that the game is designed and balanced in a way that if you want to survive long periods of time (that's the point, isn’t it?) you should spend several hours of your game time in:
-evaluating if doing an exploration trip is going to be worth it in food and resources, and once you know the map several entire regions aren't worth it at all.
-staying in your hut during bad weather, sometimes for days.
-stockpiling food, medicines, water, ammunitions, tools and wood. Enough to survive for several days as previously explained.
-planning your inventory carefully because everything weights too much and your character eats like a 9 months pregnant with quintuplets. And has the same stamina too so plan where you'll take naps during the trip.
-continuously repairing your clothes, tools, weapons, etc.

This list will take hours of your time, isn't entertaining at all and doesn't mean anything because the game may then decide that you are going to have several days of heavy snow, storms, strong winds and a pack of wolves so you have to wait until the weather allows you to do something in the outside and guess what comes next: it's time again to stock food!, and water! what a joy!.
At this point I usually start thinking why the **** would I spend my time repeating a bunch of tedious tasks for hours to see if I have better luck in a couple of days to see if I have then luck in the trip and basically I decide that I can spend my time in several more entertaining ways.
So no, I don't recommend this game.

You'll end up doing a lot of combat with the plasmids, which are kind of like spells. Plasmids are generally simple, nothing to advanced, but you can carry 8 at a time and get some good combos, and some are used for more things. For example, the lightning plasmid deals light damage to enemies, but it also stuns them. These stund enemies take increased damage from you wrench afterwards. It can also electrify water for high damage, and fix some doors. You'll figure these out as you go, and it's fun to try different combinations.
Bishock is also a bit on the easy side. You really wont have much trouble up untill the final 2 or 3 levels, where enemies deal high damage and have high health, but they're never really bullet sponges. Big daddies are the toughest enemies, but they're aren't too bad. They're mini bosses you'll encounter that are neutral to you, unless you threaten them or their little sisters. Little sisters are guided by these beasts so they may collect adam off of dead bodies. Adam is used to buy Plasmids and other buffs. Big daddies are a challenge your first few times, but they're also easy to cheese, and have various weaknesses to ammo. Each gun has 3 types of ammo, a more generic ammo, and 2 special kinds. They can be crafted or found.
What Bioshock excels at though, is the story and atmosphere. You'll find tape recordings around the game, and they'll teach you about the backstory of the game. A lot of back story is told through imagery, and whats laid around in the world. The main story of Bioshock is Ok up until the last 2 or 3 chapters, were you learn some things and the story ends up becoming quite engaging. The atmosphere of this game is also superb, with the intercoms coming on to give pre recorded messages, and the splicers speaking to eachother, and a lot of the ambient noise. While Bioshock isn't scary, it may creep you out with some of the stuff that happens.
In the end, I like this game, so go buy it.

I really enjoyed this game. It's similar to games like Civilization or Warlocks: Master of the Arcane but the details are all heavily changed to create a very unique entry into the genre. Given how much there are to games like this, I'll just highlight things that stood out to me that I liked and didn't like.
What I liked:
+Each leader/faction felt significantly different from the other factions -- There's a lot of different units, spells and bonuses that each faction gets to make you get a different experience playing with each one.
+The game's combat is really fun -- You can play in a top down view isometric grid type combat or auto-calc. The auto-calc is weird, so sometimes you suffer some bad losses and sometimes you win a battle you could have never won, however I found this feature to be more in my favor than ever against me and I normally only did it in situations where I would obviously win to save time. Additionally you can create very large armies with very powerful units so that a combat victory is much more feasible than in a game like Civilization.
+The random stuff on the map is quite fun -- The game has a quest system which, while basic, is actually pretty fun in short bursts. Additionally there is the option to have a ton of monsters and animals to keep yourself busy with them. On top of all that there is a dedicated area on each map where a ludicrously over-powered monster reigns who you can fight for some sweet items.
+The hero system is pretty fun -- At first heros seem awesome. Heroes can use spells, equip gear, have special properties that buff your army or a city they occupy. In combat they aren't useful later in game because their stats just don't scale well, but their spells/city/group buffs can be worth it. Each hero is very different so it's something to explore.
+The city system is really good and has great progression -- Each city levels up and as they level you can choose a specialization for them, offering bonuses to that particular city. This is really cool and offers you a new level of customization. I found myself regularly creating 1 resource heavy city and then making several combat cities to amass a horde of overpowered soldiers.
What I didn't like:
-The game isn't technically perfect -- Sometimes you try to click something on the map and the game has it's own mind. Sometimes walking to a particular place is a real pain. These were fairly minimal interruptions, but over the course of 50 hours it was enough to make me complain about it. Also as mentioned earlier the auto-calcuation battles can be wonky. Sometimes I would start a fight manually, then once I realized I couldn't win, I'd auto-calc to end my suffering. However, I'd end up winning a fair amount of those battles somehow. It didn't bother me because it was a nice surprise, but it may be a break in realism for others.
-There is a steep learning curve -- The game has a lot of stuff to it, much like civ. The difference is that in this game the combat is more present, so you do need to be more up to snuff. I found myself being demolished in about 3 (...practice) games before I could finally conquer others, even on easier settings. The monsters can be a real threat, which is nice later on, but at the start it can be overwhelming.
If you like any sort of strategy, please try this game. I was sad I was so hesistant in buying it (I didn't buy it until it hit $10, easily worth $40). Please note this review is based on the game without any of the DLC.

I spent money for it so I'd hope to be able to recommend it. Alas, not to be.
It's not a bad game, really. It's just that, in 79 hours, I've figured out how to utilize the tech tree and can advance faster than the Hard AI can. Having done that, I just take what I want and no one ever tries to stop me.
Some of the Rulers are pretty weak, so, one could handicap themselves by playing those, I suppose. Here are what I see as problems.
1. Everyone will tell you that the random mobs are often vastly superior to what you can field, especially early on. That these advanced mobs attack your armies AND your cities, long before you can cope with them, is very frustrating. It's the cause of a lot of re-starts.
2. It takes long periods of time to recruit army units. Thus, it's long into the game before you can mount any credible force UNLESS you simply allow your research and tech improvements to just languish and build weak units. The AI will happily flood the land with pioneers that take control of the valuable areas while you fall behind while building troops. But, he won't bother to defend them! He'll allow you to take his outposts and the resources there with no opposition. Instead, he waits until they're again undefended to send in some throwaway units to re-take them...maybe.
3. Happily, you can leave your cities pretty much unguarded against the AI opponents. They NEVER attack you. They'll build outposts and garner resources and, left entirely alone, create 4-5 units in their cities. But, they never put together any large forces to attack, just a few units that putz around doing nothing aggressive to you. The AI sends in lone heroes to battle vastly tougher mob armies and, of course, lose. The heroes usually don't die, just return to a city, maimed, to recuperate. Maybe that's the AI's method of getting them experience? It's fruitless, though.
4. There's Epic (that's YOUR army) and then there's EPIC (that's the AI mobs). Taking YOUR epic army to battle and watching a dragon eat 4-5 entire units in one turn let's you know that you can't trust the game's evaluations. Weak and medium, well, they're not too badly graded. Once you get to strong, deadly, and epic, it's prety iffy as to your relative strength.
5. Why does the AI declare war and then just sit in his cities, waiting for you to take them? Why does the AI declare war at all? I know they fight each other and take cities. I think they're just as handicapped as the player when it comes to fielding armies.
So, I won't be buying any DLCs for this game and I don't advise anyone to spend money on this game.

I've played all of the virtual pool series, and this one was a high disappointment.  Let's start with a few of the -good- points, and there are a few.
1> Visually nice to watch, the textures and over all graphics are good.
2> Physics are - decent.  And it pains me to say that because you can find spots where the physics are painfully obvious to be on vacation.  What would stop dead last shot, happens to roll JUST enough to **** you over next shot.
That's - about it.  Now for a shortened list of the bad points, points that aren't just me gnit picking.  Yes I only have 5 hours on the game, but it is very much enough to tell you what I've learned so far.
1> One of the game's selling points is "Tracking so you can learn the mechanics of the ball."  Which it does do.  In practice.  Only.  The minute you load up one of the tours you can kiss the tracking lines goodbye, you won't be getting them at all.
2> Another point is the ghost ball aiming assistant.  Which you do get. On tours, but it's a deception.  You line up perfectly only to have your ball miss the pocket and JUST happen to line up perfectly for your opponent.  Not all of the time mind you, sometimes it doesn't do this until you're on your last shot that would win you the game.
3> The second ghost ball that is on the target ball to help you line up your shot.  Again this is very deceptive and not 100% accurate - more like 75%.  Maybe I'm not quite lining it up perfectly - but I'm playing on a 50" monitor so there's that.  It's not accurate.
4> Poor controls and Deception in features.  So you spend a good 10-15 minutes going through the games tutorial.  the tutorial teaches you to use the F key to set the stroke power of your cue.  Remember the point about tracking lines?  This feature is GONE in anything other than practice, and the actually mouse controls of the cue is painful at best.  You line up your shot, you pull back on the cue, you push forward hard to break and the cue stops moving and doesn't hit the balls, in confusion you try again only for it to react way too early and your cue ball travels a pitiful inch across the table.  Bad controls = hard to play game.
5> For those of you who have no idea what M. Bisoning is.  You will learn, oh yes you will learn.  You want to learn the game so you play the story on the easiest setting - which means NOTHING.   If the game decides you need more of a challenge.  The 10 year old girl who has been missing every shot suddenly becomes a crack shot and sinks everything, performing bank shots, jump shots and masse shots.  I - wish I was exagerating on this, It tries to issue a 'challenge' by having your computer opponents running with the equivilant of you using tracking lines - it's obvious if the computer decides the computer is going to win, the computer is going to win, going as far as obviouslly curving or increasing the speed of your last shot to have you scratch.
From someone who's played all of the VP Series, I have to say I'm disappointed with this one, There's just no logic in what they expect you to accomplish.  It's clunky, it obviouslly ****s with your shots to emulate difficulty and the controls are lacking.  If you could look past the downfalls, it is a VP game, It can be fun in some instances,  But I wouldn't play it for the competitive side, you'll have a heart attack.

This classic version has been around for a while, and makes a welcome arrival on Steam. The usual varieties of Pool (and rule variations) are available and while it is simple to pick up, it takes time to become skilled. It really can improve your actual game in real life, although the AI skill 'rubber-banding' gets quite noticeable when you are good. The graphics are fine, and the physics realism is high.
You can save a lot of time offline by pressing Z immediately after any shot, to skip to the point where the balls are at rest. Playing online therefore feels nowhere near as quick, and you have to play more carefully and strategically.
If you enjoy pool, this simply has to be in your PC games collection. 5/5.
*** IMPORTANT NOTE: If you want to play online unrestricted, you have to pay a tiny bit extra, but it's still not much compared to paying for access to real-life tables. ***

If however you want to develop and learn about billiards and pool in general then it also can cater to your needs.
From the Video totorials by Steve Daiking you can learn the very basics in the art and skill Of Pool to the more advanced positioning and cue ball control and once you think you have mastered that phase you may want to start a hustler career and gamble your bux against the Poolsharks at the various and sometimes seedy locations  available to you.
You also have a varied and comprehensive  career mode at your disposal.Start of as a lowly amateur and see if you can progress your way through the ranks to take on what seems to be a brutal Champion level in the game.
You have a trick shot mode,you can set a table and the balls the way you want and try perhaps to recreate a shot you seen one of your heroes play in the past.
In short there is a whole host of things to keep yourself interested in the game,above all though this is not simply a game,its a learning tool that anyone who has a mind to can progress and advance their own understanding of how to shoot a ball and  and makes runs and start winning.
Virtual Pool does all this with the best control,method of all,the mouse.
Your mouse controls your cue stick,you draw the mouse back and push it forward to take a shot,it could not be simpler.
Using the mouse is the simplest and best way to give you the weight and feel of a shot and its also through time has proved Celeris have got it right since way back in 1995 when Virtual Pool first saw the light of day.
Other games of this nature have always used power bars and meters that take so much longer for you to set a shot up and actually hit a ball.Virtual Pool does not mess about and very quickly you will see that they got it right.
It can improve your reallife game but only if you want it to as its down to what level you want or think you may be able to acheive,the sky is the limit as far as that goes.
Ok some will say the graphics although a vast improvement on the fore runners in the series, they dont jump out at you like some other nicer looking games of that ilk.You may be right and there is still room for improvement as the game will be a work in progress and is being improved all the time.
What  stands out by a country mile is the game play and once you have mastered all the key controls as that will take time I think you will find that Virtual Pool 4 has got all the rest beat in comparison
Its not simply a game its as true a simulation as you can possibly get on PC and for the time being still hold onto the title of Best Pool and Billiard sim of all.
If you are new to this type of game please dont judge it after a few hours of struggling around and feeling your not getting anywhere.Use the tracking lines as a help if you need to,use the ghost ball to show you where to hit the ball.
The most important thing is to give it time and if you want to learn and progress,you will and it will grow on you all the more.You will keep coming back to it and you will develop as a player and you also will get a better understanding of the art of billiards and Pool in General.
You have tried the rest....now try the best. Virtual Pool 4 Its what sitting up to 4 am in the morning is all about.

Your mother is missing. She is a brilliant inventor—perhaps
brilliant because as a result of her tinkering, she now resides past the visible colour spectrum in what is known as impossible colours. You must use the Amular Spectrum—a device your mother created that can shift the very colour of the world around you—your problem solving hat, and your lightning quick reflexes in order to gather up all the colours, find your mother, and live happily ever after.
Gameplay consists of a series of areas in which you need to solve a puzzle in order to continue to the next area. Progression is blocked off by obstacles that are a colour (or two) not yet found on your Spectrum and so you’ll need to find the appropriate colour before you can proceed. This forces you to approach the game in a linear fashion, which makes sense because Hue is heavily story-driven. More on that in a moment.
Puzzles are intuitive and, more importantly, satisfying to solve. They are challenging, but not impossible after some careful examination and reevaluation of your approach. They come in a few flavours:

Every so often, a new element—different shapes of block, spigots of paint that will change the colour of said blocks, lazers, etc—is added, which keeps gameplay fresh. I found myself smiling on more than one occasion when I figured out how several elements worked in conjunction with each other.
The mixture of puzzle solving with stretches of less taxing platforming during which your mother speaks to you while you press onward is effective in fully immersing you in the worlds of Hue. Your mother serves as the narrator, communicating with you via letters scattered throughout the world, and the tone and pace of narration is just lovely.
In fact, the soundtrack as a whole is a wondrous, somber collection of melodies played on classical instruments that fits the game’s atmosphere to a T. It’s reminiscent of a more upbeat
where no horrors lurk in gloom and tasked with adding a splash of colour to the shades of gray. It also embraces
's instant-death formula where taking damage ends Hue’s life.

Hue is a beautiful, interesting puzzle platformer that I would definitely recommend to everyone. The game caught my attention right away, and I completed the entirety in one sitting.
The way Hue is played is different than most platformers in the manner used to solve the puzzles that you must get around. Your means to solving puzzles requires use of color, hence the title of the game. As you progress along, you will gain the power to morph the background colors of the world you are in. Doing so will cause any objects in the foreground to disappear if they share the same color as the background. You will unlock new colors as you play the game, and you can shift to any of them using a color wheel that pops up for your control.
That right there is pretty much the crux of gameplay for Hue. While it is also a platformer and requires some running and jumping, most of the puzzles do not force you to perform tight-knit platforming actions. They are usually more focused on the actual color puzzles themselves. A large amount of the game is easily doable, at least it was in my opinion, and not many of the puzzles will confuse you too much. But that did not make me feel bored, and the puzzles were not bad. In fact, I prefer when I can figure out most of the puzzles, instead of feeling like I would need to look up suggestions or answers.
The game does progress in difficulty as you go along, so everything is not the same. Each new area that you enter adds in a different level design, along with new obstacles in your way. For instance, later in the game will have some puzzles with colored gel spraying (like Portal 2), which can paint boxes into other colors, requiring you to figure out which colors need to be used to set boxes in correct places for holding switches or blocking lasers.
In terms of difficulty, however, the game does get a sudden spike in the final area. And the increase in difficulty here was not exactly positive for me, as it seemed like the puzzles suddenly degraded into being tedious and not as fun as the rest of the game. While I was a little sad with some of those puzzles, I still completed the game and overall enjoyed the experience greatly.
Important to the gameplay is the controls, and I will let you know that keyboard and mouse work completely fine. The game recommends controllers at startup, but I usually try games out with keyboard and mouse anyway. I had no problems whatsoever with the controls in the game. Everything worked perfectly and I could move around and react efficiently. In fact, the controls and motion of the game are extremely fluid - everything is smooth.
The art style helps show that too, with how your character moves, other objects bounce around and move in great motion. Graphics are amazing in Hue! You can see from the screenshots how the monochrome world can look, along with the changing colors. Other NPCs you meet, the puzzle objects, level layout with buildings and design - Hue is one of the prettiest games I have played in a long time. All of the colors fit together in such a beautiful way.
Music and sound are also quite amazing. I really love the background music as you play, with the soundtrack of the game having a decent amount of songs to cover your time. It really surprised me how comforting the noise is to the point that I want to listen to the soundtrack again right now. The only downside I had is that the game occasionally gave loud, bothersome audio fuzz or distortion noises, which doesn't occur with anything else I have played recently. It got better after I closed and restarted the executable, but it still didn't go away entirely. I really hope that gets fixed, because it damages the beauty of the game's audio.
Besides the music and sound, there is also some voiceover mainly related to narration of the story - and the story is something I have not gotten to yet. The reason for delaying my story commentary is that I was actually disappointed with it. While the narration you hear is pretty nice in voice quality, the story premise of Hue is nothing exactly new. Hue seems to act like it has a big philosophy... as if the story has large depth and great points about the world.
Some people seem to think that the story is amazing, but all it really does is try to argue about perspectives of the world. The main character's mother is researching this color technology, the ring itself that you control to shift the world's background as you play. She is challenged by a Dr. Grey at her university about the power of the colors, as if she is ruining something about the world by wanting to shift it from monochrome to colorful.
I honestly do not think the game actually gives you any new revelation or philosophy, though it seems like the developers think it will. And in fact, the game wastes a bit of your time because of their thoughts about the story. You "learn" about the story after every handful of puzzles in the game by finding letters that trigger narration sections. What the developers do here is have the narrator talk for a minute or two; and, in order to force you to hear it all without doing anything too confusing, they have you run through almost empty linear sections with no puzzles. The paths of these sections are intentionally boring and long enough for you to hear the entire narration without getting to the next puzzle. One of the sections is even a poorly-done maze.
Those narration sections intentionally waste your time, which is one of my big criticisms to the game. Similarly, the game has hidden collectibles called beakers, which also are meant to artificially bump up your gameplay time if you wish to find them. The collectibles do that because each area of the game requires a set of colors to get through the puzzles; but usually the areas will have one or two colors blocking certain pathways - colors which you have not yet received. What you will need to do is receive those colors from the NEXT area of the game, and you must return to the previous area, replaying the same exact puzzles until you find those previously-blocked doorways.
A shorter way to describe the above collectible complaint is this: Say there two areas of the game, A and B, with many puzzles that take a while. You must complete A entirely, complete B entirely, and then return to A, replaying almost all of its puzzles (with no difference from before), but use colors from B to find a couple of collectibles. It is a poor artificial way to extend the length of your gameplay.
Altogether, the game took 5 hours to complete, but that is with some idle time as well as those bad collectibles just mentioned. Further, certain puzzles in the game are rather lengthy for a single room, and if you die during them, you will typically repeat all of the easy portions over and over until you finally complete the more difficult part. I would say that the game is actually 4 hours or less, so it is not quite a long game for its price.
Despite the criticisms I have laid out for Hue, I would still recommend that you try the game out, as I greatly appreciated the experience.

Hue is a puzzle game where you use different hues to make pieces of the world appear and disappear.  It starts off strong, with lots of basic puzzles and a Metroidvania feel.  About half-way through (once all the colors are collected), it turns into a straight puzzle game, with some lateral thinking and quick reflexes required, and a fair bit of frustration.  To be honest, the concept got a bit stale by the last couple of levels.  The story, about a boy separated from his parents, is okay but not much of a motivation.  The gameplay works pretty well though, and it is a novel experience. It took me 5 hours (I didn't collect all the secret flasks), but could probably be done in less. Nice but not something to go out of your way to play.

I generally stay away from horror games because most horror games try and scare you with cheap jumpscares, making your expierience feel lackluster and boring. That's not the case with Outlast. This game uses jumpscares but they are used in creative ways and are kept to a minimum. The game relies on tension and stress to scare the player and it works extremely well. Dark themes are present within this game and don't aim to disappoint.
In the game, you play as a reporter who is on a mission to uncover the secrets that lie within the walls of Mount Massive Asylum. You enter the asylum uncertain of the horrors that awaits you and things in this game start to escalate really fast when you see the amount of blood that has been spilled. It's a very intense horror expierience meant to bring stress to the player.
The gameplay is simple and heavily stealth based. You cannot attack enemy NPCs' and the only way to defend yourself is to run or hide. It is rather challenging to escape your enemies and requires quick decisions to be made if you want to survive. You have a nightvision camera to help you record events and see in the dark.The goal of the game is to find a way out of the asylum but it's alot harder than it sounds. There are exploration aspects which allows you to find documents containing information and lore of the world you are in.
This game is for people who want to invest in a thrilling expierience which can make you proud upon completion and can be played in one sitting or more.
It is a great game for youtubers to play on their channel and for a bunch of friends to get together and see who is the "bigger man".
Outlast relies on gritty-looking visuals to set the tone.The game is dark and relies on the nightvision cameras' green effect to add a 'found footage' factor into the art-style. (reminding me of movies like "The Blair Witch Project")
The visuals look good and realistic enough to fully immerse the player into the game.

The music in this game isn't particularly "beautiful" but thats how it should be since it ups the tension whenever you are spotted and allows for fear to enter the players' mind. Hearing the screams of people behind the walls in the building is oh so terrifying and the sound of a chain dragging on the floor as you desperately hide in a locker, praying for your life, is absolutely dreadful.
The sound is realistic and allows for full immersion into the game.
Outlast is challenging, but requires a minimal amount of learning to complete. All you need to know is that you have to run and hide when enemies are unaware of you. I had alot of issues with platforming and jumping felt unnatural. The game has controller support but is best played with mouse and keyboard.
The game is very linear, but benefits from that by making it easy for the player to know where to go at all times.
The only replay value this game offers is if you want to complete it on a higher difficulty or if you want to hunt some achievements. The game alone is mainly there for a "one-time" expierience.
I recommend Outlast to fans of the horror genre because it is absolutely terrifying. The quality of the game is nothing short of amazing. The game is very entertaining and defines the genre it is placed in. It is a unique horror expierience that lives up to all the hype surrounded by it.

I don't want to write an extensive review because, perusing the reviews already posted, it appears that many of my complaints have already been fleshed out in greater detail. I'll give you the point-form reasons I don't recommend Evolve to any player. You can find my reasoning repeated in post after post in the forums and in these reviews.
- DLC setup intentionally manipulative, relying on normal DLC structure expectations. See "hunting season pass" debates. To say they have been clear about the additions is a innacurate simplification of their deception.
- Upon release, there were many bugs, which is normal. One I couldn't forgive was the mouse cursor being present the whole time.
- Forum moderation isn't a part of the game, but check out their tactics. If the word "moderator" is mentioned in any context, thread immediately locked. If you're talking about how the season pass problem was unfair and/or manipulative: "We told you about it in this post before, your complaint is invalid, thread locked". If they can lock a forum, they'll do it without hesitation.
- DLC content overpriced, for little reward. Evolve sometimes just feels like a big DLC shop.
- Experience and unlocking system is strange and unbalanced. You are expected to repeat using items to level the class, but these requirements are often arbitrary at best and force you to adopt tactics that don't work in order to use more characters.
- Finally, here's a post from a moderator that pretty much sums up 2K/TR's entire defense strategy. Note how they lost almost 90% of their intial players, who were evidentally *all trolls*.
"OP,
You will lose your bet since the post you've made isn't against the rules. What was the bet again? Did I win anything? (reviewer's note: this was in response to the OP assuming he would be locked or banned, because in several cases near-identical complaints were locked immediately...)
Back to the topic.
What 2K has learnt is that, if you want to make a good game, you don't have to be heartbroken because of all the trolls saying your game sucks. As a gamer, I don't really care about what the trolls say for Evolve or any other game.
If publisher and developer is happy about the product they have made, then how about making this product get better without listening to all this trolls saying "your game is dead", "rip evolve" and many more.
I've been watching developers trying to tell the trolls that if they want to support the game they can always purchase it. Saying "omg this game sucks" without playing the game is really a shame.
I've pre-ordered Evolve myself, and even if I've not played the game as other veterans did, I always enjoy a match or two I once in a while play.
What I'm mad about is that, if we take games as an art then Evolve has to be one of the best art ever created. Evolve achieved something the other games couldn't, but none of the trolls understands it.
What also sucks is that in current day if you make a Call of Duty you'll earn a lot of money, but if you create a game such as Evolve you will be spammed with hate emails every day.
If you want to discuss the game, then please purchase it, give it some try and come back to us. But if you will only stick around and discuss how the forums are managed, then sorry but this discussion forum only cover the game. Plus the discussion of moderation isn't allowed, as it creates spam topics which really achieve nothing.
If you want to talk Evolve, come to
, where the community will be the one answering your questions and not just a single dude trying to "make Evolve look good" with a star next to his name."
Got a complaint? You're a troll. Think there are problems with the game? Evolve is a new style of game and therefore art. Thread locked. Want to discuss why you think the season pass idea was intentionally misleading? Thread immediately locked, read the stickies.

Disclaimer; I don't often write reviews, and I'm not good at doing so. Everything included below is my own opinion.
This game is the absolute top "realistic" zombie survival game. You can customize your zombies how you want them. You can play on several different locations/maps, and you can do whatever you want to do in game. There's no forced story, no lore, nothing. Unless you want it.
Here's the situation. You wake up (after creating your character) in a temporary safe room. The odds are good there's zombies in your house. You have nothing but the clothes on your back, and your house key. Your only goal at the moment is to survive... GO.
The zombie's AI is well written, the music is fantastic, and the game is ALWAYS improving.
Ok, so normally we talk about the bad? They're still working on stability, and features. It is an early access. But, it's certainly worth the $15 purchase price.
Like zombies? Like sandbox games? Like searching for loot, food, and surviving? Get it. Get it for a friend, too. Playing together is a lot of fun.
I hope this review assisted in your decision.

Most realistic cuesport sim ever... and that's what this is really; a sim.
If you're into cuesports in any capacity this is the game for you. It has its problems, and they are being fixed albeit slowly.
Pros -
+ Almost completely realistic ball physics. Any shot you can play on a real table you can play here, apart from a few (See cons)
+ Most variations of popular cuesports available.
+ Nice online community - most players are GOOD :P
+ Will definitely help your real game, especially by watching other people play.
+ Addictive once you get the feel for the mouse stroke
+ SO MUCH FUN when you're in a tourney with good people.
Cons -
- Some things aren't modelled correctly. Snooker pockets are wrong. Cushion compression on the pockets isn't modelled so you can't play hard shots (a staple of snooker) into the back of the pocket... you have to hit the drop perfectly. It also means in 9ball if you get stuck straight on a ball frozen to the rail you can't do the trick of shooting cushion first. Throw is modelled (slow thin cuts with draw push off line) but it is exaggerated and unrealistic... will frustrate some players.
- Slow update process. It's a one man team as far as I'm aware. Hire somebody!
- Online community for the most part are nice but you will be destroyed until you know what you're doing... I've been playing this game for about 7 years but for a newbie they might get frustrated. People pull no punches.
- Graphics aren't the best, but very serviceable.
- Currently community is too small - steam realease has helped this and it's getting bigger all the time!
- The game is NOT CLEAR that multiplayer is more or less $10 a year... I don't mind and this is nothing when you consider that if you like cuesports you will be playing this game for life, but it is not well advertised at all.
If you like pool or snooker, you can't go wrong. Puts every other game to shame.
9/10, even with the cons!

I found Hue to be a delight.  The puzzles were fun, with concepts being introduced to help equip you for solving some of the later, which were naturally more difficult.  The controls were intuitive, simple, and felt really good.  I did not try it with keyboard/mouse as the game suggests a controller at the start.  I am glad I followed that advice because it just felt right.  Especially when you alter the colors from the color ring (wheel).  Just a slight movement of the right stick on my gamepad and the color ring is up for you to choose the needed color to solve the puzzle.  The slow-mo of the game during the color changes was also not only useful for solving, but a really fun element to play with.
To round out the game, I found the story to be interesting and special with an almost mystical element paired with science and personal perception.  A complete game where the story and puzzles are one.  I would personally be hesitant to make any Limbo/Braid comparisons.  Though you might see roots of either of these classics, Hue stands on its own as a delightful entry to the genre.

This game rules!
I've not gotten around to reviewing any of the games in my library yet, but I think it's fitting that I feel compelled to talk about this one first. I love platformer games, and this one's aesthetic similarity to Playdead's classic, LIMBO, caught my eye. Add to that a color-based main mechanic and a narrative-driven story, and you've got Hue. If you're into puzzle-platformers, this is a real winner.
The color wheel mechanic (as seen in the trailers) drives the puzzles in the game: when you change the background color, any objects of that color disappear, allowing you to move past them. It seems like a one-trick-pony at first, early in the game, but Hue makes very good use of it and includes a great deal of variety, as well as some very challenging puzzles (the final level in particular is quite difficult). It also may seem like using the color wheel (which you control with the right thumbstick on a controller) would get in the way of the flow of a platforming game, bu it actually runs  very smoothly, slowing down your character as you use it so that you can change colors even in midair. Which you will have to do during the game.
The game's story mode took me about 4 hours, but a lot of it will depend on how quickly you can make it through the puzzles. There are also collectibles in the game, which will require you to return to previous areas after you've unlocked additional colors to access secrets, ala Metroidvania games.
The music in the game is beautiful. I've only ever bought the game soundtrack for one other game (that being Undertale), but I suspect this one may not be far behind.
There's even a colorblind setting. Kudos to the Hue developers for nipping that potential problem in the bud. So even if you have colorblindness, you can still play this game and enjoy it.
If I were to pick out one weakness in the game, it's the story. The narration is beautifully spoken and offers interesting commentary on the various colors, and there's always times to listen whenever you reach a room with narration. It's only that the actually conflict of the game ends up feeling a little weak at the end. Also, the game would occasionally minimize and go back to the desktop. Not closing down or losing progress, but forcing me to click back in (however, I have no idea if the game is at fault for this, or it's just my computer). But these are minor complaints. Overall, this game is worth the money, and deserves any bit of attention it can get.
I really enjoy puzzle platformers, and the indie products I've played in this genre (LIMBO, INSIDE, Thomas Was Alone, and now Hue) keep me coming back for more.

Hue is a game were you control a big-headed boy in a side-scroller, you must accomplish your objective by solving the puzzles in this dark and perilous world, thus, growing and losing your innocence, no, wait, that is Nihilumbra; no, wait, that is Braid, no, wait, that is Limbo, no, wait…
You get the idea, this is a completely overdone and unoriginal concept, the reason game designers keep making those it's because they almost always win awards. Loss of innocence is such a touching topic, but after playing dozens of games like these, I've grown to kind of despise them.
But this is not the main reason I disliked this game, I'll get into that a bit later.
In Hue, you live in a monochromatic world, but nevertheless normal. Now, your mother didn't invent colour, but she invented something to perceive it, and this research basically drove her mad and uncaring of her family, and the University she researched the useless idea of colour exiled her for trying to change the laws of reality, until the day something probably went wrong and she disappeared, well, she was warned, after this the University destroyed her possibly world-ending artifact and scattered the pieces. But your mother didn't disappear completely, she leaves letters that you can read, so she asks you, a little boy named after her research (Hue), to risk your life and commit the same mistakes she did so you can find her, so you venture out into this perilous and monochromatic world to save your degenerate mother.
But there is something worse that the unoriginal story, this game is nail-bitingly pretentious, my God, you get a new colour and your mother starts to be all philosophical, but she just spews things that the developers probably saw in the colours VSauce video, she also likes to describe trivia about impossible colours and visible wavelengths, things not usually known by the general public, but not impressive at all, her British accent also doesn't help, but maybe I'm just projecting. The thing I hate about this game is the same thing that makes me hate the Matrix series. Don't try to make your games, movies, or books sound smart and complex to impress people, when in reality it's actually something pretty simple and sometimes overdone.
The gameplay is clever, I give the developers that, so, you've got a ring of colours, and when you pick one, it changes the background to that colour, and everything on the foreground with the same colour, stops existing, and this game nails it on puzzle design, it's all really simple, and sometimes rather easy, except for the last few levels, where the levels start to get longer, and when you die you restart, if gets frustrating when you hit a spike by mistake and have to do the puzzle again. Also, the game's got some rather lackluster collectibles, you just get them for the sake of the achievement, that's about it. The games seems like a browser game at times, I've played really clever sidescrolling free puzzle games on my browser when I was younger. Yet this game will set you back 15$.
The graphics are also really good, all the characters are well drawn, and the scenery looks nice, the colours really pop out,, also the music is good at times, specially at the Electricity level. But it kind of feels that it works against the atmosphere the world is building, as in, your mom is missing and probably DEAD, but this lime colour is real cute though. Maybe the boy is happy by losing his workaholic mother, you never know.
Overall, the game is really unoriginal, almost like a Limbo clone, but still, it's got some really good puzzles and scenery, and you can always mute your mother's voice and turn off subtitles, that'd actually make it a good game. But the price tag of 15 dollars makes me unable to recommend it, but I also don't think it's a bad game, I'm neutral towards it in the end.

Hue is a really nice, enjoyable, puzzle-platformer.
It's extremely intuitive, and aside from one or two difficult timing sections, there's nothing that could come that close to making you 'rage'. You're eased into the new mechanics, which get progressively harder as the game goes on. As you can probably tell from the Steam store page, Hue is all about colour and that forms the basis for the puzzle and platforming mechanics.
Despite this, although I never used the option myself so I can't judge its effectiveness, there is colourblind support, which I understand use symbols instead.
The graphics are pleasant to look at and the music is amazing, and at times almost soothing. This helped make Hue relaxing to play. The storyline is also a very good one but, perhaps crucially, doesn't get in the way of the platforming & puzzles and instead serves alongside them to provide a brilliant game to play.
Overall, I would recommend Hue to anyone, especially people who enjoy Puzzle games and Puzzle Platformers. Hue is a lovely game to play.

Ah, Cossacks: Art of War.
The strategy game of my childhood.
Since 2004, when my father'd introduced me to the world of PC gaming, this is perhaps the most wonderful RTS game I've ever played.
There were three RTS games back then for me and my uncle (my father preffered playing Max Payne);
Cossacks, Empire Earth and Battle For Middle Earth 2
My uncle had spent thousands of hours on the latter two, he's playing Empire Earth now as I speak!
Yes, I loved all three games, Empire Earth's fantastic editor, always making up stories in my head, or Battle For Middle Earth, imagining how I was trying to get the ring for myself. But that's enough about those two, this is a Cossacks: Art of War review, after all.
My favourite RTS game was, and still is Cossacks; Art of War.
I remember how I was always frustrated when I had to install European Wars first, because it'd take too long.
I remember how the first thing I did when I installed and booted up the game was to enter the editor and write "money" dozens of times, and then the party would begin.
I'd turn the peace mode on, generate the map of Europe and imagine that I'm a conqueror who's main goal is to destroy his enemies, make alliances with other factions (controlled by me, of course) and just create a lot of building and units and make them fight.
My uncle still refuses to play 1vs1 against me, he preffers to play vs. AI.
But I'll make him play multiplayer one day, and people of Cossacks will celebrate that day as the day Tycho the Glorius defeated Uncle the RTS Master.

It's difficult to write a review that people would really look at or find helpfull at all. I could tell you about the amazing things I saw when I just started this game, after I finished Little Big Adventure 1 and I defeated FunFrock back in 1993. This is going to be a very long review.
A game originally produced by Adeline Software in 1997, with help of Frédérick Raynal and Phil Vacey. Sadly, Adeline Software didn't make it further then 2004, where their company had to close. Luckily for us Frédérick Raynal has gained control over the rights of Little Bid Adventure, so... maybe there is a third one coming up? For more reviews from professional people I have copied wikipedia and posted it here;
" Robert Coffey of Computer Gaming World said, "With its unparalleled sense of marvel and imagination, engaging story, and deft mix of action and adventure, Twinsen's Odyssey is a true delight and simply the most charming game I've ever played". GameSpot's Ron Dulin gave the game 8.1 out of 10, stating "Fans of adventure games will not want to pass this one up". José Dias of Adventure Classic Gaming said "Relentless: Twinsen's Adventure is among the most original and intriguing adventure games ever released." and gave it a 4 out of 5. "
But let me tell you. Do you remember the first time you launched a game that you were so excited about? Like many of us we played black and white games like Castle Adventure ( 1984 ), Pac Man ( 1980 ) or one of the best-sellers from Apogee like the Duke Nukem, Cosmo, Crystal Caves and I could continue for hours! And suddenly you find this game with a UFO on the cover, a blue coated man with a S-pendant around his neck and this beautiful woman next to him. You flip the big carton box and you see these amazing 3D pictures. You are thinking " Is this real gameplay or just a short clip? " Remember, back in the days we didn't had any source of information about videogames like we have today. I bought the game and decided to give it a try.
That, my friends, is where my adventure began. I never seen anything so well detailed in 3D graphics. I could turn 360 degrees and see my character from all sides. I saw all these funny, but not terryfing creatures that I never seen before. There are bunny-people, fox-like creatures, walking sausages and evil citicens from Esmer who are trying to invade your world. The magic is in the storyline, where Twinsen needs to save a terrified group of schoolchildren who were abducted by an evil villian ( no spoilers! ). One of the best parts of this game is the humor that Frédérick Raynal and his designers put into this game. Trashcans and catuses have villians in them, funny conversation lines, pun-intended puns and an amazingly well formed story. Where Link would raise the item above his head, Twinsen is happily waving his arms up and down! Don't forget about Joë, the clumsy but joyfull elf that always seems to get Twinsen and himself into trouble! And what about Dinofly? You ever played a game when you were young where you ride a dinosaur?
TL;DR
Combat 10/10 --> Combat you never seen before. There are many magical spells that can help you fight enemies, but there are obstructions in this game that you need to overcome. Your magic ball is standard level 1 and can only hit certain enemies. You need to find ways to upgrade your magic ball to hit tougher enemies. The magic ball bounces which means you can kill enemies from afar bouncing the ball against the wall. The allout powerfull Ring of Lightning will make all those juicy sausages feel like they just came of the barbecue! And don't forget about throwing pointy darts, spit seeds with your Blowgun or simply fight of your enemies with your Emperor's Sword. Your behavior is a big part of this game that is relevant to how you throw your ball, how you wield your sword or how you preform certain actions with items.
Adventure 10/10 --> You travel from Twinsun, the planet of our hero Twinsen, to the Moon together with Baldino, you go to the casino on Zeelich and you are trying to follow a robot-chicken to find a key. Biddi Biddi! Biddi Biddi! And don't forget Island CX, that is the most deadly island in this world. For those who are willing to explore the whole game there are special items and spells you can collect that can help you later in the game. " What is Island CX you say... I... I don't know. I been there before but now I am all burned selling souvenirs next to this giant statue... I advise you to not go to Island CX... "
Music 10/10 --> The biggest part of what made this game for me was the amazing music that Phil Vachey made. The Temple of Bû from Little Big Adventure 1 and Emerald Moon from Little Big Adventure 2 are amazing classic masterpieces. What is that you say? Voice acting? Yes ofcourse there is voice-acting! Gameplay 10/10 --> Twinsen has different behavior he can adept to. Normal behavior is used to interact with people, to find hidden objects or to flip switches. On the other hand, you are ALLOWED to beat LITTLE BRATS on top of a ROOF that shoots at you with his SLINGSHOT ( Please, go punch him! )  Discreet mode is the opossite of aggressive, in certain cases you want to align yourself a little bit better, or you want to throw your magic ball higher in the air over a wall to kill an enemy, or if you want to sneak past enemies to avoid confrontation. Comparable to what Half Life 1 and Unreal or Quake did amazingly well for their time, Little Big Adventure 1 and 2 did that for their time. We could almost say that Little Big Adventure is the start of the 3D adventures which we see today, like Wolfenstein was that for the future of shooters. Everything seems fine and dandy until the weather suddenly gets worse, your friend gets badly injured and even aliens land on your homeworld, so you better go grab your magic ball and tunic and prepare yourself for some more adventures.
You don't necessarily have to play the first game to completely understand this one - you'll get everything important by interacting with books, signs and busts - but it certainly helps to get into the right mood.

Red Faction: Armageddon is a game developed by Volition Studios and originally published by the now defunct company THQ, now published by THQ Nordic (or Nordic Games) and is also the fourth game in the Red Faction series
Red Faction: Armageddon is an action packed third person shooter which follows up from the previous Red Faction: Guerrilla game and continues the Red Faction story line. However, this time the game sticks with the third person view from Red Faction: Guerrilla and also drops the open world concept and is linear like the first original two games
The storyline and missions are still fun as ever and works out well even though the amazing open world from Red Faction: Guerrilla is gone. The gameplay is pretty standard, but lots of fun and you also have a new nifty magnet gun and some powers with the Nano Forge
Once again the highlight of the Red Faction series is blowing stuff up, and you can blow up all the structures and also repair things since enemies will often be attacking you and stairs and other things you need to access will be gone. Lastly, there's an Infestion (Horde) mode which is tons of fun where you have to stay alive and fend off all of the enemies
Overall, this game is a lot of fun and is not like the previous game, however for what it is - you'll have a blast playing by blowing things up and fighting off evil cultist and aliens
