Frankly speaking, not as enjoyable as Guerilla. Personally I'm not even a fan of open world games, but RFG gained a lot of being one because of all the destruction you could do and all of the ways how. Not to say that this game doesn't have it. It does, but it's limited to corridors and ruins. The only "up" side it has over it's predecesor it the Magnet Gun. It's really fun to use even in the limited areas. That being said, it would have been way more enjoyable if this game was also an open world one.
Other than the general setting, the game play seems fine. Not an expert on shooting, but some of the guns felt appropriate (nano forge ones) while some not so much (heavy stuff like rocket launchers).
Enemy variety is not all that huge. Most of what you'll encounter are bugs, more bugs, bigger bugs, shooty bugs... You get the idea. There is the occasional human enemy, but they're far too few in far too apart.
Vehicle segments feel a bit clunky. Shooting is fine, but the movement is a bit chaotic. It was clearly designed for the console first.
The 'powers' you have seem a bit out of place as well. For some reason you can control The Force. No idea what went through their minds when they made that option.
There's not a lot of replayability outside of NG+ which gives you two new weapons, but can't really speak on that matter.
With all that said, the game is not boring. Started playing and never stopped until I beat it. Sure, the campaign might not be the longest, but I don't know what you expected of a corridor shooter. At least it's not a cover shooter. Here you use the cover to kill your enemies (with the magnet gun).
Bad story, cool concept, wasted potential. That's the short of it. Depreciated the elements of the previous title in the series that made it stand out.

I have bought Project Zomboid multiple times over the years, on multiple platforms. I was there in the beginning. I have spent countless hours losing myself in the game...
But right now, even though I love the game, I cannot recommend it at this time. Prepare for a PZ Fanboy turned realist's opinion on the current state of Project Zomboid.
*FINAL WARNING, BIT OF A RANT AHEAD, SKIP TO SUMMARY IF UNWILLING TO READ THE WALL OF TEXT.*
And before you read on, it is not because of the slow development time that I am disappointed, at least, not entirely. You see, the developers have said time and time again that they need to, and will, take their *sweet ol' time* with the development of the game. However, what I find comepletely unexcusable is that lack of information being provided by the developers, who were once the best Indie company I had ever known.
Every monday, the Indie Stone, developers of Project Zomboid, release a "Mondoid," which is an informative blog post detailing development that had taken place over the week since the last Mondoid. Well, informative they are no longer.
In the beginning, I looked forward to seeing a Mondoid every Monday. Unfortunately, for the past six months or so, the Mondoids have become little more than bland, generic blurbs that the Indie Stone don't seem to feel the need to put much effort into. If I'm wrong, it'd be hard to prove it; look at some of the recent posts on their website. Actually, the content in recent Mondoids is so similar that I can basically summarize every one you might read.
Intro of the Mondoid:
-Begins by saying that it's a "Short, sweet Mondoid this week," or, "Not much to write in this Mondoid," etc.
Meat of the Mondoid:
-Proceeds to blurb about how a lot of "good work" has been done on the coding aspect of the game, but doesn't go into much detail.
-Talks about some "secret exciting project" they have coming up for the game, that almost always is way overhyped.
-If lucky to get a post larger than a few paragraphs, you might get lucky and see a picture or thirty second video of features that were said to be, and should have been, added years ago.
Ending of Mondoid:
-Usually just a copy-paste message talking about the thumbnail of the Mondoid, or how you can subscribe with your email to get notifications on every Mondoid that comes out, as soon as it comes out. (Although, from the way thing have been, you won't need this feature, as you won't likely be missing much.)
Their Mondoids rarely provide any new, noteworthy information, creating a film of dishonesty and distrust between the player and the Developer. Now I know what those Project Zomboid Fanboys are going to say; "The Devs need their time, Tyler! You can't rush them! Be patient!"
I have been patient... For almost seven years, I believe. Since then I have seen little change after the first four years or so. I have been told to sit tightly, and have been promised a new, interesting Mondoid where all my concerns will be adressed; yet each time I am very disappointed.
And I know I said that the slow development wasn't the reason I gave this game a negative review, but it did have a hand in the decision. NPC's were said to be released in 2016 at the latest. Were not even close to seeing them, if we ever will. We have been promised proper animations, and although there has supposedly been some work towards adding them into the game, they are quickly taking the NPC direction. This game is slowly becoming vaporware. The updates are getting fewer and farther between, and are adding fewer and fewer features with each one. Most of the time we are told of "AWESOME FIXES" to the code and game, but I have seen nothing change.
Oh, and the Indie Stone often says that the reason why it takes so long to add things to the game is because the features are in need of polishing... Well, I agree with that, but your game is in Early Access. Everything doesn't have to be ♥♥♥♥ing perfect to be added in, just workable. That way you can get better feedback on issues and suggestions, which is sorta why Early Access became a thing in the first place. Just give us all something, ANYTHING that you have promised; show us that you have actually been working on the game, that you haven't given up on it, because right now, that's what it looks like.
There is a bubble surrounding the Indie Stone community that filters out a lot of criticism; I know, because I was in that bubble. But my eyes have been opened by the repetitive Mondoids, and obvious lack of content being added over the years.
In fact, let me think of the most notable additions that I've seen in the past six months...
-A TV and Radio system, consisting of Meta content and text-based broadcasts that add little more than lore to the game.
-A nutrition system, I think. (I'm not even sure it's been released.)
-Multiplayer. (Quite broken, from my experience.)
-What else... Oh, what every ♥♥♥♥ing game ever says. Numerous *fixes* and *changes*.
If there is anything else I missed, well, I'm sorry. But the features I missed are probably so uninteresting and overdue that my brain has literally rejected it.
*SUMMARY*
I love you Indie Stone, you're a great company, at least, you used to be. But you need to give us something to go on. Right now were getting little more than your "word" that content is being added and will arrive "shortly." You need to quit being so generic with your Mondoids and actually put some effort into them again. And you need to get some help with developing your game, as I've seen much more impressive work done in a much shorter time. And don't say it's because you're a "small indie team," I've seen a hell of a lot more come from two person teams, sometimes even one-man projects. That's no excuse, and there's no excuse for the lack of information you have provided in recent times.
I will gladly recommend this game when some actual content is added, but that may be quite a long time. So for now, bookmark this game, write it down somewhere. Then come back maybe five years or so. You *might* see a weapon or two. If you're lucky, and are an extra good boy or girl this year. Maybe. Probably not though.

There is not much left to say about BioShock that has not been said before. From the anxiety inducing opening to the tense crawl through the underwater city, the immersion and atmosphere of BioShock doesn't stop nor slow down for a single second. Within the first few frames of the game, the entire plot is laid out for you, and you don't even know it. The constant almost mocking way that the characters in this game throw the plot in your face makes you feel like a massive chump when you discover the twist halfway through the game (Which I won't ruin but let's get real-- who hasn't played BioShock by now?).
Rapture is a fantastic city, and will always beat Columbia, in my opinion. The feeling of isolation and the look of the dystopian underwater city has never been matched in any game I've ever played to date. The socialist influences are very blatant from the very beginning, and that isn't a bad thing. A true spectacle, I died twice in the part where Jack's heart was told to stop (a very confusing sentence for those that haven't played the game).. because I couldn't stop looking at the environment. Did you know you could die at that part if you wait too long?! I didn't.
The environments are also insanely huge for a linear game, and /almost/ feels open world. It feels as open world as an underwater city can be, where there are no invisible walls but logical reasons that you can only access a certain amount of the area. I mean.. you're on the ocean floor. You would die if you left the boundaries of this city.
Ammo is scarce and friends are even scarcer six miles underwater. Adding even more to the feeling of hopelessness and isolation, Jack can't carry that many bullets. A strategy of run and gun might work on easy or normal, but on hard (the TRUE way to play) you will have to pick your shots and pick them well. One wrong shot and that splicer will run to alert his friends you are there, and you could very very easily die. I believe the max amount of pistol rounds you can carry is 46, which is not a whole lot, considering that a single leadhead splicer can take 5-6 body shots later in the game (you won't always be going for headshots.. there's too much panic involved in this game).
Swapping between weapons and plasmids feels great, and you quickly learn the fastest way to take out enemies with combos using your favorite tools in your arsenal (I prefer the bees and the crossbow, myself). The enemies get rather difficult near the end, and playing on the hardest difficulty my biggest challenge was the Nitro Splicers and the Leadhead Splicers. You'd think it would be the Big Daddies, but when you use the uInvent as much as I do and have as much electric gel as I do, Big Daddies are nothing but Big Chumps.
You'd think that after the first few encounters with splicers, you would become desensitized to them. This is not the case.. at all. The fear they induce never stops, and they only become MORE terrifying as you progress through the game and they begin to use more and more plasmids against you. Spider splicers in particular have a very creepy way about them. The way they crawl on the ceiling, clanking about, and screaming about Jesus and such.. gives me shivers (though I am always relieved to see one, I desperately need those organs and one well placed shotgun blast will put 'em down for good).
There was not a single gunfight-- and I mean that, not a SINGLE one-- where I didn't have an "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; moment. A single misfired bullet or ill used plasmid can open you up to a relentless assault from your enemy, draining your health or forcing you to move out of your bunkered position to rethink your strategy. The splicers seem to just run at you endlessly, and that's okay. They're crazed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that have used plasmids and destroyed their humanity and now only crave more ADAM, which they can only get off of you or the Little Sisters. There's nothing like walking into a room and seeing a Big Daddy wailing on six splicers at once, realizing there's no XP in this game and therefor no reason to get involved, and sitting down with a Pep Bar to watch the battle unfold. Splicers will ACTIVELY hunt out Little Sisters. The second one spawns in the map, the splicers will find it, and they WILL engage. This was always just such a cool little detail to me, it really made the world feel more alive.
Overall, this game is fantastic. It's terrifying, it's intense, it's action packed, it's fast paced, and it's a world that really comes to life and grabs you. The storyline is FANTASTIC, and the twist is a true "What the ♥♥♥♥" moment the first time around. And every subsequent playthrough, you will notice just how much the characters in this game have mocked you.. throwing the twist in your face any chance they get, but you NEVER noticed until it was all revealed. The struggle between Ryan and Fontaine is a believeable struggle, and I would not change a god damn thing about this game if I had done it myself.
Oh, plus little sisters.. yeesh.
I guess that's one thing I would change, though. There is a tale that early in development, the devs intended for Jack (the protagonist) to be able to choose between using plasmids in abundance and 'splicing' to survive, or retaining his humanity at the price of less safety. This would have been much more impactful and dramatic than the little sister saving mechanic.. because the game LIES about that mechanic. You will ALWAYS get more ADAM by saving the little sisters. Also, that choice does nothing but influence the final cutscene in the game. There is no true moral dillema in BioShock, but if they had gone the splicer route, there would have been..
And the hacking game. It is boring, by the end, and a little ridiculously hard at times for no real payoff.
Even so, with that one nitpicky gripe, this game is a very very very very solid 10/10. It is worthy of being in every gamer's collection, and replaying it now (after straying for years since I broke my Xbox), I can truly see why this became such a massive franchise.

While I don't have many hours in this game at the time of the review, this is an addictive Civ5-like "just one more turn" 4X game. Set in a medieval fantasy world, Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes pits you against AI-controlled factions, each of which contain a Sovereign, the titular "Heroes" of the game. While there are preset sovereigns for you to choose from, you can create your own custom sovereign and choose which of 10 factions it belongs to. You can customize your army, as well, ranging from simple colors to starting equipment and whether or not they are mounted units. Keep in mind that adding stronger arms and armor to your troops will increase how much resources it will cost to create. You can, however, find Champions roaming around the world, seeking the aid of a Hero. Whenever you find a Champion, you can add them to your Sovereign's party or form parties of different units of your choice. There are multiple quests to perform, ranging from finding gold and resources to pillaging a dark lair full of spiders and necromancers. Combat has 2 forms; turn-based isometric view and standard Civ5-style quick attacks. If you choose the turn-based option, you are brought to a tactical overview of the battlefield and all the units within the party will appear on screen. Spells, abilities, and items can be used in battle, as well as many other spells, abilities, and items that can be used outside of battle. There is so much to do in this game that its hard to put down in this review without describing the whole game in detail. For $10 on sale, its worth the price for the base game. If you get hooked, the DLC adds more quests, enemies, loot, etc. If you like 4X games and the fantasy setting, give it a try!

Do you ever feel like you should control an army? Would you like each soldier to keep track of how many enemies they kill? Well you better be able to pay them! This is Cossacks a no nonsense RTS for those who like an indepth game but still casual capable.
Game play wise this is easy to pick up if you ever played the AoE series or Rise of Nations. Excpet you only live in the 17th and 18th C. Build a town or more, control citizens and put them to work, build army, build defences, build navy, and upgrade tech. Simple right? Well no. There is more than just gold to mine for. You have coal, iron, ect. Then you have wood and stone.(they are located typically close to each other) You have mills and fishing for food. If you can not pay an army they will rebel, and if they can not eat they will die. The thing is numbers matter here. You can have over 2000 citizens and so can your enemies. So be aware you need to grow. Also you can capture enemy citizens if no military is near them. So you can absorb your enemies culture. The naval battles are really cool and controling waters with a coast line city is a big advatage. A frigate can easly destroy a incoming army when in range.
Now the indepth part. The technology trees are massive and pricey. Do not upgrade your 17th cent soldiers and just rush to 18th instead if you have a western euro nation. They are pricey and take time, then you will not use them once you are in the 18th cent. Each mine can be upgrader to support more workers. The military and agriculture upgrades are very indepth. Rifling and gun powder advancments make all the difference. So you can have a highlander or other ranged soldier on a hill snyping and weakening a passing army. Remember when I said each soldier keeps a tally of how many he has killed. Well I have had a soldier kill more than 2500 troops due to time and a cliff.
Now for stradgey. This is kind of a grand RTS at times. It can take a long time to complete a game. So you can take advatage of the land. elevated troops(on a hill or cliff) shoot farther and well placed cannons can turn the tide. Dragoons and other horsemen are great for fleeing troops and artillary, but aweful in a siege. Naval control is a massive advantage but very expensive. If you lose a man o war to muntiny you will struggle to get the sea back. Picking a wise local for your city is near impossible. If you are on the water and you lose control of the sea you're lost, if you take a valley you can become a sitting duck. Think of your entrances and exits.
So what about the nations? Each has their own advatages and unique troops. The middle eastern and eastern Europe counrties are all better early in the game. If you pick these nations like Turkey or Russia be aggressive, cause man the computer will be. These troops cost the least but have major weaknesses. Once you get to the 18th C the power drastically turns. Countries like Britain, France, Prussia, and Sweden are the stronger. With countries like Spain some where in the middle. This game follows historic fact so some technologies do not get developed in some nations.
Now for the bad. Back to War is the last expansion but does not recoginize any resolution other than 768 and 2160p for me. 2160p is not compatable with this game and it will crash. It also will not take a custome res. This game, the Art of War does support all resolutions. The highest it will support is 1440p. Since it is 2D it will just zoom farther out. The game also crashes at times. Typically around the 3-4 hour mark. Loading is fast and it does auto save.
So if you like AoE II or any other RTS. Give this or Back to War a try. It's like them but bigger and more focused on historical accuracy. For a game hitting the 15 year mark I would still strongly recommend it.

D: First monster is pretty damn weak compared to the other 2. I never even see people use it. Needs buffs.
E: Another problem I had with the game was how biased this was towards the monster. The monster has no control over which maps get picked. The monster also has no way of really escaping the players becauseoo it's literally set up so that just when you run out of abilities to escape with their fuel runs out. Their tracking skills are also borderline broken. Make one wrong move and you probably are not going to escape their sights. So if you've had it easy as the monster it's because the players weren't working as a team or they were playing inccorectly. A good team of players can easily dominate the monster mostly because of the movement capabilities of both the monsters and the players being identical but the monster should have the advantage there but it just really doesn't.
F: The player revive mechnic is broken. I'm sorry but if I put in that much work to take someone out and they just get revived that takes all the fun out of the game for the monster and the will to even fight the players. If a player dies they should be punished and forced to respawn when the ship arrives. If the ship gets a shorter spawn time or the res time for players gets cut down or they take longer to revive I would be okay with that but um, I really get tired of having to stand on a dude and hope that the enemy is too stupid to attack me properly to make sure that he/she is dead. I don't mind the mechanic too much but at this point the game is so biased towards the monster it's just not even fair which may also be why they are so overpowered to an extent.

It's difficult not to appreciate the class of Cossacks. Its gameplay focus is well split into all the aspects that characterise an RTT game: game rhythm, upgrades, buildings, unit variety and relevance, population realism, battle simulation... One has got to admire the effort put into crafting the unit functioning and overall building management in this one. Superb.
Cossacks offers plenty of pleasurable elements. First, there's the outstanding number of nations, each with its own architectural identity (wonderfully done, by the way); as well as the outstanding number of unique units and their precise importance on the battlefield or in the development of one's domains. Second, there's the realistic representation of population growth, with civil infrastructure costing you more as your settlement expands, although there is no set limit for your population. Third, there's the artillery/infantry details, amazing to watch as they engage in battle. Fourth, there's the customisable gameplay, as the options for a skirmish match are reasonable (type of terrain, type of elevation, game speed, resources, etc.), gathering all the good and fair choices everybody should have when playing a free-build or skirmish game mode in any RTS/RTT. Last but not least, the naval conflicts: it's just too exciting to watch your territories and riches grow and have to formulate quick strategies with your coffers and coal reserves so you can build a solid, fearsome fleet that can outrun the enemy's.
Whether you're playing the main campaigns or the 17th and 18th centuries battles in quick match mode, Cossacks: Art of War shall bring you strategy-ecstasy. The huge battles (details of hundreds of men can be formed), the realistic artillery ballistics, the exciting invasions on the enemy's settlement, the fast-paced management of your resources (wood, gold, food, iron and coal) and workers, and the extreme attention that one has to keep on the keeping up of improvements and specific upgrades, will determine who prevails in the hot war scenario of this game. Cossacks can give you this kind of thrill, if you're fond of the genre.
Bear in mind that, while I'm writing on the Art of War page, this goes for all its "sister" games (European Wars, Back to War).

I can safely say that Outlast made me jump out of my chair more often in its four-hour descent into Hell than any other game ever has. It's a tense, brutal trek that strips you of any power to defend yourself as you try to avoid the deranged mental patients that roam the halls of this horrifyingly gorgeous world.You'll run, hide, and just generally be terrified as you discover the horrors that reside within Mount Massive Asylum. But in between the wealth of scares and beautiful environments, Outlast has a tendency to bog down via uninspired mission objectives and a few disappointing design choices.
From the get-go, Outlast is one of the best-looking and sounding survival horror games to date. Everything from the dynamic lighting to a fantastic soundscape work together to keep you on edge every second of the experience. On both PC and PS4, I dreaded entering any new areas or opening any closed doors for fear of what lurked in the dark unknown. Little details that are often forgotten in games, like leaving a trail of bloody footprints after stepping through a pool of blood, really help sell the illusion that Mount Massive is an actual place.

Outlast + Whistleblower DLC: Fun times in the mad house. (Warning of ending spoilers for Outlast)
Outlast is considered to be one of the scariest games of all time. I was well aware of the game’s reputation. When Humble Bundle emailed me about a giveaway for this game with the Whistleblower DLC I had to take it. God, what a game....
Outlast opens up with Miles Upshur, an investigative journalist arriving at the sinister Mount Massive Asylum after receiving an anonymous email about inhuman treatments at the Asylum.  Miles, always wanting a good story sneaks inside to see for himself and everything goes downhill from there for him.  Now he must try to make it out of the Asylum and avoid the violent patients while discovering what happened at the Asylum and record as much evidence to destroy the Murkoff Corporation who drove the patients to murder in the first place.
Gameplay is simple at first glance, you are armed with a camcorder which has night vision and is used to record sightings for Miles to build his report. While you have night vision on the battery life drains so you have to balance using the night vision and finding batteries which are scattered throughout the Asylum. You can peak around doors and you can run, you can also hide in the lockers and under tables to help escape should anyone spot you. That is it. There is no combat in this game and it does not need it. It helps add to the nightmarish situation Miles is in. He is just a reporter lost in a place where almost everything wants to kill him. Miles and the player have to use their wits if they want to survive and it is done so well in Outlast.
The atmosphere and the sound design are the strongest points of this game. Just playing this game puts me on edge, the simple act of pausing the game makes the smallest unnerving sound that puts the player on edge, there is very little music with the exception of key moments to insure the full effect is set in. But asides from that all there is Miles terrified mummers, irregular breathing patterns and whatever sounds the docile or hostile patients make while hunting you or busy warped up in their own little world. It is so effective. One standout moment for me is when I was trying to escape one special encounter, hiding in locker hoping and praying that he would not find me. I was such an emotional wreck.  That was one of many moments that bring Outlast close to my two favourite horror games, System Shock 2 and Bloodborne. I do not say this lightly. The game’s atmosphere is that brilliant.
So with all of that said Outlast should slide neatly into my Hall of Fame correct?
Wrong.
If it was not for the final moments of the game it would have been in the Hall of Fame quite happily but it sadly does not stick the landing due to one stupid element that is out of place and unnecessary.
Please be warned I am about to spoil a bit of the ending so if you do not want to read this part then please skip over the next paragraph now.
Outlast is one of the best horror games out there, that is a fact. I am really disappointed that the final stage of the game had to take such a silly turn.
Whistleblower is a short (about 2 to 3 hours give or take) piece of DLC that serves as a prequel and parallel story to the main Outlast story. You are Waylon Park this time, a software engineer who was working at Mount Massive and is the one who tipped off Miles Upshur to the treatment of patients. He is discovered and is placed in the Asylum to shut him up. After all hell breaks loose he tries to escape and tell the world. Gameplay is not different at all from the main game and a few familiar enemies appear and some new ones which I will not spoil here.
I would say that Whistleblower is better story wise because even though the silly element is still there it is not quite as prominent in the DLC as it was in the main story. I do consider it a plus.
Outlast + Whistleblower is a terrifying nightmare though hell. It is one of the best horror games out there but sadly it just barely misses being one of the best games due to that one stupid story element.

Hue is a puzzle platformer and here is my short review of it.
The basic gist of the puzzle mechanic is that you can turn the world into a set of colours and any object with that same colour would vanish. So basically suppose there is a pile of rocks or a wall with say orange colour and you turn the world orange that pile of rocks or the wall would disappear and you can pass through. You get the colours as you progress through the game. Once ou get a few colours the puzzles are basically hiding objects of various colours by changing the world to the appropriate colour. The puzzles involve switches over which coloured blocks can be placed, walls of different colours,lasers and so on. The puzzle design is good and there are a few interesting puzzles to solve but the game becomes quite repetitive till a new mechanic is introduced which are very few.
Also few of the puzzles make you believe that they need to be perfectly timed but that is not the case. Every puzzle has a way without involving any precise platforming which is not explained well until you figure out that this game is pure logical puzzles and does not involve any precise platforming. There are a few obvious places and the game has a mechanic where time slows down so that you can change to the appropriate colour.
Pros
Excellent music which keeps you playing through the various levels
Good puzzle design
Heart warming story if you care about it
No precise platforming required it is purely logical puzzles and the time slowing mechanic is good and negates any precise
platforming required
Cons
A bit repetitive
New mechanics are combined in a way where it is not explained in advance though the tutorials prior give you an idea
Recommended if you like puzzle platformers with good logical puzzles which are not too hard. The puzzles are fairly easy and do not require mind melting solutions. It is fairly casual game which is very easy to get into it. This is not a hardcore puzzle platformer like Braid or recursed which require out of the box solutions and involve game changing level design. buy iy for a stressfree puzzle platformer experience.

I now play on a Mac (hush!) and was originally looking for a game that could replace the survival aspect of DayZ after my PC blew up, this so far has been the closest thing to it.  Even though this is a single player game and there are no zombies or other players to keep you on your toes, this is still a great game if you're into survival like simulators and I am really looking forward to August 1 when they implement the story mode.
Basically you spawn in the northern Canadian wilderness, your objective is to survive as long as you can by strategically moving from place to place hoping there will be enough within your surroundings to keep you alive for another night , as you travel you not only do you have to fight off hunger/dehydration/hyperthermia and fatigue but also the wolves/bears/blizzards that will cross your path on occasion, it's easier said then done but once you get into the swing of it and learn about the crafting system and how to turn yourself into a survivor/hunter, all that's left really is to explore as much of this world as they have currently created... and I guess have a go at the challenge scenarios they have currently implemeted.
Definately give it a try, there is a lot of potential for this game and I think when the story mode hits on August 1 it's gonna breath more life into what's already shaping up to be a great sandbox survival simulator.

Red Faction: Armageddon is an action packed third person shooter which follows up from the previous Red Faction: Guerrilla game and continues the Red Faction story line. However, this time the game sticks with the third person view from Guerrilla and also drops the open world concept and is linear like the first original two games. The storyline and missions are still fun as ever and works out well even though the amazing open world from Guerrilla is gone. The gameplay is pretty standard, but lots of fun and you also have a new nifty magnet gun and some powers with the Nano Forge which sometimes make you feel like a superhero or a Jedi. Once again the highlight of the Red Faction series is blowing stuff up, and you can blow up all the structures and also repair things since enemies will often be attacking you and stairs and other things you need to access will be gone. Lastly, there's an Infestion (Horde) mode which is tons of fun where you have to stay alive and fend off all of the enemies. Overall, this game is a lot of fun and is not like the previous game, however for what it is - you'll have a blast playing by blowing things up and fighting off evil cultist and aliens. I spent around 12 hours beating the story and also the DLC campaign (super short) and playing around in Infestion mode.
Note: If your game crashes during checkpoints in DX10/11 Mode, turn Shadows OFF. This worked for me and the game never crashed again since I did this.

First off, the game has an amazing soundtrack in my opinion. Try looking up World 3's theme on Youtube if you want. It's by far my favorite. Now, onto more gameplay-related things:
A possible friendship destroyer if you've got that friend who loves to jump on your head and then commit suicide at the end of the level that took you 30 minutes to beat.
Even if you lack any friends to play it with, there's still usually one or two unlocked rooms you can join and make some more friends in. 10 people who I am now friends with on Steam came from random open servers in this game.
The way I see it, this can either be classified as one of three things: an unfair platformer (troll blocks), an impossible platformer (speed run challenges in race mode that are far more difficult than they should be), or a good time (watching friends rage out).
If you're an achievement hunter, this game might not be for you because of the speed run challenges. They're all possible (personal experience), but you best be willing to devote a lot of time and accept a lot of failure to do so.
There's one or two levels that have a bug or two in them, but the game has over 60 campaign levels and 60 more race levels, so the vast majority of levels are bug-free. Some of them even have extremely cheap tactics to complete if you have a friend.
Overall, this game is definitely one of my favorite platformers, but it's no walk in the park on the first playthrough.

It feels and plays a lot like Civilization with a quest and individual hero system built in.
The combat can be automatic outside of quests, like Civilization, or you can choose to battle turn-based style on a grid map (which I suck at in this game).
The questing system is unique with this kind of game, and I really enjoy it. I played on easy and felt that the pacing was a little to fast as far as difficulty advancement, but this didn't hinder how fun it was. The quests have stories to go along that may involve getting new equipment, general, or army guys, which makes questing very worth it.
I don't really like the tutorials, but as someone who still hasn't done it, I really suggest doing it. I can't seem to figure out how to get "guild points" as they don't seem to act the same as in Civilization even though it looks like it came from that game. There are little differences that if you have played or haven't played Civilization, it really makes the tutorial quite appealing.
I was disappointed to have so many characters and only about three (way less than half; not even a quarter) were female. However, the female characters that were there had great backgrounds and characters, unlike other games where females are token characters / boring sex symbols.
There is no customization except for naming stuff, and the buildings are automatically placed in order that you choose to build them.

There's a lot of promise here but ultimately, this is a bit of a disappointment.
The biggest flaw is perhaps the UI, which is buggy, missing really basic features and seems generally poorly thought out.  Eg. trying to reorder building queues (in the cramped 5 items at a time icon list) will often select the wrong item.  The mouse isn't locked to the window, so on multiple monitors, you can't hit the screen edge to scroll right.  There's no way to combine or rearrange armies occupying the same tile.  I frequently found some stray click when trying to cast a spell, or even in the loading screen inadvertently ordering armies in the wrong direction.  And a bunch more minor, but frustrating issues.  It just makes the whole thing a pain to deal with.
The game itself is decent, but it seems like it could have done with a lot more balancing and polish.  So far, I've only played through 2 games, but so far it seems like certain strategies and factions are OP, while others struggle.  The optimal strategy seems to be to cut taxes completely, pretty much ignoring gold altogether for the early game, since the unrest penalty isn't worth the tiny amount it gets you, meaning a third of the buildings are pretty much pointless.   It seems like there's the potential for a great game here, and maybe mods could help with this, but as it stands, it doesn't quite come together as well as it could.
If it weren't for the UI issues, I'd definitely recommend giving this game a try, but as it is, I don't think it's worth the frustration.

The world of Hue has a physical dimensionality rooted in color. The player has the ability to switch between these “dimensions,” making objects of a particular color phase out of existence, while objects of other colors remain or are brought back. The designers made good use of the mechanic, exploring several varied, yet synergistic ideas.
I thought the puzzles were a bit too simple and repetitive, but the game was objectively fairly well executed. While it doesn’t quite meet the standard of the genre’s greats, it would be a good choice for people looking for a light introduction to puzzle platformers.

Combines the best parts of Limbo (gently-ramped puzzles and beautiful aesthetics) and Outland (color-switching mechanic).  It's not often anymore that I make time to sit and play through a game in one sitting, but for Hue I had to.  Absolutely recommended for anyone who likes puzzles or self-paced platformers.  A few of the later levels require fast reflexes and accurate color switching, but for the most part it's a logic game.

So. Here is Evolve in a nutshell. The concept is great. A balanced team of hunters trying to take down a monster.
Your classes are standard.
1. Damage
2. Medic
3. Support
4. Tracker
The monsters are strong and hard to kill, they can get away, they move faster than you. Its what you would expect, and really, its fantastically done. I love the concept, and when the game came out, it was amazing. I got it upon release and played it tons.
Now, here is the rub.
One monster has destroyed this game for me.
They placed in one close range bruiser
One long ranged sniper
and one close ranged assassin.
Great in theory, and everything is well balanced EXCEPT for the assassin.
The assassin, AKA wraith, is a monster of monsters. I have seen mediocre players pick up wraith for the first time and take apart teams that were doing very well in a matter of seconds. The wraith has invisibility, cloning, self buffs, and the ability to pull opponents away from their group and begin a pounce style attack where the hunter cannot escape unless the wraith is damaged.
Despite the wraith's low health, it is easily capable of taking out the entire team in its weakest form, stage one. If you do not have a well balanced, well communicating group of verteran huntesr, its almost guaranteed that a semi-decent wraith player will win.
Now. In games like this, there are always ill-balanced characters. I expect that. It happens. It doesn't normally make the game unplayable. In fact, I still love this game. My issue is that wraith is all you see now. Becuase it is so easy to win with, people make a time out of picking it, and it alone. during the release of the title, when no one had access to wraith, games went well. I won or lost about half, depending on my team and the opponent. Once wraith became available however, I stopped seeing both the goliath and the kraken at all, and soon I dropped the game.
Now, this was a bit of a rant, I accept that. My point is that 2K made an awesome game, with a great concept, and they introduced a game breaker into it, and though this has been an issue since release, it hasn't been fixed. Even with this major issue, I still recomend this game, though I do ask if you main monsters, that you do not pick wraith every time. I however, am dropping this game for the time being, because I cannot stand seeing my team wiped out again and again by stage 2 wraiths, without ever once seeing a different monster.

I consider myself a veteran of TDs, willing to try out any that look even halfway passable. This could have been a good one. But..it just failed.
It has some aspects which *could* have worked well, such as the minigame where you can manipulate the upcoming wave's buffs. That's something new rather than just warning the player what sort of minions are approaching next. I'm not sure if it's very well implemented though, as most of the time all you are doing is reducing one buff that has an extremely high number and would cause you to lose instantly if you didn't do it, such as a 12x hit point buff. Hardly fun or interactive.
The towers are quite limited in choice, there are only 5 types that do any noteable amount of damage, with no further upgrades. Most of them feel incredibly weak, which makes mazing highly necessary.
There is no variety of minions, it is nothing but 'chompers', a generic rodent with sharp teeth, occasionally given a different colour according to it's buffs. Occasionally there is also a mini boss in the form of a tree, dog, or golem, so perhaps small versions of these could have been used for non-boss levels.
There is no campaign (!), just 1 single 'map' which is generated randomly, with a square also randomly placed somewhere on the map that minions must touch before they then go for the exit. This means there can be some points on the map that they walk past 3 times if you do it right. Unfortunately the map gets generated with randomly placed statues and small annoying walls which all get in the way of an ideal maze most of the time.
When I find myself quitting and restarting the map just to get an 'optimal' layout where I won't wipe on the 3nd wave, something is very wrong with the design.
One downside I noticed is after you spend all your gold, you only gain 1-2 towers worth of gold per round, which means if you are even slightly behind, you can't do much at all and it quickly snowballs into a sudden loss from there.
Back on the topic of levels/maps- the existence of this single 'RNG' created map means there are no actual levels, which furthers my thoughts that this is an incomplete beta version that I've just paid money for. Perhaps a series of maps with fixed walls or other fixed obstacles/paths would be worth adding as soon as possible as it really makes it feel like the game was just thrown out to get money before it was finished - I actively avoid 'Early Access' games due to being burned by this exact issue so I feel mega duped here and will be requesting a refund as soon as I submit this review.
Also, even as a veteran of these types of games, the difficulty is extreme, so I can see new players giving up in disgust or boredom within a few hours.
Overall verdict: this game has some potential if big changes are made, but should still be marked as a beta or early access, as it is hard to argue that there is enough content to call it a full release. Do not buy it, there are much better uses for your tower defence money such as the Kingdom Rush series which are highly polished, cheap, and available on multiple platforms.

===
===
- Absolutely essential purchase
- Recommended purchase
- Purchase only if on sale
- Purchase only if on heavy sale
===
- Environment destructiblity always gives good enjoyment in combat, in this also this Red Faction does not disappoint
- Decent variety of weapons, skills and such
- You can repair structures, which is a new mechanic as far as single-player campaign is concerned, in Red Faction series
===
- Everything else apart weapon realization, which is decent, is MEDIOCRE at best.
- There is no free-roaming: the game takes place in closed environment where you have to follow a straight path most of the time. You have freedom to destroy whatever you want, but in the end you will be on a pre-chosen path and that is what you follow. A big step back from the very good free-roaming of the previous episode, Guerrilla.
- No side-quests or challenges: only one objective at a time, linear story, no chace of doing some other activity than main quest.
- Storyline, which has never been a strong point in Red Faction, granted, is even more uninvolving and stereotyped than other chapters of the series, and that's something... something bad. The incipit which triggers the whole event that leads to the Armageddon is just ridiculous.
===
- Difficulty is really low if you know what you are doing: this is because the player has access to some ridiculously overpowered weapons. Most weapons you find are real crap, but one in particular, the Magnet Gun, is completely overpowered.
If used correctly this weapon can just destroy any enemy in a short time, because it allows you to throw pieces of environment towards enemies to cause massive damage. It has UNLIMITED ammo and a very long range. You can also throw enemies with it, and most will be instantly killed by the impacts
Combine this with some upgrades to health, armor and powers to get rid of close enemies, and there you have a really easy game. The ONLY sections with difficulty are those where you are forced to stay in tight spaces such as platforms moving and such.
===
This Red Faction is what really ruined the series in the end. Volition tried a combat-focused, alien mash up instead of doing another great red faction as Guerrilla has been, removed the key gameplay points that made the previous title great and instead of them put just a few innovations that just do not save the overall picture from being mediocre at best.
This is a game i suggest only if you are a real fan of Red Faction and want to see how LOW it has gone, or also if you enjoy REALLY MUCH blasting aliens with overpowered stuff.

This game, despite being early access and made by an independent developer team, is, put frankly, THE BEST survival game on the market right now.
Content updates have fleshed out the game mechanics and play area to the point where I can't give it a negative review. The dev team is so dedicated to this work of art, and this dedication is what sets it apart from all of the other same-old copy-paste zombie-survival trash that's been pumped out these past couple of years. It's one of the few early access games I've bought into that actually made an active, wholehearted effort to get released. It was almost entirely funded by fans on kickstarter, so they don't have any higher-ups to answer to, unlike most other dev teams. They have the creative freedom to deliver a product under their own vision. This is key; it is one of the main points that make this game a success and allows them to set the bar high for other survival-game developers to shoot for. The team pours tons of hours of hard work into their product, and their going the extra mile shows in the polish of the general gameplay and visual art style.
Gameplay is brutal and unforgiving, with your character being given only one shot to make it as many days as you can in the everlasting post-apocolyptic winter you trudge through, searching for supplies just to make it out on top one day at a time. In the sandbox, you forge your own path, be it to salvation or death. How will your story end?
+ HUGE map. Like, REALLY ♥♥♥♥ing big. It'll take you a while to explore everything, and with the updates that keep rolling in, it'll only get bigger. There are many zones and transition areas that make traveling from place to place a real adventure. You never quite know what to expect on each journey through the various territories available.
+ Brutal, but fair. Wolf killed you? Try planning a more efficient route next time for avoiding them. Run out of food? Set up snares by rabbit grounds, try fishing in a hut on a lake, or go hunting deer while staying watchful of your surroundings. No water? You should have boiled more snow when you had a fire going. Froze to death? Don't underestimate the power of mother nature, bud.
+ Immersive. Isolation in the wild brings you back to reality. The game really puts you in the shoes of a survivor trying to make it just one more day. Hearing wolves howl when you're knee-deep in the snow at night while a blizzard begins to settle in is truly something that'll send some chills down your spine. The ambient noises of the wilderness, followed by a soundtrack that truly captures the essence of what it feels like to be all alone, makes you feel like you've got some skin in the game.
+ Amazing, extremely dedicated developer team. These guys mean business. Being independent allows them to express themselves in the manner that they want, and without any set deadlines aside from the ones they make for themselves, nothing they do feels rushed or thrown out the door too early, unlike many of the AAA games we see now.
- Some of the game mechanics are confusing to beginners. The game's got a steep learning curve. At first, you will find yourself getting killed long before your first week of life alone has even built some momentum. Over time, this becomes less and less of a problem, though even experienced players may find themselves caught off guard by a stray wolf or hungry, moody bear having an off-day.
- Long wait period between updates. Though when content actually gets released, there are tons of new features provided, it might take a few months or so of testing until content gets pushed from the test branch (unstable) to the main release (stable). Some may not like this, but it goes a long way towards ensuring quality control in the long run.
- Slow paced. Again, some people might not like this, but due to the concept of the game itself, it's not something that can really be changed. This is a survival game, not Call of Duty. Your gameplay will take place over the course of potentially months or years (in-game time, not IRL) if you're good.
This is a great survival game for pitting yourself against mother nature and testing your skills against wildlife and harsh climates. It is a slow paced, brutal game of attrition that will see to your inevitable demise. This game is not for everybody; if you lack patience, and prefer games you can just hop into and half-@ss your way to the top, you will find this game to be either boring, or too difficult. The developer team is amazing, and being indie, they make the rules, not the higher-ups in suits. If you want to test your limits, enjoy highly-polished gameplay, and appreciate a unique visual artstyle over fancy graphics, this game is for you.
A decent balance of challenge and fun. There is a real sense of "more strategy to survive" compared to some other "more luck or die" roguelikes.

. It's just too hard and a little niche.
: For the hardcore puzzle/tower-defense-but-not-tower-defense player. Otherwise, get it on >50% sale.
Don't get me wrong, it's fun, have put a few hours into it myself, but the amount of time one run takes is a little exhausting.
Each room is 10-45 mins, with 13 rooms, each longer and harder, riding an exponential curve type-of-deal. I poured ~5 hours with a friend and have only gotten to level 11 (unfinished though).
Thankfully you can save and continue, though. And multiplayer is essentially bug free. (You can even save and continue your multiplayer games!)
It may be that I came into it expecting a "sit down and finish in one sitting" type of game (there is no save button in the interim/elevator screen, but only actually in the level can you "esc") and got a "sit down and REALLY WANT TO CONTINUE but you can't because it's already been 3 hours and you're only 75% done".
Also rage inducing when you run out of resources / never have enough light / the music is a little depressing / it's dark / the item rolls kept giving you assault rifles when you need a sword / did I mention the atmosphere was a little depressing?
Otherwise, beyond the complaining, the ship models are FANTASTIC, the textures are excellent, the animations are good, there are shadows, yes *REAL SHADOWS* in a pixel game. Sound design is good too, but I mean, you're stuck underground so it's gotta be a little dark and moody.
Overall:
Visuals: 9/10
Sound: 6/10
Gameplay: 5/10
Multiplayer/Gui/MetaSys: 10/10

This is a great little puzzler! With an art style similar to Limbo and other silhouette games, atmospheric music, and a challenging but not evil difficulty with a great interface, puzzle-fans will enjoy this one! You play as Hue, a boy in a black-and-white world. Slowly, you acquire colors with the help of a mysterious figure, as you unravel the connecting story about an experiment with color gone wrong. You are able to switch between colors to reveal hidden platforms, doors, and other obstacles like lasers and paint to solve puzzles. The difficulty curve starts off easy to get you accustomed to switching between colors, and the switching mechanic is very fair, as it slows down time while you pick colors so you don't have to have split second timing (though at times you do need to think quickly). The difficulty increases steadily as more colors are added, and the last few puzzles are very thought-provoking but never impossibly hard. Save points are well-spaced and fair. There are several "run away and switch colors many times omg!!!" sections where you have to think on your feet but most you can take your time and plan. Music is great; very atmospheric. Honestly, my one complaint is that during the voice over story bits, instead of leaving you idle or doing them over actual puzzles, you traverse through a long maze of ladders, stairs, or jumps with no point except to keep you busy and to listen to the story. This means that you can be just holding arrow keys for a long time without any purpose except to get to the next area. Annoying, but not a deal-breaker.
10/10. Great puzzler.

Awesome platform/puzzler! Played it in one sitting because it hit just the right niche between frustrating and "Just one more try!" Gameplay is around 5~10 hours, depending on skill.
Pros:
* Art Style
* Nice piano music
* Uplifting story
* Possible to get all achievements with normal skill
* Levels introduce new components at a nice rate. Game teaches you how to use them without needing a tutorial.
Cons:
* A little short (once you've finished, there's no replayability)
* Piano score in a few sections is a little jarring. Mostly the tense sections. (Fixed by muting those parts)
* If you miss a hidden section on your first go-through, it can cause a lot of backtracking.
Similar to "Thomas was Alone" and "Nihilumbra" -- if you've tried those and liked them, give Hue a shot! If you're a fan of the genre, it's a nice title that adds a splash of new while still keeping the tried-and-true platform puzzle style.

TL:DR Buy it if you are a fan of TD games, or if you are eager to try one. And also help support/fund the game.
I have played tons of TD games before, and If you played those old Warcraft III custom TD maps, get ready for a big nostalgia trip.
First of all, I've been searching a long time for TD games on steam with the maze aspect in it. Found this game and have been waiting the release for some time now. It really adds some depth to the gameplay, It's not just "place towers wherever the game feels like", and as the maps are "randomly" generated, there won't always be the exact best and only way to place towers.
For a game in Early Access, this game is fairly good already. It's playable, haven't encountered many bugs, and totally worth the money even while in development (not to mention it's realtively cheap, just buy it and try it). Devs are talkative and you can freely talk to them in their discord channel (+1 kudos to them).
The shepherds's mechanic is a good throwback to those WCIII heroes, only 3 have been implemented so far but they have a good variety by themselfs. For now there are 4 basic towers and 2 variation for each one via upgrades.
My only complaint for now is problably the sound/music, which can sometimes get repetitive. But don't take my word for it, I normally play games on muted.
I'll edit this review after I play some more. But so far it's definitely a buy if you are a fan of Tower Defense games. And if you never played one before, you might as well just try it for that price tag.

Shepherd of the Abyss takes well known Tower Defense mechanics and provides a heafty twist. Allowing you to building your towers in any location on your map to direct the flow of monsters coming from the portal. But there is more, you can select monsters for their next wave and heroes. The Heroes (Shepherds) you control with hotkey abilities. Allowing you to freeze towers, spawn waves of spiders, or even heal your wave monsters.
These changes make for some fun gameplay and removes the wait to see your results on how well your towers tackeled the wave as there is some skill involved in making the best use of your Shepherd's abilities.
Positives:
Great twist on an existing style of gameplay (Tower Defense)
Added mechanics (Heroes)
Wave Control - you control what comes out of your opponent's portal!
Negatives:
UI needs some more work
Heroes can be slightly confusing when you have 3 active at a time
Overall - Its worth picking up if you have a friend who wants to play too!

Ever since the Warcraft 3 Tower Defense community died out it's been hard finding a solid tower defense game with an emphasis on strategy, they are usually very straightforward and don't require much thinking. Shepherds of the Abyss on the other hand has delivered everything I have been looking for in a TD and more. While many games have abilities of some sort, they never really feel genuine, it feels like they were tossed in last minute before release, whereas in SotA you make up your own "army" consisting of some default creeps and your own Shepherds, these Shepherds all have special abilities much like DOTA/LoL and truly feel like they have their place. Items is also something SotA has done very well, you can buy items for your Sheps, some are active and some are passive bonuses, and they all feel very in-touch with the game.
But the part where SotA really shines as a bright star above all other Tower Defense games is in its mazing. The martial art of making your enemies walk the longest, most tedious path, through tight corridors of flame spitting towers and axe slinging statues. No competitor even comes close in this aspect of the game, some lets you block one route so the creeps will take maybe 10% longer to finish their run, in SotA you can make them walk five, if not ten times longer. And yet it never gets into a repetitive pattern.
SotA is tower defense taken back to its roots.

The game looks great, but plagued by performance problems.
The art is great and the maps have lots of fun details. I find upgrade mechanic interesting from what I've seen so far.
The performance problems are constant and incredibly frustrating. They seem related to the UI, but not completely. Any action that opens a window often takes a second+. It's so unresponsive that you start wondering if you didn't actually clicked the right spot. This happens even when you're out of combat such as between maps and you want to look at different upgrade options.  If I click on my hero, the FPS goes from 60 to 27 and the game often freezes for a second+. If I  let the battle run without touching my keyboard or mouse, there will still be significant FPS drops. Keep in mind there are not many units on the screen, maybe 30 total.
As for gameplay you can construct towers or support buildings and there are seperate build locations for each. The tower size determines the number of units and their strength. A level one tower has one unit. If that unit dies, it will eventually regenerate. The support structures determine the type of units. This allows you to balance between melee, range and magic attacks. From what I've seen the towers never fire or attack on their own. It's all about the units that they create. It's almost like your only towers are barracks or guard house type towers from other tower defense games. Maybe this changes at some point, but that's all I've seen so far.
You also have three powers: area attack, unit heal and slow. You get them starting with the first map. They seem to regenerate quickly.
Each completed map opens up three upgrades which you can spend stars on. You earn stars by completing maps. Three initally then a couple more from increasing the difficulty. This is a maximum of five per map and the upgrade costs were 3, 3 and 4 stars so it might not be possibly to have all the upgrades. Again I haven't played very far so maybe this changes later in the game. None of the upgrades I saw really stood out and I took the 'archers do more damage'. I hope this changes, but none of the 18 or some upgrades I've open looked fun.
You also have a hero and apparently can open up more heroes at some point. The first thing you learn in that your hero is stupid. You will tell him to stand in front of the archers and 10 seconds later he's a third of the map away leaving your archers exposed. I've never seen him return on his own. The heroes don't appear to have any player controlled abilities nor advancement potential. The units themselves are also stlightly stupid. Enemy archers will slowly pick off each melee unit from a distance and the unit will just stand there until dead. You have to send in your hero to take out the archers or maybe micromange the unit locations.
The game has been out for several month and I don't see any patches. My game says it's 1.0. There are a couple old developers posts in the spartan forums. It doesn't like any of the issues will ever be improved.

Great game. Story is interesting, somewhat linear, but ties into the lore and key plot points from the other Red Faction games. The voice acting is good, visuals are fantastic and the gameplay is really, really fun. Plenty of vehicles and walkers to use and the gunplay is the best of the series. Fans of Red Faction Guerilla will enjoy the continued emphasis on destruction and will appreciate the new weapons (and the return of some old favourites). Whilst some may be disappointed by the decision to go back to a linear campaign rather than an open world, from my point of view it was a compromise they made into order to change the environment and make the gameplay work in regard to fighting the alien race known as the 'plague'. I don't think fighting in tunnels and caverns under the surface of Mars lends itself to an open-world campaign.
Red Faction Guerilla was a fantastic game, and had open world elements, but it was in no way 'open world' in the way we see it nowadays in games such as GTA V, Fallout and Skyrim. You could traverse the entire map and mess around, but the missions were all in set locations, were very similar and the objectives did not vary greatly. Anyway, I love every game in the Red Faction franchise, Armageddon is no exception. Thoroughly recommend purchasing it as the campaign is a blast to play through - one of the best singleplayer experiences I have had to date. Tower Dwellers:
~~~~~~~~~~~~

A beautiful and rich land where strong, hairy farmers happily work the soil until hordes of scary monsters force them to escape and take refuge in deep caves. After long discussions, they come up with a plan to take back their land. This is the tale of Tower Dwellers!
Tower Dwellers is Defense Tower/ Strategy game where you take control of a settlement of farmers who want to reclaim their lost land.
After being introduced to the story through a comical narration, you will have to conquer your first territory. But before that, you can select one of six heroes available to you. Each hero has their own set of skills. Some are strong in melee combat, others can be effective from long range, and some can even use magic. When you are satisfied with your choice, it’s time to push back several waves of monsters to beat a level.
You can construct towers on the site, which has three quarry stones and a sign with the tower craft on it. Each time you build a tower, it will cost your treasury fifty gold coins.  The first unit this tower will produce is a farmer. Next to the tower you just built, there is a small site where you can build swordsmen, archers and wizards barracks. You might even have three small sites linked to a tower, and depending on what you build and in which order, you will produce a specific unit. For example, if you build three swordsman barracks, you will get the knight unit. The maximum number of units a tower can produce is three, so choose your strategy and units wisely.
The enemy consists of monsters on foot and in the air; you must eliminate them. Each time you destroy of one of their units you earn gold coins. There is a variable number of waves per level and the last one will feature a boss. Waves will become harder and harder to destroy as they come along and you might need to use special abilities, like the chicken free range (a bombardment of chickens against your foe), and the freeze ability to slow them down.  If you manage to clear the level without letting through a single enemy to the other side of the map you will win stars. If you played on a normal difficulty the maximum number of stars to be awarded is three, and five in the nightmare difficulty. You can purchase upgrades within the territory you conquer by using the stars you won.
I like the artwork and the game runs smoothly without any issues. One small point I noticed is the loading time between levels, which could be faster in my opinion. The game has a good encyclopaedia too.
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Good artwork
-	Good number of units (you and enemies)
-	A good number of upgrades
-	Funny narration
-	Achievements and trading cards.
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	A bit slow too loading between levels.
A well-designed Tower Defense with a funny narration.

Aah, The Long Dark. A so called gem under the survival games. "There are no zombies -- only you, the cold, and all the threats Mother Nature can muster."
Seems a really smart game choice, doesn't it? Leaving the mainstream zombie behind and going for full on post-apocalyptic survival in the Canadian wilderness where the wolves, bears and the cold are your 3 main enemies. Sounds good, if it was executed well.
Let me tell you a story. I've played The Long Dark for 16 hours now (Currently almost 8 days on Pilgrim difficulty and 4 on Voyager) and I'm nearing the end game on the Pilgrim difficulty. I mean, let's be fair here. Your only objectives in the game are these:
1. Find a settlement.
2. Stockpile on food and water.
3. You're done. Go hibernate for the next 25 to 50 days.
This just pisses me off. When I see a crafting tag next to a game, I expect a crafting system that really gets to me. For example, making a better weapon than I already have or armor, etcetera, etcetera. There are only 17 items in the game that can be crafted from scratch. 3 of which must be crafted at a forge which is a 3 hour (real time) walk from Mystery Valley (Including wolf and bear encounters, sleeping, etcetera)
The UI was a thing that I really liked, telling me what I really needed to know. Cold, hunger, thirst, fatigue and of course, a sentence how many hours of daylight I had left (I will come back to this later. Very nice.
Until after the Faithfull cartographer update, it completely screwed that nice menu and the gerneral sense of time with it.
I still don't really understand how time really works in this game. I know the rough ends. 13 hours of daylight and 11 of night. 24 hours in-game trace back to 1 hour in real life meaning that 1 hour in-game is roughly 2.5 minutes.
But enough of math and science, the point of this section is the sleeping mechanic and time. If I say that I want to sleep 12 hours, I want to sleep 12 hours, not 9, not 6, not 11. I've had so many instances where I wake up in the middle of the night when I asked for 12 hours. The new UI doesn't help with this either, because there is only a moon in the right corner of the screen. Also, there were some instances where I could walk outside and it was already light when the moon UI thing was still up. Limit my sleeping time based on my fatigue and tell that to me.
Story mode will come out in August and I know that. But still, 31.99 for a story mode that lasts 10 hours? And what will the missions be? Fetch this, fetch that, look for that person, scare the wolves away. You're paying 25 euro's for the sandbox and 7 for the story. Which means the sandbox must be good right? It's fine, if you execlude all the points mentioned earlier (except for the purpose part) . And let me tell you, that sandbox isn't worth that much.
Enough of my rants now.
- Beautiful Atmosphere.
- Ok-ish graphics (For Unity, that is)
- The voice acting is pretty nice.
- Nice setting.
- It's almost realistic.
- Crafting system
- New Ui
- Time
- Purpose in the sandbox (Just survive or whatever)
- The price on Steam (Really, just buy it from a third party site if you're not planning to refund it.)
Wait until it's finished, that is for the best.

I saw it on Twitter randomly, and my eyes immediately fired up. What captivated me at first was the mix of cute anime girls and super juicy graphics. But even better—it seemed like Puyo Puyo was finally revitalised and brought to PC, Mac and Linux all at once, in Steam. I couldn’t pass on this.
But with a few hours in, my opinion of it quickly evolved and I saw what it truly is. It's not Puyo Puyo… perhaps it’s something even better.
Raining Blobs is a falling-blocks-style arcade puzzler inspired by classics like Super Puzzle Fighter, Columns and—of course—Puyo Puyo, but the rules here are a bit different. Not so much different as to be confusing, but fresh and unique enough to entertain even the most diligent fans of the genre. Anyone who played any of the aforementioned will feel themselves right at home, but newcomers should get in the zone quite easily too—the game is very beginner-friendly with a nice tutorial and abundance of easing options.
In my opinion, the true benchmark of a solid arcade experience is a set of rules as simplistic as possible, that yet creates a nigh-infinite horizon for self-improvement, while of course being fun and never getting boring over time. I think Raining Blobs perfectly gets all of these points. I keep returning to this game often, and every time I find myself learning some new techniques, setting new standards for my skill, and realising it might be deeper than I thought. But most importantly, there is an online leaderboard for all of the modes—making it a complete package of a highly-competitive game with a skill cap as high as the sky. I would love to see more players get in the community, so the game can flourish in all its arcade glory!
Now, apart from the decently enthralling collection of four single-player modes (which are, by the way, all unique and truly different from each other, unlike most cheap knock-offs in today’s games made only to increase the number in their description), Raining Blobs offers brilliant multi-player experience! Whether it’s on-the-couch with controllers or on-the-knees with one keyboard, it’s guaranteed to bring a fine time of co-op and versus action. The rules here are a tad different from Puyo Puyo too, with a lot of smart tweaks and careful tunes which make for deeper strategic performance. Each of four modes can be played both alone and together, and each mode provides a different gameplay objective for the leaderboards (be it classic highscores, story mode speedrunning, a test of brainpower or endurance), effectively quadrupling the competition. There’s a flavour for everyone.
And of course, Raining Blobs doesn’t fall short in the way it looks and sounds either. All the sprites and animations are polished to bring maximum juice. The music is full of cheer and pumping. The sound effects are wonderfully reminiscent of the arcade era, adding to the nostalgic feel. The animated backgrounds drip with atmosphere. The cast is fully comprised of cute anime girls with distinct personalities, which breathes a lot of character into the game… All of this comes together to deliver a stream of very special light-hearted, playful vibes.
Despite being as deep and quick as an arcade should be, Raining Blobs feels very «light» and chill. It’s a game I can launch at any time for a few quick rounds of action, and I know I am always welcome here and will never be disappointed.
As you can see, I love this game a lot. Its developer, Endi Milojkoski, is an incredibly nice and super passionate indie developer from Macedonia. Making this game has been a childhood dream of his, and now that he has finally fulfilled it, he keeps on polishing and adding new things. His wife Magdalena is a fashion designer, and she developed all the girls illustrations, isn’t that lovely? It’s always been a great game up from the Beta as I remember it, but it’s very impressive to see just how much more it improved, with all the added modes, unlockable features like the Gallery, achievements and even
… This is highly inspiring to me as a wanna-be game designer at heart.
So yeah, whether you’re a long-standing fan of puzzlers or a beginner like me, you won’t regret grabbing this adorable sweet roll of a game! Now somebody go get VyseTheLegend off the charts. This guy is
.

I first played Hue during Insomnia 58, it left an impression and when it was on sale the previous week, I had to get it.
The art style is very stylistic. It won't take your breath away like a more realistic game like Steep but it has charm and a glorious use of colour that the whole game is based on.
The gameplay itself, is rather intuitive and new mechanics are introduced throughout which helps to keep it fresh. Changing colours - the main gimmick of the game - is a simple and fluent process, the developers have incorporated it well into the gameplay. There is a little bit of momentum which can be annoying at times ("Goodness! Stay still box!"). The levels do get increasingly complex as the game progresses but except for one or two levels, they are intuitive and not frustrating. I really do wish it was longer though!
The music - very calming, very soothing (much wow), it really suits the game.
The plot is told via letters is thought-provoking, poignant and a touch philosophical. There isn't much substance behind it does raise a few interesting ideas.
And another completely relevant point - it's Hue, a game focused on colour. The pun deserves credit.
I really enjoyed playing Hue. It's a game that is very relaxing and although it does have a little short-term replayablity (you could probably play in a years time when you forget all the levels), it can leave a lasting impression. Would I recommend paying the full-price? Maybe. But if it's on sale and you want a short and well-made game? Get Hue!

I don't know about full colorblind, but you can play this if you're partially color-blinde! Go to options, under video, and check the box! The option comes with symbols that distinguish the colors. Also, because it took me like 10 minutes the very first time I opened the game, ALL your options are under ESC. This is a fun game, and once you've figured out the way each type of zombie works, it's not hard to figure out what you need to do in each level. The blood spatters and chain reactions are incredibly satisfying, and the upgrade system is self-explanatory. My only complaint is that, if you're a perfectionist with achievements, the one for prestiging 20 times is a bit of a bear. I've got almost 49 hours of play time, and I think I've prestiged... five times? Six? There's no way to tell how many times you've done it, as far as I can find, either. And it's not like each time you prestige it gets more challenging; it's just the same stuff all over again, clearing levels, buying upgrades, clearing more levels, and then hitting the prestige button again. The first couple of times it's fine, there's still satisfaction to be had from getting platinum on all levels, but after that it's really just a timesink, all for a single achievement. The devs are aware that people don't like it, and have even agreed in threads on this topic that perhaps it's a little excessive, but they still haven't patched it to make it less tedious. So I'd say, if you don't care about 100% achievements on games, get this, it's a fun way to pass time while watching TV or Youtube, but if you're a completionist, maybe stay away. It's fun, but not THAT fun.
Edit, 9/28/17: Just 100%'d the game, and I've never been happier to uninstall something. To do that, I had to download someone else's save file that was up to 19 prestiges, and get to the 20th one myself. I still can't recommend the game unless you don't care about achievements; it's so incredibly tedious trying to get that last one that all possibility of fun is sucked out of the game. If you only had to prestige, say, five times, and it got a little more difficult or ANYTHING changed with each prestige, that would be a lot better, without feeling impossible or tedious.

You begin each level in
relatively safe from the zombies. You can take your time and pick them off at will, the twist comes when you realise you only have three bullets, not nearly enough to slay them all.
Your bullets are coated with a special pathogen with causes the zombies to explode on impact. As one explodes it will cause others nearby to do the same thus causing a very satisfying chain reaction. With careful consideration, a good aim and a bit of luck it is possible to clear the whole screen with one shot.
Adding to the game there are also different types of zombie that will react differently upon there expiration. Police zombies will fire a single shot across the screen, bloaters explode, corrosive zombies leave a pool of acid behind, soldiers fire bullets which ricochet and so on.
A well placed shot which obliterates all the zombies feels absolutely gratifying. There is an element of luck involved due to the random placement of enemies but, this does not stop
from being any less addictive. To platinum every level will take some time and once it grabs you won’t want to stop until you have them all.
- An interesting approach to the zombie genre.
- Setting off a huge chain is very satisfying.
- Very well designed.
- The puzzle and tactical elements are fun to figure out.
- Some levels will need to be replayed over and over to advance.
