Old review:
Evolve got too much hate around it, mostly cause of ridiculous DLC model. But how does it really make game any worse? Anyhow, I decide to make Pros/Cons list, to answer vital question "Is it worth it?". Here we go:
Cons:
-Worst DLC model I've ever see. Really. Skin packs, 2 (!!!) season passes, deluxe edit., etc. And the price is enormous.
-Skins are really pathetic; they are literally using just another color texture. Really lame comparing with TF, Dota, Lol or anything.
-Most of the player feels lack of the content. Well, I feel like TRS could bring us 5 monsters and 5 of each type of hunters from the beginning. It would be fair for 60 dollar tag.
-small but annoying bugs with cursor
-minor crashes and disconnects
-Game base are dropping down pretty fast and it's hard to say how bad it would be. Frequent updates with new FREE characters would save it for sure.
- and THE BIGGEST ISSUE (is it a real issue, tho?), game is far from being casual, it very exacting to player's skill. One lame random player would easily ruin whole match for your team. If he is a trapper, you got a chance never see the monster until it would come to your power plant. If he is a healer, you team probably would lose first teamfight, etc. It could cause frustration in first case or rage in second? or most likely both. Teamplay is critical here. One hunter could not win whole war, but could win a small battle and make something right to save whole crew. If everybody doing right (including monster) here Evolve shines. So its “boring and repetitive” if you or your teammates don’t really know what you should do. Most complains come from the people who don’t understand the game and not willing to learn it.
Pros... and conclusion.
Well, it's quiet a list, so do you think those things are more important than actual gameplay? Cause gameplay is brilliant, and pretty well balanced for asymmetrical game. Before you start to argue about wraith, I want to say that Evolve reminds me about MOBAs a lot (jungle, 4 abilities + ult, monster's farming, different roles and importance of teamplay, etc), so as it would have more and more characters to play, every new one would be accusing of being op, just because it’s new. Anyway game would need frequent updates and game balance. Let’s face it; it’s hard to balance even non asymmetrical MOBA games. And by the way would you call MOBA games repetetive? Cause their have 1-2 maps to play and victory conditions are the same from game to game. Their find variability in big numberf of playable champions and the fact that different people got different playing style and most importantly skill. So why do I recommend it? Well if you have decent team (even random) you would have a great joy out of it. Battles are totally epic and beautiful, hunt process is keeping you in your toes (your heart is rushing when trapper following you hard on first level), every member of the team is matters and could save all others in some situations, so gameplay is thrilling. If you are ready to learn the game (if you have a full team it would be even greater) you would enjoy it. But I would recommend waiting for updates with new characters, just to be sure about developer’s intentions and plans. It won't hurt to wait sale either, cause it's kinda costly. Evolve got its issues, its not that great as developers told you, but its definitely not as bad as community trying to make it looks and for sure Evolve is unique.

The game i pretty much a demo for the game broforce and is not a full titel that will take you hours to complete. But that dose not change the fact that the titel is 10 minuts of pure awsome!
Presentation:
If you hadn't geussed it this is parody of the movie "The expendabels" whitch stared a lot of action heros. The same fasion as broforce apply here. Every charecter is diffrent and they are all parodies of diffrent action heroes, but here we only get the 5 charecters from the expendables.
As mentioned the game is not very long but it is there to hype you up for the real game "beoforce" whitch have even more charecters levels and so on. if you have ever thought about buying broforce and are not really sure if you should get it, try this out since it free. And if you want a fastpace shooter for 10 minutes check it outtoo.
Gameplay:
Run and gun, thats basiclly what it's all about. Each charecter plays a bit diffrent since some have long ranged weapons and some have short, there is also a melle charecter. Each charecter also have there oen speciel move like trowing three grenades or pound the ground so hard it explodes. After those awesome attacks you can also chose to go in with just melle.
The goal to each level is to get to the other end of the level. Along the way you can get more lives by freeing the bros. When you free a bro you become that bro, so you can quickly learn all the charecters.
Each enemy dies more or less with 1 bullet, so you are an unstobebal force, unless you misstep and get youself killed, you also dies after only one shot.
The levels are all jungle themed and can't really be explored, there are a few alternative ways to go, but you pretty much stick to the main raod and keep running. The entire plaiying field is destructable, so you can quiqly make a mistake and destory some important runways or buildings, whitch you know have to find or created an alternative rude for. It is not easy getting stuck luckely.
The AI is not really smart, and you easily outsmart them with no problem. This really works well with the fast pase.
Overall the gameply is really fastphased and it is nice to make it all the way to the end of a level and see everything explode.
Charecters:
Here I'll give a short bio of all the playable charecters:
Broney Ross: his main attack is his duel handguns whitch fires really fast for long range, his special are laying down three bombs infront of him.
Bro Christmas: Main attack is throwing knifes whitch fires really fast for long range, his special is trowing knifes into the air and rain them down upon your enemies.
Trent Broser: his main attack is a rifle with a very long range but slow fire rade, his special is throwing a grenade that calls down an air strike.
Broder Jenson: His main attack is a grenade launcher with sticky grenades with a slow firerate, his pecial is makeing a bomb car that can be contrloed and detonated for a huge explosion.
Bro Caeser: His main attack is a minigun that fires a very fast long range line of fire that also pushes him back, his special is fireing his minigun behind him, so that he flies up into the air and smashes down to destroy everything infront of him.
Broctor Death: The only melle charecter whoes main attack is his knife, his special is to fly forward and stapping anyone in the way.
And finally Toll Broad: his main attack is a short range flametwrover, and his special is a napalm grenade that sends fire everyehere.
Every charecter is easy to tell apart and fells very uniq.
Visuels:
The visuels is 8-bit style, and dose not really deliver anyhing to visuel impresive, that would be the weakst part of the game in my opinion, since you don't really take a look at the visueal. The fast pase in this game, also make it very hard to aprisiate anything, but that is what it is designed for. There is no reason to make a beutifull scene if you are just gonna run past it right away.
Music/Sound:
The guitar solo at the end of each level is the only really memrebal thing when it comes to sound, the rest of the sound effects are pretty much gunfire, explosions, screams and desturction.
Story:
The Exspendabros have been send out to find and interegate Conrad Stonebanks, who aprently knew they where comming or just had a whole army ready. There is not really more to the story unless you want me to spoil the ending of this 10 minut game. Just play it for youself and you'll see the conclution to the story.
Conclution:
For a very short game that is only made to highlight another game, expendabros shows how the entire game works in only a few levels. Every charecter fells great to play and the overall game only makes you whish for more. If you are into fast pased shotters and are not to concerned when it comes to visuels give this a try, and the best part, you won't have to pay a thing.

The dynamic cover system from Guerilla is gone- though the havok engine is still there from Guerilla, which is cool. Aliens are there- but they are pretty meh. The third person camera sucks; it's so close to the character it becomes an eyesore less than halfway through the game- reducing awareness and reducing my interest in the game. Music is dull and is washed out- drowned in the incessant sounds of aliens, your own weaons, and the general cacaphony of overwhelming sound design. Horde mode is also there, which is an alright improvement. There are a few other modes- but the gameplay made me unintersted in playing these modes.
The campaign is pretty cool though- fighting against crazy cultists is cool, and exploring the marauder cavern is cool. Fighting cultists in the storm was pretty cool. The bulk of the game is spent fighting aliens, but that is actually pretty dull- compared to the cultist sections. The main character is unappealing, and so are most of the other characters- their personalities being completely interchangable.
Look, the point is: Buy Red Faction Guerilla. It's the same price, though it is more fun, and just overall more satisfying.

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers here from Universal Gaming Reviews to bring you a short summary/review for Raining Blobs!
If you'd like to read our full review for the game, you can find it here:
Raining Blobs is a very entertaining and addictive puzzle game that harkens back to the puzzle games of old. It feels like a combination of Tetris and Dr. Mario but it adds it's own setup to give it its own feel.
The game is competitive in nature and features gameplay for up to 16 players (8 Humans and 8 AI players) so it's great for some intense couch co-op gameplay.
There's also a tournament mode where you battle your way through each of the game's 8 characters until you defeat the boss Enya. A new mode called Puzzle Mode was released the day we released our review as well.
The game is an excellent addition to the overcrowded puzzle game genre and if there's one game in the endless sea of puzzle games that you should try out, it's Raining Blobs.
We gave the game 4.5 Stars out of 5 and since we enjoyed the game quite a bit we're giving it our recommendation here on Steam as well.

Really good tower defense game that borrows many elements from roguelikes, mainly permadeath and the RNG-dependent gameplay. It also has rudimentary RPG elements, but they are not that crucial. The main protagonist is the "team", not the characters. Research progress and resource inventory are not character bound and characters can also be easily replaced if necessary.
So, to be precise it isn't a roguelike. Combat is real-time. The step-wise door opening doesn't make it a roguelike. It's more in the vein of FTL, where you advance from system to system.
It also needs to be said, that it is very hard and very luck-based. You can dominate one floor and be completely destroyed in moments on the next due to bad luck on door opening. It's easy to cros sthe threshold where you don't come back into the game and you will lose.
Update 2017: Finally installed it again and gave it another go. Won my first game after 3 tries and, well, lost interest. I  kind of want to like the game more than I do, but beneath the nice art style and the general gameplay, but I feel there is no motivation after my first win. There are other ships/play modes, but I feel there is no real reward in playing them.
One thing that still stands, is that the RNG greatly influences your game. The RNG is the difference between a failed game and a won game, but it is heavily slanted towards devastating loses for new players. And sadly the games doesn't give you enough options to fight the odds. Sure, experienced players will find many smll things that make the game easier, but this isn't what I look for in games.
The game also does a very poor job in explaining itself to the player. I get that modern games rarely have manuals, but this one also has no proper introduction of the game mechanics. Or, e.g. the special abilities of items aren't shown in shops unles you buy them.
And again, this is not a roguelike. It is a roguelite. The door opening is not equivalent to turns, it is more the case of expanding the playing field and progressing into increasingly difficult stages. It's a heavy mix of several genres, but has the least to do with roguelikes.
But since everyone thinks it is one, maybe some more conceptual comparisons: DotE doesn't give you the same amount of choices to deal with the RNG like real roguelikes. And with real roguelikes you get a different story every time and game can be vastly different, even if you choose the same classes. DotE feels the same every time. The RNG levels have barely any significance and you won't visit them again anyway. Your team can vary, but that's not the same as having a unique character. I felt that most characters are mostly interchangeable.
Well, I still recommend the game for what it is, but for me it was about 2x 15 hours of fun, but not more. I'd rather play games that offer me someone new over time.

I've played a little bit of time in here and after their latest update and changes to the game, I figured it's about time I write my own review for this game.
The game is fun. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy it, but I think there could be a lot more done with it and I think too much time was spent on "look how pretty this looks now".
Example:  The information screen that you saw when you held TAB prior to the last major update was superior in every way compared to how the information looks now.  Before you had bars, it stated what condition your character was feeling in that bar.  Let me explain.  Not thirsty?  No problem!  You're "slaked".  Getting a little thirsty and watching that bar diminish?  Now you're "parched".  Things like that.  It was those little details I enjoyed.  Now?  It just looks like a drop of water and it gets uncolored as you go.  It's like the information regressed from what it was.  How it is now seems like how it SHOULD have been before. I don't like it at all.  Seems like a step backwards. big -
The world itself looks more crisp though, and for that I am grateful.  You can see more like you would actualy be able to as you walked around, maybe not see it the best, but you can still see more.  I hoped there would be more significant places to visit with something fairly important to do (the safes in the game were a nice touch, but I think that just playing with the tumblers makes it less dramatic when you finally open it.  I'd rather hunt down the combination and then return to the safe.  Only if you're going to do that, then make the rewards in the safe actually worth something. I don't want to keep getting matches and socks out of them), or something else that is a little more quest involved.  Because wandering aimlessly seems boring and gets kind of annoying after a while.  I'd like some direction. + and -
Speaking of direction, it's nice that they finally added a feature that let's you be able to map out the areas around you.  Gives it more of a sense of "Ok, I remember this house, this is where I stashed my pelts to dry. I've got to remember what it looks like here so I can come back later" and helps to add a little more realism to the game. +
The items need to be tweaked more.  Finding the exact same pair of socks over and over again makes it seem as if you're running around in a world where there was only ever 1 place to shop and people all bought the exact same thing, they are the exact same size, etc.  Why not vary it up?  You're playing the male character, so you need to find Large clothes to fit into.  Didn't find large?  Do you have 2 Mediums?  Then use a sewing kit to make a large. Better hope you don't screw up! because then you can't even salvage a Medium out of it.  Got all that lantern fuel you're carrying around? Let's condense it down into 1 bottle,  or as few bottles as possible, and then we'll clean up our inventory a bit more. I understand the conditions of things, but if you've got a 95% good conditioned bottle of lantern fuel, why not take that 34% condition bottle and pour it into the other one?   Don't tell me that there is a possibility of wasting it, because you waste nothing filling the lantern up, so that isn't a factor at all.  another big - from me on this.
I also think that some of the time frames for things are a bit.  Just starting off building a fire?  Well, you need to build 20 fires to get better at it.  No you don't.  You build 2-3 fires, in real life, and you're automatically better at it.  Want to make the differences more dynamic?  Then wait until about level 7-10 before you get rid of the part of needing kindling.  Or make it so that you only use a portion of accelerant to ignite the fire instead of an entire bottle.  Who needs that much!?  You stuggle to get through levels 2-??? (not sure how high they go just yet) just as much as you do level 1.  Depending on what the skill is, there should be no way you need to perform that task that many times before it makes a difference.  There are smaller changes you could apply from each level increase as well.  Example:  better at making fire? You can now, at level 4, shield the starting of the fire process, but will still have issues with the wind once it is lit.  Things like that.  It is, after all, called a "fire starting" skill, not a "fire keeping" skill.  another big - for me here.
Overall I'd have to say that the game is good, but I would just love to see some legit tweaking done to the game instead of the same rehash we've had for almost 3 full years.  Get creative, let US get creative!  I'll still recommend it because it's fun to play through, but it does get monotonous really quickly.
Overall:  +

My full review right here:

Looks and feels very similar to Kingdom Rush, but with slightly different game mechanics, which is exactly what you want out of a tower defense game if you're a KR fan. I don't think there are any units that slow / charm / paralyze enemies, push enemies back up the path, insta-kill or anything like that. Just regular projectile/melee attacks all around, making the strategy a bit bland.
The towers don't necessarily target the furthest advanced enemy, which can be a bit frustrating since flying enemies sometimes just sail by while the archers are busy shooting ground enemies that are much closer to the beginning of the path. There are no options to change the targetting AI either. Instead, you can click on a single enemy at a time to make everyone within range focus on it.
Overall happy about having bought this game. Haven't experienced any performance issues or serious bugs like that other guy.

This might be the stupidest game I've ever played, but it's also the most addictive. Objectively speaking, I should hate it. But it just keeps sucking me back in again and again.
The premise is simple. You have limited ammo, and must kill as many zombies as possible. So how do you do it? A strategically places shot sets off a chain reaction of zombie explosions.
Who are we kidding? This game is ugly as sin. All you see is black and white with a little bit of red. One other reviewer said he nearly went blind playing this game. Frankly, I believe him. If you stare at this all day, your eyes will hurt.
You want to annoy everyone in your house? Play this game on a surround sound system like I have. Every time you select a zombie, it groans. And not in a nice way, in a repetitive way. As for music? Ha! This is like chains being dragged along a metal stairwell. I'm not joking.
This is one of the best aspects of the game. You can play with either a mouse or a controller. There's no configuring. You can just go straight into the action. Mind you, this isn't a game that requires dexterity since you're really just pointing to a zombie and shooting. Still, you have to precise since it's just so easy to shoot the wrong zombie.
I can play this on any modern PC. I got it working on my gaming rig running an A8, my cheap 11" laptop running a Celeron, my Lenovo tablet running an Atom. I realize PC gaming culture is mostly about pushing specs higher and higher, but there's something to be said about a game that really can run anywhere -- provided it's running Windows. Speaking of which, I really would like to see this ported to Linux or Mac.
Here's an example of gameplay absolutely trumping specs. There is nothing visually appealing about this game. I have seen Atari 2600 games that look more aesthetically pleasing than this one. But so what? There is nothing so satisfying than shooting one zombie then seeing the rest of them explode. Doing it all with one shot? That's the definition of fun.

This is a perfect puzzle game for those who love puzzle fighters games with an element of Super Puzzle Fighter and Pochi and Nyaa with a great cast.

People, please stop comparing this to Puyo Puyo or Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine. It's not that. It's more akin to Puzzle Fighter. Heck, it is basically Puzzle Fighter except with a few but important rule changes.
That said, this is a pretty good multiplayer block dropping game, and in an increasingly saturated marketplace there still aren't many of these. It's like puzzle fighter, except with a few rule changes that creates real good push/pull between players: You rack up block clears and combos to create garbage, but the other player will only receive that garbage if it clears four or more blocks. So your opponent can dump 20 garbage blocks on you, but you can recover given that you have a good amount of blocks or a combo to clear.
It is a little bare, the tournament mode is very simple and it's various endings for each character are only in the form of a few sentences at the end. There isn't a whole lot of visual content to look at, the faux-anime girl style only exists in the character select and backgrounds.
But what is in the game is very solid and polished. Stacking blobs results in a satisfying squish, effects stand out enough and in such a way that you can read your opponent's status with just your peripheral vision. The music is charming and the sound effects are perfect for this type of game. The rules are simple enough to learn quickly and rewards tactful thinking and working under pressure. Also, since indie games do less of this as time goes on: It works. Everything works. No weird glitches, no unpolished bullcrap to swallow, everything just works.
8/10

Raining Blobs marks the Steam debut of talented game developer Endi Milojkoski. The game is one of the brightest and fastest arcade puzzle games to hit Steam in some time.
Although the concept of the game is not unique it is definitely one of the best games in its specific genre in years and arguably the very best that the PC has ever had. Games that it compares favorably to include Dr. Robotnik’s Mean Bean Machine which is considered one of the all-time great SEGA games being first released in 1993 on the SEGA Mega Drive, Game Gear and the following year on the Master System, Puyo Puyo and to a lesser extent Columns and Tetris. Game play is extremely addictive as you match blocks of the same color but can only clear them when you connect them to two same-colored blocks with stars in them. It’s not just a game that requires hand-eye coordination but also a quick and strategic mind.
The game is suitable for one player but you also have the added benefit of playing alongside up to eight other players through the game’s multiplayer. Those who do not have anyone that they can play with are not left out of the game’s competitive mode either as the global leaderboards present enormous challenge to anybody with any desire to compete with the best in the world. It’s the type of game that many players will find themselves trying to claw their way to a higher standing. Even if you’re not such a talented player Milojkoski made the game accessible to everybody by including six difficulty levels. The implementation of a colorblind option further increases the game’s accessibility for the colorblind, an oft-forgotten feature that can render these games unplayable to those who suffer the unfortunate problem. The game makes full use of the Steam platform with achievements, trading cards, the aforementioned Steam global leaderboard system and the Steam cloud. The game is also completely controller friendly.
The anime fans will delight in the anime art throughout the game but as somebody who isn’t passionate for the interest I found that it didn’t detract me from the game one iota as my brain was too busy concentrating on connecting the colors to take much notice of it.
Unless you’re simply not a fan of arcade puzzle fan there is absolutely no reason why you shouldn’t purchase Raining Blobs. At under $10 it is certain to be enjoyed by most gamers.

Wow what a great game! Bought this game about 2 weeks ago expecting to drop a few hours in abandon and come back every so often. Afterall, for me survival games are more a  fun thing I do on the side every so often, not a main game for me. Oh how I was wrong. Closing in on 70 hour mark in that time period. Would be more if not studying for an exam.
The game does not hold your hand and death can be a common foe. Some might be turned off to that. However, I am not. Every death I find myself not being able to wait to get into a new game. How will I die this time? Will I live longer? Will I get the loot I need this time? What did I not explore last time? Can I get my 200 days alive badge? While in the game you find yourself saying just one more day or let me loot that building before I go and end up spending 2 more hours.
The game mechanics, visuals, and the like are very well done and really immerse you into this lone survivor world. By far the best survival game on the market and actually will release from early access in August, unlike most survival EA titles. It is a huge map already with more coming In August. The game pushes you to your limits in survival and has a difficulty level for all types of players. The try hards, the casuals, and the tweeners. This game balances realism with game mechanics and components that may lack some realistic compnents in favor of gameplay expereience. It works very well.
The game just went through a massive UI overhaul. A point of contention with some in the community. Although it seems an obvious attempt to make the UI more console friendly, I like it much much more than the old UI I used. It is cleaner, smoother, more immersive, provides more options, while still giving you all the information you need to survive. IMO it is also easier for new players to pick up then the old UI. Regardless of your thoughts on the UI with mouse and keyboard, with a controller it is simply fantastic. Overall, the UI complaints are either just some tweaks to be made still or, IMO, long term players that dont like change because they were used to something for so long.
There are only 2 reasons why this game does not get an overwhelming positive in the reviews instead of very good from my research. One was that a few months ago the devs gave a timer that many anticipated as the story mode release timer. It was not. It was merely the announcment of when story mode would release and not the actual release. Now as I can understand the frustration in the community, I look past this. Afterall, it is a small dev team and what not so taking any opportunity to market your game is understandble to me and will not recive negative attention from me although I do understand the frustration.
The other reason is that the devs have been saying story mode is coming around the corner and then it does not. Basically the studio gives tentaive plans since I think 2014 of when they expected story mode. At one point even saying they were hoping to relese in 2016 I believe. But those were just "hope for" timeframes so to speak. Nothing concrete. The game was delayed to make a better game after switching from 2d character models for story to 3D which they had never done before. They did not just abandon the game or stop updating. This game has recived many updates and recives consistent dev attention. Bottom line is they never released a definitive release date until recently which is August 1st. That is the launch date and when it will be released.
I add in why this game seems to have some bad reviews because I want it known that it is not because of the game itself in many cases. In fact, even the ones that leave bad reviews in many cases say the game is good, but dont like what the devs did. It is also to establish that the main 2 reasons for bad reviews will not effect a new player because story mode does have a firm release date unlike before and new players wont have to worry about being given a timer.
My suggestion if you are on the fence is to wait for a sale price or the story in August. If you love survival games then you will absolutely dump the hours into this game and 35 is worth it. Especially with story mode coming August 1st.

The game is worth buying for the price, since it is very cheap (49 JPY, about half a dollar).  However, if you want to have a fun time and get all the achievements done, I would not recommend this game.
In this game, you shoot exploding zombies to make a chain reaction with three to six bullets in a level.  There are 100 levels and they can be quite tough to beat if you make mistakes in upgrading on zombies, explosive barrels or your rifle.
The idea of the game could be fun, but the current game is not because of the fact it almost depends on your luck, not on your skill.  It seems all the settings (starting locations of zombies and exploding barrels, moving directions and duration of zombies, and so on) depends on randomness, and the player cannot control this randomness at all, except to choose retry.  You will have to try around 15 times (in average) to eliminate all the zombies in a level.  If you prefer fulfilling achievements, you have to repeat beating all the levels 21 times.  It is a long journey of rather just throwing a dice so many times, not challenging your skills. There is a seldom chance of joy in watching your careful one shot resulting in a complete massacre of zombies.
There should be some modification to allow players to apply their skills; a bait, a yelling, barrels located more dispersed (or designed), environmental kills (falling obstacles to kill zombies and limit their movements afterwards), or zombie attributes attracting other zombies.

Enjoyable and addictive once you figure out what the hell it is you're doing.

All you need to know is that "for cool and unimportant reasons", Redfield City's army of the undead literally explode when shot. Under normal circumstances, this would make clearing the streets of drooling beings rather simple, but this is video gaming we're talking about. Since when is anything straightforward?
With all but one of your team having been wiped out, you arrive at the epicenter of the outbreak inexplicably short of ammunition. What this means, soldier, is that you have three bullets to deal with the undead horde, and have to set off chain reactions to rid the streets of this menace.
Not all zombies are created equal, and some have more explosive energy, while others loose off a few rounds of their firearm in their death throes.
The upshot of a good performance is money, and once you've got enough of the stuff you can set about buying upgrades that, for example, give you more bullets or inflict more damage. Others, meanwhile, grant you more explosive zombies, or increase the radius of their acidic ooze, which generally makes it easier to make a big bloody mess.
All of this adds up to a monstrously addictive quick-fire affair that utterly nails what on-the-go handheld gaming should be about.

I have to admit…. I wasn’t entirely thrilled to feature another apparent mindless zombie game on Steamified. The genre has been done to absolute death – pun semi intended. Then I saw the entire first page of reviews were thumbs down (at least to me) and I thought “Oh, great… Here we go again.” For someone who really tries not to go into any game to be featured on Steamified without too many preconceptions I knew that I was going to be full of them this time around. And yes, I had heard of the game prior to the creation of the site.
The game starts with a comic book style presentation that introduces the game, its story, characters and the setting. It’s actually pretty neat and a very nice touch. It certainly immerses you into the game in a smart manner. The action then gets underway and we discover a game that is easy to learn and pretty difficult to master until you’re very comfortable with how the plethora of different zombie types splatter. The object with each shot is to create the greatest chain reaction. Every zombie that you kill does a different thing upon death. For example, you might have a police zombie that will fire bullet(s) in different directions and for each bullet that hits another zombie will cause that zombie to perform its splatter pattern which may be creating a pool of zombie matter that destroys every other zombie that touches it, etc. In order to advance further into the game you need to kill a certain percentage of zombies on each level.
Thankfully to aide your zombie killing spree there are upgrades. Each level that you successfully complete will give you a reward in the form of cash that you can spend on getting upgrades. You can upgrade your weapons or you can upgrade the different zombies and have their damage increase over total damage, time, distance or even increase their population, Upgrading your weapons allows you to even have more bullets at your disposal. It’s a good upgrade system and one in which you will have to strategically plan for which upgrades will benefit your playstyle the most.
I really enjoyed the time that I spent with OMG Zombies! It’s not the greatest game in the world but it’s certainly one where given it’s level structure you can spend a few minutes just firing away on zombies and have a bit of relaxing fun over a short period. In that respect it’s a pretty solid game. It achieves what it sets out to achieve and on that basis I can recommend it.

There is no such thing as 'the perfect' game, nor can a game objectively be called 'the best' within a genre. With that said, Project Zomboid comes close to the idealized zombie survival setup that I enjoy. The game has a high level of complexity which requires the player to think carefully about decisions and strategy, while at the same time not being overly complex once you learn the ropes. There is plenty of content to keep the player occupied and more on the way. Though admittely some areas don't shine as bright as others, the devs are active, responsive, and generally make good decisions about where to polish their game next. The game can be challenging, but is set up in a way where that's part of the charm, and there are plenty of settings to allow the player to tweak both the environment (which is massive, ambitious, and by and large delivers) and zombie lore.
With this in mind, a few things come down to preference. Zomboid has an overhead PoV. I'm fine with that. I like first person games too, but Zomboid doesn't need to be first person to be fun. Indeed, there's a certain charm to the chosen style that in my opinion is lacking in a lot of games today. There are no super zombies or wildly fantastical elements. Zomboid takes a "realistic" approach (as much as a zombie game can be realistic, that is). I enjoy both realistic zombie games and the more off-the-wall offerings in the genre, but would not begrudge anyone on simple tastes alone. Above all, Zomboid is a rather unique experience. I encourage anyone on the fence to look up some gameplay videos online, read the dev blogs, and decide if you like what you see. Zomboid is definitely a very particular take on the zombie genre, but an important offering nonetheless.

Wow.... where do I begin...
So I got this game for free from HumbleBundle and decided to play it. Heard a lot of good stuff about Outlast and that it's the scariest game of all time. This is my 2nd horror game after Amnesia TDD so I got pretty pumped (I love the spooky atmosphere). Oh boy, there were some really good jumpscares. The story, if you pay close attention to it and find hidden documents, is pretty dark and bone-chilling. So you're a journalist (an amateur) and you've heard of Mount Massive Asylum, a place in which inmates are treated badly. You decide to go there and investigate (idk who tf would do that) and then there's the whole game, you get trapped in the asylum. The level design is very well made, there are a lot of tight corridors, underground passages, narrow rooms, dark hallways and bloody walls. Believe me, it's an extreme scary feeling that you'll get while playing Outlast, this game is amazing. I'm not that easily scared so only a few jumpscares got me. Now, the thing that probably will put people off is the gore. The game is FULL of blood, guts, ripped off heads and other limbs, mutilation, necrophilia, cannibalism and so on. I really don't understand how Hatred is an AO game but Outlast isn't. The ending of the game made me feel disappointed and it failed to deliver that horror factor it had from the beginning until the end. It was pretty sci-fi (don't worry, no spoilers). But here is where the DLC comes in place. "Whistleblower" has a different protagonist, with a different backstory, although the dlc is set exactly after the base game ends (the dlc is way more disgusting and it has even more blood and guts. Be prepared for gruesome images). You can't play Outlast without "Whistleblower" because you won't understand the story 100% and there would be no point in playing one without the other. After I finished the dlc I understood everything. This game is a must for every horror fan out there. Faint-hearted people stay away from this!
Gameplay: 10/10 (smooth and easy, although you get to know how the game works and you'll start to expect jumpscares)
Soundtrack: 10/10 (intense)
Scare factor: 10/10
Story: 8/10 (because of the ending)
DLC: 10/10 (simply amazing, it's a must if you want to understand the story)
Gore factor: 100/10
Overall: 10 (must buy if you're into horror)

There is no other game I know of that even comes close to capturing the atmosphere and gameplay that the Long Dark has to offer.  The painting-like beauty of the game world is completely at odds with your character's desperate struggle to survive.  The game and its developers make no efforts to "hold the player's hand" and although this means that some lessons are learned the hard way, it also creates a real sense of accomplishment when you devise your own unique strategies for evading wolves or conserving your ever-dwindling food supply.  However, this is not to say that the game is more punishing to new players.  On the contrary, with a range of difficulty modes the game does a wonderful job of easing new players into the "quite apocalypse" while also allowing the more sadistic veterans a chance to really test their skills.  I could go on about this game for days but I think that it is best experienced first-hand, especially in the early hours of gameplay when everything is new and surprising.  I strongly recommend this game to anybody who is craving a truly unique and immersive survival experience.

As my first BioShock game (I know, I'm late to the party), I couldn't have asked for anything better. Prior to starting the game, I was doubtful whether this game that came out 10 years ago had aged well but DAMN after a short period of playing time, I realized how wrong I was.
-For a 2007 game, the graphics are pretty nice and detailed
-The world is SOOO DETAILED and IMMERSIVE. I can't emphasize this enough; the surrounding world is everything in this game
-I have always loved Atmospheric games, and this game did an amazing job. The atmosphere of the game (the colorings, lightings, ALL that stuff) is absolutely perfect for this game and only enhances the BioShock experience
-Gotta say at times I was a bit spooked/nervous just because the game does such a nice job with visuals and sound and at times it can even feel a bit like a horror game which is awesome
-The story...where do I even begin. It's full of intense moments, interesting twists, and most importantly it's a story that you actually care about and are eager to see how it'll play out. -The combat is very unique and satisfying and there are sooo many different ways to utilize combat in this game whether it be the numerous selection of weapons you can have, or the vast variety of differnet Plasmids- each unique in its purpose
-Last but not least, the game has depth...a lot of it. There is just so much to do, so much to try, so much to loot, and so much to think about. You can hack just about everything, loot just about everything, buy just about everything, upgrade just about everything, and there is more and more and more...it seems as if everything in this game has a deeper layer to it which is fantastic IMO
I will definitely be re-playing this game some time in the future, but for now, BioShock 2 here I come!

March 14, 2012
Akira Yoshizawa's 101st Birthday
We’re excited to have Robert J. Lang here to talk about today’s doodle in honor of Akira Yoshizawa. Lang is considered one of the world’s masters of the art of origami. His design techniques are used by origami artists around the world, and he lectures widely on the connections between origami art, science, mathematics and technology. - Ed.
Akira Yoshizawa (1911–2005) is widely regarded as the father of the modern origami art form. Over the course of his life, he created tens of thousands of origami works and pioneered many of the artistic techniques used by modern-day origami artists, most notably the technique of wet-folding, which allowed the use of thick papers and created soft curves, gentle shapes and rounded, organic forms. He also developed a notation for origami that has now been the standard for origami instruction for more than 50 years.
Yoshizawa took up Japan's traditional folk art of origami in his 20s, and eventually left his job at a factory to focus full-time on his origami creations. His work came to the attention of the west in 1955, after an exhibition of his works in Amsterdam, and rapidly spread around the world. In his last decades, he received worldwide renown and invitations from all over, culminating in his award in 1983 of the Order of the Rising Sun.
I had the great fortune to meet Yoshizawa several times. In 1988, he came to New York to visit The Friends of the Origami Center of America, and spoke at a panel discussion I attended. There, he addressed a wide range of topics: one's mental attitude, the importance of character, of natural qualities, of having one's "spirit within [the artwork's] folds." Although he was the consummate artist, his work and approach was infused with the mathematical and geometric underpinnings of origami as well as a deep aesthetic sense:

“My origami creations, in accordance with the laws of nature, require the use of geometry, science, and physics. They also encompass religion, philosophy, and biochemistry. Over all, I want you to discover the joy of creation by your own hand…the possibility of creation from paper is infinite.” - Akira Yoshizawa
While there were other Japanese artists who explored their country’s folk art contemporaneously with Yoshizawa, his work inspired the world through a combination of grace, beauty, variety and clarity of presentation. To him, each figure, even if folded from the same basic plan, was a unique object with a unique character.
In 1992, I was invited to address the Nippon Origami Association at their annual meeting in Japan, and my hosts arranged for me to meet the great Yoshizawa at his home and studio. When I was ushered into the inner sanctum, Yoshizawa greeted me, grinning, and then proceeded to show me box after box after drawer of the most extraordinarily folded works I had ever seen.
When I was first approached by Google to help create a doodle commemorating Yoshizawa’s work, I jumped at the chance. Google set the parameters of the design: the Google logo, of course, but to be folded with origami and then decorated with examples of Yoshizawa's designs.
I created examples of two logo styles for Google to choose from: one in a classic origami style and a more three-dimensional version based on pleats. Google liked the pleated version, so I set about designing and folding the rest.



Two versions of the Google "G," each folded from a single sheet of paper.

To design these (or any letterform in this style), one can take a narrow strip of paper, fold it back and forth to trace the outline of the desired letter, unfold it, mark the creases, then arrange multiple copies of the strip pattern on a larger rectangle. The resulting crease pattern is moderately complex, and it gives a lovely 3-D form when folded, but conceptually, it is quite straightforward.
If you’d like to try to create your own origami doodle at home, you can download PDFs of the crease patterns for each of the letters. Print them out and fold on the lines: red=valley fold, blue=mountain.



G                          o                          o                         g                           l                          e

The butterflies in the doodle are folded from one of Yoshizawa's earliest, yet most iconic designs. It is deceptive in its simplicity, but can express great subtlety in its shaping and attitude. The combination of simplicity and depth is part of the essence of origami, and is key to Yoshizawa's work and legacy.
"Geometry alone is not enough to portray human desires, expressions, aspirations, joys. We need more." — Akira Yoshizawa, 1988
Posted by Robert J. Lang, Origami Artist

I'd like to preface this review by first saying that while I am giving this game a positve review, I cannot recommend buying it at full price. Five dollars is a bit much for this game, in my opinion. If you are thinking of trying this game out, get it while it's on sale.
I'm really surprised at the amount of negative reviews on here for this game. I've personally enjoyed playing it so far; it's a nice game to kill some time with when you don't feel like immersing yourself into a less-casual, more attention-consuming game. But you have to keep this in mind - it's a much more casual game than most other zombie-themed games out there. While it's hard to describe exactly what genre OMG Zombies! fits into, it's clear right from the beginning that you are going to have use strategy to plan out how you will complete each level. It's something of a puzzle game, forcing you to carefully plan out each shot that you take (as your ammo is extremely limited). The zombies all have unique attributes that allow them to set off chain reactions with other zombies upon their death, giving you the ability to take out 10's of zombies at a time with a single bullet.
There is something of a skill tree in this game, in which you spend money that you earn from each level to power up not only your own weapon and ammo, but also the attributes that the zombies possess, allowing each zombie to deal more damage, or deal damage for a longer duration. It isn't the greatest application of a skill tree that I've seen, but it could have been far worse. The one contention that I do have with it is the complete lack of variety when it comes to weapons; you have one gun for the entire game (unless I'm mistaken, but it doesn't look like it so far).
The levels themselves are ok. Visually, they are pretty bland, but I feel that it actually goes well with this game. While the layouts change slightly, the gameplay remains virtually the same. You may have to occasionally alter your tactics very subtly, but not by much. The difficulty rises at a good pace, I feel. Some levels prove to be fairly challenging, but once you finally kill off most of the zombies and get a gold medal for the level (or all of the zombies, on a rare occasion, securing you the platinum medal), it brings you quite a sense of accomplishment.
In short, OMG Zombies! is a good game if you can get it for the right price. It's not a game that I can see anyone pumping a hundred hours into, but you can get a decent amount of fun out of it for the price of a candy bar.

OMG Zombies!. How can one come up with a title so great and yet so stupid at the same time? Laughing Jackel found a way.
In OMG Zombies!, you play as a unnamed riot armour clad police officer who is the sole survivor of a zombie apocalypse in the city of Redfield. For reasons unexplained in-game, the zombies in OMG Zombies! literally explode when shot, showering their zombie brethren with gore and causing chain reactions of showering zombie gibs with just a single bullet. Your cop is going to have to learn to use his rifle to it's fullest potential if he's going to escape Redfield alive.

If you like stratagy, you should try this game out. If you don't, I wouldn't recommend OMG Zombies!.

This is a weird one. The game itself is pretty unique, and has a few interesting ideas...
On the other hand, it's very unpolished and often has contradictory mechanics that end up making the game very tedious.
OMG Zombies! is almost like a puzzle game, as it has been said by other reviewers. Each level has a certain layout (there are 100 levels, but much fewer layouts), and a set of zombies. There are several types of zombies, each with a unique destructive ability. Once you kill one, that ability activates, killing more of them around him. It makes for a pretty neat chain effect!
The most succint way to describe this game is one with
.
What do I mean by this? Well, each level has quite a bit of room to breathe, since the zombies start in random positions. Exploding barrels do as well. This makes each restart almost a different level.
The game hasn't been carefuly tailored for you. While that has its negatives, it can create some pretty surprising situations and chains that one couldn't predict!
And I like that a lot!
On the other hand, you unlock level by getting Gold medals on specific levels. These gold medals are awarded for killing 90+% of the zombies in the given level. That's where the randomness and "breathing room" creates a problem. It's often very unlikely to achieve that goal without some starting positions.
Another problem is how unclear it is the chain that you'll create. Each zombie is moving randomly, and their range isn't very clear. So, it's nigh unpredictable.
All of this boils down to luck, in the end.
You restart until you have a good starting position, and then you try to judge which shot will have the biggest effect.
... Then, there's the upgrade system. You upgrade each zombie  with credits you earn from medals. The shinier the medal, the more money you get. This could have been a cool feature, but it fell short for a simple reason:
each zombie has 3 stats to upgrade, but you don't get to choose which! It's automatic. This stops any possible creativity in upgrading certain zombies in a certain way to develop your playstyle.
It's also very grindy in the late game, since you need to perfect almost every level to upgrade everything.
The biggest problem, perhaps, is that there are 100 levels. This is far too much. Simply because the game is pretty repetitive. Lots of similar zombies exploding. The levels tend to get dilluted pretty fast, and instead of creating interesting situations, it's simply tedious to grind through them all.
Not to mention how perfecting a level often end in you waiting up to several minutes for the 2 remaining zombies to align so you can explode both of them with your last bullet.
...
Aside from this, there are other technical problems that don't help. Visually, the game is really weak.
It has a solid aesthetic, it was what appealed to me at first! But the actual quality is poor. The game is just a set of backgrounds with poorly aligned blood pools. If an enemy dies in a set of diagonal stairs, the blood is still horizontal and just looks off. Resolution is low as well... It's not good. And it's unfortunate, since it had potential!
The grayscale also affects perception a lot, often missing a zombie because it blended with the background. Of course, there's an option to color zombies (just get some green paint on top of it), but that ruins the aesthetic. So yeah, another problem not solved.
Finally, I'd just like to say how awful the interface is. Jesus Christ, the level selection was infuriating. I can't even describe it. You basically have a sort of grid that doesn't fit on the whole screen, so you drag it to all sides. But it has acceleration, so it can sometimes get off the screen for no reason.
Come on, use pages, ou a smaller grid... anything but this.
Anyway.
The game started out very nicely! I enjoyed the concept a lot, and chains were cool, at times.
But the game dragged on for far too long, and the tight objectives didn't go well with how free the mechanics were.
So yeah, interesting idea, poor execution.

Hue is a colour-based puzzle-platformer. You are given a palette of colours and an array of obstacles, interactable objects and hazards in these colours. Each time you change to a colour, all of the objects of that colour disappear and you can move yourself and other objects through them. The core gameplay consists of switching through colours and manipulating objects, phasing some in and out of existence in order to make your way to the end of the level.
Unlike many puzzle games, however, these puzzles are always intuitive and never infuriating. You will usually know exactly what to do very quickly, and even if there is a little thinking outside the box involved, these levels are not particularly long or complex, so even later levels will not take more than ten to fifteen minutes in total to figure out, and can be completed in thirty seconds once you know what to do - though there are quite a few curveballs where you get close to the end and realise things aren't going to work the way you intended, so it's back to the drawing board! They are also well-designed; each level has a few hazards, but dying will never take you back more than a few moments. There are also very few situations where you will be stuck and need to reset the level. The end result is that you will never be too frustrated at a level. You will always know where you went wrong and what to do to proceed, and you will never feel that your deaths were unfair. Many times I entered a level, looked at it, and thought 'oh no, this is going to be a rigmarole' and was always proven wrong by how intuitive and simple it really was. The levels are always fun and interesting to play, throwing in new mechanics every few levels so you never get bored or complacent. There are also a few short pure platforming sections mixed in to shake things up a little and keep things varied.
As well as exemplary gameplay, Hue also exhibits a fantastic soundtrack and aesthetic. A simple, cartoony art style with snappy animation makes everything stand out, and really helps with making the levels intuitive. The soundtrack is an eclectic acoustic mix of mostly slow piano tracks, with the odd bouncy, fun song mixed in to keep the mood high. The sound design is also snappy, with everything having its own distinct, fun sound.
The one area where the game is not so great is the story. There are many sections where you are merely wandering down a corridor, listening to some narration. The story is a little interesting, but the writing is not fantastic, often very simple philosophical musings that don't really add anything to the game. The voice acting is great, but while these sections are short, they take a minute or so each, which is quite a lot in a game like this where levels are also short, and only serve to slow down the pacing.
Overall, Hue is one of the few puzzle games I have played in which I never got frustrated or felt the puzzles were unfair or padding (apart from the story sections). The levels being short really helps the gameplay, so that you are never stuck anywhere for too long. The level design is some of the best I have seen in a puzzle game; always intuitive and simple, but still making you think differently every time.
Highly recommended and one of the best puzzle games I have played.

Purchased The Long Dark on sale almost purely on its aesthetic appeal. As a big fan of survival games, it was exceptionally refreshing to play one that was equal parts relaxing and challenging while also being a nice break from the zombie/surival genre.

Hardcore surivalists will appreciate Interloper difficulty which requires some pretty serious forward thinking to survive even 2-3 days while easy mode catering to the explorers at heart, while still being challenging at times (i.e. if you get caught in a snow storm at night). Easily playable as a casual game and yet I capable of binging on for long sittings.
At the time of writing, The Long Dark is in Early Access but has recently had an overhaul of the UI and developers have unlocked Story mode - which I am yet to explore. Certainly not a game that has been abandoned by the devs by any standards - infact, The Long Dark appears to be getting very close being fully polished in preparation for BETA launch.

Wow what a great game! Bought this game about 2 weeks ago expecting to drop a few hours in abandon and come back every so often. While in the game you find yourself saying just one more day or let me loot that building before I go and end up spending 2 more hours.
The game mechanics, visuals, and the like are very well done and really immerse you into this lone survivor world. There are only 2 reasons why this game does not get an overwhelming positive in the reviews instead of very good from my research. One was that a few months ago the devs gave a timer that many anticipated as the story mode release timer. It was not. It was merely the announcment of when story mode would release and not the actual release. Now as I can understand the frustration in the community, I look past this. Afterall, it is a small dev team and what not so taking any opportunity to market your game is understandble to me and will not recive negative attention from me although I do understand the frustration.
The other reason is that the devs have been saying story mode is coming around the corner and then it does not. Basically the studio gives tentaive plans since I think 2014 of when they expected story mode. At one point even saying they were hoping to relese in 2016 I believe. But those were just "hope for" timeframes so to speak. Nothing concrete. The game was delayed to make a better game after switching from 2d character models for story to 3D which they had never done before. They did not just abandon the game or stop updating. This game has recived many updates and recives consistent dev attention. Bottom line is they never released a definitive release date until recently which is August 1st. That is the launch date and when it will be released.
I add in why this game seems to have some bad reviews because I want it known that it is not because of the game itself in many cases. In fact, even the ones that leave bad reviews in many cases say the game is good, but dont like what the devs did. It is also to establish that the main 2 reasons for bad reviews will not effect a new player because story mode does have a firm release date unlike before and new players wont have to worry about being given a timer.
My suggestion if you are on the fence is to wait for a sale price or the story in August. If you love survival games then you will absolutely dump the hours into this game and 35 is worth it. Especially with story mode coming August 1st.

A chain-reaction casual game where you have a limited number of triggers to create the most possible damage. In this case, the triggers are gunshots that draw from your tiny pool of bullets, and the chain reactions come from zombies that erupt when killed (and various special zombies with differing effects).
While this game is cheap I would caution against buying it unless you're cool with a lack of polish akin to something you might find on various free flash game index sites. Rather, it plays like a freebie mobile game (and if memory serves me right, this is in fact a PSP port). While it is passable to start with, it quickly becomes about the grind for cash to upgrade the zombies, to allow you to get the same kind of combos on later levels. For instance, early on you are fine with standard zombies which have a small eruption radius, but as you progress so too does the zombie health bars, meaning that they won't erupt until hit several times by upgraded zombies.
The grind doesn't fit in a chain reaction game at all, and given the behaviour of the special zombies you will rely upon to create these chain reactions, you can end up force-restarting any given map a crazy number of times just to get workable zombie positions. While all the zombies do stagger slowly around, there is no fast-forward, and the special zombie effects are directional or range-limited. Then there is the issue of your own clicked gunshots being approximate. If there are three zombies stood close together, and you click directly on the head of one of them, it may simply decide to damage one of the other two by virtue of hitboxes and layers, rather than what you actually clicked.
I wouldn't recommend this game, but if you really must, I would suggest looking for it on a mobile platform or waiting for a steep sale.

-When you begin and even when you have many hours on the game, there will be alot of dying, especially from enemies you don't even see.

I purchased The Long Dark about a year ago, clocked in roughly an hour and didn't play it again for a year.
Since I've redownloaded, I'm greeted with enough content to warrant a review.
Upon starting a new game on The Long Dark (albeit only Sandbox mode available) you are plonked into a world, barron with snow, a glorious vista sprawls out before you in every direction as far as you can see, you are equipped with a few warm clothes, and not much else, my first thought was to find a building that might have materiels for crafting. Within 5 minutes I had found said building, raided the entirety, decontructed all the wooden frames I needed for firewood, gathered food, found a hatchet, a prybar and a light source.
Happily I began to explore the darker areas of the building with my new found lightsource, whilst having my head stuck in a metal container suddenly a shrill wolf howl peirces the air, horrifyingly, I realise I am unarmed.
Carefully I tread now, I round a corner and my fears are realised, a lone wolf (takes a little while before noticing me) begins to charge at me, I 180 spin and haul my chilly little cheeks back towards the door, the wolf nipping on my heels.
I throw myself at the exit and dont stop to turn around, I sprint as far and as fast as I can cramming energy bars and grape sodas down my gullet as I marathon for escape.
The wolf growls die down, I am alive, however, during this encounter, and how engaging it was, I didnt pay any attention to where I was going, I find myself now, in the midst of a growing snow storm, with only 3 hours of daylight remaining, genuine panic sets in as my field of vision becomes smaller and smaller until I am able to see only a few feet in front of me in all directions, here i began to feel truly lost.
I drudge ever onwards, my food supplies are sparse, my water is disapated and I am dehydrated and freezing at an alarming rate, risk of hypthermia sets in, I pick a direction and travel, sure that my game is over and this harsh environment has claimed me.
I am exhausted, through the snow and wind I think I can see a rippling red flag so make ground for that.
Under the flag is a wooden hut, I push for sanctuary, my condition reaching a critical level as I turn the door handle.
Inside are two stoves, here I am able to keep warm, melt snow for hydration, cook tins of meat I found earlier after crudly opening them with a hunting knife, I brew a cup of coffee, set the fire to a few bars and get into bed and drift uneasily into sleep.
This was my Day One in "The Long Dark" a truly unique and genuinely quite nerve racking experience.
None of the above is dramatised.
While the graphics are shaded, I feel this adds to the gritty, post-apocolyptic environment "The Long Dark" is trying to promote, the mechanics and well thought out crafting system are just about balanced enough to keep you engaging in the environment to survive and explore, after one or two days, you begin to plan your 12 hours of available daylight, and prioritise expiditions based on what immediate resources are paramount to your survival, that is of course, before you find a reliable source of food, water, heat, and a warm place to lay down and get some rest.
Overall I am very pleased with my return to "The Long Dark", this title is showing alot of potential, and I look forward to future updates from this developer.

Verdict: This is the 4x game I always wanted. A grand turn-based strategy game, comparable to Civilization IV but in a gorgeous high-fantasy setting with tactical battles and RPG elements. Most significantly for me, it is fully customisable: design your own faction, leader and units to suit your personal playstyle and role-play. Longer games have stability issues, but I fixed mine by turning off anti-aliasing. 8/10
Story: It may be misleading to speak of story in a game like this, and I have not yet played the campaign scenario. The premise of the world, elaborated here from previous Elemental games, is interesting enough. And the customisation allows you to create your own story as you please. 6/10
Gameplay:  Despite some AI and balance issues, the gameplay is solid and very engaging. It’s not long before that classic Civilization “one more turn” syndrome sets in and takes over, and single games can easily steal away 20-30 hours. Though the fashion in 4x strategy is towards hexagons, square-based maps do the job here, and it is fun to explore rich landscapes dense with monsters, treasure and quests to fulfill. City and resource management are interesting, and it’s satisfying to see your metropolises grow and your empire expand. Research is broken into three tech trees (Civic, Warfare, Magic) you advance separately, making it a strategic choice of where your focus will be. Tactical battles are fun, if a bit on the simple side; tactics emerge solely from your unit design and the composition of your armies, without regard for other factors such as terrain. Auto-resolve can be a bit wonky, and can sometimes beat otherwise unwinnable battles, but it is not game-breaking. The UI is a masterpiece and provides all the information you need to manage your empire. Detailed faction and unit customisation are what tie all these factors together and make Fallen Enchantress a superior experience to similar 4x games.  9/10
Graphics: The graphics will appear a bit dated to some, but the art style fits the unique setting nicely resulting in a somewhat cartoony, but still beautiful, dark and broken world. 7/10
Sound/Music: The sound is not exceptional (ambiance is decent), but the music is great with some truly epic themes to conquer to.  7/10

An enjoyable mash up of roguelike, tower defence, dungeon crawler and small part RPG.
Take a party of up to 4 characters (who can be swapped out as you go) thro a series of levels escorting a crystal (power supply) that must be safeguarded to the exit before progressing to the next area.
On the way to finding the exit you travel thro rooms/areas that allow you to place modules (research upgrades and provide resources for leveling up) and minor modules that act as various types of buffers, debuffers, crowd control and dps. As you enter new rooms/areas waves of creatures attack and attempt to reach the crystal you are safeguarding. One problem you have is that power is limited (dust - from the endless series of games)  and can only power a limited number of rooms prompting some tough decisions at times. Unpowered rooms equals spawn points for the enemy.
Finding the level exit brings about a mad dash escorting the crystal being pursued by endless spawns of creatures.
It can get a little repetitive which I suppose is the nature of roguelikes. But it also manages to capture that one more turn feel. So if you like roguelikes it will probably be your cup of tea,
Genuinely original mash up attempt from a company that tries to innovate and not emulate. Well Done.

What can I say about this game....
My main comparison is to Darkest Hour - a mod to Red Orchestra. I bought this game to replace that amazing mod. I have 400 hours on DH. I dont see why you would play RO2 over Darkest Hour.
Features RO2 has that DH does not:
♥♥♥♥♥♥ Cover system. Main use for it is blind firing. Otherwise youre just stuck to a wall and sometimes stick out more than if you werent in the cover system at all
Campaign mode. Sort of cool, but ultimately pointless when it comes to gameplay.
zeroing. Good, but not that important. Most engagements are up close anyways or you could just aim a little bit up.
Checking Magazines/reloading single bullets for a bolt. Good. Pretty much the only thing that matters that was added.
Bandage system: honestly pretty pointless. buggy and sometimes youll start the animation but wont finish it and cant start it again so you die. most shots just one hit you anyways.
spawning on squad leader: could be okay, but pretty lame in a "realistic" game. a lot of the time, squad leads are dumb and die or put you in a really bad place to spawn anyway.
Progression system: Ro2 decided to jump on the modern fps bandwagon where you need a progression system to keep players. So now you have a rank, which is fine as your total rank doesnt do too much. What isnt fine is that you need to get kills with weapons to unlock attachments. Meaning unlike in DH, you cant just equip a bayonet. It either spawns on the gun or doesnt. A real soldier always has a bayonet and can attach it and detach it depending on the circumstances. You shouldnt be penalized for being new because you havent gotten enough kills to earn a bayonet or scope or drum mag.
What does DH do better than RO2?
Maps. They feel WAY better. Their layouts make sense. Spawns: You dont spawn in ♥♥♥♥♥♥ locations where you can be spawncamped like in RO2. So many times ive been suppressed while i spawned, died where i spawned, or walked a few feet and died. People know where the spawns are and just camp them. The objective could be 200m away, but it doesnt matter. In DH spawns arent always one dimensional. You could spawn in a halftrack on one map. Or spawn close to the objective. They're placed better. You dont get killed immediately. The quality is just much higher.
Aiming. When you aim in Ro2, you dont move your camera like in a traditional shooter; you mainly move your gun. This makes aiming way harder for snap shooting because your gun is moving and not you. Both games have the same hipfire system, where you move the gun and the bullet comes out of the barrel instead of in the middle of your screen. But when you aim a gun, you put it close to your face and aim down the sights. You can move your body and acquire targets fast. it feels sloppy the way ro2 has it work.
Supression. It feels more useful in Darkest Hour. It doenst just make it hard to see by making your screen black and white like somehow youre colorblind by getting shot at and making it blurry. It jerks you around making it hard to return fire.
More vehicles and tools: Mortars. Halftracks. Jeeps. Many different tanks. German tanks felt better, but the Americans had M1 Garands, giving a contrast to each side without them being blatantly one sided. If you want to play Russian vs German or Commonwealth vs German, those exist on certain maps, as many RO1 maps were ported.
Community seems way better, but I guess that point isnt a solid one.
And it's a free mod for Red Orchestra 1. Which I luckily got from a video card purchase. You dont have to pay $20 to get Rising storm on top of Red Orchestra 2 just to get a different front of the war. You dont have to go through progression systems. You dont have an intrusive hud that just feels wrong. Honestly, the DH spawning system isnt that much better, but it was executed better than RO2. Obviously, something like Squad's spawning system would be more realistic, as you couldnt spawn right next to an enemy on a squad leader since rallies are destroyed with an enemy coming too close. Or having FOBs for bases to spawn at that are different depending what squad leader you have in a game since they can be placed almost everywhere.
Give Darkest Hour a go. If you want a more realistic, larger feel to the game, Squad is good. Once Post Scriptum is finished, that'll be your WW2 Squad.

To give you some perspective I was playing Rogue Survivor and Survival Crisis Z, not to mention flash games, in early 2011. Someone mentioned PZ to me and I backed them before their first demo was even out -- an outrageous idea at the time, but common now. What initially came to fruition was a polished and focused tech demo with a good art style, simple animations and aesthetic, and clunky but functional inventory system.
I fired Build 34b up this week and I can say with assurance that almost nothing has changed. The art style has shifted to a pseudo-realistic stop motion, with a useless zoom feature and glitchy lighting. Running from house to house, room to room, fighting back awful controls and the exact same terrible inventory/looting system was a chore. The netcode is Direct Connect IP/Serverbox, with no dedicated servers or IP to IP hosting -- which makes no use of Steamworks.
Combat is downright impossible with static repeating animations (or none at all) with each subsequent hit. Weapons break too frequently and are too rare, there are still no NPC's 5 years later. To close my review do not bother supporting Indie Stone, for I truly believe that high profile robbery that transpired years ago was the death of the "real" project zomboid. What we have now is an expensive tech demo.

It turns out that work just isn't worth it. Red Faction: Armageddon keeps basically nothing of what made Red Faction: Guerrilla so fun and swaps the big open world and destructible environment mayhem for a humdrum alien shooter restricted to caves. The Magnet Gun is a pretty sweet gimmick but is only as strong as the amount of debris made available to you. I purchased The Long Dark about a year ago, clocked in roughly an hour and didn't play it again for a year.
Since I've redownloaded, I'm greeted with enough content to warrant a review.
Upon starting a new game on The Long Dark (albeit only Sandbox mode available) you are plonked into a world, barron with snow, a glorious vista sprawls out before you in every direction as far as you can see, you are equipped with a few warm clothes, and not much else, my first thought was to find a building that might have materiels for crafting. Within 5 minutes I had found said building, raided the entirety, decontructed all the wooden frames I needed for firewood, gathered food, found a hatchet, a prybar and a light source.
Happily I began to explore the darker areas of the building with my new found lightsource, whilst having my head stuck in a metal container suddenly a shrill wolf howl peirces the air, horrifyingly, I realise I am unarmed.
Carefully I tread now, I round a corner and my fears are realised, a lone wolf (takes a little while before noticing me) begins to charge at me, I 180 spin and haul my chilly little cheeks back towards the door, the wolf nipping on my heels.
I throw myself at the exit and dont stop to turn around, I sprint as far and as fast as I can cramming energy bars and grape sodas down my gullet as I marathon for escape.
The wolf growls die down, I am alive, however, during this encounter, and how engaging it was, I didnt pay any attention to where I was going, I find myself now, in the midst of a growing snow storm, with only 3 hours of daylight remaining, genuine panic sets in as my field of vision becomes smaller and smaller until I am able to see only a few feet in front of me in all directions, here i began to feel truly lost.
I drudge ever onwards, my food supplies are sparse, my water is disapated and I am dehydrated and freezing at an alarming rate, risk of hypthermia sets in, I pick a direction and travel, sure that my game is over and this harsh environment has claimed me.
I am exhausted, through the snow and wind I think I can see a rippling red flag so make ground for that.
Under the flag is a wooden hut, I push for sanctuary, my condition reaching a critical level as I turn the door handle.
Inside are two stoves, here I am able to keep warm, melt snow for hydration, cook tins of meat I found earlier after crudly opening them with a hunting knife, I brew a cup of coffee, set the fire to a few bars and get into bed and drift uneasily into sleep.
This was my Day One in "The Long Dark" a truly unique and genuinely quite nerve racking experience.
None of the above is dramatised.
While the graphics are shaded, I feel this adds to the gritty, post-apocolyptic environment "The Long Dark" is trying to promote, the mechanics and well thought out crafting system are just about balanced enough to keep you engaging in the environment to survive and explore, after one or two days, you begin to plan your 12 hours of available daylight, and prioritise expiditions based on what immediate resources are paramount to your survival, that is of course, before you find a reliable source of food, water, heat, and a warm place to lay down and get some rest.
Overall I am very pleased with my return to "The Long Dark", this title is showing alot of potential, and I look forward to future updates from this developer.
EDIT: I'm no good with degrees.
