Awesome developers who are very active. I submitted on the forum a problem I was having and the very next day they had a patch fixing my issue, despite my issue not being a widespread issue by any strech of means.
Great concepts - Yes they take a lot of queue's from Terraria & Starbound but they add a significant twist that makes the game compelling and enjoyable. For example, combat in Terraria is very simple, swing a sword do damage, shoot a gun do damage, dash. In Planet Centauri you have a skill tree that allows you to learn a ton of new things which feels progressive.
Visuals - Some of the visuals are lackluster at best but the majority is very enthralling, sucking you into the world especially if you like games like terraria.
Performance - Runs like minecraft but better.
Cons (DUH DUH DUUUH)
Developers can be agressive in their marketing strategy and defend their IP w/o any thought to what others might think about that. This is a good/bad thing all at the same time. I have mad respect for a developer that loves what they're doing but everyone has an opinion and it's better to keep that to themselves. (Mom always told me, if you don't have something nice to say, don't say it at all.)
Items - I've watched the dev vLogs about how long it takes to create one animation (3+ HRS for a character animation O.O, WOW!) but in the games current state there isn't much diversity in the way of armor/weapons/sheields etc... most of which simply takes a ton of time to accomplish. I'm sure this caveat will be resolved upon release. They have plans to make some major changes in the coming patches up to release.
Visual Caveats - No in game cursor, UI needs an overhaul (Make it feel like it's part of the game plz.), a few animations could be a bit smoother such as items falling to the ground etc. Like I said above it takes a long time to craft the art you guys are putting into this game but it's the smallest of details that break the immersion w/o much effort.
I hope my review puts your mind at ease. This game is going to compete on the scale of Terraria and Starbound w/o a single doubt in my mind, I just have to be patient and wait. I will not be playing this game any further until the release, I've had my taste, and it tastes good. I'd rather wait for release and binge the game for 4 weeks straight than to burn myself out, that's how good it tasted.

I would honestly say that this game; whilst on the surface looks like a Terraria rip-off, and visually it is very similar to Terraria, is in my opinion in many ways an improvement on terraria.
There are several things in this game I prefer to Terraria:
1: Farming exists and adds another layer
2. The game spawns you in with actual help, not just a useless guide that falls down the first hole he sees.
3. There are quests that give you rewards
4. There is a somewhat safe zone where you won't just get mauled by mobs
5. The progression from surface to bottom of the world is much better. It eases in difficulty as opposed to Terraria where it's like suddenly everything is out to kill you after you dig a little.
6. Small improvements like eating a type of food for the first time raises your max XP
7. Much more straightforward crafting progession.
There are a few issues though:
1. Some big de-sync issues with multiplayer. The game host is the only one that can raid dungeons because the barriers that disappear when you complete a level only disappear for the game host.
2. There seems to be a point where you've gotten the best armour you can but you're still not good enough to do the next step. I haven't played past this point yet so I'm not sure what the next progression really is.

I don't know about other people but by focusing on the store page alone it was hard for me to understand exactly what was going on. So to set it more clearly:
There is only limited bullets with which to try and kill as many zombies as possible on the level by setting of chain reactions. There's different zombies that each does something different when killed. The zombies move around alot, so you must time the shot perfectly while also considering what zombie to shoot.
For example the normal zombie will only explode when shot, damaging other zombies around it. Not all zombies explode, based on what the other zombies are they will either explode if a normal zombie, melt and create a shortly timed acid pool, fire a bullet in the direction they're facing, or run and explode when they collide with something. These are only half the different zombies and as can be seen you must also take into account the facing of the zombies. As the levels get harder the zombies get more health, so it's better to shoot a weak zombie and have it's effect chain to other zombies.
There's also upgrades that allows you to increase your ammo and the potency of zombies when killed. So this makes for a very fun little game where you must think before you act, time it perfectly and try to kill as many zombies as possible with the limited ammo.
The levels are short and fun and alot of replay value as you buy upgrades and try to reach the 100% zombies killed mark!

It's fun to see dozens of zombies of all kinds randomly splatter in a massive chain reaction, but the operating word here is 'randomly'. The entire game is based on luck, mostly, while the skill part consists of your ability to wait until the remaining, randomly moving zombies that you failed to kill in the randomly occuring chain reaction bunch up the way you want them to, which is rarely. Can't recommend.
This game is based more on luck than skill...

This is a flash-style game in the line of those old websites with minigames. It remimds me (in its own style) to Infectonator but in reverse. Very funny and fresh to play, but 4,99€ is a bit too much. Season sales are the best moments to get it.

+
* Addictive
* Fun
* Easy gameplay, works well with mouse
* Different zombie characters with different killing abilities (explode, scream, fire bullets, electrocute, melt)
* Runs smoothly on my very-old-laptop-with-WindowsVista
* Toggle colorblind mode - easier to see the different zombie characters
* Toggle health mode on zombies, you don't need to hover your mouse over *every* zombie in order to see which one is most likely to get killed by one shot
* 100 stages
* Very retro inspired, I like the zombie roars and screams
* Encouraging you to find the longest chain of exploding zombies - snipe out the right one and you can wipe out the whole stage with one shot - it's very fulfilling to see the bullets bounce
-
* The randomness of bulletspreading when you shoot a cop/soldier zombie - never rely on them to take out others if you only have a couple of zombies left and one bullet yourself, their bullets bounce however they like AND the zombie often turns a completely different direction exactly once you shoot it
* Some zombies stop exploding past stage 3 or whatever, they only go "poof" and that's it - shoot the wrong one and you only take out just that one instead of 30
Overall a very fun and well done game, I'd recommend it to everyone except those being achievement hoarders and complaining about the 20 prestiges you have to do in order to complete the game 100% - it will probably take more time than you're willing to spend with it, no matter how fun it is. No, I don't have the last achievement, but I still enjoy playing the game occasionally, but yeah it does bother me just a little bit...

Hue is a slow paced game but one that has a ton of potential; when you first start you're thrown into the pit with a grayed out world with the backstory of Hue's mom that is lost within the world she constantly guides in the right direction but it's Hue's job to bring the color back into the world, although I am not a big fan of puzzle adventure games at all i thouroughly enjoyed Hue; it mized tough strenuous puzzles with amazing backstory that keeps the player on its toes; i wouldn't be surprised at all if this game gains more accolades as the time went on.
and the rest of the review:

I've only been into the indie games for few years now and I have to say Hue is easily one of my new favorite puzzle-platformers.
You play as Hue. As the story goes Hue's mother is a scientist who, with the help of another scientist named Dr. Grey create a ring called the Annular Spectrum. The ring is used to alter the perception of color. Unfortunately Dr. Grey gets paranoid of the rings power and Hue's mothers obsession with the project. Dr. Grey steals the ring and destroys it. This accidentally sending Hue's mother into a shade-like area making her invisible. This is where your story begins. You have to find all shards of the ring, put it back together and find your mother. Throughout your adventure you get to collect letters left behind by your mother. These letters explain what happened to her leading up to the accident.
The art style of the game is beautiful and full of color. The game might start out black and white but as you collect new colors, the game really begins to fill out and looks amazing. The level designs are right up there with the art style. They looked great and are very creative. Everything down to the way the levels look, to the way they were layed out, to the platforming and how the games unique color changing mechanic was incorporated into everything couldn't have been done better.
The soundtrack to Hue was surprisingly large. The steam page says that there are 30 tracks in total. Most of the songs I remember hearing were very calm and soothing, which was very helpful for later on in the game when the puzzles start to get a little harder. Even in the beginning, the sound track to Hue made for a very casual feeling game. I personally didn't find Hue to be a casual game though. Maybe at the start yes but later on you are tested on your puzzle solving skills. The sound effects were very realistic. You get to hear a wide range of things from running waterfalls, to falling bolders, to flaring fires, to the creeking sounds of gates opening and even the simplistic sounds of moving a box. All of it sounded real.
The Good
- Controller compatable.
- No crashes or frame drops throughout the entire game.
- Awesome voice acting.
- Great story and build up with narroration from the mother. Could have been a very generic story if not for the extra explanation from the letters you collect.
- Narroration made me involved with the characters. Both Hue and his mother.
- Amazing controls. Responded very well. With one minor issue. (In "The Bad" Section)
- Very unique and fun puzzle solving mechanics.
- Difficulty progression is great. Later puzzles get more challenging and really test your problem solving.
- Fun and challenging platforming mixed in with their unique game mechanics.
- New ways to solve puzzles added throughout the game so the puzzles don't get repeatative.
- Collectable beakens for completionist that you can later go back and collect.
- 4 to 5 hours long.
- Great conclusion to the story.
The Bad
- No replay ability outside of achievements and collecting beacons.
- Colors didn't always register if I tried to change them quickly.
- Price 16.99, A little high for my liking. Personally more around the 10.99.
Final Thoughts
Considering I went into Hue expecting a copy and paste like a lot of other games in this genre, I was more then impressed. I completely recommend Hue. I would prefer a lower cost but to be honest the games story and overal gameplay experience would be worth the buy.
If you're interested -

+ The gameplay is fun and very unique. You have the power to change the color of the background. This will turn some things in the foreground invisable which will allow you to pass through them. You will have to change colors frequently to avoid obstacles while doing some light platforming to complete a series of puzzles.
+ Great narration by a girl who sets up the story of how she found a "impossible" color and is trapped in a unseen void and askes you to save her. She talks to you through various notes she has typed out and creates some very interesting theories whether or not we as people even see the same colors as others, and about colors not seen by the human eye.
+ Nice relaxing soundtrack
+ A surprising amount of content
+ Great level pacing and variety that keeps the game feeling fresh the entire time.
+ I really enjoyed the minimalistic sort of black and white art style with little details that are appealing to see spread out through the background of levels.

What can I say about this game....
My main comparison is to Darkest Hour - a mod to Red Orchestra. I bought this game to replace that amazing mod. I have 400 hours on DH. I dont see why you would play RO2 over Darkest Hour.
Features RO2 has that DH does not:
♥♥♥♥♥♥ Cover system. Main use for it is blind firing. Otherwise youre just stuck to a wall and sometimes stick out more than if you werent in the cover system at all
Campaign mode. Sort of cool, but ultimately pointless when it comes to gameplay.
zeroing. Good, but not that important. Most engagements are up close anyways or you could just aim a little bit up.
Checking Magazines/reloading single bullets for a bolt. Good. Pretty much the only thing that matters that was added.
Bandage system: honestly pretty pointless. buggy and sometimes youll start the animation but wont finish it and cant start it again so you die. most shots just one hit you anyways.
spawning on squad leader: could be okay, but pretty lame in a "realistic" game. a lot of the time, squad leads are dumb and die or put you in a really bad place to spawn anyway.
Progression system: Ro2 decided to jump on the modern fps bandwagon where you need a progression system to keep players. So now you have a rank, which is fine as your total rank doesnt do too much. What isnt fine is that you need to get kills with weapons to unlock attachments. Meaning unlike in DH, you cant just equip a bayonet. It either spawns on the gun or doesnt. A real soldier always has a bayonet and can attach it and detach it depending on the circumstances. You shouldnt be penalized for being new because you havent gotten enough kills to earn a bayonet or scope or drum mag.
What does DH do better than RO2?
Maps. They feel WAY better. Their layouts make sense. Spawns: You dont spawn in ♥♥♥♥♥♥ locations where you can be spawncamped like in RO2. So many times ive been suppressed while i spawned, died where i spawned, or walked a few feet and died. People know where the spawns are and just camp them. The objective could be 200m away, but it doesnt matter. In DH spawns arent always one dimensional. You could spawn in a halftrack on one map. Or spawn close to the objective. They're placed better. You dont get killed immediately. The quality is just much higher.
Aiming. When you aim in Ro2, you dont move your camera like in a traditional shooter; you mainly move your gun. This makes aiming way harder for snap shooting because your gun is moving and not you. Both games have the same hipfire system, where you move the gun and the bullet comes out of the barrel instead of in the middle of your screen. But when you aim a gun, you put it close to your face and aim down the sights. You can move your body and acquire targets fast. it feels sloppy the way ro2 has it work.
Supression. It feels more useful in Darkest Hour. It doenst just make it hard to see by making your screen black and white like somehow youre colorblind by getting shot at and making it blurry. It jerks you around making it hard to return fire.
More vehicles and tools: Mortars. Halftracks. Jeeps. Many different tanks. German tanks felt better, but the Americans had M1 Garands, giving a contrast to each side without them being blatantly one sided. If you want to play Russian vs German or Commonwealth vs German, those exist on certain maps, as many RO1 maps were ported.
Community seems way better, but I guess that point isnt a solid one.
And it's a free mod for Red Orchestra 1. Which I luckily got from a video card purchase. You dont have to pay $20 to get Rising storm on top of Red Orchestra 2 just to get a different front of the war. You dont have to go through progression systems. You dont have an intrusive hud that just feels wrong. Honestly, the DH spawning system isnt that much better, but it was executed better than RO2. Obviously, something like Squad's spawning system would be more realistic, as you couldnt spawn right next to an enemy on a squad leader since rallies are destroyed with an enemy coming too close. Or having FOBs for bases to spawn at that are different depending what squad leader you have in a game since they can be placed almost everywhere.
Give Darkest Hour a go. If you want a more realistic, larger feel to the game, Squad is good. Once Post Scriptum is finished, that'll be your WW2 Squad.

I would love to give a game neutral review but since I can't do that I will go with negative for now and will be more than happy to change it as things improve.
Game has been out for a while and we are seeing big shift in reviews scores over recent few months. I would like to explain to all new to the game and mostly to developers them self why is it happening. I have recorded video that deals with that issue but if you would rather read than watch I understand and you may want to check transcript below.
To truly understand what what is going on lets talk about what Early Access is and yes I know you are aware of it but humor me and listen for just few seconds so we are all on the same page.
According to steam: Early Access game is not complete and may or may not change further. If you are not excited to play this game in its current state, then you should wait to see if the game progresses further in development. I agree that you should not buy game just based on promises but lets be honest we don’t just buy games hoping that development will stop.
Lets look at promises Project Zomboid makes to their fans.
Two major features are yet to be implemented into the game, both of which are currently in full-time development each with dedicated full-time developer support:
NPCs and Vehicles
We want to have all this in the can this year. However, we tend to avoid ETAs because Early Access development in particular is often filled with unknowns and we want to ensure we get these highly anticipated features right.
With that in mind we can imagine customers that buy this game. People bought into a product mostly 3 years ago when it was released on steam it was beginning times of Early Access and Zombie games were at their prime and thanks to huge success of minecraft so were survival and crafting games. Most people bought it for those 2 reasons survival and zombies. NPCs and Vehicles were nice additions that were to be delivered at some point in not too distanced future.
Project Zomboid is perfect survival game it progressed nicely over last 3 years and according to most of hardcore fans on reddit they are all overwhelmingly fine waiting longer for other features and happy with development progress. I have not seen a single negative comment on reddit about a state of a game.
Project zomboid released on Steam Early access on 8th of November 2013 with Build 25 and is currently in Build 35 on average game features 4 updates a year and stayed consistent in that. Game sold slightly over 700 000 copies. And in the last 2 weeks 27 000 people had played the game that means that less than 4% of game owners still plays the game. I would say not bad for 3 year old game if it was over and done but not so great for game still in development. There is much smaller influx of new players to the game and most of a game owners have forgotten about it or moved to other products.
Game is qute rich in content has good repeatability and there is many players with 100s of hours put into the game. Overall I feel that if project zomboid never made promises of NPCs and Vehicles they could finished development today and have a decent product that would be satisfying to customers.
However they did make those promises. And here we come to a source of recent surge of negative reviews on steam. I think developers overestimated what they will be able to deliver in a timely manner. This is not a great problem at the end of a day it is part of development process sometimes you underestimate how consuming new feature will be. What you do you either cut that feature from a game or readjust release date. Trap with early access is once feature is promised to customers it’s almost impossible to cut it out without outcry of people accusing developers of scam and lies. For better or worse Indie STone are stuck with features they promised to deliver.
It has been however 3 years and some of customers are getting impatient. Those people bring their complaints to forums, steam discussion and reddit. Anyone who ever worked in retail knows that unhappy customers can be right ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Complains range from desperation to right down abuse.
And here is where Indie Stone fails the most. Unhappy or even entitled customer is still customer. It is vital to treat that customer with respect and ignore angry language. You wouldn’t expect someone at retail store to tell you that you are just pathetic troll and should be grateful for what you have so why do community managers do just that I have no idea.
After reading many if not most of recent reviews one things is present in almost every one of them.The Indie Stone are extremely bad at communication with their fans.
I went to the forums and read few of responses to criticism I have seen from community moderators ranged from ignorant to dam right rude. you can see just few examples of responses devs and community managers give to the people on a screen right now. Seriously one would have impression they talk to 13 year old kid not a professional Community Manager. Every John or Jane Doe at your local retail store knows that offended customer is lost customer. Community manager job is to keep community nice and friendly, making fun of your customers, taunting them and abusing your power is exactly opposite of that. If they were my employees I would fire them on a spot reading those responses.
People feel that they feedback in discussions is limited, they feel disrespected and that what is valid complain in their mind falls into deaf ears. What do you think customer who was offended does? They use the only tool they have that developers have no control over. They go to steam and write angry review. Some negative reviews come from people with 100’s of hours put into a game. Those are your most loyal customers, guide writers and community influencers. They clearly love the game but because communication with dev team is almost non existent, their post get deleted or they receive stupid comments by community managers, they feel that this is the only tool that will force devs to respond.
And it will work if game comes out on steam as Project Zomboid 1.0 with mixed reviews from Early Access it will not sell it will hurt developers and they know it. Rather that continue to argue with people Indie Stone should have hard talk with their community Managers teach them how to respond to complaints with respect and hope they can turn this around before it’s too late.
So what’s the final verdict in here you may ask. In my personal Opinion Project Zomboid is great game worth the price at it’s current state and if you are looking for zombie experience with focus on survival aspect more than mindless slaughter you will greatly enjoy this game.
However if you are like me fan of Early Access because you want to influence the development process and take active part in shaping the game future and be seen more as a partner than customer to developers unfortunately until Indie Stone changes its ways you are better off looking elsewhere.

First of all there is nothing at all wrong with taking an existing formula and innovating based on it. People complaining about this being a "terraria clone/ripoff" are out of touch with reality. Most games are inspired by something else, terraria itself used to be critised as being a 2D minecraft clone. At this point I'd consider 2D sandbox a genre in of itself, one that terraria pioneered, and there are a lot of games in this genre that take the formula and add their own take to it, many that are worth playing including this one.
This game takes everything I love about terraria and makes it better by innovating it, adding welcome RPG elements, polishing the controls and interface, and adding a ton of features. The interface is very user friendly, and the game definitely has its own feel and charm as well. It is at the moment in early access so it doesn't have the content of terraria, but it definitely is not short on content and things to do. If they devs add a workshop, then there will be even more potential content for the game.
I'd recommend this an an easy buy for anyone who has played terraria and enjoys it, as you will get the same kind of enjoyment with this game. If you think this is just a "terraria ripoff" then nothing is stopping you from going and playing terraria.

At first glance, Planet Centauri appears to be just another clone of Terraria or Starbound. Although, once you dive into the wonderful world that is Planet Centauri, you discover that Permadeath has created something *inspired* by those titles formerly mentioned, yet something unique enough to stand alone on its own.
The sprite art and animation is absolutely brilliant. I can't stress that enough. In fact, Planet Centauri's developers have a YouTube channel where they show off their animation skills, and it really is something to behold.
The gameplay mechanics have improved significantly since it's early alpha phase. The combat can be very confusing at first, since they don't really teach you how to use the special attacks you purchase with "souls". However, once you grasp the combat system and have it down, the real fun begins.
The world is filled with awesome monsters. Some cliche, but they've put their own spin on them (ie. zombies = Night Crawlers). Every once in awhile you'll run into a GIANT form of one of these monsters/creatures, and they're more likely to drop more loot/souls.
Also, it is possible to capture & tame (and sometimes RIDE) almost every monster (AND even the T-Rex Boss!!). You are also able to craft the "transformation table" which allows you to *morph* into these creatures, which allows you to fly and use special attacks.
The developers, Permadeath, are pretty consistent with their updates, which is very important to me when I purchase any Early Access game. Their latest update, the Technology Update, offers a brand new biome (presented as a new alien world), new monsters, new boss, guns and more.
There is so much potential for Planet Centauri, especially if you wath their video on IndieGoGo you see all these items and features that have not been implemented yet (skateboard, motorcycle, boats, wings, robots, etc.).
This is a game that I truly believe in, and I cannot wait to see what Permadeath does next.

The popularly accepted theory that Jazz stemmed from a simple combination of African rhythms and European harmony is in need of a little revision. Both African and European rhythms were employed. African music supplied the strong underlying beat (absent in most European music), the use of polyrhythms, and the idea of playing the melody separate from or above the beat. European music provided formal dance rhythms. Combined, these rhythms give Jazz its' characteristic swing. Likewise, the harmonies and musical ideas of both continents are present, the blue notes derived from the pentatonic scale, "call and response" and unconventional instrumental timbres of African music together with "conventional" harmonies and, most important, the formal structure of European music. The multiplicity of ethnic, cultural and musical conditions needed to spawn Jazz was thus unique to the United States, and specifically to New Orleans. The necessary philosophical impetus for Jazz, i.e. , democracy and freedom of individual expression supported by group interaction, are also American institutions.

Super Furball is a 2D action platformer in where some dude in a tank blows up your house and a statue of a furball comes to life to take revenge. The areas near him are filled with other evil black furballs that want to kill you. To defend yourself you have an energy gun with unlimited ammo to blast your way past your foes. Enemies also have energy guns so it becomes a duel of who shoots first and is able to land a hit three times that will prevail. That becomes much harder to pull off when the enemies have the high ground and you are forced to jump to their height to land your shoots. Luckily both you and them can only shoot horizontally so you need to be right in front of another to shoot them. Hidden within the levels are a few different more power guns like a plasma thrower which works like a flame thrower and a Repeater that fires three bullets in a single shot. You will have to be careful when firing with these as they have very limited ammo and will disappear rather quickly.
The levels have plenty of endless pits that will spell your doom if you are unlucky enough to fall into one. There are other hazards scattered around like bouncing mines, missiles being randomly shot from a turret and mines randomly floating in the water. Your little furball has the ability to swim without the fear of drowning so you can take your time navigating underwater. Red gems are everywhere in the level and collecting a life grants you an extra life though they are often placed in very dangerous locations. This is not an easy game by any means and will have your head if you play recklessly. It will help a lot to keep your eyes open for any secrets that can be found like extra lives, guns or just letting you skip a difficult area. Once you finish the first mission you will be taken to the main overworld where you can walk around and go to the next mission or replay previous ones. The next level is where the bad begins and I was unable to continue past the second level due to a glitch.
Second levels starts off well enough and starts to ramp up the difficulty which is all well and good. Unfortunately once you reach a place with a snake pillar there is no way to progress any further. I'm guessing that pillar is supposed to go down but after multiple times retrying that level it never did and I was not able to play past the second mission. I was not able to play the game to give a detailed review and I do not know things like if the repetitive, slightly annoying music gets any better, if the levels are varied and how the boss fights are. From what I've played it did seem like a fun game with solid controls but I obviously can't recommend a game by playing two levels alone. I don't know if this is a common issue though looking through the Steam forums it does seem like the game has other problems like crashing and being unable to start which I have not experienced. It did not seem like a bad game but I will not recommend it due to this and would advise that buyers beware.

Unexpectedly fun casual puzzle game. The gameplay consists of a rather simple point and click control mechanic, where the goal is to create chain reactions of violently dying zombies. The levels are made of varying types of randomly spawned zombies placed within a rather open arena artificially inhibited by obstacles. The goal is to clear as many of them as possible with the limited ammo and properties said zombies have. Additionally, there are upgrade paths which enhance favourable characteristics of the enemies and the player for easier perfect completions of levels.
Since it's a PC port from a mobile platform, the on-screen menu system is a bit awkward, and the graphics look like they're from pre-millennium era, which would have been forgivable as a stylistic choice, but most likely is a side effect of poor upscaling.
Replayability-wise, getting 100% on all 100 levels amounts to about 6h-10h of playtime, including replaying some of the stages after getting all of the upgrades. However, the achievement suggesting fully finishing the game for 20 times is down-right ridiculous.
All in all, considering the game has trading cards, it's worth picking up for it's addicting gameplay and relatively cheap price, especially if it's on a sale.

Project Zomboid is the game that got me playing games again. Having owned the game since 2011, I've watched Project Zomboid grow from little more than a 10-15 minute "coffee-break" game one that supports dozens and hundreds of hours of play, solo or MP.
PZ nails the Brooks/Romero zombie survival experience, from massive hordes visible in the world to the crippling isolation and sense of hopelessness characters feel within that universe. Zombies are slow shamblers -- weak and easy overcome by themselves, but overwhelming en masse. There are no "special" zombies here -- and no need for them, with an engine that can support hundreds of entities on screen without noticeable lag (though once it gets up to 2000 or so, the Java-based engine stumbles).
Buy if the game being feature incomplete for another year or two doesn't phase you. The game's main weakness right now it's lack of human and animal NPCs, as well as vehicles. Much of the included systems are rather bare-bones and need additional content / balancing to really work well together.  It'd say it's about 70% complete at this point.
Though the stable build takes 2-3 months on average to update, the IWBUMS branch tends to update weekly.
I'm sure my grandchildren will write a better more detailed review but, until the game actually gets out of limbo, I can't recommend this.

This is one of my all time favorite fantasy 4x games.  It's basically Civ set in a rich, fantasy world meshed with an RPG heroes type system that allows both units and champions to level up, get better and gain skills.  I've put WAY too many hours into this and am testing their newest game - Sorcerer King.

Hands down my favorite 4X game.
The art, music and overall aesthetic resonate like crazy with me for some reason, even though it's far from the "best" looking game in the genre.
The game mechanics make more sense to me in this one than in any other 4X game, too. For instance, I love how a stack's damage is calculated as "individual unit damage x number of units" so that killing some of the units in a stack actually makes the stack less effective. This makes the choice of who to target a little more interesting, especially when you factor in their different powers.
This is also the only 4X game where I actually value the ability to design units. You can unlock some seriously powerful artifacts through the research tree, and along with unit-boosting city enchantments and a whole slew of interesting custom unit traits, there are lots of fun possibilities.
Designing your own ruler is also very rewarding since this game does a great job with giving you cool powers that actually matter. For instance, one of my all-time favorite faction traits is "Beastlord" which allows you to play the risk/reward game of converting beasts that you fight on tactical map. Few things are more enjoyable for me than successfully taming a huge bear and bringing it into battle with me. Bears (and a few other select creatures) have a "Maul" ability where they get to keep attacking as long as each hit lands successfully. It's not uncommon to have your bear maul a high level enemy unit to death before it can even hit back. Combine Beastlord with a ruler that specializes in the summoning part of the mage skilltree, and now you have entire armies consisting of both natural creatures and horrifying creatures from the underworld. This is really ♥♥♥♥ing fun.
I also love that "Essence" is one of the resources that you need to consider when placing new cities on the overworld map. For each essence on the city's tile, you can cast an enchantment on the city that boosts certain things like mana or production, or something even more interesting like boosting the power of units trained in that city, causing enemies to be stricken with fear when trying to attack the city, etc. It's fantastic!
I could blab on and on and on about how much I love this game. I know my thoughts are scattered, but I honestly don't feel the need to put together a comprehensive review on this one. Hopefully the few things I've pointed out here will be appropriately indicative of how great this underrated game is.

I expected something similar to contra. Old hardcore game. The issue with this game and why it fails to capture previous magic is quite simple:
1) Terrible controls. With no mouse aim 4 direction aiming feels restrictive. Especially in the game where reflexes and precision is required. You die from one hit and terrorists tend to spray battlefield with bullets. Game quickly devolves into exploiting since it is impossible to beat it "fair".
2) Random characters. I mean seriously? Who thought it is a good idea to put a completely unique character at random in the game with one hit kills? Random characters completely mess me up and makes game feel like a chore. Like it is trying to actively screw with you. They could at least given us a roster if they wanted for random badasses approach.
3) One life system. It is bad. In the contra you could continue even if hit. It promoted high skill gameplay without pulling you out of action. Furthermore, it gave you a chance to react. In this game it is completely different. You have to exploit dumb AI since you cannot fight it. It does not feel fair nor entertaining.
Due to these following reasons I do believe that developers had failed to deliver. It is pity really, since I liked their presentation and I really want game which would capture contra's magic back.

I really like this new indie genre of games that has really shocked the game developer establishment. You no longer need to be a AAA game developer to produce something that resonates with large audiences, and The Long Dark is No exception.
The Long Dark in it's current state is all about surviving longer for each game. For this you need to watch your body's status. You need to hydrate, eat and sleep. Since you are trying to survive in and endless winter body temperature is important. To manage this you need to melt snow and then boil it to get drinking water, gather or hunt for food and then cook it, and scavage the landscape to find more equipment such as weapons, matches, clothes.
Hunting is two-folded; it brings you food but also material to construct new equipment. Same goes for those things you gather when you go scavaging. You can break down most things you collect to pieces to construct something you need.
The Long Dark is a really free game only restricted by your vital signs. But in order to survive you need to find routines for each day, plan your sleep, food and water intake accordingly. And every action you take has a reaction. If you shoot a deer, extracting mest, skin and guts will probably get you to risk dehydration, starvation and hypothermia which could leave you with having to rest in a shelter when you need to collect things, and if it goes far enough kills you. But leaving the carcass out in the open will make it decompose. In this you need to take into account day and night cycles. So you need to harvest everything rather quickly. It's a weigh off in terms of what you are willing to risk to survive.
Also you need to repair things collected and constructed. If your clothes for example becomes worn down they will function less good, and soon ultimately break down completely and you can only harvest material from them. Same thing goes for all things collected including food.
You can't carry everything you collect so you need to find a good place, for example house with a bed, workbench and a stove, where you can sleep, cook food, store and construct things. If you can find food, shelter and build up a supply site with reserves, this game becomes interesting and allows for more scouting and more freedom.
It might not have the best graphics but The Long Dark has revolutionary ideas and unique systems for surviving. It's gameplay is addictive and I can only say I'm looking forward to the story mode. I'm just looking forward to the day when developers of large scale open world games take a similar approach. Think of ArmA style game with survival elements as well.
This game is highly recommended if you like indie games and and games that guarantee problem-solving! I'm just looking forward to Hinterland taking a similar approach on another climate zone!

I'm doing my review a bit early, despite not fully playing it through as of yet. Normally I like playing a game to it's completion before reviewing it, but because of several negative reviews that I read prior to buying this early release, I feel I need to do one to counteract a lot of trolling that has been going on.
Before I get into the game itself, let me explain a few things for people who do not fully know what an early access game is. This may change your view hopefully in the future and cut down on bad unwarrented feedbacks  not just this title got, but other titles as well.
Early access games, are games that are in the early stages of production. Unlike the olden days where you would see an advertisement in the magazine or demo included in a game where you see an interesting game you really like and have to wait months to several years to be completed, then wait to hopefully nab it in the store, to find out there is a 6 month waiting list and wait even longer to hopefully get your own copy, you end up getting a partial started product that is no where complete, but at least playable until the game is fully produced.
Early release games are done now a days for many multiple reasons. It gives the writer an idea on how popular and wanted their game is, plus brings in some income to keep the lights on and even possibly bring in more people to get the finished product out faster. Many a times these incomplete games are advertised with features that plan to be included, or were but had to be taken out because there were too many problems, and had to be worked on more. These companies are not trying to fool us into buying their products with false advertising. They most of the time are trying to show us what they have already included, or hopefully put in at  a later date which is also why the game is very cheap. Lot of times, the final product has to  actually be purchased again under a similar name and the ones who helped to keep the lights on get a discounted copy. Sometimes yeah, we get a company like with edge of space who takes the money and splits. Those companies, you report for adandoning a title. Especially when you see the distributer trying to still leach money off it in sales yet not life a finger to fix it. Putting up a review the title has been adandoned, when it has in fact not been, not only hurts the people who put money into the game already, it hurts others who are waiting for the finished product because false information was put up and we didn't want to get burned yet again.
I originally passed this title up because of a review with 22 people who agreed the game was abandoned. It wasn't till another pointed out that this was not true and to check the forums, which I did and found out that this awsome game has not only not been adondoned, it has been getting updates, slow I might add, but updates non the less plus dev actively replying. I talked with them and to my shock, they know about the fake negative reviews. They just choose not to respond to them, and heck, that's their choice. They said it's the buyers in the end who will get their name out. Unfortunately, many hit the not interested button and will never see this game again unless a friend tells them like myself. So before you do that with this title, look in the forums and see for yourself. Early access games are cheap and you need to understand, if your buying it for like $5.00, this is not going to be the final product and its going to have bugs. You most likely will have to pay again as well, but also not full price. Any decent company, and most are give their supporters a deal on the final product. That being said, now for the review:
Planet Centauri is a sandbox/adventure/rpg/build it type of game similar to Dig Or Die, Terraria, and Spacebound. Not all the features you see in the video are in the game yet, or have been temporarly taken out until bugs have been weeded out. The game is fully playable, and rarely crashes. The quests are fun to do yet a little confusing due to the totorial needing work as their have been many changes and updates since it was first made from what the dev told me. (Not in those exact words, but close to it)
Planet Centauri is not a rip off of any of the above games. It has it's own unique feel and play to it and has gotten my attention to the point I am writing this review early.
You control a character who crashes onto a planet. Not sure if it's my driving or some chicken cut me off in some insane road/sky rage incident. The fact is, I'm on this planet and need to survive!
The object just like the other games, start off by learning the controls, building shelter to avoid getting killed by the monster spawn. Unlike past games where you have to rush to get this done, or die by nightfall, the game doesn't throw stuff at you forcing you to rush and not enjoy the game. You can go your own pace and even go several days before you get your first home built without the worry of dying. The game only throws spawn like that at  you when it sees your prepaired for it, and that happens as you level up and build better items.
Planet Centauir's building system is unique in it's own. As you find new ores, you can build better tools. Build better tools, you gain exp to build better weapons and armor up which also helps in higher health and stamina.
Im still trying to figure out the magic system. As of right now, there is no character type you have to choose. You just equipt what you want, how you want to be what you want. Simple as that.
Designing your character is quite simple to, and you have a really good choice of colors for both male and female characters. Unfortunately, the only 3 things you can color right now are the hair, eyes, and skin. No choice for clothing, at least for now.
The game gets updates several times a year. The dev just choose to not to reply to reviews and are only active in the forums like I said above.
At this time there is no dedicated server program, but there is a server program built into the game to host multiplayer as long as your logged in.
Crafting is pretty simple, there is a menu that shows what each item is, and how much is needed so non of that having to guess what items in what order makes what.
Game just got an update today, so will update this review soon as I see what is new, what has been fixed, broken, removed, yadda yadda yadda.
This early release game, is definately worth the risk of investing in. It took a lot to pull me away from the game just to do a review for it.

I recommend this game if you really, really love any and all third-person shooters and/or anything in the Red Faction setting whatsoever; If that's all your looking for it fits the bill well. The weapon selection is good, hit detection and overall control is solid, it is an entirely functional TPS that delivers the essentials well. And if you really like the Red Faction IP, well... It's set on Mars and uses the storyline, as well as the spiffy building destruction system.
However, if you're looking for more of Red Faction Guerrilla's open-world gameplay, or just want something more than competently executed ultra-linear corridor shooting, this isn't a game I'd recommend. To be entirely clear, it does what it does well, it just... doesn't do all that much, at least compared to what you probably expect based on its predecessor or maybe just newer shooters in general. Unfortunately, this game is an absolutely linear set of hallways with occasional larger rooms, for all intents and purposes. You never have a choice of where to go or what to do, backtracking is minimal at best, you just keep going forward and shooting more of either basic armed human enemies or bug-like aliens. To be clear, I'm not saying all games must be full-on open world by any means, but, for example, having town hubs where you get to choose from a handful of missions would have been nice.
Sometimes you get to use a vehicle, but even then it's a linear trip through levels designed specifically for vehicles. Which does provide some variety, but having a powerful walking tank, for example, doesn't seem as cool when it can only be used in maps designed for only it. In Red Faction Guerrilla, the design was open to being on-foot or having vehicles, which meant a vehicle was an actual improvement over the minimum the game was designed around, which made them feel like meaningful power-ups. Tanks in tank levels only aren't really upgrades at all.
And speaking of upgrades, the game does have an upgrade system, but they aren't generally all that exciting. Overall, the power progression feels more like taking the handicaps off your character than making your character more powerful. Still, when it's all said and done you do get more fun and interesting abilities than you ever got in the previous game, so that's an improvement at least.
And speaking of improvements, you also get much more fun ways to break all the many, many destructible buildings this time around, so that's nice. The magnet gun makes demolishing buildings a breeze, and you get a quickly recharging force blast attack that tears through structures, in addition to the ol' sledgehammer being a little more powerful. (And of course, there are plenty of guns that blow stuff up too.) However, while breaking stuff finally became reasonably fun, this game's change in structure means you ironically have much less need to tear it all down in the first place. Some mission objectives do need you take down structures, but not exactly a lot, and never in any particular hurry. So while this game gives you the destructive tools you'll wish had been in Red Faction Guerrilla, it doesn't have Guerrilla's need to tear down entire military bases, or to do it in a hurry. We finally got the really cool can openers, but without the cans that made you want them in the first place.
Also, maybe this is a really personal gripe, but the ammo you can hold at once is MUCH more limited than what's laying around. So in a fight, you can easily empty a gun entirely with plenty more monsters to go, but between battles you'll leave tons of ammo behind. That combination of always either having too much or too little really bugs me, if I'm running out, it should be because I took it all and used it all. Not because I merely used the small amount I could carry out of the huge amount I left in the last room.
And as long as I'm potentially nitpicking: While it mostly has all the configuration options you'd expect of a PC game, it doesn't include any options for increasing the very narrow default field of view. Luckily, there's a fan-made fix out there, otherwise it would have been a much bigger problem. Still, the game should have the option built-in, that's one of the few flaws that makes the game feel cheap, as opposed to merely bland.
So overall, it's a well-made , but very straightforward bare bones third-person shooter. If I could give games a neutral "okay" vote I would have, but since I'm limited to an absolute yes or no, I can't say Red Faction Armageddon is bad enough not to recommend it. So that just leaves recommending it, because it delivers what it does well enough, it just doesn't really do all that much. It's a good execution of an unfortunately simple, uninteresting game design, I recommend it as halfheartedly as I possibly can.

So, I had the opportunity to try this on a free weekend, and I was enjoying it quite a bit until I ran into a couple of bugs that resulted in my being unable to progress.
The bugs in question seem to be collision or pathfinding in nature. One involves a cross shaped room, where if you place a module it can prevent you moving past and, if your character is close to it when it deploys, can cause the character to get stuck and be unable to move even after you destroy the module. Loading and reloading will allow you to move again and resolves the pathfinding problem, which would be a little irritating but overall a small issue, however I encountered a problem with the enemy pathfinding that caused them to get stuck inbetween rooms and due to this, you can't save and quit.
I ran into this scenario 3 times when I was around 3/4s of the way through the game causing me to waste about an hour to an hour and a half of my time altogether. Because of this I do not recommend purchasing this game, although I may revise my opinion in 6-12 months when they, hopefully, patch it and if I find it on sale for a few dollars. There's a bunch of stuff online about how this game isn't as good as it's predecessor, Red Faction Guerilla. From my perspective, that simply isn't true. I admittedly have a somewhat unusual point of view, since I played Armageddon first, but the improvements to the central mechanics of this series mean there's really no going back. In Guerilla, you can destroy just about anything in a variety of interesting ways based on the actual structure of whatever it is you're destroying. In Armageddon, this degree of endlessly entertaining destruction is maintained, but it's just as easy to REPAIR those items, even if they're damaged the first time you see them. Guerilla is also an open world game, whereas Armageddon is quite linear, but while I usually appreciate open world games, I guess Guerilla is old enough now that it just seems...empty, outdated, and boring. It took me about 12 hours to finish the main campaign of Armageddon, and while it's a much shorter game than Guerilla, I wasn't bored at any point. It left me wanting more, which led to the relative disappointment that was Guerilla.
note: This review was originally written to warn new buyers that the games save system had been broken by an update from valve (the game stopped being able to create new save files and crashed when trying to do so, immediately after a steam update, and the last update to the game itself had been some time beforehand). This issue has since been fixed, so I deleted my rant from the beginning of the review.

For anyone who has ever played Commander Keen or the Apogee DOS platformers, that is basically what Super Furball is.  A skilled player can complete the game on the hardest difficulty level in less than three hours.  The levels are well designed, and it's a good bit of fun but the game lacks replay value.  Also the Game Over screen looks cheaply made.  A good effort for a small team.

I will say this: The game entertained me enough to 100% it on the hardest skill, which took roughly two hours. Yes, it's that short, which is one of the primary reasons I can't strongly recommend it.
The visuals are soft and colorful 16-bit graphics which I can't fault much, though the character designs are awful, since they're basically all circles with hands and feet. Controls are tight and responsive for the most part, though the main character has a bit too much hang time when jumping, which can make quick mid-air maneuvering tricky.
If you have experience with these types of games -- the Mega Man series, for example -- then the challenge in Super Furball is virtually nonexistent. Checkpoints are generous, retaining all your progress right down to the enemies you've killed, and you're given a new bushel of extra lives each time you start a level, meaning you have plenty of chances to fail with minimal consequence. I never once got a Game Over.
The game does offer leaderboards that rank players' best times, but even this doesn't offer much challenge, as the community is so small, you might end up at the top by default since almost no one has played the level you just beat.
Settings are minimal; you can't even configure controls. The ending is literally a joke. Only buy this if you're desperate for a platform shooter.

1. This game is in conflict w/ itself but it's still really good.
2. On one hand it is a moody, slow simmering sci-fi thriller.
3. On the other hand, it is an FPS in which evil mutants fly at you in rapid succession.
4. Both of these elements hold their own but they don't work together strictly speaking. Each element works despite the other element not because of it. There is no synergy.
5. The first person combat is great. A combination of melee, gun and magic attacks as well as a well thought-out progression of upgrades makes for a rather deep experience that allows for a fairly wide variety of play styles.
6. The focus on combat doesn't really allow for your gameplay to have much of a plot. You basically get dropped into this undergrwater city and do what some guy tells you two for a dozen or so hours and then there's the ending.
7. This is different than me saying there isn't a plot. The majority of the plot just happens before the player is ever involved and is told by having the player discover tape recorders throughout the course of gameplay. It all gets kinda laid out to you no matter what you happen to be doing at the time.
8. Who cares? The atmosphere is cool and it's fun.
9. There is some minor illusion of moral choice in this game. You chose between "harvesting" and "saving" what appear to be little girls. They try to add some ambiguity as far is what is the right choice but, honestly, if you are scratching your head over what to do in this situation, I don't want you around my children.
10. There are multiple endings but they are not worth replaying the game for.
11. It is worth replaying to try out new combat mechanics or just for fun. Higher difficulty levels are worth checking out because in addition to making enemies more powerful, it adjusts random loot drop frequencies and makes certain powers take more energy to use so you do really need to adjust how you go about things rather than just aim and dodge better.
12. There are vending machines that yell at you in this and it's the most annoying thing ever.
13. And for last: The inevitable comparison to
: I like this one better. The in game storytelling in the later game is better but since the combat in that one is faster paced and more frenetic, the disconnect between the thriller atmosphere in the combat is even worse. I prefer the survival horror tinged feel of the original. Both are great games though and you should play both.

(easy mode is pretty friggin easy)
First thing is that if there are a couple compatibility issues with Win10. You have to find the .exe file and run on compatibility mode for Windows XP 2/3. There's a couple other compatibility issues, and certain things will make your game (and computer) bug out, but it's not that big of a deal.
The first thing you see when you start the game is an ominous entryway into the city; your plane crashes near some sort of towering structure, and the inside doesn't light up until you enter and the double doors close behind you. You slowly descend, the lights flickering on as you proceed, and eventually you get to the bathysphere and begin your journey to the underwater city.
The opening scene is just *twang* mmm, delicious. The initial events set up the expectations for the rest of the game quite nicely. The entire city seems to be the worn-down remnants of some wonderfully fun place, very carnival-esque with all its glowing neon signs and jingles, but teeming with crazy people spiked on 'plasmids,' which I'm going to explain as genetic modifiers that allow you (and them) to use superhuman abilities such as zapping people with lightning, telekinesis, etc.
For anyone looking to create a world of their own, play through Bioshock and pay attention - this game gets many things right.
As for gameplay, you tend to have to do a lot of scavenging. Money, ammo, other resources, are all fairly difficult to come by unless you scrounge up everything in an area, including searching dead bodies and checking for weapons near recently deceased attackers (seriously, you have to figure out where they dropped the gun before you can claim their ammo). If you really do search everything and you're good about not wasting too many resources, you can end up with a lot of excess, so it's not too bad.
The controls are a tad complicated because there are two 'categories' of weapons for you to use and multiple weapons for each category, but there are enough keyboard shortcuts that you can set everything up and be able to manage everything pretty quickly.
There are a variety of ways to handle enemies that can be pretty fun - hacking security bots, for instance. Igniting gasoline makes everything catch on fire, water spreads lightning, and other such interactions. The only thing I don't really like is the security camera things. Maybe I'm just blind, but I have never spotted a security camera before it's spotted me, so I have to deal with these security bots for a full minute while the alarm blares, every single time.
The story itself was underwhelming, because of its considerable reputation for having an incredible story. No, the story is not incredible. It's pretty good, definitely not bad. But not incredible. What I'm going to praise instead of the story is everything else - the aesthetics of the game are really good. The VOs, the characters, the sounds, the environment, and game progression compliment the story very well.
Final score 8/10. Very fun gameplay, great voicework, a wonderfully carnival-esque world of horror, and also very nice music and sound. The song about some lady looking to buy a doggy with a waggily tale is still stuck in my head.
btw pro tip - when you're choosing between 'harvest' and 'rescue,' always choose 'rescue.' It'll be worth it.
NOTE: I got the entire BioShock collection for 16 freaking dollars, so I'm going to be very lenient about any mishaps.

Cuphead has to be by far one of my all time favorite games and not just because of the artstyle or the music. It's because of the challenge this game has to offer. YES this game is a challenging one and YES you might want to buy a couple extra controllers in case you break one or two in rage. The casual gamers might fight against the first few bosses and never pick up this game again while the hardcore gamers will do whatever it takes to beat this challenging game.
Something that a lot of the most recent videos game have in common is that they aren't challenging. They may throw in a puzzle or two that you might force you to search the internet for the answer but that doesn't change the fact that most of these games can be completed by five year olds without any trouble. And I know that some people don't like challenging games and I get that (You probably don't want to play Cuphead then). But you have to admit that a game that has absolutely no challenge, no trial-and-error, no strategy, etc. is boring af.
At this point I'm just rambling so I'm gonna sum it up. This game is hard but fair. Love this game and it will always have a special place in my game collection.

The game isn´t balanced very well, but will provide challenge for up-to average gamers. Cons:

•	no hall of fame to record the result of past games

Other:
•	graphics and sound are average but suitable for a low-budget TBS game
•	the game does provide some single-player scenarios (not as deep as HoMaM by far), but focus is on random maps like Civ

This game made me blind in my left eye. No joke.
I discovered OMG Zombies! on the PSP, which only has a screen size of 4.3 inches. I am 47 years old, which means my eyes don't work as well as they used to. I should have known better. This game is so addictive that I literally spent somewhere in the neighborhood of eight to ten hours playing it. Continuous. I finished the game, deleted my save, finished the game, deleted my save, and kept right on playing. As a result, I had a massive headache, and the inner lining of my left eye separated, as the ophthalmologist put it, "like peeling off a sticker." My eye filled with thousands of tiny,  black dots (which were actually quite beautiful and which, I later was told, was blood inside the eye). It required laser surgery to repair, and I was told to avoid using the eye and not to lift anything. Two weeks later, it separated again (because I was being foolish and started using the PSP again). I told you all of that in order to tell you this: I regret nothing.
Nothing!

OMG Zombies (which I've just found on Steam in a bundle that did not interest me, but which I had to purchase
in order to share my opinion of the game) is one of those games that offers amazingly simple mechanics, but creative, open-ended strategy (okay, strategy-lite). You are in the middle of a zombie apocalypse, you only have three bullets (to start), and you need to
clear the area of dozens --sometimes, hundreds-- of zombies. Sounds impossible, and it would be were it not for the fact that there are many different types of zombies, and each type behaves differently. Some explode, some shoot rounds off upon dying, some dissolve into pools of acidic goo that, in turn, dissolve any zombie that steps into said pool. Clearing each area awards a bronze, silver, gold, or platinum medal and, with it, different monetary bonuses that allow you to upgrade the zombies, yourself, or the environment (such as exploding barrels).  As the levels progress, zombies gain hit points (requiring more damage to kill), and different combinations of zombie type, as well as environmental hazards, appear.  You can replay each area to try to gain a  higher award.
Let me tell you this: There are few things more satisfying than selecting one specific zombie, firing off a round, and watching it set off a chain reaction that decimates every (un)living thing on the screen.  So powerful was the need to do this, that I kept resetting after completion to see if I could handicap myself.  How far could I get in the game without purchasing a single powerup (pretty far, as it turns out, although killing every zombie in the area is all but impossible)? Could I successfully complete the game upgrading only soldier zombies? What if I played the game while only upgrading my weapon?
Digital crack, I say. Blind in one eye.
in one eye!!  And still, I played.
The Steam version adds three more zombie types (the Mortar, Runner, and Zapper), and the graphic novel story presentation, which offers some beautiful artwork, has been expanded. All of that said, the Steam version unfortunately suffers in its execution (no pun intended). The design of the PSP version is one of the most elegant and sleek I've seen; it's intuitive, and virtually everything you need to see is on one screen. On Steam, it's clunky, waaaay oversized, and confusing. Not only that, but the display resolutions are extremely odd (640x362, 1024x580, and 1920x1088, to name a few), resulting in
, no matter the resolution, no matter if the game is fullscreen or windowed. On the PSP, it was easy to tell what upgrades did; here, it's difficult and unintuitive, and that's coming from someone who's played it before (have I mentioned I've played this before?). (EDIT: I've discovered that you can click and drag the level select screen. Maybe a mouseover tooltip would be appropriate for the next patch?)
Still, confusing layout aside, this is a must purchase if this kind of quick-to-pick-up-but-hard-to-put-down game play is your thing (and I suspect you already know if it is). The price is right and, as I said at the start of this review, it's currently bundled for much less. Either way, I'm playing.
Until I lose
my eyes.
(Just a quick note to give the dev peace of mind: My eye is almost completely healed now. :) No lawsuit is pending, and you have my eternal gratitude for creating such a great game.

I am loving this game, and I'm not really a survival player.
I have to think about every decision - do I carve another kilo of meat off the deer and risk hypothermia in this blizzard or do I just go with what I have and find somewhere to cook it? - and when it works, thanks to chance usually, I feel amazing.
I don't like this level of choice in many of my games. I've played the Borderlands games quite happily knowing that there are a few paths to take but one main one. I've played a lot of Cities: Skylines and made a lot of mediocre cities. I've played the Half-Lives and the Metros (the latter were good games but sexist af) and they all give one way of doing things. TLD however has one goal - survival - and the game is figuring out how to do it!

A few reviewers have said it before: GREAT game, average business practice. Granted, the developers are an independent team, and they communicate remarkably well for a small team, but some of those PR/marketing methods leave much to be desired.
The game itself is incredible, if realistic survival/exploration is up your alley. The game can be challenging, stressful, and given certain environments and scenarios, downright terrifying. However, it also is extremely rewarding and fun to play!
I've folllowed the game since 2014/15 and although it has been a slow process, the development is promising. Storymode is set to release sometime in late 2017 or 2018, but the sandbox mode is charming as well.
Overall, the game is EXCELLENT and I would recommend it to fans of survival games. In fact, I would recommend to gamers in general. I wasn't a huge fan of survival games before I played TLD, and ended up loving it.

EDIT: the game has become unplayable for me. It freezes and crashes far too often.
tl:dr: good mechanics, interesting spells, poor AI and shallow tech tree. Fun to play.
The best thing is that you can create your own troops by choosing their traits and equipment. Too bad that game is balanced so that your only option is to pile up as many magical items on your troops as possible and thus eliminate the power of choise whenever to supply many troops with poor equipment or few troops with expensive equipment.
In the endgame spells are a bit too powerful. Since there isn't any multiplay, the developers haven't bothered to tune down some cataclysm spells like Volcano, which can eradicate whole cities in few turns and alter the environment so that AI has no clue how to cope with that.

BLUF: The game isn't worth $30, I paid a total of $14 for Elemental (the first one), and FE:LH (this one) - I'm a sales hunter. I have no misgivings, FE:LH (this one) has everything in it that Elemental did. So, if you're going to buy one, skip to this one.
Detail:
So, I enjoy modding this game. I'm going to say that right up front... so let me break this into two separate sections, vanilla and not.
Vanilla:
It's a passable strategy game with elements of RPG but not enough to call it an RPG game. Don't come in expecting Civ because that's stupid. Aside from the developers, I see nobody saying anything about Civ in relation to the game except in reviews from people saying its not like Civ (which they expected due to Devs who worked in ome way on Civ).
The game play is pretty straight forward - make units, fight on a tactical grid-map. Use Block to reduce damage from hits, Dodge to avoid hits (even ranged), and spell resist to avoid magic or damage from magic. The built in options to customize a faction, a hero (sovereign), and your own units lend replability to the game. The AI will use created factions as "minor races" if you aren't using them in a scenario. Always nice.
While this is billed as a the Fallen Enchantress come to enslave the world, thats really not it at all. There is a minor campaign that took a tops of 3 hours to complete (and only that cause I like to wander). That dealt with the enchantress, but even then, she was one of the easiest to beat factions. The game is really about random scenarios against random (or selected) factions including your custom ones.
It IS buggy in some annoying spots:
-  Basically anywhere that you enter text runs into issues (such as custom facions backstory and custom Hero Backstory).
-  Custom maps have issues erasing each other in the cartographer tool
-  Altering generated maps in the Cartographer Tool will sometimes cause creatures to spawn on ocen-cliff tiles and make them unkillable outside of magic
-  You can only kill the Vanilla "Ridiculous" difficulty setting (well all of them) aren't vastly different from the normal in my experience.
-  It crashes infrequently, but the autosave feature makes it only a mildly annoying issue (for me).
Modded:
The scripting is pretty easy and straight forward. You can even port in 3D models if you're so inclined. The game was intended for modding but isn't set up for the Steam community. If you get it on sale, this is worth the price. It's a fun little casual game, shoot zombies and try to get them to chain react. I've beat the game, it's not a serious game, watch the trailer if you are still wondering.

First of all, OMG Zombies! is a puzzle game. A bit crazy, random-generated, puzzle game where winning is based on a well-calculated and timed click and the ensuing chaos. Your success is ultimately dictated on that crucial first click and statistics. Oh, and there are a lot of zombies too.
That tickles your interest? Basically, in each level you find yourself somewhere high, surrounded by zombies and with limited ammunition. Each zombie has a special power triggered on their death, like explosion or acid pool or shooting a weapon. With just a few bullets, you have to kill as many zombies as possible, preferably all of them.
This is difficult at first. Then you begin to see patterns within the horde and also accumulate money from winning levels, so it gets easier as you can upgrade your weapon and the zombies. It's left unclear how the zombies can be made stronger, but somehow that happens when you pump enough money in them. Whatever really, as it surely is surprisingly addictive. Several times I decided that the next level would be the last but then kept on playing regardless.
There's also a story. No, it's not very detailed or good, but it explains where the zombies came from and why you find yourself in this dire situation. Also, it's told in an artsy comic manner, so it's cool and it works well for this game. The whole game is drawn in greyscale, except the blood that's (you guessed it) red and everywhere. The unique style works well. Sounds are repetitive and uninteresting, but the cacophony of them can be amusing when you pull a great combo.
For me it lasted 8 hours for the first playthrough (100% completion until first prestige). That brings me to the one thing that kind of bugs me: there's a bad case of "that achievement" in this game, as to earn the last achievement you have to (you get to?) beat the game completely (100%) 20 times. That's going to take a while (UPDATE: I finally beat it after almost 2 years real time, 88 hours gametime). I'd recommend the game regardless as it's cheap and fun. It's also a good game to go to when you're waiting for something but only got a few minutes to spare as it's fast to play through just a few levels.

I used to like this series.
However, many things have pulled me away from it, including the community, successfully making this series not scary over time. Have you seen the childish animations and fanart this community makes? The series is supposed to be scary, right? It isn't the developer's fault, but still.
According to my experience of scary games, it is usually this type of scary game (the type that relies on jumpscares and have childish elements to them, including games like Tattletail) people ruin with the things I mentioned above.
And also, I have the first 4 games, but I don't feel like buying Sister Location (at the time of writing this review, I haven't bothered to watch any videos or read about Sister Location to know how it works). The jumpscares have become more tame and the series has become more boring. I don't think it is a good idea to make scary games based of constant retries that can make the game more frustrating. I think it ruins the scariness. The last time I have played a game in this series (at the time of writing this review) was over 10 months ago. I have only finished 2 of the first 4 games, back when I found this series good enough for actually trying to complete a game from this series.
The lore is also interesting. That's one good thing.
I also don't think it is such a good idea to make a non-scary game, FNAF World (which isn't on Steam anymore), after previously making scary FNAF games, because the aim of the franchise was to be scary. The franchise is better off staying as scary as it can be.
I just can't get back to the series.
I haven't used the word "horror" to describe anything I've mentioned above, because I think it is an overstatement.
The community is the main reason why I can't come back to the series.
I can't recommend a game in this franchise nowadays. I would've in the past.
Also, the franchise isn't the worst horror franchise ever.
