I really like this new indie genre of games that has really shocked the game developer establishment. You no longer need to be a AAA game developer to produce something that resonates with large audiences, and The Long Dark is No exception.
The Long Dark in it's current state is all about surviving longer for each game. For this you need to watch your body's status. You need to hydrate, eat and sleep. Since you are trying to survive in and endless winter body temperature is important. To manage this you need to melt snow and then boil it to get drinking water, gather or hunt for food and then cook it, and scavage the landscape to find more equipment such as weapons, matches, clothes.
Hunting is two-folded; it brings you food but also material to construct new equipment. Same goes for those things you gather when you go scavaging. You can break down most things you collect to pieces to construct something you need.
The Long Dark is a really free game only restricted by your vital signs. But in order to survive you need to find routines for each day, plan your sleep, food and water intake accordingly. And every action you take has a reaction. If you shoot a deer, extracting mest, skin and guts will probably get you to risk dehydration, starvation and hypothermia which could leave you with having to rest in a shelter when you need to collect things, and if it goes far enough kills you. But leaving the carcass out in the open will make it decompose. In this you need to take into account day and night cycles. So you need to harvest everything rather quickly. It's a weigh off in terms of what you are willing to risk to survive.
Also you need to repair things collected and constructed. If your clothes for example becomes worn down they will function less good, and soon ultimately break down completely and you can only harvest material from them. Same thing goes for all things collected including food.
You can't carry everything you collect so you need to find a good place, for example house with a bed, workbench and a stove, where you can sleep, cook food, store and construct things. If you can find food, shelter and build up a supply site with reserves, this game becomes interesting and allows for more scouting and more freedom.
It might not have the best graphics but The Long Dark has revolutionary ideas and unique systems for surviving. It's gameplay is addictive and I can only say I'm looking forward to the story mode. I'm just looking forward to the day when developers of large scale open world games take a similar approach. Think of ArmA style game with survival elements as well.
This game is highly recommended if you like indie games and and games that guarantee problem-solving! I'm just looking forward to Hinterland taking a similar approach on another climate zone!

I downloaded and played this game during the time period where they allowed it to be played for "Free".
Would I pay 40$ for this game? Absolutely not.
Would I pay 30$ for this game? Absolutely not.
Would I pay 20$ for this game? Yes.
This is based off of roughly 10 hours of play time.
FIRST HOUR.
The game has a somewhat clunky UI. It doesn't fully teach the player what to do when it comes to building a city or, better yet, maintaining a city properly once you level up a city and begin to expand. I don't care for a game holding my hand throughout but I feel with a game like this, you need to actually teach a player how to get their feet on the ground before thrusting them in the middle of a "Civilization-esque" RTS. I had no idea what to do for the first 45 minutes or so and even afterwards still had to sit and think how to do certain actions. Yes, I played through the tutorial. It did not help. Its very basic.
CHARACTER/FACTIONS.
I played with 3 different characters (roughly 3 hours apiece), 2 premade characters and one custom made "Aragorn-like" character that focused on using a bow and buffing his allies. This is where the game shines. Each character and faction is unique and interesting as well as potent if you expand and progress correctly. Creating a character took roughly 10 minutes and was enjoyable through the entire process. One of the things that is very different and seperates this game from others is that your hero levels up and becomes stronger. Skill trees are always a plus.
QUESTING.
One of the activities you can do in the game is do "Quest". Basically your hero walks into an Inn and someone says "Hey, go across the map and do this. If you succeed, I'll give you something." Then you do it. It's pretty basic but its something to do and it rewards your hero with neat little items and gear.
WOULD I RETURN.
I would buy the game (I've already deleted it once it regained the 40$ pricetag), if it dropped in price. I enjoyed the majority of my time and I'd love to go back and see how my character (which was directly based off my Dungeons and Dragons character) dealt with this ominous Black Gate area that was locked off from the rest of the map.
This game is a STRONG 7/10. Its fun but it definitely has its problems that taint the total product. At the current price I can't recommend it. Wait for the price to drop or a sale THEN buy it.

Red Faction: Armageddon is mostly judged because it wasn't Red Faction: Guerrilla. Guerrilla was the better game, but this is by no means worse because it's not an imitator. For what it is, it's just not very interesting.  It's pretty obvious that the fun factor in Guerrilla made it so well liked, because this isn't nearly as interesting.
Most of the game is spent fighting repetitive assaults of alien insects. In fact, other than the first mission, it takes you literally half the game to fight human enemies again. I really liked fighting humans because using the destruction against them was actually fun. Enemy on a ledge? Bring the ledge down. Enemy holed up in a building? Bring it down on him. This was when the game was most fun. However, it's only the minority.
Also, the game will crash if you start a new game. There are save files you can find online that start after the first cutscene. Drop them into the save data location, restart your PC, then you can just hit continue.
If you really want it, buy it on a really cheap sale.

OMG-Z FTW YOLO
As a lone soldier fighting his way through hordes of the walking dead, you must make your way unscathed to a helicopter and flee the area. Unlike most zombie themed games (that don’t feature snowball spitting flora) OMG-Z is a single screen, mostly black and white affair that will test your puzzle skills far more than your agility or ability to perform a head-shot, and is much more akin to Bust-A-Move than Left 4 Dead.
The allure of the game is in its simplicity – shoot a zombie and it blows up. If another zombie is in close enough proximity, it too will explode and so forth – creating a chain reaction that coats the grey tones of the hand drawn backgrounds a pleasing pixellated red.
The portable roots of OMG-Z make for a fast paced game with each level taking anywhere from a few seconds to no more than a few minutes. Gamepad support is there for traditionalists but after utilizing the added keyboard and mouse option we can’t see playing it any other way. It also sports a windowed display option that’s great for getting in a few levels between tweets or writing paragraphs for a video game review.
While it isn’t perfect, OMG-Zombies! is a bloody orgy of viscera and strategy that engages and rewards your tasty, tasty brain. If you only get bitten by one zombie game this year, this one comes highly recommended.

Pros:
An absolutely incredible PvP experience that feels like two totally different games depending on which side you play. Playing as monster is a very tense, lonely experience where you live and die by your own wit and skill. Playing as hunters gives you all the trials and tribulations of any intensely competitive coop game, but with the added challenge of fighting against a single player-controlled enemy. Your teammates often make or break the enjoyment. Bring a friend.
Balance is pretty good, and has been consistently tweaked (for the better) since release. It's not perfect, but it's good enough that when you lose you usually have an idea why, or what you could have done better to make the difference rather than feeling like you had no chance.
Cons:
The DLC strategy 2K games has chosen to pursue with this game has left a lot of people feeling like they are being treated like a walking wallet.
Because the game really is two different games in one, sometimes you are forced to play the side you don't want to play, and because it's such a completely different experience it may not be what you wanted. I personally think this is the biggest contributor to the relatively low active player count.
Even so, I've been playing almost daily since release and I've never had trouble finding a game, even at 3am.

I see a lot of people saying a lot of the same things and giving the game a bad review, which I believe is a bit unfair.
The Bad:
"It has many bugs, some of which are really noticeable;" this is true, but they aren't so bad that the game deserves a bad review. "Matchmaking is imbalanced", I don't think this is consistently true but when it is true, it is likely that it is less due to a poor matchmaking system and more due to the fact that the player community is small. "The DLC pricing is too high" I agree on this one, Turtle Rock made a bad judgement call on quality vs price. They clearly put a log of work into their custom models, animations, voice acting, etc. but if it means charging the prices they charge for the DLC then it is not worth it, BUT... and this is a big one, YOU DON'T HAVE TO BUY DLC FOR THE GAME TO BE FUN. Tell 2k and turtle Rock that the price for DLC is too high by not paying it and eventually the price will come down... We may lose custom voice work in future DLC as a result, but it is a small price to pay for getting new content at a reasonable price in my opinion. The last point that most reviews agree on and, incidentally, the most important is that...
The Good:
THE CORE GAMEPLAY IS VERY FUN. This is true despite all of the bad points above. This is something that most games fail to achieve. Most games are content to take something that exists today, slap a new coat of paint on it, and expect you to pay the same price as the last time they released the game. The sad part is that most people do and love said companies for it. It is shameful that a game like this has less than 70% positive reviews and yet the newest Call of Duty gets great reviews for adding a few new skins/guns/maps to the same old multiplayer modes. Turtle Rock took a huge chance on making something completely new with the same aesthetics as other AAA games and made something great, but they suffer from bad reviews because some of the minor chances* they took went awry (*when compared to the chance of creating the new, awesome, core gameplay).
Every gamer should buy this game and give them a chance to fix some of the mistakes they made along the way.

Dungeon of the Endless is probably the best rogue like dungeon crawler that I'll ever play, because it takes the genre and adds a tower defense mechanic to it with a science fiction theme. The object is to explore randomly generated floors all while defending your crystal. The crystal gets used to power rooms that you'll place defenses and harvesters that bring in extra science, food and industry for every new door that you open. Once you discover the exit, one of your party members needs to lug that crystal from the elevator to the exit as the floor floods with enemies. Any party member not in the room with the exit gets left behind if you chose to exit without them.
Your characters will defend a room automatically and fix any damaged equipment if there's nothing happening. You only need to have your people in the right room at the right time. Its a fun and casual way to play the game. If someone gets too low on health, you can click a medical bag near your character's card to use food for more health. Some difficulties even replenish your health for each room or wave of monsters that you clear. You can spend food on each character to level up.
The more rooms of a floor that you clear out, the greater chance of enemy waves attacking. There are still rooms full of enemies, but its the waves that make things a true challenge. These waves will spawn in any room that isn't powered. Your foes can't go through doors and they'll only spawn in rooms you've uncovered so its best when you start a new floor to choose one door and work down that path instead of opening all four doors to each elevator.
You've got your choice of four characters from the start and plenty to unlock as you progress. You can find new recruits and purchase them with food, but that doesn't mean they're unlocked. In order to unlock them you need to have and keep them for at least a floor. The game lets you have a maximum of four per party and it can be difficult juggling them, because you can only control four at once. Under normal circumstances, I have three of them guard the crystal and explore with one.
Dungeon of the Endless has an amazing multiplayer that gives each player one character. Its a much easier experience. You pick a server locally, with your friends or even global. Then select who you want to be or let the game chose randomly and hop into a game. Once it starts no one else can join, even if a player drops out. When a character dies, they can't be revived and this goes for single player too! Instead you'll need to find a new character in the dungeon and recruit them. If you have more than one character under your control, you can pass them to another player. If you play global, its just as smooth as someone in your own region. The only issue that I have with the multiplayer is when the host leaves, the game ends!
The controls are easy, right click to move. That's it. Right click a door to open it and watch your character go to the door. Right click to interact with something. Right click your character icon to open their stats. Of course there are still hot keys and you can scroll the screen or focus in on your character. If you ever need to see the map, mouse wheel back to see the entire dungeon along with icons where the players, enemies and highlights are. Even see unopened doors in red. Its all streamlined, then mouse wheel forward again. Again, its super easy, a joy to play.
Along the way you'll find merchants to sell you things, but the game doesn't bog you down in equipment. Most characters have two or three equipment slots. There are science crystals that you spend science to research upgrades. You'll need to wait a while and open more doors before the research is complete, so don't spend science to research then exit the floor immediately. The recruits and merchants you find will also be attacked, so you'll need to defend them or they'll die.
There are plenty of things to find throughout the rooms: treasure chests, capsules to unlock at the cost of industry and even things that give you science, industry or food. Everything takes a second or two to unlock. Even doors take a while to open, but once they're open they can't be closed. An odd thing about the game is when you open a door, you've commit to walking into the room beyond it. So if its full of enemies, you will still walk in. Even a room full of enemies doesn't feel like a threat, you can still fallback to a room full of turrets that you've setup.
As for placing defenses, you can't just dump a bunch of turrets into a room, you need empty modules in a room to place modules. Some rooms don't even have any modules available, but 90% of them do and the trick is powering the rooms. You've got a limited amount of power your crystal can generate. If the crystal takes damage, it can power fewer rooms. Of course exploring will find more power to beef up your crystal and charge more areas. In terms of defenses, you've got health, defense and weapons. Defense things such as holograms that will attract enemies. Weapons like turrets, Tesla and sentries. New things can be unlocked at science crystals.
Once you find the exit, its best to deactivate some of the powered rooms in order to power ones along the path. After they're powered setup defenses, because when you pick up your crystal every door opens automatically. So every undiscovered enemy is activated, but more pressing than that are the waves of enemies that spawn.
Instead of classes, there are characters. Each character has their own stats for speed, damage, health and so on. Every piece of equipment can change those stats slightly. Things will boost your speed while lowering your damage per second. Some characters use swords, others have a pistol or a gun. Characters all have their own defense needs, some rely on armor, shields or devices. These characters all look and feel unique to be and play as.
Dungeon of the Endless does have only fifteen floors before you'll need to play again from the start. So there is an end game for anyone that needs a goal. Its just reaching that fifteenth floor that is a challenge. Floors become longer, more difficult and dangerous, yet still doable.
Since the game revolves around a sci-fi setting, the premise is simple, you've crash landed in your escape pod. Why am I telling you that now this deep into a review? Because its never an issue in the game, the only time it is an issue is before you start, you'll select your escape pod. After going through the game, you'll unlock different escape pods, each with its own perk. There are a few different difficulties, very easy and easy. I assume that you can unlock more, but after 8 hours into the game I still have two difficulties.
As for the graphics, they're simple and pixelated, yet still drip in atmosphere. Dungeon of the Endless is a dark and eerie sort of beautiful with a futuristic alien twist. The music gets relegated to ambiance and near chip tune music. Its barely a memory in my mind even after 8 hours of playing.
With everything said, Dungeon of the Endless is definitely worth your time for fans of both dungeon crawlers and tower defenders. This isn't a genre for everyone, but what's here is addictive, engrossing and easy to play.

What also bothered me a bit was the weird Walking Path's of the NPC's who always seemed to come from upfront, even thou they logically couldn't have been there. That imho made almost every tactic plan one could have made a bit to ruins, which annoyed me after the fifth time I ran into our fat soldier friend cuz he just decided TO POP OUT OF NOWHERE. [It also wasn't that scary anymore, you have been expecting it after the first two frights.]
That aside, I understand the NPC's have to be walking towards you and get some movement into the Game so. Still bothered me a bit.
So, on to the Pro's, yey! Well basically everything besides the above mentioned Con's. I loved the eery feeling and the setting, that not only got us chased through the entire Asylum, but also outside in the yard, aswell as (yuck) Down the drain! It was pretty amazing and I found myself staring at the screen, anticipating the next move I could make or if it was safe behind that dark corner.
So! I also got hyped on that absolute and total helplessness of our protagonist. Like cmon, even those half-degenerated not-so-human Zombies had weapons to slice us up and all we had, was a Camcorder. Which we also lost. Good job, Miles. Really.
Anyways, it really gave off the 'scare-me' feeling, creeping behind the corner, crouching through drains and trying everything to not get caught. Without saying too much, also the religious fanatic fit perfectly well into the setting, and I liked deciphering all the scrambled messages on the walls-or recording the Altar-or the sacrifices. Besides the fact the 're-activate something' tasks were rather repetitive I never had the feeling about the Asylum or its surroundings. Also the many, many rooms and ways that were just there for us to explore them, really made me feel like this is not one more game, where there is only one way.
It was creepy, scary BUT I actually had one or another good laugh, playing 'Open-Close-Destroy the Door' with our very lovely Soldier friend!
So, overall, I have been very into the Game and I'll possibly get myself the DLC and Outlast 2, because this really got me hooked up and I really enjoyed the Run-Hide-Seek I have been playing.
It's definitely worth a play and I'd recommend it for anyone who wants to be helpless and delivered for Mercy of some very unfriendly and naked Experiments!

I downloaded and played this game during the time period where they allowed it to be played for "Free".
Would I pay 40$ for this game? Absolutely not.
Would I pay 30$ for this game? Absolutely not.
Would I pay 20$ for this game? Yes.
This is based off of roughly 10 hours of play time.
FIRST HOUR.
The game has a somewhat clunky UI. It doesn't fully teach the player what to do when it comes to building a city or, better yet, maintaining a city properly once you level up a city and begin to expand. I don't care for a game holding my hand throughout but I feel with a game like this, you need to actually teach a player how to get their feet on the ground before thrusting them in the middle of a "Civilization-esque" RTS. I had no idea what to do for the first 45 minutes or so and even afterwards still had to sit and think how to do certain actions. Yes, I played through the tutorial. It did not help. Its very basic.
CHARACTER/FACTIONS.
I played with 3 different characters (roughly 3 hours apiece), 2 premade characters and one custom made "Aragorn-like" character that focused on using a bow and buffing his allies. This is where the game shines. Each character and faction is unique and interesting as well as potent if you expand and progress correctly. Creating a character took roughly 10 minutes and was enjoyable through the entire process. One of the things that is very different and seperates this game from others is that your hero levels up and becomes stronger. Skill trees are always a plus.
QUESTING.
One of the activities you can do in the game is do "Quest". Basically your hero walks into an Inn and someone says "Hey, go across the map and do this. If you succeed, I'll give you something." Then you do it. It's pretty basic but its something to do and it rewards your hero with neat little items and gear.
WOULD I RETURN.
I would buy the game (I've already deleted it once it regained the 40$ pricetag), if it dropped in price. I enjoyed the majority of my time and I'd love to go back and see how my character (which was directly based off my Dungeons and Dragons character) dealt with this ominous Black Gate area that was locked off from the rest of the map.
This game is a STRONG 7/10. Its fun but it definitely has its problems that taint the total product. At the current price I can't recommend it. Wait for the price to drop or a sale THEN buy it.

This game seems to be somewhat controversial due to being a standalone expansion to a previous game. I bought it without having played the previous installments, and I find it awesome. I have tried several of the latest fantasy 4X games in the spirit of Master of Magic (Age of Wonders III, Warlock: Master of the Arcane) and this one is by far the best IMHO.
The balance between strategy, city development, hero development, tactical combat and adventure/RPG events is just right. The magic is great. The tactical combat is good - not as deep as in AOW3, but more than enough in my book. Very similar to that in Master of Magic. The variety in sovereigns and the possibilities for roleplaying ensure replayability.
But the best feature is that you can create your own units! Instead of having only a predefined range of units, you get some guys, give them a particular weapon, armor, mount, special boni and characteristics, art, etc. and you design your own kind of troop - of course the more powerful you make it, the more it will cost to actually build one. I spent hours fiddling with the unit builder alone.
The AI has been criticized, maybe it's not the best but to be honest I don't see the difference with other complex 4X games. Even in an universally appraised franchise like Civ games, the AI is just not that intelligent and higher difficulty levels work by cheating, giving the AI boni and knowledge that the player doesn't have access to (those nuclears that always went to your only city without SDI in Civ 2, lol). I suppose adding extra elements like magic doesn't help with making human-like AIs - the AI in Master of Magic was notorious for doing really dumb things and cheating a lot, even more so than in Civ, and all of us that are old enough to have played that in its time had a great time with it. I'm having a great time with this one too, and to be honest the AI didn't catch my attention for being bad at all, I only learned people had a problem with it by reading reviews. Maybe it was worse in previous versions and they have improved it over time, as I bought the game when the latest version was already 1.7.
My only gripe with this game is that it doesn't have a hall of fame: even though it gives you a score and a rank, it doesn't keep track of your best scores... it's a somewhat dumb thing to care about, I know, but I'm competitive and seeing my best scores and trying to beat them motivates me a lot. The developers said they are going to add this feature eventually, I hope they do.
But in summary, great game, lots of good content and many hours of fun in it. I think it's very underrated and it's a pity that such a gem is not better known, that's why I have decided to write this.

Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes aspires to be a great game, and all the elements of a good turn based fantasy strategy game are there, unfortunetly, after 40+ hours of playing it, i have to say, while it is addicting, it is not very fun to play it.
I am sure there are people who have lots of fun playing at the start like an ant wich has to be careful where to build it howel least the many wandering beings of power trample it. Scurry around with you units like rats in a field full of cats and larger predators, and pray that none of the monsters, who are at this point unbeatable, notice you.
I know what others playing the game will say, that nothing is unbeatable given time. Well sure, but time is not something you have for it when there are AI rivals on the world, who are absolutly unnaffected by the same creatures building their empires, (And don't you dare claim othervise, i have seen unescorted pioneers of the AI walk around dragons and wandering ogre armies unmolested. And no, they did not have the stealthy trait.) this is frustrating at the least.
That is not to say it cannot be an enjoyable game, and that you could not beat it. (Sometimes easily, even on harder difficulties.) But luck is too much of a factor, and it is infuriating to realise that you are screwed after an hour of playing, because a creature with physical immunity wandered into your territory (And you have no magic yet), or a random event spawned a swarm of giant spiders on top of your capital that is stronger as your entire armed forces.
In a faster game these issues could be looked over, but Fallen Enchantress is Slooo
I love empire building, i have no problems with a game being slow, but when it is slow, and a bit of bad luck can be game ending, and you have to restart over and over again to get a starting position that is not full of nasties you cannot beat until after midgame tech, that is simply bad design.

Not sure why people are clicking "No" (perhaps trying to get their review to the top?), but my review is pretty spot on. Don't let the votes fool you.
What can I say? OMG Zombies! is an addictive game until you reach Prestige level 1. Play dominos with Zombies by watching them explode, shoot other zombies, scream (causes wide spread damage) and other crazy effects. You start off as an officer that appears to have gotten himself into a bit of a pickle. The way for him to survive is to down as many zombies as he can to proceed to the next areas in your journey.
Although you don't lose any health and you have no health for that matter makes the game too easy. You're basically on top of objects in the game, sniping zombies to try and cause a massive widespread train wreck. At first you only have 3 bullets, but upgrading let's you increase your clip size. The upgrade system is pretty fluid. Upgrade zombies, barrels or your own weapon.
The in-game comic that spams is quite annoying since it spams after every game at 80-100 levels. Don't get me wrong, you can skip it. It would be better if it showed different comics but it doesn't until every 10 or so levels completed (as far as I remember).
Do I recommend this? Well, if you want to waste a bit of time it might be worth playing as a time waster or if you just want to farm achievements it might be worth it (beware of 20th prestiege achievement). However, if you're looking for a game to play well over 30hrs, OMG Zombies! isn't that.
: 4/10

Honestly this is one of my all time favourite games. It's a survival game, sure, but where the thralls of other survival games struggle to get footing over one another, the Long Dark stands proudly and triumphantly above the rest. It's unlike other survival games for a number of reasons. It's setting is in norhtern Canada at an undisclosed time in the near future (?) after a geomagnetic storm essentially ends like as we know it. You play as the sole survivor of a downed plane are tasked with.. well... surviving. For now, at least, as the story is still in progress. That being said the sandbox is amazing. There are an abundance of explorable areas, with more being added periodically. The survival aspect boils down to you managing your hunger, thrist, warmth and rest, though in a landscape that is constantly below freezing temperatures, all of these things can be difficult to get a grasp on upon first playing the game. Once you get the ropes, however, you can settle into one of the most peaceful, haunting and introspective survival experiences I have ever had the pleasure of being a part of. The musical score is beautiful, the audio is incredibly refined, the visuals are unique and pleasant, the wolves and bears are spooky, the storms are accurate (I'm a wee canadian boy, I know what I'm talking about) and the male voice actor is Commander Shepard from Mass Effect, so let's bang, okay?

Hi folks and welcome to a brief review of this game.
I can sum it up all pretty much in one sentence. "This game is beautiful"
The only thing about it I would love to see added, is the chance to share the experience with another player in co-op.  The aim of the game is to survive, and the games intention is to invoke a bleak sense of being alone.  It accomplishes this so very well, but it would be nice to share the bleak wilderness with just one other person.  A bit like don't starve alone?
What I love about the game are the mechanics. Even a simple thing like lighting a fire becomes a dangerous roulette.  Will it light? or will I freeze to death out here in this cold?   I love the graphic art style and suggest that even if you don't like survival games in general you should still give this one a try.  It will change your mind.

I totally recommend this game to anyone looking for a chill, yet challenging survival sandbox.

I just had to stop playing this to write a review. And I'm not doing those very often, let alone getting such urgent impulse to actually close the game for it. But this game deserves it... I guess. Well, I'm just an hour in, reached only W3-1 but oh boy, it gives me some sweats – sweats of joy!
Never have I played such a challenging yet achievable plattformer.  Admittedly it's not my preferred genre of choice on my computer, and console gamers could eventually prove me otherwise, but I'm having a blast!
The gameplay is as easy as it gets – jump, run, duck, avoid deadly objects, just don't die reaching the exit. One lvl is merely one screen, no scrolling. One world has ten screens (plus some bonus stages), as far as I can tell, I'm in the last lvl of the 2nd world. For the adventure mode that is. There are also a race and a deathmatch mode which are obviously multiplayer modes. I've only tried adventure so far, as I'm testing candidates for the next local gaming party, but lacking a buddy right now. And this one looks very promising although you might gather a more experienced crowd. Now, it is hard as stated before and on entering a lvl you might think “how I'm ever going to make this?!”. But you are! It may take a while though*g* It's always doable, never unfair. It takes some plattfoming skill and timing. Controls are precise and responsive. Levels are riddled with – well – traps... where some of those aren't visible when you enter a new screen. But you won't succeed on your first attempt anyway... so.
The graphics are – as you can see on the screenshots – retro styled, inspired by the 16 bit era. They're not particularly unique, but by no means dull or ugly. The gore effect which covers the environment with more and more blood as you're being constantly crushed by the fist of doom or saw blade of horror gives a weird sense of accomplishment. It's got a great soundtrack, I don't like the soundeffects though. Often they don't fit or sound awfully generic.
I definitely recommend Bloody Trapland for solo players and I will vote for it on the next game night with friends.

Project Zomboid is an isometric zombie apocalypse survival simulator. If you don’t actually know what any of those words mean except ‘zombie’ you may want to play something else.
Though the game has been stuck in early access hell for years now, I have thoroughly enjoyed my time with it. I’m not really up on the current build, but I can give you a pretty good idea of what to expect if you decide to give it a go.
It has a fantastic little character creation system, with tons of mixing and matching positive and negative perks for customization purposes, but that’s not all! It also lets you customize the nature of the zombies you’ll encounter, though that’s only in sandbox mode, I think. Fast zombies or slow zombies or uber tough zombies or smart zombies or insane hordes or NONE.
Whatever you choose!
As there is no real plot to speak of, like many other survival simulators. You should probably just play in sandbox mode and ignore the other gameplay modes, unless you have some kind of death wish.
Speaking of, there are many ways to die in Project Zomboid.
Here are some of them:
Drink bleach.
Burn your house down!
Get EATEN.
Catch the virus.
Fall off something.
Go on a shopping trip to the mall.
Starve!
Eat rotten food.
Die of dehydration.
Freeze to death.
Collapse from exhaustion and heat exposure.
And many more!

Hello everyone,
OMG Zombies!!! LOL!! What a fun game to play. What you have to do is to shoot Zombies to create a chain reaction and kill all the OMG Zombies per level.
You start with 3 bullets (but do not worry, you will soon get up to 5 bullets), watch their movement and shoot and create that chain reaction.
The first couple of levels are quite simple but soon you are very thankfull to be able to upgrade your weapon (increase bullet, more damage per bullet and more range)and OMG Zombies Too.
Your objective is to get a platinum medal in each levels (bloody hard when you keep moving forward) and you will need upgrade to reach it!

OMG Zombies lets you play a cop that has to get rid of all the zombies in a level. And it wants you to do this as efficiently as possible. Your bullets ricochet off of zombies and the zombies that get hit will explode or emit lightning, or shoot bullets, for example, killing other zombies in the process. So it involves some strategy, but also luck, because the zombies walk around freely. This makes it hard to hit enough other zombies sometimes.
There are 100 levels in total and each one rewards you with a medal and money. Money that can be spent on upgrading your gun or zombies (that's right, you can upgrade the zombies; awesome !). You can choose to upgrade your zombies so that bullets from cop zombies will hit more zombies, or that explosions will be bigger and timers will be extended. Your choice. In the end you need to update them all if you want to platinum every level.
And even though there 100 levels, most of them can be finished within minutes. So completing the game will take just a few hours.
The graphics aren't the best in the world. In fact, I wasn't impressed by them at all. The 2D artwork isn't all that attractive, and the levels are too crudely drawn, as are the zombies. The animations for the zombies are also fairly basic.
But graphics is not what this game is all about. It's all about the kills. And it feels very satisfying to kill all of the zombies with just one bullet, or see that last bullet kill the last couple of enemies.
OMG Zombies is a game I'd definitely recommend, even if you had enough of all these zombie games lately. This one is worth it, absolutely.

Regarding the ending you can have more than a different ending and you can have a" good" or a "bad" one. The Story itself is presented in a Comic Book style which is a nice thing. As for the price it's a no-brainer (eh!)

UPDATE:
I would like to share my personal take on the pros and cons of this game to help people decide on whether to buy this game or not, because the game gets torn apart by many players and independent reviewers, while praised by game magazines.
The reason is simple: the pricing of things in this game is controversial.
Some do not mind the 8 bucks per new character because they will simply just pick few of them and stick to them anyway.
Others will hate it because they want 100% of the game content for a reasonable, worry-free one-time price.
And game magazines probably don't even care at all.
Apart from the money debate, here is what you should consider:
+ NOT pay2win
+ a unique experience, especially when you enjoy less mainstream and more innovative game designs
+ really solid, really great looking, sounding and feeling game
+ keeps getting updated, patched and rebalanced
- expensive base game unless you get it on a discount
- poor customization
- a lot of the cosmetic cash shop items are pointless, plain bad
- cash shop characters are not OP, but still feel like a cash-grab if you want more than just a few of them, due to pricing
= Bottom Line: Do your research where you want to get the game from and once you tried it you will know whether you really want to spend money on it, how much, and which characters you really want to get.

As someone who usually absolutely despises roguelikes, I have to hand it to these devs. This is a roguelike that is actually pretty good! So many roguelikes just create "difficulty" with brute force randomness, but this game actually has a lot more strategy and a lot more interesting decisions to make. I especially like how the light switch mechanic works to shift the monster spawning around, and the fact that you can switch it up on the fly. Sort of reminds me of Desktop Dungeons where exploration itself is a resource. Similar principle at work here, which is very interesting. Even though escort missions tend to be an infamous no-no in most games, it actually serves a fun and interesting purpose here.
Ultimately, though, I still don't think this game is for me, so I won't be playing it any further, personally. Because as much as there is a TON of stuff in here that I like, it still has those classic roguelike annoyances, such as opening a door and getting insta-ganked because randomness. Don't get me wrong, some people LOVE that, but it is one of the main reasons why this player specifically does not care for roguelikes.
Tower Defense? Yes.
RTS elements? Yes.
Turn-based strategy? Yes.
Squad-based tactics? Yes.
Resource management? Yes.
Survival? Yes.
Roguelike randomness + permadeath? No thanks.
But even as a person who has no taste for most games in the roguelike genre, I have to say that this game is really really interesting and worth checking out. Even though it's not for me, I can tell it's something special.

What can I say about The Night Christmas Ended? It's a fast-paced action shooter, which starts off pretty slow for those who aren't familiar with the genre. As you progress however, it practically becomes a 2D bullet-hell and I'm A-Okay with that!
You play through as the biggest goblin of all (by an inch), who basically goes around blasting ghosts and the likes. Mostly because he can, of course. You're sent on a quest (for a hefty sum of gold in return of course,) to go and save Christmas.
The graphics are really fun in this game. I mentioned in my full review
that there is a graphical issue I found when an enemy dies. They leave behind some blocky debris, which is intentional. However, this can cover up the purple "debuffs" you encounter in some levels. You can still see them going down, so you just have to be careful.
If you're picking this game up for children and aren't fond of swearing, this might not be for you... However if you're totally okay with swearing in your games then get this. This costs less than some pints of beer where I come from - and this lasts longer.
TL;DR: Pick this game up. It's cheap enough, it's got some silly humour and it's overall great fun. Some minor points aside, you'll have a laugh... And the game gets pretty tricky for those who love a challenge!

A slower paced zombie survival game that places an emphasis on methodical supply gathering and skill acquisition. Top down, 3D isometric view. Windows and doors can be boarded shut with a hammer and nails, sheet ropes can be created and affixed to second story windows to climb up or down. You have to account for hunger, thirst, rest (and sleep in single player modes), as well as boredom and depression. There are a variety of recipes one can use to cook certain foods. Collected rainwater must be boiled before drinking lest the player makes himself sick. Power and water shuts off over time in-game requiring the use of gas grills, or wood fires to cook on. The environment experiences degradation overtime - weeds overgrow, houses begin to look more dilapidated, etc. It's about as close to the book "I Am Legend" as you're going to get with a zombie game. Love the game, but it would benefit from the ability to use vehicles for the sake of long-distance supply runs that can become very tedious and boring if you survive to late game. There is a mod for this, however.

OMG Zombies is a great example of a fun puzzle game that was ported poorly. I have played this game to completion(Platinum Medal on all levels) on both the Playstion Mini version and the Playstation Mobile version. The PC version is practically the same game but with 3 new zombies thrown into them mix. The core of the game is shooting a zombie in hopes that its "power", or death action, ends up killing the zombies next to it. With practice and a little bit of luck(a lot of luck at the beginning) you'll be creating huge domino effect chain reactions using a single bullet. Points are earned at the end of each level that are used to "upgrade" the zombies or your rifle. Upgrades consist of increased range of power, increased damage of power, or a larger population of that zombie on the map(this is good as it creates more opperatunities for the chain reactions). There is something great about clearing an entire map with one well placed shot.
The issue with the port is the GUI, both for the menus and the gameplay. The entire game seems to have been ported line for line from the Vita version, which is touch heavy. Unfortunately, the HUD is sized for a portable system(leading to buttons that are way too large for a PC) and the level select screen is navigated by dragging, a feat that isn't exactly natural for the mouse. Hopefully Laughing Jackal sees this an works towards creating better menus and HUD for the PC crowd. Other than this slight oversight(seeing as the game is still extremely fun and rewarding) this game is well worth the $4 that it launched at.

So... I really like  The Long Dark.
But, I have some gripes.
Thus far, I've only been playing in sandbox mode, because that's the reason I bought the game - that's how I wanted to play. I'm a bit of an achievement hoarder, so I'd like to get this achievement related to harvesting 10 complete deer carcasses - and I'm still not understanding why it is so difficult to make arrowheads. Why do you need arrowheads? Because the game is so incredibly miserly about rifle ammunition. And the rifle itself seems (at least to me) to be notoriously inaccurate. Of the five rounds I've fired through the rifle only a single one has killed a deer. I shot him from behind, from maybe twenty feet away. Yeah, it better have hit!
But all of the other shots I took from similar distances, with even better placement, all whiffed.
Okay, I can deal with that - the game requires you to get better with firearms. Makes sense. But, what do I use if I am always out of rifle ammunition? Well, I'd really like to have some sort of back-up weapon! But, making a bow and arrows is egregiously difficult! Thus far, I've found one broken arrow. I took the arrowhead from that guy, and I've been working on making a bow and new arrows. The catch is - you need cured guts and cured maple and birch branches for the bow and arrows. Curing those takes five days. Five days! And you can only make an arrow with an arrowhead! So after all of these five days of curing (+the time it took me to find the uncured saplings)... I'll have ONE arrow. That, so far as I've read, is also expendable. One shot only.
WHAT. Why would arrows immediately break or be lost every single time?! That's not how it works in the real world - why in this, particularly if it's intended to be a fairly realistic survival simulator!? Why do you even need an arrowhead in the first place - let alone a metal one?
Okay - end rant. But, seriously, c'mon. Love the game, HATE that mechanic. If we  have to deal with hostile animals all of the time, allow us to defend ourselves. Otherwise, it's just a "run from monsters" survival horror game.

If there were a way to write a review with the thumb sideways instead of up or down, I'd do so for this game.  5/10.  It is a reasonable execution on a good concept: a 4X game somewhere in between Civ and Heroes of Might and Magic, with a few unique but not exactly mold-breaking twists.  I'll give it the thumbs-up, but only at Steam sale pricing ($9.99 or below).
It does require a second account registration, but the login is unintrusive after the first time.  I already had a Stardock account from playing Galactic Civilizations II.
The unit customization options are good and something that others could emulate.  Same with faction customization.
The hero development is average.
The graphics are downscale for a 2013 release, but that's never bothered me; I still play Heroes of Might and Magic III somewhat regularly and the graphics there don't bother me, either.
The characters are flat and unvoiced, and the writing for the quests and scenarios is not really interesting.
Tactical combat is fairly standard, though the move highlights could be better and it's easy to accidentally move to the wrong tile due to a mouse error.  There also don't seem to be a very large number of tactical maps, and they appear to have terrain but not actually do much with it (it at least does not appear that cover actually provides protection from ranged attacks or that attacking downhill is easier and uphill is harder, for example).
Strategic movement is somewhat awkward.
A solid effort, but it could have been significantly more polished.  5/10.

I've never heard of this game before but I saw it at a 'free weekend' and, remembering my fond feelings for turn-based strategies, decided to give it a try. Well, after playing through the night and finishing one random game, one thing is for sure: I'm not going to buy it after the time runs out.
This game is tedious. I started with the tutorial and, boy, were the introductory videos long and unnecessary! I got to the end of only one of them, skipping all the others, and didn't feel like I was missing something. Then there was the main game. For me it went like this: settle down, start expanding - ooh, it's getting interesting - die trying to explore, meet neighboors, avoid their units and wandering monsters while trying to explore and expand, upgrade your cities and lose your units on the way to join main guy's army - repeat for many turns until you know the map - start negotiating, get into a war, sign a peace treaty - rinse and repeat, that's where I lost the last of my interest for this game, during those many turns where
happened - finally be strong enough to follow the main storyline and immediately after wait again for who knows how long for new units to be trained in place of the fallen ones. Yeah, boring.
I got three endings: the ultimate spell (which I did only out of curiosity, not knowing that it will end the game), by losing to the final dragon behind the gates and by killing it (last two with the use of cheats because of the difficulty jump - I could easily kill any monster or AI unit on the map but this thing obliterates me in, like, three turns? Yeah, no, I'm not grinding for that - and by the way: those cheats? Did not help much). I didn't try to conquer all the other nations just because I couldn't be bothered anymore and wanted to be done with it. And my rating was always 4/10 (I think) despite having, like, twenty fully upgraded cities and finishing all reasearch and quests.
Also, this game doesn't have window mode which incredibly bothered me and the loading process took way longer than it should. Maybe my machine isn't powerful enough, although I thought it didn't have to be to play a top-down strategy game! On the technical side of the things, thank god there is an auto-battle option, cause I don't think I would have gotten this far without it! Never played a battle on my own (except the final dragon one but that one doesn't count) and immensely grateful for that.
TL;DR
Actually, this game is not so bad - for the first few hours. After that, if you're not a fan of the wainting game, it becomes too much. Maybe it's supposed to be played in short sessions, who knows, but for me one run was more than enough.
Never would've thought of buying this game before; certain that I'd not now.

This game has some advantages and disadvantages to a similar title with a lot more polish: Endless Legends. I thought I'd compare the two.
Advantages to Fallen Enchantress:
+ You can rotate the map, which is nice in tactical mode (during battles).
+ The quests you get have less variety compared to Endless Legends, but in Enchantress they invariably involve combat of some kind, which is good for people who like combat. Also, there are sometimes branching paths in quests, a concept pretty much unheard of in Endless.
+ The fantasy setting is great if you like that kind of thing. I do, and it's the biggest reason to like this game imho. Endless Legends has this strange cyberpunk/fantasy hybrid thing going on which rarely makes sense.
+ Huge customization. You can create your empire or kingdom from scratch, rather than the civ standby of picking from the list of pre-made leaders. You can pick and choose bonuses (and penalties) to fit your playstyle, as well as having full control over the color palette that will appear on your units and cities. While equipping units is done in Endless Legends as well as Fallen Enchantress, Enchantress has a tad more variety in the early game and also has the advantage that your units change their appearance with their gear, a feature Endless lacks.
Disadvantages to Fallen Enchantress:
- The maps. City placement is restricted to fixed locations, and battles play out in an instanced flat plane with no variety. In Endless Legends you can build wherever the hell you want like a normal civ game and when two stacks of units fight, the overall game pauses and the units spread out into the surrounding tiles, to duke it out for six rounds. This means that units are affected by terrain and elevation, and it also means battles can be stalemates or attrition fights rather than the forced fight to the death in Enchantress.
- Diplomacy is wonkier than Civ. When I played, I regularly had enemy civs offer me money out of the blue. There's a demand tribute button on the diplomacy screen, but there's also a give tribute button which will automagically give the recieving player 10% of your gold income for 30 turns. If your arbitrary point total (if you played any recent Civ game you know what I mean) is above a certain point, your opponents will shower you in gifst in the hope that you attack them last. It's funny at first, until you realize that ten percent of their income is almost always nothing and it's a completely hollow gesture in the first place. If you accept tribute from them, it gives the other civ a negative diplomacy moodlet becaude 'you demanded tribute from them'. Which, ironically, makes them more afraid you'll attack them and more likely to give tribute in the future. Also worth noting is treaties and trade are separate options in this game and that treaties must be picked one at a time, so you can't do things like sign borders agreements or take cities in exchange for peace. You either mutually accept peace (with a possible bribe in gold if needed), or you surrender everything and quit the game. There is no other way to end a war prematurely.
- No navy. The sea (and air) are sorely lacking in Fallen Enchantress. Any lakes you encounter (and you will) are impassible voids. This is a shame, because a heavy focus into earth magic (if you're lucky enough to randomly generate a champion unit that knows some) eventually nets you the ability to terraform the land around you. You can turn sea into land, land into settleable land or hills, hills to mountains and vice versa. The problem is that, as mentioned, terrain has no impact on combat and cities don't work neighboring tiles, so there's very little motivation to actually do this.
- The minimalistic approach. Numbers in this game are very small. You'll spend ten turns on a building that nets you +1 science per turn. Every customization option in this game, from making units to leveling champions to constructing buildings to upgrading them to using spells in or out of combat to making your empire in the first place, all of them are minimalistic tweaks. Despite all the options you have, none of it actually does much of anything. You might see a building that generates double the science that your city already produced, until you realize you built every science building available and you're only producing seven, and that building replaces another one which already increased your science output by 75% so instead of netting +7 science for your twenty turns of production, you're actually only getting +1. Your units will get damage buffs of 10 to 20 percent at a time, but that translates into 1-2 extra damage on your attack, which won't make a difference to the vast majority of enemies. Whenther they had the buff or not it'll still take the same amout of attacks, same number of turns in combat, to kill anything. The result is that the game feels very hollow, where it looks on the surface like there's a lot of replay value but there actually isn't. Seeing as replay value is the ultimate goal for a 4x game, this is a serious shortcoming.
Summary:
If you just rewatched Game of Thrones and you REALLY want to play a Civ game that uses a fantasy setting and magic and whatnot, if you want to play dress-up with your units and if you really don't care if the game is actually any good, you might as well play Fallen Enchantress. But if what you're looking for is a 4x game with any level of depth, a game that will entertain you for more than a few hours and a game where your choices have a drastic impact on the flow of the game, go for Endless Legends.
Oh, and Legends has multiplayer, for the people who care about that.

So i played evolve since the release day, and it was a mixed feeling! Now the game is for free and people start playing again which excited me a lot, therefore i started playing it again. Running Through Russia is a Russia themed runner game. The game's main purpose is purely for achievements.

There are potions that can move you to heaven or hell. The scenery will then change and you'll have some pitfalls on the ground where you'll be back to the normal area if you're in heaven or die (ends your current run) if you're in hell. I find it difficult to navigate in these areas because the pitfalls are placed very close to each other. There is even a death potion which will end your run after you "take" it.
However, the game has an annoying bug where you'll stuck in a bear's top and can't do anything else if you jump on the bear in the wrong spot. You'll have no choice but to restart the game.
You'll need some luck if you want to get far into the game because there are some cases where you have no choice but to die (especially when you are in hell).
Pros:
- Achievements, if it counts as one.
Cons:
- Bug
- Semi luck based

In OMG Zombies you take the role of a survivor/shooter, perched on top of something higher than the Zombie horde below you on a 2D single screen, encompassing the various obstacles and challenges of each map. Armed with just a sniper rifle and 3 bullets (which you can upgrade to 6 as you earn cash by completing levels), you are tasked with taking out the entire screen's worth of undead. An impossible task if one bullet equaled one zombie death, but this is where OMGZ's strategy comes into play.
Each and every zombie in the game has a chain reaction ability which helps take out other zombies around it. Some explode, some fire off gunshots of their own, others run through the level screaming (taking out others at their destination), some even melt into acid; all of which helps clear the screen and earn you the higher ranking, providing you with more cash and allowing you to beef up your abilities.
Each level has a Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum medal to acquire, each earning you more cash for upgrades. Don't get discouraged if you can only pull off the lower medal awards at first, it'll become easier once you've spent some of that award money on upgrades. Better medals open up more and more of the 100 levels included and you can go back any time to any level and try for a higher score; some levels being clear-able in a single shot if timed right.
Thankfully the mouse is the most precise tool for the shooting, giving you an advantage over it's previous versions (on PSP/Vita). The game runs wonderfully in windowed mode and goes along at such a pace that you can continually go back to it between browsing and chatting if you prefer (which I liked during my play for this review).
What unfolds is a game that feels a little over-powering at first, as you clamor to get even a silver medal, then opens up and gives you the upper hand as you progress, only to keep challenging you with levels that make you wonder how even 6 bullets will help you be victorious. Sometimes timing is key and you can sit there with hand on mouse for what feels like forever, trying to line up the perfect chain reaction.
Then when you've completed all 100 levels on platinum, you have the choice to start all over again in a prestige mode, in which you lose all your upgrades and must start from level 1 again. Reminding yourself just how hard it was starting out. If you're brave enough and have some serious time to dedicate to it, the game has an achievement for prestige-ing 20 times over.
The game isn't a super action romp and you shouldn't get it thinking it is. It's a strategic game that employs a very well ramped difficulty curve which makes for an engaging and addicting experience. I've enjoyed my time with it and feel it's well worth the asking price.

Now, if you are currently looking through the reviews and have found my little review, take this to heart before you buy. This game, is not an amazing rts. If you buy this game, you bought it not becuase you wanted to see darth vader completley destroy an army of infantry (though, you can see that if you want), you play it to watch as your army of only empire capital ships gets completly destoryed by thousands of rebel bombers because you thought you didnt need any anti-fighter ships. You came to watch the rebels snatch victory from insurmoutable odds, obliterating what you once thought to be intimedating star destroyers. You came to laugh with a sick twisted sense of pleasure as you defend the death star before, while the match is playing, you press a button to activate the death star, and watch a rebel planet expload.
but, most importantly, you came because this is star wars game. A Star wars rts at that, a very rare breed. So, just remember before you buy, if you wanted to have epic, fun and awesome GROUND BATTLES, you may not want to buy this. Oh, and btw, mods add a lot of longevity to the game, some mods just make the game better, more then a few that put this game in the clones wars (one focuses more on the cartoon series while the other is more just general clones wars stuff, noramlly stuff in the movies with a couple mentions to the cartoon). It took me a while to decide whether to recommend this game or not. Ultimately, I decided not to because if asked "would I play this game ever again?" the answer is a resounding no.

Cons:
Just one: This game is a repetitive slog because of its difficulty. I usually enjoy a challenge and pick hard when offered the choice, but here, it's your only choice. You'll die over and over again to memorize a boss's attack patterns, then die over and over to learn his next form's attack patterns and so on. The difficulty jumps up and down all over the place. 5 hours in, I just wanted this game to end so that I could say that I'd seen all the nice art and creativity, and be done with it. Wound up using cheats to get through the last two encounters, they were just so tedious to go through.
Had they included some selectable difficulty levels, I would gladly recommend this game. As is, only buy it if you are a glutton for punishment.

This game is often rated down because it doesn't have an open world like the previous in the series: Red Raction: Guerilla. What is often forgotten is that the open world in Guerilla wasn't any good. What was good about it was the destruction engine. Red Faction: Armageddon takes that destruction and goes absolutely bonkers with it. The trailers really don't do justice to the madness found within.
This time around gameplay is standard linear 3rd person shooting. The world, story and characters are horrific schlock. Cutscenes look cheap, voice acting either sucks or is out of place. It's totally mediocre without ever raising to either good or so bad it's good levels. These are not the elements you should be looking for here.
Destruction engine, the same as in previous game of the series, on the other  hand is awesome and will never not be. I can't belive how much stuff you can destroy in this game! While the game is set in caves, there are plenty of structures, bridges and such that can be blown to million pieces. It's great! This is especially true with modern pc's since the frame rate doesn't dip no matter what goes boom. Around the midway point a thing happens and so does intrest in the game. At that point the basic shooting is already familiar enough and more of the same starts to feel like a chore. The action picks up the pace towards the end though and there is even a suprisingly decent flying section.
I completed the game on normal with an xbox360 controller which took around 7 hours. On normal the game is ridiculously easy. Enemy AI is dumb and if they actually try something, their damage is laughably low. Dying really takes some effort in this game. At the same time the player is given loads of explosives at all times. Personally i mostly used rocket launcher, which always had plenty of ammo. If for some reason that ran out, i switched to granade launcher and if that ran out there was always plasma cannon (basically another rocked launcher) or a singularity rifle (which sucks everything toward it's projectile and then explodes) Couple this with the destruction engine and gameplay is just endless carnage! Enemies die by the dozen, buildings collapse and stuff explodes non-stop. There is an upgrade system but most of them are pointless. You can get extra skills but i can't name them because i never used them. Didn't need to. One useful ability is a repair beam which can rebuild everything that is destroyed. Since almost all structures can and will be blown up there is often need to rebuild bridges and such. It's good kind of silly: First you unload dozens of rockets and whatnot into a room only to repair it later.
There are few issues in the game itself and also some techical stuff. Getting this game to work at all  gave some serious 1990's flashbacks. New game caused a crash to desktop so i had to go through forums to find out why. Turns out that i needed to download someone else's save file (which is why i had to play on normal) to get the thing even started. This appears to be an issue with the steam client and might be patched. After that i had to download a config file to change FOV. This is not how gaming should be in 2016. Also because of the non-stop explosions the screen shakes constantly which might be an issue to some. Also the game is often really dark so it's hard to see where to go.
Red Faction: Armageddon isn't intelligent entertainment but it sure is fun! For the price of admission (i got this on sale for 2€) it's well worth it!

It’s important not to judge a book by its cover, so let me be perfectly clear: Toricky does not look good. Toricky looks like a deviantArt profile transferred into the Unity engine. The colors are garish, the art is ugly, and half of the UI is mysteriously cut off at the edge. There’s no way around this. Toricky looks bad, and half the screen is mysteriously cut off. But let’s look past that. So the game looks bad, fine. Some of the greatest games of all time look bad. There’s a lot more to a game than that. The music, for example, is pretty nice, and the story is simple and silly, something about crystals and goddesses and pig pirates, and the game seemed to lay it on a bit thick for a game of this sort, but it’s inoffensive enough. Localization features dialogue such as: “It’s round?” “Indeed, it is… round.” It’s kind of endearing, frankly.
As for the gameplay, Toricky is based around gathering “crystars”, these little collectible MacGuffins in lightbulbs that are scattered around the level. They usually require some exploration or some light puzzle solving to figure out. Crystars are used to open doors and advance the story. Each level has a multitude of crystars hidden inside it. (They function like stars in Super Mario 64, to keep it simple.) Because you have to return the crystar back to a checkpoint, every level is basically a fetch quest. The level instantly ends after you return a crystar, which means you can’t get several in one go, you have to start over every damn time, and you start at the same checkpoint every damn time, and fly and open the same gates every damn time. It’s repetitive and annoying to do this over and over. It gives you a time stamp for your run, which might encourage speed-running, but I can’t imagine wanting to go back and play any of these missions again. The game cycles through day and night, and to the game’s credit, this does actually serve a mechanical purpose (some things only occur at certain times of day), but the primary cause is just to make the visuals less appealing and less parsable half of the time, as they’re drenched in black as you fly through these flamboyant levels.

Most crystars are hidden behind some form of puzzle. Occasionally, there are boss fights, as well, but the primary gameplay loop is exploration. The puzzles to get your crystals aren’t particularly great, either. They’re generally basic rote or a simple exploration of areas. This isn’t inherently bad, but the act of exploring itself doesn’t feel very good. The trek through these areas will take you past enemies, which, for a while, you can only combat by picking up and dropping objects on them. For a while, I was completely stuck. I had checked each level and around the hub area, and couldn’t find a way to advance. Eventually, by chance, I stumbled onto some fake blocks I could fly through hidden within the hub area. This wasn’t a fun little secret; this was a necessary discovery to continue the game, within the first hour or so. Pardon my French, but: that’s bull hockey. The whole game is filled with this feeling of aimlessness. Collecting these crystars doesn’t feel good. It feels like a chore, another reason you have to fly blandly through these multi-colored environments.

Flying just doesn’t feel that good, either. Moving up and down and around feels awfully twitchy. It feels imprecise, but most of all it just feels… empty. You turn on a dime, which feels ill-fitting for a character who is entirely airborne. Your character flies in an arc, sure, but there’s no reason to go through this arc when you can just mash the directions you want to go in. If you kill an enemy and start flying down, you can die on a dead enemy. Your only method of interaction with the world is picking up or dropping objects. On one hand, this creates a clear line of thought for problem solving. On the other hand, it makes play feel incredibly limited. The whole game feels wrong. My actions don’t feel connected to those of Toricky’s. This, along with an unsatisfying gameplay loop, makes the whole game feel just not worth the effort.
I think what bums me out the most about Toricky is that there was clearly so much love put into this game. The Japanese indie market is a somewhat elusive scene from a Western perspective, and I, personally, am always excited to see what comes out of it, and ready to support it. The developer is responsive to its players, communicating with them and updating, and the art, as unappealing as it is, is all handmade. There are a multitude of language options. The voice actors are clearly putting energy into their lines. Anything from a developer that would indicate a commitment to the project, it’s here. It warms my heart in the same moment it breaks it. They had a vision, and they aimed for it. The devs cared; they really cared. But all this motivation and passion doesn’t translate into good game design.

Having put nearly 200 hours into Terraria and over 150 hours in Starbound, I can say without a doubt that, even as an early access game, Planet Centauri has a lot of potential and is already a very enjoyable game.
The controls were slightly different, took me like maybe 5-10 minutes to adjust, but using the right mouse button to swing your weapon or whatever you put there works well. I also found the system where by you eat food to permanently increase your health and stamina to be quite interesting as I shoved every piece of food into my mouth that I found.
Here is a list of things I've accomplished so far in almost 18 hours:
-Met a giant talking green crystal from the Sim's who told me to do things.
-Built a cozy wooden house surrounded by about a thousand chickens.
-Turned cozy house into a castle of death and awesomeness.
-Gone exploring in the couple of other biomes.
-Went into a cave and found lots of interesting things and things that wanted to eat me.
-Ate every single piece of food I could find at least once.
-"Liberated" the Chloridians from their cozy dungeons, built on their homeland, and forced them into labor like a proper American would.
-Killed a crazy necromancer in a dungeon that had a built in magic escalator, because even in games I'm too lazy to walk.
-Started my journey to become a Pokemon master and captured my first pet.
-Bent the elements to my will with magic spells.
-And discovered the learned the joys of turning myself into a myriad of monsters.
Overall I'm certainly enjoying the game and looking forward to the future of Planet Centauri.The devs seem cool and responsive and are constantly updating the game and adding new things.
If I were to suggest anything based on my time playing would likely be:
-More jobs for the Chloridians (After I got one of everything, I just started having a ton of soldiers).
-Invasions where monsters attack the crystal or player or something along those lines, otherwise my castle is just sitting full of soldiers for nothing.
-Possible weapon diversity/rebalancing, one of the things I've read and experienced myself is in the late game the swords do a lot of damage while magic options and other weapons like bows and other ranged attacks are a bit underpowered. This might be in part to having not fully expanded the magic system, but the other weapons could use some love as well.
-Personally I'd also love some sort of shop or market npc that you could spend some of your extra souls on, or alternatively that you could sell your items too for souls, I've always enjoyed the economic systems in these types of games.
-Lastly I'm looking forward to more story/lore content, like why were we flying over this planet in the first place? Why did we have cool armor in the first place? Is anyone in the universe looking for us or knows that we are missing? Etc.
All in all great job so far Devs, can't wait to see more in the coming months. Keep up the great work. Definitely a recommend from me.

This is my review for FNaF (Five Nights at Funky's), and after lots of in-game time, i have reached the point in time where i must write a review. Following many trials, ups and downs, and much thought, i am ready to take on the garguantuan task of writing this review.
Firstly, lets review the pro's and con's of Fifteen Nights at Denny's
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PROS:
+ Very good graphics, considering this game was made in 1996, the polygons and pixel textures are masterfully done, almost resembling real life in some points.
+ Audio is utilised very well, to make the game feel more like one of the MMORPG genre, yet are unique enough to seperate it from other games in the genre (such as sonic adventure 2), and even those in the Two Days at Benny's series.
+ The use of customisable weapon skins adds a unique collectible aspect to the game, and the method of obtaining them (a delightfully fun bingo minigame), is also very entertaining
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
CONS:
- The ambience of the game is trash, and often times, doesnt even feel like a platformer anymore!
- The paid micro-transaction DLC costumes for Jenny and the Gang make the game unfair, adding a Pay2win element to the game
- Strays away from the sandbox formula the first 2 Minecraft games followed
- The 4 mappacks added (Freddy's revenge, shiver me timbers, adventure at the kwusty kwab, and enderchest-blast) feel like cop-outs, not offering a good enough experience for the price paid
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
FINAL THOUGHTS:
Although the game is very enjoyable, i would not recommend it to the mainstream audience, simply because of the skill required to progress throughout the intensive levels.
Overall, i give Seventy-Two Quadrillion Eavenings at Pappa John's a 6.3/10
