This is one of those cases where I wished that Steam had more than two options for "rating" a game. I'll have it to 'recommended' in any case; for the 40-or-so hours I've put to the game, most have been quite exciting. It's a good game, not one without its flaws, but a good game nevertheless.
By far the most interesting part in the game is the unpredictability of death. It can come very fast; Step into a dark bathroom, have a zombie leap at you from behind the corner, and you might just get yourself scratched. In the next few days, you'll find out whether the scratch is going to be theundoing of you.. or if a simple bandage will be enough! In your first play-throughs, when you know the electricity and water are going to be cut off, you are in for the thrill of gathering food and filling every usable container (like mugs, cooking pots, bowls, etc) with water. It's awesomely exciting!
There's also a degree of faithfulness to realism that is very refreshing. Unrefrigerated food rots. Bandages get dirty (and you can clean them with water and then sterilize them with disinfectant). Players who die in multiplayer stick around and turn to zombies, carrying whatever items the players had at first. The list goes on.
The amount of customization is also good. You can change how long zombies follow you, how strong they are. You can change the electricity and water shutoff days. It's good, and makes the game suit more playing styles with a bit more easiness.
Beginning the game, the act of exploring new places is absolutely thrilling. Not knowing what to expect, the game rewards long journeys to the by-the-town warehouses and keeps up a steady stream of new things to try and do.
Unfortunately, that stream is not a particularly lasting one. My 40 hours to this game have been split over 3-or-so years. Compared to some other survival and management games, the learning curve is relatively shallow. If you're a fast learner for this kind of stuff, surviving basically infinitely is doable after your first 10 hours in the game. Even less if you took liberal use of the wiki and strategy guides.
Overall, not much in the game is going to come as a surprise to you after the initial learning curve. There's a very strong feeling of lack of purpose. There's relatively complex crafting systems in place. You can build a stronghold of skyways and escape routes, just to never need them since no zombie horde ever happens by your stronghold.
There's also the winter. I've never reached it without changing the starting date closer to it. Not because it was
to reach it, but because every time I've tried, I've gotten bored to the game before I'm even past October (the default starting date is in middle of the summer). Anyhow, you'd guess that winter had its own complicated challenges of survival; well, not really, you just put on a sweater.
The game would benefit greatly from more metagame events and more challenging, higher-tempo survival requirements. There could be events for zombie hordes spawning near by to your base and starting to move towards its direction. The winter could be much more dangerous.
I do see great potential for the game, but to be honest, it's been in development for 5 years. To me, the development process has seemed very slow and at times, somewhat haphazard (updates breaking stuff or not working properly etc are not unheard of). I still trust they are working towards getting their goals fulfilled however, and it's true that when you're doing your first big game from ground up, things are always much more challenging than one might expect from the outside!
Lastly - since this is something I saw some negative reviews criticize - one of the highlights of the game is the community. Yes, people are banned, but no, it's not a bad thing. As a community, Project Zomboid is really good relative to how most gaming communities are. The moderators are not afraid to tell people to back off, and are not afraid to ban abusive people. By no means do they aim to censor criticism; for one to claim so might be betraying more about themselves than the moderators.

I wasn't really looking for much more than what I got - interesting, utterly destructible environments, good graphics that ran smoothly, big booms and crashes and lots of enemies that presented a hazard but also went splat rather nicely. The story isn't all that bad either, even if it takes a back seat to the action, and of course it doesn't pay much attention to the Red Faction storyline of the first or third games but who gives a crap? It's a good game.

It's not Guerrilla, but that's not a pro or con, just a difference. Armageddon is a very linear game, void of any of the usual little side missions found in sandbox games. I happen to prefer this, but that's obviously just a personal opinion.
There is far less focus on demolition, as combat in this game is more fleshed out. Guns feel much better, and unlocking the enemy healthy indicator really adds to the weight of the shots. You also now have abilities that you can unlock and upgrade from your nano forge.  The game also introduces a repair mechanic, which is neat, if not a little underused.
I thought the humor in this game was great. Definitely something I liked over Guerrilla, where the intended humorous dialogue was one-sided and overall more serious.
All in all, Armageddon was enjoyable, if not a little short. The difficulty is certainly a step up from Guerrilla, but I didn’t find it very difficult to overcome, and thought it was a good choice to make to go along with the linear path.

Although this game was a big step backwards from Red Faction Guerilla (removing the sandbox was a BIG mistake after RF:G showed us how awesome an open world destruction sandbox could be), it's still worth a playthrough (provided you get it on a big discount).
The gunplay and physics are improved from RF:G and the new toys (especially the reconstructor and the magnet gun, and also the flying missions) are awesome, but unfortunately this feels a bit wasted since there isn't a big open world to play with them in. You'll be restricted to using them in relatively small caves.
Overall I still had fun with this, but I really would have preferred a proper open world RF:G sequel rather than a return to Red Faction's corridor shooting roots.

This game does some things really well and really badly at the same time, it plays out like a good early access proof of concept, but ultimately feels unfinished.
Let me explain,  The actual gameplay is tight, I wouldn't change the steering at all, it feels good, but from the 2nd track on where you need to brake, the brake just doesn't feel like it does anything more than releasing the boost. There's no wipeout-style air brake or tight turn bank you can do.
The decision to have the 'path' clip through horizon is a good move, so you have a chance to react to blind turns following hills (although I would like to see it draw further ahead), but the track design is just full of cruel noob traps so even if you react in time there's no way of preparing for the rockl/tree/wall that is placed far to close for any margin of error. This would be ok-ish if it was only later on the harder tracks, but it happens on ALL tracks from the beginning, and to compound matters the game makes it clear that one mistake is fatal, Making it more a memory game than a skill game. (Also the green/black course 'turn arrows' dotted around are pracically invisible I would like to see those re-designed as a further aid to turn warnings)
Part of the unfinished feel comes from the lack of music variety. 1 track in menu, and 1 in game (in my first hour), which even though siimlar in 80's style, don't fit together and feel a little abrupt. if the menu music faded in when you pause that would polish this.
Also contributing to the unfinished feel is the menus. It's not clear what your goal is, (there's no tutorial, just a practice run) and if you do finish a mission you can't try the next mission, you have to quit out to the mission select and pick a different one. Also there;s no real crash animation to speak of if you crash hard your craft just turns black and theres a fire texture placed on top. some kind of explosion would be much more satisfying.
I know I've written alot about such a simple littel game but I feel there's potential here, especially for speed runners, ( the near instant restarts and good gameplay feel are great for the one-more-go factor)  but within the hour it becomes an excercise in frustration.  It is not freindly to newcomers AT ALL and I can't reccommend until it's 'finished'. I hope BinaryDream keep working on it.

PolyRace isn't a bad game per se, but I can't imagine recommending it to anyone.
It feels unpolished in most aspects, and I encountered two bugs. The first session I played there was no UI while racing, and the post-race UI regularly goes outside of the screen. It seems to be made with love, but feels more like gamedev practice or a free-for-a-day mobile game than a proper I-would-pay-for-this game.
My main gripe however, is that the core gameplay just isn't that fun. The idea is there: trying to find the quickest route through a randomly generated landscape, using quick wits to come out ahead. Yet the line that shows you where to go doesn't go far enough ahead (especially when hidden behind terrain), the obstacles are frustrating, and the insta-kill ledges are sometimes hard to see.
Most of the mechanics go against this core idea as well. The whole idea of replayability raises some questionmarks as far as those quick wits go, and slow wits don't work either, since the terrain rarely has clear landmarks for you to recognise. Shields and brakes are pointless as well, since if you don't go flat-out, why even bother instead of restarting? Better to pick the fastest ship.
The 20 tracks in the missions don't flow particularly well either, and the ones I played didn't take very long.
All in all, its heart seems to be in the right place, but none of the other bits are.
PS: I got this game for 3000 coins on Chrono.gg, so it wasn't quite free. I wouldn't spend real money on it, but I hardly mourn the coins I lost.
If you are low on cash to buy Redout, this is a good alternative.

Another problem is that the gear, even the end-game gear, have too few slots for the enchanting stones. (1 for head and foot armor, and 2 for body). Despite the disadvantages of it being a game in an alpha stage, it is clear in the game that the developer plans to add much more content. Also on the plus side, the game right now runs really well on a somewhat low-end (but new) PC. It does not take up a lot of memory.

I do like this game, its fun and has a lot of potential. A clone of Terraria with some changes to keep the formula interesting, with some outstanding animation work. However, there are a few fundemental issues with it that need to be resolved. Those issues are what this review will focus on. While yes I recomend this game, only do so if you are desperate for another Terraria styled game right now because as the game is improving, I can imagine the following issues being a deal breaker for a lot of people.
1) The combat, it feels off. Its floaty, the attacks fail to feel impactful and what actually happens during combat is not communicated clearly enough. In addition to that, the enemy spawn rates are generally fairly high, a lot higher than you can deal with, especially early on. This needs a lot of tweaking, as early on the combat is a chore rather than a fun aspect of the game.
2) The terrain, and world in general. Its bad. The slopes sound cool in theory, having all this natural looking terrain around the place, however this does not work with the rest of the game and honestly just looks bad. I honestly think this is the main aspect that needs improvement. In my opinion, the sloped world should be cut and a more traditional blocky world should be used. Don't get me wrong, trying new things out is fun and good, but this creates more issues than its worth. For example, there are several inclinations, each having a different hit box. This can create issues when platforming, making it harder to aim jumps than neccessary, or during combat where your attack is just outside of enemy range because he is on a slope.
3) It can lack engagement in some mechanics. Either due to poor explanaition, or just poor design, some mechanics are not engaging or interesting. For example, farming has some cool aspect to it (mainly how seeds are thrown to the ground) but after that it seems like its just a wait with no real way to interact. I'd be fine with that, if there was more of an indication of how the aspect works, and the other mechanics were a bit more fleshed out.
Overall, the game does have some very cool mechanics, and ideas going for it. Food for example increases max HP for each new food you eat. It just needs a lot of polish and maybe some more content and I can see this being a great new game of this type.

Bioshock is the game where the "recommended/not recommended" dichotomy loses its meaning. It's very well made, exceptionally well made. It's got the most gorgeous and interesting surroundings - an art deco dream of a city underneath the sea, frozen in time in the 1920s. It's got an interesting premise, telling the tale of a society free from all norms, creating itself away from all other interference. A veritable utopian experiment. So why don't I like it? Why don't I like it...
I guess the thing is that it's well set up, but leaves me feeling like I'm missing something. And I very well may be. Either that, or whatever it's trying to get across just doesn't... come across. A lot of people are praising the story, but compared to games whose story I thoroughly enjoyed (Deus Ex, System Shock, GTA) this one just isn't very well told. The encounters seem random, the locations feel like just an assortment of oddities and what little I learn about the events that led to the situation I find myself in leave me with more questions than answers. Because really: How DID anyone survive the 40 years between the collapse of Rapture's society and my arrival?
The thing is: I can't really say anything bad about it, but still, after having finished it, I've been left deeply disappointed. Really, that was it? That's all there is to it? Don't get me wrong, it's pretty and all, and interesting, and varied, and... everything a lot of people seem to like. So I guess I just didn't get it.

The game's first mission level starts off with a reasonable track, but most likely, you are either going to crash on your first run, or dial in a slow time. From there, it only gets more and more "challenging".
I say challenging, because this game is basically a mix of track memorization and trial & error. See those little triangles? yeah, you won't be seeing them all the time, and the mix of obstacles scattered so close to this "racng line", and your desire to take as straight a path as possible while boosting, you're going to see each track a few times, until you either memorize it, or get a lucky run. I got up to about the 10th misson (of 20), and decided I would rather play a racing game that was fun, and didn't just get my panties in a twist.
There is a challenge mode where you can challenge other's tracks (not many from what I can see), there are "tracks of the day" (I got 1st on today's because no-one has bothered racing it), and of course leaderboards, but seeing how few people were on the leaderboard by the time I got to mission 10 (there were only about 40 total), I'm guessing other people also got the idea they'd rather be playing something else.
Which is a shame - everything is there for a good game, but the cruel track design just kills any enjoyment.

I like speed.
I don't, of course, mean methamphetamine. And I'm not referring to the movie with Keanu Reeves and Sandra Bullock (in this instance. )  I like the sort of speed that makes you go "AAARGH" at your monitor; the kind of speed that the term "breakneck" was originally coined for, where you think "oh look, a wall" and you hit it before you've even finished thinking the word "oh". This game has that in spades. It also manages to get from me something that I thought I'd left behind; that "just one more go" mentality that seems to wipe hours off my day.
I used to love the Wipeout series; it seemed to be built around the same thing that I love, albeit with a nice gentle learning curve that eventually ramped you up to the aforementioned "AAARGH" level. The thrill (to someone like me) of negotiating a particularly difficult stratch of corners without coming into contact with anything can't be overstated. Polyrace has also apparently been built with these things in mind, although the inclusion of procedurally generated tracks adds a nice "exploration" vibe to it; I've thought a few times now that I've refined my racing lines through a level down to near perfection - only to see on the leaderboard that I'm still 5-10 secs off the pace, then watching the ghost of my self appointed nemesis (more on them in a mo) skate through a gap I'd never even seen before.
There are currently only 3 game modes available, to my knowledge - it claims to have 4 but I've yet to get the "Challenge" option working at all (that or nobody has created any tracks yet, which I'd be surprised by.) Training is more "free run" than any kind of actual training and Missions are pre-generated maps created by the developers in which you can unlock new colours and ships. The real fun at the mo is to be had"Race of the Day" where you attempt to beat the ghosts of other players (and they can teach you a thing or two about how to thread through tiny gaps at over 600km/h, I can tell you; I feel like I'd give Luke Skywalker a run for his money after today's track.) And I have been known to roar in triumph at my screen when I've finally put my nemesis's time down (getting to them!),
There appears to be a quite a small player base at the moment, and I don't understand that - I've just picked this game up for a tiny amount of money and I can't recommend it enough. If you've bothered to read this far, then you must already be interested. My advice would be to stop dithering and by the blimmin thing. Honestly, if it takes you this long to make a choice of left or right round a rock in Polyrace, you'll already be wearing your ship's♥♥♥♥♥♥as a hat - and subsequently reaching for the restart button for "just one more go".
Oh, my nemesis? His or her handle is Joker. And I'm coming for them. (In a friendly, competitive and totally non-confrontational way, of course.)
TLDR; It's fast, cheap and awesome. Buy it. Just be prepared to swear at it and be all twitchy by the time you put it down again ;)

Story Pros:
- The main character is easy to understand and grasp his personality.
- The importance of the previous games in the series is minimal; what you need to know to understand the story is all contained in dialog etc., so you won't feel lost if you haven't played the previous games.
- The main character is able to communicate important details of what's going on without directly talking to the player, thanks to his dialog with his "S.A.M." AI on his wrist.
- The comraderie of the main character and a number of his acquiantances makes it easy to enjoy dialog, instead of it feeling like dead-pan exhibition.
Story Cons:
- Due to the importance of your character's past, you cannot customize your character at all visually.
- The S.A.M. AI on the character's wrist is near omnipotent at times, like finding routes for you through completely uncharted caves, yet other times seems completely oblivious to certain details.
- The story will frequently, intentionally mislead you through certain portions of the story, often through the AI either not providing all the details, remaining silent, etc. This tends to create a feeling of Deus Ex Machina when the Story says you can do X thing to fix the situation, long after you should reasonably have been told, or even after it made it seem like that thing was impossible (No spoilers, but the ending definitely reeks of this)
- There are a number of cuts the story takes through Cutscenes. The cutscenes themselves are actually quite nice, however, there are a number of occasions where the game will painstakingly walk you through every detail of a particular scenario, and the abruptly move you to the next chapter with no details of what happened in between (I.E. cutscene shows you loading up on a truck with your buddy, talking about where they're going, and then it immediately goes to another cutscene where you've been at that location for some time and are already talking about heading out again.)
Gameplay Pros:
- Physics & Destructible terrain are immensely enjoyable. This is seriously the best thing about the game. As you progress, you get a number of unique weapons and skills that will wreak havoc on your surroundings. And once you've had your fill of destroying buildings and sending your enemies flying, your AI can use a 'Nano forge' to repair things like bridges, so you need not worry about accidentally destroying your path to the next objective.
- There is never any time where the game takes away your progression through the skill tree, nor any of your weapons. Once it's unlocked, you can expect it to be available for the rest of the game.
Gameplay Cons:
- Objectives aren't always clear as to how you should get where you are going, unless you use the 'Compass' tool which projects the direction to your goal onto the terrain around you. There's no middle ground between, "I'm lost" and Handholdiong from the game. I would have liked more well-designed levels that make it a little easier to find where you are going without asking for an explicit map.
- Gameplay time is fairly short. Two full playthroughs took me just under 12 hours.
Visuals:
- Textures are magnificent. The developers knew what they were dealing with, and didn't leave anything blurry or pixelated.
- Meshes are a little angular at times, but instead of looking odd, they made sure to make the artistic style incorporate angles as seeming intentional (i.e. crystals on the walls, angular architecture, and spiky enemies)
Overall, I definitely recommend the game simply because of how enjoyable it is to be able to destroy the large majority of your surroundings. It makes you feel in control, and powerful.
It's definitely not a legendary game like Half-Life 2 or Portal, but it's a good 6 or 7 out of 10. Definitely worth a shot if you see it go on sale.

Procedural generation often brings practically endless replayability to a game while focusing on quantity over the quality of immaculate, tight design. That is somewhat the case with PolyRace, that rather than having a handful of tracks to choose from, opts to generate tracks procedurally giving the player some 45 million tracks to choose from. That is not to say that there isn't quality to be found, the game can be really entertaining for a certain type of gamer.
Despite the amount of tracks technically available, the game is slightly barren on content. There's the Training mode, where the player can generate tracks using a short string of letters and numbers, choose a hovercraft and race until their heart's content. There's the Mission mode, where there are 20 pre-chosen tracks available, ranging from Easy to Extreme in difficulty. From each Mission a maximum of five stars can be earned with a good enough result. Stars unlock new Missions, new hovercraft and colors to use with them. The two hardest difficulties can be quite challenging and take a relatively lot of time to clear with five stars. As far as strictly single-player content goes, that's it.
Then there's the Challenge mode, where after generating a track, the player is given 10 minutes to race on it and put up their best time. After that the Challenge is published and other players can take a crack at it, also for 10 minutes. Finally, there's the Race of the Day. As can be surmised, it's a generated track that's available for 24 hours for anybody to race on. The multiplayer is asynchronous, so the player never races against someone else directly. Instead, races take place against ghosts, either another player's, the developer's, or the player's own previous best run.
These four game modes are all the game has to offer. It's a bit spartan, but considering the game is so focused on improving one's results in short courses, it's appropiate. Combined with the amount of tracks, it's all that's needed.
The tracks themselves are short, only around 20-40 seconds. And they aren't tracks in the traditional racing game sense, rather, they are open areas filled with destructible and non-destructible hazards. There are two main race types, Time Attack and Distance. In the former the goal is simply to reach the finish line in the shortest time possibly, in the latter the aim is to simply get as far as possible until the time runs out, while collecting orbs that add to the timer. In Training mode there's also Endless, where the player can race in a randomly generated world until they crash or get bored. The player is guided by a string of lights that leads towards the finish line or the next time-extending orb. But the guiding lights are not strict instructions, they are more like suggestions. If there's a faster path towards the destination, it's up to the player to find it and be good enough to dodge the hazards that may be there. This makes shortcuts feel incredibly dynamic and fresh and not just something the developer came up with.
Overall, the game is fairly simple. There's very little to unlock, there's no improving your craft's stats, no story. And the game's all the better for it. This is strictly a game meant for the type of gamer who can race on a short ~30-second course again and again and again and again until they get it just right, and actually enjoy the experience. If the gamer has likeminded individuals to share their times and favorite courses with, all the better.

This is a: Go ahead and get it if it's ridiculously on sale recommendation, but recognize that it's not a really GREAT game...
I played Red Faction Guerrilla before this, so I was relatively familiar with the whole, "We do physics engines and destruction!" thing.  The game provides you a broad set of tools to continously destroy just about any man-made structure around you- from grenade launchers, to singularity bomb cannons, to the much appreciated and highly satisfying Magnet Gun.  I say "man made" because you spend most of the game underground- a very steep departure from the previous game's open world sandbox feel- and you can't really tunnel through the rock around you.  Still, it's satisfying that you can blast your way through walls and truly weaponize your environment in a way that makes combat feel really unique and resourceful.
Yes, the physics and the destruction are quite satisfying, but the main problem here is that that's just about all there is to enjoy.  The game goes by in a complete blur- much much shorter than I feel the last one was, and the 'story' progresses by so quickly in a set of cut scenes that you find yourself saying, "...I could just skip this and it wouldn't make any difference in my playing experience".  There are audio logs scattered around- a feature which I've liked ever since Bioshock, but they never reveal any information that you feel like you can sit down and appreciate- or which in any way makes you feel more involved or invested in this world.  Everything is pretty contrived and the characters are kind of annoying cookie cutter stereotypes down to your Cortana AI who drones at you with the impatient nag of a Self Check Out machine.
The enemies are different kinds of alien bugs- again a pretty big difference from the EDM soldiers/trucks/helicopters of the last game.  The trouble is that there's only (what feels like) 6 different kinds of them, and you fight them truly endlessly- with very little relief toward the end of the game.  And while it is great fun to splatter a whole herd of the lower tier aliens with a clever use of the magnet gun- it became a bit frustrating that toward the end of the game the stronger aliens were just about impervious to it- causing me to rely on the most over the top weapons the game had to offer just to survive an ordinary mission.
Overall - if you're familiar with Red Faction games, this one has some nice mechanic upgrades over the former installments, and almost everything you remember and loved about them is still here (including some walker levels).  But other than that it's kind of a frantic 3rd person sci-fi one trick pony.
No thanks.

I don't know if it was the pressure of early adult life or the demands of college, but I began to experiment with huge ships in my late teens. I began by looking at huge ship magazines in the basement when my parents weren't around. Then one day, my mom came home early and unexpectedly caught me in the act. Both of my parents were furious. They asked me where I go the magazine from and I said I found it and that I thought it only contained articles on small watercraft. As a result, I started to sneak out at night, telling my parents that I was headed to a friend's house to watch Full House, but in reality, I was in the library, reading up on huge ships. As my career developed, I found an apartment that I could afford and I moved out of my parents’ house. My interest in huge ships only grew. My apartment became a center for trafficking huge ship paraphernalia: model huge ships, pictures, of huge ships; life preserves – you name it. Eventually some neighbors complained and the owner of the apartment building had me evicted. By that time, I was so far gone that I didn’t care and I moved into a hostel. It was the perfect place to continue my pursuit of huge ships. The rent was cheap, drifters came and went, everyone minded their own business, and once in a while a new person would come along with scale models of huge ships in Turkey. We had a lot of wild nights and I was having trouble holding down my job. Eventually got fired. One day it dawned on me that if I don't get away from huge ships, I'll end up dead. By pure luck, I ran into a fellow who went through the same thing and he recommend Trimmer's book. Between the book and my support group, I made progress and got back on my feet again. Last night I almost turned left out of the parking lot instead turning right, as I've done routinely for the last 6 months. Turning left would have meant that I was heading to the Port of Baltimore where huge ships are present everywhere: horns blowing, sailors lashing gear to decks, and merchants teasingly gesturing to the gangplanks as they ask passersby if they want to go for a voyage on a great, big, huge ship. I started to imagine the wakes in the bay and the frolicking of tugs as they pull and push these huge ships in and out of the port. There was a burning desire inside of me: my mouth started to salivate; my hands were trembling; and my eyes darted left and right as they searched for an answer. I thought that maybe I could just go to the port and find one or two huge ships and it wouldn't be that big of a deal. Call it a voice in my head, an angel on my shoulder, or Trimmer's book in my glove box, but I turned right and headed home instead. My support group had a meeting last night and I told them about my near stumble. It felt good to tell everyone that I did not fall victim to weakness. I have my beloved support group and my dearest John W. Trimmer to thank for 6 months - huge ship free.

The long dark is a gem that I keep coming back to which is rare for me in video games. The game has beautiful stylized graphics and the developers are some of the best one's i've seen for an early access game. At times sandbox mode can feel a bit tedious, but the goal of survival keeps me intrested and engaged. There is crafting and a needs bar that you need to fill.  I love that things can turn on a dime in this game. You could be harvesting a dead wolf and after the hours pass be stuck in a blizard. There are no do-overs in this game once you die you die. This is a great feature though because it heightens the stakes of survival for each game. You could be doing great then take a wrong turn into a bear get mauled and bleed out. Hypothermia and (I believe) frostbite is in the game. If you run down a mountain there is a chance you can twist your ankle. I would enjoy additions such as a weapon's training mode. I can't kill anything with the bow.  It has been mentioned before but a dog companion would be nice as well. The developers have  a roadmap for future additions of the game that you can follow. Project Zomboid is my favourite game but I'm writing this review solely to offset the negative ones that seem to be popping up. PZ is the best anxiety simulator I've ever played. You scavenge, barricade and kill zombies, but it's so much more than that. If you've ever watched The Walking Dead and scoffed at the bad decisions the writers make characters do, this is the game for you.
People complain about "missing features" and while NPCs are obviously sorely missed (and the development team KNOW THIS), there is a huge amount of things to play with already, including a fully functional multiplayer filled with things better than NPCs ie. actual human beings. This game is well worth €14 right now, but if you bought it a few years ago based on "future features" you only have yourself to blame for not knowing how early access works. Ignore the people who say the devs are lazy (only someone who doesn't have a clue how game development works would say this) or are ignoring or insulting players (they are friendly and always approachable).
I would also like to specifically point out as idiotic the two people who said that someone modded in cars while the devs didn't (the vehicles mod is basically pictures of cars, the real vehicles in PZ would be 3d and actually good and not awful), and that they're "holding back" the animation update. They are obviously still working on it and testing for bugs. Why would they hold it back just to annoy players? And they do not put "major features" on hold and do small ones like giving food calories instead. They are a small team but obviously can work on more than one thing at once. It is amazing how ignorant some reviewers on here are of how the real world works.
Anyway, ignore all those people and enjoy the game for what it is. Updates can be slow, yes, which is not because of "laziness" but because the devs are making an ambitious game. If you don't like that, then stick to playing iPhone puzzle games of 3mb or whatever. Games as ambitious as PZ require a lot of work and testing. PZ is my favourite game. Ignore the ignorant and let it become your favourite too.

Underneath this seemingly by-the-numbers corridor shooter, lies an outrageously fun and inventive 3rd person shooter.
A game extremely ahead of its time in terms of destruction and reconstruction, you not only get to destroy everything you see, including entire vertical levels, you often need to reconstruct what you have destroyed (in an astonishingly fascinating way, using the nano forge) in order to continue on.
The graphics start plain, but are increasingly amped up with amazing particle effects and explosions.
AI is impressive and works in team effort utilizing the 3d environment to its fullest.
The enemies are bugs, and this has been done before (lost planet like), but are graphically done well.
Weaponry in the game is some of the most fun I can recall in recent gaming.
The Singularity gun is an incredible and gorgeously animated black hole firing weapon.
The game even has weapon that is a unicorn that fires rainbow particle beams, anally.  Not kidding, its spectacular and it is real.
GPS is well designed and much needed in this maze of level design, albeit very fun and well layed out.
The story is well fleshed out, but takes a lot from Bioshock/Borderlands using Audio Logs.
Overall this is a far meatier game than Red Faction Guerilla (even if it doesnt have a jet pack... hey its got a spaceship!) and a worthy successor to an already great game.
Many people missed this game, probably quitting after the first couple levels, but I assure you, if you salvage, buy weaponry and powerups, you will be waiting for more bugs to pummel with your overpowered weapon rack!

**8/10**
-THE GOOD-
---#%$@ING STAR WARS: Empire at War puts you in the command seat of the immense Galactic Empire, the tennacious Rebel Alliance or, with the Forces of Corruption expansion, the Zahn Consortium; a brutal criminal cartel that dominates the galactic underworld. Games like Battlefront (the original games, not the half-baked EA remakes) let you live the battles and see the struggles of each soldier but Empire at War makes you the commander of entire fleets of Star Destroyers, swarms of X-Wing fighters, or legions of brutal Consortium death-squads. It's difficult to understate how satisfying it is to invest thousands of credits into building your fleet and executing the perfect strategy to take-apart your enemy's most formidable defences. The level of joy I feel when I hear the Imperial March playing in the background as my massive AT-AT walkers crush rebel troops underfoot (literally) is really what makes Empire at War special.
---SCALE: Empire at War gives you the tools, resources, and authority to take-on the entire galaxy in the game's 'Galactic Conquest' gamemode. In Galactic Conquest, you choose between a number of unique scenarios and are given a pre-set loadout of planets, heroes, and resources and one goal: annihilate all opposition and conquer the galaxy. Maps range from small handfuls of worlds to the ENTIRE Star Wars galaxy! On top of all that, each planet includes both space and ground combat and comes with their own unique sets of advantages and disadvantages. For example: Tatooine, the desert world Luke Skywalker grew up on, is prone to sandstorms which significantly reduces the accuracy of rocket weapons. That means any invasion of Tatooine must be planned ahead of time because, if the defenders have tanks or defense lasers, your rocket weapons won't be very effective and you need to get creative.
---THE FACTIONS: It would've been very easy for the developers to simply make the Rebellion, Empire and Consortium factions functionally identical with different reskinned units but that's definately NOT what they did. All three factions have definate strengths and weaknesses that must be taken into account. The Galactic Empire has access to far more resources than the Rebels or Consortium and can create fleets and armies very quickly but they rely on strategy to be used effectively. You can't just charge a fleet of Star Destroyers into a Rebel attack force and expect to win, for instance. The Empire also has another unique advantage over the Rebellion and the Consortium that I'll discuss later. The Rebellion can't engage enemies directly because their units, though able to do significant damage, don't do very well in sustained combat. That means Rebel players must be willing to use hit-and-run tactics to fight their foes. The Rebellion also has the most powerful starfighters in the entire game and good Rebel players learn to use this to their advantage. They also advance themselves by stealing technology from the Empire and Consortium; gaining access to cool and unique units allong the way. By the end-game, the Rebellion ends-up with an extremely flexible fleet that can handle almost any threat. The Zahn Consortium, however, is much more brutal. They rely on the 'Corruption' game mechanic which, by doing special missions, the player can sabotage their enemies, move through their territory unseen, and gain access to powerful new units. Be careful, though, because your enemies can use their charismatic Heroes to purge your corruption! The Consortium relies on it's tough units to beat their foes; their fleet is built to brawl up-close and personal and their ground forces are capable of fielding units that counter even the most powerful enemy units. For example, they can build a Ysalamiri Cage that prevents Force-users from using their powers, and can turn an extremely powerful unit like Darth Vader into a much more managable threat!
---THE DEATH STAR: Yes, you heard me right. The Empire, in Galactic Conquest mode, can build the Death Star. By constructing expensive Research Facilities on various worlds and researching various parts and technologies, the Galactic Empire can build the Death Star (or the Death Star II from Return of the Jedi if you have the Forces of Corruption expansion). Once construction begins, all players get a warning message "DEATH STAR CONSTRUCTION HAS BEGUN" and a 5 minute countdown. "DEATH STAR CONSTRUCTION COMPLETE" heralds the completion of the most powerful unit in the entire game. As you might expect, the Death Star is capable of utterly destroying entire planets. A fleet with the Death Star in it can engage in space battles as usual. However, you will see a graphic on the HUD with a countdown "ENEMY BASE WILL BE IN RANGE IN...MINUTES". Once the countdown is complete, you can pull the lever and watch a demonstration of your fully armed and operational battle station. The resulting blast will completely annihilate any structures, ground forces and heroes stationed on the planet's surface and turns it into a lifeless asteroid field. The Death Star II, from the Forces of Corruption expansion, can even target Capital Ships and Space Stations with the Superlaser and instantly destroy them in one blast (at the expense of a delayed countdown). The Death Star is easily the most powerful unit in the entire game; so powerful that it cannot even be attacked in a regular space battle! It lingers ominously in the background, inching closer and closer to firing range of the planet. Fear not, however! It can be destroyed! If you manage to locate the Death Star, the Rebellion can stage a daring, desperate assault on the Death Star using the Rogue Squadron Hero Unit and destroy it. The Zahn Consortium can send the cunning droid bounty hunter Hero Unit, IG-88, to sabotage it's main reactor and cause it to self-destruct. If destroyed, it CANNOT be rebuilt so use it wisely!
---MODS: Though not as numerous as games like Skyrim and Fallout, Empire at War does have its own modding community (ModDB). While they range in quality from utterly unfinished to out-of-this-goddamn-world, they are fairly easy to install and it even has Steam Workshop support if you're new to modding! I personally recommend the "Thrawn's Revenge" mod, otherwise known as "Imperial Civil War" which totally overhauls all the units and planets in the game to reflect the old Expanded Universe post-Return of the Jedi continuity. It's easilly the best mod out there for Empire at War and it's totally free! *cough* Bethesda Creation Club *cough*
-THE BAD-
---BUGS: As is inevitable with video games, Empire at War does have it's share of bugs. I haven't encountered any game-breaking bugs in my play sessions but I've noticed a few audio and graphical glitches. Nothing huge or game-breaking (you won't see units distend like overcooked pasta or anything like that), just little things that might irk you if you're the kind of person that notices those things often.
---FPS: I've noticed that Empire at War tends to struggle to maintain a stable 60 fps when you zoom out in large space or ground battles (especially on the more graphically intensive maps like the Maw Installation, Taris or Coruscant) but nothing major. Most of the time it's temporary and I haven't had it dip bellow 45 but everybody's computer is different. It's a fairly old game so most people shouldn't have too much of a problem running it.
---GAME BALANCE: None of the game's units are especially powerful (okay, besides the Death Star but that doesn't really count), but there are a few instances where your faction might struggle to compete. For example: I find that the Rebel Alliance tends to struggle more against Zahn Consortium in space because they're so heavily armoured and they have weapons that can penetrate shields (the main source of Rebel Ships toughness). Using their powerful fighers and bombers tends to fix this, though.

I have played for 7 hours, at the time of writing. That is absolutely untrue. I have played this game for over 12 days. The Long Dark takes survival and freezes it into your brain. At first, you're playing it like any other game, exploring, laughing at the cheesy-cartoony graphics and the occasional bad placement of an object. Then you actually decide to play. Suddenly, you're looting houses like it meant something, trudging painfully through the freezing snow because you need everything on your back, even though it makes you easy for the wolves. Then you're being mauled by bears and falling through the ice, and eating wolves and kissing your rifle because it's the only reason you're alive.
The Long Dark absolutely lives up to its expectations. The immersion becomes powerful, and Jennifer Hale of Mass Effect fame, who voices the female survivor here, absolutely drives it home, saying exactly what you're thinking. The game is tough, it's relentless, and it's fulfilling. It isn't a crafting game, where you build until resources are cheap and you've conquered the galaxy, it's a survival game to its very core, where you either make it or fall flat, and most of the time is spent bouncing across the thin line between success and failure.
Graphics are good, if simple. Gameplay, likewise as simple as possible, which works, if a bit confusing at first. Moderate replayability, depending on the kind of success you've had. I don't imagine, if I lived for a hundred days in-game, I'd be eager to go back.

I played this game for the first time in the PS2 way back when I was a child. Even then, the amazing scenery, PayJ and the unique (for 12 year old me) gameplay got me totally hooked on it. At times I found it difficult, but never boring. It was exciting for me to photograph all the different animal species there are on Planet Hylis, and the moment I unlocked the Beluga I wasted hours just flying and not doing much else.
Many years later I found this game on Steam, and I bought it. In my eyes, this game has aged considerably well as far as the story goes, and even the gameplay (while a bit repetitive) is fulfilling and enjoyable. Its graphics, while top notch for its time, can get a bit buggy but that's to be expected from a 2003 game trying to run on 2017 computers.
It is one of my favourite games, however, not because of the gameplay, or the scenery, or the open world elements to it. The story had me going on an emotional roller coaster. From comedy, to tragedy in just a few short steps. Young me and adult me still weep in the scene where you know who gets taken by the Alpha Forces. I recommend it to anyone who likes to play games for the story and doesn't mind going through some repetitive gameplay or facing a few bugs to get to experience it. This game has been one of the best gaming experiences in my life. I will adore it forever.

I mean, everybody knows about the sensational "Beyond Good and Evil" right? (looks at the friends owning this game)... Ohhh, I see.... Well let me illuminate you why you owe it to yourself to play this game right now.
Mixing up action adventure, platforming, fighting game, driving, telling epic Sci-Fi story... and taking pictures, Beyond Good and Evil is a love child of the designer of Rayman, Michel Ancel, that will awe you from the start to the very end with super-likeable characters, wacky yet engaging story about sticking it to the man, very pretty and imaginative graphics, urban, rebellious and crazy soundtrack, tight and fun shooting, platforming, fighting and driving gameplay, and a big and crazy world to explore. Let me make a quick note regarding the tone of the community & some of the other reviews at this moment in time.
, it's good for you to be objective & aware of two very important things. (1) This game's story mode, its crowning patch and mark of completion, has been a long time coming, and (2) its fans are really, really, looking forward to it. They want it
. Even if they seem not to sometimes.
To be clear, I'm not an angry fan. I have always highly recommended this game at all stages in its development, and have no problem publicly professing my disdain for the throngs of players that are brazenly pushing a hyperbolic—and often dishonest—narrative toward the public eye about the villainy of Hinterland for daring not to cave to pressure and to take the time to get this masterpiece right.
Without going too far down that rabbit hole... what to make of all that frustration?
It's straightforward. The anticipation for August's (!!) Story Mode release—and don't believe everything you read; this month marks the first time Hinterland have ever announced a definite release date—has been drawn out over so long, and has been intensified by multiple new, ambitious additions to the game's original vision by a small, self-funded team that has fought hard to make it to this landmark point in development...
...that people are
.
Just remember that when you're looking at all the vitriol-laced rants that have been popping up the week I'm writing this. People are angry because, after more than two years in early access,
. If that doesn't tell you something positive... well, it should. It really should. They'll get mad at me for saying it, but the reality is that no-one would be so worked up about the game taking longer than planned to come out if it wasn't (a) very good and (b) hotly anticipated.
As it stands, you're looking at the game at a great time, because you don't have to go through any of that. Cheers.
Story Mode is on the way in August, and a new update is coming toward the end of this month (May, 2017). You're getting a very fully-developed and immersive Sandbox mode with an order of magnitude more content than early adopters got to start with a few years ago. The objective of sandbox is blissfully, elegantly simple: Survive as long as possible. There's nothing supernatural about the game except for some extra-aggressive wildlife (for which there is a lore explanation). There are no zombies, no monsters, and no NPCs (for now) to attack you in the world. You're alone, with tons of ground to cover and scavenge, an array of tools to discover and craft, countless new types of clothes to layer onto your character thanks to the most recent major patch, and your only adversaries are your own vitals.
You can play the Sandbox on multiple difficulties, from the pacifistic, borderline-therapeutic Pilgrim, where you have to provoke hostile wildlife before it even notices you... to the utter brutality of Interloper, which is bar none one of the most if not the most challenging survival modes in contemporary gaming. The world will literally try to kill you, because as the difficulty setting's name attests, you are an interloper and you do not belong. And, of course, there are two difficulty levels in between those as well. So whether it's a brutal challenge you seek, or a beautiful world to explore, The Long Dark has both in spades, with considerable expansions to the game's features and entertainment value coming just over the horizon.
And that's to say nothing of the game's gorgeous, minimalist soundtrack, of which I will never be able to get enough.
I'd write more, but as I have said countless times, The Long Dark is at its best when you are brand new to the game world, completely unspoiled, and know nothing about where you are, where you need to go, or how to survive for more than a day. The first time your life drops to below 5% and you manage to stumble into shelter, patch your wounds, stuff your face, quench your thirst, and close your eyes in respite just before death takes you, then find yourself waking up to a recovering body the next morning... you will have discovered what makes The Long Dark such an incredible and visceral survival experience.
I'm obviously an ardent fan, so take away from the above whatever extra layers of positivity you feel you have to, but objectively speaking, this is a rare game crafted by rare people. It will make you feel cold, it will make your heart race, and it will draw you in. The likelihood that you will regret your purchase as a newcomer in May of 2017 or later is really quite low. This isn't hyperbole. I'm not that easily excited. I'm actually in my 30s. I had an NES controller in my hand when I was 5, and have been a gamer ever since. I have a multi-genre list, spanning decades, ranking my favorite games of all time. It's populated by Bioware RPGs, City Builders, Real time and Turn-based strategy titles, Chrono Trigger, and more.
This is not only one of the games on that list, but is easily one of the highest. And I'm just talking about the
.

What you have to understand about this game is that it does what it does almost too well: create an oppressive zombie apoc simulator. This is both the game's greatest fault and strength. Strength, in that the environment is consistent and engrossing; you will need to work to survive every day and form a long plan towards sustainability lest you perish.
Fault, in that survival is a tedious activity in this game as it no doubt would be in real life. Once you figure out how to build an effective safehouse, establish a primary food source and achieve a relative margin of safety then the game takes a more boring and repetitive turn. Eventually, you will find yourself branching out more and more out of a need for exploration more than for actual survival- and this is probably when you will get killed because one wrong encounter, one miscalculation or mistep off a ledge or wrong turn in the woods can have disastrous consequences.
Single player is lonely and oppressive as the game currently stands. It will challenge you. It will make you cautious. It will make you bold. But when you prevail it will bore you. Oh, how it will bore you. Granted, should the devs input things like interactive NPCs, allies, antagonists etc., the dynamic will no doubt change towards the more interesting. For now, we will have to wait.
Multiplayer is another beast entirely. For local lan you will find hours of fun here. But the problems I mention with survival tedium will eventually become true but w/friends.
I believe that a guided antagonism is the best way to soak up the most fun from this game. I forsee that a closed server with sided teams playing one camp against the other would provide oodles more variety, fun and political intrigue- but online random servers is a very hit or miss affair (mostly miss) where grief spawners can and will destroy everything you have created for the spammy thrill of it without any sense of sportsmanship or teamwork toward a more engrossing experience. This is its own kind of tedium, unfortunately.
All the same, this is a wonderful game with wonderful potential. A new animation release is around the corner that looks to revitalize and gel this entire experience. So I will continue to subscribe and enjoy in the hope that this game continues to improve.

Honestly, I'm not quite sure why I bought this game. It's not that it's a bad game, it's the fact that I'm too scared to even play it that has me questioning why I bought it in the first place. Sure, playing it for my YouTube channel (that never really got off the ground and has been left in the dustbin until I can find proper time to make it of decent quality) SEEMED like a good idea at the time, but in practice, I found this game almost impossible to play. This game terrifies me into a state that's practically paralysis (which really isn't good when trying to use a mouse and keyboard), so this game accomplishes, and quite effectively, it's goal to be a horror game.
The gameplay itself is rather original. I've never played a horror game where I was stuck in one place, and mostly powerless to do something. Sure, there's been games where you can't defend yourself, but I've never seen a game like that where I couldn't run away. Although the doors provide some means of defence, you can't use them forever due to the drain on limited power. Being forced to work within such tight parameters makes the game challenging and frightening. Also, you never quite know where the animatronics are going to go, especially during the later nights. Their chaotic movement makes you constantly worry that, perhaps the next time you check the cameras, one of the animatronics will be waiting for you when you put your monitor down. Suspence really shines in this game, not only in the previously mentioned scenario, but also when you run out of power and wait for Freddy to come and make a mess of things.
A few people say that the jumpscares presented in the game are just a cheap tactic to make a weak horror game stronger (I'm sorry, I couldn't resist), but in this case, I will have to disagree. In my experience, jumpscares are only as good as the atmosphere that accompanies them. This game does a pretty excellent job of setting up atmosphere. The darkness obscures your view when you look through the cameras, and what you DO see is pretty frightening on its own. The restaurant honestly looks pretty rundown, which probably adds to the atmosphere as well. And, back when the game first came out, it had an air of mystery and unknown about it that made the game all the more frightening to me.
The character design alone would make the game unsettling. Bonnie in particular gives me the creeps, though I can't really put my finger on why. Chica also makes some unsettling expressions in the game, but even when Chica ISN'T making unsettling expressions, the off-putting feeling remains. For whatever reason, Freddy didn't scare me much at first, but Freddy's sudden change from slightly not-menacing into aggressively menacing is startling in the later nights. Unfortunately, I have little to say on Foxy. The only thing I found scary was Foxy's tendency to suddenly attack.
The story also adds a different kind of horror to the game. Animatronics on the fritz can be scary enough, but in this game, finding out WHY they are adds both horror and sadness to the game. Digging into the story is an adventure in itself.
This game also carries a fair bit of nostalgia for me. When it first released, I quickly became very invested in the story, and I spent most of my time watching videos on the game. This game also really inspired me to make art as well, which was very helpful for my drawing skills. When it released, I was in the middle of a very difficult time during my life, and this game and series really gave me something interesting to focus on.
There's few flaws I can attribute to this game, but there are certainly flaws. Gameplay can (and most likely WILL) get repetitive after playing the game fully through. The video camera mechanic takes a back seat the further you go along in the game, which is kind of sad considering a lot of the atmosphere is seen through these cameras, but this is less of a flaw and more of a personal irritation of mine. The randomness of the game can also be quite frustrating, and in later nights, Freddy is absolutely unforgiving. One mistake can end a run.
Overall, I have to recommend this game.

Tried the demo. A hybrid between Heroes of Might and Magic and Civilizations.
PROS
1. Story looks interesting
But I couldn't grasp anything interesting from the introductory video beyond "you must tame the land". So, I got pretty bored but I'm sure there is a lot of backstory.
2. A lot of stuff
A lot of tech which happens to resemble the Civilization tech tree for easy recognition.
CONS
1. Same problems as HOMM
You're going to have problems with scaling up. Automating battles may cause your units to suffer damage which you try to avoid, thus causing you to play every tactical battle to min-max and prevent troop loss.
2. Actions that could be passives
Have to be next to your town to cast "Inspiration" (adds 1 research) for 0 mana is something that should be a passive. Getting additional techpoints are quite important in 4X games e.g. helping to wonder rush.
It would be quite ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to have a hero stand around to cast some sort of "bless thine city" spell.
If you want to have to make a choice of which spell to cast, force a choice between 2 passives.
3. Redundant spells
You have to play a tactical battle with a spellcaster that begins with up to 9 spells and only 1 move, 1 action per turn. A lot of pretty redundant spells. Lots of choice but not able to execute everything.
Spells/abilities cooldown in about 5 turns, so unless you want to play an ultra draggy battle that will be a game by itself, I would not suggest this.
I do not see the fun of dragging out "click and attack" battles.
4. Tactical combat - Direction of Attack
Can't see which direction I'm going to attack my enemy from.
There might be direction arrows in the game but I couldn't easily find them.
5. Tactical combat - Ending
The battles end like HOMM, one winner one loser, which is a problem. There is no tactical retreat or running away. Auto-resolve just ends with one side dead. No kiting, hit-and-run or guerilla tactics, just a ringed match.
6. Tactical Comabt - No of turns
Drags the game on for a longer period of time.
In the strategic map, only 1 season (day) would have passed.
7. Extreme similarity to Civ
Settler is a pioneer, Scout is a Scout, Library is a Library, etc, etc.
I was hoping for uniqueness from Fallen Enchantress, not a portover from Civilization.
Do not buy: Stardock DRM.

Well, I played this for a grand total of 43 minutes, since it's on free demo on Steam at time of writing. I realise this isn't a full review, 43 minutes isn't very long, but the point of a demo is to entice you to want to play the game further, so I can say the demo failed for me.
Having never played a Fallen Enchantress game before, I found the controls not very intuitive, and felt frustrated a lot of the time. I don't know if there are ways to choose which things you research in what order, clicking on them didn't do squat, so my research carried on automatically. I couldn't easily see when things I was building would finish, or view or edit my building queue. It took quite a while to work out how to combine units into an army, and the relative limitations of army sizes.
Combat is a huge mess. I'm used to being able to wait and move my unit turn further down in the queue, like Heroes of Might & Magic, but instead in this I guess if my unit can't reach the enemy and isn't a long range unit he just has to pass a turn he could still have done *something* in, just not move. Most of my combat turns involved me passing turns, everyone was out of mana pretty much immediately and I wasn't presented with any information on how or when they regained it.
I then ran into a battle in which I had to fight a ghost. The ghost is immune to all physical damage. No one has any mana.
That was when the 43 minutes elapsed and I decided I'd had enough.

It's been a while since I've been into an online FPS game. The co-op nature of it is a _huge_ plus. Graphics are great, and the gameplay tends to be far more exciting than not when online. Surprisingly the bots are well designed and even if you don't have a full party, you don't feel like you're hindered.
If you approach it like a Quake-style shooter, or tend to prefer that kind of gameplay, you'll find yourself frustrated. The movement mechanics, while pretty freeing, feel still at the same time limiting. Movement speed, jumping, jet fuel, it's all balanced more on the side of "slow and methodical" rather than high-octane twitch shooting.
I don't know if that style of movement/aiming is a product of the game having to work with a controller as well as keyboard, but it's nice to have the option.
Give this game a go if you're looking for something to grab a few friends with and take on bots or other players in 4 vs 1.

I'm confused by a lot of the negative reviews.  Many say the game is abandoned or incomplete.  Some say they bought years ago and feel ripped off because it is no longer being updated.  I only recently bought the game and 5.5 hours in, I feel like I'm playing a fully developed, complete, and polished game.  More than all that, it is also a rather fun and engaging game.
I didn't follow devolpment, so maybe I'm unaware of unfulfilled promises from the developer, but I can't really imagine what people feel is missing from the game.   I suppose more robot types could be added, but I've already encountered quiete a few different ones, all with different traits and behaviors.  I don't think I've even encountered all of them.  I find their hunting AI to be very good.  They actually hunt you the way an Englishman would hunt a fox.  When they spot me or I draw attention to myself, they put ot a pretty decent dragnet in the area and I can't always get away.
I find the proceedural generation of the islands to be solid.  A convincing, English countryside with lots of interesting terrain to consider.  Over time you come to know the various copses of trees that you use to travel through.  some reviews complain about how easy it is to get lost while simultaneously complaining about lack of depts--but a lot of the games depth comes from navigating the land, finding your way around, using the landmarks such as those weird towers to orient yourself, and finding good routs to get around without getting detected.
Lot of complaints about not being able to go in buildings.  Honestly, the game would get very tedious if you had to go in each building and click on some drawers and cabinets to find a few scraps of food.   That level of looting gameplay is just not necesarry in a game that isn't about loot.  If you could go into the buildings, then the robots would have to go into buildings to look for you, taking them out of their field searches--which is the whole point of this game--being hunted across English Country side like a fox.  If you could go into the buildings, you would spend tons of time hiding inside of buildings, which would also get boring.  Its fun to sneak around the alleys and buildings of the hamlets--I'm glad I don't have to spend 15 minutes going in and searching 6 buildings everytime I encounter a hamlet.
Sound is great.   The robots make all these computer bleeps and boops that sound like something out of an creepy, 70s sci-fi movie.  Its actually kind of ominous, when youre hiding behind a building, and a robot is coming your way.  You get nervous as those bleeeps and bloops get louder, and you know he's probably going to come around that corner at any minute.  The game is actually very atmospheric, with an ominous sense of dread haning over everything that I wasn't at all expecting from this game when I bought it.  I thought it was just going to be a funny tone (and it is funny) but its also a little dark and ominous.
At 5.5 hours, so far, I love it.  I feel like I'm really just now digging into the meat of the game--learning the lay of the land, developing competence at foraging, finding meteorites, and avoiding/destroying robots.   It has lots of content, and the proceeduring generation of everything ensures that new, unthought of tactical situations appear all the time.  Last time I played, I got spotted and ended up finding myself between two hunting parties with a variety of robot types.  I vanished into a ditch in a copse of trees, and the robots were hunting all around, but hadn't found me.  Then that balloon started drifting my way.  I have watched that thing hunt the island for hours, but this time, it actually happened to come my way.  All I could do was lay still and hope the search beam didn;t hit me.  When it hit me, the alarm went off, my hiding place was revealed, and I had to make a quick decision about how to flee.
These are the elements of good gameplay.
I got it on sale for $5.  I guess $20 is a little steep, but this is a high-quality, complete, and fun game.  I just don't think $20 is really that far off the mark.  If you see it for $15 or less, I suggest you go for it, and if you like stealth/survival/proceedurally generated games, I say go for it at $20

Fun turn-based tactical battle hex board game with power cards and 5 piece types: melee defender + melee attacker, ranged, healer & boss.  Three different decks mix up the details of those basic 5 types.  There are also enhancement cards to assign to pieces and general affect cards too.  Finally, you have a deck of power-cards that can be applied up to a max of one per turn to sway the game in your favour.
It's a small download, so give it a try and just play through the tutorials for each deck available and see if its the kind of game you'd like.
It's a fun free-to-play game, with micro-transactions for buying other decks and sets of power-cards.  But it doesn't appear to be too pay-to-win.   Could do with a larger player base, but great fun if you have friends to play against.
Blitz style live games are similar to blitz-chess, or you can play Duels which are not timed and allow you to play turns over hours or days.
If dev's continue to add further decks, cards, etc. and maybe more polish then this would be a 5-star game.
Also can be played via app on tablets, mobiles, etc.

8/10 - Overall a great game, here's the breakdown:
Story: Pretty simple and easy to follow, By today's standard (2017) it doesn't surprise nor bring anything new (maybe for it's time it did?) However it's strength comes from it's characters and setting which are rather endearing relative to other games. See tilt-factor for plot objectives.
Gameplay: Its really Good mix of puzzles (don't worry no real head scracthes), good stealth portions throughout and serviceable fighting portions that don't wear out even with it's simplicty.
Presentation: As always a non-realistic approach to graphics tends to hold up with time and Beyond Good and Evil does just that. Even if a player finds the lack of detail & textures disappointing the art style and aethtic still does well.
High praise to the soundtrack though it is excellent and you'll find yourself pumped and trying to follow the beats and non-english lyrics as best you can
Tilt factor: I really enjoyed the cultural diversity or at least the multiple cultural insiprations present throught the games presentation and is a very refreshing aesthtic against other more common aesthtics like Pos-apocolyptic, war torn, cyber punk and so on.
Another commendable feat is that the games obejective is mostly non-killing ones and often involve investigative journalism. It's uplifting to see a game that isn't about killing outright and yet still be fun and rewarding; a real + 1 here

There are some glaring graphical bugs on modern systems, such as flickering textures and effects, which can *sometimes* be fixed, but it's hit-and-miss. I was able to fix them on my old PC, but the same method doesn't work on my newer gaming laptop, so there's nothing I can do about it, and the game looks completely broken. I also experienced framerate drops today, which should NOT be happening with a game from 2003 playing on a 960M.
If you have a PS3 or an Xbox 360, do yourself a favour and get the HD edition of the game that was released for those systems. I finally broke down and bought this game after eyeballing it for several months. Overall, I have to say there is good and there is bad about this game.
I'll start with the bad:
The mech shown in the game trailer is not yet implemented. Nor are the riding dinosaurs.
The magic system is a joke. The build your own spell concept is a very neat idea, but is still very lacking. On top of that, stamina regenerates so painfully slowly it's unrealistic to expect to be anything other than a sword fighter.
The mining is still a bit wonky. Mining foreground blocks is fine. Auto and free both work fine. Mining background blocks is a pain. Auto doesn't work on background blocks. Instead, you can only mine background blocks by specifically pointing at them. I'd love to see a mode that strips front and background blocks with a single stroke, to make strip-mining more efficient.
Now the good:
The game has some features I haven't seen in other 2D sandbox RPGs. Namely capturing monsters and shapeshifting.
I like the music, and the scenery is also nice.
Your stats and abilities don't rely entirely on the items you can equip.
Ovarall:
I would recommend this game. Even in its unfinished state, I've enjoyed it immensely. I eagerly look forward to future updates. If you like 2D sandbox RPG style games, this is a must buy!

So I picked up this game for the free weekend, having never actually played a build civilization stratagy game before. A stand-a-lone game by Stardock, upon the opening intro I see interesting artwork and fantasy. The story line or plot is pretty basic. You choose between 10 soverign or heros, who aim to rule/conquer the world of Elemental. Witch has been torn asunder and is in ruins ripe to be brought together again by cataclysm. The soverigns themselves and their civilizations are very themed and have a style of their own. A unique gameplay for whoever you choose. I selected Magnar. I was drawn to (naturally) by his warlock abilities and the story line of ( I'm a dragon/human thing called a Quendar, Were old and ancient and you're not. So I shall make slaves and use fire and death magic to rule the weak. ) Cool huh? A short tuturial and you can jump into the game.  Using you'r soverign you build and take over the world of Elemental. Build settlements and watchposts to increase your economy and research warfare/civilization/magic. It took a while to get the hang of all the micro-managing but after a while I think I got the hang of it. More heros DO join your civilization, while it grows in fame and fortune. Witch they want a part of , butt chose wisely your heros to your strengths and game play. Also you have to build an army or two to kill wild animals, bandits, undead, demons, trolls, ogres and everything else you can think of in the fantasy world. I was rather impressed by the monster library in the game. During all this you can also pick up quests to complete mainly by killing or collecting things while your doing your build civilization thang. And then you have the other soverigns to deal with ! Oh yeah and there is these huge epic elemental boss guys that'll pop up that'll try to destroy you....This game was interestingly addicting by the fact of I MUST BUILD MY EMPIRE BIGGER.  and level up my soverin and heros to rule the weak. An almost primal urge of destroy and conquer kinda takes over. A lot of content to get lost in while you play It's defineitly a game to pick up if you have a chance.

The concept behind Evolve sounds good on paper, but the implementation is very lacking.
There are basically two ways this game can and should be played. As the Monster you're often starting out with a need to be stealthy, as you're not strong enough to attack the hunters yet and will likely die a quick death if found. During this period you have to avoid triggering events that give away your location, like birds scattering into the air. You also leave footprints that the Hunters can follow, except through water. Meanwhile, you have to kill and feed off local wildlife so you can evolve and get stronger. This stealth portion of the game works pretty well and will get your heart racing more often than not as the Hunters are rarely far behind you. Once evolved you may choose to engage the Hunter team, killing them all to win the match or, alternatively, completing an objective on the map.
The Hunter team are tasked with tracking, capturing and killing the Monster before it evolves to its maximum. Tracking prints and predicting where the monster will head next are big parts of this. The Hunter team consists of a damage dealer, support, medic and a trapper who have to work together very closely to succeed. Communication is vital to find the monster in time.
Sadly, the game simply gets frustrating on too many levels. There is no balanced matchmaking, which often results in one side being completely slaughtered by the other. Be it a newbie monster against a team full of level 50's, or a team full of newbies against a level 50 monster. Both are equally frustrating and feel extremely unfair. Voice communication also tends to be completely absent in any of the matches I've played so far.
On maps with objectives it's also very frustrating that you are required to complete objectives, but at the same time can't realistically complete those objectives without feeding and evolving first, which takes too much time. By the time you're ready to fight, the hunters have already completed the majority of their objectives or have already downright won the game. Especially in the Nest gamemode, you can't realistically do ANYTHING against the hunters for the first 10 minutes, which is extremely frustrating.
There's also the issue of lack of replayability. Even though the concept isn't that much different than, for example, Left 4 Dead, this game becomes boring extremely quickly. Maybe because the game forces long periods of hide and seek between big badass fights. Either way, I've played for about 5 hours now and can't say I have an overwhelming urge to start the game up again. Gameplay is enjoyable, but only for one or two matches at a time. And even then, being slaughtered in some unfair unbalanced fashion just makes me want to ragequit the game sooner rather than later.
Then there is the issue of DLC. When I bought the game, it was on sale so I got the Monster Edition for 47,99 Euro. This supposedly included a Season Pass, which one may assume means that you get all current and future DLC along with the base game. Good deal, so it seemed. Only to later find out that the biggest reason one would WANT the Season Pass, namely the new Monsters, aren't even included in it. There's a whole list of DLC packs that aren't included in the season pass or in the Monster Edition, which is downright ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
So would I recommend this game? Meh, it's a tough call honestly. It's amusing for a while, but certainly not worth 60 bucks. If you can get it for a good price during a sale then yes, go get it and you'll have your money's worth of fun. But don't bother getting the Monster Edition. It doesn't have anything in it that makes the game better or more enjoyable and you'll just waste cash.
Due to lack of replayability, bad balance matchmaking and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t DLC practices, I'm gonna have to say no, I do not recommend this game.

Evolve is a really well made little game. It's gorgeous to look at, the controls are smooth and the gameplay is fun. However, it feels very half-finished.
There's no campaign, only three monsters (unless you pay...) and the game modes are rather un-balanced. Above all though, Evolve is hollow. Hunters track monster, creating tense and gripping skirmishes if they can catch the weak creature, and when the monster hits level 3 you get this fantastic raid boss-like battle as a finale BUT that's it. There was a lot of scope for a campaign, character development, history, ANY kind of story really!
The game has been sold at full price, despite a criminal lack of content. Not only that, but day1DLC... as far as I'm concerned that is despicable. I can't help shake the feeling that we're being sold a platform to buy DLC from.
It's a real shame, the core idea is great fun, the gameplay is sound, but the experience is shallow.
Also, the menus and progression are awfully implemented, the console-itis is strong here.
