Ah, Empire at War. Where to start?
It is, as the name helpfully implies, a Star Wars game, an RTS to be specific, released in 2006. The vanilla game having a Rebel and Imperial story campaign, the latter being a what-if? and the former following the old canon before Disney. Both of them are rather easy, the Empire one moreso, and are functionally, in my opinion, little more than extraordinarily long tutorials, mainly prepping the play for Galactic Conquest. The DLC Forces of Corruption adds an entirely new faction, who are functionally a galactic crime syndicate, with their own entirely new campaign as well. The story is signficantly imrpoved from the previous two, and is rather enjoyable overall, as the new faction also has entirely new units, vehicles, and ships.
Cons-wise, the base game is rather outdated graphics wise for obvious reasons. Ground battles are generally repetitive slogs. The AI is as dumb as a sack of braindead kittens, even on higher difficulties. Auto resolve, as in the vein of almost every game to ever have the feature, is bound to only end in heart break. There are also still some bugs and similar hanging around, although I haven't encountered anything truly game breaking. But the biggest issue overall is balancing in Forces of Corruption, as the new faction introduced is hilariously, utterly, and completely overpowered, capable of casually swatting aside either the Empire or Rebels.
However, dont be fooled. It is in of itself one of my favorite games of all time with ease, and I have been playing it for nearly a decade now on numerous computers, and for good reason. The space battles are the highlight of the game, and watching a Star Destroyer swarm obliterate a Rebel fleet is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic. The strategic layer/ galaxy map portion is also strangely enthralling, watching a stack of Star Destroyers build up while you station AT-AT's on literally every planet of value, then some for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles. And finally, mods. So. Many. Mods. You do yourself a diservice not to play Republic at War, Thrawns Revenge, or EAW Remake, which has updated the graphics in space battles to more than easily match any modern standard for most people.
Overall, it has flaws, but this game is still one the very best Star Wars games out there, and for very good reason. Buy it. Do the tutorial and a few campaigns, maybe a few galactic conquests and skirmishs. Then mod it like its going out of style.

Yes, I recommend this game.  The decks are balanced, from what I've seen.  You win gold every time you play, which varies with how long the game actually goes.  If it's only a couple rounds, you win less gold than a game that goes on for awhile.  The gold can be spent on booster packs for the power cards, which can change the game dramatically. Other decks can be purchased (albeit kind of costly) with in-game gold.  Yes, there are microtransactions for some items, but none of them are game breaking.  No one that spends real money on the game has much of an advantage over the F2P players.  It's all in how you play the game.  If you like turn-based strategy, get this.  The only real drawback is that live games don't happen too often.  However, there is an async mode to make up for this, and at this point I have 8 games going.  So, really, that's not even much of a complaint, although I would love to see the player base expand so that there is no shortage of games.

The options menu is also very lacking, not that the options menu needs to be grand for a game like this, but it helps if some things can be tweaked. The only things that could be changed regarding graphics was the resolution and "effects", whatever that entails. However, you could turn the effects all the way from ultra to off, with no noticable difference, so i am still confused as to what it actually does. The texture quality makes this game looks like it should be on a flash games site, like Newgrounds or Mousebreaker, not a site like Steam.
Overall, this is a game that could be played on co-op with a friend, but it doesn't have much about it that is compelling. It's more of a "Get drunk with your friends and bugger about on a game" kind of game, if you get my meaning.
Anyway, mediocre game with nothing that sets it apart from other platformers. This game was the winner of the Game Concept Challenge 2011, but it doesn't seem like the devs have added anything much to the original game back in 2011.

The first time I played this game was in 2017 so I have no influential nostalgia.  I have played other old classics and many of them have not aged well.  The same is partially true for this game however it is still a decent / good game even by today's standards.
This is primarily an adventure game with varied mechanics & interactions, it manages to maintain a wholesome feel and makes the player feel well involved in the game universe.  This game has well done; story, characters, settings, themes, varied game-play, and all of these elements are connected together fairly well.
There are a few pieces of the game which are problematic however they are mostly tolerable.  Game optimization / graphics was a constant issue for me (FPS / graphical issues) despite trying to tweak settings for 45 minutes.  Game play controls & cameras were often crappy (the camera would often start rotating when I want to travel in a strait path creating control issues).  The game is only about 7 hours long (with about 40% of side quests completed) and I will probably never touch this game again (low replay-ability).
With all that said, I am not fond of adventure games however I did enjoy this one.
Ratings;
Year 2003 (game released, estimated score if I played it then) – 8.5/10
Year 2017 – 7/10

Beyond Good and Evil is an Action Adventure game where you follow the story of Jade.
Beyond Good and Evil has a rather short story but an interesting one with some humor as well. This interesting story combined with an original universe makes for an enjoyable experience. Something fun as well is traveling with a companion for 90% of the game. However, it's a shame they didn't expand the story. At times you'll get the feeling what you did the past hour could've been done in around 10 minutes and the universe has tons of opportunity's for extra content.
What they did really well, is really make the universe feel alive and give it a character. There's interesting and likeable characters and some mini-games & side content to explore. The game itself is rather linear but if you really feel like it there's some places to explore that aren't needed for the main story.
Combat is fun and well done, and ranges from melee combat with a mix of range and even hovercraft and space battles! The game isn't afraid to try out new mechanics either. Which is a good thing. The game does lean heavily towards stealth gameplay most of the time. However, I had no problems with this as i really enjoyed those missions.
Now the game has a couple of cons as well. The camera can be horrible at moments and makes certain points in the game harder than they should be. And for some gamers knowing what to do next might be hard at times, the game doesn't always hold you hand and will require you to look around and use your brain at times. Instead of following a waypoint on your map for example. However I doubt if this is really a con since it's well done.
Overall Beyond Good and Evil is a really solid game. It's a lot of fun and has a great universe. However, although i really enjoyed my time in this game, it's not a mind-blowing experience or a perfect game.

well I played like half of the game so here's my review so far
Story: pretty generic just like the predecessors
Gameplay: WAY more linear than guerrilla, but with more diverse enemies. Armageddon is a third person shooter compared to guerrilla's free roam gameplay
Sound: Good, the music fits well, weapons feel decent and monsters don't sound half bad, voice acting is pretty good as well
Graphics: improved from Guerrilla, holds up today, can run on most rigs due to good optimization
STRONG POINTS: -Destruction system which is a trademark of the Red Faction series works very well here as well, being able to use a magnet gun to take down structures and throw them into enemies (or vice versa)
-Varied arsenal & upgrades system gives the game some slight replayability and gives you things to use in any situation
WEAK POINTS:
-Campaign has a very short length, I played 50% of the story within 3 hours
-Multiplayer is pretty much dead, not a lot of people online
-Moving can feel weird if you're coming from Guerrilla or the other RF's, since sprint is limited and jumping has a delay
Get this game on a sale, or pick it up along with the others in a pack. you WILL have lots of fun with this if you like toying around with physics and such

If you collect the purple bottle, the game ends. If you collect the light blue bottle, you go to the sky (presumably heaven). The game also ends if your character touches a cute looking bear.

This is the most I have laughed at a game in ages, probably since the early days of Newgrounds.
Well, what's this game about?
It's a 2D runner type game. You try see how far you can get without dying and picking up the alcohol bottles.
How do you die?
Either by drinking the Death Bottle, falling through Hell, or landing on the Bear.
And that's the first thing that gets me - see, you're told it's a bear. But it isn't. It's part bear, part buffalo. A Bearfalo, if you will.
I giggle everytime I see that sad, confused animal. Sometimes, if the Bearfalo is positioned right, when you touch a Sky Bottle (which transforms the stage into one in the clouds) it'll fall through a hole in the clouds, waggling it's sad, pathetic legs in a doomed attempt to get back up.
And then there are the bottles - there are 4 in total. One kills you, one is for achievements/collecting, one transforms the stage into Hell, the last one transforms into the Sky. And they spawn randomly. Anywhere. This can be annoying - your jumps are all the same height - so dodging the Bearfalo means not being able to dodge the Death Bottle behind it. Or, falling from the clouds and landing on a Hell Bottle and immediately falling through the floor.
Sometimes, though, sometimes they spawn
our cross-bred buddy. Or on it's silly face, and go rolling away...it probably drinks them to forget about its worries and its strife (yea, man!)
And the bugs...so so many bugs! The small platforms aren't actually platforms and you'll fall through. At least 10% of the time I'll jump and get stuck on a ledge, flailing my arms around and pelvic-thrusting like it's going out of fashion.
If you land juuust in front of the bear's horns it'll headbutt you backwards 3 screenlengths to your death.
The achievements. Oh boy. This is where I've been giggling the most.
See, the dev decided to add 4000+ cheevos to this game - one for every time you jumped. People responded by making auto-clickers and wrapping them up in a few minutes.
"Oh no," says the dev, "not in my game!"
And now they got changed so that every cheevo bottle will award one - because the dev wants you to play their game, see?
But now you can't - the whole point of a 2D runner game is to be able to see what's coming and time your jumps. You can't do that if you have achievement boxes constantly popping up and blocking your view, can you?
Honestly - don't get this game because it's good.
Get it to laugh at that stupid Bearfalo's face.
Get it to laugh at the devs brilliant achievement plan.
Get it to try figure out how, or why, it's Russia.
The dev has locked some achievements, and is very involved in the community and discussions.
It's a good sign, and maybe might be another reason to give this a shot.
The new achievements were added - they removed a bunch (which will have an effect on stat-tracking sites; something that was explained to the dev, who didn't care) and added a new "Speed up" bottle which has the effect of making the Hell levels virtually impossible. You now need to avoid 2 bottles and a Buffalo...
Still recommend this game for the same reason I have a picture of me when I was 10 - we need to remember the mistakes of our past so we don't do them again. It's painful, but has to be done.

In short I highly recommend this game, especially if you love RPG's and post apocalypse survival games.
I kept putting this game off time and time again when I saw it come up on steam because I thought the graphics looked a little old school for me, but what this game lacks in graphics it tenfold makes up for in content.
This game really portrays the apocalypse well and provides an authentic, claustrophobic feel when travelling to loot or find a place for the night. Unlike some other games in this genre you cannot tackle hordes with ease clocking countless kills as you simply cannot risk a bite or scratch as in this game, if you get infected you die. If your cuts/scratches get infected, you die. If you bleed out before you get chance to apply bandages you......well you get the idea.
Project Zomboid takes most things into consideration when surviving including weather (you can get too hot or too cold and if you get too wet for too long you can get a cold and attract the hordes with your sneezes), thirst (you have to boil rain water before you can drink it or you can get sick....I don't recommend bleach as a beverage), hunger (even a nutrition system included now), boredom, tiredness, sickness and many more.
There is an incredibly robust crafting system which is continually evolving. I have still got so much to craft and I have 130 hours (at the time of this review) invested in the game.
Multiplayer is even more fun if you can find a good friend or two to play with although you will all need to have plenty of spare time to get the most out of this game.
On a final note and one of my favourite features about this game is that the terrain around you ages and cracks and grows wild as it would in real life which really adds depth to the overall apocalypse feel. I love running through the overgrown streets and looting cracked and overgrown buildings as I pass the fields of grounded corpses from my escapades earlier on in the game.
I have probably left loads of important bits out which is what usually puts me off writing reviews but if you are still on the fence JUST BUY IT ALREADY! You won't regret it!

Project Zomboid is a realistc zombie survival game where death is commonplace. The focus on minute details that a person might overlook in another game make this game enjoyable and unforgiving. A must for fans of the survival genre.
Pros:
Amazing Music
A survival game that actually becomes harder as time goes on, not easier, alleviating the boredome that one experiences late-game.
A focus on many different things that adds depth and gives a feeling of realism
Even lower difficulties have some degree of challenge, while higher ones can be absolutely unforgiving. Something for everyone.
Cons:
Hard to pick up
Developement is VERY, VERY slow.
Some things are not explained as well as they should be.
The controls are sometimes a bit finnicky.
Neutral Points:
Perma-death and many ways to die, along with RPG-esque leveling means that this is a game where survival is at it's core. Perma-death might not be your thing, though, and this game takes it to the extreme.
Pre-made maps might be unappealing to some, but it means that you learn the game easier and allows for some degree of realism in the map that procedural generation can't generally provide.
Oh yeah, you can also drink bleach and kill zombies by tossing a lot of spoons at them.

First of all, this game is not for everybody. This is a hardcore, realistic, survival game. And to many people that means it will get very boring and repetative. The art style is fantastic and there are many, enourmous, fleshed out regions to loot and explore. It's not enjoyable to write something negative about something that is quite unique in some ways -- above all, I really enjoy the setting of Sir, You Are Being Hunted. Some complain about the lo-fi graphics, but they make the absolute best of what they are -- and I expect my robots to look "clunky".
Sound is more of a mixed bag. The voice effects are entertaining through and through, and distinct enough that you can quickly tell who is in an area and what they might be doing at that moment. At other times though, I hear rustling grass as  proceed over a stone bridge, or no sound at all in the water. It brings you out of "the moment". I quite enjoy the spooky narrator though, and the music always fits.
Gameplay wise... it turned into a slog by the time I had finished my first three (of five) islands. I didn't try more than one character, but there doesn't seem to be much to gameplay besides avoid-avoid-avoid, which basically means to move slowly in crouch position. Attack is naturally limited because, well, you're the one being hunted, but it would have really helped the game to have a few other creative ways of eliminating the danger of the robots. I managed to get every collectible piece of my matter transmogri-whatever by using glass bottles, alarm clocks, and toy trains. None of them felt all that different.
If it's $9.99 or lower and you live these open-world survival games, give it a try. Unless something truly great is $9.99, then buy that.

Sir, You Are Being Hunted is a survival and stealth game.
The game has you placed on an odd British Island where groups of robot hunters are hunting you down. Your job is to find stones to put into a machine to escape.
The gameplay can be pretty fun, you need to hide in bushes away from the robots, loot houses for food and supplies, and eventually get a weapon to help defend yourself.
There is a large variety of robots that can hunt you down. There are normal hunters, poachers, air balloons, a robot scarecrow and more.
For me the gameplay did get a bit repetitive after an hour of looting and running away and it can take a while to find all of the parts to escape which can get boring.
The AI in the game is decent. They see you based on a visibility and sound system which is a bit flawed. If you're sitting in some thick grass and don't move the robots can basically step on your toes, but if you even shift your foot everything in a 10 meter radius will immediately storm to your location and fire.
If you can past those couple of flaws and don't mind spending a couple of hours doing the same thing then this is a pretty solid game although it is a little pricey.

A minimalist puzzle game with non-unique solutions, a simple mechanic that is easy to understand and extremely well-explored, and soothing graphics and sound.
Let me start by saying that, although I am not recommending this game, as it did not appeal to me personally, it will very competently scratch an itch that a lot of players may have. If the trailer video appeals to you, you will probably end up liking it well enough.
That said, I personally found myself getting more and more aggravated the more I played it.
As far as what it did well: It is easy to understand, simple to play. There are tons of levels. The graphics are nice and the colors are customizable. The sound is fine, and when it gets aggravating you can always mute. The difficulty curve is not steep. Everything plays very smoothly and feels very polished.
Unfortunately, some of those strengths end up being weaknesses in the long run. As mentioned in some other reviews, there are a ridiculous number of puzzles, not to mention the never ending firehose of daily puzzles. This, and the fact that they are procedurally generated, means that they get very repetitive and very boring very quickly. I would much rather have had a smaller number of hand-curated level packs. I've not quite put in two hours, but already I've given up trying to progress to the actually difficult levels, it just takes too much time and effort to get there, and beating the easier levels is not rewarding.
Another problem is that I found the mouse controls annoying. A touch screen would have been infinitely better. For a PC release, this is unfortunate, but there isn't really a good way around that for this specific game that I can see.
The sound was another minor problem. There is very little of it. What there is is nice, but gets very old very quickly. Muting the sound fixes it, of course, but then I don't have any sound :-/
It's really hard to fault him for creating a solid, well-made puzzler with a very low price for an awful lot of levels, but I think in this case quality would just edge out quantity, for my money.

A good WW2 FPS notable for it's high skill ceiling and one-hit deaths.
Stuff I like about this game:
-1-hit deaths. Seriously, (almost) every gun kills you in one-hit (besides the SMGs which might just wing you at longer ranges. This is a very realistic FPS.
-It doesn't hold back with how challenging it is. Working off of the 1-hit deaths, it made me legitimately SCARED when I first started out in the game. I would hide in artillery shell craters, prone to the ground, it was very immersive as a game that depicts the Eastern Front of WW2.
-Good class-based combat. You have: Riflemen who are guys who capture the objective. Squad Leaders who serve as a spawn point for everyone, throw smoke to conceal your team while they advance, and mark artillery bombardment locations. Machine gunners who lock down an area with 1-hit killing rapid-fire machine guns. Snipers who pick off priority targets from long range (machine gunners, squad leaders, other snipers, the Commander). Assaults who have close ranged weapons to clear buildings. And the Commander who play this game like an RTS, he orders recon planes, artillery, amoung other stuff.
-In conjunction with those classes and their roles, this game encourages team-play. No matter who you are, actually killing the enemy doesn't just get you a higher score. Killing the enemy IN the objective while STANDING in the objective though, DOES.
-Bullet trajectory. Bullets sink over longer distances and take time to reach the people you shoot at, there is no hitscan. Thank goodness, because this makes the game a bit more complex.
Downsides:
-Punishing for newer players. The other people playing probably know where to hide and you need to learn how to cope with the 1-hit kills. You get used to this over time, but just take my advice and play your first few hours as a simple Rifleman to just get the hang of everything.
-It's a bit janky. Sometimes I have to hit a key twice to do something, it lacks just a 'little' bit of polish. It doesn't break this game, it's just sometimes the controls fight with you a little bit.
tldr, This is a great realistic FPS that places a greater emphasis on playing the objective, being a sneaky sh*t who knows how to hide while shooting the enemy, and playing the specific role of your class. I reconmend it.

Although this game was fairly linear it was still an action packed romp.  Good story, decent visuals, a host of weapons to use, and a variety of ways to play.
This is *nothing* like RF:Guerrilla with the open world.  This whole story is on tracks, but that's not entirely a bad thing.  There's some exploration to be done to find things, but you always have to "get back on the rails" to get the story moving again.
You can upgrade weapons and abilities using the ever familiar scrap which makes for some progression.  As you play, after you've unlocked your core upgrades (or before), you can unlock features using scrap that can be used on future playthroughs.  Many would consider these cheats (super weapons, unlimited ammo, etc), but if you've played through the game and story already, some of the features are great fun (like Mr. Toots) and you can choose what you want to use and not use.  In this way, you could supplement a boring section of the game with a super weapon, just to make it fun.  I never used unlimited ammo; it's just an option if you like that sort of thing.
Best game ever?  No.
Great fun?  Certainly :)

It hasn't aged quite as gracefully as some games that are a decade older or more, but it's still fun. My only two big complaints about this game are that the controls are pretty poor, both in the hovercraft and while fighting, in my opinion, and the graphics have "artifacts" that don't exist in the game world flashing and flickering on screen, which is incredibly distracting. You can go to the forums and look up fixes for this including getting the game to run in 1920 x 1080 etc (Jade looks reeeeally fat if you don't). It's doable in under half an hour.
Some folks might take issue with a third thing, but I didn't. Specifically, there are some animal people. Your adoptive uncle is an anthropomorphic pig, your character's kids she cares for (orphans) are humans, and some anthropomorphic goats, there's an anthropomorphic cow in the bar, as well as sharks of the anthropomorphic persuasion. None of it is sexualized or obsessive, in my opinion. It's sci-fi, so I suppose they're aliens...who just happen to look like earth animal species. Kinda lazy, but whatever. ;)  Unless you're insecure with yourself to the extent that you cannot feel comfortable playing a video game with an anthropomorphic pig talking on the screen, then you should be fine. I was cool with it.
With those issues out of the way, I dig most everything else about this game. The music was really enjoyable for me, the world is compact but filled out enough and charming, the characters are cartoonish but likable enough, and perhaps best of all, the game has a lot of variety in its gameplay. For instance, leaving out story spoilers, and solely talking about stuff you do, the game has you fight on foot, explore while photographing like a less annoying version of Pokemon Snap (i.e. sitting still, by golly!), fight a boss in a vehicle, explore a city and make purchases with money you looted in-game, explore and fight through an area, boss fight on foot, hovercraft races, competitive minigame against a shark guy in a bar, stealth sections with enemies you can take out sneakily, avoid, or fight if you dodge and don't get too outnumbered, high-speed chases in a hovercraft through coastal bandit caves with quickly-shutting doors, on-foot scripted chase sequences in which you run away, typically toward the screen, escaping otherwise certain doo, and more. A couple of things might be too spoiler-y to mention that are features, so I'll leave them out.
What I'm getting at, though, is that this game has a lot of variation in what you're doing from one minute to the next, and that keeps the game fresh. You can complete it in 8-12 hours or so, and that includes getting all of the collectibles, which I find pretty darn addicting. In regard to the collectibles, there are collectible detection devices you can purchase pretty cheap in town, which are totally worth it. This way, you have a general idea of where you need to find collectibles, but there's stll some challenge of hunting them down when you're in the right area and actually sometimes figuring out how to get them.
I don't want to be too redundant, but the music really worked well for me in the setting, so I simply have to bring that up again. Between the music I enjoyed and the varied gameplay, this was a very enjoyable game. Some meh controls and the fixable graphical problems keep it from being as magnificent as it otherwise could be, even as it ages, but on the whole, it's definitely a great game, and you can typically grab it for $4.99 on Steam sales, which is definitely a good price in my opinion.

You would expect a game called "Beyond Good and Evil" to actually go beyond good and evil, just as the book by Friedrich Nietzsche, which the game loans it's title from, does. But no, this game does not do that at all; In fact, I'm not even sure what it does. It's a full bait-and-switch. While the game does have some lovely music, a great lead character design, and some fun mechanics sprinkled here and there, it doesn't have any kind of wow factor. And not to say the game doesn't have it's merits as I've listed, it's nothing special to me.
To improve the game, firstly, I would have given it a better story with themes which actually go beyond good and evil. You play the noble reporter trying to bring down the corrupt government and conquering aliens; that is the definition of good and evil. I would have been impressed if they loaned themes from Nietzsche, such as talking about how the opposite of the good man is not the evil man; that they have the same desires and thoughts, just different expressions and actions. Or just anything which brought up moral gray areas would have made a more compelling story.
Second, have the story make sense. Near the end we find out a vague twist which isn't fully explained, then the game ends with out having mentioned it again. After you defeat the final boss, who talks cryptically through the whole fight, they just die, nothing else is said, some weird powers happen, and credits roll. So much was left unresolved or just flat out unexplained. It made me feel like I partially wasted several hours of my life, which is the last thing I want from a video game.
Thirdly, improve the controls a bit. Mostly, the game handled well, but when you're in the hover craft or running around a corner, the camera which suddenly change to a different view, throw off the character direction, and you fall of a cliff or run into a wall. Again, it takes away from the experience.
All in all, this was a good game which could have been a wonderful game, I'm sure, but it feels as though they gave up half way through. Hopefully the recently announced sequel will actually go beyond good and evil.

Let me make one thing clear: I do like the game. Keep that in mind whilst reading this review, which is /full/ of spoilers.
tl;dr: I like the game, but it does still need work. Lots of bugs. 5/10.
------------------------------------->>
I, like many others, played both Starbound and Terraria, and thoroughly enjoyed them both. Naturally, when Planet Centauri came up on my Steam Queue, I wa excited beyond words, and promptly added the game to my wishlist. When I finally recieved the game, I immediately installed and booted it up, and was met with this overwhelming feeling.
That feeling, dear friends, was disapointment.
The art style is pretty, the music is calming and relaxing, something I expected from playing Starbound and Terraria. But Starbound and Terraria had something that this game severely lacks at this time, and that is the feeling of a living, breathing world. Allow me to expand on this:
There is no water in the game that I have found. There are trees that dot the landscape every now and again, and you have to travel a ways away from your little crystal buddy to find different trees. The land itself is flat and wholly uninteresting. There are occasionally hills, and occasionally there are holes in the ground you can fall into, break all your bones, and cheerfully continue digging until a legendary cavern slime comes along and devours you and everything you hold dear. The only passive animals I have found are the chickens and the wisps, and they aren't entirely interesting either. That being said, maybe I haven't travelled enough to find more passive animals, but every time I've tried I've either gotten my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by enraged owls, or gotten my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by enraged boars. Either way, lack of diveristy on that front.
On that note, the enemy types from what I can see are varied, if you venture away from home far enough or dig deep enough in the earth. If you just hang around the crystal the most you can hope for is a few zombies that you can bonk on the head for souls.
AND THE SOULS.
This was something that was new to me, and I find myself feeling mixed about this. You need souls of the things you've killed in order to open chests found throughout the world. The minimum requirement is 150, and the most I've seen is 1200. It's an interesting take on finding loot in the world, but I often feel cheated, spending 400 souls to get food and salt, most of which I've already eaten. And, should you not have enough souls, you cannot open the chest at all, and must leave it. It's problematic, as I've found numerous chests to open underground, but haven't had the soul count to open them. Now, you might say I could hang around and grind, as guaranteed I'll get some enemy spawns on my location, but that isn't necessarily fun for some people, and it certainly isn't fun for me, so I suppose that's my loss.
Another bit on souls, this time with the transformation mechanic. I love, love, love the idea of being able to transform into things. I thought that was super radical and innovative. However, in practice, I don't feel it works super duper well. For starters, you start off as a slime. A cute little blue slime that moves really. really. really slowly. And you have to grind up souls to unlock the next transformation. Which is another slime. And then you have to continue to grind up souls to unlock the next transformation. Let me tell you, grinding souls as a slime is no bueno. It's just not fun. My  tactic ended up being to chase chickens from around my house, pinning them against the wall, and then transforming into the slime to kill them. Chickens only give a paltry amount of souls, so I was at it for a good while.
Digging is SLOW. I have the 4th pickaxe you can make, and though it does chew through dirt rather quickly, you can only dig 1 block at a time. it makes clearing things out very tedious. If there was an area dig, say, 2x2, I would be so much happier.
The game also has a LOT of bugs, a lot of which I haven't found fixes to yet. I have a notification for a quest complete that just won't go away, no matter what I do. And it's a quest I completed a long while ago.
Now, there's been a lot of negative stuff here, so how about some positives:
Pets are GREAT. I absolutely LOVE the pet mechanic in this game. You catch a pet, and then it's your friend. It gets experience as it kills things, and if it dies it goes back into it's
soulgem and you have to wait until it's healthy to be able to summon it again. There are some AI issues, of course. The pathfinding from the flying pet I have is a bit wonky, and it will just kind of noodle around while I kill things, but my scorpion is pretty on the ball and I love him.
I would love if you can name your pets at some point~ I think that would be super duper radical.
The spells are great as well; I love the mechanic and look forward to playing with it more as I eventually get more souls.
In conclusion (at long last):
I like the game. It has great ideas and it's very very innovative for what it is at the moment. I am very much looking forward to the game as it develops. However, I am not going to reccommend the game just yet, as there is just too much here that I find frustrating to deal with. As time goes on, and as updates are released, I will inevitably change my opinion on the game, and will write a new review for Planet Centauri.
A few things of note:
1) This game is NOT Terraria or Starbound. Do not get this game if you are expecting Starbound or Terraria. This is an early access game that I believe will do a lot of different things, and I do hope that it continues to be as innovative and adventurous as it is showing now.
2) Do not immediately go looking for the chloridians until you have a decent pickaxe, armour, and a fireball spell. Do not fight the big brutely guys hand to hand. Hole yourself up with some dirt and spam them with fireballs out of their reach. It'll be fine.
Overall, 5/10. I am going to play the heck out of this game, and so looking forward to future updates.
To the Developer: Good luck, and have fun!

This is the most I have laughed at a game in ages, probably since the early days of Newgrounds.
Well, what's this game about?
It's a 2D runner type game. You try see how far you can get without dying and picking up the alcohol bottles.
How do you die?
Either by drinking the Death Bottle, falling through Hell, or landing on the Bear.
And that's the first thing that gets me - see, you're told it's a bear. But it isn't. It's part bear, part buffalo. A Bearfalo, if you will.
I giggle everytime I see that sad, confused animal. Sometimes, if the Bearfalo is positioned right, when you touch a Sky Bottle (which transforms the stage into one in the clouds) it'll fall through a hole in the clouds, waggling it's sad, pathetic legs in a doomed attempt to get back up.
And then there are the bottles - there are 4 in total. One kills you, one is for achievements/collecting, one transforms the stage into Hell, the last one transforms into the Sky. And they spawn randomly. Anywhere. This can be annoying - your jumps are all the same height - so dodging the Bearfalo means not being able to dodge the Death Bottle behind it. Or, falling from the clouds and landing on a Hell Bottle and immediately falling through the floor.
Sometimes, though, sometimes they spawn
our cross-bred buddy. Or on it's silly face, and go rolling away...it probably drinks them to forget about its worries and its strife (yea, man!)
And the bugs...so so many bugs! The small platforms aren't actually platforms and you'll fall through. At least 10% of the time I'll jump and get stuck on a ledge, flailing my arms around and pelvic-thrusting like it's going out of fashion.
If you land juuust in front of the bear's horns it'll headbutt you backwards 3 screenlengths to your death.
The achievements. Oh boy. This is where I've been giggling the most.
See, the dev decided to add 4000+ cheevos to this game - one for every time you jumped. People responded by making auto-clickers and wrapping them up in a few minutes.
"Oh no," says the dev, "not in my game!"
And now they got changed so that every cheevo bottle will award one - because the dev wants you to play their game, see?
But now you can't - the whole point of a 2D runner game is to be able to see what's coming and time your jumps. You can't do that if you have achievement boxes constantly popping up and blocking your view, can you?
Honestly - don't get this game because it's good.
Get it to laugh at that stupid Bearfalo's face.
Get it to laugh at the devs brilliant achievement plan.
Get it to try figure out how, or why, it's Russia.
The dev has locked some achievements, and is very involved in the community and discussions.
It's a good sign, and maybe might be another reason to give this a shot.
The new achievements were added - they removed a bunch (which will have an effect on stat-tracking sites; something that was explained to the dev, who didn't care) and added a new "Speed up" bottle which has the effect of making the Hell levels virtually impossible. You now need to avoid 2 bottles and a Buffalo...
Still recommend this game for the same reason I have a picture of me when I was 10 - we need to remember the mistakes of our past so we don't do them again. It's painful, but has to be done.

TL;DR - Evolve is OK, but hollow and expensive. Not worth playing solo.
Evolve is a really well made little game. It's gorgeous to look at, the controls are smooth and the gameplay is fun. However, it feels very half-finished.
There's no campaign, only three monsters (unless you pay...) and the game modes are rather un-balanced. Above all though, Evolve is hollow. Hunters track monster, creating tense and gripping skirmishes if they can catch the weak creature, and when the monster hits level 3 you get this fantastic raid boss-like battle as a finale BUT that's it. There was a lot of scope for a campaign, character development, history, ANY kind of story really!
The game has been sold at full price, despite a criminal lack of content. Not only that, but day1DLC... as far as I'm concerned that is despicable. I can't help shake the feeling that we're being sold a platform to buy DLC from.
It's a real shame, the core idea is great fun, the gameplay is sound, but the experience is shallow.
Also, the menus and progression are awfully implemented, the console-itis is strong here.

Project Zomboid is a realistc zombie survival game where death is commonplace. The focus on minute details that a person might overlook in another game make this game enjoyable and unforgiving. A must for fans of the survival genre.
Pros:
Amazing Music
A survival game that actually becomes harder as time goes on, not easier, alleviating the boredome that one experiences late-game.
A focus on many different things that adds depth and gives a feeling of realism
Even lower difficulties have some degree of challenge, while higher ones can be absolutely unforgiving. Something for everyone.
Cons:
Hard to pick up
Developement is VERY, VERY slow.
Some things are not explained as well as they should be.
The controls are sometimes a bit finnicky.
Neutral Points:
Perma-death and many ways to die, along with RPG-esque leveling means that this is a game where survival is at it's core. Perma-death might not be your thing, though, and this game takes it to the extreme.
Pre-made maps might be unappealing to some, but it means that you learn the game easier and allows for some degree of realism in the map that procedural generation can't generally provide.
Oh yeah, you can also drink bleach and kill zombies by tossing a lot of spoons at them.

This little indie game has couch-side multiplayer.  And it's still kinda in Beta.  Or is it?  I have no idea.  Project Zomboid advertises itself (currently) as having "partial" controller support.  Well, they're doing a pretty stellar job so far...
My pal and I were going without internet a few days, and wanted a game to play together.  I don't think Steam properly shows how many hours we put on while we were in Offline mode.  But we plugged in two wired X360 controllers, and loaded up PZ.
Now, it's a bit fragile.  You need to start the game with the controller (not doing this only allows the mouse/keyboard to control the character), but once you're controlling player one, your pal can simply create a new character, and it split-screens.
This, is ♥♥♥♥ing, beautiful.
I don't know what happened when we decided split-screening, or couch-side multiplayer wasn't a "thing" anymore.  ♥♥♥♥ that guy.  He made a bad call for the entire multiplayer community.
(the game even re-loads both characters, and if only one dies, they can respawn, making multiplaying easy, and long-lasting)
So bless these developers for being -cognizant- enough to realize that their game is awesome; especially when played in pairs.
That being said, you can customize nearly everything about your survival scenario, from when the utilities shut off, to how well the zombies can smell.  This is excellent, and allows for some pretty self-abusive scenarios.
All in all, this game rocks.  For the price, you should already own it.  Missing this game when it's on a Steam Sale should be a federal offense.

Im not sure about this game but here's a delicious chocolate cake recipe.
:INGREDIENTS FOR CAKE:
2 cups white sugar
1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 cup unsweetened cocoa powder
1 1/2 teaspoons baking soda
1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder
1 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1 cup milk
1/2 cup vegetable oil
:INGREDIENTS FOR FROSTING:
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
1 cup boiling water
3/4 cup butter
1 1/2 cups unsweetened cocoa powder
5 1/3 cups confectioners' sugar
2/3 cup milk
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
:INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Grease and flour two 9 inch cake pans.
2. Use the first set of ingredients to make the cake. In a medium bowl, stir together the sugar, flour, cocoa, baking soda, baking powder and salt. Add the eggs, milk, oil and vanilla, mix for 3 minutes with an electric mixer. Stir in the boiling water by hand. Pour evenly into the two prepared pans.
3. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes in the preheated oven, until a toothpick inserted comes out clean. Cool for 10 minutes before removing from pans to cool completely.
4.To make the frosting, use the second set of ingredients. Cream butter until light and fluffy. Stir in the cocoa and confectioners' sugar alternately with the milk and vanilla. Beat to a spreading consistency.
5. Split the layers of cooled cake horizontally, cover the top of each layer with frosting, then stack them onto a serving plate. Frost the outside of the cake.

This game falls short of a great game. on a scale of 1 to 10 it barely makes up to an 8 while falling just short of getting a 7.
The tutorial is very easy to understand. Not only that but the UI interface is simple and easy to navigate. The menus are easy to navigate around so you won't get lost.
With that being said the game is divided into three modes, a typical PVP mode. a duel mode, and a mission mode.
Your main objectives are either getting rid of the enemy. Or destory their "base of operations" complete one of these and you win. Also within each mode you have these "power up tiles" that allow you to boost your attack, defense, etc.
So what is the problem with this game? Well how the game uses it's odds system is a joke. This can be heavily seen. In the mission mode, unless your expert in these sort of games. Good luck trying to complete missions where the odds are stacked against you. This game barely makes any helping hands. Sure they give you hints. But it's the complete obvious.
Now you are probably wondering "wait there isn't there a '?' in the game?" so can that help me out? Um nope it just tells you what is what on the map and on the U no hints or helping hands here.
Not only that but getting three stars in this game is a joke. Unless you want those achievements. The game requires that you beat the map in ONE round. For an expert this is easy, for a novice....well
For a novice. I highly recommend watching let's plays and play with your friends first in order to understand how this game really works with the odds system pit yourself in Dark Souls style situations or make it smooth sailing like a typical PVP match up. The choice is up to you. But don't tackle these "odds are against you" scenarios till you fully experience the game for yourself.
This game isn't a P2W. By the way, once you fully understand how the game works, etc. Then why should you need to use the microtransaction system in the first place? Also the developers are community friendly so any issues, etc. post on the forums and they or the community will help you out.
So why do i recommend this game? after all or most of this negativity about the game, or postive. Whichever you see fist. It's because when it's all said and done it's a comfortable game to enjoy nothing serious, or stressful. The game can run on just about any PC ranging from average to meaty PC's. So FPS won't be a big issue here.

ok so im going to write this review as well as i can. i apologize in advance for grammatical errors.
First off, the good.
This game first attracted me when someone showed me a video of them playing. I was first introduced to survival games with fallout new vegas and ever since that game i have been looking for the next level ever since. The Long Dark hits that survival genre like a brick through sugar glass. you start off like a lot of the minecraft survival games: no food, no tools, very little of anything. my first 30 minutes in this game i died twice. my first death was 10 minutes in. without a weapon, a shelter, or food i was forced to wander in search of such. after 10 minutes, i encountered a wolf, and was quickly dispatched.  my second attempt lasted roughly 15-20 minutes, but my character ended in a similar fate: wolf-turds. the next 11 hours and 30 minutes was the most wild ride ive had in a video game in years. from running my♥♥♥♥♥off on my first bear encounter to bringing down my first deer with a home made bow, this game does not hold back on the adrenaline rush.
Now then, the bad.
The learning curve for this game is BRUTAL. if you like video gaming while inebriated, this game is not for you. every single decision can mean death. if you miss with an arrow during a wolf attack, then thats pretty much game over for you. after about 11 hours i found that all the interiors were the same. there is a major lack of weaponry, even though there are simple weapons EVERWHERE. you would think that you would be able to fend of a wolf with a knife or an axe, but alas, there are only 3 weapons in this game: flare gun, le olde mosin nagant, and the trusty bow+arrow. there is a decent amount of clothing variety, but theres really no need for it all. once you find the items that give you the best weather protection you will find yourself ignoring all other clothing. there is a lack of variety in the animals as well with only 4 different animals: bear, wolves, rabbits, deer. the rifle, which is admitedly the most powerful weapon, is very wonky, you can find it in one spot on one playthrough, but on the next it wont be there. you can end up with 16 rifles and not a single bullet for them.
this concludes my review. overall i rate this game, in its current alpha state, a 5/5 UNDER THE PRETENSE THAT EVERY NEGATIVE ISSUE I ENCOUNTER WILL BE RESOLVED ONCE THE GAME IS COMPLETED! this is so much GREATNESS in this game. even in alpha i highly reccomend this game.

One of my favorite games to play. very high replay value since items spawn differently each time you play, and you spawn in different locations with each new game. Incredibly challenging to play at first without looking at user-created maps (I dare you to see how long you can survive without looking at any maps on your first play). It is different than any other survival game because it is actually well balanced between staying fed, hydrated, and well rested along with the weather always changing and never knowing when wildlife is going to be around the next corner.
The mechanics of the game are quite detailed and yet still simple to get used to right away. I really appreciate the archery in the game since many games cut corners with bow and arrow weaponry, but Hinterland really put some time into the archery as distance, wind, and experience all play a part in how accurate you can shoot an arrow, most games are terrible at this.
The only downside of the game is when you start stocking up mass amounts of supplies and get the best clothing, and the rifle, as the game starts losing it's difficulty around then (thats when its time to go to the next difficulty setting)
I also love that the game also has challenge modes, so you can play certain challenges instead of the basic survival sandbox.
Overall, this game is worth every penny and I cant wait to see what Hinterland Studios has in store for future updates.

What a fantastic game. Many other survival games are a "survive + X" experience. The Long Dark is a pure survival experience. Come prepared. If you stop paying attention, you die. If you make a dumb mistake, you die. On the other hand, the difficulty settings are very thoughtfully tuned, and not simply a matter of "everything is harder"— They are actually different experiences. This is a deliberately-paced game, and the careful, thorough player is rewarded. Also, this game has some of the most incredible sound design I've ever experienced. It's rare that a game conveys substantial information through its sound. In the Long Dark, if you pay attention, you will be able to tell if you are near a man-made structure while you are in the midst of a snowstorm, and that can mean the difference between life and death. The devs for this game are passionate and dedicated, and have proved it over 2+ years of continuous, quality updates. I continue to enjoy this game and look forward to what the future brings for it.

TL;DR: Get this game. Very few weakpoints listed in the pro/con section. I made a video featuring a last man standing amateur tournament with 18 out of 20 playable characters, added to this review.
Dungeon of the Endless does a lot of things right, taking the positive aspects of various genres and
surprisingly manages to mash them together without creating a big pile of crap.
Not only is it fun to play, easy to pick up and hard to master, it also offers a great deal of replayability
and nice community.
PRO/CON
I won't go with a full pro/con list here, let's focus on the very few cons.
-- A few (currently 2 out of 20) playable characters need to be purchased separately and cost way more than what would be reasonable. Josh N'tello is included in the Dungeon of the Endless Chrystal Edition
and Kreyang in the Endless Legend Founder Pack, an addon for a different game of Amplitude Studios.
It has been stated on the forums that the Kreyang-situation will be adressed at some point in the future.
-- Some footage from the trailers isn't actually included in the game or simply outdated, like the overworld view with the Necrophage Nibblers, or Max opening a door that takes a lot longer to open in the actual game.
-- While the game features coop-mode, at this point in time it lacks a savefunction (will be added) and also offers a different and in my opinion not as enjoyable experience because of the missing pause-feature, which is an essential part of the singleplayer mode as you can issue orders while pausing.
-- The secret hero of the game is rather a gimmick and in my opinion way too weak in comparison to the other heroes.

-- often slowpaced, heavy focus on strategy and ressource management, also permadeath. Stuff like that isn't for everybody.
That being said I thoroughly enjoy the game and can easily recommend it. Not sure about the chrystal edition because of the unreasonably high price, but that's something everybody should decide on their own, I got it anyway.
I also created a video featuring a fully edited last man standing amateur tournament of almost all playable characters, where I not only shoutcast but at the same time explain the basics of the game in more detail.

A good WW2 FPS notable for it's high skill ceiling and one-hit deaths.
Stuff I like about this game:
-1-hit deaths. Seriously, (almost) every gun kills you in one-hit (besides the SMGs which might just wing you at longer ranges. This is a very realistic FPS.
-It doesn't hold back with how challenging it is. Working off of the 1-hit deaths, it made me legitimately SCARED when I first started out in the game. I would hide in artillery shell craters, prone to the ground, it was very immersive as a game that depicts the Eastern Front of WW2.
-Good class-based combat. You have: Riflemen who are guys who capture the objective. Squad Leaders who serve as a spawn point for everyone, throw smoke to conceal your team while they advance, and mark artillery bombardment locations. Machine gunners who lock down an area with 1-hit killing rapid-fire machine guns. Snipers who pick off priority targets from long range (machine gunners, squad leaders, other snipers, the Commander). Assaults who have close ranged weapons to clear buildings. And the Commander who play this game like an RTS, he orders recon planes, artillery, amoung other stuff.
-In conjunction with those classes and their roles, this game encourages team-play. No matter who you are, actually killing the enemy doesn't just get you a higher score. Killing the enemy IN the objective while STANDING in the objective though, DOES.
-Bullet trajectory. Bullets sink over longer distances and take time to reach the people you shoot at, there is no hitscan. Thank goodness, because this makes the game a bit more complex.
Downsides:
-Punishing for newer players. The other people playing probably know where to hide and you need to learn how to cope with the 1-hit kills. You get used to this over time, but just take my advice and play your first few hours as a simple Rifleman to just get the hang of everything.
-It's a bit janky. Sometimes I have to hit a key twice to do something, it lacks just a 'little' bit of polish. It doesn't break this game, it's just sometimes the controls fight with you a little bit.
tldr, This is a great realistic FPS that places a greater emphasis on playing the objective, being a sneaky sh*t who knows how to hide while shooting the enemy, and playing the specific role of your class. I reconmend it.

"In modern war... you will die like a dog for no good reason."
A brutal experience that punishes you for the mistake of not using cover, teamwork, and/or effective tactics. Be prepared to die repeatedly until you learn how to effectively maneuver with your team, play different roles accordingly, and adapt to different situations. Your skills will be strained and you will often find yourself in the muck with enemy fire whizzing overhead as you pray that you're in sufficient cover. Tunnel vision will sink in as you're constantly reminded of the overwhelming stress of imminent death with every bullet impact and explosion that lands in front of your eyes and ends the lives of your comrades around you scrambling for shelter, their disembodied limbs flying and their dying screams echoing. You may even break down and give up hope while facing the enemy's war machine and find yourself asking the very meaning to life.
Overall a great family experience for the children! 10/10

Would I recommend it? Hell no!
While Guerilla was fun despite sad bleak red sky, dull story and mostly empty world, Armageddon takes all these cons and makes it double.
Now we have to travel through dark underground caves filled with monsters, with very limited ammo supply and 2-3 destructible objects 90% of the game time.
Also, cutscenes look really ugly and voice acting is like bad 90s action movie.
While game can be fun it managed to crash me to desktop around once an hour, so my experience was not good from technical standpoint as well.

Intro:
I got intruduced to the red faction series with RF: 3 and was inpressed woth the open world dynamic. Going into Armegeddon I was worried that the games more linear level structure would be a hard sell.
Negatives:
I was unfortunately proved right on this, the plot is decidedly shallow and straightforward. It incorperated many of the tropes included in a zombie game, and mixes them into the red faction stew to produce a game that is untimatley dissapointing. The linear structure of the game makes the destruction engine less relivant, and the plot struccles to hold attention. You could feasable play through the entire game without knocking a building down, except where you are requred to destroy something. Levels fell long and often fell clostraphobic, with many redundant fights that struggle to contribute anything new. Certan bugs have to be killed in specific ways, while others are effectively bullet sponges whose soul peopose is to maul you before you can empty enough rounds into the target. Vehicle combat is almost non existant, there are only three vehicles that are useable in the base campign, and all two are used on levels that dont let you get in or out. While you get involved in large spaces within the campign, they can be tedious to cross and ultimately become boring. The in games sound bites you recover do enrich the experience, and they imply a grand conspiracy as to why the world was allowed to collapse in game. The conspiracy narrative never really gets flushed out, and there are entire levels that could be cut out without having any effect on the plot. For example, the level where you fight the bug queen fells like filler once you actually beat the game and discover that fight (and the death of your girlfriend) was not even nessary because you could have repaired the terraformer and killed the bugs and any point before the point where the game allows you to do so. Replayability is encouraged by the salvage mechanisim, which carries your upgrades over to multiplayer. Of course, the campign struggles after one playthrough, and it makes other playthroughs feel like a real grind, especally when you have to trade large amounts of salvage to unlock the games array of cheats. The disadvantage  to the salvage system is that you have to play through the campign to stand a chance in multiplayer, because the base player stats are pathetic in comparision. You hold less ammo, reload slower, have ferer hit points, and no nano abilites. Veteran players will steamroll you, then scrape you off the street and beat you into a fine pulp before tbagging you all the way into the respawn que.
Positives:
The repair mechanic is a cool idea, and was desparately needed in this games prequel, since that envirnment never regenerates. The nano powers you can accumulate through collecting salvage add a fun dynamic that becomes critical in later levels, it struggles to overcome the eventual grind that later levels become though. Griphics have been tuned up, though not by much. Building destruction is smoother thatn in the previous game, but its hard to notice because most weapons make the pillers and colums you hit vanish rather than get blown off. However, when you do get the chance to conventally blow up a building it looks awesome. Multiplayer can keep you interested, but its a personl intrest thing.
At its current price I dont recommend it, I managed to get it as part of the RF pack over the thanksgiving sale and so paid a lot less. The game was worth waht I paid for at its sale price, but I would recommend waiting for the price of the game to come down under five dollars before diving into this.

I think this game is fantastic! Having read the current (and largely negative) reviews, I felt like I had to add my own.
This game is unlike any I've ever played. The closest similarities can be drawn to Left4Dead's versus mode. The ability to play as the monster - the enemy - in a variety of game modes and utilising various monster abilities adds huge replay value and novelty. For so long, gamers have called out for original concepts and IPs. Here's one and they did a cracking job at it in my view.
In regards to the bugs and issues relating to the game:
I played the beta release extensively and I can see why people would write negatively about the technical aspects of the game. However, the vast majority of these have issues have been fixed! I encounter only one issue (albiet a freeze/crash). Outlast isn't really a game of skill, and as it turns out, that makes sense. You're not a cop or a soldier or a genetically enhanced superhero. You're just a reporter. And as a reporter, you don't possess many skills with which you can fend off the hulking brutes, knife-wielding stalkers, and other homicidal maniacs who lurk in the halls of the dilapidated Mount Massive Asylum. You can't shoot them, or punch them, or rip pipes from the walls to clobber them with. You can only run and hide. You're always in danger, and when that danger is nipping at your heels and all you can do is flee, desperately hoping to shake off your pursuer, Outlast is a terrifying roller-coaster ride. Unfortunately, the pacing stumbles in a few instances when Outlast stops coasting forward on its own momentum and requires you to go hunting for the track yourself, but these are small setbacks in what is usually a deeply unsettling experience.
Drawn by an anonymous tip, you come to Mount Massive to investigate allegations that an unscrupulous corporation is doing horrible things to mental patients in the pursuit of profits. You move through Mount Massive in first person, and your weighty movements make you feel physically grounded in the environment. And what an environment it is. Mount Massive is supposed to be a place with a long, dark history, and as you make your way through it, you come to believe that it has been home to many horrors over the decades. You can almost feel the damp, moldy air infesting your lungs, and every shadowy room fills you with apprehension, since you never know when someone might be waiting to leap out at you.
There are plenty of effective jump scares in Outlast, but they don't feel cheap and opportunistic. The atmosphere of Mount Massive is so cohesive and so convincing that the horrors lying in wait for you feel right at home in its pervasive darkness. Luckily, you can penetrate that darkness with your trusty camcorder's night vision, which lets you see your immediate surroundings but doesn't make them feel any less terrifying, bathing objects in an artificial green glow and doing nothing to dispel the darkness.
Mount Massive's crumbling walls and bloodstained floors successfully create the illusion that you're in a once-functioning facility where unspeakable horrors have occurred, but the path you must take through the asylum is rigidly linear. You might occasionally venture off of your narrow route a bit to find batteries to power your camcorder's night vision or documents that shed a bit of light on what has taken place at the asylum, but you won't get far; there's only ever one way forward, and as you bump up against the game's restrictive nature, you're reminded that you're in a video game after all, one designed to usher you from one terrifying situation to the next.
There's nothing wrong with that when the situations are effective, and in Outlast, they usually are. You're hunted through much of Mount Massive by a massive man who doesn't hesitate to rip your heart right out of your chest if he gets his hands on you. Seeing his silhouette in the darkness ahead or hearing his heavy footfalls somewhere nearby is enough to make your pulse quicken, since you know you have no recourse against him but to flee and to cower. When he does spot you--and he will--you can only run, hoping that you might shake him off by finding a locker to hide in or a bed to slide under. He's so threatening that in these situations, your own breathing might become as ragged as the shallow breathing of your character.
But Outlast runs into a bit of a problem. Your encounters with the hulking brute and the other homicidal denizens of Mount Massive are terrifying because your opponents are so lethal and because you can't defend yourself against them. But when you fail to elude them and meet a grisly demise, and then have to face the same situation a second or third or fourth time, the tension dissipates, as if you're watching a scene in a horror movie you've seen before and you know exactly when the killer is going to strike. When you need to repeat scenarios, Outlast's gameplay takes on a rote feeling of trial and error; you know that what you did last time didn't work, so you try something else, until you find an approach that does work.
In the end, though, Outlast's few weak moments are overshadowed by the effectiveness with which it so often gets inside your head and scares the hell out of you. You sometimes end up feeling like you're just going through the motions the game requires you to go through, but when the ride is as well designed as this, the best thing to do is just get in and hold on

Epic Arena is a simple turn-based game - and I think that simplicity is both a blessing and a curse.  It is very easy to learn.  Of course, there is a lot of strategy involved when playing against other players - since knowing how pieces move doesn't mean you know what the opponent is going to do.  The cards are well designed and the game provides all the info you need to know for how to use a card or piece.  The tutorials and single-player missions are fairly helpful in "training" you to know how to play as well.
However, the simplicity of the game also comes with a downside for me.  I have gotten accustomed to having more units and cards in a deck-based strategy game. This is just not that kind of game.  Instead it is more like chess insofar as, aside from power/boost cards, players start with the same or equal decks.  This, of course, is what is necessary for balanced duels.  However, it just makes the game lacking in depth, as far as the cards are concerned.
Now, admittedly, the point of the game is not RPG-type card growth or finding those rare cards.  As a result, you never feel like you "need" to spend money on extras, since you can get everything you need to earning coin (passing missions with 3 stars will get enough coin to eventually buy the most expensive item, the spyglass).
Regarding multiplayer and duels, blitz games (which are the default game) move fairly quickly.  Without experience or good handle of the game, a more experienced player will almost always win.  I found it helpful to play with a couple duels with friends without time limits as a way of better learning how the battles went.
All in all, it is a pretty fun game.  For people who like a "chess match" of sorts, this is perfect.  For people looking for any sort of story or card depth, this may not be for you.

ok so im going to write this review as well as i can. i apologize in advance for grammatical errors.
First off, the good.
This game first attracted me when someone showed me a video of them playing. I was first introduced to survival games with fallout new vegas and ever since that game i have been looking for the next level ever since. The Long Dark hits that survival genre like a brick through sugar glass. you start off like a lot of the minecraft survival games: no food, no tools, very little of anything. my first 30 minutes in this game i died twice. my first death was 10 minutes in. without a weapon, a shelter, or food i was forced to wander in search of such. after 10 minutes, i encountered a wolf, and was quickly dispatched.  my second attempt lasted roughly 15-20 minutes, but my character ended in a similar fate: wolf-turds. the next 11 hours and 30 minutes was the most wild ride ive had in a video game in years. from running my♥♥♥♥♥off on my first bear encounter to bringing down my first deer with a home made bow, this game does not hold back on the adrenaline rush.
Now then, the bad.
The learning curve for this game is BRUTAL. if you like video gaming while inebriated, this game is not for you. every single decision can mean death. if you miss with an arrow during a wolf attack, then thats pretty much game over for you. after about 11 hours i found that all the interiors were the same. there is a major lack of weaponry, even though there are simple weapons EVERWHERE. you would think that you would be able to fend of a wolf with a knife or an axe, but alas, there are only 3 weapons in this game: flare gun, le olde mosin nagant, and the trusty bow+arrow. there is a decent amount of clothing variety, but theres really no need for it all. once you find the items that give you the best weather protection you will find yourself ignoring all other clothing. there is a lack of variety in the animals as well with only 4 different animals: bear, wolves, rabbits, deer. the rifle, which is admitedly the most powerful weapon, is very wonky, you can find it in one spot on one playthrough, but on the next it wont be there. you can end up with 16 rifles and not a single bullet for them.
this concludes my review. overall i rate this game, in its current alpha state, a 5/5 UNDER THE PRETENSE THAT EVERY NEGATIVE ISSUE I ENCOUNTER WILL BE RESOLVED ONCE THE GAME IS COMPLETED! this is so much GREATNESS in this game. even in alpha i highly reccomend this game.

One of my favorite games to play. very high replay value since items spawn differently each time you play, and you spawn in different locations with each new game. Incredibly challenging to play at first without looking at user-created maps (I dare you to see how long you can survive without looking at any maps on your first play). It is different than any other survival game because it is actually well balanced between staying fed, hydrated, and well rested along with the weather always changing and never knowing when wildlife is going to be around the next corner.
The mechanics of the game are quite detailed and yet still simple to get used to right away. I really appreciate the archery in the game since many games cut corners with bow and arrow weaponry, but Hinterland really put some time into the archery as distance, wind, and experience all play a part in how accurate you can shoot an arrow, most games are terrible at this.
The only downside of the game is when you start stocking up mass amounts of supplies and get the best clothing, and the rifle, as the game starts losing it's difficulty around then (thats when its time to go to the next difficulty setting)
I also love that the game also has challenge modes, so you can play certain challenges instead of the basic survival sandbox.
Overall, this game is worth every penny and I cant wait to see what Hinterland Studios has in store for future updates.

What a fantastic game. Many other survival games are a "survive + X" experience. The Long Dark is a pure survival experience. Come prepared. If you stop paying attention, you die. If you make a dumb mistake, you die. On the other hand, the difficulty settings are very thoughtfully tuned, and not simply a matter of "everything is harder"— They are actually different experiences. This is a deliberately-paced game, and the careful, thorough player is rewarded. Also, this game has some of the most incredible sound design I've ever experienced. It's rare that a game conveys substantial information through its sound. In the Long Dark, if you pay attention, you will be able to tell if you are near a man-made structure while you are in the midst of a snowstorm, and that can mean the difference between life and death. The devs for this game are passionate and dedicated, and have proved it over 2+ years of continuous, quality updates. I continue to enjoy this game and look forward to what the future brings for it.

If you like Rougelike games, buy this. No questions, just do it. You'll thank me later.
For those of you that need extra convincing, here's a rundown. You play as a group of crashed prisoners on Augira (the same planet as the setting of Endless Legend, and the implications are there that the survivors of the crash go on to be the Vaulters, and possibly the Ardent Mages too, in that game) who find themselves needing to ascend through twelve floors of abandoned laboratories, filled with colonies of escaped experiments that take none to kindly to your intrusion. Gameplay  consists of moving your heroes to new rooms, with each newly opened door counting as a turn in which monsters may spawn and resources are gathered, and setting up static defences in order to defend your crystal and ultimately allow you to safely transport it to the elevator that will let you escape.
The game keeps you on a leash at all times, starving you for resources and forcing some tough decisions as to which rooms to keep powered in the face of oncoming hordes of monsters, which will form an unending tide once you start moving that crystal. And if you die, don't even think you get a saved game, it's right back to the start and twelve more floors of tense, randomly generated nightmare for you to scrape through. Summary: Terraria-clone with some fine ideas/art but no content/balance.
Veredict: Wait 1 year (late 2017) and check again.
Good:
- The single-player engine: not complete, but mostly bug-free with good performance. Props to the programmer.
- The art: some enemies in particular are well drawn & animated.
OK:
- The interface. however, it feels it is suited for a generic MMORPG.
- The "transformation" system: you can play as a monster to have some good laughs.
Bad:
- No content: game is about 10% complete. No real quests, few enemies/bosses, etc.
- No balance: many things are either OP or UP.
- Multiplayer is still in development: this can prove to be tough to finish.
- Too many gimmicks (food, taming, gems, runes...) that are not really deep/interesting for the player at the current state.
As per Steam's definition, Early Access games should be playable games. In my book, this means that a game should have both the tech and the content at least half-way done. In Planet Centauri's case, while the tech is there, the content is not. There is less than 10 hours of content for this game, and most of it is unfinished or unbalanced. While it seems it can be a fun game in a some time, there is still a long, long road ahead before recommending this game!

I say this as a relatively easy to impress and also probably pretentious player of art games and indies - I love me some metaphorical stories - this game is using a pretentious story that's about 90 seconds long and told almost entirely with weak metaphors to prop up 5 hours of repititive and tedious 'puzzles'
almost every puzzle was solved eithr by realizing i could interact with something i hadn't before after ten minutes, or solving the puzzle immediately and attempting the same jump for twenty minutes. The puzzles are generally simple, but with needlessly narrow timing required to complete them.
I loved the first the ten minutes. They were filled with a load of variety and grim visuals that had me asking and revising a lot of questions ... but then the game went another four hours without ever addressing those questions or ever showing a character again.
The game clearly has a story, and it isn't uninteresting. Me and a friend talked it over for a while after the game ended, and i thought it was pretty satisfyingly grim and sad and all that to justify the game's aesthetic -
but the story really only comes after you play it. It's so dense and impenetrable while you're playing, the game barely gives you a drop of actual, honest story in the middle and end that it's almost impossible to develop an idea of the narrative while playing. The only reason the metaphors of the environments and hazards mean anything is because the game ends after giving you almost nothing, and you're forced to squeeze an implied story out of a place where there might not even be any (thought there might be), in order to justify the time you spent. The narrative, for the player, comes only after they've played the game, which isn't super great.
If this game were to flourish it would have to do so with its puzzles, or choose to populate those puzzles or in between space (of which there is too little) with real story and effective imagery. But it does neither, choosing instead to give the player its take on the same sliding blocks, timed obstacles, gravity switches, and traps that they've seen in a hundred puzzle platformers before and after.
I think the context for this game's release was probably different - it's been some years and dozens of notable puzzle platformers have come around, and as harsh as I'm being, this isn't a bad game. It excels beautifully at the vibe it's expressing, and it's visually interesting. I don't think it lived up to the hype very well at all.
