Are you ready for a strategic RPG with tactical combat and a vast world to explore?
Well too bad! First you need to build your first city, then set research, then maybe you can wait a few turns to build a scout, then maybe find something interesting outside of a two tile radius of where you started the game, and a few turns later, maybe finish researching sticks with pointy ends so you can make spearmen.
Or in other words, in spite of how this game tries to sell itself, this game is basically just Civilization with a new coat of paint and a spellbook mechanic.  (Notably, spellbooks are also tied to tech trees, so you get even more "sit and watch a progress bar fill up" fun.)
One would think that after over two decades, the formula for these games would be getting refined - even Civilization itself has, for the past decade, done much to try to lessen the micromanagement - but this game and the other low-budget Civ clones prove that some people are just averse to new ideas.
In essence, the point of this game is to build cities, expand cities, kill barbarians - I mean monsters - and finally get a conquest/diplomacy/research/whatever ending.
There's also a unit customization screen, although that made a whole lot more sense in Galactic Civilizations than here, and the low polys on the characters and fact that selecting a cloak makes your character go bald make it both a bit frustrating and unsatisfying as a means of customizing your troops.  At best, you can make one class of soldier have a red hat instead of a green one to tell them apart more easily.
I can't recommend this game, as anyone who would want to play a 4X like this might as well play the much better-polished Civ V.

Dungeon of the Endless (DotE) is said to be a merge of dungeon crawler and tower defense, with random level generation and RPG elements. But is it really so? Let's find out.
The game starts with two characters chosen from a pool of sixteen (many of them locked at the beginning) on a crashed spaceship. Their only source of energy is a crystal they must protect at all costs, and their objective will be to escape the "dungeon" where they have landed. The dungeon has twelve random generated floors, each of them considered a level. On each level, you explore the rooms in search for an elevator to take you to the next one. But it's not enough to find it. Once you find the elevator, you have to carry the crystal there.
Both in the exploration and the transport phases, monsters will attack you, but in different ways. Here comes a key element of DotE: the dynamic combination of real-time and turn-based gameplay. A new turn begins each time you open a door. At this moment, you receive resources and monsters spawn. From this point, you control your characters in real time to fight the monsters or build new defenses. When you take the crystal to carry it to the elevator, the game becomes full real-time, with monsters spawning continuously until you reach the level exit. Or die.
The game takes elements from different genres. First, you have a party of up to four characters. You start with two and recruit more during the exploration. Some will die, and death is permanent, so you'll need to hire replacements. Each character has three item slots that can vary from one to another, in which you can equip stuff found on chests or bought from merchants. They also have a particular level system: you don't level up by fighting monsters and getting experience points, you level up by spending food (one of the resources avaliable) on the characters. Higher levels lead to better stats and new abilities, both active and passive. Characters are different enough to have different gameplay styles.
Next you have the resource system. There are four resources in this game: industry to build things, science to research new things, food to heal and level up your heros, and dust to lit rooms. Lit rooms allows you to build things in them, and also prevents monster from spawning. You can increase your production in any of the first three resources by building modules, but dust is only obtained when found through the dungeon, and resets at every new floor. There are also a lot of minor modules to build. From stat bonuses to plain offensive towers to enemy mind control modules.
DotE comes with two difficulties: "very easy" and "easy", which in fact mean normal and hard, respectively, and also some pods that determine certain gameplay changes, like no health regeneration in exchange for better heals with food. This, in combination with the different character choices and research decisions, help to increase the game lifespan.
In my opinion, this is a highly original game, an unique combination of genres with an identify of its own, and probably one of the best indies of the last year. It's hard and it's punishing, and many gameplay aspects are left for you to discover for yourself, but beating it is really rewarding.

Drag out lines around a grid from multiple start to finish points, filling up all the blocks on the way. It controls well, the graphics and sound are servicable, and I give it a positive rating, but there are issues here.
The main problem is that there is a ridiculous amount of it.
26 letters 25 levels a piece, if you are completionist like me youll want 10 daily mission sets done as well each having 25 levels themselves. Ive literally done in excess of 900 levels.
Well, okay, but why complain about a lot of content? because it can be kind of dull. The level types do actually change, it does periodically shake things up, but you have to go through one, two, even three hundred levels before you notice a distinct change. The difficulty curve is quite subtle as well, it took until around T, thats 475 levels in to the game before I found any real challenge.
Whats more, the changes arnt big: A slightly bigger grid size, a third colour, etc. There arnt remotely enough mechanics being introduced to warrant such a huge number of levels. It really is like someone worked out a generator for it, put in a huge number and dumped the lot in to the game. (Also, a bunch of the levels appeared to be near identical duplicates as well, differing in maybe a single easy move to complete.) I think it would have worked better as a much tighter game with a fraction of the level count in interesting plucked out level designs, then have endless modes at different difficulties with which you could rack up score to unlock palettes and maybe throw in some other things to unlock as well.
That all said, its quite... zen to play. You can put something on to watch, and play LYNE absent mindedly, just keeping your hands busy and such. Thats how I clocked up so much time in the game and finished off everything. Just know that thats what you are getting in to, its not a huge challenge, nothing will surprise you or blow your mind, but it can pass the time, is competently made, and is very cheap.

I almost never review games, but had to put this out there to counter some of the IMO overreaction from the community. If you haven't been paying attention to the furor, Hinterland basically pulled a bonehead PR move by launching a countdown timer on the game (which has already been delayed for years, mind) at the end of which was an announcement of a future release date for the story mode and a new trailer.
Lots of people had reasonably guessed that story mode, or some other big update was coming, and Hinterland didn't do anything to temper expectations. People are justifiably angry.
That all said, this game remains one of the best I've ever played. If it wasn't a fantastic game, the community wouldn't be so enraged over not having more of it. Check the hours played for most of the recent negative reviews, they're much higher than an actually bad game would have.
Anyway, the game itself is amazing. I usually don't like survival games, but the atmosphere of this one is top notch. You get a soothing calm over the entire game world and atmospheric music to enhance the feeling of being truly alone. Hell, the sound effects person IMO needs a freaking Oscar for building an immersive world. It serves as a fantastic contrast to the actual action of being attacked by a wolf or mauled by a bear.
Crafting is basic and immersive, and the survival techniques seem to be more realistic than you would expect from a game. Scavenging is genuinely fun and finding a magnifying glass under a filling cabinet is a WAY bigger endorphin rush than it had any right to be.
In summary, The Long Dark is already a fantastic sandbox game and worth the asking price, but the project itself has been plagued by delays and recent bad PR moves, and future releases look promising, though I wouldn't be shocked if story mode we're delayed again. I would still buy all three copies again.
10/10 for the price.

The Long Dark is a game that seemingly taunts its players. Dying a couple of times, sometimes "losing" hours of gameplay, that's the way I learned how to overcome its challenges. The struggle to survive is what's fun to me, even it can be stressful.
Mechanically, TLD is about managing multiple progress bars, each of them increasingly standing for an unmet requirement of prolonged existance. Players can die from the cold, hunger, third and apparently sleep deprivation, although I can't confirm the latter. For the adventurous type who likes to leave the house in search for supplies, there are also more violent options available. Get mauled by a bear, bitten by a pack of wolves or drink a can of expired soda to meet your maker.
Oh and also there's a large beautiful 3d world to explore, which reminds me a bit of Fallout Las Vegas, only in a Canadian apocalypse and currently without NPCs to feed on. If this game interests you, why not watch a video? You'll know when you want it. Personally, I got a lot of gameplay out of this, strongly recommended.

I picked up this game because Beyond Good and Evil 2 was shown off at E3 2017 and I had never played the first one, even though the concept looks super rad. I wasn't sure what to expect when I booted up the game, but boy, I was in for some video-gamey fun.
The menus are and overall controls are a little weird, this being and early 00's game and PC ports haven't really been perfected (still hasn't been, mind you), but it doesn't take long to get used to it. I browsed the button mapping menu that shows up before the game boots, and there aren't many controls in the first place, anyway. The camera con go wild in-game sometimes, too.
There are also some bizzare visual glitches that happen when there are too many particle effects on the screen, I think. It's very jarring, but I've managed to look past them. There might be a fix somewhere, but I haven't read up on it.
The combat is alright. It's simple, to the point: you got your attack button and dodge button, hold attack to USE YOUR SUPER ATTACK, JADE! and such. It has a soft lock-on feature that can trip you up sometimes. Some mix-up comes into play with the various companions and their attacks which you can use in conjuction with Jade's, like Pey'j's rocket boot attack can be used to launch enemies and objects with your staff. It's interesting.
When you're not fighting, you're going around levels, solving puzzles and taking pictures. The camera is a big part of the game's function. It's the main source of money as you use it to take pictures of animals and get paid for them, in addition to a myriad of other things. Between levels you drive around a hovercraft that you can upgrade with a special currency, called Pearls, which you get from defeating bosses and finding secrets and such.
Perhaps the strongest point of the game is the cool setting and characters it has. You get really attached to them, which makes plot twists that happen all that more effective. I really like the way they handled the player character, Jade. Too often in a lot of story driven games, you start off with a long dump of exposition about the main character and their background and they usually become the most uninteresting part of the game. In Beyond Good and Evil, the first thing you do is pick up a flaming peice of wood and beat the snot out of alien monsters to save some orphans, and you find out bits and pieces about Jade's character later through the story. I wish more games nowadays would follow the "show, not tell" rule more.
Overall, I'd recommend this game. I got on sale, but it's probably also worth it at full price.

About Red Orchestra 2: Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad, the leading tactical multiplayer WWII shooter on the PC, will take the award winning Red Orchestra franchise into the next generation of gaming. Cutting edge graphics and audio built using the Unreal Engine 3, inventive features and streamlined realism will deliver an unrivalled tactical shooter experience.
Heroes of Stalingrad will focus on the Battle of Stalingrad and the surrounding operations, both German and Russian, from July 1942 to February 1943. The game allows the player to experience one of the most brutal battles in all of human history. Delivering unrivalled accuracy and attention to detail, along with gritty, vicious combat in multiplayer modes the game will feature everything from quick, brutal firefights to more intricate and challenging tactical modes.
Rising Storm: Rising Storm is the next game in the award-winning Red Orchestra franchise. You know the great gameplay, innovative features and realistic audio and graphics of RO2 - Rising Storm will take this to the Pacific Theater, adding even more features, new levels, new weapons and new factions. The game will allow the player to fight across iconic locations from the famous island-hopping campaigns in the Pacific from 1942 to 1945, as the US Army and Marine Corps fight it out with the Imperial Japanese army and Special Naval Landing Forces. Players will experience beach assaults, jungle fighting, close quarters night fighting and more across Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima and Saipan, among other iconic battles. The player is able to take the part of either side – American or Japanese – battling it out online in multiplayer on up to 64-player servers.
Rising Storm also introduces an entirely new type of gameplay to the franchise - asymmetrical warfare. The American’s have the apparent advantage in firepower with their fast firing semi-automatic rifles, fully automatic weapons, and devastating flamethrower. The Japanese balance this out with gameplay elements that model their raw courage, ferocity, and cunning use of equipment. Their knee mortars allow them to rain indirect fire down on their enemies from anywhere in the map. Grenades can be planted and turned into booby-traps for unwary GIs. The Japanese put very high store on close-quarter combat, with a bayonet on almost every weapon – even machine guns and SMGs. Their banzai charge suppresses the enemy making it difficult for them to return fire and gives them an opportunity to close in to use bayonets and katanas on their opponents.

I did not have fun playing this game.
The "dark, gritty atmosphere" you see it praised for so often is little more than just an aesthetic choice: it looks cool on the screenshots and whatever, but it doesn't contribute anything towards the actual game itself, other than adding to the simple minimalistic presentation. It feels like an excercise from the developer, trying to get the player through game with as little input as possible. And if that's your thing, cool! There's no guidance, no instruction, no narration or any sort of story-telling; you've gotta figure that all out yourself. Which is fine.
From that, I wouldn't call this a puzzle game. These aren't puzzles you're solving. Because of how there's no input whatsoever, a majority of the levels are, in some (usually big) part, trial-and-error based. And if that's also your thing, cool. There's no real brainteasers, nothing you have to sit and stare at for a while to figure out: it's all trial-and-error and timing, especially in later parts of the game. You've got a very little window of opportunity to make just the right action, and if you miss that window, you're either gonna die or have to try again.
Because of both of these, there's pretty much no way you're gonna get the "complete the game in one sitting with <5 deaths" achievement unless you've played this before or watched someone play it. I started writing this review when I had about a quarter of the game left - and it took me that long to discover that you gotta squish these little glow-worm-type-things to unlock achievements? Which, with there being no input or guidance, is not immediately apparent. So if you go into this game blind like me, you possibly wouldn't have discovered that until a while in.
Several years ago, the necessity of the player using the physics engine to advance in the story was something super cool and awesome, but these days it's pretty much expected. The controls and physics in Limbo all feel slow and clunky, and that really doesn't mix well with the time-sensitive nature of what feels like most of the levels. About halfway through the game, I felt like I was checking the "Load Chapter" menu every five minutes to see how much longer I'd have to slog through this thing.
Also, the lack-of-narration, you-figure-it-out thing feels... well, feels kind of tryhard. This game is no Amnesia where the player filling in the gaps between the given plot points amount to something big and huge and amazing and mind-blowing. In Limbo, there's just simply... much there. You're in this weird, vaguely apocalyptic somewhat steam-powered on-and-off crumbling urban world, with what seems to be clans of other kids that are trying to kill whatever comes their way with traps. No other background, no explanation, nothing at all to help you figure out the What or the Where or the When or even the Why. It just felt like a attempt at "hey, I'm gonna make this super cool vague environment, and the player will have a great time figuring out what's going on" that really fell flat.
(My game also slowed way down right after I got past the last obstacle of the last level, and the only way to get it to continue was to repeatedly pause and unpause to advance it frame-by frame; I thought this was a glitch so I repeated the chapter, but then it did it again, and on top of everything else I'm not 100% that's not intentional? Later when checking this, apparently it's a known bug with Nvidia when v-sync is off + some other frame-related settings)
So. Yeah. I did not have a good time playing this game, and wouldn't recommend it unless you get it for cheap or free - and even then it's a far shot.
Quick edit: I was talking to my friend about this game, and she put into words what I'd been feeling the entire time - this feels like a flash game. Good thing I got it for free (Steam or Humble was giving it away for free or something, I don't remember), or else I'd regret spending the $2 it costs as of writing this

Cuphead is a fun thrilling third-person shooter with the majority being boss battles and some platformer levels. The difficulty isn't easy, even in Simple Mode; the difficulty doesn't change and bosses are only shorter, so this game isn't for you if you can't keep up with the game's pace. (Actually, the game doesn't even let you progress if you play the bosses in Simple Mode.) However, the controls are fluent and gameplay is great. All the levels require memorizing how to dodge/counter a boss's attacks or safely get through a platforming level. In the Regular Mode for boss levels there are usually three main stages, and they always have different attack patterns. All the bosses stages are very creative and I applaud the developers for this. Every boss comes off as original even if based on something else, such as the cat that resembles Tom from Tom and Jerry. (Is that technically a spoiler?) For both the boss and platformer levels, there's no checkpoints, making you get it in just one try. The platformer levels are literally run and gun, so run, shoot, jump, and dash your way to the goal! You could also play as a Pacifist in the platformer levels by not killing any enemies. Every time I lose a level I have the urge to play it again and again until I succeed, which makes this game super addictive and a great time-consumer. The artstyle is exactly like "rubber hose animation" used in cartoons from the 1930's. All the traditional hand drawn cel animations and watercolor backgrounds in this game were done by the creators and their animation crew, so this game took a lot of time, effort, and dedication to make. Then there's the music! Cuphead's OST (Original Soundtrack) was composed by big band recording sessions, creating the original jazz recordings and other themes of music the game's description mentions. All the music works great with all the levels! Like the visuals, Cuphead's soundtrack is just like the times it captures so well. This game's price is currently $21.99 CAD and let me tell you, this price is a bargain considering this game's visuals looks so beautiful and is just super fun to play (with the vibe of feeling like I'm immersed into a cartoon). Yes, the game may be short, but beating any level can take a very long time. You can have multiple playthroughs because this game isn't one that gets old after one playthrough, so you can play this again in the more challenging Expert Mode after completing it normally if you think you're good enough! Or try co-op mode! I do recommend using a controller (I use a PS4 controller but whatever works for you) because it feels better than with the keyboard. This game has full controller support. And for local co-op, all you have to do for that is open the game, open your game file, and then connect your controller, simple.
Difficult, but not impossible. A controller is highly recommended.

After spending over 50 hours on the game, I think it's safe to say that I enjoyed myself enough to play that long. Although it's not action packed, it's everything a survival game should be: You have to think your way through situations and worry about things other than a horde of zombies. But it does have it's letdowns, so lets go through the pros and cons.
Pros:
- Base making: You can create your own base, whether it be from scratch or building on a pre-apocalyptic construction with lots of building options to choose from
- Realism: You can get diseases, you can get cut, burnt, cold, indigestion, hunger, thirst, exhaustion, boredom, unhapiness and you have to tender to all these different things, giving the game the sense of realism a survival game deserves.
- Graphics: Although the graphics aren't ultra-high-def GTA V, they are nice to look at in the good old retro fashion.
- Multiplayer: This game is very fun to play with a friend, and I have not yet tried on a server but I can imagine it being close to a walking dead scenario.
Cons:
- Grinding skills: Despite the numerous skills letting you do lots of things, you still have to grind A LOT to get the skills up. In carpentry for example, I must have made dozens and dozens of trips cutting down trees and building fences before I even got to level 5. (on a side note: a person with the job carpenter starting at lvl 3 can't make a simple set of stairs until level 6?)
- Fps Lag: If you have a decent/intermediate computer then you should have no problem. But if you're on an old computer and think that this game is for you because of its retro style, then think again.
- Lack of life: There is a general lack of life in the game. There are no vehicles at all (although I hear they are implementing them), and appart from the mission npcs, there are no survivors appart from you and any online player.
- A sense of repetetiveness: This may just be me and my uncreativeness, but as with a lot of survival and exploration games including minecraft, terraria, dayz and others it gets repetetive when you've seen what there is to see, and there isn't a HUGE amount of content to discover in this game.
To conclude, there are some points that could definetely be improved on, but I think it's definetely worth the 13 euros if you like survival games.

It's an apt testimony to the skill and passion of the Amplitude folks that Dungeon of the Endless has become my go-to timewaster. The premise is simple: Your prison ship's been attacked and you've crash-landed on an uncharted planet. You and your motley band of inmates, ship staff and exotic natives must navigate the twelve floors of the mysterious dungeon you've found yourself in by finding the elevator on each floor and using the "crystal" generator from your escape pod to power it and move to the next level up. That crystal is also needed to power the rooms of the dungeon, providing a variety of resources conducive to your survival, but it is limited by its supply of "dust", and each room left unpowered has a chance to spawn a wave of hostile fauna whenever you open a new door on that floor.
The gameplay is an elegant combination of roguelike, tower defence and classic RPG mechanics. It's both accessible and challenging, with a bit less of the luck factor of, say, FTL (you'll rarely be thrown into randomly unsurvivable situations) and more strategic decisions to make rather than a roll of the dice. While plotting your route through the dungeon, protecting the crystal is your primary concern. You'll have a range of modules to install in a dungeon, from resource generators to defensive weaponry, and as your power demand starts to exceed supply you'll have to get clever with which parts of the dungeon you keep powered and where you open new doors. Your heroes' abilities and attributes vary widely. Some are slow but powerful tanks, well-suited to holding a static position; others are technically-minded and can operate or repair the modules you build; others still are nimble speedsters ideal for responding to trouble spots or running the crystal to the elevator. Managing your heroes is therefore crucial to success.
The understated soundtrack and the pseudo-pixellated, hand-painted graphics are both surpassingly beautiful, and taken with the game lore (which frequently ties in with that of Amplitude's other titles, Endless Space and Endless Legend) they create a truly unique atmosphere and sense of immersion. The heroes will treat you to some fun banter occasionally, and are great sources of emergent stories. The tale of how you brave robotic swordsman sacrificed himself keeping a horde of nasties from his beloved crystal carrier; or how two of your most dissimilar dungeon explorers form an unstoppable monster-slaying, best-buddy team; are experiences that remain with you long after their runs have ended. Some combinations of characters even have unique backstories of their own, which unfold as they ascend the floors with sometimes-shocking outcomes that I won't spoil here. Simply put, the game oozes personality.
Whether you're a fan of the genre, or simply someone who appreciates an old-school challenge or a lovingly-made game, I can't recommend Dungeon of the Endless enough. Keep your eyes on Amplitude, because they've just had an amazing year.

This game rules, but good luck explaining what genre it is to somebody.  You've got 2-4 heroes exploring rooms trying to find the elevator to the next floor.  Every time you open a door, that's a turn, but then combat takes place in real time.  You have to collect a very limited resource to supply power to rooms, and if you don't light them up, monsters can/will spawn there most of the time that you open a door.
To help your heroes fend off these waves (which run for your crystal and attack it, robbing you of the powering-up resource), you can build modules on hardpoints in most rooms, like turrets and stuff.  You've got to balance exploring for the exit with making sure the pathways that you're opening up to your crystal are defended.  You've got to make sure you keep your heroes leveling up and equipped well, while also researching new tech at certain special rooms you'll come across, so you stay caught up with the increasingly nasty monsters.
Once you find the exit, you'll need to make sure that the path from the crystal to the exit is well defended and clear, then pick up the crystal and make a mad dash for it, as all the doors you didn't get to opening fly open on their own and endless monsters spawn from any room you haven't lit up.  If the crystal-carrying hero dies, or if you lose all your heroes under any circumstances, welp, start over idiot.
It's incredibly unforgiving and takes some getting used to, but the game flow is actually less complicated and more intuitive than I'm making it sound.  There's lots of scenarios to unlock in the form of different "pods" that change things about the game, and there's LOTS of heroes to find and recruit as you play, with plenty of variety.  A lot of them have history and stories together that you'll find out if you have the right combo of people in your party, too.
I really like this game.
Protips:
1.  Start on "Too Easy" so you can get the hang of things.  "Easy" is actually pretty hard.
2.  Don't try to power every room you open.  In fact, you want to power the minimum number of rooms possible, and create corridors to farm dust off of the waves that spawn.
3.  Heroes have wide variations in their stats, and definite roles to play.  If you mis-use them, they can easily die or not be very effective.  Pay attention to how you build your team!
4.  Somebody on your team needs to be fast, period.

Had a team of 4 heroes. Opened a door. Monsters pour in the now opened door and two heroes die. After this, I open the next door, and a zillion more monsters pour in. My remaining two heroes die. 10/10 would open two doors of death again.
This game has a lot going for it, and it spans lots of genres and types of games. Turn-based? Yup, resources are gained based on turns. A turn is completed when a new door is opened. Real-time? Yup, combat, building, and movement takes place in real time. Roguelike/RPG? Yup, you level up your character and collect items to equip them with while running around each floor of the dungeon. Tower defense? Got that, too. You build different types of "towers" in rooms for defense, resource production, or boosting your heroes. You level up or heal characters by using food, build towers by spending production, and when you find a science crystal you can spend science to research new types of towers or upgraded versions of ones you already can build. There is also the interesting element of dust, which can be collected from some types of monsters when they are killed, or some rooms occasionally grant dust when entered. The use of dust is to power rooms to be able to run the towers you have built in them. The limited quantity of dust makes for some interesting decisions as you discover more of the floor, you will never have enough dust to power all of the rooms, so you must make choices as to which rooms to power. Unpowered rooms without heroes in them can also produce more monsters when the next turn is begun, so that also plays into the strategy of which rooms to power. Finally, once you discover the exit to the floor, it becomes a mad dash to take your precious crystal from the entrance to the exit and escape with all of your heroes alive. There is also a story element to it in that the characters have a back story, some of them involving other heroes as well. And it's in the Endless universe, which is quite a clever setting IMO, I already enjoyed the lore from Endless Space. This game continues with the same lore. This game is very fun, if you like dungeon crawlers or tower defense games, you won't be disappointed unless you despise the genres combined in it.

This game has an old soul.
When I say "it has a retro platformer feel with RPG elements" most people will take that to mean that it's a Castlevania clone.
On the contrary.
Planet Centauri features many similarities to games like Castlevania for sure, exploration, transformation, gear upgrades, and unlockable power moves all feature in this game.
But that is only the surface of the gameplay, the GUI so to speak.
From there, the depth of customization is immense.
The open ended storyline allows players to embark on any kind of adventure they choose, be it a base builder, a farm simulator, a dungeon crawler, a collector, a hunting simulator or all of the above as a low spec version of Ark Survival Evolved.
At a glance this game looks like Castlevania or Megaman, but it has all the best elements of titles like Metal Slug, Abuse, Elfland, Wonderboy, Crystal Caves, Cosmos Cosmic Adventure, Commander Keen, Jill of the Jungle, Digdug, Ultima and so many others but this list is long enough already, you get the point...
It feels retro as.
That's not to say it's leaning on the fact that it's feature-heavy to support shabby game design.
The learning curve is understandably steep and the tutorials are somewhat vague, but the natural progression of the game introduces new features at a comfortably staggered pace so a new player doesn't have to learn to build a hut and a fire before they starve to death within the first few minutes of gameplay (in fact, starving doesn't seem to be a thing at all, i'm not complaining).
Overall, Planet Centauri is a great way to enjoy the features of more modern games, while capturing the feel and system requirements of some of the more classic, somewhat forgotten, titles that made PC gaming great in the 80s and 90s.

Not a bad game.  The controls take a bit to get used to, combat is tricky in my opinion (slow if you're constantly trying to avoid getting hit in melee battle, losing a ton of health just rushing in, not a whole lot of knockback to give you time to try to back off), and most of the tutorial quests are ranked 0 stars (easy I assume) while sending you way off to find the items needed, which are generally around tougher mobs when you don't have the gear to face them without nearly dying, or straight up dying.  For me (who plays in borderless fullscreen with zoom checked, that'll be useful information for the next few things I say), the hotbar at the top overlaps the enemy bar that pops up on the right, so I can't see the first couple of buffs they might have.  Opening anything such as the workbench, anvil, etc, gives me an oversized pop-up screen of what I can do with that particular crafting station, and it's always off the bottom of the screen, and I always have to move it up to the top of the screen to see what's at the bottom when I scroll down, to which the information that pops up when you highlight an item is off the bottom of the screen still.  Playing without the zoom checked fixes the bar overlap and the size of the pop ups, but then everything is too small in my opinion, and a pain to read.  Changing the resolution doesn't do anything for me, even after switching out and in to fullscreen again, or restarting the game entirely.  Also, while in fullscreen, when I make a character, everything under the hair/skin/eye icons under the center color grid box are off the screen.  I have to get out of fullscreen to see the Random Validate Cancel options.  I feel like there needs to be a 1.5 zoom, something that gets you a little closer to the character, but not so much that you get interface overlaps, oversized pop-up lists, and having certain options cut off from the bottom of your screen.  That, or a slight reconfiguration of how things are placed within fullscreen, and a configuration to how big the UI can get before overlapping occurs.
Aside from all of that though, it is a good game.  The fact that you have to get enough souls from monster kills to open chests and to increase your skills is a nice feature.  It makes finding chests that much more fun, since you have to decide "Do I get the chest, or save up to get a new skill?".  Transforming into a monster is AWESOME, although it's a pain at first (trying to time when to jump as a slime into another slime, or land next to it to bite it..).
Hopefully, by the time this game is finished, all of the kinks will get worked out.  I know it's early access, and I don't expect perfection (early access or not), but all in all, don't be discouraged by the start of this review, they're just minor annoyances.  This game is definitely worth checking out, for what it has, and what it'll have in the future.

out of the many crafting based games i have played over the years, this is the first i have ever felt the urge to write a review related to.....namely i will break it down in a simple manner...mind you this is merely my own personal opinion
potential for creativity:8/10......with only seven metals being introduced and limiting the current weapons they have released....as well as not sofar creating any gem weapons that can be manually crafted.....this game has some shoes it can still grow into, but i would honestly feel they would have more growth potential with 1-3 more metals being introduced....maybe even introduce floating metals like some games have, where you cant find all resource types in the same map....this maps people explore multi mapping potential....also having the same biome layout every time reduced the potential for creativity imo because it limits how much it makes people adapt to their surroundings.....
gameplay:9/10....smooth, precise, very little if any lag....npcs have a clear glitch related to platforms that i think the game makers might have to address eventually, but otherwise it runs clear and to the point.....
replay value:6/10......mostly it lacks some replay value due to how every map is mostly the same....sure the location and layouts of some of the underground special biomes vary...but otherwise it is pretty cookie cutter in its repetition......and while this isnt always a bad thing, especially for gamers new to crafting gaming....even they would get bored after awhile.....
would i recommend playing this game:9/10....as long as they keep adding new content and fixing bugs i could happily recommend this game to people i know offline, on steam, and on the various net groups i run with.....once they got a decent variable flow to it hell i wouldnt even mind if it was only updated once a week because with what they could add at this point, applying variable attributes for randomization if they wish to incorporate such aspects....they could have a game that would eventually make terrarria and minecraft seem mundane at best......the potential is there, they have but to seize it.....
suggestions:maybe enable a workshop option in the future so players can help create content......just an idea noting how much it helped add fun variables to the civ series which otherwise i found after two playthroughs more boring then watching paint dry.......maybe branch off weapons into not just long range and swords....maybe add a mid range of spears,whips, halberds....maybe introduce in some hammers or other forms of weaponry...ie...stone weapons, gem weapons, stone armor, gem armor, etc......maybe introduce some new metals to add more choices...introduced timed events that after X amount of gameplay can be triggered....or say after someone kills the dragon,chicken,master, or necromancer......maybe add more ranged weapon variables, like instead of just two boomerangs which are extremely generic...introduce maybe a chakram that spins a single loop around the player when used, or a throwing spear like the reptiles use....maybe introduce a way to level up ones hp and sp so one doesnt have to rely purely on luck of chests and food ingredients.....because tobe honest sp is lacking compared to the spells one can craft eventually....i do love the variable monster system they have in the game, and how you can catch even legendary and divine creatures.....pretty black legendary skeleton :D......i love how the pets you catch can lvl up and become insanely stronger.....like my new pet mage from the recently released dungeon....well worth the exploration imo......maybe tweak the giant apes so they dont take up so much of the screen because they can be easily killed just by having a hole to sit in and a boomerang i noticed, while a smaller ape maybe wouldnt fall into the same trick trap.....maybe add a new bomb or two that doesnt explode right away, or even crafting exploding arrows combing dark arrow with say a small bomb?......maybe add a new axe because honestly having a single model axe feels kinda like a waste.....especially since the intro chest always has one, then you find you can craft one later, but since its the same as whats in the intro chest it feels like....meh whats the point of crafting this axe......now maybe if the axe was an ingredient for a weapon tobe crafted, like a halberd or battle axe that might bring more appeal.....
overall:i would give this game in my opinion...imo for those not familiar with the acronym....a 9/10......needs some variable options to keep it fresh but for a new game its quite worth its price tag i would say.....and with some improvements it might actually be considered actually a real bargain.....

It's Cold Out.

Possibly the most beautiful and immersive survival games I've ever had the pleasure of playing.
You find yourself in the middle of the Canadian wilderness after modern civilization has been wiped out by a geomagnetic storm. With nothing but the clothes on your back and a handful of variably useful items, your goal is to survive for as long as you can. Your enemies are not zombies, assassins, or nazis, but something far more terrifying: Nature.
You have to stay hydrated, fed, clothed, rested and unhurt. You must scavenge, hunt and trap for food. Light fires with whatever fuel you can find to stay warm, and find whatever shelter you can to rest in. All this while avoiding being mauled by a bear or a wolf.
The environment is hostile, but Hinterland's Art Direction means that you nevertheless find yourself stopping and staring at the night sky when it's clear or the mountains as the morning sun lights them up.
Hinterland's PR department needs some work (That countdown was a bad idea) hence the recent poor reviews. But the game itself is one of the best I've played in my life. A close look at the sheer number of hours put into the game by those who gave it a bad review after the countdown fiasco shows just where the anger is pointed.
The game is definitely worth the money, even without Story mode. Just keep your expectations in check.

I usually don't write reviews, but after 170 hours of so much enjoyment I feel that I need to leave a positive review given the amount of negative spam due to a poor PR decision on behalf of Hinterland. Review the game, not a decision the CEO made that will be forgotten in three months.

The story of Red Faction Armageddon can be easy to forget as it strikes as something bland without many surprises aside from a couple of plot twists moments a bit of love here or there and many, many explosions. However, while many games have a deep narrative with a strong storyline Red Faction is worth a play, especially for a nice fill if you are looking to relax and play something easy-to-follow with a love for destruction (and construction). Just like many movies, there are the ones that you can’t wait to go to the cinema and watch it while others you just stumble while zapping on your TV in a lazy Sunday. Red Faction Armageddon is the latter but by any means does this means that it was not an enjoyable experience. Despite being short my time with the game was worth my time investment. In under 6-7 hours I finished the main story and I was happy with the ending although I wish it could have lasted me a bit more.
The bigger fun factor has to be all the destruction and the variety of weapons. While I got stuck in the geometry a couple of times after destroying things, nothing like make use of my hammer with the combination of the reconstruction ability to get out of a mess of concrete wall that just crumbled on my feet. From sending grenades and then hit “detonate” to sticking enemies in the walls there is a bit of everything for any gun lover. Assault Rifles and Shotguns are also present in the game but considering the satisfaction from shooting the other weapons these tend to be forgotten through most of my play through.
Besides the standard shooting the enemy with said weapons, some vehicles will be at your disposal during certain missions. These will be armored vehicles to destroy the enemy and can be driven by land or air however, the sound effects felt a bit poor when firing some missiles or other bigger weapons. The visuals are nothing out of the ordinary but considering the time the game was released (2011) my experience in 2015 was not diminished by this, it was all about destroying and exploding things from start to finish and overall I can say it was a positive experience. If you have a little time to spend on something to play in little chunks of time without having to worry about complex systems or controls I would recommend giving Red Faction Armageddon a fair chance. You can play the game in short bursts since it provides a gentle checkpoint system.

Red Faction Armageddon
Rating 7/10
Overview: Linear Third Person Shooter
The Good:
+ Varied locations, despite taking place on Mars every location feels unique and varied.
+ Good sense of pacing, the game introduces new vehicles, enemies, weapons throughout the journey to keep things fresh
+ Variety of different weapons that are very unique and fun to use that fit different play styles.
+ Like previous Red Faction Games, this game features impressive building destruction.
+ Solid controls
+ Destroying buildings, killing enemies allows you to gain salvage which is used to upgrade your character, weapons and abilities
+ Infestation Mode (Horde Mode) allows you to fight wave after wave of enemies.
The Average:
Ruin Mode allows you to destroy environments within a time limit to score as many points as you can. It is a great idea that seems very underutilized given it only has a handful of maps. The previous Red Faction game had the same mode but it was much more fleshed out in its execution so this was a bit of a disappointment.
The game has a lot of enemy variation but it certainly doesn't feel that way. For most of the game you will be fighting the same 3 types of enemies over and over again.
Main campaign will take around 6 hours to complete
The DLC is decent but also very short. The levels are not as well designed as the main campaign.
The Bad:
- The story is decent if a bit simple in its premise, it doesn't feel as developed as it should and serves more as an excuse to kill hordes of enemies. Given the location and history of Red Faction it seems like wasted potential.
- Multiplayer achievements which are now almost impossible to obtain.
Conclusion
I can't recall another series that has had more changes each entry than Red Faction. The first game was a linear first person shooter similar to half life. The second was a level based first person shooter with bosses. The third was an open world third person shooter. This game is a linear level based third person shooter with upgrades. At this rate its only a matter of time before we see Red Faction the real time strategy game. This is a good game but plays it entirely safe with its gameplay and design. The potential is here for something special but never achieves it.

Beyond Good or Evil is a game I played for the first time in 2009. I adored every moment. The world and setting was so unique. The gameplay was fun and the pace was great. I still have the disc but decided to buy it on steam, and to have a digital copy if I lose by disc.
The game still holds up well 8 years after playing it and almost 14 years after release. You play as Jade, a action reporter and caretaker of the local orphanage. The planet they live on was peaceful until they were attacked by the Domz armada, who is trying to take over the planet. Protecting the planet is the Alpha Section. After some events ,not told to avoid spoilers, Jade needs to find the truth about a conspiracy.
Gameplay is mostly exploring (kind of linear) locations while solving puzzles, fighting some enemies and taking pictures. The puzzles are mostly simple. The combat is great and the animations are amazingly smooth as Jade moves between enemies. The photo element is very cool. You have to take picture of every animal species that you come across. This gives you credits as a reward. There is also races to enter with your hover boat, a few stealth sections, mini games and a flying part.
This a great game that everyone should try.

As a fan of Co-Op gaming I am a big fan of this game!
There has clearly been a lot of work in this game. You see this in how you play it, how
it looks and in the possibilities /limits each playable character has.
Since I am a real team player, I played mostly as a hunter and I loved the fact that you
depend highly on each others skills to survive the confrontation with the monster.
As soon as one team member is neutralised/killed/inactive/off alone you feel this in the fight with the monster. As it should be in any respectable co-op game!
The hunter classes + weapons are really well balanced and I have very few remarks in how to improve them.
(The passive role of the Trapper as soon as the dome is set is the only thing i can come up with...)
I was very surprised, disappointed and frustrated to see that the game did not live up to its potential and this is probably caused by 2 major reasons: 1) For a Co-op game with repeatable gameplay it was way too expensive. The high priced Hunter expansion didn't help as well...
2) The developers waited WAY too long to launch the first real update that fixed some issues about balance en bugs !!! And even when they did, the patch didn't live up to the expectations...
In short:
+ A great Co-Op game where you depend highly on your team mates, as it should be!
+ Nice graphics (for a multiplayer game).
+ Very unique concept because you can play the monster too!
+ Every hunt is different despite the fact you play the same maps over and over.
-  Patching took WAY too long!
-  Too expensive for this genre, especially if you include the Hunter pack.
-  As a result of the negative remarks, the number of players keeps dropping.
Finding a full team to play a human monter is nearly impossible now...
My score: 85/100
Update review for Evolve Stage 2 (Beta)    !!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
The makers of Evolve decided  to make Evolve free to play in he hope of rebooting the game and make it live up to its potential.
I can honestly say they succeeded in their intentions. Not only did they make the basic game + basic hunters and monsters free to use, they have also understood that a game like this needs constant updates + new features from time to time.
Since the game was rebooted, several new/modified hunters and a monster have been added, which is fantastic!
Since they still call it "beta", i presume many more new features will turn up.
I hope to replay the old game modes of the original game (nest, rescue or new ones) and I still look forward to the rumours of a 2 monster vs 8 hunters mode...
One remark could be that the role of the trapper is now a lot less important...
In short:
+ Still a great Co-Op game where you depend highly on your team mates, as it  should be!
+ Nice graphics (for a multiplayer game).
+ Very unique concept because you can play the monster too!
+ Every hunt is different despite the fact you play the same maps over and over.
+ Several patches and features were already added, they seem to have seen the light on this matter.
+ Now free to play, which is the main reason the reboot is so succesfull.
+ Easy to find other players on different parts of the day.
+ You can unlock every hunter or monster with coins you can earn in game.
+ Some nice remakes of old characters/monsters have been added with small changes in weapons and abilities.
-  The trapper's role has been greatly reduced now we can all place the dome
-  Only one game mode available for the moment, hunt.
-  Lack of fresh looking, new maps to play on. There are some new ones, but sometimes you rarely notice it...
My new score: 95/100

With your trusty wrench and pockets filled with guns you have fun shooting waves of enemies and turrets through the levels, well at least for the first few levels, enemies just become damage sponges even after you get the camera and get the max rank for a basic enemy you’ll find that they still take multiple headshots without a worry, it makes sense for the big daddy there the tanky sorta-enemies of each level but the not the ones you fight so many of. When it's claimed that this game is the "Hardest" Zombie Survival game, they're correct, partially. The only real difficulty that I've perceived in this game has been one based on random luck. The combat system is simplistic at best, and trivial at worst. It's very easy to grab the nearest stick-like blunt object and fend off the meagre zombies you'll need to fight clearing out the area. If power and water are still on (a random event turns either off, that while mean time to occur can be changed there's no real "safe" choice, either immediately possible, or not for months) food is plentiful and water infinite, if they aren't food is still a common resource even without farms setup, making water the only scarecity. The only times I've died is to being bitten, a random chance, and dieing of being infected (which is possibly guaranteed, the multiple wiki's are very info scarce on the matter, some not being updated for quite some time.) There's no way to cure or become immunized to the infection, so it's entirely a war of attrition, that can't be won because the zombies spawn in infinitely (oh sorry, wander.) The interface is clunky and interaction with the world-environment is confusing (I can't count how many times I've right-clicked on a sink and instead select a window over an oven on the other side of the room, there's a tile-selector for destroy/pickup/putdown/rotate, why not interact?) The world is persistant (you can continue playing in it as a new character after your old one wasn't lucky enough) which is a strange choice for what I'd define as a game with elements from a more 'rogue'-like genre, but some people find it a plus.
That's not to say I haven't enjoyed myself playing this game, the moments are few and far between, but they shine fairly bright. This game is just still too unpolished and features half-implemented (like a nutrition system, really? nutrition? what is this, ♥♥♥♥ing life simulator 2008?) for me to reccomend at this time. Will update review as necessary upon replaying after major patches, though I doubt the challenges being based on a luck factor wont ever go away.

A very ambitious game with a lot of potential, hindered by weak AI.  FE:LH is a 4X with combat elements similar to Heroes of Might and Magic.  It's a very complex game with a lot for the player to learn, but unfortunately the AI just doesn't put up enough of a challenge to make the player learn more.
THE GOOD
- Empire has many customizable elements, such as enchantments for cities and items/traits for units
- Decent random map generator
- Deep, complex game with a lot to experiment with and a lot to learn
THE BAD
- Very weak AI can't handle even the basics of the game
- Unit customization could have had more options
- Poor graphics relative to performance of the game
The big draw for FE:LH is how customizable everything is.  You can create your own heroes and empires and even your own units.  In many ways this is very fun; players can opt to create their own super-mage or their own highly specialized raiders and see them work to great effect.  It's quite interesting compared to the generic units of most games of this genre.
Unfortunately, the options for customzation aren't incredibly varied; most empires have mostly the same options, with the unique ones being straight upgrades from the usual.  The "traits" you can give to units are very straightforward and not balanced enough to encourage very much decision making.  Every race's armor and weapons look the same.
The AI that comes with the base game is incredibly lacking and is easily the game's greatest weakness.  I understand it's very difficult to create a good AI for this genre of game, but the one in FE:LH is simply pathetic.  Opposing AI will constantly declare war on the player without any intention of actually attacking, or if they do attack, it will be a pitiful couple of units raiding resources rather than presenting an actual threat.  The AI is also poor at managing its resources, opting to found cities and immediately train units rather than build some actual infrastructure.
Fortunately, there are mods available to help mitigate these issues, some of them very good.  The developer is still continuing work with the game and a number of DLC have been released.  Overall, the game doesn't present enough of a challenge to a power gamer to purchase at full price and may be too complex for the more casual type of gamer.

This is a 4X+ fantasy game that shows the years spent in its development and polish.
Standout Features:
- Huge game with a large technology tree, and many rules.
- Easy to learn but difficult to master (I take this as a plus......)
- Many ways to play, and many ways to win
- A variety of maps
- Resource Management - RTS Style for mana, iron, horses, etc
- Abilities for units
- DLC adds to the game and makes it much better
- Customization for everything: factions, leaders, city upgrades, unit design (alpha centauri style)
- Notably, good customisation for game start and in-game options. Really fine controls help you tweak things.
Standard 4X features:
- City building, unit creation, resources, unit leveling, maps, technology tree
- Good graphics
- Nice cloth map when you zoom out
- Modding
Fantasy features (not usually found in a 4X):
- champions
- faction attributes
- sovereign (leader) attributes
- magic: spells, mana, magic paths
- quests
- items
- wounds to champions
The only cons are:
- The AI is bad. This is typical, however, for the genre. Even Civ V AI was bad.
- No multiplayer. In any case, games are usually too long for efficient multi-player
- Help could have been more detailed for the more intricate aspects (and power players)
- Tiny game-provided campaign (but the customization should be enough to keep you occupied)
- Game balance could be slightly better

This game has always been the one that provided the most intense and atmospheric emotions. I've always felt that adrenaline when my squad was entering the buildings covered in smoke just to execute the remaining victims of grenade orchestra.
Even though the game engine seems quite old, you can still enjoy the physics at their finest. Lovely sight of body parts flying around after artillery barrage, accompanied by the tasty screams of wounded and shouts of charging soldiers will blow your senses away.
The game is really tactical, although you'll find yourself placed amongst veterans, who are probably planning to spend the rest of their lives playing this game (fully understandable, because it's a masterpiece). Solo play isn't really going to get you anywhere, because the scoreboard doesn't only reward killers.
All in all, it's a game that will see me returning from time to time.
